It's difficult to give this game a binary recommendation, because I feel it could be either deeply resonative or utterly mild depending on one's personality and attitude going into it. I personally felt the latter, so I will err on the side of a non-recommendation for this one.
Basically, it examines the psychology a depressed creative through the medium of a series of unreleased short games that were never intended to be played by the general public. You progress through these games while listening to a running commentary about the developer that theorises about the thought processes that went into each game. That's as close to a plot synopsis as I can give without giving away major spoilers, but I was encouraged to buy this game with little more than "I can't tell you anything about it, but you have to experience it!" and came away disappointed. I feel like it's at least helpful to give people an idea of what they're getting in to. There's little to be gained going in completely blind.
If you are, or know someone who suffers from depression, personal anxiety, a need for validation, loneliness, or if you simply have empathy for or a fascination with those thoughts and feelings, then this game could well be a powerful experience for you. That being said, I do struggle with depression and self-doubt, and wasn't particularly moved by it. It feels too personal, like watching someone air their dirty laundry in public. It asks us to relate to and empathise with issues that not everybody can relate to, and if you don't share those feelings then there's really nothing for you.

Think SNES / DS style overhead style RPGS like Final Fantasy 1,2/4,3/6, Dragon Warrior, Lufia, etc. and imagine being able to create games in this style.
There are some caveats which I will get to in a moment, but first...
If you're looking for a game that absolutely demonstrates everything RPGMaker has to offer, look no further than Last Dream, also available on Steam. Among some of its numerous features are a custom crafting system, a completely unique class system, an 'endless cave' of sorts (Lufia), a very complex leveling system, gear, 8 unique classes, a 1000 page strategy guide in pdf form etc. Dont let the rather bland 'create your party' stop you, its my one complaint about Last Dream.
The only reason I mention playing Last Dream is, it was created using RPG Maker which will give you a very good idea of just how much is possible, and believe me when I say, the sky is the limit with RPG Maker.
The editor is simple enough to use for basic functionality like creating maps, creating monster groups for use in your maps, shops, npcs, modifying / adding characters, tiles, items, monsters, etc. and I would strongly recommend grabbing the demo, which I KNOW is available on their website but I think its also available on Steam.
The problem with RPG Maker comes in what is required to make anything outside of the most simple things like doors (which require scripting). There are templates that make things a bit easier, for example, to make a door, you have to create a portal and thankfully, there is a wizard that will create the script automatically for you, but it gives you a glimpse at some of the potential compexity involved if you want to do anything more than the most basic of basic things.
There are torrents and websites that have LOADS of resources that are free to use / public domain (make sure to explore the licensing restrictions, some are free for personal use, not commercial - ie. should you decide to sell your game). Also be careful as some assets are ripped from other games which may violate licensing agreements that usually include copyrights on art and sound restrictions. But, there are also many free and open resources, including very complex scripts, sounds, music, monsters, characters, objects, etc.
Also of notable concern is the severe lack of any assets that come with the base game, as I recall, there are 2 monsters and only about 30 or 40 tiles in the base game so be prepared to go on the lookout for additional assets (or make your own).
All of the art uses BMPs (possibly JPGs/GIFs), the sound is either mp3 or wav so its very simple to import your own assets into the game, although a bit time consuming if you download a large amount of assets (you dump the assets into the appropriate RPG Maker sub folder, then you have to import each asset one at a time through RPG Maker...disappointing).
Overall, I think its a fantastic little program if not overpriced given what you get out of the box. And if you are looking to do anything more complex than having maps with doors, shopkeeps, and some dialog in your game, expect to learn some scripting / graphics editing / sound creation / stat tweaking.
As one final note, there are TONS of tutorial videos on Youtube for learning how to use RPG Maker, I strongly encourage any users to make extensive use of these tutorials, it will make the entire process much less painful.

First Impressions:
I love the viking theme of this game, and that's really about it.
Pros:
-Textures look alright for the most part.
-Music is decent enough.
-The style is somewhat unqiue, but not very mature.
Cons:
-Most systems within the game are fairly basic
-Combat is simple with skills that are fairly static and simple.
-Skills never really advance beyond doing some damage and upgrades appear to just increase stats (exciting, I know)
-AI is pretty stupid, they just throw themselves at you to do as much damage as possible. Crows, for example, just dive on you to do some minor damage to widdle you down and you just kinda smack them away.
-Quest system has you doing raids (quests) that involve you tearing your way through something while killing and collecting everything to complete additional tasks. This system often requires back-tracking, which not long prolongs the game artifically, it makes early levels *really really boring.*
-The raids seem to repeat the same deign every level
-The story is hilariously simple that it made Diablo 3's look good. Nothing is expalined, no connections are made, characters have no defining traits, they all kinda look the same.
-Voice acting is hilariously basic and sounds like it was done in one take.
Overall:
The game is worth it's money on sale and I would pick it up if you like game's similar to Diablo or Torchlight. However, don't expect to become immersed in the world with hours of content, because there really isn't that much sauce in the pasta.
I wish this game the best of luck and if you can support it, then please do as I can see this going a long ways with enough time.
Edit: After my initial review, I have now seen the extent of the creativity this game has... or rather its lack of. Let me explain:
Every single raid I have done has the same layout. As you can imagine, it's mind numbingly boring and I've only put 7 hours into this game.
Enemies are reused more than I would like. Even boss abilites are shared with some high level trash mobs, making damage patters easy to remember.
Player skills can only have their dps numbers increase with time.
Skill upgrades are also bound to the amount of resouces you have, so I need wood to rage longer... great.
There is a pitiful amount of skills, which is worse considering you can't mix and match since weapons determine what skills you can use.
A lot of the trash mobs become a sponge at points, which is espically anoying when you are in an enviorment where you have to take shelter every 2 minutes. Attack for a few, run a lot, attack for a few, run a lot, it gets boring real quick.
The main character is chliche and is increadibly 1 dimentional. Imagine generic a-hole that just wants to kill.
When given branching dialog paths, they all seem to be the same as well as don't give you what you are acutally going to say. Some serious Fallout 4 vibes.
Gear upgrades and skill upgrades come at a snails pace.
Gear has no skill altering affects other than some generic damage boost, exp boost, attack speed boost, armor boost, or skill boost. Beyond simple.
At this point all I can say is that this game is so simple and safe it makes my head spin. If this game wants to stand out, it acutally has to do something new.

After many months of pining for its release I finally have my hands on Towerfall for PC. After many hours of shooting, jumping and powerups, I can tell you that this is an amazing experience; one I will be playing for many years to come.
The controls are tight, the options are super robust and the frenetic gameplay is wicked fun. It reminds me of great couch co-op games from the past, Smash Brothers, Power Stone, and WCW Vs. NWO. It brings friends together and tears them apart at the same time. What a wonderful experience.
Some may scoff at the lack of online multiplayer and while that is entirely understandable I also have to say that as the previous owner of a long running internet cafe as well as being a brother among three; I have learned that couch play and LAN play offer a significantly different and in my opinion, a better experience. If online multiplayer is a must for you, I suggest you look at something else for the time being as this is not what you're looking for.
If you have a couple controllers, some good friends and many hours to spare; you will not regret this purchase.  Towerfall provides endless entertainment in simple 30 second rounds, causing immediate satisfaction and chaos.
Highly suggested purchase.

TowerFall Ascension is not for the faint-hearted. It may appear very simple, but it can become extremely challenging very quickly. Here's a video giving you my thoughts on the single-player side of the game (for those of us who have a hard time getting friends over).
In summary, here are the pros and cons of the game (some as ? because it varies on the person)
+ Simple controls. It makes it easy for anyone to pick up and play.
+ High skill ceiling. While moving, shooting, jumping, and dodging are the only controls, using them all in combination to navigate the diverse courses while shooting down foes is more than challenging to say the least.
+ Fluid gameplay. Everything responds exactly how you expect it to and when you expect it to.
+ Local Multiplayer is a blast. It's very competitive, and when you win, damn do you feel good.
+ Highly satisfying when you perform well. It takes a lot of skill to do this, and when you do, you know it.
+ A lot of enemy variety with different mechanics.
? Extremely challenging. You can make it so difficult, that you will never beat a level unless you perform near perfection. The one-hit-kill system makes this so.
? Even on normal, it doesn't hold your hand. You will die and fail multiple times before you learn the map's patterns and enemies so you can complete it. The time will differ greatly from person to person.
? The single player is decent. It's nowhere near as fun as the multiplayer, but that's to be expected of most games.
- No tutorial. The best I could find was something in the options menu that gives you hints, but you have to look for it. With something as difficult as this, anything that helps is greatly appreciated.
- IMO, I wish they used better quality sprites like the ones they have when you select your character. Just a small ding for this, though. Graphics only matter to a certain extent.
- This can be very frustrating in later levels. You just can't see everything that's coming at you, and when enemies fill the screen, it only makes it that much worse. Best thing to do is set it down and come back later, but that may be never depending on how bad it♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥you off.
- It's local multiplayer only. It cuts off a really good part of the game for those people who can't get people over to play. And I can't help but feel this game would've really benifited from having online servers so you can play multiplayer anytime.
In conclusion, get it for the multiplayer. You're gonna have a blast with it. If you have time to kill and like a challenge, then consider getting it for the single player. It's not bad for the price.

The game is Early Access and it shows.
Being a free to play game and about 6GB in size, there is no reason not to play it if you enjoy tower defense games.
All transactions for the game are cosmetic or inventory increases (basic quality of life).
The game is definitely enjoyable for a while. However the flaw is quite clear with a game following the road of "item levels". It turns into an MMO. Each hero only has 4 towers meaning a current total of 16 options. For those who enjoy a bit more complexity and variation, this gets boring fast. Using item levels forces you to grind for gear for most of the game to reach the next difficulty, ultimately putting you in a position of what to do after getting through the hardest maps. Also for the hardest difficulties, there is little room for variation on towers, there is a specific towers requirement essentially and also a gear requirement for heros to play certain roles properly in order to succeed.
The use of heros is fun and fine, but in the end due to the power of enemies and many lines, you have to rely on towers more. Unless you enjoy grinding for gear or can find some form of enjoyment after obtaining the best gear without being bored, this game ultimately falls short.
The more classical mazing tower defenses or those with 40+ variations and multiple upgrade options will remain a more entertaining option for those seeking a true tower defense game. The only reason I can truely recommend it is because it is free. Otherwise it would be worth $5 at most.

Dungeon Defenders II is a highly enjoyable game, particularly given its Early Access status. It has been relatively bug free for me so far, with only two glitches in over 20 hours of playing. I've been playing as an apprentice, a ranged attacker with a decent set of defensive towers. This class seems well balanced with each of the towers doing something different and strategic choosing and placing your towers becomes quite important.
The levels are well designed, with some of the levels being quite tricky to figure out best tower placement the first time you play them. Mobs are good and well balanced, they could do with a larger variety of mobs but they do their infuriating job well. I've only seen one boss so far, Betsy, who is excellent and well balanced.
I haven't tried the other classes yet. The huntress appears to have the best DPS and her traps can be powerful but they don't impede enemies. The monk seems a little weak compared to the other classes at the moment being both close range and having weaker traps/towers and is more of a utility class. The squire has very good towers and their barricade health eventually scales with character health, making them very effective at blocking the enemy's approach.
There are a few issues though. The points you receive on level up make so little difference to your abilities that they may as well not be there - and they suffer from diminishing returns on top of that.
My main gripe, though, is the game select. You choose which map you want to play on, click go, and then you may start off solo or start off in the middle of a match and there's no way to choose. If you start off 20 seconds after someone else just created the map then you don't get any gems to build towers and traps with. This can result in a frustrating start to the game and it would be better to be able to choose to start a new game, or have some way of distributing the gems once the game has started.
Still, this looks very promising and hopefully issues will be resolved before release.

First off: I don't like plattformers… at all. I bought a good number of them, almost never finished one.
After entering the world of LIMBO though, I could hardly stop playing. This game is all about atmosphere - which is delivered right at the beginning.
The whole game has a very eerie feeling to it, mostly due to the lack of music and the fact that almost the whole story is shaped by your own imagination.
The gameplay is very solid (personally, I suck in most plattformers and ragequit sooner or later ^_^) and there are no frustrating encouters, though I got stuck for a minute or two at some puzzles which had me thinking hard about how to solve them.
To sum it up: LIMBO is the first game in this genre, which really captivated me since "Another World" back on the Amiga
and this is probably also the only plattformer for a good while, which I can recommend. The only downside IMHO is the really short playtime (~3-4 hours).

One of the strangest game I've played in years this one! When you hear the title of this game, you think it could be a party game. Instead, it really is a dark, horrifying platformer, where you have to guide a cute little boy through the dark world called Limbo: A place between heaven and hell. At least that is what has been told.
In fact, there is no storyline at all. All that you know is that the boy wakes up in a dark forest, and has to make it's way to the end.
It will not be an easy walkover, though: The further you get, the harder it will become. The boy will easily fall victim to a cruel and painful death.
Overall: Limbo offers a variety of incredible puzzles, outstanding visual/sound design, and an immersive world that you will not want to come out of.
If you would like to play an original, challenging platformer, Limbo is surely recommendable.

Your lover is being accused of a murder he didn't commit. While you're a lawyer, you want to find the artifact he was hunting in order to make the culprit come out of his hidden place. However, you would have never imagined to travel through time...
The plot is kinda going everywhere, though you visit places from an hotel room that are very different (an airport, the village in the winter, a old mansion, a cabaret) to find pieces of totems.
What? Oh the title? Yeah, I'm still searching the connection with witches, warlocks and the main plot.
Anyway, the gameplay is the standard one: hidden objects scenes, mini-games, everything is well balanced. However, there is a little problem at one moment: the item you need is an axle jack but is not in the list  - in reality, it seems that the lists were inverted for that scene.
The graphics are quite good and I loved the unique track.
However, I'm quite mixed of this game because of two things. The first one is a game breaking bug out of nowhere that made me do a second profile. Indeed, I couldn't access anymore a scene where a vital piece was stuck. When I start the game again, suddenly, I lost my diary, my totem case and my map. And the scene was still unavailable.
The second one is the problem met for the achievement with no skip and no hint for scenes. In reality, you have to avoid any click on the hint button, even outside of the hidden object scene. You have to wait until the skip button is charged for the mini-game because you may risk the hint button to resplenish itself and counting as a skip/use of hint. Some people got a problem when exiting by accident an HO scene. And you need to do it in one go: you can't leave the game if you want these achievements.
So, yeah, I'm still letting a thumb up but I would wait for a discount or another bundle to get a key, even if 6 euros isn't expensive.

The Beginner's Guide is the first solo work for the creator of indie smash hit The Stanley Parable, Davey Wreden. While it was an interesting concept, it lacked the charm, wit, or playability of TSP.
Even at the opening sale price of $8 it felt overpriced for essentially sitting and watching a slightly more interactive video. It honestly felt like it should have been a free game. There's only about an hour and a half of story here and absoutely no replayability. It's basically an $8 movie ticket.
The story polarized me. On the one hand it did something no game had ever really done by abolishing the fourth wall, the story itself came across as pretentious and, at times, tone deaf in a way I think was unintended. Itseems to bill itself as a 'true' story about the relationship between Wreden and Coda, but after playing it I can't help but think its 'true' in the sense that a horror movie is 'true'; maybe based on real events but given significant artistic liberty. While I won't spoil too much, the narrator by the end came across as entirely unsympathetic in an entirely unintended way. By the end, I felt nothing but contempt for him as a self-centered, selfish, and massive egomaniac of a person. The "poor me" ending just makes it seem like an abuser begging the victim to forgive him. The eventual moral tries to make a big point about understanding the characters in an abstract way but fails because everything up to that point contradicts the eventual 'revelation' at the climax.
The level design itself was varied and colorful, though completely linear and utterly devoid of anything, but after all the story is the focus, not the gameplay. There is little for you to do besides wander around as you listen to the background behind the levels and the personal story attached. Literally about the third chapter the game tells you the engines excells at linear, blocky coridors, and boy did I get that in spades. In TSP sequence breaking, clicking everything, and doing the unexpected generally got you interesting, funny, or intelligent easter eggs. I got literally nothing here. Therefore I can honestly say if you really want to experience this game, your best bet is either to watch a Let's Play or someone streaming it. Unless you can get it for free its really not worth your time.

I'm going to start this out by saying I don't fancy war games too much. Yeah I've played Call of Duty and such but this game really is nothing like it. Red Orchestra is possibly the most realistic war game I have ever seen.

You've got no HUD but a small map in the corner to help direct you and keep you informed. You don't regenerate health, you must use bandages, which you have only two of. When you are hit or take damage you will see a flash of a body showing the damage and location. The bullets actually have react, like falling and wind. Finally, there is the panic meter. Like a normal living person, and not the robots in Modern Warfare, youd panic. If a bomb goes of next to you or you get shot at.. you start to spaz. The screen shakes and your heart starts beating fast, until you calm down.
The game is reasonably priced and worth taking a look.

I had high hopes for this game, and was looking forward to playing it blindly as I did with The Stanley Parable. I had my hopes crushed fairly quickly, as  this game does NOT live up to the entertainment value of its predecessor AT ALL.
And I'm just gonna put it bluntly: The Beginner's Guide sucks.
All it is, is just you walking through a series of half-baked, barely interactive levels  made by some random nobody, who is not the developer of The Stanley Parable, and you don't even get a sweet british narrator...
It's a shallow, unwitty, melancholic and pathetic  barely one and a half  tale about how a "~2 deep 4 u, oh woe is me~" amateur game developer that was friends with the creator of The Stanley Parable struggled with his first world problems and issues. While I was enthusiastic at the start, as the game does have potential with neat ideas for a very unique and interesting story, it fell apart quite shortly after the first few levels. The problem is just that I'm not emotionally engaged or interested in a story about how some asocial whiney person struggled with his personal issues while making pretentious games.
The Beginner's Guide is nothing more than an interactive documentary that should have been free, it's dull and boring, and dont expect anything funny or witty, cause TBG is all about depression and self-loathing and whatever.
I don't think it's all bad, it has cool concepts but It's just not fun to play, this should have been a free game or a youtube video, because it has ZERO replay value, unlike TSB.
Some people might enjoy this game though, if they can relate with the subject matter, or find it more engaging than I do. I'd much rather find this person and tell him/her to make The Stanley Parable 2 instead, and stop being so whiney.

Secret of Magia looked like it was going to be a retro RPG, taking me back to the days of the Nintendo and Super Nintendo.  Playing Dragon Warrior, Faria, Times of Lore, or even Ultima to some extent. Starting out, you are in a room with Two characters, while you control a black sphere.  I was given the option choosing which Hero I wanted to play as by going through One of Two doors on either side of each Hero. I selected a character and was taken to a black screen where dialogue appeared. It seemed there was some sort of overarching villain who wanted "the elements" and threatened to reap your soul if you didn't get them for him. You then wake up in the bed of an inn, where you find a memo telling you to go to the bottom of a well to prove your worth.
There was no tutorial playthrough where you learn how to open the menu, switch between various screens, equip items or gear, or to even orient you to your basic surroundings. I thought this was a little clumsy, because a lot of the good RPG games have these basic features. So it took a few moments to explore the keyboard to figure out how to open the menus and switching between things. Instead of my usual exploring I decided to follow the storyline and proceeded to a well where I descended and encountered rats. The game told me to equip a sword, but didn't explain how to do that: Luckily, I fooled around with the keyboard so I knew where to go and what to do. Rat-Kabob coming up. Then, I was told to equip a lantern, but for the life of me I couldn't find it in the inventory. Finally after 3 minutes of frustration I was able to locate a lantern, by going to my armor, selecting equip and there it was, hidden. Frustrated, I equipped it and proceeded through the cave slashing at rats.
I think this game has some things going for it. Visually it is retro, but done in a good way. The story seems interesting, very Final Fantasyish; However, Ithink the dialogue is a little weak and the menu system is clunky. Perhaps playing further will alleviate my frustrations and I will be pleasantly surprised. For now though, based on my initial interaction with the game I think it is mediocre. Some things are done well, others not so well. It is playable and it is still an interesting RPG. I give it a thumbs up, but would urge caution for those who are easily frustrated or have unrealistic expectations.

I was curious about this game because it was on sale and the great reviews about how scary it was caught my attention. These kinds of horror games usually don't scare me (Amnesia and Slender: The Arrival did nothing for me). I can safely say that Outlast is the first game I've played that managed to make me jump a bit. I'm not going to exaggerate and claim that it gave me nightmares or made me crap my pants. No, I wasn't shrieking from my computer chair, but I did find it to be a somewhat startling experience which is more than I've come to expect from horror games. What that says to me is that if you have less of a tolerance for horror games than I do, then you will definitely be scared by this game.
Graphically, the game looks great (and runs great). The visuals create a dark and foreboding atmosphere that works to draw you in and is very immersive. The voice acting and music are also excellent, and the characters are very believable.
My only real complaint with the game was that it can become a bit tedious and boring at times. There are certain points where it is very unclear as to where you need to go, and you find yourself stumbling around in the dark just looking for an objective. Blindly walking around like this (no matter how creepy the atmosphere) isn't really that tense or frightening, especially after you've been doing it repeatedly for ten minutes at a time.
Overall, this is a great game. I must admit I was skeptical, I'm normally not a huge fan of games where you can't fight anything and have to run and hide all the time, but I was really drawn in by Outlast and found it quite entertaining. So if you are a fan of games like this, then I am sure you'll be very satisfied.

One of the best Total War games in my opinion and still competes with newer total war and RTS titles today.
+ Huge variety of historical units and regiments, like the Old Guard or the Blackwatch.
+ Awesome Combat
+ Great balance overall between units and unit types, Cavalry can kill light infantry easily, but line infantry kills cavalry and so on.
+ Alot of Nations to pick from, who all bring different units and "focuses" to the table (for example: Russia has very good melee stats)
+ The maps are very big and dont feel too clumbed up like in newer titles.
+ Most Maps provide a variety of strategy you can use
+ Siege Battles feel great and pretty balanced, which is hard to do
- Minor Nations (Like the Dutch or Denmark) dont have alot of unit variety and their units are practically worse than the units of big nations in every department
- Some maps encourage camping due to 2-3 choke points that have to be pushed through
- Artillery has infinite ammo
- Most Players dont allow Artillery which leads to constant camping/skirmishing fights
Overall, I highly recommend you buy the game (especially when it is on discount). It is one of the best Total War titles out there and definitly worth your money.

I was given this a copy game by the developer(s) (or someone in contact with them) to review.
Secret of Magia is a bit of an interesting title for me, at first I was rather enjoying it. It had an OK story, some character progression and even some nice things like a HookShot! Unfortunately it went downhill from there (and before that even).
I personally played this game with an Xbox 360 controller, as that's what I generally enjoy playing this style of game with. Sadly there appears to be no documentation of the controls for it.
So here's roughly what they seem to be for me:
A - Run/Walk + Hookshot
B - Menu (Really odd binding IMO)
X - Attack/Interact
Y - Magic
LB - Shield
Select - Quick Menu (also used for cycling between quick menus)
Start - Also used for cycling quick menus, but cannot be used to access it in the first place)
RB/LT/RT - Appear to be unused.
Now while the game was fun for the first hour or so, unforunately it simply became a grindfest of bugs and dull combat. It is worth noting that I played as a Paladin class, so other classes *may* be more interesting, but for me it simply consisted of standing diagonally from an enemy and spamming the attack button (the cooldown on combos seems very short IMO).
This tactic ends up changing slightly for enemies that have a ranged attack as I will simply attack them head on because they have no melee secondary attack, leaving them essentially paralyzed while I attack them. Magic attacks are OK, but they have no cooldown meaning they can easily be spammed. (I only seemed to have access to a fire spell and ice spell as a Paladin, with the ice being a sort of ball shot straight ahead, and the fire being multiple revolving fireballs).
Now you might seem to think that combat isn't so bad from this, but enemies get tougher the higher level you are, the problem is that while their health gets ever higher my attack doesn't seem to level at the same rate (or at all), with most monsters now taking up to 70 (yes
) hits to defeat at level 16 with the best weapons I currently have.
I also have ended up with virtually endless money as well from every monster I come across up to the first boss, meaning I can basically never die by drinking as many life potions as needed due to them having no cooldown.
It is also worth noting that the game has no hint system or in-game map (short of the maps you can find on tables in some houses). I have played through as much of the game as I can, but I cannot find a key item, despite knowing roughly where it is, this is also despite having the key item that should come after it (as far as I know).
Now I suppose we must move onto the bugs I discussed earlier. Some of these have already been mentioned in other reviews, but I will mention them again nonetheless.
- The lighting engine appears to be broken entirely, I didn't realise this until looking at the screenshots now with their lovely lighting, yet my game appears to be running at max brightness with no shadows or dynamic lighting of any kind, the game looks almost
- Many objects are solid for no apparent reason (such as foliage, there are some flowers that are seemingly identical, yet one is solid, the other isn't)
- Many walls aren't solid (e.g. Multiple walls in the Church aren't solid meaning you (and NPCs) can walk on them.
- There's a key that you can pick up
that I can pick up as many times as I want for no apparent reason, I now have 7 of said key in my inventory.
- This is not necessarily a bug per se, but I noticed that after a couple of hours of playing my ears were beginning to hurt, the sound effects for melee attacks appears to be rather harsh, thankfully I was able to disable this via the RPGMaker menu (F1).
Really I just don't think I can recommend this game, it has too many bugs, combat has become tedious (I avoid as many enemies as I can now), and it just wasn't a particularly fun experience (apart from the first 30min-1hr). Maybe once Secret of Magia gets updated a bit I'll revisit it and update my review, but for now I cannot recommend it.

This is one of those times when the sum of all parts is better than they should be. Nothing in this game is outstanding or excellent, yet the game is competent most aspects. This creates a fun and enjoyable game, and i really want to recommend it. There are still problems with things, like targeting enemies and movement etc, but these are all issues with it being a console base game, and kb/m control.
I don't recomend it though. In fact i vehemently suggest you look elsewhere, for one single reason.
The save system in this game is terrible. In a normal console game, anything the game gives you baring exp in a rpg, is still there when you die, that chest you opened you will need to open again, but the items you get are still there. In a normal action rpg/hack n slash with random loot (like this game), your character is saved at all times, you pick up an item and die, ou still have that item, or if an enemy drops something and you die, it will still be there on the ground when you make your way back.
Not in Vikings. If the game gives you that lucky drop, gives you that amazing new weapon you've been hunting for, and you happen to die before the next checkpoint. It's gone forever. This and this alone can kill any fun this game could give you.
Do not buy this game, unles they introduce a secondary save system or change the checkpoint save system completely.

Do you remember playing multiplayer games such as Goldeneye or Smash Bros. with friends for hours on end? TowerFall is that experience and more. Matches are fierce and exciting. They are the perfect length to allow players to rotate out without feeling too short. You’ll be cheering and yelling alongside everyone else as you wait for your turn.
TowerFall is a masterclass example of intentional game design. Nothing feels out of place or missing. The controls and pacing have been fine tuned to create the best possible experience.
While multiplayer is the main focus, and is amazing, there is a substantial amount of single player content. I’d like to focus on that in this review since everyone else is going to talk about multiplayer.
In quest mode you take on waves of enemies with a friend or by yourself. There’s one level for every tower with normal and hardcore difficulties, which I would rename to hardcore and insane. Waves and enemy movement are not random, they have been carefully designed to provide a varied and challenging experience. Even the simplest of enemies can be a huge obstacle with so much going on at once. The boss fights are epic too.
Perhaps the most challenging mode in TowerFall is trials mode. It’s like break-the-targets in Smash Bros. but way more intense. Each trial is like a puzzle -- figure out the optimal way to beat it -- then figure out how to pull it off. Gold times are set so someone moderately good at the game might have a chance with practice. Diamond times are even harder with most set to under a few seconds. It feels very satisfying when you pull it off. Each trial feels unique and like the game is trying to teach you something.
TowerFall is a beautiful game with an insane amount of visual polish. While its character and environment designs stand out, the details and animation are what puts it over the top. Everything from how the character moves to the environment details such as dripping water or crumbling skeletons.
This review is not complete without talking about the audio design. Each character has a unique set of sound effects. This not only gives them individual personalities but also lets you know what’s happening elsewhere on the screen. The soundtrack is also worthy of much praise. Each tower has a unique track that matches the visuals perfectly. It echos the gameplay both in tempo and mood and tells a story at the same time.
Multiplayer is what you buy the game for but single player is very good too. TowerFall is an amazing game and is worth both your time and money.

A pleasant, if unremarkable, hidden object game.  It's a relaxing way to spend two hours.  All the usual trimmings are there - hint/skip buttons so you're never stuck, a teleporting map that indicates the areas in which there are things to do, and a journal to keep track of the (minimal) story.
The graphics are nicely done. The music is inoffensive.  There is no voice acting, and no extras of the sort you'd see in Collector's Edition hidden object games.
The hidden object scenes are list-based junk piles with the occasional interactive object (e.g. pick up the sponge and wipe the mirror with it to reveal an image that is an item on your list).  Each hidden object scene is revisited, but not really repeated, since the objects you found the first time remain found.
There aren't that many puzzles, and those that are present are mostly of the tired old slider variety.
Most of your time in-game will be spent point-and-click style, finding an item to help unlock a box that has another item you can use to reach another locked box and so on.  These inventory... interactions? They're not really puzzles.... are satisfying in the same way that popping bubble wrap is.
Harmless fun at a reasonable price. Recommended for fans of the genre, as long as they know going in that this is just more of the same.

This is arguably one of the greatest online multiplayer games ever. For those of us born in the 80s who were there for the advent of FPS games and then also online gameplay, this and the other early Half-Life mods are some of the true cornerstones of some of the most eternally excellent gaming exoerience off all time. I remember playing this around 1999 or 2000, I had traded my friend from Junior High burnt copy of Rainbow Six Rogue Spear for an actual copy of Half Life, and this was before Serial Codes were really enforced as they are now, and this was before Steam too, there was the Sierra online network and WON IDs. Phenomenally grand memories of badass battles and classic funny moments that can take place during a game. This is one for the ages, and I played a ton of Counter-Strike back then too. Along with Action Half-Life (an amazing stylized-action movie style mod) and Firearms (a great approach to early realistic combat, with a vast array of weapons) and then there was The Opera, and Natural Selection. But they all came from the first, which was this, Team Fortress Classic (which yes, is techically a remake from a Quake mod, but IMO better in a handful of notable ways). So that's why I wanted to write a review for this awesomely eternally replayable online multiplayer team-based FPS game. I remember playing in Drippy's 2fort server and ViBig before I'd go to school in the mornings, it was so fun being able to play online through fast cable internet against other people probably doing the same thing. That's why this game is important, it's arguably one of the best multiplayer games of all time. Period.
Real talk: this game is cool. Play with lights out and headphones on.

-You can attach/detach bayonet whenever you want to. (Just like in Rising Storm 2.)
-No stupid suppression system. The one they have in the first RO was simple. When you get shot at, you point of aim moves a little, whereas on ro2 if an mg shoots at you, your screen has a seizure AND plus they can hip shot mg's in ro2. Not a fan of that whatsoever.
-A minor detail I liked about the first RO is class descriptions but thats just me mostly.
-In the first RO hip shooting was MUCH better and easier instead in ro2 its kind of a gamble for life but not completely.

I had high hopes for this game, and was looking forward to playing it blindly as I did with The Stanley Parable. I had my hopes crushed fairly quickly, as  this game does NOT live up to the entertainment value of its predecessor AT ALL.
And I'm just gonna put it bluntly: The Beginner's Guide sucks.
All it is, is just you walking through a series of half-baked, barely interactive levels  made by some random nobody, who is not the developer of The Stanley Parable, and you don't even get a sweet british narrator...
It's a shallow, unwitty, melancholic and pathetic  barely one and a half  tale about how a "~2 deep 4 u, oh woe is me~" amateur game developer that was friends with the creator of The Stanley Parable struggled with his first world problems and issues. While I was enthusiastic at the start, as the game does have potential with neat ideas for a very unique and interesting story, it fell apart quite shortly after the first few levels. The problem is just that I'm not emotionally engaged or interested in a story about how some asocial whiney person struggled with his personal issues while making pretentious games.
The Beginner's Guide is nothing more than an interactive documentary that should have been free, it's dull and boring, and dont expect anything funny or witty, cause TBG is all about depression and self-loathing and whatever.
I don't think it's all bad, it has cool concepts but It's just not fun to play, this should have been a free game or a youtube video, because it has ZERO replay value, unlike TSB.
Some people might enjoy this game though, if they can relate with the subject matter, or find it more engaging than I do. I'd much rather find this person and tell him/her to make The Stanley Parable 2 instead, and stop being so whiney.
Thanks for wasting my money, Davey. (and for having a "skip level" button)

Fallout 3 was a great step in the franchise.  It also was the bigest change to the franchise.  I know that you're looking at my hours and you think "this guy has not played this game enough".  Just like New Vegas, I had the game of the year edition on my Xbox 360.  I got it on my PC for nostalgia reasons, and It didnt work.  Its optimized for Windows XP, and I have Windows 7.  So if you plan to purchase this game make sure you know how to run it on a higher OS, or you better have a mean XP machine.  Now on to the game.  Fallout 3 was a game that was a big building block to FPS+RPG.  It had a great story along with a fun enjoyable journey.  The main game has a fantastic story.  The game has you helping the Brotherhood of Steel, but you can help the Enclave(their enemies) in some ways.  The main questline is linear and somewhat short, but its best if you take your time and explore the Capital Wasteland.  Fallout three has 5 DLC's.  Unlike New Vegas, in this game its more easy to scramble the order of the DLC's.  The first one I did was Mothership Zeta.  This was my second least favorite DLC, but it was still enjoyable and hilarious.  You get abducted and you and a crew of survivors from different time periods have to fight your way off the ship.  You get cool loot and there are interesting characters.  My favorite character would have to be Sally and I would have to give a honorable mention to Paulson.  The next one I played was Operation Anchorage.  This one is the DLC thats right in the middle(third).  It lets you participate in the lore of fallout, and it shows what the war between the U.S. and China was like.  It gets you cool loot, its fun to explore, and its interesting because of the Fallout lore within.  Its pretty easy, just be cautious at times.  My favorite character is Benjamin Montgomery.  The next one I completed was Point Lookout.  Point Lookout is by far my least favorite Fallout DLC.  It was somewhat hard, the story was boring and wasn't justified in the end.  Plus you dont seem to get rewarding loot.  In this DLC I didnt really have a favorite character, I guess the ghoul, Desmond.  I didn't like it, but that doesn't mean you wont.  Next I did Into The Pitt.  Into The Pitt takes you to post-war Pittsburgh and bring the first faction system into FPS Fallout.  This was my favorite from Fallout 3.  Its story rich, cool loot, great setting, and introduced the faction system.  My favorite character was Wernher.  This last one to play takes place after you finish the main game, Broken Steel.  In Broken Steel you take the fight to the Enclave and finish them off.  Its not much more comlex than that.  It also adds loot and enemies to the game, and increases the level cap.  Another great DLC that is number two for Fallout 3 DLC's for me.  If you do get Fallout 3, take it slow enjoy it.  Thanks for reading this long monster of a review, have fun.

My favorite part of Zachtronics games is the feeling of moving tangible objects in the game world. That's what elevates it above awkward programming for me. Out of the Zachtronics games I've played, Infinifactory captures this aspect best.
The workshop integration also adds a lot of value. The built-in puzzle design, as in all Zachtronics games, tends to favor big-and-messy puzzles as the game progresses, and I'm more a fan of small-and-clean puzzles. Many of the workshop puzzles offer this sort of design, in particular Aap op Sokken's "Way Too Fast" series.
Compared to 2D Zachtronics games, it is less challenging to complete puzzles in Infinifactory because having 3 dimensions available means you are less space constrained. Those looking for pure difficulty may be disappointed, but for me the increased immersion makes up for it.

Note on recommendation: This game is roughly the length of a movie, and I got about as much enjoyment from it as I would a movie. Therefore, I'm going to go ahead and recommend this game despite its length and lack of interactivity. That being said, this game is for a very niche audience. I would not recommend it to the general gaming audience.
Note of reviewer: I make games for a living, and this game talks about people who make games. As a result, the messages in this game are going to reach people like me. It will not mean as much to others.
Note on the game: This game deals with depression and people pleasing, which could be uncomfortable for some players. Be sure you're ready for some heavy material before diving in.
Actual review:
What more needs to be said than what I already said? This is a rather heavy examination of some of the psychology that goes into creative works. There are parts that feel very contrived throughout. I didn't actually feel like I was looking at what I was told I was looking at. People don't really make games exactly as presented here. Nonetheless, there are facets of it that ring painfully true for anyone who has attempted creative work like this. It'll get you to think about your relationship not only with your work, but with other people's work. For that, I think this game was overall a success.
If you're considering getting this game, I suggest you find someone who has played it and who knows who you are first to see if they think you'll get something out of it. Otherwise, you may find yourself disappointed.
Steam offers a refund for any game you've played for less than 2 hours. As this game is about 90 minutes long, this means that theoretically anyone who buys it could get a refund after playing through it. Please don't do this to indie developers. If you buy this game, keep it in your library. If you're not willing to part with $8-10 on 90 minutes of entertainment, then... well, maybe these kinds of games just aren't for you.

This game is terrifying and amazing at the same time. I've watched Let's Plays on this and even when I know what's going to happen this game makes me jump and completely forget I knew it'd happen. Just about everything is against you and it really makes you anxious while playing, thinking that in every room something is going to get you. Let's just say:  I love being terrified in gaming but alas very few horror games have been able to chill my blood to the bone and leave a path of sweat trickling down my back.
It really captures being a Horror/Survival game, because you can't attack your enemies. All you can do is run and hide, and outsmart them (because, the's admit, some of the enemies can be pretty stupid).
Taking place in a Mental Asylumn where everything is against you(what doesn't get scarier than that?), you take control of a journalist, Miles Upsher, who acting on a tip-off that things are not well at all at the Mount Massive Mental Institute decides to take look around to see if there is a valid story worth printing. As far as story goes that is about as much I will say - its better the gamer goes into this sick and twisted world with as little information as possible.
Gameplay wise, Outlast employs the mechanics set like any other first person game (moving your character by WASD) but that the main character can now vault over obstacles in his course whilst fleeing from some of the most grotesque characters ever created for gaming. In between filming what you see you will be doing a lot of frantic running and hiding lest you forfeit your life.
On a scariness level - Outlast succeeds admirably. This is truly a terrifying experience (up the ante by turning all the lights off and playing with headphones on) and with AAA style graphics truly immerses you in a world of horror that is coupled with a sparse but very tense soundtrack. The audio for Outlast and the various sound effects it employes to scare it players is top notch.

Wolves of Midgard s an excellent Diablo type of game; in some ways even better then Diablo. With 45 hours in the game as I write this review, I can only recommend this game! Every runs are big enough to keep you going for a couple of hours, with enough treasures and obstacles to make it quite enjoyable. You can even run them again to gather more experience and resources. Treasures offer a variety of equipment and it is not hard to find something better then what you already have which is the aspect I find it very frustrating in Diablo 3. There are even artifacts that when you have completed the set are very handy but to get them, you need to solve puzzles of the sort. There are skills tree for each type of weapons and it is easy to switch between them, even while your are in an expedition. Graphiques are really well done and the story is complemented with a bit of humour just as some monsters are. I am playing this on the MAC computer and aside for a long loading time when you start the game, the game runs very well and I haven't experienced any bugs or crashes. It seams that I still have quite a lot to do yet in this game and apparently, you can replay the game in a harder mode once you finish the first run and there doesn't seem to be any level limitation. If you enjoy hack and slash games with lots of loot to find and improvements to be made either on equipment of town development, go for this game!

I saw a short video of this game a while back displaying some of the gameplay. I thought the concept was really cool, and the gameplay looked smoothe, but I didn't really pay very much mind to it after that. Until it showed up one day in my dicovery queue, and, being the curious person that i am, I picked it up at it's Christmas sale price.
I was completely blown away by just how fun this game is. Creating large assebmly lines and factories and watching all the small storage units come through from a nice top down view, or witnessing the creation that you spent hours on make a tiny mistake somewhere in the middle and fall apart with storage crates piling up and falling off cliffs due to your small error, and then procceding to pick apart your assembly line piece by piece to find that tiny little mistake.
On top of this amazing "create-> test-> fail-> change-> succeed" style gameplay, there is a dark, but still somewhat goofy plot, that made me shed some tears in the early game. The unnerving corpses that litter each level, each one holding the last recorded audio log before they failed their task. This game brought me right up to my screen with so many different emotions. And, dare I say it... The dog. Being an overall animal lover, and an owner of a dog myself, witnessing the horrors that lie in that one level brought me to tears the moment I picked up that audio log, and really brought to light the horrific acts commited by the games antagonists.

This is one of the best "puzzle" games I've ever played and is one of the best games overall I've played in a long time, certainly in 2016. I put quotes on puzzle because it is basically a 3-D programming game, you have stuff, you need the stuff to be arranged in a certain way at a certain endpoint. You use the tools you have been given and the methods you have learned to make the stuff fit what the endpoint wants. And it's all you, thats why this game is so great. Any frustration comes from you not yet getting the desired result yet. But it never feels like you're out of things to try, there are always more approches you can take, and so it might take an hour to solve a stage, you're trying new stuff and refining that whole hour, not sitting there stumped. Also there are little nuggets of story to be found that make the world you're solving these puzzles in more intriguing. 9.75/10, because I havent finished it yet and dont know where the story is going, so I dont know how satisfying the conclusion is yet. But if you enjoy puzzle solving at all, in any way, I'd recommend picking this up right now without hesitation.

Secret of Magia is an Action RPG developed with RPG Maker.
I was given a key by the developer and I am sorry to say I do not recommend this game and here is why.
Let's start with the good things first :
The game offers not only between the choice of a female or male character, but features a class system that determines what can you equip. The HUD is nicely done and the quest system is rather original for a game like this.
The combat system is pretty good and the enemies are implemented in a smart way, the skeletons in the mines were one of them, as they genuinely surprised me and made me paranoid.
Another nice thing is that you can gather flowers and butterflies for the crafting system, sadly after an hour and a half I have not tried this system yet, but I gathered quite a lot of stuff.
Now for the bad parts :
I'm not sure if the developer has tested this game, but it's full of bugs, you can go inside walls, letters become plants when you read them, some blocks that should be solid are not, some that shouldn't be are, glitches here and there, couches have teleport blocks inside them, I was joking with a friend that in the first chuch you come across you can ascend to godhood by straight walking on the wall, most of the walls there are passable, even npcs climb them.
The combat while original for the first half hour, is kind of unbalanced, at least as a melee class, I was getting oneshotted the first levels which was pretty frustrating (slimes), I had to align myself diagonally so the monsters wouldn't have a chance to attack me but I could. I farmed a little, when I leveled up though, the monsters leveled with me and became a lot more tanky, giving more gold too. Now, the first real boss was not a big problem because by the time I had so many money I invested in health potions, he could never kill me, doesn't matter how much damage he did to me. After that you drop a legendary weapon which is a bow, a weapon my assassin shouldn't be using but he was using anyway (not sure if legendary weapons do not have class requirements). Some of the resources are inherent to RPG Maker and not original by the developer, you can judge if that affects quality or not.
I do not feel compelled to complete or continue the game as I did not have much fun with it, but thank you anyway for this chance (since I received the key by a developer or someone in contact with him).
All in all it's a low quality rpg maker title with some smart ideas here and there, but with a weak story, characters and quite full of bugs at the moment of writing, so personally I would not recommend you this game.

Well, Creative Assembly have managed to do it again. Their top-notch mix of grand strategy and battlefield tactics comes to tumultuous Napoleonic Europe, and you'll be guaranteed and good challenge and your expected dose of Total Fun.
The Napoleonic era may have been a cultural, political and social turning point for Europe, but as far as battlefield tactics go, it was one of the most sterile points in human military history. Line a load of poor peasants dressed in desperately uncomfortable rough-wool uniforms up in rows, arm them with poorly-perfoming, inaccurate muskets, and have them shoot at each other until what is left of one of the armies runs, then hound them with your sabre-wielding cavalry.
And yet, CA makes it work brilliantly, like they always know how to do.
There is a great deal of historical accuracy in this one, from the number of buttons on the Austrian Army jersies, to the types of units present during the time. Both sides of the gameplay (campaign mapping and battles) are very strong and engaging, and as always, look great.
Take control of any of the major powers (France, Austria, Prussia, England, Russia) of the war, and see where it leads you in a campaign. Or try out one of the many set piece battles from the time. They've even managed to make the naval battles work well, too.
I've always been a greater fan of the classical era of humans murdery side, but Napoleon: TW makes a great change, and you won't be disappointed.

Banished is a city builder that is great when you start playing it. Gather resources and build buildings to support your town like woodcutters and blacksmiths, while constantly being on guard for shortages of important items like food and firewood.
Once you get to about 200 population, the game is easy mode however. You will not be doing anything different from 200 to 2000 population, but simply recreating the same working center and support structure you have elsewhere.
Disasters are supposed to add random events to mix up the play, but they always destroy a large chunk of your town. You would think if you had wells everywhere, and had everyone working to put out fires they would... but they don't. If something catches on fire, it doesn't matter if you have wells and 1000 firemen; your town will still burn down.
This is a game that feels like halfway through gameplay design they gave up and said "it is good enough". Which it is for the price, but I feel let down. When you are trying to figure things out the game is great; once you do figure things out, you'll do that same thing over and over and over and over.
TLDR; good early game, but repetitive after a certain population with zero changes in gameplay as your city grows.

This is a good game.  It's a great little survival simulator for a small band of "middle ages" people, that hopefully will make it to a big band of people eventually.  The graphics and sound track are crisp and relaxing.  And your decisions will make and many times, break your little colony.  The first 20 or 30 hours you'll be pretty amazed with most of the content.  After you survive your first 10 years or so, your biggest concern is surviving a number of dreaded natural catastrophies, that are rare but can be really devestating.  (These can be turned off, but where's the fun in that?)  ..   (Stupid tornados.)
That said, this game isn't for everyone.   There aren't any goblin invaders or even natives to attack you.  You don't have a military to build up.  Your best defense is a lot of food and firewood in your stockpile.
The only real negatives I have about the game is that you need  to micromanage all your people in their professions, and moving them from farming in the spring through autumn, and back to other professions in the winter such as mining or forestry can be kind of tedious.    The road system sometimes doesn't allow you to build a path where you people can clearly walk is a little frustrating as well.   There could be some additional content as well, the possiblities are pretty endless, but there's some nice mods out there to help flush it out a little.
Otherwise though, it's a nicely polished little game, especially for the limited resources the developer had.  And the price is right.
I'd definetely be interested in seeing a Banished 2 with a little more content, some additional professions, and perhaps some sort of further danger for your colonists, such as wild animals.

Not playing UT 99 is a crime to gamers everywhere. UT 99 is arguably the most competitive multiplayer FPS game right next to Counter Strike. This is not a friendly game, don't expect to come in and start whoopin'♥♥♥♥♥instantly...no, no...expect to come in and start getting YOUR♥♥♥♥♥whooped instantly. Fast paced, gory, frag fest action at its finest. UT 99 is a game that is simple, you grab a gun (My personal fav being the Flak Cannon) and go find some meat!
The graphics of course may not be all that amazing, but graphics don't make a game, gameplay does and man does UT 99 offer that. With an arsenal of weaponry at your command and over a 100 maps, both by the dev, and the community, this is a game that I think will never get old, and the best part is after all these years, UT multiplayer is still going strong, just make sure you join a game with actual players and NOT bots. Trust me, you'll know if you are playing with bots or not. Single player is simple, you play in a tournament against bots, but personally, I skipped the campaign and went straight for the real deal multiplayer since I find fighting against bots...well boring. The soundtrack is foot-tappin awesomeness with fast techno tunes that go perfect with the sounds of rocket launchers and screams in the distance followed by the sound of body parts hitting the floor.
There is a ton of gore in this game so be prepared. I think UT can stand up to any game today and still win, yes, even Battlefield 4. I like UT a lot more than Quake III for many reasons. It seems what Quake III was flawed at, UT 99 was improved in. Now don't get me wrong, I like UT 2004, but there is something about UT 99 that I like a lot more than 2004. I'm not sure but 99 is just wayyy more fun and awesome for me that 2004 ever was. What else is there to say, it's fast, it's action-packed, it's gruesome, it's frantic, it's insane, it's intense, it's UT 99! And no need to worry about specs, any modern CPU can run this game perfectly smooth with no lag at all, believe me, I have a 1.0 GHZ processor laptop with AMD c-50 dual core. This is essential if you call yourself a PC gamer, and for the price of a book, you'd be silly NOT to buy this game! Don't let the difficulty of this game turn you off at first, UT is a game that is fun to play, but hard to master, it just takes time and patience to finally start getting into the swing of things and starting to get kills. So play UT 99 today! I'm sure you'll enjoy seeing your avatar die in an explosion of blood and limbs...:3

TL;DR - Dis game gud.
If you've ever dreamed of living in the campiest action movie ever, then by all means, welcome to your dreamworld. In Just Cause you play the ultimate action-hero protagonist, Rico; a walking cliche. Rico has the chiseled chin, endless supply of guns, ladies hitting on him left and right, explosions for every eager enemy, and a parachute to get out of trouble. The game plays to it's own absurdity. You'll constantly find Rico in ever-escalating situations with characters as equally cliche and over-the-top as he. This makes for a hilarious cinematic experience while still being awed by the top-notch action we've all come to expect as the standard.
As far as game play goes, you will find a few key elements of this game that quickly help it stand apart from the crowd. Just Cause 2 has an amazing grappling hook mechanic that allows you to hop from vehicle to vehicle, zip quickly away from danger, tether cars to the ground while they're driving, and even tether enemies to vehicles where you can then drag them mercilessly around. This makes for tons of hilarity while being extremely functional for navigating danger and the environment. The second key element in JC2 is the open world. This game is a sandbox done perfectly. Perfectly. I don't know that I've had as much fun in many other open-world games as I did with JC2. I constantly wanted to explore the map and find new villages, airbases, and harbors I'd not yet visited... and subsequently decimated.
Apart from these key elements you will find what you'd usually expect, pistols, grenades, shotguns, a vehicle-theft system (boats, planes, and choppers included), NPC alliances, and a gorgeous environment for it to take place in. The only complaint I'd have to log is the vehicle controls were occasionally difficult to deal with. Trying to take turns in the wrong vehicle and navigating a plane on anything other than a runway can prove a challenge. In addition there were a few times I tried to grapple away from danger only to find my character stuck floating in air; tethered to some unseen object. That being said, I'd hardly call that much of a complaint. The fun-factor in this game easily covers any frustration by these issues and keeps you drawn into the game.  10/10 would play again.

A technically flawed but mostly charming and low priced action adventure/RPG title, Secret Of Magia harkens back to older action adventure RPG titles and the inspirations and love for the Zelda titles is clear, and things like the friendly dialogue, brief random encounters, art style and music all fit nicely. There's also a fair amount of content, areas and enemies for the cost, and overall, while it has problems and does nothing special, it's good value for money and a competent aaRPG.
Full disclosure: I recieved a Steam key prior to this review.
The variety of environments and pretty good intro level were enough to get me engaged, and the casual and unlimited nature of exploration from an early stage are worth mentioning. It's easy to skip ahead if you're impatient, but equally easy to spend an extra hour or two just exploring and grinding. There's also a variety of competent and occasionally funny dialogue from many different denizens in many different towns.
The music is also very pleasant to listen to, and sets the tone really well without getting annoying at all.
Overall, if the developer releases a patch or two and clears up some issues, this title will be worth picking up for what is essentially the price of a coffee.
I feel like a patch or two would fix up most of my complaints, but for the sake of completion and honesty here they are.
There are tons of small technical bugs. I routinely found myself clipping through walls and into inaccessible areas, I was unable to equip or de-equip items after certain encounters, and had no way to continue but to slowly suicide, menu systems sometimes became disabled for unidentifiable reasons and plenty more small annoying technical mistakes that should've been play-tested and fixed.
The support for using a mouse is great, and makes playing a lot faster and smoother, but the out of the box key bindings are frankly awful, and the in-game configuration panel isn't listed in the controls, nor accessible by anything other than messing around (it's F1 in all RPG Maker titles), and even that isn't properly labelled or actionable, and F12 causes crashes due to a bugged RPG Maker script. Again, these are little things that can be fixed fairly simply, but that's all the more reason to highlight them.
There are design mistakes too, namely the save system relying on positional altar markers. This means that, like some of the older Zelda systems, you can only save before entering an area or after travelling to a specific place. For a game that encourages player grinding and a slow death screen, this makes little sense. An auto-save or simply just a save button would've been a far better choice.
The main issue for me, however, was the combat. There is arguably a small level of skill required in coordinating where to position the player in regards to each enemy and the environment but, at least as the soldier class, it's mostly just about finding the next diagonal tile and slashing ad infinitum and became repetitive and bland after a short time and even boss fights are mostly about predicting the next move and getting in position.
Priced at just £1.99/2.99€/$2.99 at the time of review, this is actually priced fairly, and will probably be worth picking up on sale for someone looking for a casual aaRPG with a nod towards older Nintendo titles, just not until some of the technical problems are corrected.

Slightly inclined toward recommending this game. For aboslutly casual players like myself it is an okay-good free game if you so decide. The game has two types of currency, F2P FW$ which you can earn by just playing, and Kredit which you purchase with real money.
In general there's no need to spend any real money on it unless you want to be really competitive. Repear cost for weapons and armors are somewhat expensive comparing with the reward from a match, but you can always withdraw back to the default guns and armor which require no repair, and still be able to do reasonably well in Hard PvE to farm/save some WF$. My suggestion would be keep away from Insane PvE and those multiple Tower Raid special op which will require players to have very good gear and team to complete and gain any noticable reward. Oh and unless you are buried with real money and have no idea where to spend them, stay away from Kredit random boxes, the drop rate is neglectable.
The game has some good ideas, like deviding into four classes with specific types of guns and ability: Rifleman the general DPS output with rifle or LMG, and who keeps the team supplied with ammo; Medic that is generally needed for any PvE mode, can heal and revive teammates though not every player is willing to play it so be prepared to be it a lot, equipped with a shotgun that can be deadly in close range; Engineer the sidekick DPS can resupply teammate's armor hp (which reduces dmg received) and carry one claymore which can be handy; Sniper, the class many newcomers like and hardest to be good at, as its name tells, dealing precision strike with sniper rifle and the easiest one to be killed when things get messy.
The game requires quite a bit of teamwork on higher level difficulty. And like all other team-based games, suffers from idiotic players which can ruin everything. After playing a while you can friend some decent players and/or join a clan for a more steady gameplay. The game is not perfect, with many glitches, like enemies spawn right behind you, and bad balancing of difficulty, like some bosses are very hard to fight in certain maps. But for a F2P it does its work to be entertaining, and when you are tiredd of it, just quit and leave it in your library until the next time you feel like it.

I started near a lake, with many ice fishing huts littering the frozen surface. I searched them all, taking all that I could find. Some wolves were nearby; best keep my distance.
There are some cabins on the shores, I rummage through a few, only to emerge from one confronted by a wolf. I retreat back inside, sleep for a few hours to wait the wolf out, and reemerge.
The wolf is gone, but it's getting late and the wind has picked up. There are still a few ice fishing huts to search, as well as a rather large cabin across the frozen lake that I have yet to visit.
I begin my trek across towards the cabin, checking out the last few huts. The wind now brings snow. Darkness is quickly descending.
I search the last hut, I am only a short distance away from the shore now, but the storm has become a blizzard and I am freezing.
I need to warm up. Luckily the hut has a pot-belly stove, which I am able to get a fire going in. The hut has no door, so I stand with my back to the fire, staring out into the whipping wind and snow. It howls at me, daring me to venture forth into its icy embrace.
I don't want to indulge it, but I have no choice; my fire is about to go out as I have no more wood to fuel it.
I burst from my shelter only to realize I can no longer see the shore. I stumble blindly in what I pray is the right direction. I find the shore, but it is unfamiliar, and too steep to climb. I keep following the shore to the right, hoping I still have my bearings correct. I am beginning to freeze again. I just want to sleep.
The incline of the shore decreases, a sign can be seen.
"Rangers Station"
Never have I been so relieved. I burst inside the cabin. Food. Medicine. Tools. A wood stove.
I am safe, for now.
10/10

One of the hardest, yet most rewarding WW2 shooters on the planet..
This is the only FPS that keeps me coming back for more, now 900+ hours, it does have a steep learning curve but it's rewarding once you learn your way around the controls. If you are considering this title I would recommend playing territory games on realism mode either team DM's or Campaign ( Campaign is my favourite), much more immersive and difficult but  the best way to experience RO2 in all it's PTSD inducing glory!
If you like to fight for the Axis or Allies, experience the weapons of both sides and the famous battles of the Eastern Front or the Pacific campaigns, look no further.
The randomness of battles never ceases to amaze me, from being a lone survivor of a artillery strike when everyone else around you vaporises to being pinned down by a tank in the open and unable to do anything because you are being supressed so much you can barely think straight, no game has ever produced the gameplay RO has. The weapon and class progression system keeps you pushing yourself onwards towards Hero status, but even then the cruelty of war means that even a new players bullet can easily have your name on it...
The community is great and you will find some great servers with custom maps with large spaces to fight in, once the team gets organised and communicating you can overwhelm the enemy against all the odds.
The recent updates such as the MG42 and new maps really keep this game fresh.

In Amnesia you could compensate much more easily for ♥♥♥♥ups and explore more easier since pretty much every shadow was a place to hide. Makes this game feel alot more static in comparision.

After an hour of having green burn into my retinas those sections of the game became a ♥♥♥♥ing annoyance rather than scary. For a clone, this is actually a decent game. Although it's not as bright and as colorful as Bomberman is, this game is has an attitude of it's own. Get into a good match online or locally and your set for some fun. This game is actually quite difficult keep in mind (even on the lowest setting)!
The
resembles that of bomberman except with a few unique features. Each character comes with their own abilities (two to be exact). The Girl is able to teleport and throw a knife. The Toymaker is able to deploy a totem and detonate them. The Sad Clown is able to "sneeze" and confuse. The Puppet Mistress can use her gaze to slow opponents and petrification. The Dummy is able to freeze bombs and detonate them. The Wrestler can charge and smash opponents. The Thief can go invisible and use his special ability, shadow step. The Mine can silence and cage opponents. Of course just like Bomberman, there are pickups available in game to make your bombs better. Some of these pickups include being able to hold and deploy additional bombs, increasing the range of the bombs, giving you ammo to use a special and increasing your health.
Additionally, players can detonate bombs whenever they please. I'm not sure exactly how the bomb detonation system works as sometimes when I press "detonate", they do not detonate instantly (I'm guessing maybe I simply chose the right player). They have also included the option to take away the blood and gore. I'm sure most gamers will play with it on but it's extremely appreciated to have such an option available. Single player is interesting as it follows each character and their diverse story/history. The narrator can be a bit annoying but does his best to immerse the character (especially when you die over and over). He's sort of corny but the twisted storyline makes up for it all. It is true that this game is sort of hard and some parts are extremely difficult to get through. On easy, some of the levels are possible! Seriously, this game has a steep difficulty to it at times. Opponents come in all shapes and sizes. Some have shields while some are able to eat your bombs! Single player missions will try to diversify by having you protect something or play through levels that are not of equal dimensions.
The
are exceptional. They tried to visualize everything for the player so identifying which bombs will blow up next is perceivable. I definitely like the diversity within the characters. The mood and tone
they chose to introduce this game is appealing even though I'm not a big fan of dark or scary themes (unless it's the Darkness)! The interface is quite friendly and is easy to use. They seemed to really try and nail the details with the music and the quick button switch from keyboard to gamepad.
There are different game modes available in local. Although the classic version is usually the best, players will also like to try sumo. It's isn't actual sumo where you run into one another.
