I wish I could give this a mixed review. I like the game, but it has issues that prevent it from being easily recommendable. The biggest issue is the A.I pathfinding is horrible at times, and you kind of need to micromanage  a bit too much with tanks. I mean that when you command a single soldier or tank it doesn't seem like there is any way to make it rotate at a move point, however when commanding groups you can for some reason. When commanding individual units you need to use the "Defend" command AFTER it gets to it's destination to get it to face the right direction. And the games tutorials are practically pointless, they don't explain really anything. I was getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off for the first half hour because I kept losing my tank in the tutorial mission because the game didn't tell me how to make them go in reverse. They also don't tell you how to make soldiers pick up weapons, change ammo types, or even how to manually use a grenade. You use the "retreat" command to make them go backwards (i assumed it made them flee). If you do get the game be sure to play around with the U.I a bit. If you can deal with the at times abysmal pathfinding (Hold shift and use waypoints) then the game is amazing if you want a realistic RTS game, although I probably would still prefer Combat Mission. And it's worth mentioning I did have a random crash, so I would save often. But if you can put up with it's annoying playability issues, you will get a lot of value out of it.
But if you don't know what kind of game it is, it isnt a RTS like C&C or Starcraft. There isn't any of the rock-paper-scissors countering ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t. One of the reasons I gravitated towards these kinds of games is because I was tired of games where a sniper can take 100 bullets because the attacking unit didn't say "good against snipers" in it's description.  I would still say that Men of War is realistic enough for most people, but if want something that's more realistic than even those, this would be a good starting point, mostly because of it's low price tag.

Dungeon Defenders II is a team building game and it requires teamwork and communication building between team plays while offering three different levels of difficulty. Since I played in a team of two and a team of four, I would prefer a duo team play becuase it's more challenging. But, in a group of four, it offers a more relaxing gaming environment, which is perfect for casual gamers. Moreover, it can be played in the single player mode which I'd assume it's more challenging than a duo play.
In the game, the different levels of difficulty and types of maps allows gradual improvement from easy mode to normal mode, and to hard mode. Personally, I find this really helpful. Also, the graphics, missions, quests, and features of the game are okay.
However, the game gets glitched easily and there's a lot of server problems, connnectivity errors to the taverns, and adding and joining a friend's private taverns. Also, the limit on the amount of players per party is only 4 four people, so those that wants to play in a team on 5 is impossible.
Overall, I would recommend this game based on the development of this game. However, I would not recommend this game if you seek to play in a group of 5.

Real puzzle games, and I don't mean cheap match-3-tiles or the weird dream logic of point-and-click-adventure-games, are rare. Zachtronics continues to be the leading, if not only, producer of fantastic, fun, and brain warping puzzle games.
Sadly I must admit that I delayed buying this because I was scared off by the reviews calling it too difficult. Spacechem broke me and the thought that Infinifactory was harder put me right off. After getting this game from a bundle recently I was pleasantly surprised to find it completely accessible. People call it hard but it's not at all, every puzzle in the game can be easily brute forced to solve. If the abstraction of Spacechem scared you away I would definitely recommend this.
The real challenge, and fun, comes from trying to be as efficient as possible. Build a factory that works then go over it cutting out the fat and speeding it up. Or maybe try building a vertical compact factory, it might be slower but you'll have a much smaller footprint. Each level conviently gives you a chart that compares your results to the global stats. Banished is a sandbox, open-objective, strategy game with the aim of maintaining a thriving community in an isolated geographic location.  The game includes no violence, other than natural disasters and accidents, and is based entirely around wise resource management to ensure a healthy, happy, and productive population.  The technology level within the game can be described as medieval, although no specific time period or location are given.
This may sound like a simple and boring game, but it is far from it. It is both relaxing and highly addictive at the same time. The developer (One impressive note to make here is that this game was made by a single person.) did an excellent job at balancing the types of resources that the player needs to manage.  At no time does the game feel overburdening or too complicated.  Conversely, neither does it at any time feel simplistic, or boring.
Staving off starvation, population decline, cold winters, and natural disasters poses unique problems often overlooked in today's flashy, ultra-violent games. Banished is an excellent addition to any strategy-fan's library.  Its focus on problem solving, its addictive nature, and its non-violent atmosphere make it especially recommendable for pre-teens and teens, although they may need some adult assistance to start them off.
The full price of this game is $20, and to be honest, it is probably worth twice as much. However, if you are on a budget, you can find it on the steam sales for considerably less.  I highly recommend it.

As I'm only 30 minutes in, this review will be a basic impression of the port itself.
Overall, it's relatively solid for a Japanese dev. It's got a good range of resolution options, even going up to 1440p for my monitor. Preset graphics selections, FXAA support, draw distance, and a few other things to modify for graphics on top of that. It runs smoothly without any signs of stutters or crashing.
The biggest caveat for some would be the ugly textures in places and 30 FPS lock. However, I'm able to forgive them as it's a port of a PS3 game.  Allowing higher than 30 FPS would have broken the combat system, according to the developers.
Still, hopefully with this game successful, they'll see PC as not a place to port, but as a primary release for future Tales games. And maybe those games will be designed around 60 FPS from the get go.
For the game itself, I can't judge. Only 30 minutes in. But so far, it seems to bring the standard Tales flavour, with its own unique charm.  If you love Tales games, you'll love this game.
EDIT: After 3 hours of playing today, I've experienced a few graphical issues. Screen tearing and flickering happens extremely rarely, but it's noticeable when it does. However, this happaned maybe once an hour.
The battle camera can also be an issue: But only in the specific instance of battle starting while you're in a cramped area (like a doorway).
Still, these two problems are not nearly enough for me to not recommend it. In those 3 hours, most of my experience was good. The battle system is deep, and a good flow of tutorials and new mechanics means that it won't get stale for awhile - even once they stop I'll still have a lot to learn.

Okay everyone, I'm just doing a quick review of Banished to give you a general idea of whether or not you might like this game. I'm not going into deep strategies here, but I'll try to give some pro tips. Thanks for reading.
Banished is about a group of people who have been banished from their homeland and must re-establish themselves in their new land while trying to survive exposure and deprivation. It's essentially a city-builder where your enemies are time, weather, starvation, sickness, and poor planning. You start the game by setting a few basic conditions that will determine much of your fate before you even begin. In my experience, even on the easiest settings, I rarely have a group last more than 20 years. I haven't studied any strategy guides or gone into the forums much, so I'm sharing just what I've learned through the school of hard knocks.
Banished can be an unforgiving game. If you frustrate easily, you may want to give it a pass. Let me add, however, that when your strategy works, there is a sense of an actual accomplishment that many far less challenging games fail to deliver.  And you're going to need some type of strategy and some luck to survive more than 7 years in many instances.
After you've made your starting choices, you hit the ground running. You can let the clock tick along fairly slowly, but where's the fun in that? Pause the game, have a quick look around, open your most critical reports and let them hang on the edge of your vision, assign initial tasks to villagers, and pump the clock up to 10x speed (if you get bored easily like me--otherwise, just let it go). You may feel an inclination to go big, but I judge that would be a mistake. Don't clear huge areas of land or build the largest farms you can in the hopes that you will survive the first winter--you probably will regardless of what you do.. but that second winter might be your end-game even so. There will be time for going big later after you've learned the basics.
Go moderate, but go quickly. Consider these as your first tasks (not necessarily in this order, but order can matter a great deal while you're learning... and even after that). Assign a few builders from among the general laborers. Clear some land. Plant some modest farms and an orchard or two. Build a place for the firewood provider to do his job.  Bump up your resource limits for food and fuel. Keep the list of future tasks assigned fairly short so you can change strategies easily when you're first starting out. You'll need more storage space. You'll need more tools. You'll need more iron, stone, wood. You'll need more fuel and food. You'll need medicines, too. The list of tasks keeps rapidly expanding, but choose wisely and try for some moderation. Don't be afraid to switch people around to whatever job is most needed at the moment. Keep in mind, too, that if things get moving along in a good way, you may be faced with a population explosion that might rapidly deplete one or more essentials. If you run out of fuel or food and someone dies of old age or starvation, you may have consigned your settlement to a slow withering death, or a quick one depending upon your skill and luck.
Never give up. You may find yourself down to three people, but if they are hunting, fishing, or engaged in some other food production activity, and if they have enough fuel and other necessary items, you can bring them back from the brink. Just be careful. An abundance of good things combined with a population explosion may leave you without the resources to keep from going over the other direction--then you run out of food, your older workers die from some cause and your children are left to starve or freeze to death. Did I mention the game can be unforgiving? Or perhaps the younger ones already died, and there's nobody but the old and infirm to keep things going just a little longer. Okay, this is getting a little repetitive, but the game can be just that at times.
Banished currently has an active modding community, though the mods seem pretty much limited to tweaks: a new type of building, an improved harvest rate, better schools. Consider adding some. Using the right mods, you can change some important aspects of the game that can give you enough of an advantage that you find yourself lasting longer. However, in my experience, having a few mods does not necessarily guarantee a stroll through the park on Sunday afternoon. A few dumb mistakes could leave you without the things or people you will have to have to survive your first 5 years. Who knows? You may even decide to mod it yourself and make it just the way you'd like to play it. Or not. The choice is yours.
If you need a big pay-off, I don't think there is one. Nothing in the game gives me any sense that there is anything more to hope for than to survive and grow as a community for one more year. Also, watch out for the time dilation effects. hahaha... No, but you must seriously pay attention to the passage of time in the game because it looks like the seasons pass and only a year has gone by, but your people seem to age far more rapidly than they should. And death is always waiting for your people. Watching and waiting. It's all a delicate balance that you must maintain. Fortunately, there are tweaks for these things as well if you desire to change them.
I think that's enough to give you the general sense of how it plays and what it is. I hope that helps. Thanks again for reading. The game isn't for everyone, but it is worth playing. If you played it before, consider trying it again because, even without mods, it seems a bit easier than it did when I first purchased it--I think the developer may have taken some of the community feedback to heart, in other words.
Peace.

Absolutly the best Total War. Here's why:
- I have over 400 hours in this offline and 260 online, so I've played it long enough to know it's solid.
- Improved from the ground up: Empire's engine is used to great effect here. The map is larger, but the campaign as a whole is smaller. Not a problem though; you'll be too distracted by the enhanced strategy of it to notice this.
- Story Mode; Story mode is great for those who are after a more story driven experience. Imagine the Rome 2 Caesar in Gaul expansion, but in the 18th Century and with more scope.
- Darthmod Napoleon. There is no better TW mod. You'll hear fanboys saying this, but it really is true; try it for yourself. The ai will stun you. The stability will awe you. DM Multiplayer is also still very much alive, though you do always have the option of switching to Vanilla on startup.
- Polished; it is second to only Shogun 2 in terms of polish; graphics, gameplay; it just works. I also have yet to have a single crash in this game.
- Naval combat; pretty much the apex of Naval in the series imo. Great selection of ships, tactics and variety of battle possibilities. Quite simply superb.
- Versatility; runs on any system; OSX, PC, Old, New.
- Re-Playability; I find myself keep returning to NTW. Sure, new ones come out and i'm distracted. But I always find myself back with Musketeers and Jagers.

I give this game a 1000 out of 100. I'm not exagerating, I had a blast while playing it!
First of all: if you are looking for a good, ol' fashioned otome game... you won't find that here. This game is not to be taken seriously and you should not be angry or disappointed just because of it. In fact, I invite you to sit, read, laugh, and relax with it.
So... let me try to point out three good things - at least, because I think there are more - about this game:
No. 1: This game doesn't take itself seriously (I think it even breaks the 4th wall a tiny, itsi-bitsy bit if you pay attention to what the characters say). I said this at the begining, right? After playing otome games for a long time, you start to expect a pattern... you can even start guessing correctly which is the best answer to achieve the best ending without even paying attention to the story, just to the displayed answers in front of you when it's time to make a decision; and then "playing" just becomes automatic... which feels a bit dull. But this game, makes fun of itself... so much, that it gives you - and itself - the chance to "not take into consideration your choices" (I'll try to talk a bit more about this in the next point).
No. 2: This game is perfect for noobs and seasoned players alike. (You may probably think: what are you talking about? what kind of person cannot understand how to play an otome/dating game? Is not rocket science!) I know, I know... but still, this otome game gives you the "peace of mind" of being able to chose the worst possible answer and still not fail to reach the appropriate ending (please, those always reluctant to chose the worst answers in any other 'serious otome game' - despite of knowing it unlocks one of the endings for the collection - raise your hands... *rise hand*). See? That's what I'm talking about! Here you don't have to burden yourself with being right or screwing up... the game doesn't care - it even points it out in a very sassy and comical way -, (and you shouldn't either); and that makes it quite enjoyable.
No. 3: It is simple yet absorbing. Ok, the game doesn't care for your choices so you can really - for once - relax and play a game really paying attention to it's story instead on focusing on your best tactical way of approaching the best ending possible. And when you don't have 'the burden of choosing', and you enjoy this game for what it is - a beautifuly crafted and pieced together parody of what otome games are -, you realize that the story is catchy, the characters are well-defined (so well, that they even mock their 'place in the game'), the music is nice and suits the game. Also, the heroine is easy to approach (from a player's perspective... I have clashed so much with the usual otome game heroine that I usually use that as an indicator to know if I want - or can - play an otome game) and you can also see her as part of the story... not just the avatar that lets you interact with the possible suitors.
Well, I hope you give this free game a chance... you won't regret it. I sure didn't.

gonna review the game after i finish it but for now here are some troubleshooting for common problems (i didn't encounter any of them)
1. Screen tearing: Force v-sync through nvidia/amd control panel
2. Audio issue: Set audio frequency to 48khz or below, 98khz will give you the problem
3. AVG issue: AVG is detecting false positive for Zestiria files, put the game folder to whitelist
4. Crash issue: switch to Windows sound Config or take off your headphones
5. No voice when character speak: turn the audio to stereo not surround and it should work.
6. Rebinding keys doesn't work: try restarting the game after rebinding.
don't rush into refunding, try those fixes for now till the devs patch the game soon.

Starting out it's reminding me of a mix between Tales of Graces / Tales of Abyss nostalgia with the combat artes and titles.  If you're a fan of the tales series it seems to be more of the same.  I expect the same tropes and new twists on some things.
The skits are a return to Tales of Graces with full character models instead of the usual boxed heads.  The combat is focused more on the main protganist with the other characters able to enhance him better (without spoiling too much of the plot).  It is an interesting mechanic.  Xillia 2 locked Luger in place for the entire game (allowing you to play anyone but he had to stay in the party of four).  In Zestiria while you can control any character you choose (just like most other tales series) it's in your best interest to stick with the main protagnist as you add more members to your crew.  Additionally you have to have a human in control and there are other limiting factors to potential party make-up.  I'm taking a "wait-and-see" on how much this ends up bothering me.
I haven't had any issues with the PC port and have been using my PS3 controller with no issues.  I also switched to the keyboard/mouse controls for a little bit and those worked fine as well.  English voice acting is also well done.
The equipment/crafting portion of the game seems to be a bit more convoluted then it needs to be, but I think as time wanes on I'll figure out my way around it.  Also the addition of being able to slot things into the zone (eventually this happens to avoid spoilers) that level up the monsters might give the player control to keep any zone relevant to your level.
I will say that the motley crew didn't start to round out really well (even skit wise) until Edna came along for me.  So if you're finding the crew to be a bit dull or not your cup of tea... tough it out until her.
I look forward to losing more time to this game!

Preface - I pre-purchased the game and have completed it on normal difficulty. I played with a mouse and keyboard and had no issues with that.
All in all, the game is visually appealing, the story and gameplay are OK, but nothing surprising (except maybe the elemental resistance system - the game forces you to take a rest from cold around a fire, and so on), soundtrack is nice and matches the game well.
It had quite a few bugs starting off and still has a ton more, at least according to forums. The bugs that I came across and never saw fixed were not game-breaking to me (pretty much all of them were like 1 second "meh" type, and the few that were bigger could be fixed by reloading the last checkpoint), but there was one serious bug - if I had all parts of a legendary weapon (Thor's Hammer and the like, basically the best weapons in the game), when combining the parts, sometimes it took the parts but did not actually give me the weapon. Fortunately, there's a couple of workarounds for that (1 - exit to menu, reload, try again, 2 - combine a weapon you don't care about first, and if it bugs out, then combine your weapon, and it will be fine), but it's still a crap situation.
However, it is not worth anywhere near the full price of 45€. Not even if it had no bugs, which it has tons of. I'd say a fair price would be 20-25€, if they fix the most prominent bugs (like inability to sell runes, which you get quite a bit of during the playthrough). There's also a lot of minor inconveniences with the terrain - you get stuck on many invisible corners and things that other games would allow you to slide past. It feels like this game has not been playtested properly and just rushed out with all its bugs because someone in management just really needed the money.
Crafting was very boring and basically an rng-fest with mostly crap results, which resulted in a lot of wasted resources. Thankfully you get a lot of them during normal playthrough if you try to do the challenges in each map, so I never ran out of normal resources, only Jotunjarn.
TL;DR - do not recommend, unless on a 50%+ sale and you're fine with obvious, but mostly harmless bugs.

I'm rather tempted to throw a thumbs down here, which I probably should - and I won't.
The promise of the game to throw you into a rather grim scenario that adheres widely to Norse/Scandinavian folklore and culture has been fulfilled - mostly.
The idea of creating an ARPG in the lines of Diablo and whatever came after it has not.
Still, it sticks to lore, to rather historically accurate representations of gear (probably with the exception of 4-meter large hammers, but you'd just call your guy BONK and get on with it . .), you're offered decisions after "visiting the neighbours" where you can sack them one-off for big gains or keep them around so they can pay tribute, you level up your vendors as you level and overall it's a grand piece of troll and jotun whacking.
The part that bites are the diffficulty levels.
Other than that the guys in the toughest setting are harder to kill, there's no difference in rewards to the easiest difficulty, loot, X and progress are pretty much identical.
More effort = same reward.
Shoult I decide that Easy is too easy and I'd rather notch it up a bit for personal challenge without material rewards . .
I can't.
The character is permanently locked to her/his specific difficulty level selection when it is created.
Selecting "New Game" to change this will reset the character to zero, loses all items, X, progress. It creates a brand new character and you start over again.
I sincerely hope that this will be addressed because if that's not happening, I see the idea of re-play value severely clipped.
As Blizzard demonstrated with their Diablo titles, people DO play the same content again, five times over, when the rewards scale with the difficulty and it's a process of improvement and progress to do so.
As it stands with this title, I'm inclined to roll me a new toon, set it to the easiest difficulty, play through the story and then do something else because I'm finished with the game.

Doesn't have the quality and playability of something like Skyrim, Oblivion et al, but in it's own way it's addictive and fun. I was looking for more RPG games and this, although different to my favourites and feels a little old skool, is perfect.
There are monsters that will own you easily along the way, progressing through training and doing some quests gets you progression with the monsters. The key to combat seems to be avoiding taking on more than 1 enemy at once, or manoeuvring so that only 1 enemy can hit you at any one time and not trying to take down anything above your abilities at that point. If you do then there's a high chance of dying, but hey quicksave, quickload, not really a big issue.
Most of the quests can be solved in multiple ways - I even finished some and didn't even start them properly due to exploring randomly in an open world way.
The interface is fairly basic in terms of maps and such but it is usable. Exploration feels rewarding, as there are always herbs and treasures to be found which you can sell and then use to pay for training and items etc.
There is no inventory space or weight limit, you can collect everything to your heart's content. For lore lovers, it's a little lacking but there's enough to back the game up.
Well worth trying if you pick it up on sale.

Absolutly the best Total War. Here's why:
- I have over 400 hours in this offline and 260 online, so I've played it long enough to know it's solid.
- Improved from the ground up: Empire's engine is used to great effect here. The map is larger, but the campaign as a whole is smaller. Not a problem though; you'll be too distracted by the enhanced strategy of it to notice this.
- Story Mode; Story mode is great for those who are after a more story driven experience. Imagine the Rome 2 Caesar in Gaul expansion, but in the 18th Century and with more scope.
- Darthmod Napoleon. There is no better TW mod. You'll hear fanboys saying this, but it really is true; try it for yourself. The ai will stun you. The stability will awe you. DM Multiplayer is also still very much alive, though you do always have the option of switching to Vanilla on startup.
- Polished; it is second to only Shogun 2 in terms of polish; graphics, gameplay; it just works. I also have yet to have a single crash in this game.
- Naval combat; pretty much the apex of Naval in the series imo. Great selection of ships, tactics and variety of battle possibilities. Quite simply superb.
- Versatility; runs on any system; OSX, PC, Old, New.
- Re-Playability; I find myself keep returning to NTW. Sure, new ones come out and i'm distracted. But I always find myself back with Musketeers and Jagers.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

I'm having a pretty fun time with this game. However, after reading some other folks' reviews and giving it a bit more thought, I'm going to lay out a more critical review than initially planned. Needless to say, here are the pros and cons.
Pros:
-Combat is fast-paced and engaging; never feels like a chore or a "grind"
-Devs did a good job creating a game world out of Norse mythology
-Clan upgrade system is solid and rewarding
-Game is pretty nice visually
-Raid maps are pretty distinct from one another in terms of setting and enemies
Cons:
-Limited character creation (more hair colors + ability to choose head/face type would be nice)
-Clunky mouse+keyboard controls; I found myself having a lot more fun playing w/ a USB controller
-Not enough to do between campaign raids - besides the option to hunt creatures on previous maps for resources and XP, there are no side quests or other ways to interact with the world outside of your clan
-No way to really interact w/ your clanmates outside of the barter/crafting services they provide; might as well not have a "clan" at all considering that you do pretty much everything alone anyway
-We don't really get to know the player character at all; s/he mostly just delivers battlecries and snarky one-liners - makes you question why this game's even classified as an RPG
-Poor excuse for an endgame - no one wants to have all their best gear stripped away just so they can replay the same content all over again
Overall, I think this game would benefit most from greater customization all around, as well as a more rich and nuanced game world (including ENDgame world), and more interactive and developed characters. This game's plenty of fun if you're in it for the Old Norse goodness and the combat, but beyond that, it just doesn't have much to show for as an RPG.

Big edit: Originally I gave a "do not recommend" as there were some critical issues that were taking a while to get addressed. I am pleased to say that all the critical issues with the game (at least for the solo experience) have now been patched out.
This isn't D3 or Path of exile, do not expect a 1k+ hour experience with a big mapping system at the end of the campaign, the game features an NG+ system and 5 seperate wave based arena challenge maps but that's the extent of its post-campaign. If you want a fun ARPG to put somewhere between 10-100hrs this game will do nicely.
Pros:

- Fully voiced
- Easy to learn
- Visually pleasing
- UI is neat and uncluttered
- Very fun first playthrough ~8-20hrs depending on OCD level (if casual play easy or normal with dual wield swords, if hardcore gamer just start on highest difficulty and go sword+board, prioritise upgrading the shop to lv2 then buy a fox ring).
Cons:
- No respec system depite early encouragement to experiment with builds (can lead to bricking a character)
- The entire spec for bows is useless unless you intend to play the game on easy mode, the weapon only exists to be swapped to for destroying breakable environment objects and birds.
- Slow weapons don't work with the game's targetting system as the attacks are synced to a faster base speed, using hammers for example will result in missing about 50% of your attacks and getting hit by enemies while using skills that should kill them.
- Cannot repeat bosses.
- Enemies with the ability to block tend to break your combo meter and interfere with the game's pacing on higher difficulties.
- Artifacts (Mythic tier items) Roll random affixes and socket slots upon creation despite the effort that goes into finding all their pieces and the fact you can only make them once per NG.

I thought that this engine was so strict as people said before. But after I read the manual and found that this engine is expandable using Ruby, I think it's more than enough.
1. If you think this is expensive, the price is for the 'built up' system that included in this software and for the license that allow us to distributing the game that we created. For professional developer, this is very cheap. Comparing to the framework library that I used to make a professional software, that cost $999+ (it's just the library license, not the tools nor software). With just $70 you have all that you need to build RPG with all of that 'engine' already writen, want more? Use Ruby. It's more than enough.
2. Never compare it to other game engines like Unity, Construct, whatever. They all have pros and cons for themself, including this one. This one is built for 'RPG Maker' (especially JRPG). What engine that exist today that have all writen functionality like this for creating RPG? Yes, all of the engine can do that, but how much time will you consume just to write the basic RPG engine? Battle system, map generator, etc.
So I think, if we are early in game design, this tools is helping so much (for creating JRPG of course). For pros, the Ruby is more than enough for extending the functionallity. So I recommend this software for you, who want to creating RPG. That's why it's named RPG Maker :D

An outstanding puzzle game by Zachtronics which poses a great danger to your free time.
Your objective is to build assembly lines to build specific products for alien overlords. This gets increasingly harder as you progress through the levels, as you have to choose the right tools in the right order and with the right timing.
There are many ways to solve a level, so you can build your contraptions to your liking. This gives the game a lot of replayability, because you can always optimize your solutions to be just a few cycles faster, or to be a little cheaper, or to use up less space.
While later levels can get really hard, this is still a very accessible game, especially when compared to other titles by Zachtronics. If nothing else works, look up a guide. This won't spoil the fun too much, because you might learn some methods for future levels, or you could try to improve on the design.
Summary:
If you like puzzle games and / or building contraptions, then do yourself a favor and get this gem.

It's hard to find something to say about Five Nights at Freddy's that hasn't already been said. I'm a huge fan of horror and have played just about every horror game, watched every horror movie (even the cheesy ones) and read every online ghost story and creepypasta there is so obviously, I'm a bit more harsh when judging a piece of horror. I can't necessarily say Five Nights at Freddy's is "scary" as much as it is tense. VERY similar to Slender in that the game relies on the tension caused by the feeling of paranoia and the feeling of being hunted to get into the player's mind. The problem though is that this game's tension is built more so out of the fact that you don't want one of the animals jumping up and screaming at you loudly, not so much that you actually feel in danger like you would in Slender or games similar. Because of that and the fact that while you don't know EXACTLY when the jump scare will occur but get a good idea of when it's coming (animal is close to your room in the camera feed, clicking sound when trying to turn on light, etc.) leaves this game feeling more like a digital version of a jack in the box rather than a real, horror experience. All that being said, I still very much enjoy this game and (especially considering the price) would definitely recommend it to anyone interested in it. A good piece of horror? No. A good experience? Yes.

Searching a cabin I found a can of dog food. I was hungry. I smashed it open and ate it with my hands. I lost some of it when I smashed it, but it did the trick.
Later I found the Camp Office. The dead man had nothing on him. I put on a heavy wool sweater I found in a drawer and tried to build a fire. I failed twice and ran out of tinder. There was some newspaper on the ground on the first floor so I took it and shoved it into the stove and tried again. Finally, a success. After getting warm I foraged for supplies like wood and tinder. Ate and drank some food. Then slept for a good 12 hours. When I awoke I felt dehydrated and a drank some water. Very good, despite some profound flaws.
GoNNER is an arcade game with a very original graphics and some nice twists in the gameplay: describing it would be pointless, the best thing you can do is watch one of the promotional videos. Yes. No misleading advertising there: the game is really like that…
It's the kind of game you would expect (and hope) to play for the rest of your life, to come back and plain again in 5 years, and yet after a couple of hours, the fun is gone.
Why? Well, because GoNNER IS NOT REALLY A ROGUELIKE GAME, whatever the authors, the store page or other reviewers might say.
The reason? While the layout of the levels is slightly different in each run, there is no other random factor.
In the proper rogue-like games, like Nethack, Angband, but also Diablo and Binding of Isaac - to cite more recent champions of the genre - you start with a barebone character, and it evolves out of chance and your own choices during the course of the single game, which leads to each playthrough is a unique experience.
GoNNER throws away all that: the loadout can be decided at the start of each game, and the roaster of available weapons and perks contains all the items already discovered. Sure, there are shops where you can change the equipment (but mind you: it's always the same inventory), but what's the point of that, when you can have the best possible equipment from the start?
To make things worse, bugs in the game logic spoil the experience: you are supposed to earn the equipment through minor hidden achievements, or by finding it in secret levels - a nice touch that would have given the game stamina - but a problem in the code allows you to "discover" them for free by re-rolling the store content.
Balance is also a serious problem: what IMO is the best weapon of the game hands down, can be obtained early on in the game.
One minute I was having fun trying to get better at the game and passing level 2, using the shotgun and combining heads and perks in an uphill battle, the one after getting the final weapon, I blasted through
the levels effortlessly and finished GoNNER in a matter of minutes. It took an extra half an hour of play to get 100% competition, with all the achievements.
What a bitter victory.
I think that a review should reflect the merits or faults of a game for what it is, and in this regard, GoNNER deserves a solid thumb: it's a small gem, and you will enjoy it, but I can't hide the
disappointment.    It could have been so better.

Parts I did not like:
-The little cutscene for every single action
-Useless actions (sitting on a bench, smoking a hookah, etc.)
-The last boss fight was pretty unfulfilling
-The lack of armor availability (there are armor upgrades but you only get it per chapter, you don't for example find an iron chestplate, or some variation)

Ambience and atmosphere is the first thing I look for into a game. You can't go wrong.
Never in my life have I seen such an immersive WW2 game. The gameplay is wonderful, The cover system is well designed with blind-fire options as well as a very smart engine with realistic weapon placement, recoil and mechanics. The music is simply amazing and perfectly fits the game, the mood of the music changes whether your team is having a beating or is advancing quickly through the enemy lines. The sound effects blends really well with the battlefield, bonus points if you own a quality headset or a wicked sound system. Be sure to activate "Native voices" in the options to hear soldiers speak their native language, which adds up even more for the atmosphere of the game.
Russians crying to go back to their motherland whilst bleeding to death, And Nazis screaming "MEIN FUHRER" just a second before their last breath... You feel like you are INSIDE the game, You are the soldier. Deaths are painful, weeps are intense and you can clearly hear the suffering of the soldiers right before they pass away. If your leg gets gibbed, don't expect a light response from your soldier. This game is so traumatizing and representative of an actual WWII battle that many people have reported suffering post-traumatic stress disorder from it. You have been warned.
The developers of Tripwire has not failed to their duty. They have delivered a realistic, dynamic and truly immersive WWII first-person shooter in all it's glory. The game is not designed for an average player and it is unforgiving. You will get mercilessly massacred if you're a casual. This is, without a doubt, Multiplayer Game Of The Year 2011. You'd be a fool not to buy it if you are an adept of World War II.

What's with these glyphs? Whose skull is that? Why is there a hovering whale? GoNNER offers these and other questions, but explains almost nothing. It's up to you to figure out the world and its rules. As a procedurally generated side-scrolling shooter, all you ever need to do is move, jump, shoot and—hardest of all—not die.
GoNNER is best played with a controller, although the keyboard controls are workable – and you'll grow arms and legs. Collect a head, a gun and a backpack, and you're able journey through the surreal corridors, chaining kills to earn glyphs and increase your score multiplier. GoNNER quickly transitions from eerie mystery to quirky action platformer.
The art style oozes personality, despite its crude look. The variety of enemy designs ensure that each monster type is immediately identifiable—handy as each behaves in a specific way. Bats will chase you down, slugs move languidly across walls, and porcupines can roll up into a invulnerable state. Later, robots explode when damaged but not killed—often leading to a deadly lesson in being aware of your surroundings.
Despite GoNNER's difficulty, aesthetic and mystery, there isn't a whole lot to it. It doesn't take long to work out an enemy's patterns, and there's isn't much variety within the level generation. While loadouts offer some tactical planning, the range of equipment isn't diverse. GoNNER doesn't offer the longevity of the best roguelike shooters, but it's nonetheless a stylish, weird and just shy of being a genius entertaining action platformer.

I just finished my first playthrough and given the remarks on the experience of NewGame+, I think I will leave the game at that. I had a rather good time with the game because I loved the theme, music and the unique aspect of environmental hazards drawn into an RPG.
Lets do this the ol' pro con fashion:
Pros:
- Vikings! (who don't like them some vikings?)
- Almost omnipresent environmental hazards explores new design space for an RPG (although...)
- Music
- Basic charge-attack
- Shop-items matter!
- Town expanding
Cons:
- Almost omnipresent environmental hazards (because it's done so trivial and generic that it feels more like a chore)
- Poor linear storyline that lacks actual character motivation (most boils down to; some lass tells you you need to beat someone up and being a Viking, that's what you want to do... ain't it?)
- No actual meaningful choices on story or character progression (I'll elaborate below)
- Scripted loot
- Clunky controls
- Bugs that severely limits an already quite linear game
And lets follow that up with some explainations.
Environmental hazards/exposure: The idea is refreshing and to some people (me) "new" to play around in an RPG. The fact that it boils down to: some missions have hazard areas and some generic safe zones that rapidly decrease your exposure to the elements. At this point it basically becomes a chore. There are different kinds of exposures but in general they all could have been the exact same, with little to no difference besides visual/flavor. I lack a sense of better dynamic use, where you actively have to walk close to the cliff side to gain some kind of cover. They have zones that increases your exposure more than others and those were good implementations, but I lack a more thoroughly used exposure mechanic for it to be something truly unique that you had to take account of.
If you had to buy some sort of fire potion to heat you up through a blizzard rather than just waltzing from safe zone to safe zone, it would help make it a part of the gameplay and not a trivial side-worry.
Music: The music is not grand and epic as in bombastic but it suits the theme and fits quite well with the overall gameplay.
Storyline: The storyline is basically; start a mission, get from point A to B, if you want ressources and better loot do some exploration and complete challenges. Fight boss, win, get loot. Get introduced to a new segment of the story that "unlocks" the next mission. Many of these briefings on your next mission segment feels forced and the main character often makes comments on the ridiculousness of the task and it all just seems like a poor way to use sarcasm to cover the linear and often uninteresting plotline.
It doesn't help that the final boss fight is anticlimatic as all hell. It feels in no way epic or meaningful and the game ends without a choice. This leads on to the next weak point...
Character progression
You can choose between a few fighting styles; one-handed and shield, dual-wielding, 2-handed (staff or weapon) or a bow. Each fighting style has a skill tree of its own. However the skill trees are linear in progression and are limited to 5 active skills, which all can be equipped at the same time which means you have no real choice in how you build your character. If you pick one class (which I strongly recommend) you need only get a few bonus skill points and you can get every skill-upgrade on curve.
This is not befitting a fleshed out RPG. The only other choice you have in this game is; character gender and minimal customization and your decision to either sack other viking villages during the story line for a load of ressources or to have them grant you tribute over coming missions.
That being said the skilltree does have a rather smooth curve (at least for followers of Tyr - one-handed with shield) that grants you some useful skills that helps make combat a bit more fluent.
Combat charge: The inclusion of a standard combat charge that basically makes you dash towards enemies a slight distance away makes the combat a lot more fluent, especially with the roll/dodge-mechanic. The dodge-mechanic takes some getting used to (mostly only works against heavy-hitters) and at times feels clunky and not very skillful. The dodge-mechanic could have been better but is neither something I consider a foul.
Shop items matter: Most of the time when playing RPGs you can only get worthy gear from random drops - because it promotes the exploration and grinding for loot that most RPGs are known for. Shops in those games are used almost exclusively for selling ♥♥♥♥♥on of crap and then repairing gear or getting potions or something alike. In Wolves of Midgard after you get a blacksmith upgrade you can actually often craft yourself a better weapon than the legendary gear you found 4 missions ago. I find this positive as it makes shops feel useful other than a gold refinery. Which leads me on to my next point;
Town expansion: That you can upgrade and "expand" your village's shops is a neat way to make you invested to find ressources and it provides some natural power spikes throughout the missions (for better or worse). However the end game makes it all feel kinda♥♥♥♥♥♥
Scripted loot: Throughout the missions you can complete some side-missions or puzzles and unlock Artifact-weapons of the gods, which first happens around the remaining hour of the game which could be completed in 10-12 hours. I went mostly completionist on the map exploration and have a few hours of AFK in menus, which results in my 25 hours record.
Clunky controls: I touched this subject with the roll-mechanic but it also extends to targeting sometimes being sluggish to understand that you have switched targets. Hitbox or selection-box was sometimes a pain between larger enemies and smaller ones running around at its feet and occassionally blocking you. The skill aim tracking was sometimes way of so I could roll away from combat and aim back at the center of the enemies to fire up my ranged AoE, only to have it fire in the direction I was facing (away from them as I rolled) instead of the direction of my cursor. Targeting environmental ressources like dead trees was not always particularly good, at which point I simply pressed Shift to attack in my cursors direction. Some destructibles I could not even hit without the use of an AoE skill.
The UI for shops is also kinda messy with a rather heavy use of point'n'click which gets to be a nuisance when you have to sell 20+ items after a mission. This kinda brings me to my final point...
Bugs: New games tend to have some bugs here and there but some of these I cannot fathom haven't been tested and fixed by released. My most pressing being the inability to BUY or sell runes. You find runes on raids at random or through the trials - time consuming and mostly unrewarding. By the time I completed the game, I had 4 top tier runes in 2/5 groups. Other bugs include impassible terrain on grinding raids - blocking completion.
Cutting it short, in summary: If you like Vikings, low choice RPGs and can get it at a discount, try it out. Otherwise I cannot recommend it as it is. 45€ for what feels like a shallow spin-off of the RPG-genre seems lazy and unworthy.

This is the game to buy if you are a WW2 maniac like me. Though there isn't that much hardware that you can get your hands on the stuff that you do get is very well modelled. M3 medium tanks are my favorite because it's so fun to see them roll down a hill mowing down infantry with their MG turret, shooting an armored car with their 37mm, and shooting a pzIII with their 75mm. It is a shame that there aren't more vehicles. The only British vehicle that appears is the valentine (Only one that appears in campaign idk if more) but if you are expected to see the iconic british vehicles that ruled the desert like the churchhill, matilda, or the crusader, you will be kept waiting. Most American vehicles make an appearance including two variants of the M4. The only iconic vehicle missing from the germans garage are the spgs based off of the pzIII chasis like the stug. The Germans have by far the most complete arsenal as they have multiple variants of the pzIII&IV, multiple armored cars and apcs, and the famous Tiger.
GAMEPLAY
All combat is fully modelled. This is not COH where the max range of a tank gun is a 50 meters. In fact, most cannons can shoot across the entire map (though they won't penetrate armor very good that way). Any thing your units can see they can shoot assuming that their target is not outside their maximum range which will be a problem with smgs but will rarely happen with anything else. A tricky part of commanding is putting your assets in places where they have fields of fire. In most rts if a bump in the terrain or part of the crest a hill is blocking the fire the game will let the bullet travel though the obstruction. This is not a game where you can micro manage things other than the major assets. The major flaw in this game is control. It is how you say, not very good. For starters the default move order is a fire and move drill which is useful for tanks which don't have to stop to fire but will get your infantry killed all the time as they stop to fire for a few seconds, move a couple of meters, then repeat instead of just running into their trench. There is also an incredibly irritating latency to orders given to infantry and sometimes they simply ignore what you are telling them to do. Try to tell them to get in cover while they are in a fire animation? They will spend 3 seconds getting fired at before listening. The controls of the vehicles are passable at best. There is not way to tell vehicles to orient their armor without telling them to advance and sometimes they will stop firing for no reason or repeatedly fire at a target they have no hope of penetrating meanwhile infantry are right next to them lobbing AT grenades. The biggest negative is that there were FAAAR too many defense missions. More than 75% of the were defensive missions and half of those were pure defensive which means that you don't need to move your troops around at all. Some of them however required skillful use of vehicles to reinforce sectors and skillful placement of AT guns to maximize their effectiveness.

This game is bad, really really bad one of the worst strategy games I have every played. Let us talk about the selling points of the product
1. The AI
The ghost in Pac man probably are more complex than the AI in this game.
a. There is no path finding. For example units will not follow roads, even in cases where you start them on roads, but will head in a straight line to their destination unit they hit something and must turn.   There is a stage where you fight on the road between high cliffs. When the AI travels it does not follow the road but hits a straight line until it gets stuck on a hill side that is to steep so it turns a bit and repeats the procedure. So if the road has a curve to it the unit does not follow the curve but makes a zig zag motion til it reaches its destination
b. AI allies are about worthless. There are stages where you fight and your re-enforcements are AI allies. Problem is the AI allies do not want to fight. Now most of the time they will fire on an enemy if they see him, but do nto expect them to go looking.
This really gets to be a a pain in missions where the ally AI is needed to win, in such cases its a 60/40 chance you are losing the mission
c. units disappear. You will have a unit walking then all of a sudden its gone. Not shot at or in combat just gone, it's like the rapture
d. Units movement. You spend a lot of your time trying to get units to move. Now most of the time they will move when ordered, but there are many times they act liek your not even around. I am not talking a unit that is scared or injured but just under normal cases they simply do not want to move.
2. Line of Sight
I would love to meet the person who designed this system. It appears combat in WW2 involved both sides playing pick a boo. You will have two units within 10 feet of stopped looking at each other, only to have the enemy disappear, then reappear in the same spot.  I have seen whole tanks be surrounded by enemy units (infantry and tanks) disappear then re appear. This gets to be a pain in missions where you need to prevent the enemy from breaking through. it sucks to be firing at that last tank only to have it engage its cloaking device
Stage design
For some reason the developers decided not make the player guess on how to complete missions. Sure you are giving an overview on what you need to do but never told how to do it. I know you are thinking, why do you want the game to walk you through it? That's not what I mean, what I mean is the developers put hidden triggers that only they know in order to complete a mission. For example
You are to hold the line and defeat the enemy attack. Ok so you fight for a few minute and even get a "Mission accomplished" alert. Ok good, so some time goes by and your are still playing. Well this is where the fun begins, see the game said you had to defeat teh attack, what it didn't say is that in order to complete the mission you need to have an infantry unit in some random building.
Now if you are lucky it is just simple case of moving stuff around till you activate the trigger. If you are not so lucky the enemy keeps rescanning until you run out of men.
Final thought
No doubt someone will come on here and claim I am not telling the truth. Well to them I say go look at the official reviews, most complain about the same issues. It is sad this is a great game when it works and could have been something if only the developers had the skills to deliver

Currently it's one of my favourite virtual TCGs, if not my personal favourite!
It provides the player with quite simplistic mechanics so it's easy to pick up from the get go but offers enough strategic depth for interesting card combos! I adore the art style of the different cards alot! Some of my favourite illustrators in the korean gaming industry are working on this game. The overall design of the UI is very polished and certain elements have a highly nostalgic touch to it, like opening booster packs, sending you straight back to your childhood when opening physical booster packs. The strongest aspect of the game is easily the discard of fundamental TCG elements such as a draw mechanic. You might ask yourself how is a TCG going to work out without such an essencial feature? Let me tell you, it works perfectly fine and I would even go so far the system is brilliant, but try it out for yourself! Due to the deck structure only consisting of 12 cards it's very comfortable to create your own deck pretty quick and making adjustments or changes later on. The game definitely feels fresh and is entirely different from current TCGs which are mostly just "hearth stone clones". Duel of Summoners wants to be more individual in that regard and it totally manages to do that, offering fun gameplay and being a true TRADING card game. Yes trading is actually a thing in this game which ironically most TCGs don't provide.
Even if you are not a long term fan of the mabinogi universe you should still give this game a shot if you are a big fan of TCGs in general!

When I purchased this game I didn't know anything about the Fallout games other than it's a post-apocalypse after a nuclear war.  That was it.
Enemies in this game range from annoying (dogs and boatflies) to creepy (feral ghouls) to monstrous (super mutant brutes...). I find that I take a lot of sadistic pleasure in wiping out entire clans of raiders, especially once they start calling me names ("only a coward hides!" yeah? eat my bullets!).  The best part about the game, however, is the level design.  The detail in Washington, DC is really impressive to me.  I've been to DC more times than I can count on both hands and I found myself recognizing places and admiring the attention to detail.  Having been in the metro hundreds of times, I also appreciated the detail in the metro stations, which was also pretty spot on.  Heck, even the sidewalks are pretty accurate.  I really appreciate the graphics.
The story is intriguing and the world itself is so deep that I feel I won't be able to complete this game very quickly.  The last game that really grabbed my interest in this way was Half Life 2, which was a purchase well worth my money as well.  I definitely recommend this game to anyone regardless of your tastes in video games.  This one will change you!

Banished is a distillation of what a lot of city-building fans missed from newer SimCity games.  It’s a smart, fun twist on the concept -- instead of ruling over a metropolis through a mayor’s lens, you play a more intricate role in the development of a small colony.  Every citizen is somebody you can see and control (though not directly), and your role is to see that your citizens are well-fed, happy, and warm through the long winters.  The result is a more nuanced and satisfying game than the EA flagship franchise which inspired it.
Every Banished game starts on a randomly generated map, where you control a small band of settlers (about 10 adults and 10 children) who have ostensibly been banished from wherever they came from.  You have nothing but the minimal supplies they carried with them, and the resources of the land around you.  Your first objective is to survive the coming winter, which you can do by building houses, creating a source of food (a fishing dock or gatherer’s hut would do), and a source of heat for winter (firewood).  All of these things require resources such as lumber, stone, and iron, which your citizens can scrounge from the land around them.
After the first winter, your options explode.  The basic idea is to increase the population of your town by building homes, while balancing the basic needs of the citizens with the resources required for those needs.  Every citizen in your town is a resource as well; the player personally assigns jobs to accomplish every task, and must make sure their labor force is well balanced and not spread too thin.  Should the population dip and you no longer have enough farmers, for instance, the consequences can be dire.
All of this may sound a little daunting, and it can be, but Banished provides a helpful tutorial at the outset to ease the difficulty curve a bit.  I was able to get rolling with my city and survive my first winter with its help.  The mechanics are satisfying and relatively deep, although after 20 hours or so I found myself finding a groove and more or less following a formula for increasing the population of my town.  It was still fun to see my town sprawl across the map (which can be sizeable), but the gameplay got a bit tired.
Banished does come with robust mod support and for those who find themselves growing tired of the gameplay, there is an extensive library of mods which breathe new life into the game.  Colonial Charter is a large mod which adds an incredible amount of new content and greatly extends the life of Banished.  It’s great to see mod support for a game like this, and it’s a shining example of why we should see more mod support for games going forward.
Overall, I’d recommend Banished to anyone pursuing that city simulation itch, but finding themselves disappointed with recent EA offerings.  Populations of your city won’t rocket into the millions, but the level of control and visibility into the workings of the simulation is very satisfying.  It’s a game which, while probably inspired by games like SimCity, does plenty to establish itself in this genre with new ideas.

Ambience and atmosphere is the first thing I look for into a game. You can't go wrong.
Never in my life have I seen such an immersive WW2 game. The gameplay is wonderful, The cover system is well designed with blind-fire options as well as a very smart engine with realistic weapon placement, recoil and mechanics. The music is simply amazing and perfectly fits the game, the mood of the music changes whether your team is having a beating or is advancing quickly through the enemy lines. The sound effects blends really well with the battlefield, bonus points if you own a quality headset or a wicked sound system. Be sure to activate "Native voices" in the options to hear soldiers speak their native language, which adds up even more for the atmosphere of the game.
Russians crying to go back to their motherland whilst bleeding to death, And Nazis screaming "MEIN FUHRER" just a second before their last breath... You feel like you are INSIDE the game, You are the soldier. Deaths are painful, weeps are intense and you can clearly hear the suffering of the soldiers right before they pass away. If your leg gets gibbed, don't expect a light response from your soldier. This game is so traumatizing and representative of an actual WWII battle that many people have reported suffering post-traumatic stress disorder from it. You have been warned.
The developers of Tripwire has not failed to their duty. They have delivered a realistic, dynamic and truly immersive WWII first-person shooter in all it's glory. The game is not designed for an average player and it is unforgiving. You will get mercilessly massacred if you're a casual. This is, without a doubt, Multiplayer Game Of The Year 2011. You'd be a fool not to buy it if you are an adept of World War II.

Now that I've played a short while (60hrs as of this writing), I feel I can give an honest and somewhat informed opinion of the game.
This is somewhat of an updated version of the classic city/empire building sim... minus any combat. You start with a small group of settlers, and a little bit of resources. After that, it's up to you to build it up however you wish. Meet the needs of the settlers (housing, food, tools, clothing, etc..) and the new settlement will thrive and grow. Don't, and you'll quickly find yourself in a crisis of starvation, or plain old freezing to death. It can be a challenge to find a balance between having the population to man the various production facilities, and being able to feed said population. This is mainly because you need  them to not only work in food related jobs, but also work in all the other supporting tasks as well. You can't just build a bunch of fishing docks and farms... you must also have a blacksmith to make tools, a woodcutter to supply firewood for warmth, a hunter to gather game for food and leather, a tailor to create warm coats from the leather, a herbilist to keep the sttlers healthy, builders to build the different buildings, and more. Without all that, you struggle... but feeding the additional people needed for those jobs is also a struggle.
In that respect, the developers have really hit a home run. The game is easy enough to quickly understand how to play, yet hard enough to be a real challenge to master. The map seeds allow for an almost infinate variety of gameplay. Every new map is different, and requires a totally different strategy to suceed... allowing a great deal of re-play ability. This is a game that won't get boring or stale very quickly.
As for bugs, I've only found a couple. One bug is that occasionally the game crashes to desktop with a fatal error when I try to open the assign jobs tab. Doesn't happen often, but it's happened a few times and only when I select that tab. The other, and I am not sure if it's a bug or how it's supposed to be.. but it's annoying, is that sometimes a particular worker will hoard all the resources in their house.. to the point of starving the other settlers. Such as a fisherman who takes all the fish to their house instead of to the warehouse... having 300-400 fish in thier house and every other house starving. That's happened a few times to me.
Neither of those bugs are bad enough to not play, as neither happen every time. I'd say it happens maybe 1 in 10 games or less.
Pros:
Freedom to build the way you want
Difficulty well balanced
Fair amount of different careers
Seed map system is great for infinite replay ability
Good bit of mods available which add to the game
Cons:
Needs a way to upgrade the buildings to produce more as you grow.
Settlers don't follow the paths or roads you build... making them useless
No way to manually direct a particular settler to perform a task

5-4-17:
It takes 5-10 minutes to finish, maybe another 5-10 to 100%. And it's pretty easy. And not that fun.
People seem to like it for speedrunning but here's my problem with it:
- The mechanics are very straight forward.
- The sections don't always segue into one another (and when they don't, not even vaguely).
Therefore 95% of what you need to learn is the route you're taking, rather than having to master the technique at all. This would be fine if it wasn't so set in stone as to what the route is - there's no way to diversify as the mechanics and level layout are so simple.
I watched the world record speedrun (2:46.92) and it consists of maybe four or five tricky jumps, and everything else is just knowing where to go. There's no leaderboard, so there's nothing to beat except that time. And now it's just about tiny tiny adjustment anyway.
Also, beautiful? The surroundings are nice - the day/night cycle especially - but the ground texture ruins it. The best part is probably the music.
A game like this just has to feel more fluid and have more replayability. I can't see myself playing Refunct again.
Instead, I greatly recommend

I struggled to come to a conclusion on whether or not I would recommend this game. It's a shame that Steam doesn't allow a neutral option.
On the one hand, this is a beautiful game. There are some interesting and thought-provoking environments. Even after the game had ended I spent a while to take it all in; to go over everything I had witnessed and experienced. The game is intelligent and I applaud it for that.
However, the trailer makes you think that you will have more control over what happens. That you, yourself will be trailing through this random person's documents and games; trying to form your own opinions and conclusions on what they are like, based upon the things you see. However, this isn't how it really is at all and for that it feels like the game is slightly mis-sold.
The issue with the narration style is that it doesn't allow you to form your own ideas, or at least, not as much as I'd like. No sooner had my mind began to wonder about Coda and his feelings, the narrator would tell you what he thought Coda had been feeling. I felt this stifled my thoughts. I wanted more time to explore, to delve into the games and psychoanalyze it all.
I feel that the game didn't expand as much as it could have. There was a lot of potential but it fell a little short and for that it feels a bit underwhelming.

This game predates Men Of War (MoW), but will definitely appeal to anyone who is fond of those games.  It is similar to MoW in that it is an in-depth combat simulation involving anything from infantry to vehicles to planes, each with their own inventories, names, and experience.  It diverges from MoW in that the engagement distances and overall scale of things is far closer to reality.  Tanks can actually thow mass several km downrange and still have lethal momentum.  Even rifles can shoot several hundred meters.  It is slower paced than MoW, but is larger scale and is much more persistent in the single player, with infantry and crew members each gaining experience that you get to allocate into their different aspects and medals that you get to award them.  Everything carries over from one campaign battle to the next, and what you've got is what you've got: losing armor or entire squads really hurts.  All in all, it is a clunky but very respectable (even lovable) game and certainly has it's sights on what's important.  I hope they make a Theatre of War 4 with engine and interface improvements, more factions, and the ability to play a drop-in multiplayer campaign.  That will be an instant buy.

The last time I played this game was in early 2012ish, and even the land battle tutorial instantly brought flashbacks at the cannon part.
First, the classical soundtrack for the campaign map is really good and relaxing
Second, manual-resolve ship battles, took some maneuvering to win there, although the repair abilty is a bit op.
Third, the land battle tactics are fantastic. This game simulates the shock of getting fired upon for the first time, where their morale drops heavily and are vulnerable to anything from artillery to cavalry. Then after a few moments, that unit regains its courage and shoots back over and over again until either side dies or flees first. The land battle maneuvering is also very well balanced, light infantry and the like usually don't form lines, and lose to line combat, but they're LIGHT. They usually shoot farther and are meant to be skirmishers. Line infantry are a big pain in your and my ### because they have bayonets and can shoot in varying degrees of success from the crappy militia to the elite grenadiers. They even did a good job simulating armed citizens, sometimes their morale was ultra-low, other times they had 10 morale points!!! I think this varies on their public order?

I do not recommend this game after (from what I know) completing it. I am putting the uncertainty here, because I come from The Stanley Parable and was expecting a different experience. The game however does not indicate any branching paths.
First of all, the trailer feels misleading. In the trailer, you are given the impression that you will be able to explore a game world at your own pace and at your own discretion. The game itself is a linear narrative experience, where you are guided through it with almost no (to me known) ability to divert from the set path, like in The Stanley Parable. I did not enjoy it, but it probably helped keep up the pace and cohesiveness of the experience. I honestly expected to be rummaging through someones harddrive and find files on it.
Second, is that if you are expecting a Stanley Parable like experience, this is, as mentioned, not it. It is mostly about walking around, taking in your surroundings, combining it with the information given by the narrator and continue walking. The narration is serious and to the point. There are no alternatives, no clever ways to find hidden things. There are no meaningful discoveries to be made. The game tries to stand on its own without any clever subversive intentions.
Third, it is a short game and does not have replayability, because of the above mentioned reasons. Therefor the price to me feels too high.
I do not want to spoil any of the games narrative content, just can say that it is an emotional, not funny one.
If at some point, someone finds replayability in this game, then that would be great. Also I have checked my HDD to see if maybe all the games were there, like shown in the trailer, which was unfortunately not the case. If it gets cheaper and you want some quick to play narrative gameplay, which is well made, go for it. For now, I do not recommend it for fans of The Stanley Parable or as a game.

I've been playing this game on mobile for several years now, it has a great combination of being smart and being addictive. It's also pretty unique in its mechanics, has real card trading, and is very light on P2W, which is always a joy.
The port is not perfect, it's still rough and feels mobile, but it's definitely playable. I always felt this game would work best on a big screen and I wasn't wrong.
The interesting thing about the port is that you won't play against OP mobile guys but instead start from scratch with everyone else on PC. The PC version is completely stand alone, it uses all the latest patches, but so far only the first card set - there is A LOT of content to come later. Additionally, it seems like they rebalanced most OP cards and really try to take balance seriously this time.
Overall it's a very promising start. Definitely give it a try, if TCG is your thing it may suck you in for a loong time.

I walked to Mystery Lake via the West Access. I spotted three small cabins in the distance and moved toward them. I heard wolves in the distance and looked around thinking they could be a threat; thankfully they were walking across the lake a safe distance away from me. Searching a cabin I found a can of dog food. I was hungry. I smashed it open and ate it with my hands. I lost some of it when I smashed it, but it did the trick.
Later I found the Camp Office. The dead man had nothing on him. I put on a heavy wool sweater I found in a drawer and tried to build a fire. I failed twice and ran out of tinder. There was some newspaper on the ground on the first floor so I took it and shoved it into the stove and tried again. Finally, a success. After getting warm I foraged for supplies like wood and tinder. Ate and drank some food. Then slept for a good 12 hours. When I awoke I felt dehydrated and a drank some water. I felt better after that.
I decided to explore around some more outside. There was a train derailment nearby that had nothing to help me. So, I followed the train tracks, knowing that at somepoint they have to lead me to somewhere semi-civilized.
I saw an area that had a bunch of cut down trees. I thought there might be a chance to find an old axe around there or something useful. I found my way to a Logging Camp. Things were looking up!
I saw two wolves in front of me wandering the camp, probably hungry. One of them spoted a deer and took it down. My first thought was, if I wait there might be something of that deer I could use. My second thought was, the wolves will be territorial of a kill so I need to be cautious.

This is my edited review to commemorate the 1-year mark since The Long Dark (TLD) came out on early access. That's not to say that the game is neglected. Quite the opposite. In the year since the game first hit Steam Early Access there have been 49 major updates and hotfixes. That averages to nearly one update per week for a year. Hinterland (the devs) have done the opposite of abandoning TLD.
The game is beautiful and immersive. The sounds are gorgeous and occasionally bone-chilling. The devs consistently look at what the players request while not doing anything that would compromise their artistic vision for a lovely game. They have said that they are working towards a thoughtful single player, story mode experience, and while TLD is still only available in sandbox alpha everything they do to the game appears to be moving towards that goal.
You can die due to freezing, falling, failing to light a fire, wolf, bear, bear and then wolf, falling off a cliff while running from a wolf, falling through the ice, starving at your campfire, dehydration, exhaustion, food poisoning, dysentery, exhaustion or... you know, stuff and things.
The game wont hold your hand and it's not a quick fix. And I love it. At almost 400 hours of of game time, I'm still not bored with the game.

A lot's been said about this game already and here are my two cents:
It's easy to die, especially early in the game, when even a grave moth can kill you with a few hits. But when you make a few level, get better equipment (esp. armors), visit some trainers, get used to the fighting system and when then one day even the strongest monsters die by a few strikes of your sword (or spell), is just a damn cool feeling of accomplishment. :D  So: yes, it's a tough one, but never unfair (at least to my perception). Enemies don't level with you, so if you die too quickly, go training at less powerful enemies somewhere else.
There's a ton of hidden things to be found. Leave the paths and streets, delve into the wilderness to find ingredients to boost your stats (but don't forget to level Alchemy as well, brewing them to potions will make them A LOT stronger ;-) ), find caves with treasures (and even stronger monsters *aargh*), sneak into houses and plunder their chests (but don't get caught) and so on......
You can develop your character individually, while the faction you pick throughout the game defines kind of your "base profession", either a mage or a fighter class. That's pretty fun, cause you don't need to be a pure melee fighter, if you don't want to. But you'll for sure never be as deadly with spells as a mage... what my current (third) playthrough is. On my first run I paid people to hand over quest-relevant items, the next time I learned pickpocketing and got them "for free"... *hahaha*
Visually stunning for its age, especially if you install the Enhanced textures available on the net. If it then refuses to start (happened to me), apply the 4GB-Patch, worked perfectly fine for me. My only complaint is the design of the ending, but... I'll leave it up to you to find out.
Recommended, if you're not too much of a casual gamer, cause it requires *some* dedication. I took help from GameFAQs and other fan websites to help me understand some game mechanics, but for me it was really worth it.
