so this game isn't bad per say. I like it a lot. the combat is fun, fast paced, the skills can be interesting and fun. There is a ton of potential in this game, but there can be some improvements made to it for more longevity and greater fun.\
First thing which youve seen new game+. it sucks, no point, not really. You keep nothing, no level up bonuses, no new gear to be explored. not worth. if there were more loot options or if we kept more than just our skill tree there would be more to do than a first play through.
Second is the lack of items. scripted items aren't that bad if they are worth it, but theres a huge lack of variety in loot and gear. This is not a loot fest like diablo or grim down, not at all.
Third there doesn't feel like a progression of items. Some orange items from early in the game can still work at the end game with the right stats.  the only real progression of power you feel is in your skill tree and your weapons.
Fourth the skill trees feel limited. Its understandable that active skills wont transfer between weapons but there would be more replayability if we could incorporate passives from other trees to make the play style we want stronger, or cater to a specific style of game play regardless of weapon. Also some trees make you favor specific weapon types if you want meaningful damage which kinda sucks.
Despite all it's shortcomings i really do like the game. it is fun, its a fun romp, just not for the long haul like grim dawn or diablo. if it can expand on these 4 issues and make the game more varied i feel like it could stand up there with the greats. Also dodge rolling in this game has ruined other ARPGs for me. not gonna lie.

I do not recommend this game after (from what I know) completing it. I am putting the uncertainty here, because I come from The Stanley Parable and was expecting a different experience. The game however does not indicate any branching paths.
First of all, the trailer feels misleading. In the trailer, you are given the impression that you will be able to explore a game world at your own pace and at your own discretion. The game itself is a linear narrative experience, where you are guided through it with almost no (to me known) ability to divert from the set path, like in The Stanley Parable. I did not enjoy it, but it probably helped keep up the pace and cohesiveness of the experience. I honestly expected to be rummaging through someones harddrive and find files on it.
Second, is that if you are expecting a Stanley Parable like experience, this is, as mentioned, not it. It is mostly about walking around, taking in your surroundings, combining it with the information given by the narrator and continue walking. The narration is serious and to the point. There are no alternatives, no clever ways to find hidden things. There are no meaningful discoveries to be made. The game tries to stand on its own without any clever subversive intentions.
Third, it is a short game and does not have replayability, because of the above mentioned reasons. Therefor the price to me feels too high.
I do not want to spoil any of the games narrative content, just can say that it is an emotional, not funny one.
If at some point, someone finds replayability in this game, then that would be great. Also I have checked my HDD to see if maybe all the games were there, like shown in the trailer, which was unfortunately not the case. If it gets cheaper and you want some quick to play narrative gameplay, which is well made, go for it. For now, I do not recommend it for fans of The Stanley Parable or as a game.

Not for everyone, I'll just say that right now. I've been with the RPG Maker series for a long while now and Ace is probably one of the best versions they've made (debatable with XP still being pretty good, but having a more dated interface). As the title of the game says, it is an RPG Maker, you make RPG games with it, or more specifically, 2D JRPG's similar to the old Dragon Quest or Final Fantasy games. Though other genres can be made if you get creative (though adventure games would be easiest).
PROS:
- Somewhat easy to learn
- Importing custom resources is pretty easy
- The RPG Maker community is large and mostly friendly and are always willing to help you.
- LOTS of tutorials on YouTube that are very detailed to help all of people who don't know anything about the program, learn it.
- Great for making 2D JRPG’s
- Has Steam Workshop support
- Everything in the package is Royalty Free, so you can sell your games if you want to.
- Surprisingly deep. You’re even able to make your own damage formula for attacks.
- Able to keep you entertained for a very long time.
CONS:
- Not as easy to learn as one might think. “Simple enough for a child” I don’t think so.
- The community frowns on games that don’t have completely different resources; even if the game is good.
- Pretty expensive, 70USD probably isn't worth it. I recommend trying out the lite version and if you like it, but hate the restrictions of it then buy the game on a sale - it goes as low as 17.50USD.
- The default battle system is bare-bones. Pretty much requires a tweak, or overhaul to be fun.
- It doesn’t have a battle sprite for every character. Which sucks, because some RPG’s have you battle more than generic thieves and bandits.
- Set to a really weird resolution by default and can’t go any higher than 480p.
- No options menu by default for your games.
- The character generator has many flaws; for example, the faces aren’t the same style as the faces in the Run-Time Package, and they don’t have a face option for every sprite option (no hood on sprites, but there is one on faces).
I recommend it mostly for hobbist game designers, or for people that want to tell a story.

This game has a lot going for it on paper. Particularly, the Norse Mythology setting was a draw for me. The roll mechanic and more technical combat also seemed intriguing, if not new (turns out Victor Vran does this better). 12 hours in, I just don't think it really comes together. The combat feels tedious and awkward, rather than precise. The skill and loot systems are shallow and boring. Earlier on I wrote a review for Counter Strike claiming it was one of the greatest mods for Half Life ever made. Well, this one, Team Fortress Classic, is other of those. This isn't actually the first Team Fortress game, as the original was released for Quake. The original idea was to turn Quake into a team-based game giving different characters a class with different guns and characteristics, allowing fora team-based play. Half Life, being hardly based on Quake's engine, obviously received great versions of classic quake mods, and TFC is one of them. At first, if you have played HL Deathmatch, this game will somewhat feel like Half Life with classes, and it kinda is, but, it adds something totally new to the HL experience, which is team roles. If you are playing a scout, a pyro, or a demoman, you are an agile attacker, and your work is to run and gun (or grenade, or flame). If you are playing as a Medic, while you do have some damage-dealing weapons (such as the awesome nailgun) your main role is that of a, well, medic. You distribute medkits to your allies so that they can recover health (no, you don't have a healing gun like in TF2). Even as a medic, you can still be an effective assassin type character. But the real assassin character is the Spy. He can disguise as an enemy unit and use a knife or gun to bamboozle them. Another type of support/assassin character is the engineer, who can build turrets who annoy and kill your enemies. And then, there are the more specialized damage dealers. The soldier is your standard Quake-style character: he has a rocket launcher, he expldoes people with rockets, and he can rocket jump for extra mobility. The  Sniper is, well, a sniper. In maps such as 2-fort (probably the most popular map), there are very good camping spots for a sniper to deliver precise killing blows. And, obviously, there is my favorite, the Heavy Weapons Guy, or HWGUY as he is called ingame (in TF2 he's called the "Heavy"). He has a minigun and a lot of HP, and his job is to act both as sort of a tanker, and as a big damage dealer: if you get in the range of his gun, you're probablly dead.
So many different classes with their distinct gameplay is what made TFC a classic between classics. Not even Team Fortress 2 manages to be quite as statisfyingly fun as this game for me, for a very simple reason: it feels like Quake in the parts where it needs to feel like quake, such as in the very high skill ceiling, focus on mobility and fast reflexes, yet it also feels very different from quake where it needs to be different: teamwork and different roles to play. Many games such as, obvioulsy, TF2 and Blizzard's new hit, Overwatch, have learned a lot from Team Fortress Classic who will truly always be, the daddy of this whole genre (with QWTF being the grandpa).

Talk about a throw-back.  While not quite the Grand-Dadddy of team based shooters, it is a recreation of the Grand-Daddy of team based shooters.  To think that this reincarnation of the game is almost two decades old is amazing.
This game comes from an age of abstract level design, lag, and ridiculously fast paced action.  With different maps being designed for different team based games.  But, possibly the most popular of all time was Team Capture The Flag, and most likely on the map 2Fort (or if you were a Quake gamer, 2Fort5).
Younger gamers may have a little trouble adapting to the old-school style of online battle...Strafe Shooting and Rocket Jumping, all while piles of Gibs expload all around you. But the fact that almost 20 years later this game is still actively played online gives testament to the amount of fun to be had while playing.  If you want to know what the average gamer spent his entire summer, and every night, playing back in 1999...until he passed out from exhaustion, this is it (or possibly the original Team Fortress).
For the Older Gamers who wonder whether this is still worth downloading.  As of 25 June, 2017, there were about 6 dozen servers available, with about a dozen of them heavily populated.  I played nonstop in a packed server for 4 hours in one sitting before my old age got the best of me.  If you are looking to play a game you grew up with and loved, this is still a valid option.

WORKAROUND FOR LANGUAGE CRASH ON STARTUP AND AUDIO ISSUES
There is a bug in the game that may cause a crash when using a surround sound setup.
If you have Razer Surround, try disabling that and run the game again.
For surround headphone users, if you have a USB connector that you plug your headset into, try plugging your headset into a 3.5mm audio jack instead. (The round green one)
If you have speakers and headphones, try setting your default audio device to your speakers instead of your headphones.
If character voices do not play, set the ingame audio setting to stereo instead of surround.
If your audio is distorted or crackling, you can try to set your speaker audio frequency to 16 bit, 48000 Khz, DVD Quality by opening the sound settings on your computer, select the speakers you use, right click and select properties, and under the advanced tab, there should be an option to change speaker frequency.

Finally, the Tales series is on STEAM!
The Tales series is a traditional style JRPG which has stayed true to it's JRPG roots since it's first release in 1995. And since then has only improved upon and critiqued it's unique style of gameplay over the years. It is hands down, without a doubt, one of my all time favorite game series of all time.  That's because with each installment in the series it delivers what I've come to love and expect from all the Tales games , with added improvements. So here are a few things you can expect when playing a Tales game.
What to expect -
*Free Motion Battle System- A combat system where you actively move around in the battle and can attack freely in real time, using lots of cool combos and skills. The technical name for the  battle system has changed with each improvement so I'll just call it the free motion battle system.
*Engaging character's - What really brings the Tales games to life is it's characters and their interactions together. Even the small chit-chats they have, or skits, make the characters feel alive and the conversations feel real.
*Story - A story driven game over several hours with lot's of side quests to do.
*The world - Exploring the vast world, the towns, the npcs and all the hidden things within that world.
*Longevity - The Tales games are long, great, games. Not  short games you can just blast through in one sitting. And if you plan to unlock everything then it's even longer. Yay!

First of all a lot of the Tales combat will feel very familiar. Characters have regular attacks, special moves called Artes, and magical spells. Regular attacks and Artes can be chained together while magical spells require charge time, so the caster must be protected from enemies who want to interrupt their spells. The CC system appears to have been replaced by something called the Spirit Chain system, which looks like a mix of TP and CC. You spend SC to use Artes, and they replenish as you attack. As with CC, precisely timed side-steps, blocks or dodges can fill the SC gauge.
One of the more interesting elements of the game is Armatization, a super-powered combat mode that is similar to the Chromatus in Tales of Xillia 2. Armatization requires Sorey and one of the Seraphim (Team Members). Each of Sorey's Seraphim pals is tied to a specific element, and when Sorey uses Armatization, he fuses with them to gain access to new moves and weapons based on their element. For example, Mikelo provides a bow and magic-based arts while Edna gives giant stone fists and earth-based arts. Instead of the traditional Tales character swapping (Like in tales of Symphonia for example), there is a focus on different fusions to change Sorey's play style.
When you hit an enemy's elemental weakness or elemental resistance, the game displays a big glowing icon to notify you. This also makes me suspect that enemies can swap resistances on the fly, requiring Sorey to do the same.
The dungeon exploration in Zestiria feels very familiar. You'll probably have a good idea of what to expect if you've played recent games in the franchise. This game lacks any sort of puzzles in the dungeons, similarly to Xillia. So, for anyone hoping to a return to dungeon puzzles like Symphonia, will once again be disappointed. However, the dungeons are spacious and well suited to the game’s “Real Map Battles” system.
Tales of Zestiria doesn't look to reinvent the wheel. The core Tales combat system that people know and love is still there, and while there have been some changes to the basic design, longtime fans will still enjoy the game. There are some new features, such as the Armatization fusion mechanic and the new on-field battle camera, to keep the game feeling fresh, and the story is hella intriguing.
There are two last things to call attention  to before closing this review out. First, the cutscenes. Every scene with dialogue in Zestiria is actually more like a cutscene. Text bubbles have been removed in favor of the text showing up on the bottom of the screen like subtitles, and the entire scene has motion and acting to it. However, even with that all being the case, you can still press buttons to skip through lines quickly. It’s really implemented incredibly well!
Second, are the anime cutscenes. Ufotable handles all of the animation for the game, including the cutscenes (of which there are surprisingly many that are animated) and the opening sequence. Every single bit of animation that Ufotable handled in the game looks stunning and absolutely gorgeous.
I'd DEFINITELY recommend it if you are an Tales of fan or newcomer!, unless you find yourself allergic to the typical trappings of such games (you can see the typical zomg 30 fps outrage on the forums already). But it’s still a Tales of game… isn’t it?

Review of the Steam version of the game:
This game is available for mobile globally and mobile users can play across region and OS (android and ios).  The Koreans and Chinese also have a PC version but their version is crossplatform with the mobile game but for whatever reason the Steam version of the game is NOT cross platform making this game a huge waste of time.  If you play this game you will be basically playing with a small sliver of the community who aren't aware of the mobile game.
As I understand it the reason Nexon decided to make the split is because they wanted to make an enormous balance patch on the mobile version but decided that some people would leave if a a bunch of their rare hard-earned cards got changed and decided to make a separate game with these changes.  Even if they do a stellar job with balance in this version I can't see why people would toss all thier cards in the mobile game just because a few of their cards stopped being meta to play a version that boasts balance from a company with a generally bad reputation with balance.  All of this while losing the convinience of being able to play anywhere and with a much larger community.
Review of the mobile version of the game:
Assuming the Devs realize that a standalone game is a stupid idea and itegrate this version with the mobile version the mobile version is a pretty good game (at least on par if not better than Hearthstone).  You don't draw cards from a deck like Hearthstone and Yu-Gi-Oh taking a huge amount of luck and RNG out of the game, instead all of your cards in your deck are available to you at the start and you have to balance card costs to decide which cards to play and when.  There is still some RNG as your deck might have a slight strategic advantage over your opponent's or you might get super unlucky with which resources you get but you won't be in a situation where you are stomping an opponent who is vastly worse than you but all of a sudden your opponent gets a super lucky draw and destroys your entire strategy with a single card.

This review is based on the mobile version, Mabinogi Duel. I hear this version is separate, and maybe things will be different, but given Nexon's track record for both Mabinogi
Mabinogi Duel, I don't have much confidence in that. Take this as a warning.
Mabinogi Duel is quite unique when it comes to trading card games. Its mechanics will feel familiar to those who have played TCGs, and yet are different enough that the game stands out. Having played very early on in the game's release, the game was fun and felt mostly fair. It had its issues  (which still persist, by the way), but it wasn't a terrible ordeal to keep up without paying. The early sets were also quite reasonably balanced - with exceptions, of course - but playing in lower ranks in arena still saw a variety of different decks and the maintainers listened to feedback and made generally reasonable balance adjustments.
Unfortunately, it is all too easy to fall into the regular traps of TCGs, and this game is no exception. The amazing thing is that it took less than a year for that to happen. Each new set was increasingly unbalanced, the method to build your collection was changed several times - increasingly in favour of opening your wallet - and PvE was reduced to being a real waste of time. Nowadays, quite frankly, game balance is thrown out the window. It's broken. It didn't help that they merged the overseas servers with the KR ones either - deck diversity took a real nosedive.
The game has been reduced to event spamming (this should sound familiar to Mabinogi players) and constantly releasing alternate-art cards. Gold - the currency the game was originally designed around - is a scarcity unless you fullfil the mission "purchase X amount of duel coins". There are now not one, but two premium currencies. Originally just gems, there are now duel coins which don't seem to be all that different - except gems get thrown around to non-paying players and you can do more with duel coins(?). It's a confusing mess that came about in their attempt to salvage their situation when they made PvE collection building virtually impossible in any reasonable length of time.
It's a real shame too, the game had a lot of potential to flourish as a unique and creative TCG. I suppose it's like Mabinogi itself; it had so much potential before it devolved into a skill grindfest with inreasingly awful power creep and terrible game design.
That being said, the game still has its moments - building silly and gimmicky decks to face against friends is fun and I'm assuming this version is starting all the way from G1
, which was when the game was actually good. I suppose I can recommend you to at least try it out if you're curious, I just don't know how long the game will last before going down the drain.
Also, for Mabinogi players, they claim that the game is based on Mabinogi lore. There's pretty much nothing it has in common with Mabinogi aside from using a few familiar characters (including a certain blacksmith whose entire inclusion is to flog a deceased equine). Nothing ties the stories of the two games together; there's no real explanation at all.
Oh, and by the way, "Ifrit: Firora" was neither fair nor balanced when she came out.

RPG Maker VX is a very powerful game-making program that is easy to learn and a lot of fun to play around with. The game script is completely customizable, offering a huge variety of gameplay types and styles. Those who are new to programming (in Ruby) can still find a huge list of resources to customize their games including scripts, music, sound effects, tilesets, etc.
Programming events in RPG Maker is very simple, and after a few brief youtube tutorials you should have no trouble making your RPG ideas into a reality. The potential for this program is limited only by your imagination and your willingness to learn. It is also possible to create a full-length game without any modifying any of the scripting or creating any new tilesets or character sets.
RPG Maker includes a large array of tiles for most every type of fantasy map (Dungeons, world maps, forests, caves, etc.) Making maps in RPG Maker is as simple as pointing and clicking, there is also an option that allows random dungeon creation if you should so choose.
All in all, RPG Maker is perfect if you are the creative type looking for a user-friendly way to create games, or are delving into the world of programming / game design and don't know where to begin.
It's also worth noting that games you create can potentially be sold and/or distributed through steam, pending of course that they you've made something original, and worth playing!

An authentic, gritty and unforgiving World War 2 multiplayer shooter.  Red Orchestra 2 is not for the casual or uninitiated as death comes frequently, usually unfairly, and almost always from a single bullet.  Weapons feel very realistic, with rifles having sufficient gravitas to remind you of their deadly purpose and automatic weapons having recoil that will have you shooting at the sky if you're not careful.
Team play is a must. Capturing objectives can only be achieved with numerous people and the limitations of mid 20th century weaponry means classes are obligated to work together if they want to be successful. working alone or not working towards an objective is pointless as you get next to no points for kills unless you are in range of the objective.
The recent Rising Storm DLC essentially adds a completely new game, with it's own maps and brand new soldiers and weapons. An excellent value and solid addition.
If you're a serious shooter fan, with a tendency towards the hardcore difficulty, you just might like this one. It's one of my personal favourites because of its dedication to historical accuracy and realism, two things which we don't tend to see often in World War 2 shooters. It can be exceptionally frustrating at times due to it's authenticity but it's a game I recommend to those with the right expectations.

This is going to be a long review.
I am by no means a survivalist extrordinaire. I wouldn't last 5 hours in Minecraft. But this game makes you feel like you can survive anything... until you run out of matches.
For example, here is how I last died.
I ran into the Trapper's Homestead, sprinting to get out of the freezing cold wind. I was looking for food; peaches, candy, anything I could get in my belly. I looked through the locker, the box under the bed, the first aid kit on the wall, but didn't find anything but an old can opener. Then I looked up, and I swear I heard a heavenly chorus, because sitting on a rack on the wall was something so much more valuble than a granola bar. As I took the old hunting rifle off the wall, I felt a sense of awe come over me. I looked at the nicks and dents and thought of all the stories that they contain, and how many more tales I would write with this pen of steel and wood. After looking around a little more, I decided to try my hand at cracking the safe I found next to the workbench. After several tries I finally got the code down, and lo and behold, inside was a box of 5 rifle shells. By now I was feeling like Rambo. I would not die to this cruel world!
I survived by hunting the game that I saw in the clearing in front of the homestead that I had claimed as my home, and cooking the meat that I carved off their collapsed frames. I lived this way for about a week, until one very important setback to my otherwise flawless plan - I ran out of matches. But I wouldn't let that tiny detail stop me; I am the great VinyGroundhog! I will not succumb to the meager needs of hunger or cold! And thus my journey begain. I searched from house to house for those tiny life-sticks, but each and every one had been picked clean on a previous venture. I realized that there was only one place where I could find what I needed, one place that I had avoided like the plague. I was going to have to tackle the dam.
As I walked into the dam, flare in hand, I looked for Fluffy the Terrible, Killer of Men and Crusher of Souls. I searched through the entire dam for this beast of legend, but nowhere was she to be found. Not able to contain my exitement, I set about looting the dam with a newfound vigor. I looked in the main room. No matches. I looked in the closet. No matches. I looked in the control room. Still, no matches. Soon I reached the conlusion that I was going to have to go downstairs. I walked down the first set of stairs, and as I rounded the corner, there was a nightmare standing in front of me. I stared at Fluffy, and she at me. We stood at a sort of stalemate for around thirty seconds. And then I ran like a coward. I made it up the stairs and Almost made it out when I was knocked down from behind. As I looked at those menacing jaws that I had fallen to so many times before, I knew that I was nearing my end. We struggled for what  seemed an eternity, and then I finally kicked the evil beast off of me, turning and sprinting through the door as fast as I could. By now it was night, and probably had been for a while. I struggled away from that horrible place, blood dripping down into the snow beneath. I looked around in my pack, and found nothing to treat my wounds. I walked along the train tracks, freezing, starving, dehydrated, and bleeding to death. I looked around and saw that I wasn't going to make it. But I refused. I would not die on the terms of a wolf, no matter that it sent me here. And then I thought of a way that I could stand up to the tyranny of the wolf.
I sprinted to the logging area, and then I found the hill I was looking for. I started up the hill, made it a few yards, and subsequently fell off the hill and sprained my ankle. But I wouldn't let that stop me. I started back up the hill, limping this time, and made it farther, and farther, and farther without falling. And as I hobbled up the last few yards of the hill, freezing, starving, dehydrated, limping, and tired as anything, I saw the sun start to rise. I walked over to the edge of the hill, my vision rolling with every step, and sat down, leaning against a rock. And as my life reached its dusk, the world around me reached its dawn.
That is what this game does to you. It puts you on a high, which lasts a not inconsiderable time, and then it takes away one thing, and you begin this slow descent into your death. And that's why I love it. It's an Emotional rollercoaster. Everything that happens in the game impacts not only your in-game effigy, but you, as a living, breathing human being. However, there are a few things that I wouldn't mind changing...
Hinterland, If you're reading this, Please take note.
The game world is easily the loneliest one I have every encountered. It even beats pre-NPC Minecraft. Please fix this. Give me a dog, or better yet, multiplayer! What I wouldn't give to either help or hinder other players in the fight for survival.
Birds. Everytime I see a bird in the game, all I can think about is the potential meat on those hollow bones. Just give me a way to hunt them, or trap them. a shotgun would be nice.
All things considered, this is a very good buy. It's probably my favorite PC game right now. 10/10

I hesitantly recommend this game.
To start with, I wanted to play it for a while, and recently bought it on sale (cause I'm a poor people) and was quite excited to try it. However, as with certain other recent titles, I think 'style' certainly outweighed 'playability' in the designers minds. Specifically, why can I only aim forward? Yes I can 'mush' slightly up or down to help aim my shot, but really, is it so necessary no to allow any vertical aiming? I'm playing it on a 360 controller, Im pretty sure I have enough buttons to do so. I mean, Contra had the ability to aim better, I don't see how this was a positive design choice just another example of artificial 'difficulty' (read: needless irritation). I was there for retro games, I remember what it was like, I'm in my 30's now and don't feel like I need any more pain in my day-to-day.
Also after getting hit you do this cool thing where you revert to your useless goop form and have to try to gather back all your♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ok, that's cool, except it really sucks to actually play. Normally I get hit after getting swarmed, so there becomes so way to actually get out of the situation. I would rather get instakilled from getting hit than have to deal with that mechanic.
Lastly, I went to go 'visit death' or whatever from the main menu on a whim after dying a few times and getting bored. Turns out on that screen I can equip myself with stuff I earned on previous runs. WELL WOULDN'T THAT BE NICE TO KNOW. Example of pointless ambiguity leading to artificial 'difficulty' (read: needless irritation). I'm not going to complain about the double jump; it sucks but that's a valid design choice.
Aside from that, cool game. There's plenty of other reviews about all the positives, such as music, art etc. those are all true. Gameplay puts schtick over usability to the point where I don't see myself playing this unless I get bored and just feel like shooting stuff without thinking for a while. I'm an artist, art is good I like art, but it's a game so focus on making it fun before making it pretty. I bought Momodora III at the same time I bought this, and that's way more fun. It has similar gameplay, but I feel like in that case it's legit and doesn't detract from the experience (like how good Megaman games play).
TLDR; I'm disappointed in the controls, but aside from that it's cool, just not as good as expected (hyped).

This is an online trading card game. It's ported from a mobile game but despite the often low budget porting choices (you'll see) the game is highly playable and super fun.
To describe the game briefly, there are 5 "colors" (for lack of better word) that have their own unique resource like magic. Decks are only 12 cards and you start with all cards in your hand at the start of the game. You can have up to 3 colors per deck. Cards are played by their resource cost. You can acquire these resources in 3 different ways: start of turn, randomly gain 1 resource of a color in your deck, or discard a card to gain 1 resource of that color. There are 5 positions to play creatures to, spells, a graveyard, and player level mechanics that dictate the cost of cards, how many actions you have per turn, and how much max life you have. There are unique characters that have their own mechanics that will compliment your deck.
It does not feel intimidating to build decks and try new strategies. There are ladders and tournaments of different formats: e.g. a limited draft format, a daily ladder, weekend tournaments, monthly ladder. You don't need a gigantic collection to play the game, and there is a story mode to rack up some resources.
This game has some pretty rough translation strings. It's sometimes hard to figure out what a card does, but I doubt the Nexon team is going to leave these unaddressed for long (at least I hope!). I'm sure there will be a communal resource describing card interactions in detail until the translation strings are updated.
There is only one set of cards out now, but there are unreleased sets that I believe Nexon plans to release fairly rapidly. I hope they will consider not overloading players with too many cards, as it may be discouraging to keep up with hardcore players' collections if you want to play casually.
I'd consider spending money on some packs if you're new. However I don't think grinding out new cards is particularly difficult, and there seems to be a P2P trading component available (gated on player account level) if you'd rather not spend money. The number of cards in the game is not overwhelming right now and there are many strong cards that are not super rare, though it does seem like some of the best cards are the rarest.
If you don't like this kind of F2P model you might not like the game, but the gameplay itself is highly enjoyable.
Full disclosure: I did receive a collector's pass for free when I beta tested the game that has carried over to live.

The National Suicide Prevention Lifeline is independently evaluated by a federally-funded investigation team from Columbia University’s Research Foundation for Mental Hygiene. The Lifeline receives ongoing consultation and guidance from national suicide prevention experts, consumer advocates, and other stakeholders through the Lifeline’s Steering Committee, Consumer/Survivor Committee, and Standards, Training and Practices Committee.
The National Suicide Prevention Lifeline is a leader in suicide prevention and mental health crisis care. Infinifactory is the kind of game that only a certain type of people will enjoy. I can say that I fall under that category, and I thought it was fantastic. Due to its logical nature, Infinifactory is a game geared toward the same kind of people that enjoy programming; while playing, you'll likely find yourself using a lot of the same practices you might use when coding, such as building machines in "sections", optimizing, and debugging. It's also a great way to know if coding is something you'd enjoy or not; if you don't like this game you probably shouldn't try programming either. The game has plenty of content, and as an added bonus, if you have friends who play the game you can compete to see who can build the smallest and/or most efficient machine (which really adds some good replay value).
Besides the fantastic and unique gameplay, the game has some pretty solid graphics and good, relaxing music. However, there's one thing about this game I find questionable, and that's the story. You've basically been "captured" by "alien overlords" who are forcing you to create these machines for them. Any story that uses those terms is very clearly cliché and uninteresting. Of course, no one is going to play this game for the story, but I think the game would be a lot more polished if the story were to be completely overhauled or even removed entirely (I do in fact like the space setting of the game worlds, and I think the game would work out just fine without any story whatsoever).
Don't let the stuff I said about the story turn you away from playing Infinifactory – it's still an amazing game, and I highly recommend it if you think you're up for the challenge (especially if you enjoy or are looking into programming).

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

An authentic, gritty and unforgiving World War 2 multiplayer shooter.  Red Orchestra 2 is not for the casual or uninitiated as death comes frequently, usually unfairly, and almost always from a single bullet.  Weapons feel very realistic, with rifles having sufficient gravitas to remind you of their deadly purpose and automatic weapons having recoil that will have you shooting at the sky if you're not careful.
Team play is a must. Capturing objectives can only be achieved with numerous people and the limitations of mid 20th century weaponry means classes are obligated to work together if they want to be successful. working alone or not working towards an objective is pointless as you get next to no points for kills unless you are in range of the objective.
The recent Rising Storm DLC essentially adds a completely new game, with it's own maps and brand new soldiers and weapons. An excellent value and solid addition.
If you're a serious shooter fan, with a tendency towards the hardcore difficulty, you just might like this one. It's one of my personal favourites because of its dedication to historical accuracy and realism, two things which we don't tend to see often in World War 2 shooters. It can be exceptionally frustrating at times due to it's authenticity but it's a game I recommend to those with the right expectations.

RO2 raises the bar in multiplayer-based shooter realism. There will be no bunny hopping, 360 no scope headshots in this game, ever! It is an exercise in patience, a WW2 simulation where full auto weapons are in short supply, and bolt action rifles make up the bulk of the armaments. Iron sights are almost a requirement for accurate shooting, but a single shot can and often does make a kill. Realistic damage modeling rewards careful marksmanship, and treats a shot in the heart the same as a head shot... an instant kill. However, the effects of limb damage aren't made quite clear, and seem to serve no other purpose than a means to implement the self-applied battlefield bandaging feature.  RO2 is a PC-only shooter, and gives the arcadey big name console ports a run for their money.

The standard gameplay mode is tug-of-war style where teams must grab control points in sequence. Each control point is captured via a "King of the Hill" style mini-tug-of-war by the team who can maintain a higher player count within the "hill's" borders. Thus, contrary to arena multiplayer shooters, the most important task for the player is SURVIVING as opposed to simply killing. Surviving and killing alike require a certain level of teamwork, since the game can be punishing for those who prefer to run and gun.

This standard game formula is further broken down into pure Tug of War (where the map control starts with neutral center capture points and the control can go in either direction) and Assault/Defence (where one team attemps to capture the points accross a map while the other team must defend said points).  These modes are hardwired into the maps they are played on, meaning that some maps are soley Assault maps, while others are soley Tug of War maps.

There are other game modes available, but I have not tinkered around with them much since I greatly enjoy the standard game as it is.

Vehicular combat is a sore spot for me. Straight up, it sucks, for many reasons. Vehicle gameplay wasn't implemented in the normal fasion seen in most games. For example, you must commit to vehicular classes, and once spawned you actually start in the vehicle and cannot exit. Nor can other players enter your spawned vehicle. And there are other annoyances. It's just.... bad.

Another gripe of mine is the spawn system: it's clunky and counter-intuitive. For example, if you are attempting to spawn on a squad leader, but the commander forces a respawn before you can finish the selection, you will spawn at a random spawn site that is most definately NOT your squad leader and more than likely much further from the front lines than you would like. Again, there are other annoyances with RO2s spawn system.

All in all it is one of the premeire shooting experiences available. Highly recommended!

Summary of my ramblings below:
Half of this game is a wonderful experience, it drew me in in the same way the Gothic series always did. After finishing chapter 2 however, I would recommend just switching it off and watching the final scenes on YouTube. The final chapters are awful, just awful. Fetch quest after fetch quest after fetch quest with absolutely no substance in between and a ridiculous amount of aimless wandering, even with teleporter stones. If you're patient, love exploring and don't mind having to extensively fix the game before you even consider playing it, Risen is amazing.
-----
It saddens me to admit that I can't honestly recommend this game without several warnings. Having just spent 30+ hours on the campaign, completing dozens upon dozens of fun sidequests and essentially making my protagonist a walking tank, I'm so thankful to have finished Risen. My first half of the game was spent thinking about how I was looking forward to replaying the game as a mage on my second playthrough, but having finally finished the main story, the game offers absolutely zero replay value for me.
Aside from the countless glitches, broken quests and hauntingly frustrating issues with trying to climb ledges, the game just lost all momentum after the second chapter. My first ~20 hours in the game were golden, I was like an excited child running around and exploring the lush environment, beautiful ruins and wonderfully constructed towns, caves, castles, etc.
Then I reached chapter 3... That was where the enjoyment ended for me. The entire remainder of the game takes place in a labyrinth of boring, dark crypts that all look identical to the previous one. The puzzles were no longer fun, but the same mind-numbing tedium, rearranged to look ever so slightly different.
As an avid fan of the Gothic series, I expected glitches and broken quests, it's always been a part of the adventure with any PB game and I expected nothing less, but there's a limit... When you're in a cave and have to climb up 8 ledges in a row to get to the next section, around 95% of attempts to climb upwards will place you either in the ceiling or the floor, unable to do anything but reload your quicksave for the umpeenth time. This experience absolutely destroyed the game for me. I lost countless hours to reloading my game due to forgetting to save before I tried to hop up an inconspicuous 3-inch piece of raised floor. I did eventually install the community patch, which was a god-send for fixing some of my busted quests, and I wish I'd done so sooner, but it boils my blood when these game-breaking issues are left in when the developers are clearly aware of the issues. Having to alter my graphics settings through 3rd party software is not something I can condone.
If not for the jumping issues, the second half of the game would have probably been just about tolerable, but every single area was filled with ledges to climb and it drained my soul every time I saw a set of large, craggy steps.
Play half of this game, it's half amazing.

I hesitantly recommend this game.
To start with, I wanted to play it for a while, and recently bought it on sale (cause I'm a poor people) and was quite excited to try it. However, as with certain other recent titles, I think 'style' certainly outweighed 'playability' in the designers minds. Specifically, why can I only aim forward? Yes I can 'mush' slightly up or down to help aim my shot, but really, is it so necessary no to allow any vertical aiming? I'm playing it on a 360 controller, Im pretty sure I have enough buttons to do so. I mean, Contra had the ability to aim better, I don't see how this was a positive design choice just another example of artificial 'difficulty' (read: needless irritation). I was there for retro games, I remember what it was like, I'm in my 30's now and don't feel like I need any more pain in my day-to-day.
Also after getting hit you do this cool thing where you revert to your useless goop form and have to try to gather back all your♥♥♥♥♥♥ Ok, that's cool, except it really sucks to actually play. Normally I get hit after getting swarmed, so there becomes so way to actually get out of the situation. I would rather get instakilled from getting hit than have to deal with that mechanic.
Lastly, I went to go 'visit death' or whatever from the main menu on a whim after dying a few times and getting bored. Turns out on that screen I can equip myself with stuff I earned on previous runs. WELL WOULDN'T THAT BE NICE TO KNOW. Example of pointless ambiguity leading to artificial 'difficulty' (read: needless irritation). I'm not going to complain about the double jump; it sucks but that's a valid design choice.
Aside from that, cool game. There's plenty of other reviews about all the positives, such as music, art etc. those are all true. Gameplay puts schtick over usability to the point where I don't see myself playing this unless I get bored and just feel like shooting stuff without thinking for a while. I'm an artist, art is good I like art, but it's a game so focus on making it fun before making it pretty. I bought Momodora III at the same time I bought this, and that's way more fun. It has similar gameplay, but I feel like in that case it's legit and doesn't detract from the experience (like how good Megaman games play).
TLDR; I'm disappointed in the controls, but aside from that it's cool, just not as good as expected (hyped).

Even though this game is still in development, it brings a new kind of feel to the survival genre that I think a lot of people have been waiting for quite a long time. Along with that the only danger element you'll see in the game (at least currently) are the wolves that randomly patrol the forests either looking for something to eat or looking for you now this really does add more of a survival against mother nature and was a great addition to the game, but, during my time trying to find shelter I was easily slaughtered by a passerby wolf and wasn't really able to fend him off easily even though it shows that you can in the trailer. The date of the start of the history of the United States is a subject of debate among historians. Older textbooks start with the arrival of Christopher Columbus on October 12, 1492 and emphasize the European background, or they start around 1600 and emphasize the American frontier. In recent decades American schools and universities typically have shifted back in time to include more on the colonial period and much more on the prehistory of the Native peoples.[1][2]
Indigenous people lived in what is now the United States for thousands of years before European colonists began to arrive, mostly from England, after 1600. The Spanish had small settlements in Florida and the Southwest, and the French along the Mississippi River and the Gulf Coast. By the 1770s, thirteen British colonies contained two and a half million people along the Atlantic coast east of the Appalachian Mountains. In the 1760s, the British government imposed a series of new taxes while rejecting the American argument that any new taxes had to be approved by the people (see Stamp Act 1765). Tax resistance, especially the Boston Tea Party (1774), led to punitive laws (the Intolerable Acts) by Parliament designed to end self-government in Massachusetts. American Patriots (as they called themselves) adhered to a political ideology called republicanism that emphasized civic duty, virtue, and opposition to corruption, fancy luxuries and aristocracy.
Armed conflict began in 1775 as Patriots drove the royal officials out of every colony and assembled in mass meetings and conventions. In 1776, the Second Continental Congress declared that there was a new, independent nation, the United States of America, not just a collection of disparate colonies. With large-scale military and financial support from France and military leadership by General George Washington, the American Patriots won the Revolutionary War.
The peace treaty of 1783 gave the new nation the land east of the Mississippi River (except Florida and Canada). The central government established by the Articles of Confederation proved ineffectual at providing stability, as it had no authority to collect taxes and had no executive officer. Congress called a convention to meet secretly in Philadelphia in 1787. It wrote a new Constitution, which was adopted in 1789. In 1791, a Bill of Rights was added to guarantee inalienable rights. With Washington as the first president and Alexander Hamilton his chief political and financial adviser, a strong central government was created. When Thomas Jefferson became president he purchased the Louisiana Territory from France, doubling the size of the United States. A second and final war with Britain was fought in 1812.
Encouraged by the notion of Manifest Destiny, federal territory expanded all the way to the Pacific. The U.S. always was large in terms of area, but its population was small, only 4 million in 1790. Population growth was rapid, reaching 7.2 million in 1810, 32 million in 1860, 76 million in 1900, 132 million in 1940, and 321 million in 2015. Economic growth in terms of overall GDP was even faster. However the nation's military strength was quite limited in peacetime before 1940. The expansion was driven by a quest for inexpensive land for yeoman farmers and slave owners. The expansion of slavery was increasingly controversial and fueled political and constitutional battles, which were resolved by compromises. Slavery was abolished in all states north of the Mason–Dixon line by 1804, but the South continued to profit off the institution, producing high-value cotton exports to feed increasing high demand in Europe. The 1860 presidential election of Republican Abraham Lincoln was on a platform of ending the expansion of slavery and putting it on a path to extinction.
Seven cotton-based deep South slave states seceded and later founded the Confederacy months before Lincoln's inauguration. No nation ever recognized the Confederacy, but it opened the war by attacking Fort Sumter in 1861. A surge of nationalist outrage in the North fueled a long, intense American Civil War (1861-1865). It was fought largely in the South as the overwhelming material and manpower advantages of the North proved decisive in a long war. The war's result was restoration of the Union, the impoverishment of the South, and the abolition of slavery. In the Reconstruction era (1863–1877), legal and voting rights were extended to the freed slave. The national government emerged much stronger, and because of the Fourteenth Amendment in 1868, it gained the explicit duty to protect individual rights. However, when white Democrats regained their power in the South during the 1870s, often by paramilitary suppression of voting, they passed Jim Crow laws to maintain white supremacy, and new disfranchising constitutions that prevented most African Americans and many poor whites from voting, a situation that continued for decades until gains of the civil rights movement in the 1960s and passage of federal legislation to enforce constitutional rights.
The United States became the world's leading industrial power at the turn of the 20th century due to an outburst of entrepreneurship in the Northeast and Midwest and the arrival of millions of immigrant workers and farmers from Europe. The national railroad network was completed with the work of Chinese immigrants and large-scale mining and factories industrialized the Northeast and Midwest. Mass dissatisfaction with corruption, inefficiency and traditional politics stimulated the Progressive movement, from the 1890s to 1920s, which led to many social and political reforms. In 1920, the 19th Amendment to the Constitution guaranteed women's suffrage (right to vote). This followed the 16th and 17th amendments in 1913, which established the first national income tax and direct election of US senators to Congress. Initially neutral during World War I, the US declared war on Germany in 1917 and later funded the Allied victory the following year.
After a prosperous decade in the 1920s, the Wall Street Crash of 1929 marked the onset of the decade-long worldwide Great Depression. Democratic President Franklin D. Roosevelt ended the Republican dominance of the White House and implemented his New Deal programs for relief, recovery, and reform. The New Deal, which defined modern American liberalism, included relief for the unemployed, support for farmers, Social Security and a minimum wage. This will be my very first review on Steam, though my library has over 100 games and I've spent probably a couple thousand hours playing time between all of them. This is the very first game I've played on Steam that made me WANT to publicly reveiw it, as any other game I've played, I felt like my opinion wouldn't add anything to it.
This game, however... wow. I really don't want to spoil anything about this game. The summary is enough to go into. All I will say is that it is not the Stanley Parable, nor does it need to be. It's a strong game with a deep theme throughout, and I think it's an important message for anyone who creates art, be it video games, film, photography, writing, drawing, sketching, etc. This game affected me pretty deeply and got me to thinking about things I've never considered, and the ending really punched hard. For when you get there, you'll know what I mean when I say the part at the end where you walk up the stairs and read the first message from Coda to Davey really hit me hard. The rest of the game was very thought provoking. As far as gameplay goes, it's even less interactive than the Stanley Parable was, so it's not a "game" so much as a story that you walk through and experience. I personally love these kinds of games, but they aren't for everyone, so keep that in mind before you buy.
Tl;dr: This game should resonate with everyone, especially if you consider yourself an artist of any kind. For $8 I consider it a steal, I gladly would have paid the full $10. A worthy follow up to Stanley Parable, even if it's a totally different game. Good job to Davey Wreden, and I can't wait for more!

The aptly-titled Magical Otoge Ciel is a treasure. You play as the princess Ciel, travelling with two of her royal knights--Florien, her childhood friend, and his stern yet caring brother Anton--along with a mysterious trickster, Yvin,
following them throughout local kingdoms. On each route, the characters learn more about each other, and in the process, fall in love while making bad puns. What isn't there to love?
The art is incredible for a game of this price; heck, it's better than art in some paid games I own, and that's saying something. The character designs are precious. The backgrounds are gentle and painterly, simple without being boring. The CGs, also, are beautiful. I love the creator Batensan's art style!
The characters are wonderful. The writing, humorous and light, is refreshing, and the worst that can happen in this game is maybe some hurt feelings and minor drama. Florien grows so much, Anton reveals his true self
and Yvin's route, which varies from the other two in terms of direction, is fun with a bit of added character development. When there is drama, it's not cheap; it's actually very well-done, leading me to get emotional about these characters.
There's also a plethora of extras, most of which are behind the scenes stuff with the creator Batensan, and lots of fun extra scenes with the cast, which I grew to love immensely as I played.

A typical Piranha Bytes game. If you liked Gothic 1 and 2, you'll like this one too. If you need everything spoonfed and like to follow the arrow to collect free XP for quests, this isn't for you.
The world is open and nearly fully accessible right from the start, but there are monsters everywhere that will kick your butt, if you stray from the roads. Most of the quests can be solved in multiple ways that are for the player to figure out. The game doesn't hold your hand and only shows an objective on your map, if an NPC marked it for you and if you even have a map. Exploration feels rewarding, as there are always items and treasures to be found. Since there is no inventory space or weight limit, you can collect everything to your heart's content.
The graphics are also typical PB. A little bit chunky but with their own charm. The lighting and weather are beautiful and immersive. You can really feel the clamminess of a rainy day and the mellow warmth of sunny one. Nights are dark and make you want to use torches or look for a bed to sleep through them.
There are two factions you can join, which determine how you progress through the story and give the game much replayability. The main story is nothing out of the ordinary though. Impending doom, yadda yadda, you save the world. However, the side-stories from quests are enjoyable and that's what really matters, in my opinion.
The RPG part is kept simple but not in a bad way. Instead of a skill tree you invest points in a weapon or magic class to improve it, e.g. sword fighting or fireball. Leveling your weapon gives you things like an additional combo hit, the ability to parry, to charge your strikes or to wield two-handers in one hand. Weapon damage can only be improved with strength and dexterity for melee and ranged respectively.
You can also learn crafting and gathering skills which, too, are kept simple and wont take much of your playtime.
Cooking is an innate ability, but you need to find recipes for good food. There is no fishing. Thank God.
The thing that really put me off at first and made me take breaks a few times, is the melee combat. As always in PB games, button-mashing will get you nowhere. The player has to improve along with the character and get good at dodging, parrying and striking at the right time as well as performing 3-4 hit combos. In itself, this is a really good system and has much potential to be great fun. The problem is that everything hits, dodges and recovers lightning fast. You can hardly ever perform your combos because your target will instantly recover after the first one or two hits and either dodge, parry or counter-strike you. This also goes for you parrying or dodging an enemy and trying to hit them while their defenses are down. They will mostly dodge or block your strike, no matter how fast you perform it. Input reading taken to the extreme. Not fun.

GoNNER is a solid game, but I think it chose the wrong structure/genre.
The rogue-like structure is usually a way of exploring a space of possibilities more thoroughly. Instead of a small subset of situations (as in puzzle games), rogue-likes have a specific set of rules, and then place you in as many combinations of those as possible.
This can include both challenges that you have to overcome, and the tools at your disposal to do so.
I usually use The Binding of Isaac as an example, especially of the second point. You have a whole lot of items, and a whole lot of synergies between them. So the rogue-like structure is great to show you the different permutations. It also has a lot of subtleties to explore and later exploit - from secret rooms, to arcades, to interactions between items that give you consumables, etc.
You're also very dependent on the items that you get, though you also have some control over the number of items and choices you have to shape your run.
GoNNER works on a very different principle: you can carry only 3 different items at once, and all of them are available at the start of the game (assuming you've unlocked them). There are <10 items in each category.
What this means is that, after an initial period of experimentation, you've probably chosen your favourite combination, and there's little reason to stray from it.
The game has you going for a set of 4 (and a half, let's say) levels in each area, then you get a shop, followed by a Boss. Each different area obeys this structure.
These shops sell you HP (though one of your items determines your max HP, so you can only refill it in the shops), ammo, and some of the other items (randomly chosen, though you can pay for rerolls).
Now, why would you use the shops at all, given you have your chosen loadout from the start? The most obvious choice is if you like to handle each area differently. That's fine, though that wasn't the case for me - one of the loadouts was clearly better in every aspect, for my playstyle.
The other situation in which they can be useful, is if you've lost some item. When you're hit, all your items are scattered, and you can to recollect them. They're usually scattered close to you, but some of the areas make it difficult to get your items back - one has lots of pits that lead to death, another has a very clear directionality, so it's difficult to go back to retrieve them, etc.
Unfortunately, it was very rare for this to happen without leading to my permanent death. Because you only have 3 items, it's a huge handicap to lose one. Also, the game is very fast, you die very easily, but can also quickly get far in the game. Also, if you have collected enough glyphs (currency), you can restart the level at which you were on (die at area X, level Y, you restart at area X, level Y, so you don't really lose progress). This is means that you can easily forfeit a life to get those items back (usually once per game at most, but still).
From this, I hope it's clear that you aren't really encouraged to experiment with loadouts during the game. There is neither enough variety, nor are there enough constraints. Once you stabilize on your optimal, you have little reason to abandon it.
The other aspect would be exposing you to different challenges. This isn't really ideal in a platformer/shooter, though. Enemies only interact with you can close range, unless they shoot randomly from afar. So your best bet is to take care of enemies from afar as well. This doesn't expose you to many different challenges, and each run goes more or less the same way.
Finally, and this is the only benefit this game gets from being a rogue-like, comes mechanical mastery. Basically, you get better at the game - not very surprising, heh?
You get used to the jumping suubtleties, the gun knockback, how enemies move, jumping on top of enemies, etc. You slowly master all of these aspects until you can beat the game.
For me, this isn't really enough to warrant the game's structure. The perma-death, especially. Thankfully, the game is very fast paced (in both ways - you can die very easily, but you can quickly get back to where you were). But it's still very annoying to die late in the game, and having to go through all of the rest because of a small mistake.
Or, even worse, is the fact that the bosses are much, much harder than the rest of the game. The last boss is especially chaotic.
So you repeatedly go through the easy areas until you die to the last boss again.
There are other aspects of the game that I didn't think were too good.
The glyphs you collect have a cap. Also, because the shop isn't very useful, you often each this cap early on. So, their only use is almost as a second life (which gets more expensive the later you die, being very close to the cap later in the game). This means that the early game is mostly inconsequential - playing perfectly on bosses can give you more ammo, but that is also undone when you use your second life, or lose your weapon, so it's rarely significant.
All in all, this is a very purist game. It's 95% mechanical skill, at most 5% of exploiting the game's secrets, shops, etc.
This makes the rogue-like formula seem a bit scummy - favours the idea the perma-death is in the game as an artificial extension to the game's length.
If you really enjoy purist games, you can probably enjoy this a lot! The items are genuinely distinct from one another, and so require changes in your play style to use the different combinations.
You can make a challenge for yourself to beat the game with the different combinations, try to reach for higher combos/scores, etc.
But I do think the game is very difficult for most people to get much out of it. I took 12 hours to beat it for the first time, after reaching the final boss maybe 5 or 6 times. Once I managed to beat it, I had enough of it, honestly.
----
Ok, I wrote a lot of stuff I thought was wrong with the game. It had mostly to do with its structure.
That aside, I think GoNNER is very solid! As I said, the items are very different, and there are many subtleties to the movement, from the knockback, to enemy explosions, to jump height.
So it's a good game, but I strongly disagree with its overall focus.
The game Bleed seems better structured for something of this type - many difficulties to choose from, focus on time/score, much better suited for multiple playthroughs and getting better at it with each one.
GoNNER seems a war of attrition, slowly getting better at exactly the same thing until you beat it.
That aside, the game has a very unique style, both visually and musically. Both of these also change and get more chaotic with your combo meter.
Anyway, I've ranted for long enough.
I think the game's "rogue-like" aspect is a product of the times more so than a design decision, and it ends up feeling very out of place, and even artifically extending the game's length.
But, if you enjoy mastering the details of a runner/shooter game, you can probably get quite a lot out of this. It's just not what it seems to encourage, so the burden is on the player, so to speak.

A very artistic and thematic Rogue-like platformer which generally ruins itself with completely artificial difficulty and a lack of overall content.
The art and thematic design of the game is very well done, and the platforming as well as the shooting control feels quite nice. But the two biggest problems remain, the difficulty is entirely artificial and it exists to only compensate for the lack of content.
The game has around four map types and four bosses. Each map type taking several minutes to complete. Although the maps are quite artistic in their design, it is still extremely bare and simplistic. Mostly, the maps are only composed of ground textures and enemies. There is only a half a dozen or so each of weapons, back items and head items across the entire game; and most of them really are not worth using. Some of them it's difficult to even tell what they do, while the uses of others are pretty negligible or blatantly inferior to another. The game is technically very small, and while it has good randomization; it's not much of a plus when the maps are basically ground textures and enemies.
The game takes longer then thirty minutes to beat because of enemy spam, pretty much. As the game progresses, the maps become more and more flooded with enemies. To the point where reacting, dodging and shooting them all is completely arbitrary and one mistake can end it all. Or accumulated mistakes lead to the player running out of health. When players get hit, they go through a unique recovery mechanic which can lead to them getting stun locked into getting hit over and over by enemies, losing their equipment entirely, or just straight up dying instantly if they are not randomly in the right scenario to recover properly. Literally, if chance decides it, when players get hit they can get caught into a situation which ends that playthrough; simply just because. Players can sustain up to six or so hits before dying, but sometimes they just die instantly, is basically how the system works.
The game boasts how difficult it is, which is quite a joke considering that any game could acquire this same difficulty if the developers decided to just spam place enemies all over the map to the point where players are almost guaraneteed to lose. Succeeding in a run is almost entirely subject to whether the game generates some of its more scummy levels or not, and past that it is just about human error. How many projectiles can you dodge in a row before you get hit, how many flying enemies can you jump and duck through before one gets you.
There's no learning curve or adaption on the players end, because from start to finish the challenges that the player encounters are caused by the game just throwing waves of danger at the player over and over. Eventually they'll get hit, maybe they'll recover maybe they won't, maybe they won't get hit one time but they will another. Maybe they'll just keep getting hit over and over. The random number generation of the game isn't the greatest challenge but more so is the random occurence of human error, how many things can you dodge before something hits you.
That is it. When you play this game, you will initially improve by learning more about the levels and enemies. But after that, your chances of success are entirely based of random luck. Because the only challenge the game presents, is by filling the room with enemies and telling the player they aren't good enough to beat the game if they can't beat them all at once. Well of course you won't, because the room is filled with enemies. The level of cognitive dexterity required to respond to all this at once is beyond that of an average human.
So you lose, and lose, because the game is unfairly spamming you with too many threats to react to; up until the point where you randomly don't lose because of luck; and then the game tells you that you won. And then it's over, and you've spent however many hours playing a game that's only a half hour worth of relatively blank levels and little content.
For an extra five dollars, you can go buy any of the multiple other Rogue-like giants out there which not only have massive amounts of content and diversity more then this game, but have difficulty that is based on something more then enemy spam.

Napoleon: Total War is fundamentally a very enjoying RTS game. I only have two big gripes with Napoleon. The first gripe is that - much like Empire - the textures on units and structures are shockingly low res, even when set to high. Not that it ruins the game, but it's offputting how grainy it can look when zoomed right in. In Shogun, this wasn't as big of an issue. My second gripe is that the offline campaign - which is honestly about the same as that of any other Total War game - focuses strictly on Napoleon Bonaparte's real-world campaign. This shouldn't be a shock, since the game's called ♥♥♥♥ing Napoleon, but it would be AMAZING if this game had the same huge campaign map that Empire did. The time period could have also been a little big bigger - but again, it was to accomodate Bonaparte's epoch, so I get it.
I grabbed some DLC for this when they were 0.50$ a piece during the Sega sale, and I really enjoyed the addition of some historical units for all countries. Especially the UK units! Total War has a good example of how to do DLC right - some neat additions that don't make the game better or worse, for a reasonable price. All the DLC does is add some historically accurate units, so really it's just for the sake of eyecandy and to please history buffs.
The combat also feels mechanically better than it does in Empire. Not much to say about it, but it feels better. Pretty much all there is to it.
9/10, worth the money! Total War never disappoints.

THEN I REALIZED... - the lack of description is a part of the game (and it certainly adds to the aesthetic too). It becomes a search for knowledge, trying out different powerups and see what they do, finding things out for yourself and experimenting, exploring the game world and it's items, weapons, powerups, enemies, and even finding out how the game's mechanics work. Since that realization I have been largely enjoying the game and embraced the unknown things that come my way, trying to figure them out by myself. I suspect this is not something everyone would enjoy, BUT I sure have and continue to do so :)
DIFFICULTY - The game offers quite the challenge and death comes often, however I am eager to get back in there and try a new set up of items/weapons/powerups and learn from my mistakes and try once more to reach further than I did before, slowly but surely I am getting better and further and further, and a sense of curious exploration of the game world as well as the welcome challenge keeps me coming back for more!
STORY & WORLD DESIGN - The story is weird, but likeable (and kind of cute) if you are into quirky stuff. It is not a masterful storyline I'd say (although I have not beaten it yet) but it sure is a playful universe full of interesting creatures and features!
AESTHETIC - The playful, minimalistic artstyle and animation along with the funky, mysterious soundtrack adds up to a really cool atmosphere, and the curious creatures/enemies you encounter are often charming and interesting.

Team Fortress Classic Review – Raymond KT
Summary: One of the most popular online action games of all time, Team Fortress Classic features over nine character classes -- from Medic to Spy to Demolition Man -- enlisted in a unique style of online team warfare. Each character class possesses unique weapons, items, and abilities, as teams compete online in a variety of game play modes
To me, Team Fortress Classic was unfairly dumped in a bin called “a team-based multiplayer shooter like Counter-Strike only messy and guff.” As I say, I know that’s an unfair comparison, but I stand by thinking the game messy. I never ever joined a Team Fortress Classic server and had a pleasant experience. It was always chaotic; it was always full of conc-jumping wunderkids; I always seemed to pick a class that felt useless; its maps always seemed to result in stalemates around single, narrow chokepoints. I never had fun. Or, well, that’s not true. There was one thing I liked about the game: feign death. The ability to at any point press a button and pretend to be a corpse. Most players would be wise to the trick and would shoot you as you lay prone on the ground, but occasionally you’d experience the wonderful thrill of watching a player walk by you unknowingly. I think I only managed to use that scenario to my advantage a few times, but it was worth it each time. A preview of what the Spy brought as a matter of course to Team Fortress 2. Before you take to the comments to lambast me: I can appreciate that Team Fortress Classic had a lot going for it. I think maybe if I’d been in a clan then I’d have liked it. Sing its praises in the comments if you feel like it. Team Fortress Classic is awesome. There are many different game types you can play on it. You can play a game with two teams where you have to capture the flag. You can play a game where you have to hunt a important person, or you can be one of the people protecting him. There are also games where both teams consist of only snipers. You do need to have the Internet to play the game, but if you are reading this review, then you already have the Internet. This game is worth playing because once you start playing, you can pick it up really easy. If you like team-play and shooting games this is for you. For being an older game TFC (Team Fortress Classic) has very nice graphics. The levels look really good and have been put together very nicely. The teams are easily distinguishable due to their obvious red and blue colors. The guns all look god and most are based of real weaponry, they are tru to form. TFC has everything Counter-Strike(CS) has but even more. The mission of the game is to attack or defend a fort (depending on which team you are). If you are on the attack team you must do your best to invade the fort with your flag. This is no easy task though as the defending team gets high powered weaponry to defend their fort with. Using your skill you need to infiltrate the base through secret passageways or just blasting in the front door guns blazing. The movement is extremely fast, but not out of control, which make the game much more fun and easier t move around without getting blown to pieces. This is purely a multiplayer game so there is a ton of replay value. Just keep playing rounds to improve your skill or play on the different team for some variety, or even try a different type of soldier to be! There is plenty of possibilities.
