I haven't played many city sims before except for a bit of Tropico. This is very different. There is a bit of a steep learning curve, as the goal is different than other games. You are attempting to build up a town into a thriving community, but instead of doing this through currency, everthing is done through resources. The game is essentially resource management - which sounds easy, but can prove increasingly difficult as your population booms, natural disasters occur, crops get ruined, or disease spreads.
I have played a few towns, and have very much enjoyed it. Each time i've played, I have so easily lost complete track of time. It's rare for me to get so absorbed in a game. I spent a solid 8 hours playing it one day without realizing it.
On the neg side though, after building up your town to include a few other sub-towns, and get them to a point where they are relatively self-sufficient resource wise, the game kind of loses its drive (for me anyway). You could essentially play it until you have the map completely filled up with buildings and such, but at that point your population would inevitably die off due to inability to expand. This fact makes me not care to play a map longer than a day or two.
The most fun i've had is starting off, trying to make it through the first few years, and building my town up to be self sufficient, then toying with it for a bit. I think I will continue to enjoy this game for a few more maps, but can see myself losing interest in it due to resource management being the only real priority in the game.
I guess this review might sound kind of negative, but all in all i've really enjoyed this game and definitely recommend it. The nature graphics are great, controls are easy, it has a customizable UI, and is moddable. I give it a 8/10.

Infinifactory may be the finest puzzle game I've ever played. It presents you with a simple input/output problem to solve, and gives you tools to solve it. And while the game starts you out with basic routing problems, it eventually has you creating complex production lines that require multiple actions to run harmoniously in parallel. The challenge is in how you abstract and breakdown the problem in to managable pieces, which is vastly more similar to most kinds of real-world problem solving than what is presented by most puzzle games.
And I think that's part of the satisfaction that Infinifactory provides, is that it tests applicable problem solving -- it stretches your brain, creatively, and not just on arbitrary game logic (though, let's not kid ourselves, this is not a "realistic" game).
On top of the really excellent puzzles, Infinifactory is also coupled with an absurd but engrossing little narrative, presented (at first) through mostly environmental details. It leaves you scouring each area for audio logs for a little more insight -- and when that reaches a natural plateau, things really take off.
Infinifactory is truly masterful gamedesign; a must play.

It's much more convincing, at times even scary in its realistic depiction of the brutality of war, more realistic, and, while heavily (almost completely) centered around infantry combat at this point, it sure as hell does it well.

Warface offers free to play shooting with classes and co-operative modes against an ever expanding number of maps. Available for PC and at one point Xbox 360 (shut down Feb 2015) Warface is a highly rated free to play shooter.Co-op mode in Warface features a class system of Rifleman, Sniper, Medic and Engineer which each bring their own skills to ensure victory in the daily missions that you and your friends will have to conquer. This ensures a fresh challenge each day to face and gives you plenty of unlockable content spread across the three difficultly levels of Regular, Skilled and Hardcore.
While co-op is varied and a great way to hone your skills you’ll also find a solid competitive landscape offered by Warface that brings all the usual game modes to life. Warface offers the likes of team deathmatch, free for all, bomb plating, destruction and a handful of other modes where you’ll be able to again swap between the class of your soldier.These classes in both PvE and PvP fill typical roles and shine more so in the PvE where their special action can provide greater benefit to the team as opposed to the shorter lifespans of PvP spawns. The Rifleman for example carries extra ammunition for his team while the Medic can heal and revive team mates.
All of this gameplay is wrapped in the pretty package of the CRYENGINE which makes graphics sharp throughout the game modes. Other unique elements of Warface include the ability to slide which adds another combat element, the unique interactions of players (like giving a team member a boost to secure higher ground) and a solid collection of weapon customisation that can be done within the game itself. I wish I could recommend this game, but I can't. Not even for the price of 5 dollars.
Apparently the plot states that you have been shipwrecked on Rosecliff Island, and your task is to collect items to help you escape. There is no explanation as to who the previous resident(s) of the island were, or why the island is now deserted. There is no dialogue with NPCs, no narration, nothing. The gameplay consists of you bouncing from one hidden object scene to the next, and as you finish a "level," you complete a simple "puzzle" game such as a word search or matching tiles. Upon completion of the puzzle games, you are rewarded an item to assist in your escape, such as a bucket or a stack of wood. As you progress along, you begin to see the same hidden object scenes again... and again... and again. As much as I enjoy hidden object games, even I found myself overwhelmed with mind-numbing boredom.
On the plus side, the artwork is nice, with the hidden object scenes not being overly cluttered, and the items were often cleverly hidden.
Verdict: Don't spend 5 dollars for this game unless you happen to enjoy visiting the same hidden object scenes over and over. If so, buy it if it is on sale for 90 percent off.

A good is fairly standard ARPG.
Charecter creation is suprisingly (for this type of game) detailed. You select male or female, then adjust hair style, colour, and body. Finaly, you pick a name and a God. God's are this games version of classes, as which one you select determins what weapons and skills you are using. You can switch God's at any time by equiping their weapon. For example Loki is dual wield, Thor is two handed, and Tyr is one handed. As you level up , you get skill points to spend. These can be spent on any God, and are a fairly standard mix.
To level up, you collect Blood from your defeted foes. Then take it to an alter and sacrafice it. You then get a meny asking what stat you want to increase. This is not presented in the standard way of Strength, Agility, Constitution, ect... Rather, you are presented with the actual end result. For example, Damage, Attack Speed, & Health are all choices.
Combat is fairly standard mix of attack and dodge, with skills on cool downs and such. Nothing cutting edge, but fairly well executed.
As you adventure, resources drop form smashing destructables and from chests. You will need to collect these to upgrade your village, and to buy new equipment. When you sell your old or usless gear, you get resorces back. Fortunatly, you do not use invenotry space for this.
The biggest problem is pathfinding. It is very easy to get stuck in what looks like a viable path. The AI does this as well.  An are of opertunity, for the Dev's would be to add better invetory managment. There is no reall sort method, only a filter by basic type.
Graphics and preformance are good on my i5-3570, with a R9-390x, I have no complaints in this area.
Overall a well executed game, but not worth AAA 60$. Fortunatly they are not selling it at that level and this game is definatly worth a buy at the 40$ level.

After a few hours of struggling to kill moths and crickets, I was kidnapped by one of the game's two factions and forced to study in a locked barracks with other recruits.  I acted out by stealing from the other students and staff at every opportunity.  Still graduated, which makes this a great public school simulator.
Good:
- Many quests have multiple solutions.
- Both factions are flawed with good intentions.  After I joined one faction I was still able to speak to the other one.  They addressed me differently but didn't hate.  It was interesting to see how the two sides viewed each other during conversations.
Bad:
- Lots of backtracking for quests.  Fast travel is introduced after a few hours, and it helps somewhat.
- Some quests have unclear objectives.
Sadly, I encountered a bug that prevented me from moving forward.  I visited 5 required locations and dug an item out of the ground at each, but the game only recorded 4 times.  As a result, I couldn't see the game to its end.  I still enjoyed the time spent.
Other reviewers have many complaints so here are some tips:
- Force vertical sync in your GPU control panel.  If you don't, climbing a ledge will make your hero get stuck.  Weird fix but it works.
- Turn the difficulty down.  No shame in it.
- Quicksave often.  I did before and after every fight.
- You must specialize to survive. This is not Skyrim where you can master everything.
- In combat, stand very close to the enemy.  Sidestep their attacks to hit their exposed back.  This works with almost every enemy type.
Excellent in every aspect, a must have for Strategy gamers.

This is a historically important game as far as multiplayer FPSes are concerned, but is it worth playing now? Well...if it's on sale and/or if you adore vintage shooters, I'd say yes.
Comparing this to
is kind of like looking into a time capsule. It's janky, not
well-balanced, and the grenade spam is real (real stupid, even.) The Spy has no cloak or sapper, instead he can feign death as a fake corpse, and if anything that makes him even harder to play. The Pyro is kind of useless, and the Medic usually ends up launching himself at the enemy team to poison them with his medkit, which let me tell you is far, far less intuitive to use than TF2's mediguns.
Both he and the Scout have concussion grenades that let experienced players literally fly all over the map, in addition to bunnyhopping letting you go faster in general, although at least the game doesn't totally revolve around them like
does.
On the other hand, there's not hundreds and hundreds of hats bloating the game, and since there's no unlockable weapons as well as fewer hidden "pro level" mechanics to learn about, it's actually a little more intuitive overall than TF2 is at this point.
It can still be fun - it still has that Team Fortress magic, but with the high percentage of veterans in the playerbase and the age of the game, you'll have to come to terms with it like most old school titles. There's not that many players; the daily average is around 100. Some of them
clean your clock if you're new, as mentioned before. If you want to experience this, ideally you'd get a couple friends to join you, or find a 'TFC revival' group that arranges pick-up games.

I had a lot of fun with this game in my childhood, but looking back, there are a lot of problems with it. Bethesda has a long track record of developing great games, and slowly dumbing down consecutive titles to appeal to a wider audience. Unfortunately, Fallout 3 falls victim to this.
The nuanced, layered story of fallout 1 and 2 are thrown away for a much more linear, black-and-white story with clear good guys, few meaningful choices, and villains that are either so poorly developed that they barely seem like characters, or feel like they should be in a saturday morning cartoon. Sometimes both.
And when I say linear, I mean in comparison to the previous titles not developed by Bethesda. In Fallout 1, you are just sent of into the wasteland with no compass, no clear bath to your goal, just instructions to find a water chip, vague directions on where you MIGHT find one (which don't even turn out to be correct) and a vast and interesting world to explore in search of one. You discover your own path.
In Fallout 3, you are always railroaded along, gravitating towards the marker on your compass to talk to essential NPC #33 or get the next McGuffin. And don't get me wrong. The water chip WAS a McGuffin, but you weren't railroaded along a path, following a marker to get it. It took you half the game to find it, and you needed to find your own way, asking NPCs about it, travelling from location to location, and discovering quests, obstacles, and hints along the way. Fallout 3 seems like a halway-shooter by comparison.
I am a big fan of the Fallout series and the Fallout universe. Hell, I've even played Fallout Pen and Paper, but if you're looking for a good fallout game, I would recommend playing Fallout 1 and 2. If you're looking for a good fallout game that's also an FPS and a little bit easier to get into (Not requiring patches or knowledge of the rules and mechanics), then I would recommend you check out Fallout: New Vegas. In fact, check out all 3 of those games. They are some of the best roleplaying experiences you can have digitally.

I enjoy hidden object games, usually.
The problem with Escape Rosecliff Island is that, unlike a lot of hidden object games, there is almost no storyline. You don't get to explore an island, pick up tools along the way, find hidden object scenes and solve puzzles to advance like a lot of the popular hidden object games. You just pick a scene, find some objects, go to the next one, find some objects. Every once in a while, you break up the endless monotony with an extremely simple puzzle; such as, matching cards and word searches. After finishing the end-level puzzle (word search, match-3, etc.) you receive a tool to help you escape the island.
I tried to push through, until I realized that you start revisiting scenes. After that, I just couldn't take anymore.
Maybe, I skipped a cut scene? All I know is that I have no idea why I was on the island. The puzzles are flat and boring and I have no hope that the ending would do this game any justice.

Did you like Cave Story? well this is just that but with worse combat, procedural generation and dubious mechanics. Oh and the main quest is a mediocre fetch job. I don't know how this hasn't been established yet, but in a metroidish title, where you can only shoot in a straight line, DON'T PUT CONSTANTLY FLYING ENEMIES UNLESS YOU BUILD THE LEVEL AROUND IT. See the straight line shooting works in games like Cave Story or Axiom Verge because the levels are built around established mechanics and in both those games you can shoot up and down, which enables more options against flying enemies, and reduces the player's weak spots. GoNNER lacks this feature because... I have absolutely no idea. It tries to compensate by allowing you to kerb-stomp enemies Mario style, but the controls are a bit wonky and falling is faster than it should be for this mechanic. Or just have shooting be directional to the mouse pointer/analogue stick. There's also an ammo limit, a feature that was added solely to screw with flow apparently. there are a couple of other niggles, every time you get hit you drop your current loadout and have to manually go and pick it up, and if you get hit while in this state game over. This could work as a mechanic if the other mechanics weren't garbage but with how they are now it's just another problem. Level design is randomly generated, and rouge-like. No care or effort was put into thinking how this algorithm functions because the level design is just straight up awful. The game gives you an infinite wall jump to compensate for any impossible architecture which to me just seems lazy. Art style is okay. I like that it's not Pixelated because the majority of the indie market seems to be stuck in 1990 when it comes to resolution but it's still too minimalist and lacking the vibrant tone that this sort of game needs. Sound design is okay as well, didn't stand out or feel like sandpaper so I guess that's a pass. Story isn't even trying, you have to go find things for your friend, a depressed whale. That, coupled with the octo-cat elevators is desperately trying to stand out as kooky and weird, but again it doesn't match the tone and just sticks out. Overall I wouldn't recommend this game, it's inherently flawed mechanics just make it impossible to enjoy.

This is a solid tool that will enable you to create JRPGs with relative ease. And I would love to recommend it because it really IS a good and solid piece of software. Putting together a small game is a breeze- maps are designed in a WYSIWYG editor, there is a good default library of graphics and objects. And everything works just fine. Random encounters, multiple characters, shops, turn based combat, it's all there right out of the box and even a newcomer will quickly see his idea turn into something playable. In addition, you're free to release your game whichever way you see fit, even a commercial release is possible. There is a lot to like here.
Still I find it hard to fully recommend RPG Maker VX Ace. This is why:
1) It is very expensive. 60 Euros are a lot of money, especially if you're just curious and maybe want to make a small freeware game. The program has been on sale quite regularly though, dropping to 15 Euros, and that is a good investment indeed. But before you shell out even THAT money, consider getting the freely available "limited" version, which has everything the commercial release has, and only limits the number of objects that can be used. It's still absolutely possible to make decent games with it.
2) It is highly restrictive. You can make "classic JRPGs" with ease, but as a newcomer, you're truly stuck with the template RPG Maker provides. The interface, combat rules and attribute system are very, very basic and apart from a quick paint job there's not much you can do... until you're ready to dive into Ruby scripting.
3) Scripting is a pain. On the pro side, the Ruby SL is powerful enough to change virtually every aspect of a project. You can create your own combat system, you can create your own attribute system, you can create new interfaces and really make something unique. But the editor is so barebones that you can't really do it comfortably, and especially if you have ever used a more advanced code editor you'll soon wish you could write your code THERE.
4) It doesn't take advantage of ANYTHING. Multiple resolutions should be a standard these days, but here you're stuck with a relatively low native resolution that looks charmingly retro or crude depending on your personal opinion. Large games tend to stutter occasionally. And what about a decent options menu? Not to be found.
So that's the gist of it. If you like JRPGs, see RPG Maker VX Ace on a discount and feel you can live with the limitations, I daresay you won't be disappointed. It's really fun to make a plot-driven game and see your ideas walk around the screen. Then there is the vast amount of resources available; if you put some effort into it your game can look downright stunning. And there clearly IS a lot of quality in the product- it's not been around for so long for nothing and the Steam version with its Workshop support will defenitely prove worth your while.
But it could, and should, be so much better, more accessible, more comfortable to use- and that's where the tool lets you down.

Five Nights is the epitome of horror games. It is fear in gaming distilled to its purest form; an experience that forces you to give it your full attention and focus while it strips you of any sense of balance or safety. It is unnerving and upsetting to its core.
What truly makes this remarkable is how simple the game is. There is really only one action: Close the Door button only and always when you think you're about to be attacked. Close too early, and you waste power. Close too late, and you are doomed.
All the rest is window dressing to this, but what is there is so perfectly executed. I must emphasize that what I say is praise. The simplicity is to its benefit, providing you with absolutely nothing to distract you from your feelings of foreboding, dread, and terror.
This is, in many ways, the perfect horror game.

Absolutely. Amazing.
I don't write reviews often. Hell, I'm not even a type of nerd to play this kind of game. However, one day I was feeling pretty gloomy and tired. I decided to buy this game for about 2 dollars from a sale to give it a go. It met my expectations not only as perfectly as I had thought it could hold, but even added to it. The nurturing music, the vibrant lands, the skillfull thinking - it inherits it all. You're not simply trying to chill out with some nice brain music and wander the beautiful lands they give you - you try to make it complete and restore it.
You are, well, you. As you wander through the map you'll have to complete little 'missions', and by that I mean reaching a certain destination put out with a beacon flare. As you walk and run and jump and crouch towards your objective, as you do that, you change the rocky lands into grass lands. Every block must be covered to make a complete 100% (you can track it by hitting the pause menu, aka esc.) and if you collect every red-glowing block, you'll be met with 4 achievements as of March 16, 2017 - amazing quotes and expressions to really press you down and melt you. It will make you think for a second, think back and reflect on the world. It will put your body into a state of paralysis. You will die of the thought alone. Once you get used to the game, it becomes simple. A game of exploring the lands, while at the same time saving it; with your present being a nice little expression x4.
What I'm saying is this game is truly amazing. All of the graphics and details put into this game are beautiful. For a 2015 game, it's extraordinary. I'm so surprised it hasn't dazzled the market as of yet. Infinifactory is the best puzzle game I have ever played, bar none. Period. In my opinion, a good puzzle needs to meet three conditions:
1. It must require hard thinking to solve
2. It must not be frustrating when no immediate solution can be found
3. it must make you feel smart when a solution IS found.
The first point is pretty obvious, since most people play puzzle games  in order to think. point 2 is the reason I don't like puzzles as a genre; almost all puzzles can only be solved in one exact way, and if I am not thinking in the super unorthodox and particular way the author deems to be correct, I cannot solve it, and that is frustrating to me. Point 3 is the most important. I can accept some frustration if I end up feeling good when I finallly solve the puzzle. However, again almost all puzzles I have tried make me feel like an idiot for not seeing the solution quicker, when in fact the solution was by design arbitrary and for the lack of a better word, "stupid".
Enter Infinifactory. 1. Infinifactory is hard! I have sat at a single puzzle for literally 3 hours scratching my head trying different solutions only to be foiled by something. It requires three-dimensional visualization and thinking. It requires both hard thinking and creativity in order to solve.
2. The aforementioned puzzle I tried for 3 hours didn't feel like 3 hours. I decided to play the game for 20 minutes one night before bed, and 3 hours later I realize it has not been 20 minutes. I then continued for another 3 hours (I didn't need sleep *cough*). Infinifactory lets you constantly make progress towards a solution, even when I largely have to start over and delete what I did. It does this by naturally building off of previously done things, and requiring you to combine many small solutions into a coherent whole.
Finally, 3. Infinifactory makes me feel like a ****ing mastermind mechanical engineer and PhD in quantuum mechanics that just solved nuclear fusion when a factory I built works and works beautifully. I have  never rage quit this game once, since even failing is fun. Seeing the factory being built as it becomes more and more complex is satisfying and inheritantly lets you want to continue and not get frustrated. I would recommend this at 5x the price.
TL;DR: It is fun to struggle to a solution even when it takes hours to get there.

Infinifactory is, at it's core, a simple problem solving game. You must get blocks from point A to point B in a specific configuration. It's your job to figure out how to do that with the blocks given. Creating assembly lines that will move your pieces around and assemble them into the finished product.
If you like puzzle games, and enjoy building things, then this is a game you would likely enjoy.  Construction is reminicent of minecraft and other sandbox block building games, with a lot of trial-&-error required to get to the solutions.
Pros:
-Fun, unique, and clever. Well designed game
-Promotes thinking outside the box
-Easy to learn, hard to put down
-Steam Workshop, so you can pit your brain against other people's creations
Cons:
-The "campaign" is a bit short and completed easily
-Often a single solution works for most puzzles with a littlte tweaking
-Puzzles weren't as challenging as I had hoped. Looking forward to playing with community content.
Overall, I'd give the game an easy 8/10 for fun, unique, puzzle play.  If you like puzzle games and block building sandbox games, buy this. It's a great sort of fusion of the two.

I am just off a 3+ hours livestream of Risen and I want to write this review with ideas and impressions fresh in my mind.
If you're only interested in the short version:
Pretty good game that open-world game fans will enjoy even though your patience will be tested at times.
I run Windows 10 and had no problems whatsoever lauching/running the game.
Pretty graphics, funny moments at times because my character was witty, more often because he really wasn't :D
The longer version:
- Personal remark
Unlike many rpgs, I didn't identify with my character: I didn't create him, oh, he's a him too. But that's all right as I often questioned his intelligence and was indeed quite happy to refer to him as my character rather than me.
- the looks
Very pretty, npcs look fine especially for a 2009 game but I felt they all looked alike (only went to one region, full of men), the landscape is well designed. Animations looked awkward at times but really not a dealbreaker. Day and night cycles felt appropriately long (especially night that is proper pitch black, let me tell you, I used them torches).
Props to the game for immersion, letting you drink (a whole barrel), cook (an empty pan) take a bath (fully clothed). What I mean is, there was a definite effort to make the game immersive and it is successful for the most part. ;)
- the sounds
No problem with the music or the effects. Voice acting is good, sometimes funny (they swear and come up with entertaining insults).
- the story
Only 3 hours in so I have only seen a tiny bit of the main quest. I can tell there are factions which makes the game replayable. Occasionally I felt I was forced into choices I didn't want but that happens with rpgs.
- the combat system
Fighting felt somewhat limited because my actions are click, double click to attack, right click to parry, possibly double tap to jump to the side rather slowly (so not a good dodge). To be fair though, it is more than Morrowind ever offered. It is also less than modern action games that give you combos and whatnots.
- levelling up
From what I can tell, you fight, get xp, level up netting you learning points. You then use learning points (and gold) at trainers that will improve or teach you skills or train your stats.
There aren't too many skills and no skill tree. A shame as it *may* reduce how unique your character becomes. But then again, only 3+ hours in...

GoNNER is a fantastic little game that is incredibly addictive, hard and unique.
Not dissimilar to games such as Downwell this game is partially randomly generated and the goal is to survive as long as you can through random small dungeons. You control your character Ikk and try and get from one end of a room to the other; throughout this room will be a horde of different enemies each of which have unique characteristics and will present different dangers to the player depending on where they're situated or whether they're grouped together with other enemies. Like Devil Daggers each enemy has a unique tell and you must quickly assess the situation in order to move through the room without being harmed.
Ikk has 3 inventory slots: a gun, head and backpack. Guns range from shotguns and pistols to lasers and so on, each having a unique feel and ammo capacity. Heads are similar to Downwell's 'styles' in that they intrinsically change the character. The default head has 5 or so hearts but you could change this head in order to have different physics but less hearts for instance. Backpacks are like special abilities. The default backpack grants Ikk an instant reload (whereas usually he must run and collect ammo from fallen enemies) but later ones send out a flurry of extra bullets in fast succession or freeze time momentarily.
Although the game is randomly generated it still contains distinct levels and a similar sense of progression to the gameplay. Knowing what inventory to take into later levels becomes very important.
One of the most addictive elements of GoNNER is its combo system that rewards quick chaining of enemy kills. As this chain rises the music intensifies and becomes more complex and more points are earned. To keep a chain going though you must sacrifice picking up key items such as the purple cubes that are dropped by enemies that act as both continues and currency in the games many shops. Do you try and keep a chain going throughout multiple levels whilst leaving behind certain upgrades, enemies or items or do you take a slower and more methodical pace in order to maximise your purple cubes to use in the eventual event of your death?
GoNNER is a really fun roguelike platformer that I wouldn't hesitate to recommend (especially at its sale price!). It's unique and addictive moment to moment gameplay and phenomenal award winning sound design and visuals round off the package nicely too.

Not only is the game meta, but it got me pretty thinking pretty meta... up in my own head with how to interpret it. It convinced me that many times I feel like Coda and other times like Davey. There were stretches where I believed it was entirely fiction, but also moments where I thought it must be a true story. I've certainly known real creators who produced stuff like Coda (including myself at times), so it's not that far fetched. In the end I guess it's semi autobiographical and in that sense it's nice to understand Davey a little better.
I love that it's short, smooth, and self contained. Davey's final words are sort of a cop out, but after that there's some good closure. This game will definately ring true for other creators, not just game makers, and may also work for fans of "creepy pasta" stuff. It's sort of a ghost story and it would be interesting to see if the myth gains a following beyond this game. Compared to Stanley, this will appeal less broadly for lack of humor, but it's cool to see that he can do a game with a very different emotional core and nail it.

So I'm not an hidden object game aficionado.  This is only the second one I've played.  Anyway, the number one reason why I'm not recommending this is the ridiculous amount of repetition.  Each of the 25 puzzle locations has in the neighborhood of 50-70 hidden objects in them.  In the main mode, you visit each of them by level 15 but then are forced to play 10 more levels (of multiple locations each) to get to the end.  I think the justification for the repetition is that you search for 10 objects at a time per location but since the objects are also repeated across locations it just feels even more repetitious.  Secondly, the threadbare "story."  Each level, after searching several locations on the island, you collect an item to help you get to the end of the game. SPOILER
Other that that, after each level you get to do a simple game mode like card matching, match 3, word search, or some jigsaw type ones.  These are just ok.  You can unlock a mode where you get to do 15 levels of match three, but that was the least fun type.  Now on the plus side, the hidden objects are well placed within the locations and there was some fun word play in the clues sometimes.  Also, I did enjoy the simple final escape puzzle.  I was surprised to find that I really enjoyed the Unlimited Seek and Find mode that you can unlock.  Contrary to what I expected in this mode, you get to find every available item at a location (which like I said seemed to be in the 50-70 item range.)  I played through the game twice because I knew I wanted to write a review, but otherwise I only would have played through it once.   BOTTOM LINE: For half the price, Season of Mystery: The Cherry Blossom Murders is a better hidden object game buy.  It has an actual story and less repetition and Steam achievements.  However, if you're going by game time alone, Escape from Rosecliff Island forces you to spend much more time on it.

I'm currently watching the developers on the community forums to see how they respond to the players feedback and  I do keep coming back to it regularly to check on gameplay.
I bought this game believing that it would provide a viable alternative to Diablo 3 which is the nearest comparison I can make based on the hack n slash games I own and play.  The Norse-Viking theme appealed to me as it did others, and I was looking forward to a fresh series of "Acts" to play through on various levels of difficulty.
The graphics are nice, the theme is novel, and it looks like an AAA game which is how they priced it. Sadly it doesn't currently play like one, the interface being clunky and making the process of crafting,selling, enchanting, and dismantling equipment an absolute nightmare.
There is no stash, limited bagspace (with no option to upgrade) that quickly fills up with grey garbage, no returning to town to dispose of gear mid level, and no carry over of your character's level and equipment for re-runs. Effectively, no replayablity.  The Skill Trees are basic bare bones and only apply to specific weapon types while the side objectives for each area don't vary that greatly, tempting you to abandon them.
A weak story can result in the player thinking "what am I doing this for?" and I experienced that playing Wolves of Midgard.  God, I tried, but to me it didn't have any depth and I never felt that my character was progressing.
This game needs a lot of further development to make it stand up against it's better known competitors and I hope the developers  front up to the pc customers, admit they got it wrong first time, and set about fixing it.   Like I said it does have a lot of potential but some of the features come across as "half arsed" and unfinished - I couldn't play this on keyboard and mouse without the use of a controller as well, which thoroughly defeats the object.
It's also very apparent that this game was primarily designed for casual console players with the PC community somewhat of an "afterthought" given all the reported interface problems and the lack of depth in the content.
I can't recommend it in the current state as I don't think you get enough back for your bucks but I do intend to monitor the community news for updates from the developers and will log in regularly to check on gameplay.
If the game gets better then I will change the review accordingly.  I hope they sort it - this game has a lot of potential!

I'm not even finished with this game yet, but it's killing me. Unfortunately my computer is laggy and the graphics aren't as great as they would be due to that. I repeatedly run into things, can't move due to lag, and end up dying.
But anyhow, it's a great horror game, although I scare easily. The music's really nicely done. It creates anticipation, atmosphere and anxiety. While there are the cliché jump scares, setting, and artwork for rooms, it's still a very chilling game. Gore, blood everywhere, fire, darkness, chase scenes, corpses everywhere are all cliché scares and we all know it. But the fact that you don't exactly know where to go and do makes it scary. It's unpredictable and twists and turns are everywhere throughout the game. (Quite literally.) When you have to use the night vision on your camera, it's super creepy. You don't know when the darkness will go away and you don't want to use up batteries. You don't know when the next battery will show up.
Although the repetitive tasks are a bit annoying. (Pull levers, drain water, etc.) And at those points the game isn't really even scary and the enemies just become immensely annoying. And when you're not playing on insane difficulty, you would prefer to die and start over at the checkpoint rather than continue from your current place.
But so far, this game is really interesting and keeps on making me want to play. But I don't ever play it if I'm alone, to be honest.

Risen is essentially a spiritual successor to the Gothic series with the developer Piranha Bytes losing rights to the name Gothic but retaining pretty much everything else. Since its release in 2009 I've owned both the pc and xbox port of the game, although until recently hadn't gotten around to actually completing the game, and in wake of that, I really must recommend Risen.
Without too many spoilers, Risen takes place on the island of Faranga, where the hero washes up after the ship he is on crashes, and before long is thrown into the struggles of the island and the people on it.
I shall do a list of pro's and cons to make it easier to get a good impression:
PROS :
-Great feel of progression (I went from a man covered in rags to feeling like a badass)
-Very nicely designed world, filled with people, animals and looooots of hidden things to find (like caves and secret passages)
-Enjoyable combat system which grows over time.
-No need to kill NPC's when you upset them and otherwise. (you can just beat them up and that settles conflict or they will beat you up)
-Quests that don't just feel like fetch quests and npc's that don't just seem like they are there to provide you with something to do.
-2 factions to join and roughly 4 classes to choose from or mix. These Factions being fairly grey in morality and not providing just a good versus evil.
-Voice Acting by Actors; John Rhys-Davies, Lena Headey, Andy Serkis and more.
-Plenty of Loot and Skills to aquire.
CONS:
-Graphics were outdated for its time of release and can be very muddy. (This said I still overall like its aesthetics and its   graphics never bothered me, though it can be weird as occasionally you can find areas where the graphics look very good)
-Occasional bug or two causing npc's to be somewhere other than where they should be or quest not seeming to finish.
I have to heartely recommend Risen, while it may not be as pretty as many other Rpg's, Risen is a great game really worth a shot for anyone who wants to enjoy a classic Rpg that doesn't hold your hand.

Angry Joe memes aside, the Risen series is a great trilogy of RPGs created by Piranha Bytes that will please anyone who's into more old-school action role-playing games. Risen is a game that will challenge you and maybe even frustrate you at times, but it will also reward you, and the whole while will leave you to your own devices to figure things out.
Risen is an "open" world RPG from the creators of the legendary Gothic series, but it's not exactly the type of open-world you see from games like Skyrim or the GTA series. Unlike those games, in Risen you have to pay attention not to head into a dangerous area when you aren't prepared or well-equipped as you will get slaughtered in an instant. There are tough enemies right from the start of the game sprinkled in hard to reach areas all over the map, and if you can somehow survive in those areas, you can visit them and maybe even make out with a rare treasure for your effort. The world is also not as huge as Skyrim, but it feels more hand-crafted in that every plant, rare or otherwise, and every item in the game is meticulously hand-placed. So, when you find that obscured path to the top of a mountain with a small clearing, behind that conspicuous tree over near the ledge may be a chest with a sword sticking out of it, a sword you can take, a rare plant nearby and so on. You will find surprises like this all over the map, and the level design and overall way their worlds are build to reward your exploration is second to none in Piranha Bytes games.
Another great aspect of PB (Piranha Bytes) games is also the unique settings they have. In Risen, you are a stowaway who gets washed up on a mysterious island with only the rags on your back. This starts the traditional PB feature of starting with nothing and having to scavenge and do whatever you can just to survive in a harsh world. You will have to make friends, and you'll quickly realize that not everyone wants to be your friend. You will have to get stronger and explore if you have any chance of surviving. The various characters you meet will have dialogue that often has humor, wit and charm, and while it's not really a hugely cinematic, storytelling game, the story that is there is interesting enough to keep you playing the game, exploring ruins on the strange island you find yourself on and wanting to learn more about the world and its lore. These games really do a good job of making you feel weak at the start and keeping a methodical, rewarding sense of progression throughout the game where every little thing can make a big difference to how long you last in the world.
Making choices as to how you play your character also has consequences. Whether it's the skills you invest in, the gear you buy or the faction you join, you have to pay some attention and play somewhat wisely to get the most out of the game. These decisions not only heavily impact the gameplay and the playstyle you choose, but also determine the way the story unfolds for you. Character building decisions are often the difference between life and death in the game, literally. A full set of armor will make a huge difference against tougher enemies, and armor and weapons do not rain down on you from the sky, so even getting a single set of decent armor is a big achievement in the game! The loot in general is a bit more low-key, so when you find an enchanted ring or a fancy weapon, you really appreciate it. There is also extensive crafting in the game, but like everything else in the game it takes effort to figure out and accomplish. You can become a Goldsmith to create various trinkets, a Blacksmith to sharpen and create new weapons, an Alchemist to create potions that not only heal you but can also use rare ingredients to permanently buff your character and explore many other professions. The game is stricter with its progression but also gives you tons of freedom to be creative, play the way you want to and tell your own story.
As far as factions go, they are also a traditional PB feature. The faction you choose will determine a lot of things for you, from skills you get access to to what weapons and items you can use. You can't even get close to the head guy in charge until you prove yourself and work your way up the ranks. When you do, though, again the game greatly rewards you in some way, whether it's making a powerful ally, getting sent on new, important missions or just getting some sweet and much needed loot to help you. It should go without saying as this point that if you build your character poorly you may find yourself having a harder time. However, the game is not super strict, so if you explore and use your RPG Senses you will figure things out and get good results. In short, it's a bit more unforgiving than you're probably used to, with a very minimal amount of "hand holding", but if you stick with it the end result is a much more rewarding RPG that you can get lost in.
What this game ISN'T is something you're going to pick up and just breeze through. You can't really follow the mini-map to every quest location, heck, you will have to find an actual map just to get your bearings! The combat is not a button-masher and you will get rocked early and often. You can't really learn every skill in the game or even get good with every weapon type as it's going to be hard to find all the skill points, money and experience you need to do so. The voice acting is great, but it's not going to be a cinematic movie game like Witcher 3, Mass Effect or the like. You can be very creative with the gameplay, though. You can invest in sneaking to creep into people's house and steal from them as they sleep. You can pickpocket characters and even take quest items from them or relieve them of other valuables. You can learn magic and become a mage, but like the rest of the game this takes time and effort to do so. You can even levitate to access hidden areas and spots you otherwise wouldn't be able to reach. There's a lot of cool stuff like that in the game.
If any of this sounds good then you should really play all 3 Risen games and head back to the Gothic games as well where this formula was created. Piranha Bytes makes great, unique RPGs that are still a breath of fresh air in RPG gaming today. I love them and highly recommend them, but only if you are prepared for a bit more of a challenge and a slower pace. If you like open-world RPGs but want something that is a bit heavier, a bit more impacting,  meaningful and also challenging, hand-designed and with a high attention to detail, PB games are for you. I'd recommend all 3 Risen games, and to play them in order for the maximum experience.
Can't wait for their new game, ELEX. Thank you, Piranha Bytes, for still crafting gems like these!

Ive had plently of time to digest this game and have arrived to this conclusion. For the price that you pay i can find no justification no matter how hard i try as to what stands out about this project and if it offers anything worth experiencing. This title is simply a cash grab that relys completely on its predecessor the Stanley Parable. I myself have created short projects using software such as UDK, Source and Java, so you would think i would relate to this deeply. Sadly not, this entire game could be created with basic knowledge with the Source Hammer editor by simply placing sound triggers and timed events triggered by arriving at a certain point. This is not my problem however, The Stanley Parable did the same but that project had purpose for its controls. The point of the game is to oppose the narrator or follow the instructions to arrive at a certain conclusion and it was a clever idea. However I didn't find The Beginners Guide to be clever at all despite the launch hype. Everything seems to be vague and poorly put together. If there is some sort of meaning i completly missed it, to say it has a meaning is like shooting in the dark. Sure if you think hard enough you'll scratch the bottom of the bucket and find some sort of meaning that you can apply to almost anything. If you thought hard enough you could say Assassin's Creed has a deep meaning but there is no obvious reason to think so. The problem is the story tries to be something its not, a deep psychological experience. Its so far up its own♥♥♥♥♥that it costs the price it gives you. Basically the story can be sumed up as this. Imagine someone in your community lives in a house made up of red bricks. Now i assume that this person is a angry individual and does not socially connect with people and he shows this through his choice of house. I create this entire story with no solid reason and jump to conclusions and the community beleives this is deep. In my opinion this is not a good game at all, it should be free or around $3.50. I've seen free Source mods with better content than this. This may however be different for you and you may end up liking this artsy tale. Everyone is different, but if you take your paintbrush out of your behind and look closely you may find that there is nothing there to begin with. With all this in mind i recommend the buyer watch a walkthrough of the first 25 min of this and make a decision then. If still interested purchase it, if not, it dosent get any better in my opinion.

RPG Maker has is a great piece of software. It has a brief but steep initial learning curve that quickly levels off. Once you are
a bit familiar with the system and its basic capabilities, you'll see that you can create fun games with steady but unburdensome effort. You may only yield ten to twenty minutes of playtime for every six to eight hours of building time, but that is to be expected. The best thing about the software to me is that you are in control of how much depth you want. The core package is best suited for cookie-cutter whimsical JRPGs, but between the DLC, script editor, and robust community, it is entirely possible to spice up the core very easily. You can even (with a lot of learning and/or experience) make games far outside the mold of a typical early to mid 90s JRPG. Overall, not a magical artifact that makes fantasy worlds real on it's own, but a tool that anyone can pick up, and with a little dedication, make games for their friends, or maybe even for real profit.

Pros:

* Clunky battles tailored for 1v1 action. Game throws at you a ♥♥♥♥ton of enemies.
* Physics glitches out in 60+ fps mode. Advice to force vsync in your gfx card options.
* Some dialogues are sheer idiocy.
* Last boss is a joke.
Summary:
Game is long, pretty hard and tedious. Quicksave every step as glitches are everywhere. Proceed only if you are an RPG fan or crave for some good ol' Gothic fix. 5.5/10

It is free and you can see that the creators have been putting quite some heart and effort into it.
There where many things that I didn't expect from this such as being able to drive the car and some nifty weapons.
Horror snobs might disagree with this but without the guns this game wouldn't have much going on for it.
Despite the developers best intentions, everything feels "half cooked" and rough around the edges. Here is an example: The protagonist is constantly coughing or moaning when moving around...this gets annoying fast. I couldn't figure out what caused this.
There is a story going on too but from what I've seen of it, it felt very juvenile and is mostly delivered through notes. There are cutscenes and voice acting thrown in too...a nice choice.
The enemies feel rather out of place and don't cause any real dread. With a setting like this there where infinite other options rather than very stereotypical monsters.
The leveldesign is quite decent but unnecessary dark in places. I suppose this should encourage using the lantern but you could still see enough without it, so why bother.
I'm giving this a recommendation because this is clearly someones baby, its not yet another terrible horror "walking simulator" where the lack of any means to defend yourself (or gameplay for that matter) is held up as being superior and its free. HOWEVER: I recommend this only to fans of the genre and younger people. If you are in your early to mid teens you might get some spooks out of this but for everyone else.
Another quirk of the game is to constantly warn you about how important it is to save ammo yet there is way more spread throughout the levels than you could carry.
Its free, it was a lot of hard work for some folks and its visually and also otherwise sufficiently well made for a recommendation but:
I'm sorry, its just tremendously boring.

Imagine if Arma 2 had a baby with COD 2... This is what you would get.
The graphics are actually quite good and more than adequate for the gameplay. Controls and models are fluid and it is a very easy game to 'pick up and play', certainly it feels a lot more intuitive than I first thought it would be, striking a nice balance between simulator and arcade type game play.
Despite this, it is still a rewarding game for the less seasoned player. I personally prefer to play on servers running realism and territory mode though, which brings one hit kills and the like to the fore. This is not a game one would expect to gun and run in, and people expecting to be able ninja across the map like you might in modern warfare will soon find themselves dying a lot. Even the bots are good shots and their inclusion means servers are always manic and full of action when human players are limited. Hence taking cover, going prone and teamwork do happen in this game and are nearly essential for success. In this respect, it does seem to emulate Arma 2 but without being anything like as clunky to play.
Tonnes of semi-official servers are up and running and it is very easy to find a game to jump into, allowing you to choose how many human players you want to be up against and hence a rudimentary level of difficulty for multiplayer games.
Would recommend, I own numerous FPS games and none of them offer the same multiplayer replay value as this.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

If you love RPG games that really immerse you in the world and allow you to live in another world for a time, then do yourself a favor and buy this game.  Due to its age, and the fact I had never heard of it, I bought this on sale not expecting much.  What I found was a true gem.  My first impression was that the graphics looked dated compared to modern games (although not bad by any means), but as I played the game further I began to no longer notice the graphics and found the game to be extremely beautiful.
The first thing about gameplay you will notice is that it isn't easy.  Small beasts can kill you if you aren't careful, and the combat system is not merely hack-n-slash.  Instead, you will need to improve your knowledge of either axes, swords, staves, crossbows, bows, or magic.  You will need to know how to counter off of a parry, do a side-swipe, or a power swing with the sword for example.  Eventually you can wield a 2-hand ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sword in one hand and use a shield as another example.  As such, the beginning combat is brutal, because you simply haven't earned the experience to know how to expertly use your sword yet.
When it comes to magic, everyone can use a scroll, but an actual spell caster takes time to develop.  You will find  reagents and spells across the world, including stone tablets to increase your wisdom, in both mundane places and dark dungeons.
Do you like to sneak, steal, and kill people and beasts from afar?  You can do that too.  You can also multi-class and create the exact character you are wanting to play.  This may be necessary as well, because there are some times where a trap in the floor requires you to levitate across it, or a small hole in the wall requires you to morph into a small insect to pass through it in order to progress to an area where a small army awaits and only your sword and shield can ensure your survivability.
Besides class specialization and combat, the environment is very well done.  That bush you can't see through may hold a pack of wolves that you can't see.  Foliage can be passed through, but it can't be easily seen through (as in real life), and it creates a real fear of venturing off the road in this seamless, open world environment.  That dark cave isn't emitting strange noises for nothing...
This game easily offers between 40-60 hours of gameplay to anyone who isn't rushing the main quest, and takes the time to explore similar to Bethesda games.  Combat is different and can feel sluggish sometimes, but that is part of what makes the game exhilarating.  You can't just stomp your way through this world; it takes finesse.  The story is good, but isn't what I would call epic.  Despite that, the game works and works well.  I can assure you that if don't give up in the beginning this game will really pull you in and is worth far more than the $3 it costs you on sale.  Highly recommended.

If you're getting this to mess around, or because your kid wants to make a game, or because you want to make free games, get this when it's on sale at least 50% off (preferably 75%), and it's a cool enough buy.
If you're planning on using this professionally or for profit (only reason to justify spending $60 on it), you better already be (or own) a sprite artist and at least a competent enough programmer to mod video games.
Re art: The program comes with free character sets and tiles that you can use with this, but you're pretty much only going to be able to make one short and limited knock-off of Final Fantasy.  The internet also has free and "free" character sets and character generators, but many of them are either limited to Final Fantasy style characters or include copyrighted material (some of it possibly copyrighted by someone else).  That said, the walking sprites are 32x32, 12 frames.  Dead simple if you ever did graphics for early 90s games or similar retro clones.  It's simple enough to find or make a template and fill it in using Paint and
(no photoshop needed).  If this becomes an obstacle to making a game for profit, you're either lazy or color blind.
Re programming: I'm no programmer, but the scripting doesn't appear to be that much harder than some of the simplified pseudo-C++'s that were common to moddable games in the 90s, but not as hard as real programming languages that cause English majors like me to carve eldritch symbols on themselves while chanting "ia Derrida, Chomsky Fthagn!"  If you can mod games by making code changes, you'll probably be able to figure it out.  If you're the sort who can read instructions, the lovely people at the RMVXAce Wikia have lots of stuff on scripting.  That said, if you're planning on using this professionally, at least make sure you can at least make a mod for existing games that required proper changes to code before buying this.  If you can't, it might not be worth the investment.

New Star Soccer 5 features a decent soundtrack, a basic menu that has a tad bit of a learning curve and simple gameplay  that requires a bit of finesse.
The game starts with the player creating a character and choosing a team. After following the tutorial, the player can join in matches against the AI teams. During matches, the player can be penalized and even injured preventing them from playing in the next few matches. After the matches are completed, the player gains funds and can gain/lose reputation among various factions e.g. boss, team, friends, etc.
If the player is not favorable among factions, there is usually some form of consequence on the player, such as a lower "happiness rating", which affects their character's playing performance. The player may participate in mix-and-match mini-games to boost the reputation of factions.
The player may spend their funds in the shop on various items. The vast majority of the items contribute to "lifestyle rating" which aids in finding a girlfriend, which drastically increases the "happiness rating" of the character.
The player may also participate in training to boost the character's stats, which helps in their overall performance during matches.
One of the most amusing aspects of New Star Soccer 5 is the Leader Board. From the Leader Board, you can see your global ranking compared to other players. This makes things competitive, as you can strive to be the #1 player of New Star Soccer 5, globally.
New Star Soccer 5 is a simple, mildly entertaining game with various features. I recommend this game, but I advise you to try out the free version that is available on the website first. This will allow you to see if $15 is a good value for being able to play the game infinitely each day.

This is an okay game with a bunch of flaws, but fairly easy to win once you have the hang of it and can be fun especially if you played games like footballer of the year back in the day, this is very much an update of that where you actually play the game in full (if abbreviated) rather than just shooting at the goal.
You start off as a lowly footballer who can't shoot, pass, run, dribble or anything. Day by day you can practise, buy toys, go out with the girlfriend (if you have one), try to build up a rapport with your team mates, fans, or boss, etc. Initially the main thing is to build the skills and you do training drills where you have to bend the ball, beat defenders, tackle, dribble around cones, etc. in a limited amount of time/attempts, if you do your skills when you play games improve in the appropriate area.
In terms of playing matches you start off as a sub only having a few minutes, and maybe not being picked at all. Based on doing well in various in game stats you try to get good game ratings, which will get you picked more often, or even a starting position in the team if you keep doing well. At this point you start to having to manage your energy by buying toys to keep you occupied during matches, NRG drinks (which often give you cramps during a game), etc. You also need to spend energy managing relationships if you want your teammates to pass to you, your girlfriend not to dump you, your friends not to hate you, etc. So you get into a balancing act of all these things, and you have to learn how to play the minigame puzzles (pair matching for relationships, "simon says" for the media), etc.
The main in game challenge isn't really about winning matches, once you know the AIs weaknesses this is fairly easy (for example the quick turn to lure defenders into sliding tackles to clear the way, the banana dribble close to the goalie to lure him out and then walk the ball into the net, the direct vertical run outside the goal to curl into the same side top corner, the diagonal curling out/in balls, etc.). The problem instead is trying to use the match to improve your ranking and stats - so doing lots of safe passing in your own half to build up teammate approval without spending energy, getting some tackles in without getting cards, and otherwise building up your stats for passing/tackles/set pieces to increase your transfer value and wages higher, etc., as the benefit from just scoring more and more goals and winning games is capped - you have to become more rounded to be the best.
Overall the game is quite good fun at times, although it can be frustrating as well, and your team mates need a lot of managing/adaptation to actually be useful to you given how braindead they are, and the out of match stuff makes for a reasonably interesting balancing act. Once you are successful it does all become fairly formulaic however, as once you are fully skilled up and have largely capped out your relationships it is relatively easy to deal with any new off the field problems, and winning matches/championshops/cups is a breeze once you have the skills and know the AIs strengths and weaknesses. I am not sure I would recommend it to most people however at full price, as I doubt most will play it for long enough to really justify the price tag, and apparently it hasn't been on sale for over a year at this point, but this could be a fun game if you like the idea (and have a controller!) and can put up with some bugs/flaws.

This isn't a game, and I don't mean "not a game" like Gone Home "wasn't a game" in some folks' minds in that it didn't have a fun (in my, and many others' opinion) interactive aspect (interactivity being the fundamental difference between a video game and a video). That was just (again, in my opinion) a bad game.
This is a program that tells a story, and contains two really interactive moments besides walking, not including repeated instances of one interactive moment, an optional interaction, and "interactions" which have no bearing on either the story nor future interactions.
Unfortunately, those few brief interactive moments would have been as effective told on video, and the story would have been as effective told on video. However, a video twenty minutes long would have been enough to sufficiently tell the story this program tells, with as much impact. This "game" is two hours long and costs $8 (at the time of this writing).
If it had been a dollar and twenty minutes long (and saved me the steps toward inevitable repetitive stress injury by way of pressing the keys), I wouldn't be upset, because a dollar isn't very much money, twenty minutes isn't very much time, and the point that the "game" sluggishly delivers is probably worth a dollar and twenty minutes. Ten dollars and two hours is more than the story can justify, and thus, I can't recommend this purchase. Go buy The Stanley Parable instead; or, if you're intrigued by the premise the trailer presents, go watch this on youtube with the closed captions turned on, the volume muted, and on 2x speed. It's not a bad story, fundamentally; it's just not (and probably shouldn't be) a damned video game, and acts like it is one.

This puzzle game is all about assembling, manipulating and delivering blocks in the right way to their destination. To accomplish this you will set up increasingly complex networks of fully automated conveyor belts accompanied by blocks that weld, rotate and more. The real fun lies in that you get to see how well your friends as well as everyone else who played did, giving you an incentive (beyond that of certain achievements) to keep optimizing your solution. The first person view and 3D environment really call on your spatial thinking. While the earlier levels can be done relatively fast as soon as you get the mechanics, the later levels will have you break down problems into little steps and iterate upon your work as you go. And as you advance you also get to know more of the story you got thrown into.

Okay, let me make this clear - I'm a big fan of HoMM V. And after I tried MMH VI I've grown to hate it! I used to consider the sixth installment an abomination of the whole series... Just until the seventh was released. And that's where my opinion has changed. Yes, the sixth Heroes were bad (compared to the fifth) but MMH VII is a ♥♥♥♥ing horrible game, which has made me realize that MMH VI is a goddamn "masterpiece". Because, despite all the♥♥♥♥♥♥we hate about it, it does have some features I wish HoMM V had. And these are:
+ A possibility to convert a conquered other faction's city to a city of your own faction. Finally! I had been dreaming about this since the third Heroes.
+ A fairer way to arrange the heroes' skills. They don't pop up randomly anymore! Now you get to choose them from the list by yourself.
+ A new "Tears-Blood" feature. It is a truly interesting new decision in developing a hero, depending upon his deeds.
+ Hiring a hero is also not random anymore. You can pick one from the list, just like with skills.
+ The marketplace's prices give players more freedom in trading resources (compared to HoMM V).
+ A totally new faction - Sanctuary. Although it probably means a lot only for me, because I'm very fond of Japanese culture.
And now we're gonna dig up some♥♥♥♥♥♥ which this game hides in its depths:
- There're no gems, mercury and sulfur anymore. Why the hell were these classical resources removed!? This is absolutely the worst and the most idiotic decision in the series ever!
- The number of factions was also reduced. In fact there were only FIVE of them at the start! And one more faction was added as a part of a DLC. Curse Ubisoft for being so greedy!
- No random map generator. Another annoying thing about MMH VI. The amount of standard maps is very limited. You have to find some new custom maps on the net (or make one by yourself). Much thanks for crap like that!
- The units' traits are completely different as these in HoMM V. I can't describe the details, but I liked them more in V.
- The graphical part usually doesn't mean much to me, but even I can tell that many of the visuals' design is totally lazy.
My conclusion: MMH VI is obviously not the best game in the series but also not the worst (especially compared to the VII). So if you're able to deal with all the negative sides here and anxious to enjoy the new good features, you should definitely give it a try. And if you'd never accept a HoMM game with reduced resources and factions, just skip this one and stick to the best games of the series: III, IV and V.

The artillery is a joke. They fire into the ground if you have a bad position and are completly useless then. The only real important upgrades in the game are for the artillery which you get very late, if you have it, you can do long range luck shots and kill hundred of units with 1 shot. Usually it only kills 1 or 2 with a long range luck shot. At short range you can do better luck shots with more kills and fear effects.
There is friendly fire on. If you place a group of units behind yours and let them fire you kill your own units. This is a kind of the battle system, which is pretty ok. Its your job to make as long as possible lines to have the biggest damage as possible. You can also try to surround your opponent if you have more units and make your opponents units running by fear of the upperhand of the opponent.
The building system is a joke. The buildings are too expensiv and too less worth. Usually you only need a training camp.

There are 4 kinds of infantrys.
The simple infantry (militia or peasants) which has less fire power and cant use anti cavalery formation.
The regular infantry which has good fire power.
The mortar infantry which has good fire power and a useless skill to make 1 time a good damage in short range.
The sniper infantry which has good fire power and a slightly higher range but have less units per group and are only good against players, because they run automatically as soon as the regular infantry come too close.
The Ai is a joke, the only thing they do is to spawn units for free from nowhere cheating like. They will attack just in a few situations, but never real. The ai isnt able to defeat you, because it never try to conquer, except in specific events. For example, if you conquer Paris the ai start to get units for free from nowhere in a other town next to you and in 3 turns they will spawn and move to Paris to conquer it back.
Furthermore the artillery of the Ai usually never shot, so you can ignore it.

I certainly wasn't allowed into any of their cities, or even near their territory. In Fallout 2, I killed a child who was throwing rocks at me and found myself denied shunned from most civilized places for the crime. In Fallout 3, I nuked an entire city, sold a♥♥♥♥♥♥load of people into slavery, massacred an entire village of ghouls, and the worst punishment I got was a single visit by comically underprepared regulators and the "I'm not mad, I'm just dissapointed" treatment from my father.
So to anyone out their looking for a dynamic experience, in a world that you feel like you can shape, don't buy this game. Buy any other game out of the Fallout series.

Where to begin? Fallout 3 takes place is a post apocalyptic world, you begin as a baby and go through growing up in Vault 101, from there you pick your perks and stats before venturing of into the world of dust and rubble, building have been either damaged or destroyed and a large amount of enemies are out in the world ready to kill or side with you, the graphics are rather bland and old looking but it's the gameplay that matters in this game, it can become very addicting fast, the leveling up system is well designed with a stat list and picking a perk for each time you level up, tons of clothes to wear that have stats on them to increase anything from armour to speech to lockpicking etc, a wide selection of guns and you'll continue to find or purchase new and exciting weapons when adventuring in the wasteland, there's also a V.A.T.S targeting system that freezes time and lets you select different body parts to shoot at which is a blast to use, overall I would highly recommend this game and you will not regret purchasing it

I've been playing this for a while now, and it still gives me a lot of fun and enjoyment. Great gunplay, music and game sounds are excellent and it manages to be a realistic military shooter, with futuristic and fun elements like the cyborg missions. There are 4 classes that have very different play styles, and are very fun to play with, and it is designed to boost the team play. In PvP, all classes have their own advantages and disadvantages, so it's up to you to choose the best tactic.
Do you like PvP? You have lots of modes for that. You like PvE? You have lots of missions for that. It has an amount of variety that I haven't seen on many other games. Yes, you have to either pay to get the good♥♥♥♥♥♥ or put some time into it, but it's still a free game to play and you won't regret to play it for hundreds of hours.
The movement system is better than lots of fps. the UI is very intuitive and easy to get around and get the loadout you want. If you play for free like me, you can manage your warface bucks and buy stuff with it on the shop like guns, grenades, armour and skins. The management system actually gives me enjoyment and it gives the player goals to achieve in the game in terms of what you want to upgrade next.
It has bugs, like any 60 dollar game has. It lags like any other 60 dollar game lags. Devs are always giving out new updates, almost every month, and fixing bugs or improving some aspects of the game. If you enjoy first person shooters, you should definitely give Warface a try.
Too difficult? Start with the easy and normal difficulty missions to get yourself up to speed. Lots of other players will help you on the co-op missions it you are new to this type of game. As you progress in experience, you'll always have different secondary challenges in each mission to keep you focused. Or if you just wanna play for fun, you can also ignore them and just have a good time!
It's free, it's fun, it's well designed, it's Warface and I love it.

The whole thing starts off with you realising you're in the middle of Nowhere, Coldas♥♥♥♥. Which, to cut a long story short, is not good. It's snowing, the winds are blowing faster than your old car could go and there's a couple of eyes in the woods. For a moment you just stare at it all in awe.
, you might say. You would be right, but now is not the time for pleasantries since you're dressed for summer in the middle of a snowstorm. You walk for what seems like hours and finally see a house with a door in the distance.
, you might think. And then you die.
The only real bad things are that after about 10 days of surviving you're not doing anything new. If you've been somewhat lucky with drops you will have found most of the clothing and tools you need. Your endgame struggle is basically finding enough antibiotics to fill a bathtub. But I guess that's what survival in harsh cold conditions is like. The map be a bit small but why even complain when it's only a month into early access and they just doubled the size. The new area is a bit less detailed, but it doesn't have to be so it's no problem.
The graphics are amazing, the lighting feels "real" in the confines of the game world and the design is so cosy you are almost bound to find yourself in a snowstorm after noticing you've been staring at nature for 30 minutes. The crafting and menu-system is great, like a way less buggy and understandable version of Dayz (mod). Every category of items can be ordered alphabeticaly, by weight or condition. There's no guides or tutorials but that only makes it feel more scary, like you're not prepared (just like your character) of what it's like to be stuck in the middle of Canada during a permanent post-apocalyptic winter.
I'd say yes. The game is fun, addicting and only feels repetetive after about 8+ (probably more) hours which is better than a whole lot of other games not in early access. Well worth the about 20€. I never played earlier version without the map upgrade, but from what I've read in patchnotes and forums it seems they are updating a fast pace while also listening to testers support.
