This game is unique compared to its genre. Enough said, Fantastic! Most real you can get, now with that said, I'm annoyed to see people going around trying to beat that generalization up saying the game isn't realistic. It's the most you can get towards it. Yes you have stuff that falls apart fast, yes you get hungry fast. Heck, you are in freezing wheather, in all reality that does mean you are burning calories a LOTTT faster. Maybe the game isn't perfect but it's fun and enjoy it for that purpose, it's a hardcore game and I'd rather have tons of food I have to eat more of than finding no food at all when I need to survive. I'd rather have a can opener that breaks than twnety of them and no worries the rest of my game. (With that, I'd l ike to say stuff doesn't even fall apart that fast anymore, on top of that you can REPAIR things. Which everyone freaks out saying clothes don't fall off you and knives don't break. Um, I never once had clothes fall off or a knife break in game, because I notice it is breaking and fix it. You fight off a dozen wolf attacks and expect your knife to be okay, alright?)
For those who don't enjoy survival or don't like exploration or don't like a challenge, that just means you're a book reader going to a magazine store. You're in the wrong genre buying a game you don't like! If you do enjoy all those aspects that this game supplies, then awesome cause I do to and this game just blows me away. It's replay value is higher then you think. If you start and read all about the places and how to play, then yes you probably won't have as much fun, if you just start and learn about it and explore without cheating online you're going to have a blast. I have yet to find every single location and I barely even played on the second map still. They have randomizing locations for loot and a special location that makes it that much more exciting to explore after each playthrough.
Wolves is a big one. I love them, another challenge to overcome when trying to survive. If you want to say what the hell wolves don't attack people, then move on. Because a hungry wolf in the middle of a post DISASTER scenario who needs ot eat will attack someone. Which brings me to another part, the mechanics of the wolves are awesome. Because at times they WILL NOT attack you. Instead they see you and run away. Very rare but it does happen. They come at you, you can still scare them away, stand your ground don't rush them, light a flare and they are gone. If you don't ask me that sounds realistic. If you just want to be that character that lights a flare and chases down the wolf and it attacks you, then complain about it saying it's not realistic. Then you sir, are a moron. Any person who understands the makeup of animal instincts will understand that a threatned, cornered animal will fight back. The wolves in this game almost act the exact same way. Their mechanics are perfect tune with this game. I love it.
Which brings me to one point, Post DISTASTER! Everyone misses the very first part of the game. Clearly a disaster has struck, and storm where your plane crashes. THIS is why dead bodies are everywhere. This is why it is cold. Not just because you are in Northern Canada. It is a disaster which explains all the destruction and death that you see. So don't go bagging the idea of its location in canada or the cold being unrealistic. The cold... Is amazing. I just one review about not being able to put on layers? Um you can... its called wool sweats under pants. Sweaters under heavy coat jackets. When you find enought of the right clothes you are able to layer them if game allows it. Yes you can't wear the biggest heavy ski vest over another heavy ski vest. It's to prevent the obvious "I'm going to run around with 50 sweaters on and be perfectly okay with absolute no challenge." The mechanics of the game are set, to limit your ability from nerfing the settings, so that you will always have a challenge in the game. Because whether you want it or not, challenge is what keeps a game afloat and enjoyable mulitple times through.
Basically said, if you want to enjoy the game for what it supplies, then awesome because it gives an experience you can't really find in most survival games. To me and to it's genre, a hardcore survival game with actual challenge other then threat of CONSTANT PVP shooting and absolutely no other obstacle like you see in all these games around us with literally no genuity or originality. This game sidesteps that completely and instead of becoming an online killing game it has become a single player REAL survival compared to that genre's name now. Basically if you want to be that player that says oh a "realistic" game okay... Then play and go "Omfg wolves attack me, oh what is this I get hungry fast, oh my gosh I'm staring at a screen playing a game this isn't real life this is so not a realistic game" Then you really should rethink your gamer life and learn to understand the fun individual originality that many games, not just this one, give to you.

***SPOILERS  BELOW***
Summary:
Davey Wreden, founder of Galactic Cafe and creator of one of my all-time-favs "The Stanley Parable" comes back to give us the "Follow-up to the Stanley Parable".
Coda is described as a shut-in, self-deprecating game designer and innovator. However, in Wreden's perspective, he feels he is encouraging Coda. Wreden adores and emulates Coda's work.
Game maker with the handle, "Coda" experiments with different game designs, and in these designs he reveals many personal things about himself. Coda's games are fun, and cleverly insightful. Wreden is emotional and a good narrator. Coda gives Wreden games he made so Wreden can comment and critique.
Wreden plays coda's games as a progression over the years, and the games start to change tone as Coda's creativity runs out, and Wreden starts to chafe Coda's safe zone.
Wreden showed his games to other people, which generated fanfare that Coda was not ready for (This is similar to what I understand what happened to Wreden with the Stanley Parable, ironically). Coda felt betrayed. Coda shut himself in further, and this game is Wreden's attempt that stopping the feud and getting Coda out of his cell he built for himself.
Coda's last level is a cold, antisocial, personal hit at Wreden. It's no wonder he wanted to show it to others.
Many of the things talked about really hit home hard. You can take home a lot of good advice from some of Coda's games. Take your time playing, read everything you see.
Thoughts (+,-):
This keeps your attention in the same way as the SP. I had to sit through the whole thing at once. I was totally captivated and waiting for the big conclusion that was kind of anticlimactic.
Would Coda even be able to come out of his shell now that his works have been analyzed by someone he supposedly hates, and reviewed by the whole steam market?
Narrator/Designer Wreden beats himself up a lot, despite his own achievements. He even admits that he, himself is depressed very often, which is scary. He genuinely sounds like someone who is battling with depression. Although these games were entertaining, I genuinely hope that anyone who feels that way about themselves chronically can get the help they need. Nobody deserves to feel that way about themselves when they obviously have so much going for themselves. Grass is always Greener.
It's an apology to Coda, but it's also a bold statement to Coda in the language of validation that Wreden understands. If people enjoy his games, what does Coda (and Wreden) have to worry about?
Coda is someone who is worth paying attention to, but you can only lead a horse to water, right? You can't force the guy to make the games you like.
I feel the game deserves attention, but this kind of thing should be free.
To be honest, with all that buildup, I was expecting Coda to be dead in the end.
There's no bad time and place to discuss mental illness, however.  If you are actually depressed, please make sure you have the support and resources you need.

The actual full version of this huge, full of info review:
This is not a game.
This is the most complete and user friendly RPG making engine available at the moment.
First of all, it didn't came out of thin air. There is a long history behind it.
The application has enough graphics layers to do what you need.
A few more (or infinite) would be a nice feature though.
Anyway.
If you need more you can do parallax mapping anyway,
a technique with infinite power.
Rpg maker  supports Scripting!
So to be fair, if you learn Ruby programming language,
and dive into RGSS (the engine the game is using)
you can do anything you want, even an action RPG engine!
Don't expect too fancy stuff, but it will do for mini games anyway!
I would appreciate if the creators would implement 3 systems.
1] Default Menu based
2] Side Battles
3] Action RPG
Those 3 things can make VX Ace a perfect out of the box produt.
PERFECT!
There is only one excuse for that, not being implemented.
Resources for RTP and scripting would increase the main RTP file.
But is it really so important?
I mean, we can have a big RTP in exchange for a ready to do anything engine .
There might be needed new resources standards.
So?
Why don't you consider adding them all in?
Don't get me wrong people.
You can still make those three battle systems.
But that's the bad part, you are the one who have to do the job.
I have to mention though, that there are scripts of generous creators out there,
that demand only to credit them and maybe to show a link to their site.
Fair enough don't you think?
Anyway let's rate this engine.
Before I do though, I have to tell you that it is indeed the BEST out there at the moment...
for making RPGs out of the box.
As a product it takes 70/100
The price is really high!  60 Euro is not a funny price.
But there is the lite version, to check if you like it and if it fits your needs.
You are limited to use 10 things of each but who cares?
So price will NOT lower the rating of the product, due to the great marketing of the company. Congratulations on providing the lite version by the way.
Points are lost because of the lack of pre-defined scripts for more battle systems.
Also on many systems graphics are blurry on scrolling even after the flickering reduction.
Also you might need to buy commarcial anti lag scripts to do complex and fancy stuff without lag.
One more thing.
The software should have more graphics implememnted in it.
Buying a new version of an RPG maker should inherit all the previous resources, in order to encourage new users to buy it.
Otherwise, you should provide the users with enough graphics for any scenario they might in general wanna create. But the resources are just the essentials to code a game. So you lose also points from that.
Anyway.
If you could give us a free pack of scripts and initial resources for action RPG and side scroll battle system,  as a Free DLC, that would be great.
Another bad thing is that it doesn't support very high resolutions.
This is a true con of the engine.
Developers though are up to do something about that.
Do i recommend this product as it is?
If you wanna make a game out of it, to sell it, or to give it as freeware, then yes i do recommend it.
There is nothing really negative about it, except what I already mentioned.
What you see on the video is what you get.
What you do NOT see, is what those developers thought.
I am a programmer.
I can appreciate other programmer's insight!
I was away from my computer, thinking how will I do something I wanted to do, to the game i develop.
When I returned and opened the application to see my alternatives, I couldn't believe it.
I had two problems solved instantly, just because there were two features there.
I can hardly imagine something in 2D gaming that this program can not do.
If there exists something like that, it would be a really complex issue.
You will just have to script hard in Ruby to create something that will stand from the common games.
Not to mention that you can create games diffrerent than an RPG.
================================================
One thing though.....
What is this obsession with the right channel everywhere?
Whatever...
My personal opinion bottomline:
Buying RPG Maker VX Ace on 75% Discount,
along with some DLCS is a great investment,
50 Euro to have everything you need to create a decent RPG, is a cool price!
Especially when alternatives have mothly fees, or have gigantic prices.
Of course alternative engines, can do more things.
Some of them can do things better!
But you will still have to get your own resources to use.
RPG Maker VX Ace is an engine, with a GUI to work into, plus resources to use.
Finally, I believe that,  it's not an engine that makes a good game,
as it's not a guitar that makes a good music picece.
Think about it.

This is a game that I would've waited to go on sale to purchase knowing what I know now of the game. All in all its a decent game but it doesn't bring anything spectacurlry new to this genre and nothing that it does do has really made me think to myself "wow that is amazing." As of writing this review I have just cleared the campaign for the first time at with close to 17 hours of gametime put into it. I love the setting of the game and that is what got me interesed in it in the first place, having high hopes with a few reservations for the game. Theres is a story there, while not a grand peice of story telling theres is a story to the game focused around delivering vengance to an enemy who has mostly wiped out your clan. this is to be expected as ARPG selling points aren't their stories but their gameplay!  Graphics are decent, could be better but not bad. One mechanic the Devs talked highly of was the exposure mechanic, which dealth with being expoed to extrreme elemtents, cold, heat, posion, etc. Sadly exposure feels very rough and unpolished in how its currently handled. it has potential but its not reached in this game. Combat is pretty fun when theres a lot of enemies around to attack/dodge around. Theres no "loot-splosions" when defeating bosses but always a specific legendary item that drops, though the bonusues on those items will be randomized, meaning you may not get the bonuses that you want. Since all the abilities damage is based off of WDPS getting a new weapons is always a GREAT feeling the further you go. Since theres not crazy amounts of loot everywhere the developers have added a crafting system for gear but the system is pretty bland. There are 4 types of resources to gather in the game; gold, wood, iron, and jotunjarn (the latter being used for more of the later parts of the campaign.) Get enough of these resources and to to the craftsmen and select the item you want and it rolls out with a random quality and random bonuses. That sums up the crafting. In addition to spending resources on crafting you also upgrade different buildings in your village which is  nothing special as well, upgrading the buildings just increases the tier of gear/runes they can handle. Save for the altar which lets you get higher ranks of your abilities. theres no bank or storage of any sort if you're the type who hordes legendaries youll have to hold onto them in your inventory. Speaking of which your inventory has a limitied amount of size which I'm not sure the game lets you know how full it is. It may, I just haven't noticed any indication of this except for when youre full and your character lets you know your'e full everytime you run over an item. Part way into the campaign you have to upgrade your boat to progress which comes out of nowhere and could be a hinderance if you don't have enough resourcse because you've just upgraded your craftmens and are low on say wood for instance. At that point it could take a while to farm it up, but you shouldl have acces to a merchant at that point where you can trade resources for gold and vice versa. Though the game does a poor job explaining you cna buy resources with gold, it sounded like you could only sell resources for gold. You can place runes in your wepaons/armor if theres slots for runes on them. once a rune is placed you cant get the run back AND you also cant replace that rune with a more powerful or different ability runefor some reason which seems odd. The multiplayer only being able to have two players in one game is defeinitley odd but I'm sure theres a reason for this. Would love a sequal or something that included the standard 4 players co-op. Having just recently cleared the campaign I've unlocked New game+ and have just started on that. When starting new game+ you lose all items that you have which the game notifies that starting NG+ will do so with a confirmation pop up when selecting that option. In addition to losing all your items you also lose all level up improvements; %healh increase %dmg increase, etc that the game never states that starting a NG will do this. The gear that is dropped and crafted in NG+ is greatly more powerful then end game gear from the previours playthrough which is nice once you get set up again with some gear and stop being naked and afriad.
CONCLUSION: A decent game that feels like it could've been much more then it turned out to be. If you're a fan of the setting or the genre you'll probably be happy with your purchase. Though there are much better games in the genre out on the market that do expectionally better at what this game does. Hopefully this game will see support from the developers, which seems likely as they have responded to a good deal of reviews from users. If not much support hopefully a sequal that gets things under reins and becomes a competior to the kings in this genre.
*Will update if I come across any thing worthy of mentionion while playing in the future.

If you are unfamilliar with the Heroes of Might and Magic game series, its principle is basically a turn based strategy game with some RPG elements.
Having played the entire Heroes of Might and Magic series from part I to this one(i have not and will not play Heroes VII), i can say this isnt the worst Heroes of them actually. I think it still ranks above Heroes I and IV, maybe II even. Even though i dont like that they reduced the number of different resources and kind off changed the combat system back to what it was before Heroes V (that was the highest evolution of the HoMM-combat system so far imho) it is a nice, artsy game with good music. It would be all good and i could recommend it. If it werent for the main point that makes it impossible for me to recommend this game.
So, i simply cannot really recommend this game for one main reason, and that is the fact that in order to play the single player campaigns you have to stay online. Like for example i had many a battle that lasted almost or more then an hour reset so that i had to play it all over again because i was transported back to the main menu when my internet connection broke. That and the fact that i sometimes have to start the game several times in order to avoid some bugs(mainly "town freeze"), and because it is forced online singleplayer i get to wait a lot until the savegame is fully loaded every time. Dont let the many hours i played this fool you - i have to play it because i started it already and want to know how the story concludes.
I know, it might seem as if the real issue was my bad connection. No it isnt. Making a single player campaign require an online connection during play is just a player-antagonizing and thus fundamentally flawed idea. Because even if the bad consequences of this happened only once it would be once too much.
But hear me Ubi, i promise as soon as you make the singleplayer campaigns and the conflux contents available for offline play i will change this review into a recommendation. But since rather Sheogh(The demon inferno land inside the games story) will completely freeze over before you will do that, i will keep not recommending it.

This is an updated review. I have had 6 hours on the game already. I'm having a lot more fun once I got the hang of the game mechanics. That said, the game still has problems.
Fast Reflexes Required.
- I'm not a fan of Dark Souls type games where reflexes near perfect timing is required. I like to make builds that have a mix of sustainability and survive with the occasional dodge mechanic for huge attacks. This game probably has a build like that, but basic design caters more towards people who have good reflexes.
Tedious Grind for Items
- The build that I'm looking for is also probably hidden behind better gear, but the grind for gear is abominably slow due to the huge amount of materials required to upgrade just about everything and the slow gain of said materials. And forget about drops from monsters - the game seems to emphasize a lot more on crafting to get better gear, and I'm not a huge fan of endless grind just to experience a build type.
Non-Intuitive Mechanic Design
- Trying to figure out the game mechanics just through playing is frustrating. The dodge mechanic does provide 'immunity' in an extremely small window and also depends on how the enemy attacks vs where you roll (exactly as how the dev's response to my initial review says). It takes a lot of experimentation just to understand how something works and how to apply it in game. If you are a casual player, you may not have the patience for it.
Bottomline: It's fun and rewarding once you figure out the mix of game mechanics and gear to enable your character to better survive the fights, but that requires a whole lot of patience. I would recommend this game only if you have lots of patience.

Original Review 10 minutes into the game.
This game needs more polish. Here is a short list of my problems with the game just a few minutes in. Note: I was playing on a mouse / keyboard configuration. It may be a lot better with a controller, but this should not be the case for a game sold on a PC platform anyway.
1. The command mapping is unintuitive. Tab to heal. Space bar to dodge (luckily, right mouse click also initiates dodges - the game does not tell you this at the start). Left-clicking on an enemy initiates an attack, but if your mouse clicks hit another enemy midway of an attack animation, it cancels your attack and starts a fresh attack on the enemy you clicked - frustrating as hell when this happens.
2. The roll dodge isn't really a dodge per se. It lets you move slightly faster in a direction, but you are still susceptible to attacks from enemies. In a game where the healing mechanic can only be done on recharge, having a dodge skill that doesn't really dodge is extremely punishing.
It's clunky and will take some getting used to. I may update this review once I play a lot more of this game, but I just wanted to warn people first about what to expect with this ARPG.

The whole thing starts off with you realising you're in the middle of Nowhere, Coldas♥♥♥♥. Which, to cut a long story short, is not good. It's snowing, the winds are blowing faster than your old car could go and there's a couple of eyes in the woods. For a moment you just stare at it all in awe.
, you might say. You would be right, but now is not the time for pleasantries since you're dressed for summer in the middle of a snowstorm. You walk for what seems like hours and finally see a house with a door in the distance.
, you might think. And then you die.
The only real bad things are that after about 10 days of surviving you're not doing anything new. If you've been somewhat lucky with drops you will have found most of the clothing and tools you need. Your endgame struggle is basically finding enough antibiotics to fill a bathtub. But I guess that's what survival in harsh cold conditions is like. The map be a bit small but why even complain when it's only a month into early access and they just doubled the size. The new area is a bit less detailed, but it doesn't have to be so it's no problem.
The graphics are amazing, the lighting feels "real" in the confines of the game world and the design is so cosy you are almost bound to find yourself in a snowstorm after noticing you've been staring at nature for 30 minutes. The crafting and menu-system is great, like a way less buggy and understandable version of Dayz (mod). Every category of items can be ordered alphabeticaly, by weight or condition. There's no guides or tutorials but that only makes it feel more scary, like you're not prepared (just like your character) of what it's like to be stuck in the middle of Canada during a permanent post-apocalyptic winter.
I'd say yes. The game is fun, addicting and only feels repetetive after about 8+ (probably more) hours which is better than a whole lot of other games not in early access. Well worth the about 20€. I never played earlier version without the map upgrade, but from what I've read in patchnotes and forums it seems they are updating a fast pace while also listening to testers support.

This game is unique compared to its genre. Enough said, Fantastic! Most real you can get, now with that said, I'm annoyed to see people going around trying to beat that generalization up saying the game isn't realistic. It's the most you can get towards it. Yes you have stuff that falls apart fast, yes you get hungry fast. Heck, you are in freezing wheather, in all reality that does mean you are burning calories a LOTTT faster. Maybe the game isn't perfect but it's fun and enjoy it for that purpose, it's a hardcore game and I'd rather have tons of food I have to eat more of than finding no food at all when I need to survive. I'd rather have a can opener that breaks than twnety of them and no worries the rest of my game. (With that, I'd l ike to say stuff doesn't even fall apart that fast anymore, on top of that you can REPAIR things. Which everyone freaks out saying clothes don't fall off you and knives don't break. Um, I never once had clothes fall off or a knife break in game, because I notice it is breaking and fix it. You fight off a dozen wolf attacks and expect your knife to be okay, alright?)
For those who don't enjoy survival or don't like exploration or don't like a challenge, that just means you're a book reader going to a magazine store. You're in the wrong genre buying a game you don't like! If you do enjoy all those aspects that this game supplies, then awesome cause I do to and this game just blows me away. It's replay value is higher then you think. If you start and read all about the places and how to play, then yes you probably won't have as much fun, if you just start and learn about it and explore without cheating online you're going to have a blast. I have yet to find every single location and I barely even played on the second map still. They have randomizing locations for loot and a special location that makes it that much more exciting to explore after each playthrough.
Wolves is a big one. I love them, another challenge to overcome when trying to survive. If you want to say what the hell wolves don't attack people, then move on. Because a hungry wolf in the middle of a post DISASTER scenario who needs ot eat will attack someone. Which brings me to another part, the mechanics of the wolves are awesome. Because at times they WILL NOT attack you. Instead they see you and run away. Very rare but it does happen. They come at you, you can still scare them away, stand your ground don't rush them, light a flare and they are gone. If you don't ask me that sounds realistic. If you just want to be that character that lights a flare and chases down the wolf and it attacks you, then complain about it saying it's not realistic. Then you sir, are a moron. Any person who understands the makeup of animal instincts will understand that a threatned, cornered animal will fight back. The wolves in this game almost act the exact same way. Their mechanics are perfect tune with this game. I love it.
Which brings me to one point, Post DISTASTER! Everyone misses the very first part of the game. Clearly a disaster has struck, and storm where your plane crashes. THIS is why dead bodies are everywhere. This is why it is cold. Not just because you are in Northern Canada. It is a disaster which explains all the destruction and death that you see. So don't go bagging the idea of its location in canada or the cold being unrealistic. The cold... Is amazing. I just one review about not being able to put on layers? Um you can... its called wool sweats under pants. Sweaters under heavy coat jackets. When you find enought of the right clothes you are able to layer them if game allows it. Yes you can't wear the biggest heavy ski vest over another heavy ski vest. It's to prevent the obvious "I'm going to run around with 50 sweaters on and be perfectly okay with absolute no challenge." The mechanics of the game are set, to limit your ability from nerfing the settings, so that you will always have a challenge in the game. Because whether you want it or not, challenge is what keeps a game afloat and enjoyable mulitple times through.
Basically said, if you want to enjoy the game for what it supplies, then awesome because it gives an experience you can't really find in most survival games. To me and to it's genre, a hardcore survival game with actual challenge other then threat of CONSTANT PVP shooting and absolutely no other obstacle like you see in all these games around us with literally no genuity or originality. This game sidesteps that completely and instead of becoming an online killing game it has become a single player REAL survival compared to that genre's name now. Basically if you want to be that player that says oh a "realistic" game okay... Then play and go "Omfg wolves attack me, oh what is this I get hungry fast, oh my gosh I'm staring at a screen playing a game this isn't real life this is so not a realistic game" Then you really should rethink your gamer life and learn to understand the fun individual originality that many games, not just this one, give to you.

With $120 of Early Access free to play DLC I started as a skeptic. Lets try to ignore that elephant in the room and discuss the addictive qualities.
In this grind oriented treasure hunt the loot is unsortable, unsearchable, and miserable to compare.
After two games you will have 50 or so pieces of loot 40 will be drastically inferior 8 will be side grades 1 will be what you are looking for and 1 will be marked as an upgrade despite having awful stats. This drudgery starts immediately and much like the first DD item stats take their time to become relevant in the scale of the game. Items sell for small amounts of gold that is difficult to spend. Shops have 6 items every 15 minutes with a noticeable delay on the tool tip to inspect each item one at a time. Such a small pool of items having a random level requirements means you will never find a usable item let alone a good one.
The tower defense game play is just fine in spite of the above. The primary difficulty is that in a public game you are very likely to be joining a defense in progress with the majority of the limited defense cap already spent. I know it isn't a cooperative game if a bad player can't bring the team down but the current mechanics directly encourage it. Every player gets a build allowance and spending it in good faith will screw over the rest of your team.
It's free it's co-op and it's free. It looks nice even if the extra detail gets in the way of efficient tower placement. As a tedious detail oriented person I feel actively persecuted for attempting to interface with the inventory and stats.

Short of it: It's worth playing.
***SPOILERS  BELOW***
Summary:
Davey Wreden, founder of Galactic Cafe and creator of one of my all-time-favs "The Stanley Parable" comes back to give us the "Follow-up to the Stanley Parable".
Coda is described as a shut-in, self-deprecating game designer and innovator. However, in Wreden's perspective, he feels he is encouraging Coda. Wreden adores and emulates Coda's work.
Game maker with the handle, "Coda" experiments with different game designs, and in these designs he reveals many personal things about himself. Coda's games are fun, and cleverly insightful. Wreden is emotional and a good narrator. Coda gives Wreden games he made so Wreden can comment and critique.
Wreden plays coda's games as a progression over the years, and the games start to change tone as Coda's creativity runs out, and Wreden starts to chafe Coda's safe zone.
Wreden showed his games to other people, which generated fanfare that Coda was not ready for (This is similar to what I understand what happened to Wreden with the Stanley Parable, ironically). Coda felt betrayed. Coda shut himself in further, and this game is Wreden's attempt that stopping the feud and getting Coda out of his cell he built for himself.
Coda's last level is a cold, antisocial, personal hit at Wreden. It's no wonder he wanted to show it to others.
Many of the things talked about really hit home hard. You can take home a lot of good advice from some of Coda's games. Take your time playing, read everything you see.
Thoughts (+,-):
This keeps your attention in the same way as the SP. I had to sit through the whole thing at once. I was totally captivated and waiting for the big conclusion that was kind of anticlimactic.
Would Coda even be able to come out of his shell now that his works have been analyzed by someone he supposedly hates, and reviewed by the whole steam market?
Narrator/Designer Wreden beats himself up a lot, despite his own achievements. He even admits that he, himself is depressed very often, which is scary. He genuinely sounds like someone who is battling with depression. Although these games were entertaining, I genuinely hope that anyone who feels that way about themselves chronically can get the help they need. Nobody deserves to feel that way about themselves when they obviously have so much going for themselves. Grass is always Greener.
It's an apology to Coda, but it's also a bold statement to Coda in the language of validation that Wreden understands. If people enjoy his games, what does Coda (and Wreden) have to worry about?
Coda is someone who is worth paying attention to, but you can only lead a horse to water, right? You can't force the guy to make the games you like.
I feel the game deserves attention, but this kind of thing should be free.
To be honest, with all that buildup, I was expecting Coda to be dead in the end.
There's no bad time and place to discuss mental illness, however.  If you are actually depressed, please make sure you have the support and resources you need.

Seeing as how I haven't played as much as most others who have reviewed this game, I don't expect that much attention, but I just thought my opinion is worth noting. This game is good. Compared to many of the AAA titles, or even indie  that are being released as of this year, this game stands out as a clear would-buy game; even in its alpha stage. But as being in alpha, it could be better in my opinion, but not as many things drag it down as you might think. I'm going to start this off by telling you what I think was done right.
PROS:
-You almost always find items where you would in real life (i.e. Dresser=clothing items): This may seem like an odd one to some people but I just think it was a good addition to not just have random things like food in a drawer for a dresser.
-The graphics: I am usually a real stickler for graphics in games, but this game and its abstract angular approach on graphics just amazes me on how breath-taking these visuals are for an indie game. It reminds me of something that No Man's Sky is going for without all the crazy colors.
-The wolf AI: With my experiences with wolves, I have found them to be quite good. They eat stuff when you aren't bothering them, they wander the woods, the approach you with caution instead of just charging in with no remorse, they run away and whimper if you whip stuff like flares at them, and I feel like it was done right. I have no clue if there are other AI in the game, but you can just find out for yourself if there are.
-The Replayability: It may not have the social interactions of DayZ, nor as many ways to go through and be excited about a certain gun you get, but it’s taking a new twist compared to other survival games without all the living dangers, and it works.
-The Weather: I love this games weather system. Sometimes is calm and normal, next it's a blinding snow storm where you can barely see anything. It's always varying and makes you think critically in certain situations, like making sure you don't freeze to death from the high speed winds.
Now I feel it's time for the cons of this game.
CONS:
-The 'No Weapon Except for a Rifle' Approach: I personally like how this game strays away the '50 kinds of weapons spread across the map and go find them to survive' spiel, and even with the lack of enemies, except for those dreaded wolves, it can fit perfectly. The thing I don't like about it is that you have nothing to defend yourself with except for your hands or that god-forsakenly hard to find rifle. I have found 1 bullet in all my runs, and that's it as to getting close to that rifle. I found a knife and was like "Sweet, now I have a melee weapon to fend off the wolves", but to my disappointment, it isn't a weapon, only to open stuff it seems. Same with the hatchet, I would love to be able to use them as a weapon. Please make melee weapons, not even a lot of them just a few would be fine, and maybe even a pistol (Which in most cases you can find more than a rifle in many areas of the world and will make sense).
-Crouch Speed: This isn't really a con more than an annoyance but the crouch speed. Please for the love of God man; make it at least a little faster. I know I’m crouching and I don't move as fast, but I honestly feel like I'm in a pool of thick peanut butter.
-Item conditions almost always dreadful: Do people tear up their♥♥♥♥♥♥and through it in a dresser? Or even throw a can of pop on the ground and put it back into their fridge? I know it's some form of the apocalypse, but item condition almost 75% of the time are 50% or less (For me mostly less). Also, the item condition seems to waste away a bit too fast (i.e. the hunting knife/ can opener, maybe even some clothes).
-Inventory System: It isn’t too bad, but I feel like it’s a bit too cluttered for my liking, especially when dealing with my clothing items. Maybe a visual perspective of your body with what’s on it would be fine, but I feel like food and other items are pretty much okay as for as its layout goes.
-Baby♥♥♥♥♥♥Body Structure: You obviously never drank milk as a child in this game and your bones are like peanut brittle. You can take a jump from five feet and lose about 10% of your condition. It makes sense in some scenarios of falling, but your condition shouldn’t be lost so wildly.
Remember this is just my opinion, and after all it is in alpha and will improve drastically between now and it’s release date. I hope this is helpful to some of you guys on the edge of buying this it is a sure 8/10 in my book, and actually one of the first and only games in alpha I have played/seen that I ever truly liked.

This game is addicting. It's relaxing enough to be able to play it after work, when I don't need an adrenaline rush, or to think too much; but it's challenging as a long-term strategy game.
A mistake you made 5 years ago can set your town in a death spiral; you need to plan accordingly, and when you make a mistake hope you can correct it before it gets out of control. You're balancing resources, food, workers, the needs of your citizens, and city planning for the best efficiency and happiness of your town and it's citizens. There is no warfare, but you're up against your citizen's blatent stupidty, and that's enough of a battle.
You have disasters (tornados, fires, etc), disease, infestations. If you don't plan properly you'll have a large amount of elderly citizens and not enough young adults to replace them, thus causing a large collapse in population which will bring your town's production to a halt.
The mods are also a huge plus, with a large and skilled mod community to add onto the game once you've gotten all your achievments and want to play something a little different from the vanilla game.
All in all, this game is good for someone who enjoys the long-term strategy and the challenge of a game which likes making you fail.

Do I recommend Banished?
I do now.
When Banished first came out, I purchased it from the developer's website and played it for 3 or 4 days straight (note: the hours reflected on this review are only accurate from the last few weeks - I have played many many more hours than is noted on my Steam account).
I liked it then, but it wasn't completed, in my opinion. The game lacked content and the games became repetitive, tedious, and boring.
--Enter mods --
The developer opened the game to modding and breathed life into this game. Don't get me wrong, the game could have been fantastic all by itself if the developer had added some much needed content and story, but the community mods fixed all that.
You can add mods right from the game menu now; you can get extra buildings, items, etc. You can d/l mods that add story to the game (albeit linear). But the mods fixed this game and now I'm going to give this game a definite thumbs up and a definite recommend -- before I would have said wait it out.
The graphics are good enough. The RTS is great (much better with mods). The ability to fail was, however, greatly diminished with the mods (the only downside to certain mods).
If you like casual RTS games, miss Sim City, and want to plan out a city, but hate Ubisoft (Anno), get this. You'll not be sorry you did.

Wow, as a long-time horror genre fanatic, I was not disappointed.  Just to put this into perspective, I have been playing horror games since MS-Dos was the dominant operating system a very long time ago.  I've played essentially every major horror genre game you can think of, both on PC and console.
However, for years the genre stagnated... becoming more action oriented then truly scary.
This... omg, THIS game brought me back to the terror-filled nights I remember of my younger years.  This is the first game in I don't know how long that actually had me pausing it and turning on the lights in the house, subsequently causing me to do a paranoidd quick check around the house to make sure my wife and kids were still safe in their rooms and no window had been quietly broken in by some crazy person from the local asylum.  Yes, this game is glorious!

With $120 of Early Access free to play DLC I started as a skeptic. Lets try to ignore that elephant in the room and discuss the addictive qualities.
In this grind oriented treasure hunt the loot is unsortable, unsearchable, and miserable to compare.
After two games you will have 50 or so pieces of loot 40 will be drastically inferior 8 will be side grades 1 will be what you are looking for and 1 will be marked as an upgrade despite having awful stats. This drudgery starts immediately and much like the first DD item stats take their time to become relevant in the scale of the game. Items sell for small amounts of gold that is difficult to spend. Shops have 6 items every 15 minutes with a noticeable delay on the tool tip to inspect each item one at a time. Such a small pool of items having a random level requirements means you will never find a usable item let alone a good one.
The tower defense game play is just fine in spite of the above. The primary difficulty is that in a public game you are very likely to be joining a defense in progress with the majority of the limited defense cap already spent. I know it isn't a cooperative game if a bad player can't bring the team down but the current mechanics directly encourage it. Every player gets a build allowance and spending it in good faith will screw over the rest of your team.
It's free it's co-op and it's free. It looks nice even if the extra detail gets in the way of efficient tower placement. As a tedious detail oriented person I feel actively persecuted for attempting to interface with the inventory and stats.
If only I could drink vodka while deflowering the maidens of the land. Such are the spoils of war.

While I initially really liked GoNNER, it began to sink into me that the parts I didn't like were weighing down the game with my disappointment so much that I was slowly starting to not have fun. At the current moment I think I'll refund my purchase and buy the soundtrack on bandcamp. Here's my gripes with the game, in no particular order:
Ok, I love crypticity and games with it. I even love it when certain games require crypticity to win. But the keyword is
games. It really grinds my gears when a game like this or binding of isaac makes every item a complete mystery to what it does, especially since there's permadeath. Why take any risk? I don't know what any of this crap the merchant is selling is, and even if I buy it, it doesn't tell me what it is either. When I do try to buy something, it seems straight up worse than what I have currently or feels like it has no effect. Everything probably has a purpose, but i'm not going to reduce my health by two notches halfway through my run just to question what it did. Either you look up a wiki and spoil the fun, or have the game slap you around a bit until you forcefully learn everything it wants you to. This is especially stressed because...
It feels like the developer at points is trying to make it hard, especially since it calls itself "tough as hell". The main problem here is that there is simply too many enemies on the screen at all times. I think the trailer and some screenshots do it justice- but just imagine that a lot of those enemies take 2-3 hits to kill depending on the weapon and they all move at different speeds and have different AI. You walk into a room in the first world even and there is just a ton of crap everywhere and you kind of just spray and pray because you just bought the game and have no idea what the strategy for dealing with this massive wall of meat is, if there even is one. Even the boss fights are just rooms filled with a boss (two, for the first one at least) and a ton of infinitely spawning enemies until you kill them. There's just too much. Hard is fun when you feel like it's a fair challenge or you're being slowly introduced to advanced concepts, and if it's designed around it. This feels like neither- the random enemy generation feels like the computer is abusing the copy paste tool and you are thrust right in.
Not really much to say for this one, but it's a surprisingly big issue considering that jumping is sometimes what you need to do to kill enemies. I think the acceleration is a bit off or it's too low, just something about it feels wrong. There's probably an item that "fixes it", but it just feels frustrating to deal with vanilla. It's like you're constantly jumping in molasses.
But honestly, I don't totally hate this game, I'm just super frustrated it isn't better. It feels like all of these cool assets and amazing music got wasted on a totally generic trying to be hard roguelike when it could have been made into something a lot better. I love the personality, I love the art, and I absolutely love the music. I just feel like GoNNER wastes that potential.

I didn't know what to expect when I heard the game known as Fallout. I remember my friends talking about Fallout 4, one of the lastest games in the series. I thought the concept of Fallout was astounding. Since I couldn't afford Fallout 4 at that time, I bought Fallout 3 to still enjoy the experience. May I be the first the say that I truely enjoyed this game and I never regretted buying this game. In my opinion, this is a masterpiece since this game actually got me into the franchise. Would I recommend getting this game? Yes, if you are new to Fallout and wanting to get into the series, even at a affordable price!
Pros: If you are new to the Fallout series, get this game. It's not really my choice to tell you what Fallout game you should get to get into the franchise. For instance, you could probably get New Vegas or Fallout 4 if so, but this could be another choice to get into the series. One pro is that there is such a variety a choices that make a great impact on the game. This is a true RPG for creating your ideal character.
Cons: I did meet some odd experiences so been cautioned when buying this game. The game is not compatable for Windows 7 and up, only for Windows Vista or below, however, this is an easy fix when researching how to configure Fallout 3 to Windows 7 and up. So it shouldn't be complex. On the side of that, I did experience some crashes eventually, but I'm assuming it was my computer since my computer has medium specs for gaming.
For Pros and Cons, they're pretty even, I would recommend anyone getting into the Fallout series with this. Whether you want it or not, I still enjoyed it, thanks Bethesda! :)

An exceptionally atmospheric, realistic FPS set in Stalingrad as well as the Pacific Theatre. RO2/RS combines solid gunplay with a host of innovative map designs, often created by the community. The guns feel exceptional thanks to Tripwire's attention to detail.
RO2/RS creates tense firefights with squad-based tactical combat, with an emphasis on realism. Where other games allow for health regeneration or other crutches, here the damage is dependant on the weapons calibre and where it hits. With an experienced player base, the learning curve remains steep but ultimately rewarding as the satisfaction received from every successful action is that much more deserved.
One of the most unique FPS' out there, RO2/RS is highly recommended.

As many will tell you, this game is not the Stanley Parable, in any sense at all. It offers something else at looking through this person's past, as well as the narrator's with this person who makes these games. For what it offers, a whole hour and a half, as promised, it's a ride that leaves you either uncaring about the overarching story itself, or actually emotional around what goes on between these two people.
For myself I feel like I'm in the group of the former, simply because I've felt what the narrator has felt. However, I feel like for the price of (when I bought this) $8 I feel like what I'm doing is supporting the developer rather than getting a full experience for what I could have possibly expected. I can say there's something here for those like myself that have done what the narrator has done, but at the same time people might expect more out of this.
Can I say I fully recommend this? Not entirely. The strength in this is to have an emotional bond with either the person that created this, or the narrator going through this timeline with their history with this person. If you lack such a bond, then essentially you're pressing W and occasionally E and the Space Bar for an hour and a half wondering what is even going on. If you do share such a bond, then the question is; do you feel you got your money's worth or are you simply supporting a man and getting a short story out of it?

TL;DR: Not as good as SpaceChem, but still a fairly good puzzle game.
Mainly my problem with Infinifactory is that most of the puzzles just seem too straightforward.  In SpaceChem you had to worry about running out of room to place down instructions, and making sure the waldos could loop properly.  In Infinifactory you just have to make sure things get done reliably and the parts don't get in the way of eachother.  You won't even have a problem with the latter issue in most puzzles unless you increase the speed.  Most puzzles are not complicated enough to even have to think hard about how to get things done.
The plot is alright, but it likewise seems a bit too straightforward.  In SpaceChem you had huge plot twists, escalation, and the feeling of being some kind of secret super-chemist fighting against an unknowable foe.  In Infinifactory, it just feels like you're doing your job.

It's a great reminder that you can't ever win in life. No matter what your abilities are, you'll always be at the mercy of your circumstances.
Do well at your job and your co-workers will probably hate you and hinder you at every opportunity - after all, they pursue the same vague idea of glory and prosperity you do. And you only have so much time on this planet and that time, you will learn, is not nearly enough to please even a fraction of the people who matter. Do poorly and everyone will hate you - your family and fans disappointed, your friends and significant other alienated, the press chewing your fat until they decide you're yesterday's news - and then there you are, stuck on the bench with your only friend left: the drink.
But of course your boss will always be there to provide a stone cold, insatiable father figure: shouting unhelpful and meaningless nuggets of wisdom like "Take your time" and "Think about when you call" every step of the way; providing the minimal required amount of reinforcement to your Skinner box of an existence to keep you going.

I'm digging it so far. It's a fun game, with a twist on the 'usual ARPG mechanics'. They taken ideas from various other ARPGs that have tried to be a little bit different, and then made it 'their own' with added stuff on top of that.
The combat feels fun and engaging. Especially the 'Trials of the Gods' are REAL fun and can get a little bit tough, if you don't use the dodge mechanics as intended. As you progress in an ARPG, 'everything' gets easier; that's a given - but to begin with (and where me and a friend is currently at); it does a great job at being a big challenge, without making us feel like it's utterly impossible.
The skill-system isn't 'over-the-top' in any way - it's actually really simple, but not to the point of it being boring and 'lackluster'. It feels right, for this game. Not in a bad way at all. Sure, there could be more variations and such - but it's not needed (from my point of view, at least).
The only downside to the game (Apart from the few bugs we've come across so far - which aren't game-breaking at all), that we both feel is a bit of a let-down:
It is limited to 2-player coop.
I would have LOVED to see this as a 4-player coop, like most ARPGs have been for so long.
Despite that; I really recommend trying this game, if you like ARPGs - maybe even if you don't like the genre that much.
Give it a shot! :)

Do I recommend Banished?
I do now.
When Banished first came out, I purchased it from the developer's website and played it for 3 or 4 days straight (note: the hours reflected on this review are only accurate from the last few weeks - I have played many many more hours than is noted on my Steam account).
I liked it then, but it wasn't completed, in my opinion. The game lacked content and the games became repetitive, tedious, and boring.
--Enter mods --
The developer opened the game to modding and breathed life into this game. Don't get me wrong, the game could have been fantastic all by itself if the developer had added some much needed content and story, but the community mods fixed all that.
You can add mods right from the game menu now; you can get extra buildings, items, etc. You can d/l mods that add story to the game (albeit linear). But the mods fixed this game and now I'm going to give this game a definite thumbs up and a definite recommend -- before I would have said wait it out.
The graphics are good enough. The RTS is great (much better with mods). The ability to fail was, however, greatly diminished with the mods (the only downside to certain mods).
If you like casual RTS games, miss Sim City, and want to plan out a city, but hate Ubisoft (Anno), get this. You'll not be sorry you did.

Upon first impressions of the screenshots, it's fair to assume that New Star Soccer 5 would be a modern, hopefully deeper attempt at the 90s Sensible Soccer games. Besides the appearance of the match engine, I feel that this game should not be compared to any Sensible Soccer game. New Star Soccer 5 simply does not deliver the same quality of gameplay and overall polish as the 90s favorites.
In this game, there is much focus placed on the life of the athlete you play as. You will be able to choose which skills to train in, you will be able to take part in social activities with friends, teammates, and a girlfriend. You will have the chance to build your relationship with your manager and the fans, and you will also be allowed to spend money on many items and properties. Most of the time, the way you must perform these actions is by playing memory games where cards will be flashed with different images on them, then they will then be flipped over and and scrambled, and you will need to match two of a kind. That's all there is to it, and it isn't any fun.
The developer chose to implement a DRM-like system of player creation and in-game updates where you must manually create an account with a password on their servers, and every single time the game updates after a match, for example, it tries to connect again to their servers. The problem is that the connection to their servers fails almost every single time the game tries to reach them to save your progress. This means that you will need to retry the connection over and over, until it works, each time the game fails to connect to their servers, and it happens extremely often.
The career mode allows for the player to go through a maximum of 20 in-game years, and after that you will need to retire that player and begin a new career with someone new. With your player, you will go through his early development as a teenager all the way to a veteran in his late 30s. There is a simple contract negotiation between you and the clubs, there are transfers, there are relegations and promotions within the leagues, and there are international competitions for both club and country. There are some major flaws with all of these features. Very little of what goes on both in the player's career and on the pitch actually makes any sense. Match ratings are almost totally broken, with the game giving your player a low rating or a high rating apparently not reflecting anything that occurred on the pitch. Your 17 year old player will become club captain and be called up to the national team for doing nearly nothing. It's as if these events were scripted into the programming of the game no matter what you did as a player or how well you played the matches. How well your club performs in cups and championships seems to be artificially altered by more scripted programming, having nothing to do with how well you play or even if you play in the matches at all. Choosing to skip a match and not playing in it makes no difference at all in what happens in the game world or how well your club performs. If the programming of the game wants your club to win or wants you to have whatever random rating, that's exactly what will happen.
The way the match engine looks is what drew my attention to this game, and coming from playing the Sensible Soccer games in the 90s, I was hopeful to relive a modern take on those games. I was very disappointed. The match engine has many problems, including those related to your teammates' and opponents' AI. Everything seems scripted and the other players on the pitch will not do more than precisely what they were programmed to do. Asking them to pass you the ball can produce some senseless and ridiculous moments. Every match played is almost identical to the last, and can be won by using the same exact strategy as before. The controls are imprecise and can be frustrating at times. The shooting and passing mechanics perform inadequately and rarely the way you intend. It's also really obvious that the game is intended to be experienced by people playing primarily as strikers, and secondarily as attacking midfielders. Every other position won't make any sense at all. If you want to be part of the action on the pitch, you will need to travel the entire field and play out of position almost always. Even as a striker and as an attacking midfielder, if you actually want to be part of the match, you will need to run all over the place and play out of position a lot of the time. In addition to New Star Soccer 5 having all these problems and looking and feeling like a mobile game, it's just not any fun. There are rarely any moments where your actions will mean actual accomplishments, as the game is playing itself down to all the events it has been scripted to do.
New Star Soccer 5 is mediocre.

An interesting take on the Survival Horror genre, Let The Cat In is a revolutionary experience.
You play as a cat with a randomly generated name and hobby. I recieved a cat named Van Gogh. His hobby was wrestling. This gave him the ability to fight back against the deadly enemy in the game, but to no avail.
The only enemy in this game is the Cat Flap. It is a dangerous adversary. If you encounter it on a door, you will not be able to let yourself in. This is where the "Yarn" mechanic comes in.
If you use the Yarn to trigger a mechanism used to open the Cat Flap, it will be defeated, giving you entry. This is where the game gets really deep. The next level, you are on the other side of the door again, and will have to find a way to open the Cat Flap again.
My theory for this is that the Cat is in a permanent coma, caused by an accident involving a particularly deadly Cat Flap. The Cat then associated the Cat Flap as the adversary, and itself as the Hero. In it's coma, it is in a situation in which it must triumph over the deadly Cat Flap constantly. Whenever he triumphs, however, he is brought back to the beginning. This represents how the Cat Flap will never be defeated. It is a neverending cycle, and the death of the Cat is the only escape. The Cat does not have the ability to end it's own life, though. He will never escape. The constant hope of maybe, just maybe being able to escape this purgatory one day is the only thing keeping him going. But he won't. He never will.
As soon as this finally clicked in my head, I finally realized how much of a masterpiece this game was. A free masterpiece. You can download it right now.
Would you like to experience a deep, terrifying and possibly depressing story about a cat?
Get this game.

Easily one of my favorite action-roguelike's I've played in a while.  The game has such a confident and unified sense of style.  Everything pops and crunches in a really satisfying way.  The music, which builds in intensity as your combo goes up, compliments the game really well.
The game also has a lot of really nice touches in the systems and mechanics.  From the emphasis on building up combos (you can't even start scoring points until you've completed at least one chain of 5) to the fact that you have to recover all your character's components after they take a hit to restore yourself to full power, or the ammo system incentivising (and sometimes requiring) you to take the more difficult route of jumping on enemies heads rather than just shooting at them.
Its a good game.

Red Orchestra 2 has a very hardcore style that may not suit everyone. This is the kind of game where one bullet can kill, and often you'll get killed by an enemy you didn't even see. Of course that can work in your favour as well, and once you learn the maps its not too bad. If you can get past that potential frustration, there is a very good game here. Your vulnerability can contribute to tense moments, and getting caught close to an artillery strike can be particularly unsettling. Map layouts are interesting, with a mix of open spaces and tight indoor areas. The nature of the control point gametype will generate teamwork even on unorganised public servers. The community seems small, but I haven't had any problems finding active servers so far. Tripwire have a history of supporting Killing Floor long after release, so RO2 should have a good lifetime. If you're looking for a new multiplayer FPS, this is definately worth a try.

This is a spectactularly good adventure game that i wish i had played earlier. Unfortunately it does not work at all using Steam In-Home Streaming, so you will have to find the time to run it on a local system instead. The story zaps you into some magical world that is currently suffering under a regime that worships at the altars of austerity and trickle-down economics. You wander about talking to interesting characters as you help them out of the mess. What makes this game great is not the puzzles (they are essentially all just fetch quests), but the excellent dialog and description text. There is lots to click on, and everything is just the right balance of absurd and profound and laugh-out-loud funny. It might not be to everyone's tastes, but if you're into politics and surrealism and oddball comedy this is definitely worth the time.

I did not truly know what to expect with The Sea Will Claim Everything, but I was very happily surprised with what it was!
The game is a unique point-and-click adventure story. The graphics are mostly 2D drawings that do not move, though there are some places where this changes quite a bit. Many things on the screen do not drastically stand out from other objects. This is somewhat ironic, because the game is the absolute opposite of typical point-and-click games where the interactive items stand out.
In fact, nearly everything on the screen can be clicked to generate many different outcomes. Some are traditional, such as text descriptions of items or dialogue with characters. While others may cause weird events to occur, generate sounds or jokes, affect your UI, and so on. The game tends to break the 4th wall quite a lot in its sense of humor and peculiarity. There are really weird creatures to meet, or funny easter eggs for real life or other literature, for instance.
However, there is a main plotline to the game that is quite serious, even if a lot of the jokes and oddities might throw you off track. Many people might start off like I did, thinking that the game would just be a silly adventure into weirdness.
And while the game indeed keeps its quirkiness throughout the entirety of its time, the dialogue with characters and the storyline of the Fortunate Isles shows a real conflict over life and happiness. The Sea Will Claim Everything is filled with real life issues over government, news/word-of-mouth, work/employment, wealth, murder, philosophical beliefs, identity, and more.
You may continue to encounter bizarre scenes that make you look at the game as if it is crazy, but if you also focus on many serious encounters in the game, you will realize that there is something quite direct and real about the fantasy world you are visiting.
The Sea Will Claim Everything grew more interesting as I played it, though I will say that I did not read every single word or humorous scene that I encountered. I heavily focused on the plotline and more serious scenes, though I enjoyed many of the silly easter eggs along the way. The game's description on the Steam page notes "Walls of text" and it is very true. If you actually look at every single item description and read every single conversation word-for-word, your play time could be 3 times as much as mine, probably.
As mentioned earlier, the game's art style is mostly 2D without animation, with the exception of a few areas or specific scenes in the game. The art style still stands out as very nice, showing that a lot of work was put into it. There is an extremely large amount of areas to navigate in the game, and none of the exploration or backtracking ever felt boring to me. Part of that is owed to the game's ability to fast travel, and also the fact that  navigating between different areas is almost instantaneous.
Many of the places you explore also have their own distinct music, which further stands out as very interesting. I was taken aback at the number of songs in the game and the fact that many, many of them have a lot of quality work.
The Sea Will Claim Everything turned out to be an adventure that I unexpectedly loved. Quite a unique experience.

I'll give NSS5 that, it's a relatively enjoyable game. The match gameplay is reminiscent of Sensible Soccer and other early 90's, and definitely works in a retro kind of way. The drawback, however, is that the game is kind of a poorly designed, buggy mess. Save files get corrupted left and right, the game freezes with alarming regularity, and the puzzling online requirement tends to make starting new games a chore (hot tip: If you happen to buy it and struggle starting a game because of connectivity issues, edit the Settings\Settings.txt file. Change the line nettimeout=5 to nettimeout=100).
All in all, I can't recommend it. There's not enough here to defend the crippling issues the game has, and definitely not enough to defend their pricing point. Steer clear.

The last woman standing, Caldonita, spent her remaining six months constantly fishing to keep herself from starving to death.
10/10 Would wait too long for nomads again.

Gonner is a fantastic little game that I have come to enjoy recently. It's fantastic to quickly pick up and play (and then put down again when you die)
What I like -
Controls are very responsive and feel tight.
The art style is captivating. The passive animations on everything make everything look alive. The colours are vibrant and it is very clear what is and is not an enemy.
The combo system is fun and rewards risk, as you will be forced to sometimes give up currency in order to continue a combo. Watching the colours of the world change as you kill makes a god combo all the more exciting,
Text, or lack thereof. Having no text to speak of aside from the menus gives the game a comic style, as emotions and abilities are shown through visual flair instead of descriptions.
The little interactions between objects.
These little extra touches add so much interest to an already compelling gameplay.
Weekly updates!
What I don't like -
Walls being invisible unless you are near them can screw you over sometimes with regards to combos and pitfalls
When you are hit in the middle of a bunch of enemies, it is very difficult to see where you are and can go.
Environment variety is a thing I feel is lacking. You could put it down to art style, but personally I really don't like that within certain areas, rooms look identical.
Lack of variety is a big problem. There are very few guns, heads and backpacks to choose from at the moment. This issue is being resolved via updates, but at the time of this review it does not feel like you encounter enough items to cause a playstyle change mid run.
Pitfalls where you cannot see the walls feel very unfair. Furthermore, having your gear dropped down a hole also feels similarly unfair.
Honestly though, the issues I have are mostly easily resolved. Even if the game was in pixel art I'd still reccomend it for the smooth gameplay and tight controls.
I look forward to future updates from this indie gem and I wish the dev the best of luck in finding this game an audience.

Risen is an open-world RPG set in a land filled with turmoil. You play as a nameless castaway, stranded on an island with not a coin to your name. So, you make a name for yourself - getting swept up in the struggles of the people while you do so.
The story in Risen is interesting, sure. But I cannot say it was anything too phenomenal. The overarching plot (and main goal) failed to keep me interested, and I found myself more focused on the smaller quests and the lives of the individual characters.
The graphics in this game have held up surprisingly well over time. While they are not as impressive as a new game, they were certainly not jarring. There were some beautiful scenes, and never a moment where I noticed just how old the game was.
Combat... it feels like it had so much potential. I love being able to parry attacks, having to predict my opponent’s patters. Not so much when I am fighting three at once, though. I feel like the combat could have been much more entertaining if you only had one foe to face at a time.
The final boss fight. ARGH! How frustrating it was, that even with a quicksave, I lost all my progress on the boss due to a misstep and fall.
This is really not a bad game. Nothing phenomenal, and certainly not something I would pick up again just to revisit the game world. But it was fun.

In the beginning of this review I wrote "in general I can recommend...". I wrote it, because it's true, but not only. I'd like to write about some things I didn't like. Firstly, many missions that are repetitive and make you think as if you were doing it for another time. Second thing - from circa middle part from the game it got boring for me. It takes too much time to get destruction points to unlock next main quest and exploring is not as appealing as it was before.
I haven't played multiplayer yet, so I won't write about it, although I heard from my friends that it's good.
Generally speaking, there are more positives about this game than negatives, that's why I can boldly recommend it as a good, well-made and beautiful looking product.

It's certainly got its flaws, but I didn't think it was so bad as to be in mostly-negative review territory.  I'm honestly not sure whether to give it a recommendation, but I can at least say I don't regret spending the time to play through it once.  That's more than I can say for some of the games I've paid for.
To summarize the experience, it was like the gameplay from the Afraid of Monsters mod for Half-Hife with the atmosphere of the Resident Evil maps for Sven Co-op and the pacing of Spooky's House of Jumpscares.  On the plus side, you can tell time was taken to detail each area with interesting things to look at and little collectables or easter eggs to find. It was somewhat interesting (or at least at first it was) to explore there house where you spend the majority of your time.  The writing on the notes you find is at least competent, which is pretty rare for free horror games on Steam. The voice acting is comedically awful but the sound overall is actually pretty decent and helps build a bit of atmosphere.
The main problems with the game are centered around level design, however.  I understand engine limitations sometimes demand segmentation in levels, but it really shouldn't be necessary to this extreme with Source unless the dev was in serious need of a RAM upgrade on his compile machine.  If just two short hallways were made part of the main foyer map instead of separate levels, it would have cut the number of load screens to a fraction of what they end up being, but even so the door transitions and load screens are relentless everywhere you go.  There are moments where you'll have to make trips back and forth from one side of the house to the other, and this consists of what feels like ages of hall, door, load, hall, door, load, room, door, hall, door, load, repeat ad nauseum.  Just let us open some doors and leave them open for God's sake.  I've got a fast SSD which made the load screens just a second or two in most cases, but this would be torture if played on an older system with a hard drive. It literally felt like Spooky's House of Jump Scares in the latter half of the game.
By the way, the house is the Resident Evil mansion.  Not inspired by it--it IS the Resident Evil mansion. With the Resident Evil soundtrack.  I immediately had flashbacks to the Sven Co-op remake.  Not sure how I feel about that, though I'm kinda guessing it might not be so cool in terms of being legal.
The other prime issue with the level design though is the enemy placement. It is deliberately trollish 90% of the time and constantly does its best to silently spawn zombies right behind you for absolutely unavoidable hits. Even if you're expecting it, the game is designed for the spawns to happen out of your field of view.   Monsters don't have any footstep, idle or aggro sounds, so your only audio cue is getting whacked in the back of the head.  Not cool.  Could have done without this feature.  Oh, and some of the zombies might surprise you by how much of a brick shithouse they are, meaning you'll need to either have a full clip in your machine gun or find some level geometry you can use to get out of reach and cheese it.
Despite all this though I still managed to get some enjoyment out of the whole thing.  The atmosphere was decent and some of the puzzles did require a bit of thought.  Wouldn't pay for it, but for a freebie it wasn't too bad for an evening's distraction.

I only played 1.5 hrs so far but let me tell you, i enjoyed every minute of it. The graphics are not made to be super realistic and high detailed, but still look great in any way. It's just something else and i like it.
Especially buildings add a lot of atmosphere to the game if you search them for loot. Also the sound is really important, if you are indoor you hear the cold wind from the outside bashing against the building, wolves howling and the floor cracking.
Lighting a fire is the most satisfying thing ingame, nature your worst enemy and you are at the end of the food chain.
The craft system is nice already, everything is explained well (how to get rid of a cold, how to heal yourself or how to get rid of an infection)
Weather is also changing from time to time and it makes things even worse.
I had a scary entcounter with nature when i went straight in to a snow storm (dumb as i am). I could'nt see anything, i was alone with my storm light running out of fuel, on a frozen lake, luckely enough i found a small shack where i was able to light a fire. It raised my body temperature but i knew my fire would go out sooner or later. So i moved on, the wind still strong, still not able to see anything far away until i reached a nice housing with a chimney. I went in, completely frozen, gathered food and lit a fire and rest in there for 10 hours straight to re-gain energy.
This is what makes the game any special - the concept. No zombies, no brain eating. Real SURVIVAL. Only thing i dislike. No encounters with other human beings, i felt like Will Smith in I am Legend. Only a small amount of animals (wolf, rabbit, deer) by what i have seen so far. Map could be larger and i guess the game will get boring as soon as you are well equipped. But just now since its early access and i hope there is more to come. Multiplayer in form of Ko-op aka. Dual Survival would be nice but its not needed. Overall a great singleplayer experience, worth the money. I just hope it will get more content and be supported as long as possible.
Thanks for reading (i hope you did :p)
