A short, charming adventure.
As opposed to the more traditional puzzle-focused adventure game centering on complicated interactions between the player inventory and the world, making progress in this title often boils down to "just click on everything".  The focus is on exploring the fantastic locales of the Fortunate Isles and getting to know its inhabitants.  A big part of the charm is that the game is filled with many small details simply there for flavor.  As long as you are willing to take your time and soak in the atmosphere, the payoff will be worthwhile.
I will note that the game is politically-charged, but I found its approach to be both philosophical and heartfelt enough to make up for any differences between my politics and the author's.

I feel awful giving this a negative review, it's a free to play game with adorable kittens in it, I must be some kind of monster to dislike it on that basis alone.
However, the novelty of this game almost immediately wore out when I realised this was a cut down version of Contraption Maker with a lot less predicable physics and added microtransactions, and it's a not very well optimised PC mobile port to boot.
If it had the same weirdness of its trailer it might have been more tolerable, but as it stands its an average physics-based puzzle game, not nearly as poor as Bad Rats but not as good as Contraption Maker either.
One thing that would have been in its favour was customising your cats, and unlocking new features  and puzzles as you progressed, but that is strictly limited and unimaginative, plus I was too bored to continue barely 10 minutes in.
Overall, there really isn't much to say about the game other than I don't think it's worth downloading, even if you want to waste a few minutes there are so many better free/cheap games on steam. The most damning thing I can say about this game is that even cats couldn't save it.

Whenever I went to Showbiz or Chuck E Cheeses, I'd always mention how I'd hate to be locked in there at night.  This game gives you a perfect example of why I wouldn't want to be locked in there at night.  In fact, I could say the same thing about any ride or attraction that's filled with animatronic beings (Pirates of the Caribbean, It's a Small World, The Hall of Presidents...)
What we have here is a resource management game with some board game mechanics sprinkled in.  You start with 100% power and using the cameras, turning on the lights outside your booth or closing the door will all consume power.  The idea is to make from 12am to 6am without allowing the animatronic demons to enter your booth.
The unholy demon spawns from hell will start in their places on the stage(s).  Then suddenly they will disappear, and it's up to you to keep track of where they are via the security cameras as they move from room to room in a sort of chess-like/weeping angel-like manner.  Your job is to keep them out of the booth.  If you shut the door on them successfully, you'll see them retreat to another room away from the booth (and perhaps looking a little more angry...)
Unfortunately the only way to see what's immediately outside of your booth is to turn on the lights, spending more energy (and sometimes giving you a minor heart attack).   Oh yeah, the kitchen is pitch black so you will have to rely on audio only...and something may or may not be lurking behind that closed curtain.  Also, experiencing complete power loss is probably next to the worse nightmare you could possibly imagine.  Of course these Freddy and his pals are completely aware of your presence behind the cameras and will do anything it takes to mess with your head as they quietly surround you on both sides.  Oh look, it's staring right at you, it looks hungry...
...and wait a minute, where did the chicken go?  He was just down the hall a second ago.  It's at that point you panic and start looking at every camera trying to find him until you put down your tablet and find a nice surprise had entered the room when you weren't paying attention.  A couple of seconds later you're  now picking yourself off of the floor from having just fallen backwards in your chair and your housemates/roommates/spouse/family are rushing up the stairs to make sure you're okay from the scream they just heard.
I recommend playing this game at least once, and that might be the number of times you'll muster up the courage to play it.  I think this one benefits from a few people gathered around the display so you can all have a laugh after you've had your communal scream.  At least you'll have someone to hold onto when Foxy comes strolling down the hallway.

Like stepping back in time about twenty years, this is a Master-System-level game wrapped up in Megadrive-level packaging. Some of the minigames are fun for a while, and the general idea of trying to balance training, games, social life, and other responsibilities in a professional football career is a good one, but ultimately repetitive implementation, odd choice for some mini-games (a higher/lower card guessing game for contract negotiations?) and a match engine 25 years out of date (Sensible Soccer is relatively state-of-the-art) let down what could have been a deep, feature-rich professional footballer career simulator. Still fun for a time due to some fantastic ideas (online leaderboards without demanding direct PvP? Yes, please!), and a series I'd love to see progress, but this edition is simply too basic, particularly during matches which quickly become an exercise in frustration. Worth a playthrough after picking up on the very cheap, but it has a long way to go to be more than just a collection of good ideas.

Super Splatters is a super fun and challenging puzzle game. The game first starts off simple and is easy to learn, but later you will return to the earlier levels with new challenges awaiting making this game very difficult to beat all the levels. The goal is to have your splatters splat across the levels and touch firework pods, touch all the pods in every round and you beat the level. The levels become more difficult and varied requiring you to use different stunts in order to light up all the pods and past certain obstacles. If you're looking for a crazy and fun puzzle game then give this one a try. The graphics, sounds and music are all well done making this game feel very light-hearted and goofy, but do not let that fool you - the game sounds simple but is very challenging. I was only able to complete all of the easy and medium challenges, the hard ones will require patience and practice!

Refunct is a lovely little game that really gives you the freedom inside it's little world as it promises. Try again if you missed the jump, falling in water doesn't kill you, evenmore you can just stay underwater as you want, to explore the map in it's underwater state! No failstate, no timer, no points, just jumping around for nice music. I remember that I quit after my first death when it first was released on Steam.
The last few days, I replayed it.
And what do I have to say?
The surroundings, the textures and models were stunning, great work there. The weapon models looked fantastic and it all really fit to the post WWII-theme.
However, the gameplay and gameflow were both horrible.
The pistol does itty-bitty damage, you need two full clips to finish off the first few monsters (which are pretty weak compared to those later in the game).
Most of the weapons, which have a scope are almost useless when using the ironsight function. I expected the scope to cover almost all of my screen (similar to games like TF2, Half Life 2 and CS:GO).
Instead i got this tiny pin prick of a scope in the middle of the screen, which sadly enlarged the things viewed through it so much that I rather had to guess where I was aiming instead of actually aiming. It was like looking through a tiny magnifying glass.
The weapon switch speed was horrible. I get that it is more realistic when he first packs his pistol away and then slowly pulls his sniper rifle from elsewhere, maybe his bag or his back. But when have games ever been realistic? Never.
Compared to the awesome weapon system in Half Life 1/2, this just lacked the power.
Why power? Well, most of the weapons did laughable damage. I needed an entire clip with the MP40 to finish one of the later monsters. Four sniper shots for one of the grey walker things. The only efficient weapon was the rocket launcher, which you could only get when you had found an item in the middle of the game (bit unfair eh?).
Also, we have the usual Cry of Fear-type punishment when you reload, you loose the entire clip. That's one of the only features I liked about the weapon system. Oh and the iron sights of the unscoped weapons were pretty good.
We spoke of enemies earlier, I'd like to come back to that.
Most of the wicked zombies, infected and mentally insane you encounter in the mod are way too strong. This is mostly because of their movement speed, They run so fast that you cannot walk backwards and shoot at them. Also their attack speed is like they ate 6 Moon shards (obvious Dota 2 reference). Most of them will kill you in roughly four hits. I guess there's a headshot mechanic, but how in the absolute ♥♥♥♥ are you supposed to use that if you run from a 300 Mp/h Lamborghini zombie, whose head sways drastically because of the way he moves?
I actually think the boss battles are not that hard compared to what some of the enemies do. It was always a fair 1 vs. 1 fight, so that you actually had time to dodge and aim.
But especially towards the end of "The Forgotten Ones" the battles are relentless, with as much as 15 enemies piling onto you (or one of your unfortunate mates you have to rescue).
The absolute worst part of the mod was the health system. You could only carry one health kit at the time, that could heal you, but that doesn't help you anything when you are being overrun by hordes of OP mutants. If you get hit ONCE, YOU START TO HOBBLE AROUND LIKE SOME ♥♥♥♥ING ♥♥♥♥♥ WHO CANT EVEN TAKE A SINGLE HIT! Yeah, your movement is minimzed to maybe 40% of your NORMAL walking speed (which is already pretty slow).
Also, you bleed out when you are under 1/3 of your health. Just won a fight? Well, fear no more, you'll ♥♥♥♥ing die as a reward! Yaaaay!!!! ♥♥♥♥ing hell.
The puzzles are next level cryptic lard♥♥♥♥♥ Who is supposed to know that there will be a bunker under a random grate in a washing room? Who can guess that you have to cut open some random pipe covering just to get a pipe? All that is because these things are only "revealed" to you when you press the "Use-key" at a very specific area, nowhere else. It isn't hinted in the notes properly, the character never mentions anything and you'll end up searching around through the mansion with the most horrible stamina a video game character could have and one of the most terrible map loading methods I have ever seen (it is like in Cry of Fear, where you can't open doors physically but click your "Use"-button at them to be ported behind it, whilst the screen fades out and in again). The maps are tiny, a 10secs map loading screen is behind every second door.
No quicksave function. The addition of this feature would make many of the problems nonexistent.
To conclude: Don't play it. Download Grey or Afraid of Monsters if you want a proper horror mod. If you want a challenge and some pretty sweet looking WWII graphics you can try it.
But I wouldn't recommend it to the normal consumer who might stumble onto this in the horror section of the steam store.

First of all, DD2 feels like a complete reboot of DD1.
Graphics and animations aside, the few changes that felt refreshing to me were the substats you get from loot and the spheres, especially uber spheres. The substats (e.g. hearty blockade) are way more important than just the stats you add from leveling whereas the spheres gives you a diverse option to build your towers. Oh, and you can no longer add defense attack speed with equips, so that makes it different from DD1.
Similar to DD1, this game is all about the loot. Pretty self-explanatory, you progress from getting better loot and to get better loot, you gotta keep replaying maps. Essentially making the game feel "grindy". Just a disclaimer, loot isn't the most important aspect of this game, there're still ways to beat levels such as strategising tower placement and countering magic/physical resistance. I feel that loot is what drives the game, it is the 'core' of Dungeon Defenders.
Which brings me to...
What I don't like about DD2 right now 19/10/2015:
- THERE IS LIMITED BAG SPACE!!!!!!! You get pretty good loot that you wanna keep (that takes up space). You gotta wait 48 hours for an egg to rot and become a material required for evolving your pet (that takes up space). You get pet food for your pet (that takes up space). You get some other material required for evolving pet (that takes up space).
It's disheartening that you have to either sacrifice loot for progressing your eqp/pet, or sacrifice progress for loot. Moreover, certain maps gives you a lot of loot, so you gotta sell items in between waves (playing with people, everyone is in a hurry to 'g' up).
- So gems are no longer just solely for cosmetics. Since more bag space also requires gems, would this make it P2W?
- Server lags. This game just became free to play recently, so no doubt this would happen. However, playing this game every now and then, I find myself off the side of the cliff. You decide if you wanna put up with that (personally I'd give it time).
Other than the few main points above that I have problems with, the game is still in Alpha with lots more potential. Can't wait to see it in completion.
The game is free to play, so what are you waiting for? Try it.

While I'd like to give the game a positive review, something tells me to just simply put it in a nutshell: PewDiePie referances -- guys, if you're going to make easter eggs, make them be based around something other than some Swedish ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥-Youtuber. Secondly, this game has massive potential, but the voice acting ruins the atmosphere just a bit too much and the jumpscares are far too typical.
First thing right off of the bat:
- Who the hell was at the door at the beginning of the game? Just a, *knock knock*, "I wonder who that is?" and then that's it?
- The protagonist holds the reward for claiming and owning the World's Most Impatient Phone. The damn phone rang like 50 times before I could gather my gun, keys, and journal.
- The voice acting wasn't all that decent which, in my opinion, completely ruins the atmosphere. But it's not horrible.
This complaint is rather small: - When your friend, spoiler, dies, it says in the subtitles: "{Enter Name Here}! No! What the hell?!" But the protagonist says, "{Enter Name Here}!, NO! WHAT THE ♥♥♥♥ WAS THAT?!" or something like that.
Also, the character moves way too damn slow; espeically when your stamina runs out.
So, all in all, it's not the worst Half-Life 2 Horror Mod I've played, like I said, it has massive potential and I there are some parts in the game of which I did enjoy. But if you guys want some inspiration on how a jumpscare should be planned out or how voice acting should be done, I recommened taking a look at the infamous Half-Life Mod: Cry of Fear -- I'm sure if you contact the head of Team Psykallar via e-mail or whatever, he'll be more than happy to give some tips. One last thing, the animations are a bit.. robotic and unrealistic -- which, of course, ruins the atmosphere.
I don't hate the game and I'd love to give it a positive review, but I don't think I should considering the above text.

I only played 1.5 hrs so far but let me tell you, i enjoyed every minute of it. The graphics are not made to be super realistic and high detailed, but still look great in any way. It's just something else and i like it.
Especially buildings add a lot of atmosphere to the game if you search them for loot. Also the sound is really important, if you are indoor you hear the cold wind from the outside bashing against the building, wolves howling and the floor cracking.
Lighting a fire is the most satisfying thing ingame, nature your worst enemy and you are at the end of the food chain.
The craft system is nice already, everything is explained well (how to get rid of a cold, how to heal yourself or how to get rid of an infection)
Weather is also changing from time to time and it makes things even worse.
I had a scary entcounter with nature when i went straight in to a snow storm (dumb as i am). I could'nt see anything, i was alone with my storm light running out of fuel, on a frozen lake, luckely enough i found a small shack where i was able to light a fire. It raised my body temperature but i knew my fire would go out sooner or later. So i moved on, the wind still strong, still not able to see anything far away until i reached a nice housing with a chimney. I went in, completely frozen, gathered food and lit a fire and rest in there for 10 hours straight to re-gain energy.
This is what makes the game any special - the concept. No zombies, no brain eating. Real SURVIVAL. Only thing i dislike. No encounters with other human beings, i felt like Will Smith in I am Legend. Only a small amount of animals (wolf, rabbit, deer) by what i have seen so far. Map could be larger and i guess the game will get boring as soon as you are well equipped. But just now since its early access and i hope there is more to come. Multiplayer in form of Ko-op aka. Dual Survival would be nice but its not needed. Overall a great singleplayer experience, worth the money. I just hope it will get more content and be supported as long as possible.
Thanks for reading (i hope you did :p)

When I first saw this on Greenlight, I thought it was some low-quality point and click that somehow got lost among the pile of uninspired platformers and boring first-person horror games. How wrong I was.
This game has amazing worldbuilding. Despite its somewhat basic graphics, every scene has a lot of interactible elements, most of them rewarding you with strange creatures and items descriptions, puns, or twisted references to real-world things. There are sentient flowers and mushrooms (beware of the communist varieties), weird food and potions, technological plants (the game's UI is apparently made from them, and clicking its various doodads, that might look like they're just for show at first, will actually activate silly effects), and many more. The book titles in particular are great, whether they're referencing classics, fantasy and sci-fi, political and economical essays, videogames (particularly Morrowind, if you've ever played it you probably remember its peculiar literature), made-up authors or Greek writers I've never heard of. There might be a bit too much pseudoscientific stuff ("Revolving Protonic Chrono-Accumulator") and fantasy name salad ("King Xekmurg from Alkhirg") for my taste, but it's only a minor complaint. It all amounts to some kind of Frankensteinian setting, made of parts that should not work together but actually do. If you've read Harry Potter and wondered how Rowling managed to create an interesting setting while at first it seems she just threw every fantasy cliché ever into a soup, you'll get a similar feeling here.
The scenario is mostly used as a way to discover the world, although it's easy to spot it also delivers a social and political message (read: a left-winged political message, so you might not agree with it if you're leaning towards conservatism), since there are obvious nods to the Greek crisis and the Arab Spring. Despite the characters being mostly quest-givers and quest-receivers, they all have their little stories to tell, their own views on the world, and I ended up deeply caring for them (but it's easy to get hold of my emotions when you put cats and lizards everywhere).
Gameplay-wise it's a typical adventure game, click on things, get items, talk to characters, move the story forward. The few puzzles in there aren't particularly complex, or illogical (thankfully), and there's a quest log to keep track of what you need to do. It still has a few surprises in store, like the alchemy system.
While at first glance the graphics may look like they were drawn by a five-years-old, they're actually pretty competent in their use of coloring and shading. They give the game a peculiar atmosphere, somewhere between an illustrated book for children and an old PnP RPG manual from the 80s.
There are other games in the same setting available from
. I haven't played them yet, so I can't say if they're as good as this one, but I'll mention their existence anyway.
+ Excellent worldbuilding
+ Likeable characters
+ Great writing
+ Quirky UI and alchemy mechanic
+ Many hidden things to find
- Political message might rub you the wrong way

If you want to be a pedant (and I love nothing more than pedantry), you can boil almost any PC game down to clicking. Point-and-click adventures, obviously, but also puzzlers, simulators, and even FPSes if you go by the classic line about sniping being a point-and-click adventure where the only puzzle is Use Gun On Head. I bring this up because of all the clicking to be had in the gaming world, The Sea Will Claim Everything might be the most fun I've ever had clicking on things. Not because it's particularly pretty or complex clicking, but because what you get for it is so delightfully rewarding.
TSWCE is posed not as a game, but as a portal into the fanciful Lands of Dream. A fellow by the name of The Mysterious-Druid has grown this techno-organic interface for you so that you can help him solve a few pressing problems in his picturesque realm, namely the foreclosure of his equally techno-organic home, the disappearance of his girlfriend, and the political unrest threatening the Fortunate Isles. Luckily for you this portal functions much like a point-and-click adventure, with static scenes to click around, key phrases to initiate dialog with, items to find, combine, and use, and some other less-useful but plenty interesting features.
It's a cheeky premise for a game but you can't really appreciate how well it works until you get to that first scene and start clicking things. It's not a particularly strange scene, just a druid in a cave with a bunch of books and boxes and computery-things. But every single thing you click has a different, quirky description. And I mean EVERYTHING, every single book, every single mushroom, every single button, and every single bit of decor has something to say about its philosophy or political alignment or life goal or something equally irreverant. Scenes in this game brim with secrets where the reward is a clever line that's more than likely going to make you chuckle.
The Room and its sequel have long been my high-water mark for enjoyment just from clicking things, with every single switch and key and object having Blizzard-levels of tactile quality to clicking them. But TSWCE is an entirely new paradigm of clicking enjoyment, where every scene is full of things you just can't wait to click on because you'll be instantly regaled with loads of charm. That's really the key to making a great adventure game, giving players a world that is irresistible to explore, and while others have achieved that through graphics or story, this title does it through masterful writing.
That's not to say the story isn't a draw here, of course. The creativity and attention to detail that starts you off with a dimensional window in a techno-organic habitat extends fully to the rest of the game. The Fortunate Isles lie in the Lands of Dream, where goat people and elves and talking skulls and philosopher trees live and work side by side. Every one of them is a grounded, realistic character for what they are, fascinating to converse with without ever wearing out their welcomes. As your quest to aid The Mysterious-Druid unfolds you'll find a thread of plot that strongly echoes the hardships of our very real world, held aloft by subversions of myth, challengers of intellect, and some of the best writing to be found in gaming.
It took me a bit to warm up to the pace and style of this one, but rarely have I been so well-rewarded for sticking it out. Every element of the game is woven together with masterful artistry, from the detailed window that itself is used in puzzles to the random crafting experimentation that rewards you with more charming writing and secrets. You will never run out of discussions and descriptions to revel in, full of clever puns, thoughtful symbolism, and heartwarming plot. The Sea Will Claim Everything is a true treasure, a game of magnificent prose presented as rewards for exploring a rich and colorful world.

A whimsical point and click adventure game with a narrative based around humanity and politics.
The point and click aspect of this game is almost all clicking on objects to read descriptions that are typically humorous. Occasionally you will need to find things in the environment and pick them up by clicking them individually. It's not common, and they're usually in your face. The rest of the game is really done through talking to characters and helping them so they can help you. Early on, I felt sort of pressured to click everything so I wouldn't miss anything important or funny.. there were tons of things to interact with. Eventually, after the first area, it's not so bad. There's also a ton of character that you may meet all at once, but the world layout makes it easy to run around quickly.
I really enjoyed the art style; it's cartoony, whimsical and colorful. I thought the music was superb as well, fitting the themes of the areas. The overall feel of the game is extremely calming, but it can feel kind of slow at times.
The game is best played alone with no distractions, as you do have to keep track of things you need to do. I would generally explore all the new areas before going back and completing the "quests", and a couple of times I found myself with too much to remember. There is a quest scroll you can look at that sums up what you have to do, but sometimes it's not descriptive enough... if you forget who you need to talk to, or where they are, you can spend a lot of time "lost." I got pretty far in the game before getting stuck... characters kept talking about a certain person that I was positive I never actually discovered in the world. I only ended up running into them by misclicking the navigation arrows. A couple of other quests seemed vague but didn't stop me up as much.
My biggest complaint is having to click the navigation arrows to move around. I wish I could use the arrow keys for this, so I wouldn't have to move my mouse around as much. Otherwise, the UI is quirky, but I feel like it added to the feel of the game.
I ended up enjoying the game more as it went on, and I really appreciated the small little details here and there. I don't think this game is for everybody, as there isn't a "twist" or anything crazy that happens like most games. It's simply an interactive story most of all, and a social commentary of the world secondly. There's a lot to like here, but it is a slow experience and not something you should rush through.

This game begins extremely slowly and increasing the speed at which you level relies on some dubious game mechanics.  You get bonus blood (experience) if you kill multiple mobs at the same time.  No, not multiple enemies in quick sequence, they have to die at the exact same time.  Which means that the best strategy is to chip away at higher HP mobs, spend some time rolling around gathering them up, and then executing them all at once with an AoE ability.  The rate at which you level/unlock skills could probably be improved, at least early on.  It is definitely a slow haul at the beginning.  I recommend not playing on anything easier than "hard" otherwise the game is extremely dull.
I've read terrible things about M + KB, but on my XBOX 1 controller, the game plays perfectly fine.  I've encountered none of the bugs that I have seen reported.  The exposure that everyone is complaining about so far has only been in 1 area, I've explored 5.  It's also extremely easy to manage -- doesn't seem to change in difficulty on the higher levels either.  FWIW, I thought it was an interesting mechanic that you could, mostly, forget about but added to immersion.
The game is extremely linear and almost any "side area" (usually just a dead end path) has some type of chest with goodies in it.  It's a basic design, but not a bad one.  And while the graphics aren't phenomenal, the environments are pretty neat.  Quests are straight forward, ending with a boss.  All the boss fights that I've done so far I've thoroughly enjoyed -- multiple mechanics, etc.  Not sure if any of the mechanics change across difficulties.  All areas have some bonus objectives -- these are pretty uninspired, but don't detract from the gameplay experience at all (typically kill X mobs, which you easily complete if you explore the map, or burn X number of flags).
Most of the inventory complaints seem to be with regard to M + KB.  The inventory management seems perfectly fine for my XBOX controller, minus the occasional issue with "wheels" where you try to select a slot, but jump to the next one by accident.  This is not uncommon and is hardly a criticism.

Outlast promised to be horror, survival game without any fighting. Instead you have to overcome the horrors by running, patience and a lot of planning how to escape...
I have to say, that I have much enjoyed the game. Supercillious and arrogant journalist is about to film another reportage about bad corporation. However, your camcorder changes very fast to your ultimate survival item. And believe me, scared patients are your smallest problem.
This with a great soundtrack, also some jumpscares created a great story. Combined with your notes and documents found results into horrors beyond our world and capability of our minds to understand it. Night vision also sends this genre to another dimension, hunting for batteries is essential. Concluded with epic finale.
Negatives for me was too much light in the end, some jumps (but perhaps to my wooden pc :-D) and bug, when my camcorder did not break during the female-ward passage. Nevertheless, I highly recommend this game and do not forget to play with headset during the night without the light!

Story is telling us various background informations, which are filling the gaps in original game and completes the bizarre horrors created by the Murkoff corporation. Again, we have to escape and again, it was epic.
New bosses were added, Frank Manera as "Canibal" was good, but Eddie Gluskin as "Groom" overcame any limits for negative characters. Living inside his own world, I felt sorry for him in the end. Really, for a badass!
More even closer escapes, another usage of camcorder (without batteries, only with incorporated light), new locations with horrific atmosphere, more resignated and mutilated patients and more of corporation stuff even with own tactical assault teams!
I experienced only one bug, the curtain before Drying Ground location. The tempo of the game is changing, keeping the tension high and proves your reflexes in unexpected situations. Also, another amount of collectibles and epic finale with an idea to think about.
Definitively recommend this, even better at night without lights with headset!

CTD and Repetitive
FIRST THE CRASH TO DESKTOP ISSUE:  My first play session worked fine, except the menu was too small for my resolution (1920 x 1080).  A few adjustments in the settings fixed that.  However, during my second play session the game would crash after about 5 minutes of play time.  (For reference, I’m running this on Windows 8.1, 64 bit)  After some research, I finally discovered a fix which involved going into the registry and deleting some entries.  And I discovered this fix only worked as long as you didn’t start a new game.  If you did, you’d have to edit the registry again.  This is certainly something a player should not have to do in order to get a working game.
ON TO THE PLAYING:  So I bought the game because it seemed fun.  I generally like resource management and time management games.  I've played Sims, SimCity, Diner Dash, Cooking Dash, etc. just to give you an idea.
At first it was fun.  I could place buildings where I wanted.  A few like the houses even had different styles to choose from by typing the "F" key before placing it on the ground.  I liked watching my little worker ants hurry around.  I quickly got a handle on my food supply, and this was despite some of the workers hoarding a disproportionate amount of food in their houses which meant less for others.  It’s not that hard really.  Just have some farm fields during the growing season, and you also have a few hunters, fishermen, and/or gatherers.  I also got control of wood, stone, etc.
In the end, it seemed all I needed to do was sit with the workers pane open and subtract or add workers to different positions as I needed.  For example: “Subtract 3 workers from Gathering, and add those 3 to Building because I have a wave of construction projects going on.”  It’s just a matter of clicking up or down on the arrows next to the jobs in the list.  I just needed to do that and keep an eye on the resource panes.  That’s why it got repetitive, and I played less than 10 hours.  Maybe that’s all the game is really meant for.

Super Splatters is another one of those games I'd never heard of, but picked up in a gaming bundle. I'm always willing to give these obscure titles a try; sometimes you find a hidden gem. This game isn't exactly a diamond, but it isn't bad either.
You control blobs and use the environment and skills to slam your gooey goodness into bombs, trying to rack up combos for skill shots and clearing lots of bombs at one time. The game is simple, and is something you can easily kill an hour with.
I enjoy that every level feels like it adds something new to the experience, but because of this, the developer felt the need to over-explain every new element through an "instructor," and these scenes are riddled with bad jokes and are incredibly boring to sit through. It really takes away from the fluid experience this game could otherwise offer.
As with most of these indie games, the pricetag is a little bit unreasonable to me. The game is entertaining, but it's not something I'd ever throw more than a couple of dollars at. If you can get it cheap, go for it - otherwise you probably won't feel like you got your money's worth.

Super Splatters is a fun physics game that is suitable for all ages. The goal of the game is to set of fireworks by shooting blobs of liquid igniter at them. This is a fairly simple concept, but can be hard to achieve when you reach later levels. As you work your way through the levels, you will unlock new tricks to help you complete your goal. Depending on which gamemode you play on, the tricks will add another layer of challenge to the game. In my opinion, the gameplay is cute and nicely done.
The graphics are very bright and clear. The game is vibrant with color, which makes is very fun to watch the blobs explode all over everything. I don't really care for graphics as much as most people, but I find these ones great to look at. They gets two thumbs up from me.
The music and sound for the game is adjustable, so if you grow tired of it, you can always shut it off. The blobs do make unintelligible noises when they talk in their quirky ways, which I find to be really cute. For most games, I tend to turn the sound off, but I leave it on for Super Splatters, since it's enjoyable to listen to.
The reply value of Super Splatters is moderate. You can go back to finished levels to try to acheive even better highscores than before, which is a definite bonus. And while it is fun to watch the little blobs hurl themselves to certain death, it can become repetitive after awhile. I would recommend picking Super Splatters up during any sale.

I've used the rpg maker software since RPG2k3, followed by the iteration of RPG Maker XP and RPG Maker VX. All told, I've spent close to 4000 hours messing around with the different versions, with the bulk of that time spent on RPG Maker XP.
I have some reservations about the software. My biggest complaint has always been the difficulty of having one project handled by multiple people. There was never an easy way to have more than one person working on it at a time. I often ran a project in collaboration with my brother and another friend, so updating work that was done independantly into the main file was always an issue. This means that the software has always lacked a way to work collaboratively. The issue is still here in the newest version.
Another of my larger complaints with version XP had always been the heavily restricted battle system. While better coders than me had made modifications to the (shudder) ruby script, it never allowed the versitility through the user interface that I was looking for. Those issues have been completely addressed with version VX. The battle system has far more flexibility now than it had in XP, reviving some of the features that made the battle system in 2k3 so strong. Status effects can be both positive and negative, and each character can support customized skillsets. A great improvement.
But I feel they went wrong with the graphical style. Compared to the high quality 2D graphics of XP, which were reminiscent of Final Fantasy VI and Chrono-Trigger, RPG Maker VX chose to limit the design to a stylized 'chibi' which cheapened the environment and the characters. This was highly distasteful, and resulted in me maintaining my RPG Maker XP project despite the superior versitility of the VX interface and software. Futhermore, the layering for the map design functions poorly, refusing to allow too many objects to overlap. Parallaxing is the only way to fix this issue and that requires an enormous amount of time and effort to properly photoshop. Then came version VX Ace. With Ace, support was put in place to allow for larger sprites. That was half of the battle. I began an extensively time-consuming process of converting all of my RPG Maker XP content into the new wide format for Ace. Then I discovered that the 'infinite' allotment for tileset size doesn't function. The interface cuts the tileset short, limiting the amount of tiles that can be accessed on a single map page. I was a huge fan of XP because I could (and did) use a single tileset that contained literally EVERY single tile. Giving a single map a huge variety of different content. This is impossible in either version of VX. Also, the layering issue persists in Ace. I am not a fan of parallaxing.
Although my review may have more complaints than raving support, understand that I began using this software because I was looking for a medium through which to tell a story. The story was, and is, more important than the game. The game has to be easy to play and not too grinding so that people can enjoy the story and explore the world I set about creating. For that purpose, this software performs remarkably well. I bring out the worst aspects of the software because over the course of a long project, as more and more time is invested into it, these issues caused repeated frustration and waste of time to figure workarounds (which usually involved parallaxing - did I mention that I hate that?). In short, know what you're getting into.
I will endorse this software and freely recommend it to anyone looking for an easy method of releasing their creativity. As my project partners moved on with their lives the remains of our efforts are left unfinished. On the other hand, the story is really good, and I've begun adapting it into a book instead. If the software is ever improved to address the layering and tileset size limitations, I might come back. But for now I've put it aside.
PS - Making a game is an ENORMOUS amount of work. I offer my respect and condolences to anyone commiting themselve to the effort. Good luck to you, and may your project end in completion.

I'm a fan of this title.
SpikySnail's Super Splatters seems to be the only game so far by the developer, and it shows a lot of promise.  Through no fault of the game's own, it doesn't seem like it's found the player-base or market I feel like it deserves.  If you put this thing in a time machine and sent it back to the mid-90's, this would be exactly the kind of game my sister and I would sit and play for hours, trading off a controller and trying to one-up each other.
As far as gameplay goes, you have several stationary characters, Splatters, situated around an arena also filled with multiple small colored bombs, usually strung together or packed into clusters of tight formations.  When your Splatter smashes against a wall or other object, it will dissolve into a massive gush of liquid.  It's very physics-based, and you get lots of different effects by playing with different speeds and angles of approach, Your goal is to coat all of the bombs with the liquid.  However, the real goal is accumulation of points, which is accomplished by taking advantage of new game mechanics as they're introduced: stunts like sliding around curves or initiating secondary strikes in the air, manipulating time, combining smaller blobs to make larger more powerful blobs, comboing; all this stuff really comes together in ways where there's no one way to approach a levlel.
Here's why its worth your time:
First; it's polished!  Colors pop off of the screen!  Satisfying sound effects!  It's everything you would want in a casual title like this.  All of the controls are smooth on keyboard+mouse and even smoother with the Xbox controller.  There's a nice progression mechanic that keeps adding new stuff as you unlock new levels, and different level types to keep things fresh.
It's challenging!  Levels look simple, but you'll find yourself messing up or just scraping by an awful lot.  Until you practice.  There's always a way to get a higher score, and replaying levels until you get that one perfect shot is addictive.
It's fun!  It's perfect for dipping into for 20 minutes and then out again.  Never fret about the tutorials or unskippable story segments, just hold "F" or the bumper to major fast-forward through the whole thing.  This even works during level resets, too.
The verdict:  This game was given to me and I'm glad it was.  It's really good, and I wish I'd had it years ago.

Just Cause 2 is awesome. Panau is a beautiful island of deserts, jungles, snowy mountains and beaches. At 400 square miles, it is one of the biggest game maps ever created. Rico has a grappling hook and a parachute, which allow the player to do so many cool things and travel the island without vehicles. While the planes, helicopters, and boats feel great, the cars are a little bit disappointing. Drive fast and you will immediately slide out. The gunfights are not really a strong suit of the game either. There is ridiculous aim assist and Rico can take at least 20 bullets before dying. What I love the most about this game though is that it has so much to offer outside of the story. I finished the story after a good 30 hours. But to complete all of the faction missions and challenges, find the easter eggs and complete all of the settlements took me over 150 hours. Overall a great game, and hours of fun.

Ok, I am in and alive for 13 days -
I've finally made a good start.
I started slowly.
Gathered supplies from the coastal area, made an empty home my safehouse. Hell, I had a fridge with 40Kg of food. I had so much food I was forced to stuff Chocolate Bars and Cooked Meat in Drawers... I even had a special Cabinet with Dog Food only.

I will begin with the easy part: I enjoyed The Sea Will Claim Everything very much. I have been a long-time player of adventure games, games with lots of text, interactive fiction, and as such felt very at home inside the "window" of the interface. It is possible that not everyone will share this level of comfort, but I'd encourage even such skeptics to consider trying it, or at least trying one of the free Lands of Dream titles. I really do think there is a place in everyone's life for games like this: something slow and thoughtful to savor and ponder.
There are a lot of reasons why I liked this game, and the other reviews on this page do a good job of explaining them, but I will reiterate for emphasis. The music in this game is wonderful and really, really adds a lot to the experience. The tone of the writing ranges from extremely silly to extremely poignant and somehow still feels like a unified whole. The characters you encounter are twenty different varieties of delightful, and I found myself caring about their stories much more than I expected. There's a point near the beginning of the game where (if I recall correctly) you are reading someone's journal to discover a crucial yet mundane piece of information to solve a puzzle. The entries continued on beyond the point when I learned what I needed to, and by the end I was overwhelmed and misty-eyed over this person's story--and they don't even appear anywhere else in the game. That's when I knew I was playing something really special.
So, I'd say the thing I liked most about this game was the characters. Actually, as I played through the game I started to realize that essentially everything in the game's world is a character. Every rock, every flower, every box, every mushroom. Some of the beings you encounter just talk to you more than others. And this struck me as a very lovely idea: that life is a kind of fractal, that everything has its own story and experiences, that some kind of universality connects even things that seem utterly disconnected. And the game has a great many more ideas.
I am not sure I have anything particularly negative to say about my time playing. There were two places I got stuck: once because I hadn't searched an area exhaustively enough, and once because I forgot about certain capabilities I possessed. But overall the level of frustration was low.
In summary, I think people who know they like this kind of game will really like it. And I want to re-emphasize for everyone else who is not sure: try it and I think you will be pleasantly delighted.

Got it as a gift, put a couple hours into it, already decided it's one of the best gifts I've ever recieved. There will be people railing at me for comparing this to Dwarf Fortress, but it really is like a less sophisticated and more limited, and therefore much more accessible, Dwarf Fortress with graphics that are very easy on the eyes and an interface that is slightly less visually unweildy. Being one in these kinds of games to make terrible decisions, all my games so far have been on Hard difficulty starts, and believe me, it's lived up to the name. It's a long string of trial and error, with a lot of winters full of empty houses and streets full of emaciated corpses, but in the end, when you make that first milestone and survive your first winter, the constant trial and error makes that moment of triumph all that much sweeter.
I take issue with some of the vagaries of the AI, for instance the fact that the citizens of your city seem incapable of eating food unless they're in their homes (which necessitates building houses around the different job buildings, and the planning that you'd need to include with that), but all in all this is a very, very satisfying game for people who enjoy the challenge of staking a claim in untamed wilderness and, without aid, making that settlement not only survive, but thrive.
Go slow, plan carefully, and just enjoy the sights and sounds of beautiful, untainted woodland as far as the eye can see while your workers do their thing.

Pros:
Simple

Easy to control
Cons:
This game will hold your hand like your mom in a supermarket
You will have to sit through dialogue. This is a game that does not need dialogue.

Analysis:
Super Splatters. I picked this game up in Humble Bundle 14. Pretty nice bargains so I decided, why not?
Got this and a couple of my favorite PC games in it. Lets get back to this game.
There's not much to say about it.
You point and shoot. Not like FPS point and shoot. You literally click where you want to go and shoot that way.
Not much else to it. This game is a game that you wouldn't really play to get good at.
It's more like what I'd like to call a "pick up, put down" game. Meaning, you just pick this up when you're bored and put it down when you've found something better to do.
The bright and flashy colors will keep you entertained for maybe 15 to 20 minutes. That's as long as it will take. It's pretty much a flash game, but made for people who are too lazy to search on Google.
This game holds your hand. Like literally. I get that there are tutorials, but sometimes I just like to throw myself into a game and learn on the go. Not like this one needs explanation, but still. I feel like I'm 5 whenever I start a new stage.
Dialogue is not a thing that needs to happen in this game. I've played flash games just like this and some of them still stick out more than this. You know what they didn't have? Dialogue. You don't need it. It's just sort of a break in the game. You want to start moving, but here comes yellow splatter to tell you how to impale yourself on a spike. Yippee. I feel as if it's an intentional thing. Maybe the creators are trying to psych us out.
This game gets super duper easy. How easy? I'm going to answer this question with a question. How easy do you think it is to breathe? I'm quite sure (Unless you have asthma. If you're reading this and you do have asthma, I'm super sorry) breathing comes naturally to most humans. This game will teach you to flip and say it's gonna get challenging from here on.
It doesn't. I've found myself just flipping multiple times for a better score/3 stars. It almost seems as if all of the tutorials, dialogue and handholding were unnecessary to even include within the game.
This game, as I said earlier, was most likely not made for extensive periods of play. It's a game that you can pick up and put down at will and forget about.
With flashy colors and simplistic controls, this game handles well and looks great.
The dialogue will seem a bit unnecessary. You'll have to deal with it sometimes.
I'm gonna give this game a gracious 6.5/10.

This is an amazing puzzle game. The building blocks you have are simple with no special tricks, yet you can build some very elegant yet complex solutions to each puzzle.
Each puzzle gives you a rating comparing how you've done with everyone else who's done the puzzle too on a nice bell curve. The farther to the left on the curve you are, the better. There are three different metrics too (cycles aka time, blocks used, and footprint (how much horizontal space your blocks and the materials need to move to reach the goal). All of these metrics are only governed by what you've built, so you are free to try to improve your score, and often improving one score may come at the expense of another. However you have space for three different solutions to each puzzle so you can try multiple approaches to try to improve your best score in different areas.
The game feels like programming/engineering where you need to test your creations at each step of the way to make sure that they are behaving as you expect as well. You can adjust some input parameters like how often materials are provided to you (and at various speeds different materials may come out at different rates, changing how you need to build your solution).
If you liked Spacechem (by this same developer) you'll love this game!

Like SpaceChem, this is a puzzle game that implicitly allows you to choose how much you want to challenge yourself.
Normal difficulty is just trying to solve every puzzle in any way that works, which, for those who haven't tried Zachtronics designed based puzzlers before, can still be a challenge.
Hard difficulty is when you start itching to find an elegant solution that doesn't have a giant snarl of pushers and sensors each trying to fix some unfortunate stall or collision that popped up the first time you built a solution.
Obsessive difficulty is when you decide you want to find a "best" solution that absolutely minimizes cycles or size with no waste. Even some of the tutorial levels turn in diabolical puzzles at this level. If you go here, you will dream Infinifactories after hours of fiddling. You may even start scouring the web to see if someone somehow did it better (which will, most likely, make you cry or curse profusely). You can, quite frankly, devote as many hours of your life to this game as you wish to without running out of mental challenges if you set the bar high.
Rarely will you ever find a puzzle game that has the depth to admit such rewards from obsessive analytical thinking, if you are the sort of person for whom that holds any appeal.

It's the age-old story we're all so familiar with. A little kitty has gone out for a night on the lash with its mates, gotten absolutely f*cking slaughtered, against all odds, has somehow managed to stumble its way back home again in one piece, but wouldn't you know it, has only gone and forgotten their keys and locked themselves out. Euurrrgh, classic kitty! It's a good job you're still at home inside, then, and are able to set up an elaborate array of contraptions that will eventually open the door for our sh*t-faced feline and let it sleep off its inevitable hangover!
Let the Cat in is a single screen, free-to-play puzzle game where a cat waits outside a door that's connected to a series of levers or pulleys that a ball must make contact with to activate and open. In each stage, the ball (or sometimes several) begins suspended in the air and the game paused. Given a limited, pre-set selection of items, you must place and position these items to allow the ball to get from its starting point to the handle that will then open the door, interacting with any objects it needs to or collecting the optional three stars along the way. Unpause the game and let the ball do its thing, hoping that you've placed everything for it to hit all its targets. If you haven't, simply pause/reset it again and tweak the positions of your placements until you've found the right ones, then do it all again in the next stage.
There's a nice choice of different objects to play around with, from basic ramps or simple books to knock over or additional, bigger balls to hit multiple targets, to slightly more adventurous items like springs or conveyor belts. When I first looked at the game on the Store page I was a little worried that the wealth of choice and freedom to place anything wherever you wanted would be overwhelming. That, when given so many options, you really wouldn't be able to choose any and would be left scratching your head wondering what to do with everything and where it should go. But, thankfully, between the limited number of items you're given for each puzzle, and the already laid out, fixed starting structures in every stage, it's set up in such a way that you'll at least have some vague direction of what to do in most levels, and the real challenge will be finessing the precise placement to make the ball go exactly where you want it to. It also helps that there are multiple ways to complete most stages, and in many cases, if you're crafty (or lucky) enough it's possible to do it using only a single item.
The three stars you can collect in every stage act as the game's currency which can be used to purchase hints. Well, I say hints, it actually auto places all the objects so all you have to do is unpause and watch the puzzle play itself. Or if that's too cheap for your liking, you can always use them to buy extra items to merely make things a little easier on yourself. Or better yet, if you just really like cats, they can be used to unlock more, as well as some snazzy little clothing accessories for them. As well as collecting stars in-game, you can also purchase them with real money (some of the proceeds of which apparently go to charity), but unless you're really bad at the game, or really intent on making those kitties look fab-u-lous, I always found the case to be that I had an abundance of them and never had to pay a single penny to complete the game. Well, sort of complete it.
As it stands right now at time of writing, the game hasn't been updated in almost six months, and the promised additional puzzles have yet to materialise and the developers nowhere to be seen either here or on its App Store page where it's also available. There could be many perfectly good reasons why the developer hasn't been able to get around to working on it in a while, but until proven otherwise, you should probably consider the game to be abandoned for now and impossible for achievement hunters to legitimately complete as a result. For everyone else, they probably won't care and will be happy with the 143 stages that are available and the many free hours of play they'll be able to get out of it.

My game history (hard difficulty):
- First Town: Citizens didn't have enough children and the population slowly died off due to old age.
- Second Town: Expanded too fast and couldn't feed everyone; mass die-off due to starvation.
- Third Town: Managed to keep everyone from dying of starvation (barely), but fell behind on fuel production and lost the town due to everyone freezing to death in the winter.
- Fourth Town: 10 years in with a population of 60 and everyone is healthy and happy, with only natural deaths... so far.
20 hours and four games in, I'm just starting to feel like I'm getting the hang of building a small, productive town that isn't going to implode and I haven't even built all of the buildings yet, much less gotten a single one of the 36 achievements. Also, I just remembered that I've been using the default map types and there are tougher ones. There also looks like there is a pretty good mod community, although I've been kept busy enough with the default game I haven't tried any out yet.
So, yeah, basically, if you like city management games and want a challenge, pick this up.

A peaceful little game where you build your own town/village from a band of exiles. There is no story to be had, but that is not where it's charm lies - indeed, one's own mind can fill in the gaps I find, creating your own backstory & reasons for why they're there. But no, the game's true charm lies in it's atmosphere - quaint and relaxing, for the most part. That doesn't mean it cannot be challenging however - whilst you build your town, one cannot forget the needs of your people! You must feed them, keep them healthy, warm & dry away from the harshness of nature, and if you wish for them to work well for you, you'll need them to multiply, to be educated and equipped with solid tools! Never let your populace age without having kids - for all they are a drain on your resources you'll need them to avoid dying out! But if you have too many kids, you'll run out of food oh-so-quickly. The gameplay can be described as a balancing act between all this, but it's not as stressful as it sounds once you get the hang of it. Quite astoundingly, this game was made by a single person..!

Are you part of The Sea Will Claim Everything's impossibly small ideal audience? Left-wing fans of point-and-click adventures, willing to read walls of text and forgive cludgy interface to experience a labor of love? If you're even just most of that, TSWCE is worth a shot.  The game is *insanely not for everyone* but those who like it will find a lot to love.
The hand-drawn interface is primitive, but the music and writing have more than enough maturity to make up for it. Its sense of humor tends toward the "quirky" side but it usually stays clear enough of forced "randomness" to stay endearing. There are some light puzzles but most of the content is experienced by talking with the inhabitants of the Fortunate Isles and carrying about ideas and conversation topics from place to place. Two puzzles that have to be brute-forced telegraph this in advance. Overall, puzzles are fair.
But it's the story that makes TSWCE worth your stay. As a trans-planar visitor to the Land of Dreams, you find the Fortunate Isles in disarray, shaken by economic turmoil and a rightward-creeping kleptocracy. If you know what that means, you're in the right place. If you don't, TSWCE is loaded with sympathetic characters who make the politics of the Fortunate Isles concrete and real. You'll get more out of it if you know the basic contours of the Greek Debt Crisis, but even if you don't, you'll easily figure out who's on the side of common people and who's lining their pockets off the misery of others. You'll use wild biotechnology and come face to face with creatures of myth and legend as you learn about what can be done to save the Fortunate Isles.
It's a short game but an absolutely one-of-a-kind experience and if you take your time to read and enjoy this dense heap of words, it will return so much of the love that was clearly put into it.

This software is pretty complex, but gives you the potential to create your own game and forge your own adventure. I tried it out and began working on my own game, but it's taking months to make because of the complexity. It may not be simple, but this software has the potential of making a game and requires a lot of time and work to make. Thanks to the Workshop, I can possibly post a demo of my game later this year. In GoNNER, the art style, sound effects and sound track all blend together to create a truly beautiful experience. The game is worth its price tag just for this alone. You can immediately see that this is a labour of love.

As you'd expect from anything claiming to be a roguelike, you die, a lot. But in GoNNER this doesn't feel so much of a punishment, because with almost every play through you unlock something new, or discover some trick you hadn't noticed before (you can spin after jumping with the bear head!).
If you're into roguelikes, enjoy a challenge, or just want to support an indie developer that is making all the right choices, this title is worth every cent. A true gem.

A fantastic game creator. It is a bit difficult starting out, but once you figure out how to change tilesets and open scripts (witch isnt that hard, I'm just a bonehead and didnt want to experiment for risk of screwing up), its quite easy. The stats may be a bit hard to figure out at first due to the creator having its own set style of a battle engine, but in the end if you can, it is completely worth it. If you're having trouble, theres a few tutorials on youtube that can help you out. My only real problem with the game, is how difficult it is to find tilesets people have uploaded so you can download. I feel that is the reason this needs its own Steam Workshop page. Other then that, thats the end of my complaints. Now to the good parts. The character creator is quite good, it gives you a decent variety of custom hairstyles, skin tones, eyes, noses, mouths, clothes, and other things to use. The script editor is easy to figure out once you start using it, the tilesets you start out with are decent, and if you dont like what it supplies you with, you can create your own and import them. There are also several enemies it supplies you with, most of them already coming with a custom stat set in case you dont want to design your own enemies. There are also default playable characters you can use. One of my favorite things about this game, is that unlike most other RPG creators, the scripting isnt to limited to make something great easily. The price is a bit high, but in the end, if you're a huge RPG fan and always wanted to make your own game, it's completely worth it.

Red Orchestra 2 is wonderful.
The "psudo-realism" setting that most Modern-era FPS have taken is vexing.  A gaming experience shouldn't require much suspension of disbelief.
Team Fortress 2 is a great game for its cartoon fantasy setting, allowing us to imerse ourselves in the gameplay world.
Call of Duty on the other hand takes a "realistic graphic/settings" approuch, but keeps gameplay highly casual (i.e. health regen, invincible humans, no recoil, unbelievable events, ect.) and fails utterly!
RO2: Heroes of Stalingrad on the other hand upholds a deep commitment to realistic gameplay to match its unique real-world setting, the bloodest and most interesting infantry conflict of all time, the Battle of Stalingrad.
The game was pushed out early which means lots of bugs and critic reviews that are less prasing than it deserves, but Tripwire has proved itself to be a company commited to ongoing development with loads of free content and performance improvements down the line.

For version 0.183
TL;DR: A very neat game that it is very different from your typical AAA release. What you do, and how you play, is left up to you.
The Long Dark is a very interesting game due to it's emergant game play and focus on the environment as an adversary. By choosing to have the environment be the "enemy" of the game your game becomes whatever you define it as. For me, it's exploring the map although in the latest release they've added crafting so I suspect that will become my new goal. I enjoy that I can move around this beautiful wasteland (also known as home) and see just how long I can last with just the clothes on my back and whatever I can scavange or make. It is an excellent example of a true survival game. The latest build also address most of my prior criticisms. For an alpha, this game is fully playable, constatly improving and very fun.
The few criticisms I do have are:
#1. You will die. Regardless of what you do, you will enentually run out of supplies and die. The crafting system has undergone a major upgrade so running out of clothes is no longer a problem. However, means of making a home-made knife, fire striker and spear (or some other means of wolf defence) all still need to be implimented.
#2. No procedurally generated map. The maps remain constant. The only change is what is contained in the loot containers. This is great since it allows the developers to make a large, interconnected world. It is bad for players because, as you play, you will learn the locations of most important areas. As such, instead of being "stranded in the wilderness" you just need to find a landmark and go to your favourite survival location. Even a small procedurally generated map would add a lot to this game's replayability because every time you play you'll be exploring something new.
#3. Lack of a map and compass. Obviously, having a HUD with a GPS display would be very, very silly. But at least having a compass that you can check (or being able to find one) will make it a lot easier to avoid getting lost. A paper map or log book that the player can edit would also be nice so you can mark down locations as you find them as well as note where you are cacheing items.
#4. Troublesome Inventory. The game's inventory system is very bare bones in the alpha. Things that should be possible on one screen (e.g. equip and repair items) are spread across multiple pages. If you eat something, you're kicked out of the inventory and have to open it again. The biggest annoyance by far is how the game handles clothing. Different items of clothing have different benifits but there is no way to directly compare what you have with what you're wearing. The inventory is certainly functional and is slowly improving but, as of alpha 0.183 it remains one of my bigger grievances.
#5. Unrealistic wolves. All the wolves in this game have rabies. This is terrifying! Regardless of your health and armament you will get mobbed by wolves. Having a better interaction between player and wolf (i.e. they will only attack if you are vulnerable) will make them a much more effecitive psychological enemy (what are they waiting for!) and game play enemy (injuries and being unable to run become that much worse). This has been slightly fixed with the introduction of difficulty levels for the sandbox mode but I have not had time to compare the new settings yet.
#6. Possibly no female character in the release game (unconfirmed). In the sandbox mode you can select your gender and get a different voice actor (provided by the excellent Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer). I enjoy playing female characters and it would be nice to be able to play one in the main game as opposed to just sandbox mode. Although I doubt the developers would restrict character choice in the main game it has not yet been listed on their website as an option
#7. Lack of distinction between characters. Jennifer Hale and Mark Meer are both great voice actors but I would like it if the characters they voiced were slightly different from a gameplay perspective. For instance, the female character could be better at repairs or more resistant to injury whereas the male character may have a higher carry weight. People are not all the same and having characters with differenet strengths would allow, again, for more replayability
The Long Dark is certainly an interesting exploration of what a game can be and I am eagerly awaiting the full release!

Do you like puzzles? Do you like SpaceChem? Do you like MineCraft (appropriate give Zachtronics' Infiniminer being its forebear)?
Then you'll love Infinifactory. It's like SpaceChem, but in 3D, and yet surprisingly accessible. You'll be building crazy 3D contraptions with ease. If anything I'd say it's a fair bit easier than SpaceChem, given a larger working space and lack of meta maps where you need to string together multiple machines. And there's no boss fights.
The plot is a lot simpler here, but it's a case of a little doing a lot. Maybe even more than the creator expected, in that it leaves a lot up to you to interpret and question. It also has a few surprises up its sleeve. The progression of things you create is also a big part of this - from mundane to the militarstic.
I haven't finished every puzzle yet, but whilst a few may initially look daunting, a bit of thinking usually reveals a solution. You'll also learn new techniques as you go (many you'll invent yourself), and some will also be revealed that open up new avenues of production line efficiency. I don't find myself ever really stuck. Break a big problem down into smaller parts and work on those. Then you'll realise, oh wait, you need to refactor this bit because of some reason. And when you finally figure it out, it's really rewarding.
Great soundtrack and nice, simple, effective graphics (and some quite interesting environmental design later) contribute well to the overall game.
Highly recommended :)

This is an arcadey football game with interesting RPG elements.
You are playing the part of a single footballer. That's a very refreshing mechanic, which hasn't been used in many other games recently. That makes this game fairly refreshing.
There are almost two games feeding into each other: Firstly, there's playing the matches. This is a good, but not stellar, arcade style football game, with a tiled view from behind the goal, similar to the various Amiga games of the 1990s. You just control your own player rather than the whole team. The game is fast-paced and holds your attention. The "one player" mechanic is also very different to most other games.
Secondly, there's the RPG game. This has you "levelling up" your player, maintaining relationships with team mates and friends, saving up for houses, flash cars and the like. You can also do several other things, such as gamble your money at the casino or racetrack. The mini-games providing this are all very simple, but there are a lot of them and they're competently done.
The most interesting part comes where the two games overlap. Should you pass to a teammate rather than scoring yourself - because then he'll like you and be more likely to pass to you next time, or do you score yourself because you want the goal bonus to buy some new boots? When scoring a goal, do you celebrate with the fans to improve your relationship with them, or do you celebrate with the manager so he's more likely to pick you next week?
I found this interesting and refreshing, and brings some planning and thinking to the arcade-style match engine.
If you're wondering whether this is the same game as its more famous cousin on iOS, it's not. This is much more fleshed out and playable, particularly the match engine which is real-time. Incidentally, if you haven't played the iOS version then it's well worth the price.
It's worth pointing out that the game is nigh-on impossible to play using keyboard and mouse. You'll definitely need some kind of controller. I just used a cheap USB one, which worked absolutely fine. The buttons are user-definable.
The game does get a bit samey after a while - it's essentially the same game 20 hours in as it is 20 minutes in. However, at the price that's not a huge problem.
I enjoyed playing this. If you like arcadey football games, or are bored of FIFA and want something different, then this is well worth a look.

It's... interesting.  I can't really fault this game for being what it is.  But what it is maybe just isn't for me, and that's because I'm me.
The story of this game is that you-the-player are a guest in the Land of Dreams.  You run around various isles helping the whimsical pseudo-philosophical people with their troubles and trade items around to solve some puzzles.  A lot of people are oppressed by their more serious skeleton governors and an evil skeleton general, and you help them make the bad guys go away.  Its not presented in a childish manner as my description might seem (and by childish I mean overly sanitized), and there's some deep language / concepts being presented... but I think really the problem is that I've grown up.  Its a bit
abstract and whimsical for me.  I am someone who is very open and self-analytical about his thoughts and feelings, so what's presented in the game feels like an invitation to something I have explored quite well already.  Abstractions about change and the future and identity and hard times and all, I see it and nod my head not in dismissal but in recognition.  Its also the way it goes about it, as I just dont find that insightful figures of speech and deep metaphorical quandaries as useful as directly thinking about the topic in question.  So this might be a very good game for someone who hasn't so thoroughly explored themselves, but not for me.  "You can always explore yourself more!" you might say.  And that's probably true for adults who haven't got a good grasp of themselves and their own beliefs (and boy are there a lot of these).  Maybe it sounds arrogant but believe me, I know myself.  I've done that.  So the game just doesn't have that much for me.  All that being said the game wasn't a complete bore or anything as I might seem to be implying.  Some characters had some dialogue that I nodded my head in recognition of and in general I agreed with the tone of the story.
The other problem is that the game carries the kind of humorous tone that I have never liked.  I don't have a great word for it, but I always call it the 'Hitchhiker's Guide humor.'  Basically, random nonsense descriptions or dialogue added just to be random because nonsense is humorous.  Its not for me.  Saying that an eyeball plant loves to play Borderlands with a character first name 'The' last name 'Mysterious-Druid', or that a drawer is full of water with a family of sardines inside, or a dog that talks like can haz cheezburg, or random dialogue about plants chatting happily or conspiring about something mysterious whatever isn't funny to me.  It never has been, and never will be.
There's not a whole lot to get in depth with about gameplay.  You talk to NPCs, follow what they ask you about and generally fulfill their requests without much puzzling about.  If there's any gripe its in a few nitpicks of game design for the benefit of the player.
One is if you walked away from the game and came back you might end up horribly lost as some NPCs don't repeat dialogue that gives hints and you need a collection of items from them to complete the game.  These are lumped in under one objective (collecting tokens) without more information so the details will be lost on you if you dont keep the game fresh in your mind.  You'd have to talk to a lot of NPCs again to figure out what you were looking for.
Another is that its possible to miss a few items and not know where to find them.  For example, 'Tremendous toadstool' is one such item.  There's a lot of mushrooms in this game.  Eventually I just stopped clicking on them because they only gave Hitchhiker Humor quotes for doing so, and thus I ended up passing by this item and having to resort to a guide because it didn't ever occur to me that this one which doesn't appear to be exceptional in any way might be an item I needed.  I could see this occurring for someone with other items too, or not thinking to revisit one or another NPC and getting a bit lost, or forgetting how to turn off the screen for the Unspeakable Cave.  Going back to The Mysterious-Druid for a clue might have been useful for the mushroom, I'm not sure if other NPCs give hints for the cave and so on.  I also had to use the guide to find the fireproof gloves as I had somehow missed the safe key needed to acquire them, thinking I had explored the Underhome completely.  Hunting every room all over again would have been a small chore.  Once again, asking The MD would have been helpful here as they would likely know where the key to the safe was.
Suffice it to say this game will not tax your computer in much any way that I can imagine.  No bugs that I could detect and the game never crashed.  Music was blaringly loud even when set to lowest in game and 1/100 on my headset.  I had to resort to speakers instead.  Playtime is about 2.5 hours, but I got this in a bundle somewhere over a year ago probably for around the price of almost nothing.  I think the length is fair for the game, you could definitely take the game a bit slower.
The aesthetic of the game is kind of passable, its not meant to impress as much be a visual cue, which is fine.  I've played other games like that which I thoroughly enjoyed, although this game did not greatly grow on me.  The music is okay, not unpleasant to listen to so that's good.
This again where I wish I could give more of a neutral recommendation.  I really just don't know what to think of the game.    I would probably say that its okay for others to play it for an introspective angle, but I'm sure a lot of people would be turned off by the graphics and not let themselves get much into the game and the genre (hidden object/p&c) isn't a popular one these days either.
It just wasn't a game for me.
EDIT: Reading the PDF that comes with the game gives some more insight into the thought that went into making the game.  The story being an expression of the personal plights of the developer does make sense.  Those plights arent trivial, and that insight does improve my feelings on the game somewhat, but making a game about a personal story isn't by itself enough.  The game has to stand on its own too, so my rating will remain the same.
