I love this game.  I *LOVE* this game.  It always sounded interesting and quirky, and I never had a clear idea of what it was about; recently I decided to fire it up and take a look.  And I *love* this GAME.
Right off the bat, I have to say: it's not going to be for everyone.  It's gentle and thoughtful, and there's a lot of reading.  It's a game that wants patience, and we won't need our guns and shields here.  The story is dense and rich and peopled by curious daffy folk: ancient trees, talking animals, dwarves and elves and leprechauns and Greek mythological beings.  They're not drawn from a single universe, they're drawn from many, so our elf in the market greets us "Mae gevonnen," and our Mysterious Druid, from the long-lined Mysterious-Druid family, is more a hippie organic Let-It-Be sort of fellow.  His partner does science experiments with her Quadricorder.
We start in the Underhome, five floors and a cellar of tree-like habitat.  We have no idea what's going on, and The Mysterious-Druid isn't much help.  A little, but not much.  Thugs from the Mayor have been over, threatening foreclosure, and they broke some stuff and upset the tree - they even ripped up the rug, which I gather really held the room together.  We'll need to get to the bottom of things, but first we'll need to calm and repair the Underhome enough that it will open the door and let us out into the world.
There are mushrooms and books and organic machines all over the place - and every mushroom, every book, and every flower in the game has individual text when we click on them.  Every one is a hoot.  The book titles range from real to hilarious to fanciful, with references scattered through fandoms of every sort.  The mushrooms and flowers aspire to this and that, and some are communist.  There are several islands, which we can't visit until we find a compass and a sextant.  The sextant is hard.  We need to break into a tomb, and find the roots of the corruption, and of course tend to the Underhome and its garrulous, helpless residents.
There's a political message about brutalism and corruption stealing heart and life from the good and various citizens running strong through the game; I gather it specifically alludes to the collapse of the Greek economy within the EU, but these days many of us will find that the details may have changed, but the overall picture has not.  The message, ultimately, is one of wise and weary faith in the decency of time and the resilience of people.  I found it ultimately really beautiful, and this game is my nominee for the "I'm Not Crying" category in the new Steam awards.
So I'll call it "quirky," but it's so much more than that.  Better to say that it's bursting with personality, that creativity is leaking out at the edges.  It's booky, geeky, lovingly wise creativity, spread though the wild and static characters who live on these islands.  Frankly, I couldn't ever quite put my finger on it, and I was always eager to see what leap of fancy would come next.
First run took me about 8.5 hours; I had to go back to catch up on a missing achievement, thus my longer total time spent.

Banished stands out for me because it does not do 2 things that almost all other city builders do.
FIrstly, it doesn't task you with creating an economy so fragile that the slightest misstep brings your growth to a grinding halt. There are no overcooked production chains like those normally seen in found-a-colony style games. Rather than having larger quantities of buildings dealing in intermediary products, the game allows single buildings to either accept a variety of raw materials to produce a finished good, or collect the raw materials required directly themselves. The output can be adjusted based on the number of workers assigned. So instead of having to figure out the breakpoints where your population size warrants laying down the considerable expense of a second complete production chain, you can safely overbuild a little and keep on adjusting the workers assigned you only need a fraction of a facility's output.
Secondly, it doesn't ask you to build up this complicated economy for the sole purpose of sending a military to wipe out an opponent. Most often this is the weakest aspect of these games, and simply cannot compete with an RTS focused on combat rather than multiple resource economies. So instead of a token 3-5 military units and requisite production chains to get them armor, weapons, and training, you're simply fighting against the elements.
Banished lets you spin up a randomly generated world (and gives you the seed number so you can share the same starting conditions with others), and tackle its 36 achievements, or create your own challenges. If you miss complex production chains and a greater variety of consumer goods, a surprisingly solid mod community awaits you, delivering upgraded housing options and expanded farming and processing buildings. If you've enjoyed games in the Settlers series, Anno series, or Tropico series, Banished is a refreshingly different take on the same concept.

Amazing software that does exactly as promised: allows the designer to quickly and easily create an RPG without knowing any code, script or other complex langauge. The drag-and-drop interface is even slicker than Game Maker and the toolboxes are intuitive use, requiring no tutorial (though tutorials are always helpful). The kit makes it easy to get into more advanced design techniques, such as creating your own artwork, designing quests, and putting together interesting encounters. Adding music, splash screens and dialogue are as easy as clicking the mouse button. The more advanced designer will still get a very powerful tool out of this, allowing you to alter scripts, codes and modify the engine with ease if you so desire. I highly recommend this software for any designer who wants to focus on making a game and focus less on assets, music, and coding.

GoNNER is a criminally underrated Roguelike with a gorgeous psychedelic aesthetic and engaging gameplay. Similarly to the Bit.Trip games, GoNNER's music and visuals become more complex and vivid as your combo goes up. This system does a great job of keeping the music interesting, and really adds to the frenzied excitement of trying to hold onto a combo.
More importantly, GoNNER is just really ♥♥♥♥ing fun. I love the satisfaction of bulldozing through cute monsters in caves and islands, trying to perfectly skirt the line between combo-destroying slowness and reckless speed.

What Downwell was to descent this game is to lateral movement.  It's a similar concept in the roguelike genre with an emphasis on racking up combos for score.
There are unlockable weapons, heads, and items.  All have an effect on gameplay.  Weapons range from pistols to laser beams and items do various things such as refilling your ammo to invincibility.  Heads determine your health and each one has unique traits, such as triple jumping, floating, extra health, or firing an extra bullet.  As you unlock these pieces of gear, you'll be able to choose them to create customized loadouts at the beginning of each game.
On the subject of health, this game has a unique mechanic that can create some interesting situations.  You drop all held items upon taking damage, including your weapon and head.  If you get hit again before grabbing your head, you will die.  Sounds rough, but managing to survive after all your gear falls down a pit is really satisfying.
Music and sound is on point and the beeps and boops give a really unified feel with the graphical style of the game.

Where to begin... The Long Dark is a survival game that consists of many possibilities when your the last human alive in this frozen wasteland. This game's goal is to survive for as many days possible. Surviving the cold is only one of the challenges there is in this game.
Survival:
In "The Long Dark" you have to survive as many days possible. This consists of challenges the player has to go through. As you start out your main goal is to look for shelter. Shelter is one of the key things for survival in this game. Over time you might start to starve or even thirst. Food and water is also a main key in this game. Looting places will give you tools for your survival. Clothing is also something to look out for. Clothing will keep you warm enough to survive outside while you look for things.
Challenges:
In "The Long Dark" there are challenges the player has to face to reach his/her goal on surviving. Wolves. Wolves are your enemies in this game. If your not careful than you can end up dead or fatally injured. Thats one of the challenges faced in "The Long Dark". Scavenging is also one of the hardest challenge's there is. As you look around for anything possible for your survival sometimes you might get what your not looking for. Looking around on the ground you will be able to find things left by previouse surviviors. Such as backpacks, medkits, plastic containers, metal containers, and sometimes even their bodies.
Things to look out for in this game:
Things to look out for in this game is extremely important as you start. First find a good place to camp for a couple of days. Find equipment near your site so you can survive for the longest time possible. As you "level up" scavange around. People often scavenge the woods to look for bunker's. These bunkers are the JACKPOT to your survival. They have enough equipent to last 5-10 days. And there is more than one bunker.
My own experiences in "The Long Dark":
My own experiences in "The Long Dark" was pretty amazing overall. The graphics and gameplay was pretty pleasing. The enviroment and challenges that were in this game were incredible. This game in my personal opinion would be a 9/10. This game has its upsides which i have given to you. But sadly this game has its downsides. The downsides of this game is that firearms are very rare to find and they are your ownly given weapon. The wolfs are to overpowered which was explained. Sometimes loot isnt worth picking up because its a waste of space. And there is no option to jump in this game. But other then that its a GOOD game WORTH playing.
My ideas:
This is the last part of the review. But my ideas of what to add next to the game is a possible multiplayer option.
The multiplayer option would of been an option to host the server and invite friends to play with you and to survive with in this huge game. It would be perfect because the map in this game is extremely huge which is good for trying to find your friends and survive with.
Over all:
The over all rating to this game is 9/10. The makers of this game did an over all GREAT job on this game. And hopefully they continue to add more.

I really like the pacing and style of these puzzles. The easy early ones give you a chance to develop generalized techniques to apply to the later ones, as it should be in a good puzzle game. Unlike some games, the puzzles don't rely on "gotchas" that only the developer would think of (i.e., I've been able to solve all of them without spoilers so far).
The levels tend naturally to break down into clearly divided sub-puzzles, so it's easy to jump in and start making progress. But you won't get bored, as there are frequent twists that can wreck your initial plans and make you consider a reset; sometimes the pieces don't fit together as you expected. When a new mechanic is introduced, expect to spend some time figuring out the nuances. Best of all, as you solve the sub-puzzles of a given level to your liking, your sub-solutions will play and re-play in the background as you continue working on the remaining pieces, which can be oddly satisfying. The score statistic histograms add some replay value for optimization.
You can't die. Timing matters for machines but not player actions. Small mistakes are easily fixed for no penalty. The UI is nicely polished. There's a darkly comedic backstory that intrigues without getting in the way (warning, includes mentions of harm to animals). It's got very well thought out voxel editing tools (I never expected to see a usable drag and drop in 3D). It might be my ideal puzzle game, and it's making me want to try Infiniminer.

Pre-review backstory:
I am 19, first HoMM game I played was HoMM3, followed up with a small bit of HoMM2. Played HoMM between the ages of 8-15, irregularly as my uncles were the ones who had the games, then on and off for a bit the last 4 years.
Mind you, I NEVER touched the campaigns in those games, only played skirmishes with my uncles and some skirmishes solo to practice.
Now in the recent sales, I noticed HoMM6 was available quite cheaply and I said "♥♥♥♥ it" and bought it, I never had the ability to buy games before I turned 19 and by then I had forgotten about this game.
----------------------------------------------------------
Actual review: Never having played a newer HoMM game and also never having tried campaigns before, it was the first thing I did to get into the game.
Started the Dark Elf campaign and let me tell you how it went: After failing 3 times in a row on the first mission, I finally understood the mechanics of the game and also the strategy, I finally finished the first mission. So I load in the next mission. Brickwall'd. Tried it 7 times, was always either one turn too late or had too few units to finish it. But I had noticed the Dynasty weapons, and I've now looked them all up and I feel quite happy because this is progression that I enjoy - grinding exp to get tangible bonuses on permanent items.
I gave up on the Dungeon campaign and decided to do tutorial. It's a breeze now that I know all mechanics and strategies.
Immediately follow up on tutorial with Necropolis campaign, not too hard although VERY long. The content in campaigns is mostly combat and build-up to combat, which I like, it's action packed and not something you go through in a day.
Since I have limited time to play due to work I can plough through 1 mission/night if I'm lucky.
Anyways, in my Necropolis campaign I realized I could collect more Dynasty weapons playing through the campaign, and I can do it in any order I want, but me being anal about it wanted to try it in order.
So after Necropolis I tried Haven - upfront let me tell you, I hate Haven, so I wasn't looking forward to this grind. Gave up about 40% into the first mission after 3 restarts, they are so NOT my faction, and I'll go back after I've leveled up my weapons to make it easier to just hammer through it.
Up next I felt like doing Inferno, and man was I looking forward to this! Suffice to say, I love all evil factions, and Inferno are much cooler now compared to in HoMM3, where the final tier unit was a funny looking devil, while here it's this sort of Balrog-y "Pit Lord". I. LOVE. THIS.
I did the first mission, it was a blast. But the second is a bit too hard, so I'll adopt my strategy for Haven and wait on my Dynasty weapons.
Replaying Dungeon currently, and it's going great. With the experience from playing through Necropolis and doing a lot of Inferno and Haven, I am moving forward again.
----------------------------------------------------------------------
Gameplay feels very HoMM-y and I like it.
Graphics are good, nothing to complain about - I find that as long as it's not something that would return to HoMM3 graphics then it'll suffice and I hope it's enough for other players - more and more people seem to find graphics an issue, which is a bit sad. Anyways, the game is really pretty to look at, in my eyes at least.
Dialogue is silly and/or sarcastic or just caricatures. Not sure how I feel about it, and I wish I had played the older games' campaigns to compare.
Story is a bit... weak. I don't like the idea of the first 5 factions in the game (campaign wise) are all allied to eachother due to them all being siblings, all seemingly trying to complete the same goal.
Sounds are sometimes REALLY well made, and sometimes just laughable. Manticores flying sounds like something from a kids cartoon show. Don't know if it's due to me having set speed higher in combat, but stuff like that really does emasculate things.
Grind is good. I like it, and I like playing the campaign to collect more weapons. Can't wait to level them all up and use them against friends potentially.
Which brings me to the last point, I've heard terrible stories of how♥♥♥♥♥♥the multiplayer is, so I hope it's going to be no problem.

When I first started this game, I was struck by it's immediate warning, which had the words "light", "loud" and "scare" - already that sounded like the kind of passive agressive / insane temperament I was forced to grow up with as a child in Long Island, NY in the 1980's.
After many hours being in Freddy Fazbear's Pizzeria, I can say this place is one that you owe yourself, as a human being who uses a computer, watches films, and likes a good story - to vist at least once.
I appreciate the source of emotion this game uses - the fear of inanimate objects being imbued with life - the sadness of tainted childhood (let alone - LOST childhood...) - the anger at an unappreciate employer (you have NO idea what I have been through...!) - the joy of victory...that last one will only last briefly.
The plot is that you are a night watchman at a nearly defunct children's party place, akin to a Chucky Cheese, which was the source of video games/arcades in the 1980's and is what helped even spawn the popularity of games today (this game, in essence - is a twisted homage to the very origin of mainstream gaming).  The game was "sold" to me that you were making sure the puppets do not move, and do not come to your room.  I was very confused - to me this game looked HORRIFYING but there was no hint at the horror, and it felt more like a "Killer Klowns From Outer Space" mixed with "Child's Play" type of experience...why are all these screenshots so scary, yet the gameplay sounding so innocent?
Because the game itself relies on your fear: of the strange, of adults, and of corruption.
The things I love most about this game are unfortunately, what I feel most big budget developers, and most gamers now, would and will try to change.  I see "complaints" about Five Nights At Freddy's, but to me, are it's sordid virtues:
- The game cannot be played in windowed mode (which means..no distractions! - when you play, you are immersed in the game as if you were playing it on a TV/Console or Arcade - you can't multitask, typing in Word, ordering crap on Amazon, changing songs in iTunes, check your Wordpress, Facebook, Farm, etc. etc.)
- The game can't change resolution or "insert setting here" (because the developer perfected it for you - this game is an artfully created experience - it's like a video game version of a French Film from the 60's - it's an "auteur" at work - the game's creator knows what he is doing, trust him - and go with the sound settings and graphics he picked - let the "Five Nights At Freddy's" take you as its prisoner.....in every way...)
- There is no save setting (The beauty of this game is that an enjoyable play session can go anywhere from 2-20 minutes - and the learning curve is steep - save settings and short levels become redundant)
This game is worth every penny of it's price.  I purchased it based on it's uniqueness and that it spoke to me as a lover of a good story well told.  I was rewarded with an amazingly crafted and simple Puzzle Horror game that I could play at day or night - and within seconds be swept away to an intense little cramped office, where all that mattered was immediate survival - "Five Nights At Freddy's" is not just about watching cute animatronic characters in a security camera - it's about why you're watching them - are we as "dumb" as the person who took this job?  Maybe he just wanted a scare and a challenge too.
Play it, enjoy it - take your time - then go watch a horror film and play a game - "Five Nights At Freddy's" is an ode to both.

Controls... the whole idea of having the right click toss grenades OR shoot secondary weapon is absurd... luckily you can customize the key bindings. The aiming mechanic counts the angle of the aiming hand, not your own field of view, which means you will find your self looking directly at the enemy, shooting, but hitting the wall to the left or right of you, because that's where your hand is aiming at. More then a few vehicles handle like a cow on ice.
Story... well if you where planing to buy this for the story, forget about it, this is a sandbox to waste your time on side missions and fighting the ai armies.
Bugs... well from being permanently stuck in a wall, to having the black market NPC give you fast travel option, for you to die, and the option to perma disappear for the rest of the game... pretty frustrating. No crushes or errors though. My most complained issue was likely being stuck in one way or another after using grappling hook.
From the plus side, this games world is enormous and filled with huge amount of side missions, its a pretty world, and the vehicle variety is impressive. Its kind of what people wanted Farcry to be, more variety and stuff to do. Grappling hook, while fairly unrealistic, is very fun, as you can grapple on to a moving helicopter, kick the pilot out and hijack it... or grapple to soldiers or cars... well pretty much anything.
Overall... 5/10, Worth a 5-10 dollar sale. But wouldn't recommend as a good game.

For those of you who like to struggle for little reward and compensation, I sincerely hope you have fun.

One of the best puzzle games I've played. You essentially create a machine out of blocks/parts that each do a different thing, one block might be a conveyer belt while another is a sensor that can be connected with yet another block that pushes blocks in front of it whenever the sensor activates.
The mechanics of the game are simple and very easy to understand. But to create a machine that produces the goal product can be very hard and requires both logic and intelligence. You will feel very rewarded once you finally succeed. But don't think it is over yet, you will be scored and compared to other players based on how small your machine is, how fast it can build and how many parts/blocks you used for it. You will feel an urge to go back and improve upon it if your score is not to your satisfaction.
Due to the nature of the game it means that for each puzzle there's basically an endless amount of solutions. This gives you a lot of freedom which many other puzzle games lack. In fact, you can save up to 3 machines for each puzzle, this way you can experiment with your current machine without losing anything, you can even try and optimize it for production while neglecting its size and parts.
I'll definitely recommend you pick this up if you enjoy puzzles and logical thinking.

It's hard to write a review about a game that's so beautifully crafted but with whose central conceits you take so much issue.
The lands of Dream, within which the game is set, is more whimsical than really vividly imagined. There isn't really a clear set of rules that comes through; instead it's a flight of whimsy whose philosophizing is so ever-present that the game fails to hide its true purpose as a delivery system for these ideas.
I really find it a shame that such a gifted writer is so solidly steeped in one philosophy in particular, making references again and again to every communist thinker and writer from the likes of Marx all the way down to China Mieville. It's so much more interesting if the writer isn't so eager to reach his conclusion, instead presenting problems with multiple possible answers and allowing his audience to salt to taste.
But make no mistake -- this is a message game, and so I must address the message.
Kyratzes waxes poetic on the unnaturally destructive nature of debt, on capitalism as destructive force, etc. But the problem is that communists -- including Kyratzes -- again and again attack capitalism for the sins of corporatist mercantilism. Debt is destroying nations from Greece to the US because central banks fix interest rates so as to allow their governments to pay low interest on national debt. But this also drops the price of debt for everybody.
Meanwhile, oligarch kingpins -- the proverbial robber barons of old -- turn from very successful businessmen such as Jeff Bezos in to corrupt plutocrats like Rockefeller (or Jeffrey Immelt, frankly) by using their resources to corrupt the laws, writing new ones to destroy their competition through regulations that benefit them at the expense of other businesses.
This is not capitalism. This is corporatism and it's mercantilism.
Capitalism must have law as its foundation -- that is, the rules of the game must be the same for all players. This way creativity and innovation is rewarded. We can see this in the video gaming industry. Without publisher gatekeepers a more liquid market has emerged allowing guys like Kyratzes to compete with big developers on merit rather than market buying power.
Capitalism is necessarily tied to republics, because the nature of republics restricts the legal powers of the government, creating enough stability in the law for people to invest their money and start businesses.
Our (the US) republic has been corrupted for many years, the law weakened and co-opted for oligarchs' benefit. This happened by replacing many foundational laws under the banner of direct democracy, or majority rule. The majority is bought with money via media, and the crumbling law allows mercantilist oligarchy to take its place. THIS is the devil that communists point to and eroneously call 'capitalism.'
Meanwhile, Kyratzes' Greece is experiencing the wrath of bond markets looking at a fiscally insolvent country that cannot bail itself out by printing money. Greece is experiencing the effects of european central control, not the effects of capitalism.
Communism is unworkable for two simple reasons:
Firstly, man is not omniscient. There is no possible way a committee of experts can accurately predict the actual number of boots demanded by a people. The only way this can actually be done is via the price system that market economies use. But a communist system hasn't any prices, and so planners must guess at this, thus creating regular and inefficient shortages and gluts.
Secondly, equal income for all actually means a vast underclass with an extremely small ruling class. This is necessary because somebody has to decide goods production levels for the society, and the man who does this holds absolute power over everything. How many boots should be manufactured? Of course, this man will need a number of political appointee experts to assist him. Thus an extremely small, fabulously wealthy ruling class that decides the fate of everybody else. No income gap is the same as a VAST income gap. And it follows that communism is necessarily ALWAYS tied to oligarchy, because somebody has to make the production decisions. The idea that economic systems and political systems are discreet and separate is plainly absurd.
Communists like Kyratzes have a fantasy that personal freedom can exist arm in arm with communism, but this is an impossibility. Command and control economies require command and control governments to operate them. A republic under this system is a republic in name only. Representatives bow to the wishes of the heirarchical bureaucratic planners who bring the bill to the legislature, and the planners -- who control the fates of all and thus hold all the power -- ensure that the reps who are elected are those that play ball.
Further, the idea that personal and economic freedom are separate is again illusory. The freedom to make something and sell it is fundamental to the freedom to speak, to write, to live. The planners in a socialist system can simply remove the appointed job from any dissenters. And private profit -- an alternative way to make a living should one lose his job -- is illegal.
The simple fact remains that while governments never REALLY care about personal freedoms that don't threaten them -- like the freedom to dance, or the freedom to praise the government -- it is controversial speech and controversial action that must be protected.
Under a capitalist republic naive intellectuals like Kyratzes are free to promote their wrong-headed thinking, and disseminate their views unimpeded. But in a communist society ideas of liberty and markets see dissenters on the wrong end of a rope.
Kyratzes is clearly a brilliantly contemplative person, and I imagine he would present the counter argument as well should he have heard it. But contemporary intellectualism is often an echo chamber, and I doubt that Mr Kyratzes has read F.A. Hayek, or Mises, or Garet Garrett, or he might present both points of view and leave his readers to decide for themselves.
That said, Kyratzes' brilliant writing makes this game the most pleasant proselytism I can imagine. Yet that it is nevertheless.

As a people pleaser and someone who has suffered from social anxiety and depression, I kind of wish this game had come with a warning. At times, I felt almost physically ill from empathy with what was going on in the game. It's a powerful game, in terms of bringing emotions out of the player. But it's not "fun", it's not "cute", it's hardly even really a game. It's a work of art, and I don't recommend it for anyone who isn't willing to have their day a little bit ruined.
edit: I had a hard time deciding whether to rate this as a positive or negative review. The game's purpose is to move people, make them emotional, and it succeeded at that. Despite this, if the story is to be believed, then I very much believe that the creater shouldn't have posted this game for the world to see. From my interpretation of the final level (not the epilogue, the one before that), he is only making things worse for himself with the one he is tyring to communicate with. But that's not why I rated this negatively. People are saying that I should change my review, because the game succeeded in it's job, but I have warned a couple of my friends away from playing it, because the content is so jarring. Feel free to disagree with me all you like, it's your opinion, just as my opinion is my own.

The Sea Will Claim Everything is a bare bones graphic adventure, with simple puzzles and an over-reliance on pixel hunting. You're presented with single-image nodes and interact with "hotspots" by clicking on them - save for a few exceptions, there are no inventory or verb puzzles; you automatically use the correct object (if you have it) when needed.
But wait.
It's also hyperliterate, full of offbeat humor and loveable characters. It's imaginative to a fault, gentle, and filled with warmth. The story and the writing are excellent. So is the music.
I normally loathe pixel hunting in adventure games, but here it's turned into a strength - rooms often have dozens of objects to interact which, each one of their descriptions a joy to read.
The simplistic puzzling would be a problem, except that here it fits the game's pacing to a tee. And it still feels satisfying, mostly because it still depends on exploring the environments thoroughly.
Listen, this is one of the loveliest things I've played in a long time. If good, well-written stories interest you in any way, and you're not allergic to lo-fi graphic adventures, I recommend this game whole heartedly.

I began playing this game on January 1st, 2015 (before it was on Steam), and finished it the next day. Prior to playing, I was a conservative kid raised to believe every word Glenn Beck said. Today, I am a communist. And it's ALL THIS GAME'S FAULT!
You see, I belong to a narrow generation of youth who grew up on Flash games. Even today, the only consoles in the house are a Wii and a DS Lite, each with just a handful of games. It started with regular visits to Club Penguin and Miniclip, then Nitrome, and, as my desire for innovation grew, Casual Gameplay @ JayisGames. I subscribed to JayisGames on Google Reader (RIP) and once every few weeks, I scrolled through and clicked on everything interesting. This is how I discovered the work of Jonas and Verena Kyratzes. (Aside: this is also how I discovered Ludum Dare, where I would soon enter my own rudimentary games.)
I fell headfirst into the dreamy wonder of The Infinite Ocean, the lost world of Alphaland, and of course, the sweet laughter behind The Book of Living Magic. If I had to pin down what attracted me to those games, I would say "emotional payoff" -- these games, unlike most others, gave me an indescribable feeling somehow related to beauty. This feeling would cause me to babble on to my best friend for days about the games, especially The Infinite Ocean, its ambiguous plot quite the exercise for my 13-year-old brain. These games gave me my earliest notion that videogames could be art.
Now, I knew that Jonas's games were in support of communism, and that communism was antithetical to everything I then believed, but that only made them more intriguing. Bored of Fox's strawmen, I began frequenting Jonas's blog, cultivating his strong challenges to my beliefs. I even wrote a story in the comments once to counter him, but I'm afraid to dig that up, haha.
The Sea Will Claim Everything was the Kyratzes' first paid game, and being that I was a Kid With No Money, it was a several years before I bought and played it. And, well...
Games are about overcoming challenges. Your standard videogame challenges you to kill things before things kill you. But other games present a more meaningful challenge. Undertale, for example, challenges us to empathize with those hostile towards us. The Sea Will Claim Everything challenges your view of society.
You can fall in love with the Fortunate Isles like your own home, because these are the characters' homes. You can grieve the pillaging of the Isles and give your best to help, only for Lord Urizen's men to take everything away. Through the Lands of Dream, you can feel for the plight of humanity in our waking world.
But what really turned me to communism were the mushrooms. They look so dashing in red.

The Sea Will Claim Everything is a beautiful game on many levels. I have no qualms recommending it if you enjoy a wonderully crafted story, which I admit was emotional for me. The game world is also incredibly rich and feels "alive", even though it is depicted in a completely static manner.
There is a lot of reading in this adventure, which is one of the highlights to me, as it was so well done. The puzzles are not terribly complex, with only one giving me a little trouble. A lot of the joy of this game is discovering all of the little parts that make up the game world. As an example, every book in the game is unique and you'll discover just how complicated mushrooms can be. Also, the game doesn't really hold your hand and instead it requires you to explore and experiment, neither of which are downsides.
If there was a major downside to the game it would be that I wanted the story to continue, which is perhaps a very high compliment to a game. I also want to mention the beautiful music in the game. It really fit the experience and was a pleasant accompaniment to the experience.
I'm looking forward to many more adventures in the Land of Dreams!

Jonas Kyratzes, one of the writers of The Talos Principle, with the whimsical art of his wife Verena and the music by Chris Christodoulou (who did the music for Risk of Rain) united together to make a wonderful game.
The Sea Will Claim Everything is a very special and rare game that combines the exploration of a fantastic and creative world with interesting and deep analysis of modern economical and political problems.
Partially inspired by the economic crysis that struck Greek, and still holds many european countries, this magnificent game explore with a slow pace and a biting humour many unresolved problems of this situation, still aknowledging the difficulty of resolving it.
On top, or besides this, the game itself is the story of a wonderful group of magical island, whose beauty and existence is menaced. Kyratzes manages to write an interesting, moving, eccentric, dramatic and fun story, such as is life.
A truly interesting experience, with excellent music and wonderfully represented, that I suggest to experience slowly, and if needed be, with a tutorial if you encounter any empasse.
Do buy it.

I really wanted to like this game... it has potential, fortress take overs are pretty fun, but getting 100% takeover in a fortress is often more frustrating then fun because developers decided to make small boxes with money and armor count for the fortress takeover... so more often then not you are running through an area about 400 square meters, looking for that last box... while unlimited waves of enemies annoy you, if your lucky, you will spend about 10 minutes looking for that last box.
Controls... the whole idea of having the right click toss grenades OR shoot secondary weapon is absurd... luckily you can customize the key bindings. The aiming mechanic counts the angle of the aiming hand, not your own field of view, which means you will find your self looking directly at the enemy, shooting, but hitting the wall to the left or right of you, because that's where your hand is aiming at. More then a few vehicles handle like a cow on ice.
Story... well if you where planing to buy this for the story, forget about it, this is a sandbox to waste your time on side missions and fighting the ai armies.
Bugs... well from being permanently stuck in a wall, to having the black market NPC give you fast travel option, for you to die, and the option to perma disappear for the rest of the game... pretty frustrating. No crushes or errors though. My most complained issue was likely being stuck in one way or another after using grappling hook.
From the plus side, this games world is enormous and filled with huge amount of side missions, its a pretty world, and the vehicle variety is impressive. Its kind of what people wanted Farcry to be, more variety and stuff to do. Grappling hook, while fairly unrealistic, is very fun, as you can grapple on to a moving helicopter, kick the pilot out and hijack it... or grapple to soldiers or cars... well pretty much anything.
Overall... 5/10, Worth a 5-10 dollar sale. But wouldn't recommend as a good game.

My favorite game of all time has always been Condemned 2: Bloodshot... until I played Outlast. Outlast has to be one of, if not THE, best game(s) I've ever played. It's so well rounded when it comes to the genre. I mean, I like the idea of Silent Hill, but that and Resident Evil just don't feel right when playing. I like Dead Space, but it's combat oriented. I like Amnesia, but it's just too... ambient? Outlast has the perfect level of threat vs jumpscare and a great twist of "what the f*ck, that's f*cking creepy as sh*t." There are really memorable characters and the controls are really nice. I think the only complaints I may even consider are that I would have loved to see more of The Twins. They could have had so much more backstory, but even with as little as we see them, they're great! Also, I don't feel like the Walrider was as unholy as he should've been. The Walrider (Alp) is based on a folklore about a "nightmare demon." Literally lethal nightmares from hell; but the Walrider just seemed like a♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off ghost with Parkinson's. I wish there was some way that he could keep the same level of threat and difficulty, but become more unholy/creepy/frighening; something that'd make Hellraiser look like a Sunday school teacher. But that's just me. Point is, Outlast (and Outlast: Whistleblower) is one of the greatest games to touch the market, in my opinion, and I would recommend it to anyone with the stomah for it.

Great for making games in the vein of old school NES/SNES RPGs.  You have everything right out of the box to make your own complete RPG whether it's a funny or serious project but it still takes time and dedication.
The default resources are fine but some people have created commercial quality games with this with their own custom artwork, music, etc. The engine is massively modifiable through RGSS3 (Ruby) scripting.
Through scripting you can change the battle engine to include side battle systems, action battle systems (like Zelda), change the UI and so on. If you want to do anything really neat with this you'll need to dig through some tutorials though but there are mountains of resources, scripts, tutorials, etc. for VX Ace.
If you're new to VX Ace and even if you've used past products but need a refresher, Kelsper's Beginner's Guide to RPG Maker VX Ace is a must read.

Few games are as happy to be here as Super Splatters.
Its delightfully tongue-in-cheek writing and happy-go-lucky characters are quite literally bursting with charm, flinging their jelly-like bodies around the stage before exploding into gooey cascades to the cheers of their insatiable audience. Super Splatters is so unconcerned with being taken seriously, so committed to making you laugh and smile, that it’s hard not to forgive some of its more frustrating parts for the sake of how much fun it’s having.
Super Splatters is all about skill in an environment you wouldn’t expect to demand it. Your goal isn’t to do good yourself, but impress the audience watching you and in turn earn fans to help propel you to the next level of splatter stardom. You do this by making an absolute mess, shooting your wiggly body toward small balls you need to cover with your explosive fluids in order to clear a level. The challenge is you’re only given a limited number of goo-people and balls are typically spaced out so as to require a lot of tricky maneuvering to catch them all.
For a game seemingly aimed at more casual players, Super Splatters has an abundant amount of depth in its scoring system and outrageously difficult level designs later on. Different shots activate stunts, the more of which you chain together the higher your combo gets and the more fans you’ll receive. This becomes fiendishly complex when you have to deal with multiple colors, required stunts, and an increasing number of spikes ready to prematurely split you open.
Issues only arise when Super Splatters’ somewhat luck based design begins to feel as if it’s working against you. As you’re required to clear every level entirely, it’s not uncommon to end up with a single ball remaining do to you goo somehow not penetrating a stack enough, or slipping through the floor faster than you’d anticipate. Later stages are positively infuriating at times, testing my patience with little in the way of direction, and losing much of the cheerful dialogue that made earlier levels such a joy.
Maybe that’s a bit of a baseless complaint though as there isn’t ever a reason you’re forced to play past a comfortable difficulty. Super Splatters is fully focused on giving you as much or as little a challenge as you want, so outside of completionists there’s never a forceful urging to push you outside your comfort zone. And that’s something I find really refreshing: a game so completely devoted to having a ridiculously good time that you can’t help but enjoy yourself.

I purchased this just before Christmas--mostly out of curiosity, and a love for the classic RPGs reminiscent of Secret of Mana, Chrono Trigger, and Final Fantasy. This RPG maker is exactly what is says it is, however it can't be judged on the quality of the final product you make. This tool gives you a lot of freedom, to create an entirely unique game, but only if you're creative. tech-savvy, and artistic enough to handle it. If you have no experience, that's okay too--everything is straight forward and there's tons of existing content to use in the game (and download open-source online.)
The default tilesets are okay, they could have been better designed to allow first-time users to really immerse themselves in their story, and not be constantly repelled by the terrible "world map" tilesets and fear of possibly having to learn how to script. I spent hours teaching myself through youtube videos to make sure I knew how to accomplish each little detail I wanted. I was lucky to have existing experience with graphic design though. (I highly recommend this to a skilled graphic designer--the real beauty of RPG maker shines when you can draw perfectly customized images)
After nearly a week (approx. 15 hours), I had a 15 minute game that included a completely unique tileset, sprites and custom window mapping, a maze, a few collection triggers, and a cut-scene that used my own music I edited. I gave my game to my partner as a Christmas gift and it was huge success.
Patience is a virtue with this powerful tool. You'll need to commit hours upon hours, but the final result will be truly awesome and will reflect the work you put into it, it's dauntingly customizable, but the program is well executed, and you game will be entirely yours. RPG maker isn't limited to fantasy type games either, it's possible to use the engine to create historically accurate games, war-time simulators (that use an RPG engine) or culturally specific stories--but they are not built into the default maps, sprites, mobs, or tilesets; be prepared, if that's your goal, for an insane amount of work.

I saw this game a PAX West and instantly knew I needed it. I love "action roguelikes", and this is a great entry to the genre. The game may look like a simple platformer with guns, but it is far more than that. Every time you play, the levels you play through are generated procedurally. This means every time you will face a different arrangement of enemies in a different arrangement of rooms. On top of this, as you play more, you will unlock new heads, new guns, and new activated items. Each of these will change they way your character behaves. This helps you to approach playing the game differently, which ultimately helps you get better at the game itself. You will die a lot, but the more you play the more you will learn how to die less, and eventually you'll make it to the end. But thanks to the level generation and character customization, beating the game is never the end.

compete for high score.

wishing that there were more variations in level design.

I would have preferred that it had more levels, but for what
it is, I can recommend this game.  See the video review for a
more in-depth review.

Vikings – Wolves of midgard takes a lot of cues from its competition – as well it should. Its an ARPG, much like in the vein of Diablo or Path of Exile where you run through dungeons (raids), collect loot and XP and build a character that does magical, majestic, mayhem and masterful butchery of everything that moves.
Video:

Text:
While Vikings does follow the same trend and basic ideas as its competition, it does try to deviate and set itself apart with a few changes and mechanics.
First: the games leveling and progression system is a lot more fluid then that of most competitors, throwing out classes to allow free-form skill trees where a player can level up and invest in as they deem fit. This creates a more dynamic experience where you can expand beyond the limitations you pre-selected if you feel something is more cool during gameplay.
The skilltrees have a nice variety in skills and effects and do provide interesting choices to explore during leveling, tied into the weapons you’re using. This also translates to weapons with crafting and progression being a lot more fluid and allowing you to experiment more, especially as you have some control over upgrading and building your own town in terms of which vendors and crafting stations you upgrade.
The downside is that the truly outrageous stuff you can do with other ARPGS with exploding blades of flaming farts, are very much limited with the majority of items providing passive buffs. This means that while getting cool looking items is great – their actual effects are pretty boring (barring a few exceptions).
Thankfully, the combat makes up for that with varied enemies and challenges between different areas, locales, vistas and mechanics while still keeping a clean style where you just want to keep pushing forward. So while the mechanics are basic on face value, using the varied enemies and skills coupled with the limited healing available does create challenge.

Also – slow motion killcams never get old.

All good taken along, the game does have some bugs and issues, mostly focused around the interface and various problems with the inventory being unresponsive and minor ease of use annoyances.

All in all, not a bad package at all with decent replay value with NG+ and pretty nice content overall.

What I like about the game:
1. The atmosphere. It is a real fun. You can blow up raiders and supermutants listening to some kind song about love.
2. A promising start. At the beginning of the game I felt like there was going to be something epic.
3. Hacking, lock-picking, speech. It's great when you can solve your problems this way.
4. Using different weapons. In most RPGs you pick some kind of weapon and stick to it. In Fallout 3 I used nearly all weapons because you never know what ammo you're going to find.
*** SPOILER ***
5. Blowing up Megaton. The quest is stupid, but it is fun, plus you get a better apartment on the top of the tower for doing this.

What I don't like about the game:
1. The ending. It is not epic at all. The final battle is epic, but not the ending. I just wanted to try my new armor and weapons which I got from the final battle, but I could not because the game ended. It's they allowed to continue the game by purchasing The Broken Steel.
2. Hacking and science. In my opinion hacking could have been more sophisticated. And science skill is responsible only for hacking.

There are minor differences like Sir, Madam depending on gender, some options depend on your karma and some perks add some options to the dialogs. But that is nothing comparing to the previous games of Fallout where you are treated like and idiot because your intelligence is 1.
I would give this game 8/10

I attempted to get around these issues by shrinking the resolution and switching to a controller (which was more responsive for some reason), except this resulted in a smaller, heavily letterboxed screen and terrible controls that couldn't be modified. In the few brief moments when I had controls, I was having to sequence break the tutorial on account of it not wanting to continue until I'd healed. I was at max health and there were no enemies.
So yeah, not impressed.

The Sea Will Claim everything is an extremely beautiful game. The hand-drawn graphics seem crude, but they engorge you in a matter of minutes. That's not to mention the peaceful, relaxing music.

The Sea Will Claim Everything is one of those amazing niche games that you can't help but fall in love with. It has a similar style to classic graphical adventure games: travel around to various locations, click on hot spots to collect items, read description, or perform actions, and complete quest objectives.
What makes it stand out as such a special and exceptional game is the immense love that has gone into this hand-crafted world. The graphics are hand-drawn, and charmingly so. The story is well-written, with engaging characters and surprising depth. It's one of those games where you actually care about the people in it. Almost every tiny thing in the world can be clicked on to read a description, and everything is so wonderfully quirky, you actually want to click on every last thing and read the details. There are so many hidden surprises to be found, exploring the world is worth the price alone. (In fact, it's worth trying to click on everything in the game window, as there are several weird and unexpected results.)
Because everything in the world is detailed in such a wonderful way, it can be easy to overlook how well the simple gameplay suits the genre. In classic adventure games, there are often multiple modes for the mouse cursor, but TSWCE doesn't need a cursor that switches between a hand and an eye and so on -- if you can pick something up, you will. If there is an interaction to be had, it occurs. It allows you to focus on the immersion without worrying that you missed picking something up or turning something on.
Perhaps most importantly, the game treats you like a person. This may sound a weird thing, but it's a wonderfully weird game, and one that's worth playing after you've "beaten" it and solved the main plotline's problems.
It really is a special game and a special experience. Charming, engaging, curious, and wonderful. I can't recommend it enough.

I have been playing dungeon defenders since the first one and as for DD2, I have played it since they made the first stage.
I will give a summary, pros, cons and overview.
Summary: If you like team based games, this is a must, teaming up with friends to defend zones in this game is more fun than any other game. The goal of the game is to use towers, and abilities to defend objectives from hordes of enemies who also have abilities. Play alone or with up to 3 randoms or friends (total of 4 per team.) With tons of playtime.
Pros:
• Not pay to win. Money goes to cosmetics, and bag space. Currently in alpha bag space is a bit scary, because loot is pretty much doubled. But you can sell during maps, so you will honestly never run out of space.
• So much play time. The game is in alpha, most games being released this early would have 20-50 hours of gametime. Leveling one class to 50 takes about 30 hours. This unlocks the endgame and speeds up leveling for the rest of your characters. Ultimately you want to level up 4 characters to 50, farm gear in each difficulty to move to the next difficulty (there are like 6+ difficulties.) And by the time you gear all your characters, trendy will have more content for you.
• Easy learning curve, yet still pretty challenging. If you want a game to relax, this is it, if you want to be challenged, somehow this is still it.
• Vote on what you want to see from the game. Because the game is still being made you can go to the forums and vote for new content. Say they have an idea for 3-4 play modes, and they are not sure which to do first, they will ask the community and you can read about them and vote. This game takes "Listening to the community." to a completely new level.
Cons:
• Buggy as hell. Not many bugs are game breaking and this is why people still play it. But there are tons that are annoying. Like dailies, I haven't gotten a daily in 3 days. And the 3 dailies before that I completey but didn't get rewards from.
• Alpha. The game is missing a lot of QoL features and still has some things they are holding back on. Also there are some gaps in content that you may need to grind old content to get to newer content. However they are giving bonus loot during alpha and there won't be another full wipe.
• A bit grindy at the moment. Finish the campaign puts you around level 22, doing some hard missions in freeplay brings you up to around 30. From there it is pretty much spamming the same 5 missions 30 times to get to 50 to unlock the same maps but just slightly harder and drop better loot.
Overall, the game is free, so try it. And if you want a game to burn a ton of time into without ever needing to spend a dime, this is it. I see no reason not to at least download and test it. The bugs are annoying but nothing annoying enough to get me to not want to play the game, especially when I know they will fix them eventually and we are getting bonus loot for helping them through it.
*Side-note: No hackers woohoo trendy!

The Sea Will Claim Everything is a charming and unique point & click adventure game, with an engaging story that betrays its storybook visuals; it balances wry humour and silliness with a strong narrative exploring both political and philisophical themes, a hallmark of Jonas Kyratzes' writing. If you're familiar with his work on The Talos Principle, you should have a good idea of what to expect.
It will subvert your expectations of more traditional adventure games and draw you into the wonderfully bizarre world full of interesting and unique characters, all brought to life with lovingly hand-drawn art and fantastic soundtrack. It'd probably be easy to dismiss it as 'just an adventure game', merely describing the story or features wouldn't change your mind on that, but it's ultimately more than the sum of its parts and an experience that is both entertaining and thought provoking.
It's not entirely without flaws, but the faults I have with it are minor, pedantic at best, and don't detract from the overall quality in any significant way. My only real criticism would be that it's somewhat short, although not in a way that the story felt rushed or not long enough, moreso that I just didn't really want it to end.
While it may not appeal to everyone, The Sea Will Claim Everything is a game that deserves far more attention and one that more people should try. If you're still unsure, there is a demo available
, where you can also play the other games in the Lands of Dream series for free (which you should).

The Sea Will Claim Everything is a very detailed adventure game that focuses on story. Almost every object in TSWCE can be examined, giving you interesting descriptions. The game goes as far as giving each of the mushrooms their own little backstory. Reading these is always enjoyable, thanks to the great writing.
TSWCE is very nonlinear. There are two roadblocks near the beginning that restrict where you can go, but beyond those, you can do nearly everything in any order you want. There are a lot of objectives to accomplish, which can get overwhelming. Since the explorable area is quite large, it's sometimes difficult to find what you're looking for. The puzzles themselves are easy, so anyone should still be able to finish the game with enough patience.
The graphics are nice and colorful. You meet several imaginative characters along the way, all of which are well illustrated. The background music is atmospheric and relaxing.
TSWCE is one of the most underrated games ever made, in my opinion. If you'd like to explore a surreal world and enjoy story heavy adventure games, it's definitely worth playing.

Most negative evaluations are due to bugs. To be fair, my copy sometimes bugs, probably some graphical issues (black screens on battle/town screen loading). Nothing unbearable, though it's sometimes annoying to have to quit and reload at the beginning of the turn (thank god for autosaves).
I am a single player, playing official campagins, so this is what I'll be talking about. The campaigns are long, I'm already at 300 hours of gameplay and I've only just finished the first campaign and first DLC and started the second DLC. Granted, I never autoplay battles, but still if you play the whole game through it is worth your money. Campaigns are rather interesting and characters and stories usually interesting, although I guess it depends on tastes. The final bosses on some maps can prove to be pretty challenging in hard mode (as can the very first battles on a map, before you upgrade your army and hero).
The gameplay gets kinda tedious though: troups conservation is the main focus, to the point that your main goal in every battle will be to try and lose without a single troup lost. It leads to some skills being almost a requisite for any game (especially since in this game, healing can resurrect fallen units in a stack), so that any hero will have the same 10-15 skills as all the other heroes you've played, despite the plethora of skills available. Top level is 30.
This being said, all the factions are rather interesting to play, with good units and combos in each (I haven't tried dungeon yet). Special mention to the new sanctuary faction, that actually is a nice offensive faction with beautiful design and great features.
The design is actually maybe the game's greatest asset, as it is indeed very beautiful. It also runs pretty well, my computer is 8 years old (i7 860 and GTX285, 8gb RAM) and runs it without trouble.
Note that you can play the game offline, but you'll miss on some features like achievements and dynasty weapons. The servers seem stable (I've only been disconnected once in 300 hours), but playing online means you're limited to a very short number of saves, so you have to overwrite regularly on your old saves.
All in all, the game is worth buying and playing if you can see through the gameplay shortcomings. It's not the best Heroes game, but it's not a bad game, and even if you only play the official campaigns, it's got plenty of content and game time.

For those looking to make their own game, a bit of advice: Do some research and/or download the trial (RMVXA Lite) FIRST before actually buying! As well, RMVXA is wonderful in its own right, but is VERY processor-heavy and may require higher specs than the "Required / Recommended System Requirements" lets on. Just a fair warning to those with weaker computers that you should expect some lagging.
With that out of the way, for old-school SNES-era RPGs (or sprite-based games in gener), RM is absolutely perfect, once you learn the ropes for how to use it. Which may take some time, but once you get the hang of how eventing and map tiling works, it can really be quite the powerful tool. The resources available are free to use for any project, whether a free project or commercial, and there is a lot of support from both the community and the main Enterbrain website itself. As well, many aspects of the database are open for modification without the need for programming skills, and those that aren't can be changed with a few (dozen) lines of code.
The only issues thus-far that I've encountered are generally small. The largest thus-far is the learning curve; it can be rather daunting to jump into one's first project during the first couple of weeks, but once you get the hang of how the general flow works, then things become easier to manipulate. As well, there are some limitations in the editor for those with limited talent in scripting, but that can be overcome if one employs the help of a dedicated scripter or scripts designed by others that change how the editor/database works. Finally, while custom resources (scripts, spritesheets, tile sets, etc.) are generally free-to-use by their authors for non-commercial projects, those that are looking to make money off their games may find themselves out-of-luck or having to pay royalties to the creators of such content.
Other than those minor gripes, RMVXA is a great package for starting game developers, and makes a great basis for understanding the game-development process as a whole. While it can be a nightmare for those just starting out, the intuitive and dedicated user will grasp the basics and go from there fairly quickly.

Where for some reason I could not into Spacechem, Infinifactory has got me by the short and curlies. It's a genius example of puzzle design, really, in a style somewhat reminiscent of The Incredible Machine. You're given a specific input and output, sometimes a few special pieces in the middle, and set loose to design your madcap assembly line. There's no right answer, just whatever produces the desired product without causing a broken pileup along the way. You are then given a numeric breakdown of your carbon footprint, blocks used, and cycles (length) taken, on a bar graph showing average global player scores for that level. I think that's also brilliant, because you aren't competing for any specific "S Rank" conditions (although there are some achievements to that effect), you're just shown how you stack up to the player average and left to decide for yourself if you want to try to go back and optimize things just that little bit more...
Levels often look daunting at first glance, but as prodded at will usually unravel gradually as you work out where to put piece buffers, delay gates, and so on. Failing that, you can always go look at some other player builds, which in recreating you will come to understand the fundamental components thereof. Even by cheating you're learning to play the game better.
There's also a more sandboxy set of levels available, and a built-in GIF recorder for showing off your solutions. Fantastic puzzle game that basically does everything right.

Gonner is an action shooty platformer, featuring themed worlds and tactful procedural generation. (In a good way)
It's shares a lot of DNA with Downwell - stripping down the game to something immediate and instantly gratuitous. Rather, it doesn't hold back and throws you into a series of world encounters without explanation, where your weapon of choice and ability will have to contend with the enemy hordes.
Like Downwell, the game has a combo level meter that you can start off by destroying enemies. Keep the momentum going and you'll be rewarded with additional credits - credits that you can use to buy gear at the item shops that intermittently appear, or should you meet an untimely fate, that could be used to pay off Death from claiming your soul.
Visually the game is sparse, but it works really well combined with the arcade purity that Gonner does. In motion, the game is eye catching and fast, with generous 2d animated explosions and particles bouncing around the screen when the action starts. Similarly, the audiowork is subtle but provacative at times, very much in tandem with what's being presented onscreen.
In recap - Gonner is sweet, short and pure. Downwell fans, buy without question.

I almost didn't play Just Cause 2. Twice. The first time was before buying it. I hesitated because of how huge everyone made the game world seem. The impression I got was that there was more to do here than every Elder Scrolls combined. And I didn't want to make that kind of a time commitment. But when it went on sale it was too cheap to pass up.
After intsalling and trying to start the game is when I almost gave up a second time. I couldn't get the game to run for more than about 5 mintues without crashing. That meant I would race desperately to get to the next checkpoint before the game crashed. I couldn't pause or explore or do anything but rush blindly ahead. Even on normal you can't do that without dying though. So I gave up for a while and played some other games, hoping for a patch or some explanation.
Eventually, months later I tried again, but the game hadn't been patched and probably wasn't ever going to be. So I researched some fixes. Nothing seemed to work. The two biggest recommendations were to run in Windows 7 compatability mode and to turn off decals. Neither worked. BUT I got lucky and just decided on a whim to do both at the same time. The first time the game ran for 15 minutes without crashing I almost cried. Then I made it to an hour. More. So luckily, that combination fixed it for me. But the real shame of this game is that I almost missed it entirely because of such a horrible beginning experience and having to manually change things to get it to even run.
Once it did run though, it was an awesom experience. In a word: fun. And really just plain, simple, fun. The first two tutorial-heavy story missions are actually a bad opening to the game, even though they introduce all the necessary concepts. They're too linear. Too narrow. The best part about Just Cause is how open and free and spontaneous the world is. The story missions largely lack all of that. The controls also took some getting used to. Having dodge be tab - an awkward button to hit repeatedly - and aim be C - something I've never encountered before - threw me for a while. Eventually I did get used to the controls though and I couldn't find a mapping I liked more than the default one. There's just a learning curve and you have to power through it.
In the open world and used to the controls, the game shines. Largely because there is a lot to do, but you don't even have to do any of it. I spent my first 10 hours or so just exploring and causing chaos and searching for items. And it was addictive. And fun!
Then I moved on to the races. I didn't expect them to be good, but with only a few exceptions (i.e. plane flights through cities and driving on snow) I found the racing to be insanely well executed. I looked forward to completing all of them and beat all 75 even though I didn't have to.
The faction missions are also fun, although I realized that the shorter they were, generally the better. Just Cause seems to be meant for bite-sized play, with a short rise and fall of action. The longer missions, whether story related or not, were where the game suffered.
And the story itself is terrible. The writing, voice acting, all horendous. There are as many accents as there are voice actors, and most of them don't sound like any kind of real accent at all. It's quite jarring until you get used to it. But in some ways this actually works in the game's favor, because it reminds you not to take it seriously.
So if you want a third person action game akin to GTA but even bigger and less serious (though maybe a bit less absurd than something like Saints Row) Just Cause is the place to get it.

Super Splatters is an odd combination of arcade and puzzle style gameplay that will keep you competitively trying to raise your score by exploding harmless little globs for the sake of the show. Your goal is to make these globs of goop fly across the screen doing different stunts and combos building up the highest score possible so that you can flaunt your score on the leader boards. A quick 15 minutes of playing somehow flashes before your eyes as you realize you have been playing for a few hours making a strategy and properly executing it for an attempt on the top score. The are different game modes if you'd like to mix it up, and it's an overall fun and solid game. It is easy to get hooked on it and get 7-10 hours of gameplay out of it, which is well worth the 10 dollars. You can definitely get more gameplay time through actively playing through all of the different level layouts and missions if you really get hooked on the game.
You can even record your gameplay ingame so that you can post it on the leaderboards for the ultimate boasting of your skill. It really reminds me of that type of competition you would get at the local arcade as you battled your friends indirectly for the top high score.
If a good mixture of arcade and puzzle games sounds appealing to you, this is a great purchase. Have fun!

Risen 1 is a great RPG game. Overall, I think it's the third best out of 6 games from the devs of Gothic. (Gothic and Gothic 2 are the better ones).
I played this game for the first time when it was released back in 2009. Haven't played it since then, even barely remembered what the story was, what were the good or bad things.
I just finished this game on the hardest difficulty (as a mage this time) and I enjoyed this playthrough sooo much! But the very end (the last few chapters) was a bit tedious and grindy.
I know that many players who are unfamiliar with the Gothic gameplay mechanics and how unforgivable these games are - can get a bit frustrated about the way the combat works or how it's hard to know where to go or what to do (especially when you start the game). But I never had a problem with those things, I think that's what makes these games (Gothic/Risen) unique to all the others. I really enjoy the beginning of these games where even a single herb or arrow can make the difference. The character building is enjoyable and challenging.
+Still good graphics for a 7y old game.
+Amazing voice acting.
+Amazing music!
+Ambient sounds and sound effects are perfect. You really feel like you are there, in that world. It makes it very believable.
+Controls are pretty good too.
+Long game. ~50h if you like to complete every quest, kill every enemy and so on.
+Tombs and caves are well done and creepy.
+Rewards players who like to explore the world.
+Many different NPCs with different personalities.
+Multi-layered quests.
-Attack spells (utility spells are good) are a bit lackluster. There should have been more variety. They are fun to use, but you want to have more than 4.
-Bugs. There are a big variety of those. Sometimes you get stuck near the ledges just because. Especially late game.
-Lack of variety of enemies at the last 1/3 of the game.
-That freakin' sea monster.
-Nights are too dark and tombs and caves sometimes can be nearly pitch black. So prepare your torches or use the light spell, you'll definitely need it, many times.
-Too few NPCs that you can find outside of cities or camps.
And a tip for everyone: SAVE OFTEN AND A LOT. Save before/after talking to an npc, after killing creatures or turning in quests. And after many other things. This will save your nerves and you will not need to waste more time doing the same stuff if you f*cked up or misclicked something.
Oh and another tip. Don't be ashamed to use some guides if you get stuck or want to know more about some stuffs. Will save your time and/or will quicken your decision making.
+It's very cheap on sales. So grab it, it's well worth it.

I knew about The Sea Will Claim Everything for some time but only now did I finally play it. Should have done it sooner.
TSWCE is a game full of whimsical charm. The Land of Dreams as a setting is a creative and engaging one filled with the strange and magical. There’s also obscene amounts of flavor text for things such as every book and mushroom in the game. The writing is filled with corny jokes and silliness that while it may not always hit is still really endearing. The game also has a really strong fairy tale/children’s story aesthetic and the music is great too. TSWCE is also a political fable, being very critical of the economic policies that led to the Great Recession of 2008 as well as reactionary ideologies in general. Philosophy is also a major part of TSWCE and the some of the game’s major themes are the dangers of ignorance, greed, and strict adherence to dogma and that one of the most important ways to make the world a better place is for people to be open to change and have an understanding and empathy for the people and world around them. This all done well and a major reason why is because the setting and characters have so much care put into them so that the message doesn’t envelop the narrative and instead works alongside it and they enhance each other.
Gameplaywise it’s more of a point and click game, the magic screen is your UI and most puzzles are more simple stuff such as item gathering, talking to people, and exploration. As the game tells you from the get-go it’s a bit of a slow paced game, but it’s still real engaging.
Overall TSWCE is a unique and  enthralling game with a lot of heart and a well-crafted message.

This is based off of a few hours of playing over the last week. I've gotta say that this game really does the survival game (without zombies) very well. This was my most memorable life so far:
I had survived a couple days by scavenging some cabins that I had found and had collected some essential gear. Coming across things like a can opener, warm clothes, matches, some wood and a couple of tools made me feel confident enough to head out at morning to find some new food sources.

After searching the woods for a while it was getting pretty late in the day and I had luckily found a dead deer carcass. There was a few pounds of meat on it and I was really hungry by this point so I decided to put down a camp fire right there and skin and cook the meat. Focusing completely on getting my fire started, cooking my meat, and boiling water I realized it was all the sudden very dark. I looked up because I had heard wolves howling earlier and no joke, right in front of me just out of the fire's light was a pair of glowing green eyes. It was a wolf, waiting for the fire to burn out. Smart enough to keep it's distance but ready to attack. (Here is a picture:
)

This was one of the most intense moments I've ever had in a game. As time ticked by, the fire "timer" ticked lower and lower and eventually burned out. I ran away from the wolf into a cave that was right behind me and the wolf followed, running close behind. You can probably guess what happened after that, due to me being in a dead end with nowhere to go.

The spontaneity of the events that unfolded throughout that playthrough really gave me hope that this game will be great, and the devs really know what they are doing. Also, the art direction is really cool. It is highly stylized and even though it doesn't look realistic per sey, they do hit the nail on the head for authenticity. The locations are varied, the environment feels alive due to the weather conditions, sounds which are great (the indoor sounds when it is windy are amazing), and finding loot is exciting and meaningful. The only things I hope they improve are the map size, the UI which feels a little tedious with the lists, and giving us more to do!
Well, this turned out way longer than I was planning but I want to put out there my thoughts on this game and I hope the devs deliver on what could be a great addition to the survival genre of PC games!

Weirdest experience I've ever had playing a game. If I had to liken it to something, it would be like walking around the Library of Babel finding that none of the books have any meaning through the random jumble of letters. Just when you think you're not going to find anything useful, you find that one book has a single intelligible word. But its existence is completely by chance - it gives no insight to who built the library or where the books came from. Rationality tells you it's all worthless. Random noise. But the library exists to give you that idea.
I have no idea whether this situation is fictional or factual. I've no idea whether the narrator is both developer and commentator. I can't tell you whether it's a waste of time or not. But I bought a copy. I played it. And by some miracle I didn't request a refund. I still don't know why. Perhaps I feel I can work it out if I look at it again. I don't know whether ir's accidental - this sense of emptiness or it's a carefully engineered con-trick to rob the participant of any sense of understanding.
I don't even know if I can recommend this game or not. Steam forced me to pick an option but it felt wrong to click either button. I chose Yes after tossing a coin.
The Stanley Parable tried to demonstrate the ineffectiveness of trying to escape a fixed narrative. This game is trying to ask if you can find meaning in the movement of fog and sand.  Can you look at the wind and see a form? All I feel is ambivalence.
