GoNNER’s advertized as a tough as hell procedurally-generated 2D platformer with roguelike elements.
It might come off wrong but it’s not that hard in my eyes. Simply because I grew up with games like that and I play loads of such. So it might differ for you lil’ Jimmy. You just have to C4 yourself. See what I did there? Haha.
And what’s it all about?
Well you’re on a journey to cheer up your friend Sally by searching for just the right trinket in the deep and dark places nearby.
TL;DR: Still a better lovestory than twilight

Let’s start off with the roguelike elements.
So here’s the thing. The levels are, obviously, procedurally-generated so you’re getting a new layout every run. The amount and type of enemies are also random and so are the items and so on.
Now here’s where some people will be like: BUT IT’S ROGUELITE YOU SCRUB! Shush I say.
The term roguelike has (d)evolved over time anyway.
I mention this because when you happen to die in a level there’re two possible outcomes. Either you have enough runes so you can pay for a continue or you’re one runeless lil’ fella and you’ve got to start all over.
I’ll get to the runes later.
Now at the very start of the game you spawn without a head … dafuq? It’s not such a big deal dude. I mean c’mon … who needs a head anyway? In case you really want one well there’s a solution for you.
There’s one big ol’ tree and a nice fella who’s more than happy to hand you one of the heads that just happen to hang from the tree. At the start you’ve got two heads that you can choose from but over time you’ll notice that you’re able to unlock various other heads.
Now here’s the fun part. You not only look different, like your GF does with a new haircut which you probably never notice, BUT in GoNNER you notice that Ikk looks pretty damn fine depending on the head.
But wait there’s more! Not only can you choose a head for lil’ Ikk, that’s the name of the character you’re playing as in case you didn’t know, but you’re also able to choose a gun and an item.
Ikk carries those items on his back during his trip to cheer his good ol’ buddy Sally up. The guns you ask? He holds’em with his hands duh! FOCUS!
Anyway you start the game with three different weapons. A machine gun, a shotgun and a laser.
The same goes for items. There’s a lil’ ammo refill that you can use whenever you’re in need of some ammo, a shark fin which makes you go bananas and it’s best to find out what the other one does for yourself.
Now after you’ve chosen your setup of your liking you’ll jump into the snake which will bring you to the next level through it’s … let’s call it the “other end.”
Now the game features four worlds. Every world has four levels. If you’re lucky enough you might find some additional levels? Who knows … maybe I’m just making things up?!
Now after every world you’ve got the chance to hang out with your good ol’ buddy Sally, the landbound whale. Sally’s also quite cute but that’s just my opinion.
Depending on the world and the level you’re in you’ll encounter different kind of enemies. Now every world has it’s own types of enemies. However enemies will show up in later levels as well. Means world one enemies will also be seen in world four for example so beware.
Let’s get into the mechanics of GoNNER next.
You might notice that you do get points after you’ve killed an enemy and that a weird skull appears in the upper right corner. That’s the combo system you’re looking at.
Something incredibly awesome happens if you manage to keep your combo up.
Hint: LSD.
If you happen to fill a combo tier, a combo tier consist of five skulls, you get a rune. The higher your combo tier is the more points you get for an enemy. It’s also important to know that you also get more points for the amount of runes you have. So it’s a good idea to keep your combo going if possible since you might be needing those runes in order to buy youself some nice things or if you fancy a top five position on the leaderboards. That’s not the only thing runes are good for though. You’re also able to buy yourself another life should you happen to die in one of the levels and trust me … you will.
Something that I should also mention is that if you get hit you lose your head and jump around as a droplet.
Now if you manage to get your head back it’s all good you just lost one heart but if you get hit again you’re dead so be sure to be careful.

Basically you drop everything if you get hit so it can happen that you lose your weapon or back item due to’em falling into a pit for example. You’re able to get a random weapon and back item on the next level though.
Now as Ikk you’re able to RunGunJumpGun err wrong game. But basically you are.
And just like our favorite italian you’re also able to jump on the enemies to inflict damage.
Then there’s the thing you’ve got on your back. You can use that as well. If you do it goes on cooldown for a while so you can’t spam it.
Ikk can also double jump in order to get to higher platforms or to reach those pesky flying enemies.
There’re also leaderboards in the game if you happen to care ‘bout that or if you want to brag ‘bout your super highscore.
One thing to note’s also that the game will get updates every now and then and new things might be added as well.
So a lot of people question the replayability of GoNNER.
I like to compare it to Nuclear Throne as in you try to get as far as possible and there’re quite a few things to unlock. But the main reason why we or rather I still play Nuclear Throne is because it’s fun.
That’s also the exact same reason why I’ll continue to play GoNNER.
All in all it’s damn worth it’s price and with a Dev like Ditto you’re safe. You’ll get a good and solid game and a Dev that actually cares.

GoNNER is a rogue-like platformer developed by Art in Heart and published by Raw Fury. In GoNNER you play as Ikk, a small blob who enjoys wearing skulls and shooting things. He’s a bit of a weird one. Your goal is to progress through different levels and worlds killing things and trying not to die. You’ll want to try and rack up loads of points too so you can show all your friend(s) how badass you are on the leaderboards!
I’ve always been a substance-over-style kind of gamer but GoNNER is too damn stylish for me to not mention it. For a start, GoNNER is beautiful. The bright colors of Ikk, enemies and any pickups in the level contrast really well with the dark background in early levels and still look good against the brighter backgrounds`. It makes the game pop. The simplistic character design also work very well for GoNNER. On top of all that, GoNNER has a fantastic soundtrack and it’s incorporated into the game in a really interesting way. As you get higher combos the music speeds up, getting faster and faster as you kill more and more enemies without a break. I found this to really help build up tension in the game when fighting off a buttload of enemies.
As I mentioned, Ikk is a blob. How does a blob fight off enemies you ask? By picking up things he finds during his travels of course! In other words, you find items during your runs (one of each item type for each world as far as I’ve seen so far) and you can then choose which items to use next time you start over. The three different items types are: heads, weapons and equipment. The head you choose determines how much health you have and how quickly you move, some of them do other things too but you can find out about that yourself! The weapons are up next, so far there’s some good variation and while the weapons seem balanced you’ll probably end up choosing one you like more than the other. Each weapon has a set amount of ammo and once you run out of that ammo you’ll have to find a bullet casing dropped by an enemy, this is the pickup that replenishes your ammo. Lastly you’ve got equipment, basically the equivalent of spacebar items in The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth. These all have different effects and they recharge over time. One of them gives you a bullet pickup, another acts like a personal trampoline. As with weapons, you’ll probably find one in particular that you like more than the others.
There are two other kinds of pickups in GoNNER: hearts and purple runes. Hearts can be found by opening blue chests in the levels, they’re a welcome sight let me tell you. The purple runes are pretty interesting. They’re dropped by enemies (the drop rate seems to increase as you rack up combos) and they’re used for two things. Firstly, if you have enough of them they can be used to resurrect yourself when you run out of hearts/die without a head. The cost of doing this increases each time you do it and it increases each time you progress to a new world and when you do resurrect yourself you start at the beginning of the level you died on. The second use for them is in the item shops before a boss fight at the end of a world. The shops stock one of each item type as well as either a bullet or a heart. The different items have different prices and you can also spend a couple of runes to swap out what’s on sale.
So speaking of death (Ikk has a friend called Death funnily enough) it’s going to happen a lot. As you’d expect from a rogue-like game. There are two ways to fully die in GoNNER. You either lose all of your hearts and then get hit again or you somehow manage to get hit while not wearing a head. When you get hit you lose a heart, drop all your items and Ikk returns to blob form. As a blob, you have a few seconds to bounce around with no risk of losing health while you either try to grab your items back or move to a safer spot. Returning to Ikk’s headless chicken form will send out a little shockwave that kills anything standing too close to you. Comes in pretty handy.
Between each world is a sort of intermediary level home to Sally, a giant landbound whale and Ikk’s best friend. Sally loves you. When you reach this level and go see Sally she’ll be kind enough to increase your weapon’s ammo capacity and give you an extra heart container. Both of which come in very handy as the game gets even more difficult with each world. One thing that’s worth noting is that if you die and resurrect yourself with runes you’ll lose the extra ammo and extra heart container.
Going through the levels and killing enemies earns you points which then end up on the leaderboard. I really like the way the leaderboard is set out. It shows you who got how many points as well as how long that run was and what items were used during it. It seems to me like the only way to earn points is to kill enemies in the level and each enemy type gives you a different amount of points (there are four or five enemy types per world). As you would expect, the higher your combo is, the more points you earn.
As much as I’ve enjoyed what I’ve played of GoNNER so far, I do have one main problem with it. It lacks control re-bindings. Now the default bindings for the M&KB and for controllers are decent and I’ve enjoyed playing using both, however, they aren’t going to perfect for everyone and there were a couple of bindings in particular that I had some trouble with/wanted to change. It’s not a huge issue but I would definitely like to see key re-bindings patched in at some point soon.
GoNNER combines superb style with some great substance to create an all-round satisfying experience. Oh and it has a giant landbound whale. Who doesn’t love giant landbound whales?!

Another remarkable release from Zachtronics!
Puzzle games come in many different forms nowadays, and they make you think in different ways. The part that I love about Infinifactory is that I can imagine, in my head, the parts of the output contraption coming together in a certain way, and then eventually getting all the movements timed and positioned correctly to make it happen. Or whatever gets the job done.
On the more difficult puzzles, the magnitude of what is required by the puzzle can make solving it take over an hour, easily. There is a certain threshold of patience, that if you can commit enough time and thought to that problem, you should be able to get it done after a while. Once you get the mechanics of the game down it's just a matter of that. I find that sometimes I am in that mood, and I'll solve a couple more problems, but most of the time it's hard to get motivated to solve some of those problems.
The game doesn't require you to solve every problem as you progress, however, so it's a blast as you're first going through it. I think that's a sufficient offset to the inherent difficulty of Infinifactory that I'll recommend this to the puzzlers out there. Due to the spacial nature of the game, if you like manipulating things in 3D, this is much more likely to arouse your interest. Of all the Zachtronics releases, I feel like this is probably the most accessible.

This is the most innovative and terrifying video games I have EVER played. It takes the usual horror game tropes and throws them out the window. If you are used to games like Slender, Amnesia, or SCP: Containment Breach, you WILL be lost and confused.
In a lot of horror games, they try to make you feel alone and confused by presenting you with a puzzle and making you solve it without showing it to you directly, or they try and do so through the story. In this game it is so different from everything else, it takes time to get used to the game mechanics, which you don't have. You may end up floundering around a lot not realizing what does what, and you may do something wrong without knowing why. This causes panic and confusion for the player and it's not reliant on anything in-game, but rather the player's mistakes. In games like SCP: CB, which are procedurally generated, a lot of the confusion relies on the fact that you just get dropped in and are expected to go to these certain places in this certain order when you are never told any of this. In this game, they cryptically explain to you how to play, you still don't know what is happening and why, especially once you get further in.
A lot of horror games also try to create a sense of dread. A feeling that keeps you from wanting to continue down the next corridor, even though you don't want to. This is portrayed very well in a game called Dreadhalls for the Oculus Rift. Dreadhalls comes in as a close second to this one for me as "The Scariest Game Ever", and that unbelievable feeling of dread is the cause. But Dreadhalls gives off the same vibe a lot of other horror games do, just amped-up tenfold. The biggest reason I think that this game is better, is because it gives off a completely different feeling.
You get an IMMENSE felling of paranoia while playing. You have no control over your character or his surroundings other than the doors, door lights, and the security cameras. All you can do is literally wait to die. No matter how much you check the cameras, they can, and will keep moving towards you and you can't do anything about them other than closing the doors. You can only do "so much", and not everything you do actually works, so you have to try everything to find out what works while trying to do what works. You know that you will die, you just don't know when.]

I did not play any fallout games prior so I was a newby on fallout.
The good:
* engaging story. ( I personally think its a plausable story)
* Full of side quests
* 100 hours of gameplay if you want to complete all the side missions.
* Its more rpg than shooter.
* Gear that wears out. Adds a new game dynamic.
* Limited resources, makes you frugal, but adds a great variety as you end up using most of your weapons.
* Leveling has real impact on consequences
* Karma (doing good or bad things) changes how people react to you.
* You can save your game and come back to it a week later. (unlike a lot of online RPG games)
The Bad:
* Same monsters. After 60+ hours, killing the same monsters gets a little tiresome.
* Subways. Although at the beginning they were really exciting by the end they were more tiresome.
* The constant requirement to repair gear turns you into a manic horder, which slows down the pace of the game.
* The start was super difficult. Everyone and everything at the start is out to kill you. At least that was my experience.
* Storage mechanics are annoying. You have to go through all your inventory to pick out items, and if you accidentally click A you have to start again.
* Overall crafting could be better. I think I ended up crafting 4 items in total.
Overall I would 100% recommend this game for anyone looking for a cheap single player open world RPG.

Banished is a medieval town simulator where you need to balance food gathering, townspeople care, resource production, natality and death of townspeople.
Don't let the nice but lower-end graphics fool you; this game is incredibly addictive and well balanced. Despite it being a relatively "recent" game freshly out of Early Access, the game is well-polished and will find you want more.
Finding the balance for everything is key; build a house too soon and suddenly, you can't feed your people anymore. Don't have enough labourers to replace old workers that are about to die, and all your plans go down the drain...
It still lacks some features to make it truly complete; the ability to force certain resources to be stored in specific places, forcing townspeople to not use a type of resource since you want to keep it for another action (example: coal for steel tools, berries for ale...).
But despite those little shortcomings (oversights?) and few debatable mechanics, this game is truly worth the price of admission.

I've played every entry of the Heroes of Might and Magic series (except VII, but I'll explain that momentarily), and I wanted so badly to like this one. Since people seem to respond well to the pros/cons list, I'll use that format.
Pros:
-The single player campaign is reasonably fun. It has some frustrating moments, but overall the missions are at least enjoyable, if not particularly original. The cut scenes are best skipped though.
- In all the previous games, there was an element of chance to skill gain, while in this game you can customize your heroes' skills freely. This does tend to reduce the variety of skills used, but it takes out some of the irritation of not getting a skill that you consider vital to your hero.
- Combat is similar to all the previous games, but with significantly expanded creature abilities, which I like. Rather than just attack-attack-attack, there are options for using most creatures in a secondary role. I'm not a huge fan of the square combat grid (as opposed to hexes), but it's not terrible, just not ideal.
- Graphics and animations are quite a bit better than previous games. Not that graphics are a vital feature in a turn-based strategy game, but it's nice little side feature.
Cons:
- Multiplayer does not work. I know people will say "oh, have you tried ____?" Yes. I have tried whatever you were going to suggest. It does. Not. Work. I even opened a ticket with Ubisoft support, and after several weeks of trying everything they suggested, I never succesfully joined or hosted a multiplayer game. It doesn't matter how fun the single player is, Heroes is a game to be played with other people.
- Ubisoft went ahead and released Heroes VII before fixing this game, and (surprise surprise) it had the exact same connection issues as this game, plus some all new game breaking bugs. As I said, I didn't actually play VII, but you can go read the reviews for it and they will almost all cite some comparison to the broken status of VI. As of the end of 2016, VII has also been abandoned and will never be patched.
I realize that it looks like the pros outweigh the cons in my list, since the pros are all in-game features, and the cons are out-of-game problems with Ubisoft. Regardless, my recommendation is to avoid this game, and all future releases from Ubisoft. One thing is for sure, I will absolutely not be purchasing another game from them until they stop releasing broken, buggy games that never get fixed. Ubisoft does not deserve my money, or yours, or anyone else's for that matter.

First off I’ve been a alpha/beta tester for GoNNER so I’ve seen this game get better and better with every update. Here’s one of the most important things to note.

The guy seriously cares ‘bout fixing all the bugs and whatnot. So kudos Ditto.
Now that I’ve kissed some♥♥♥♥♥(because I wanted to heh) we can move on to the actual review.

Looks funky eh? GoNNER I mean. I can’t remember the name but I saw that message during a Twitch Stream and thought it’s quite fitting:
Anon: this game looks what Isaac would dream of on lsd.
And I most certainly agree. The art style’s quite unique and probably not for everyone, I love it though but then again I’m weird myself.
If you see Ditto the Dev of GoNNER you’ll see it fits 100% because he lives and breaths that style.
Sorry Ditto :P
GoNNER’s advertized as a tough as hell procedurally-generated 2D platformer with roguelike elements.
It might come off wrong but it’s not that hard in my eyes. Simply because I grew up with games like that and I play loads of such. So it might differ for you lil’ Jimmy. You just have to C4 yourself. See what I did there? Haha.
And what’s it all about?
Well you’re on a journey to cheer up your friend Sally by searching for just the right trinket in the deep and dark places nearby.
TL;DR: Still a better lovestory than twilight

Let’s start off with the roguelike elements.
So here’s the thing. The levels are, obviously, procedurally-generated so you’re getting a new layout every run. The amount and type of enemies are also random and so are the items and so on.
Now here’s where some people will be like: BUT IT’S ROGUELITE YOU SCRUB! Shush I say.
The term roguelike has (d)evolved over time anyway.
I mention this because when you happen to die in a level there’re two possible outcomes. Either you have enough runes so you can pay for a continue or you’re one runeless lil’ fella and you’ve got to start all over.
I’ll get to the runes later.
Now at the very start of the game you spawn without a head … dafuq? It’s not such a big deal dude. I mean c’mon … who needs a head anyway? In case you really want one well there’s a solution for you.
There’s one big ol’ tree and a nice fella who’s more than happy to hand you one of the heads that just happen to hang from the tree. At the start you’ve got two heads that you can choose from but over time you’ll notice that you’re able to unlock various other heads.
Now here’s the fun part. You not only look different, like your GF does with a new haircut which you probably never notice, BUT in GoNNER you notice that Ikk looks pretty damn fine depending on the head.
But wait there’s more! Not only can you choose a head for lil’ Ikk, that’s the name of the character you’re playing as in case you didn’t know, but you’re also able to choose a gun and an item.
Ikk carries those items on his back during his trip to cheer his good ol’ buddy Sally up. The guns you ask? He holds’em with his hands duh! FOCUS!
Anyway you start the game with three different weapons. A machine gun, a shotgun and a laser.
The same goes for items. There’s a lil’ ammo refill that you can use whenever you’re in need of some ammo, a shark fin which makes you go bananas and it’s best to find out what the other one does for yourself.
Now after you’ve chosen your setup of your liking you’ll jump into the snake which will bring you to the next level through it’s … let’s call it the “other end.”
Now the game features four worlds. Every world has four levels. If you’re lucky enough you might find some additional levels? Who knows … maybe I’m just making things up?!
Now after every world you’ve got the chance to hang out with your good ol’ buddy Sally, the landbound whale. Sally’s also quite cute but that’s just my opinion.
Depending on the world and the level you’re in you’ll encounter different kind of enemies. Now every world has it’s own types of enemies. However enemies will show up in later levels as well. Means world one enemies will also be seen in world four for example so beware.
Let’s get into the mechanics of GoNNER next.
You might notice that you do get points after you’ve killed an enemy and that a weird skull appears in the upper right corner. That’s the combo system you’re looking at.
Something incredibly awesome happens if you manage to keep your combo up.
Hint: LSD.
If you happen to fill a combo tier, a combo tier consist of five skulls, you get a rune. The higher your combo tier is the more points you get for an enemy. It’s also important to know that you also get more points for the amount of runes you have. So it’s a good idea to keep your combo going if possible since you might be needing those runes in order to buy youself some nice things or if you fancy a top five position on the leaderboards. That’s not the only thing runes are good for though. You’re also able to buy yourself another life should you happen to die in one of the levels and trust me … you will.
Something that I should also mention is that if you get hit you lose your head and jump around as a droplet.
Now if you manage to get your head back it’s all good you just lost one heart but if you get hit again you’re dead so be sure to be careful.

GoNNER is a rogue-like platformer developed by Art in Heart and published by Raw Fury. In GoNNER you play as Ikk, a small blob who enjoys wearing skulls and shooting things. He’s a bit of a weird one. Your goal is to progress through different levels and worlds killing things and trying not to die. You’ll want to try and rack up loads of points too so you can show all your friend(s) how badass you are on the leaderboards!
I’ve always been a substance-over-style kind of gamer but GoNNER is too damn stylish for me to not mention it. For a start, GoNNER is beautiful. The bright colors of Ikk, enemies and any pickups in the level contrast really well with the dark background in early levels and still look good against the brighter backgrounds`. It makes the game pop. The simplistic character design also work very well for GoNNER. On top of all that, GoNNER has a fantastic soundtrack and it’s incorporated into the game in a really interesting way. As you get higher combos the music speeds up, getting faster and faster as you kill more and more enemies without a break. I found this to really help build up tension in the game when fighting off a buttload of enemies.
As I mentioned, Ikk is a blob. How does a blob fight off enemies you ask? By picking up things he finds during his travels of course! In other words, you find items during your runs (one of each item type for each world as far as I’ve seen so far) and you can then choose which items to use next time you start over. The three different items types are: heads, weapons and equipment. The head you choose determines how much health you have and how quickly you move, some of them do other things too but you can find out about that yourself! The weapons are up next, so far there’s some good variation and while the weapons seem balanced you’ll probably end up choosing one you like more than the other. Each weapon has a set amount of ammo and once you run out of that ammo you’ll have to find a bullet casing dropped by an enemy, this is the pickup that replenishes your ammo. Lastly you’ve got equipment, basically the equivalent of spacebar items in The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth. These all have different effects and they recharge over time. One of them gives you a bullet pickup, another acts like a personal trampoline. As with weapons, you’ll probably find one in particular that you like more than the others.
There are two other kinds of pickups in GoNNER: hearts and purple runes. Hearts can be found by opening blue chests in the levels, they’re a welcome sight let me tell you. The purple runes are pretty interesting. They’re dropped by enemies (the drop rate seems to increase as you rack up combos) and they’re used for two things. Firstly, if you have enough of them they can be used to resurrect yourself when you run out of hearts/die without a head. The cost of doing this increases each time you do it and it increases each time you progress to a new world and when you do resurrect yourself you start at the beginning of the level you died on. The second use for them is in the item shops before a boss fight at the end of a world. The shops stock one of each item type as well as either a bullet or a heart. The different items have different prices and you can also spend a couple of runes to swap out what’s on sale.
So speaking of death (Ikk has a friend called Death funnily enough) it’s going to happen a lot. As you’d expect from a rogue-like game. There are two ways to fully die in GoNNER. You either lose all of your hearts and then get hit again or you somehow manage to get hit while not wearing a head. When you get hit you lose a heart, drop all your items and Ikk returns to blob form. As a blob, you have a few seconds to bounce around with no risk of losing health while you either try to grab your items back or move to a safer spot. Returning to Ikk’s headless chicken form will send out a little shockwave that kills anything standing too close to you. Comes in pretty handy.
Between each world is a sort of intermediary level home to Sally, a giant landbound whale and Ikk’s best friend. Sally loves you. When you reach this level and go see Sally she’ll be kind enough to increase your weapon’s ammo capacity and give you an extra heart container. Both of which come in very handy as the game gets even more difficult with each world. One thing that’s worth noting is that if you die and resurrect yourself with runes you’ll lose the extra ammo and extra heart container.
Going through the levels and killing enemies earns you points which then end up on the leaderboard. I really like the way the leaderboard is set out. It shows you who got how many points as well as how long that run was and what items were used during it. It seems to me like the only way to earn points is to kill enemies in the level and each enemy type gives you a different amount of points (there are four or five enemy types per world). As you would expect, the higher your combo is, the more points you earn.
As much as I’ve enjoyed what I’ve played of GoNNER so far, I do have one main problem with it. It lacks control re-bindings. Now the default bindings for the M&KB and for controllers are decent and I’ve enjoyed playing using both, however, they aren’t going to perfect for everyone and there were a couple of bindings in particular that I had some trouble with/wanted to change. It’s not a huge issue but I would definitely like to see key re-bindings patched in at some point soon.
GoNNER combines superb style with some great substance to create an all-round satisfying experience. Oh and it has a giant landbound whale. Who doesn’t love giant landbound whales?!

This game is basically a 3-dimensional version of SpaceChem, where you have to construct large factories of conveyor belts and welders to build objects (like chairs) out of cubes. A lot of the annoying parts of SpaceChem have been stripped out -- the controls are much smoother now, and the silly interface of arrows and reactors is completely gone. If you like engineering games or the concept of SpaceChem, even if you didn't like SpaceChem, you'd enjoy this one.
The game does a great job building in complexity over time. A few levels feel like you're just doing the same thing over again, but I was impressed with how many levels presented a new concept, given the simplicity of what you're doing. Nor did anything get too hard, too fast; each new element added had tons of use cases, and each puzzle usually explored one of these use cases to the fullest possible extent. I felt like an expert at the end of the game, and levels that had taken me a while initially turned out to be really easy when I went back to them.
After a while, there's seemingly not much that can be added to the game other than asking you to build ever greater and more complex structures out of the cubes you're given. Thankfully, the game stops just short of getting boring, then gives you a lot of new toys to play with (via the DLC) and a bunch of difficult puzzles, then gracefully bows out. It's free, so it feels like a warm "Thank you so much for playing -- play these if you still want stuff to do". The DLC feels pretty tedious (especially the laser levels), but even that's something I might appreciate in a few months if I ever want to play again.
The achievements are exactly how achievements should be -- not too annoying, but requiring you to play a little bit creatively to get. The game took me about 12 hours to beat, but it was so much fun and I'm honestly glad it didn't drag on longer than it should have. Even if the main game doesn't scratch your engineering itch, there's like 20 more hours of extra content.

Well, where to start? I will begin by saying I enjoyed this game very much. RATE: 8.5/10 (easily)
The TL;DR is that Risen is an unforgiving 3rd person RPG. (By unforgiving i mean you will die a lot. Saving is your best friend).
I won't do a pro vs con in a list fasion but I will state a couple things that I did like about the game and a couple things I didn't like.
What I LIKED about Risen is how your character develops. Trainers are required to upgrade skills and you can choose any path/style you desire. Having said that, your choices do get limited by which path you choose to progress the story in. Another aspect I liked is the "unforgivingness" of the game that I previously mentioned. It makes the game feel very "true" or "real", like death is around the corner at any moment. And this goes on throughout the entire game, there is no point at which you can amass gear or items to become a god in the Risen universe. Your character will always be on par with the strongest enemy along the story quests. The story was enjoyable and is a good premise for future plots. The characters you meet are enjoyable and create a desire to quest.
What I DISLIKED about Risen mostly is the "unforgivingness" of the game I previously mentioned. Its like a love/hate relationship. I can admit to cursing at the monitor at certain situations. Thankfully the game has a built in auto-save at points in which they know you are probably going to die. There was only 1 bug that upset me, I was leveling my skill while wearing a ring that gave me +1 in that skill and the trainer stopped training me 1 point too early (so I only had 6/10 towards the skill instead of 7/10 because i changed the ring i was wearing). It was only a minor inconvenience.
Having said all this I RECOMMEND this game as a pick up. Enjoy. :)

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

I've played this game for 44 hours and it costs 10€. Even if you wait for a sale, I think 10 is already a good price. It's worth it if you like games like Skyrim, Fable or Kingdoms of Amalur. Try a demo and see for yourself!
+
; A journey from rags to riches
+
; An action combat system that gets you involved
+
; Various strategies you think of can help you turn the tide
+
; The island is a pretty place to look at
+/-
; Not always the best voice-acting but at least everything's voice-acted
-
; It's a pretty island but eventually you've seen it all.
You wake up on an island after a shipwreck. You have no idea what island you're on, no idea what the creature that sank your ship was or why you keep feeling tremors on this island. With a weapon plundered from a dead sailor, you start walking into the jungle and see what fate has in store for you.
The atmosphere is amazing. Bit by bit, you have to keep walking forward, using whatever you can find and fighting all kinds of creatures to stay alive. The mysteries of the island reveal themselves to you bit by bit until at long last you have a complete picture of what's going on. But not before you've made a name for yourself. A real "from rags to riches" story. (I was kind of fond of the rags).
Combat system works great. You'll probably use a sword and a shield at the start of the game. You can block any attack coming at you as long as you're actually blocking. Once you see your chance to attack, you have to press left-mouse button quickly to chain a combo. Not too quick though! Do it fast but with decent interval between hits. If you do it like that, your hits will hit the enemy quicker and they won't be able to counterattack so easily. (Took me a long time to learn that).
You will also encounter a lot of strong monsters - often so strong that you should turn back - but that doesn't have to stop you from trying. As long as you keep the basics in mind and don't lose focus, you should be able to take even bigger enemies down. Additionally, you can also use your surroundings to your advantage. Use higher ground, bottleneck the enemy, circle the enemy, dodge & attack, distract... Plenty of ways you can fight. It keeps things interesting enough.
There's also dungeon exploration which is quite interesting. Some dungeons are straightforward, others require you to get various kinds of spells to get through. Nautilus spell to get through tiny cracks, levitation to cross chasms, and telekinesis to operate faraway levers and buttons, to name the main ones. Some levers can also be operated by shooting an arrow at them. In any case, there's enough puzzles and traps to keep dungeons entertaining.
Besides fighting, there's also other skills you can learn. Blacksmithing allows you to forge your own swords and repair legendary weapons that you find. Alchemy supplies you with healing potions and elixirs that make you stronger permanently (rare ingredients). You can make scrolls stored with fantastic spells, like conjuring a skeleton to help you or the spell that turns you into a nautilus. There's more than a few skills in this game. All you have to do is find a trainer for them and have them teach you. (Prospecting is kind of a lame skill though)
I'm not sure if there are any bad things I can say about this game. Graphics are not cutting-edge 2016 but it's good enough; They paint you a world that you can call beautiful. Voice-acting is sometimes... not very invested. Can't give a plus for it but it's great that every NPC in the game is voice-acted. I appreciate things like that.
The initial glow of discovering the island fades the more you travel around the island, and the ending seems a little anti-climatic. The journey as a whole is great though, and definitely worth playing through.

For Piranha Bytes, Risen was a clean slate. After Gothic 3 was a total debacle at launch due to their publisher, JoWooD, meddling with the development and basically ripping the game from their hands before it was finished to meet a launch date, PB cut all ties with the series that put them on the map. Signing up with Deep Silver, Risen was constructed, from the ground up, to be an evolution of the formulas and gameplay loops found in Gothic, while also targeting console players with a multi-platform release. Risen succeeds in a lot of what it sets out to do.  However, there are still some missteps, especially in the latter parts of the game.
The story takes place on Faranga, a mediterranean island, where after humanity cast out the ruling gods (a reference to one of the endings of Gothic 3), massive ruins begin to rise out of the ground all over the world and deadly creatures begin to pour out, forcing humanity into conflict once again. To make matters worse, massive storms are wreaking havoc on any kind of settlement or ship out in the oceans, which is where the nameless player character comes in. After stowing away on a boat commanded by a militant theocratic order known as the Inquisition, the player shipwrecks onto the island along with one other survivor and has to figure out what is going on.
The player is given a choice between siding with three different factions in three different massive areas full of side quests and characters, and this is something Risen does really well, almost to the degree of Gothic 2. The settlements all ooze atmosphere, whether it be the bandit camp in the swamps or the Inquisition monastery high up in the peaks of an active volcano, they all have distinct character and feel like real places and much of the early game is spent in these areas.
After picking a faction, the game begins to settle into a rhythm of exploring ruins, doing some light puzzle solving and finding the plot device of the day. While this can get rote after a while, the game is still very much enjoyable and the story is intriguing enough where I was playing just to see what happens next. There are some great characters in Risen too, especially the Inquisitor himself (voiced by Andy Serkis), Don Estaban (voiced by John Rhys-Davies), the crime lord leader who was exiled out of Harbor Town by the Inquisition and Patty (voiced by Lena Heady), a tavern owner who is looking for her lost father.
However, where the game lets itself down, is in the combat. Now, YMMV but I never quite got the hang of how combat works in Risen and would often resort to cheesy tactics in the later game when the difficulty curve begins to rapidly spike up. Even with endgame gear, enemies were still able to stun lock me with ease and decimate me without breaking a sweat. It's possible I didn't build my character right, but it was often frustrating dealing with the combat. However, it didn't make me want to stop playing.
Speaking of character building, the learning points system from Gothic makes a comeback and it's relatively unchanged from how it was used in previous games. When you level up, you get ten learning points and use them to learn skills from trainers (along with a little bit of gold for good measure). A really enjoyable part of this system is that each trainer has different lines for how they teach you something like how to swing a sword, with each having their own take and personality on it, though this ultimately makes no difference in terms of gameplay.
Risen is also quite a looker, with a very strong mediterranean themed art style throughout and well-done lighting. Characters don't look super hot in 2016, but it's still far better then, say, ArcaniA, which came out two years later. The game also runs very well on modest PC's, and more higher end specs can utilize tools like nVidia Inspector to add in anti-aliasing. At 2x SSAA, this is quite a great looking game.
I highly recommend checking this out if you are a fan of the Gothic games or of European CRPG's in general!

I had mixed feelings on the original Blocks that Matter, so when this game came out I was a little skeptical. So I have to say, for anyone that played the first game and found themselves infuriated by the end: this game is wonderful.
Where the original had ultra-long, ultra punishing levels, this game has an undo button. Where the original had slippery, floaty platform controls, this game has precise click-based grid movements. While many puzzles in the first game depended on you not only solving the problem at hand but also pulling off difficult platforming maneuvers, this game has gone the pure-puzzle route. Heck, even the story (which doesn't matter much in either game) is better in this one, for what it's worth. Basically, every complaint I ever had about the original Blocks that Matter has been fixed in this sequel.
I also have to make special mention of the soundtrack: while I really enjoyed the original game's chippy blippy soundrtrack, this game takes it in a completely different ambient direction, and actually really, really pleasant to listen to. For several days after finishing the game I had the soundtrack on during work.
As a final note, I played this game on a Surface Pro 2 (aka a touchscreen computer) and it played very well! There was only one mechanic that was a little awkward on touchscreen, but I was pleasantly surprised at how well it worked out, since I've found that in a lot of games, touchscreen controls do not always work for mouse controls like you'd expect.

Meh... picked it up in the sale and I am pleased I waited. I considered buying it straight away for full price because it does look like a very interesting title.
However, now I've played it a bit I have to say it is a very, very flat game. There is no depth to it to keep it interesting. In fact it is almost not a game. It is a case of finding a formula and balancing things between the margins you set for yourself.
Although the graphics are great, the interface is clunky, in fact it is unwieldy. You never really grow attached to the villagers because there is nothing of interest going on with them beyond assigning them to a job. You can't manage them well enough either. I have houses with 1 pensioner whilst other houses have 6 adults living in them.
The concept is really interesting, but the execution doesn't do it justice. There should be far more depth to the banished folk, I want more back-story, more engagement and far, far more interesting events. Most of the time it is just a case of setting up the foundation of a village and speeding through at 10X speed whilst expanding.
Shame, could be great, isn't. I realise it was made by a tiny studio but to me this game would have worked far better with less focus on the graphics and more on the gameplay.

Well, I'm fresh off completing this game after about 10 hours.  It's honestly hard for me to decided whether to recommend this game or not.  In the end, it comes down to would I recommend it to my past self?  Narrowly, the answer is no.
As far as the horror genre goes, I place
at the top of the list.  If you watch a lot of horror movies, then Amnesia is
and Outlast is the
.  The former plays much more on the mind and allows your imagination to terrorize you, while the latter shows you a bunch of mutilation and gore as well as the hands that will deliver it to you.
The story of Outlast isn't very compelling.  It seems it is just there to act as filling between the gore and the things that will kill you.  I find it far less terrifying when you see what's going to do you in, and Outlast's villians practically introduce themselves as to be like "Hi, I'm Fred and I will be you killer today."  Sure there are some frights, but there's never a real sense of dread and fear that has you really immersed in the environment.
Gameplay wise, I found Outlast very frustrating.  There are a lot of characters, and it is difficult in some circumstances to tell friend from foe.  You can't fight back in Outlast, only run and hide and try to avoid the perils that face you.  Because there's lots of villians to keep away from, Outlast plays a bit like a stealth action game.  However, you are given very little tools to outwit you enemies, and it becomes a very frustrating experience.  Too many situations required a bit of trial and error (or trial and dismemberment) to figure out how to progress, and in the end it makes the experience feel more like a game.
If you are like me and like a good compelling story, deep immersion, and more psychological horror, then Outlast will probably not appeal to you.  However, if you like gore and disturbing monsters constantly chasing after you, then Outlast should be a great game for you to enjoy.  Alternatively, if you are just dying for another horror game, then Outlast is a good enough game to tide you over until
.

Ingredients
1 cat
½ red onion
1 pimiento
1 clove of garlic
2 ½ dl coconut milk
2 ½ dl cream
2 tbsp meat extract
Juice of lime
Ginger
Butter
Instructions
Skin, fillet and chop the cat. Start your coffee maker, grease the heater and place the pieces of your cat onto it. Fry it until they are cooked throughly and tender, it will take about an hour (it depends on what cut of meat you’re using and how fresh it is). Remove the meat and wipe the heater.
Chop all of the remaining ingredients that shall be chopped. Put a dollop of butter into the carafe, let it melt and then put the onion and the garlic in the carafe and fry it for about half an hour. Season with ginger. Add coconut milk, cream and meat extract and let it cook for two hours – it should get really warm. After that add the cat meat and wait a bit longer. Finally add pimiento pieces, lime juice and season generously with freshly ground black pepper and just a little salt. Turn off your coffee maker.
The best way to serve this delicious cat stew is accompanied by a glass of a tasty red wine and freshly baked bread.

I figured Outlast would be the next Amnesia, as in it would be a horror game that understood horror comes from atmosphere and tension rather than just loud spooky monsters. I was partially right, as Outlast uses the same "run don't fight" style as Amnesia, but there's something really missing from that formula that Amnesia had but Outlast doesn't, and I couldn't really place it. Outlast is not scary, sort of depressingly un-scary, in that the big guy following you who requires you to hide shows up so often that he loses his impact after like the third time, and by the end is much more annoying than scary.
Speaking of the end, it comes really quickly, as Steam says i had just under 4 hours after the ending, and that might be inflated as I died an awful lot and looked for all the collectibles.
Outlast also has an odd way of giving objectives, as the hospital is incredibly linear, yet the game does a bad job of telling you where you can and can't go, leading to unnecessary deaths when running from enemies.
The important part of this game is the atmosphere, which, while solid, is also very easily broken as the game lurches between plot development and jump scares. Yeah, there are a few jump scares, but those are just startling, not scary. The game's atmosphere is sort of ruined whenever certain characters show up like the doctor who speaks in an oddly dissonant voice while he murders you, and the two naked inmates who constantly show up to blind the player with a frontal assault while talking about how they're going to eat you, but you only have to run from them in one segment and thats it.
The biggest problem with Outlast is that it has some good stuff, but it downplays all of it in an attempt to create an atmospheric horror experience, but fails so spectacularly at it that there is not much to recommend.

This ranks alongside Spacechem as one of my all time favorite games. Challenging puzzles, engaging story, overall a well-oiled and ingeniously-designed game. Well worth the money for programming/engineering types and anyone who enjoyed Spacechem.
Gameplay
Pretty straightforward. Given parts, build a factory which assembles the parts into a final product. New tools are introduced one at a time, and there is just enough help given to the player to get them going. Obstacles and pitfalls arise naturally forcing the player to think of creative workarounds. I found the final puzzles very challenging, but neither frustrating nor insurmountable. Solving the finale was pretty satisfying!
Story
Unlike Spacechem, whose story was as cold and unforgiving as space, Infinifactory's storyline includes some subtle humor, as well as voice acting and interaction with physical characters. To me, the introduction of humor was a bit awkward at first, especially since it still retained elements of the same grim tone as Spacechem, but it was easy to get used to. Overall, the story branches out in tone rather well, and remains in the background and never distracts.
Other
The achievements and the workshop provide some extra challenges, and the nature of the game makes it very suitable for user-created puzzles. Gotta make my own soon...

Infinifactory is the best puzzle game I've ever played. It takes something truly compelling for me to spend hours, sometimes days at the end, perfecting a single puzzle, and yet I have never felt frustrated.  This is a game that truly earns the description 'engaging.'
Everything that happens in this game is because you made it, and you need to have your brain firing on all cylinders to make it through. But fear not, any new players considering this game: the mechanics are easy to approach and you'll be hooked in no time.  Players who have enjoyed any other game by Zachtronics (like Spacechem or TIS-100) or who like similar games with similar mechanics (Factorio, Big Pharma,  even the city-builder games by Impressions) will absolutely love Infinifactory, but I think anyone willing to giving Infinifactory a chance will love it too.
In this quick review, I'll discuss the gameplay of Infinifactory, it's aesthetics, and try to answer why I've been unable to put this game down.
The gameplay is simple: from a certain point at the start of each stage, a series of inputs regularly pop out a component-usually a single box, but other times a more complex shape.  From there, the goal is to simply combine these inputs to meet at the output area, and repeat this ten times.  The player has a number of tools at their disposal, from simple conveyor belts and welders, to parts that push and destroy.  With these parts, all sorts of advanced operations may be performed- advanced techniques even allow players to build 'circuits' from these simple parts.  A later level may resemble a factory made by a mad scientist, full of pipes and blocks, with piecies whirring and whizzing by, only just avoiding disaster.
Infinifactory has pleasing visuals, notable for its sturdy blocks and the orange and blue color scheme of its factory parts.  The environemnts are colorful, vidid, and distinctly not of this world. The screen shots do a better job describing what it looks like than I can, but as you can see, there are a great number pleasant and varied stages, and for the most part, there feels like a good variety of factory components, too.
There is an interesting story being told, usually through voice logs and a handful of scripted sequences that set the stage for Infinifactory's otherworldly visuals. In many puzzle games, even those that do try to tell a story, the gameplay has no relation to the story. Here, there's a
why you're building things- and you may not exactly be doing it of your own free will. The story's tone is quirky, with a grinning undercurrent of black humor.  There are a few twists and turns along the way that delighted me.  I found that a nicely written story like this helped ground the events and kept me interested.
Puzzles in this game have a wonderful quality where the final output seems simple, yet constructing it from its individual components can be deceptively challenging.  There's a smooth difficulty curve, with tools introduced gradually and new techniques being learned organically as more challenging puzzles are introduced. By the time I'd beaten the game, I found that I could go back to puzzles that took me 90 minutes to solve and beat them in 20 minutes, with a much better score as well.
At the end of each puzzle, the player is ranked according to three criteria: how fast the puzzle was, how many blocks it took to build, and how much space it took up.  I like the way that this scoring encouraged me, because it was rare that I hadn't done well in at least one category.  This system encourages different styles of play-those who (like me) enjoy sprawling, messy solutions that strive to be as fast as possible, or those who favor a more restrained, elegant design.
The game comes with a capable level editor that's integrated into the Steam Workshop. Already, tons of user-made levels are available for play. In my experience, though, few have stacked up against the levels in the campaign.  Most are based around gimmicks or some other novel use of the mechanics.  Sometimes this is successful, but overall I haven't found it as satisfying. That said, I can't claim to have explored the workshop throughly, or to have attempted to create any levels of my own.
The true joy in this game comes from the sense of owning each solution you make. There's no single way to solve each puzzle-there are hundreds.  After completing a particularly challenging puzzle, I've often looked up how others have solved theirs- not once has my solution resembled someone else's.
I never had the feeling, like I often do with puzzle games, that I was fighting with the developer to find the 'right' way to solve the problem.  Instead, Infinifactory simply gives its players a handful of tools and asks, "Why don't you build something interesting?"
I think it's the mark of a great puzzle game that I have enjoyed my failures as much as my successes.  I have looked back at puzzles that took me hours to solve, and even though the final result was a swollen, creaky machine, I can remember all the hurdles and struggles it took for me to create my solution and think, "Yeah, I built that."

Another sublime "programming" game from the mad genius who brought us SpaceChem. This time you've been kidnapped by the alien overlords who have set you to building them factories.
Basically, you get given one or more "inputs" (usually single blocks of different types) and (usually) one "output" that's built from those blocks. You have to build a production line out of conveyer belts, welders, pistons, sensors, etc that can repeatedly turn the ipnuts into the outputs. All this is done in a Minecraft-like world of cubes (and the guy who created this game also created Infiniminer, which was a major inspiration for Minecraft).
Once you've solved the puzzle, you get three little graphs that show you how your solution compares to the solutions of all the other players in terms of how quickly it produces the required output, how many blocks you used, and how much space it took up. Then (if you're like me) comes the fun part: optimize, optimize, optimize, and try to get the best possible score in each of the metrics (most likely with three different solutions). The great thing about the graphs is that because nobody can see anyone else's scores, there's no real incentive for anyone to cheat, and because it doesn't show exact scores, You can aim for the slightly softer target of the top score bracket rather than being tormeted byt that one guy who has an insanely good score...

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Tetrobot and Co. is a puzzle game where you run a robot repair shop. Customers send you their broken Tetrobots and you deploy your Psychobot in order to repair the robot from the inside out. You do this by absorbing and spitting out blocks of matter.
Each Tetrobot has to be repaired in phases (levels). Each level consists of multiple rooms with generally one puzzle. There is a rewind button in case you get stuck. Each level additionally contains three memory blocks. Gathering those unlocks extra levels.
Tetrobot and Co. is a very difficult puzzle experience. Do not be fooled by the endearing artstyle; this game is hard, especially for the completionists amongst us. One of the things I found very difficult was understanding which blocks to use and which ones to save for another puzzle. However, with difficulty comes satisfaction when you finally are able to solve that one last puzzle that stands between Psychobot and the last Memory block.
Furthermore, the controls are simple. You only need the mouse to play. The soundtrack is nice and there are quite a few songs so I had something to listen to whilst planning my next move. These two elements allow me to focus more on the puzzles themselves as that is what this game is about.
Two (perceived) flaws I need to mention. First, there were multiple occasions where my blocks flew straight through solid walls, forcing me to restart the level. So there are some bugs.
Second, the story falls short of being interesting. You come across pictures and letters sent by the owners of broken Tetrobots - and your replies - but it never kept my interest.
To summarize: if you like a rather difficult puzzle game with a nice soundtrack and you care less about story to drive the game, Tetrobot and Co. is something you ought to consider.

Risen is a game that just simply grows on you. It starts out as a simple something and infects you like some kind of benign, beautiful infection.
It's the story.
It's combat is simple, yet effective. It's skillset is just the right balance of simplicity and growth. It's not linear, and yet, it uses the difficulty of the environment to keep you from moving beyond where the story wants you to go. It's open world and yet your skillset and loadout will keep you where the story wants you.
The mobs you encounter don't level up with you, giving you the satisfaction of whipping the siht out of a mob today that you had trouble with a while back. Each time you get smacked you can confidently nurse your wounds and walk away muttering, "I'll be back you bsatrad!" And you will be back... and you'll be back ready to utterly destroy them. Sweet satisfaction. You can ONLY get this kind of revenge in a video game. That said, save often! Get very familiar with the "Quick Save" button.
And the story moves on.
It took me well into the 3rd chapter before I had to search online to understand how to do something.
The acting is great for a video game... and unexexpected for it's age.
I have, at the time of this writing, just 54 hours in the game... and just as I was thinking it's about to wrap up the story, it continues. Fantastic! The quality has caused me to search out a whole series of games I didn't know existed.
As for "cons" I would mention the graphics... but that wouldn't be fair as I'm sure they were revolutionary for the time it was created. And they're actually beautiful with the way it does its blurring affect on things that aren't supposed to be in focus and other scenery. It's simply outstanding. It's the edges and corners that give its age away. Other than the occasional glitches that occur when you get jammed up against a wall and can see the scenery behind it suddenly, I haven't found any bugs.
In short, it's well thought out, a story that is well written, a program thoroughly baked and bug free, combat and experience growth well balanced and satisfaction in just the right places.
If you're into dungeons and RPG and over the shoulder combat, you'll enjoy it.

This is not a bad game, but in my opinion it should have been refined more, especially in gameplay. I got it in a 1 dollar bundle, and for that it's surely worth the value. What I am asking myself is whether it's worth the time. The answer for any player reading this that has not yet played Super Meat Boy, is definitely No. Their time is better spent there.  For those that are (like me) looking for more Super Meat boy, my answer remains No, and the gameplay critics below explain why. For those looking for a strange, challenging platformer, it's a yes.
The game has some hints of originality, a decent music, a hipster story telling that's not too annoying... However, it looks and feels like a prototype. Controls are simple triggers: jump can't be a small or a big jump, but just a jump. There is no dash button,  and sticking on walls feels like you have been glued to them (falling naturally is very slow). That's alright if there's no hurry, but it feels unfair when you have to perform quick tasks. Gameplay-wise, the developers made the decision of not having what the game defines Friction in every level. That means that if you are on a sliding surface, the surface will simply slide under you and you will fall on the spikes beneath it. Again, it's not a bad idea by itself, but it does not feel natural to the player.
One aspect that I appreciated is that levels don't reset when you die, making it impossible to finish by muscle memory only.  It forced me to focus on all obstacles. I also gladly appreciated the posssibility to disable distracting animations from the menu.
However, overall levels ended up annoying me more than they gave me satisfaction for finishing them. I wish there were a  middle thumb, but the honest answer to the question "Do you recommend this game?" is No.

I like this city-building, survival game for numerous reason. Are there changes I would like to see? Yes, but overall, it is a fun, addictive game that is deceptively simplistic.
First thing I always do is build at least two food sources. Those survivors don't stay healthy if you only have a single food source. Usually, I go for gatherer, hunter, and fisher - in order of preference. That seems to make my little people happy. Then there is the extra storage that I build, so I can clear out some resources and get a stockpile to work with.
It is easy to survive. Not so easy to thrive past about 80 people. You have to carefully provide the necessary housing, so you will have plenty of young to replace the deaths as the time comes. You have to think of the future with everything you do (or don't do). There are both rewards and consequences.
There is only one official end to the game, and that is death. It can come from anywhere at anytime. As soon as I get complacent, I am struck with an epidemic, tornado, or crop failure.  Took me a while to figure out my people suffer if I overwork fields. so you have to plan for letting those fields "rest". People tend to stay happier if they are closer to the barn (or food storage).
The little things make a huge difference!
What would I add or change if I could make a recommendation?
I would love to be able to click on a person and move that person to a different location. There seems to be a burp or stagnation in productivity at some points. Those people will choose finishing up a road over building a needed home, even if you prioritize the building of the home. If I could simply pick up a worker and place it on the home to get the ball rolling that would rock.
Another suggestion would be to add a "restart map" option in the menu. Sometimes I get attached to a certain map, and then can't find it easily. Restarting the map would be great.
I definitely recommend this for people that like this type of game. It isn't an intense game, but it will draw you in. My cat likes to watch the people run around, and then she attacks them through the monitor. It is family entertainment. In a world of excessive violence and adrenalin-powered gameplay, it is refreshing to find a game that slows life down and makes me think.

Think of this game as a "My First Fallout". It does a great job of introducing all the basic concepts of the series - the wasteland, vaults, factions, etc. - but is nowhere near as good as the other games in the series. Play this and then play New Vegas and you'll feel the difference. Still a fun game to play, but think of it as a stepping stone towards its superior siblings
PROS
- Art style that really captures a post-apocalyptic future by way of '50s Americana
- Soundtrack is amazing, featuring a mix of haunting orchestral pieces and catchy old-time swing standards
- Does a (mostly) good job of transitioning from isometric turn-based combat system to first-person shooter combat
- Story is more cohesive than the one in New Vegas (IMO) and gives you a good excuse for venturing out into the wasteland
- Moira Brown and Three Dog are the best characters in the series. I will fight you on this
CONS
- All RPG elements have been stripped to the bare minimum to the point where it's more of an action game with some RPG mechanics instead of a true RPG
- Player choice is severely limited - you cannot join different groups, you can't really choose a different ending, and the final mission is little more than a corridor shooting gallery
- Factions are sad parodies of their former selves
- Everything that happens is triggered by your father - you are basically a spectator to his much more interesting story

You play as a man whose parents were murdered during the Holocaust by a madman Nazi doctor, finally seeking revenge on the psychopath who's caused you 20 years of pain and suffering. The game consists of 4 chapters, where you'll discover not only the many victims and their hand-written stories smeered with blood scattered throughout the game, but you will come face-to-face with those that did "survive" the doctor's company, and you will wish very dearly that they hadn't.
Overall, the controls will probably need  some adjustments early on, as the key bindings are far from the conventional WASD, etc setup. Brightness settings will need to be optizimed as well, since the entire game is extremely dark. Object interaction and collision can be awkward at times, especially while driving or moving through piles of rubble.
The horror of the game is a combination of both jump-scares and psychological thrill, especially as the tension rises with the unpredictability of flashes or screeches, as well as the enemies tending to ambush and surprise the hell out of you very often. The World War II-era radio and classical music  consistently set the atmosphere of the game and immerse you within the past.
The enemies themselves are generally very fast and come at you during the least convenient of times, and if they hit you, you had better hope that you have a med-kit, because the bleeding effect and sheer damage can be very crippling, resulting in a need for constant supply of weapons and ammunition, though the latter can be found in surplus very easily.

Team Fortress Classic is a precursor to TF2 a highly popular Hat Simulator made by valve, so let's take a step back and look at the first game in the series.
Team Fortress Classic is similar to all early valve multiplayer games and by that I mean, Counter Strike and Half Life Deathmatch. The gameplay is similar, but there is a different gameplay spin in each game. For example in Counter Strike you use real life weapons, in Half Life you use iconic weaponry from the games and in Team Fortress you have classes.
Classes range from a heavy who uses a mini gun, to a spy and a medic and many many more. All of them have different weaponry and all function differently on the field. Some weapons do more damage, but fire slower or vice versa. It all boils down to skill and it's really fun.
Gameplay wise, I only got the chance to try out Capture the Flag as it's the only server I found which still contains a nice amount of dedicated players which is nice. Other gamemodes have a few players, but the game is pretty much dead and I will get into that a bit later.
Graphically this is a mod of the Half Life game similar to Counter Strike, so a lot of the same assets and models are in this game. It's not aged well, but overall graphics are not the selling point for this game.
Gameplay is really fun, it's challenging and rewarding and it's general a really good gameplay design.
Now the only bad thing is a major problem with the game. It has a dying community and it's dying rapidly. I only found one server that had 13 people in total, while others only had 2 or no players. It's a dying game, but the people that play it, they are very dedicated players so you can get in touch with a community and get  a game going.
Overall Team Fortress Classic is a fun game, is it as good as Team Fortress 2 ? No, not really. While I like the gameplay more in this game, I still think Team Fortress 2 is the better game.
Final Rating:
6/10
Pros:
+ In Depth Gameplay
Cons:
-Dying Community

What a wonderful experience. Smart puzzles, cute story and design, lovely clean sound and visuals.

is a hugely enjoyable and rewarding experience.
Next to solid mechanics, presentation is always important for me, and boy does this game deliver. The design is simple but clever, the different blocks and environments each look distinctive yet work incredibly well within the overall visual theme of the game. The sounds are an absolute joy, I just love the little clinks and chunks the different blocks make when they connect. They are also functional, in that they let let you know what's happening: lasers go
, fire goes
, and the Bot makes the cutest little chirping noises when you do something wrong.
All in all this is a must-buy for puzzle fans.
PS: I'd recommend playing the game on a touch device. It's much more organic and intuitive than the mouse controls.

However, if you have come for an outstanding chocolate chip cookie recipe, you've come to the right place.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
1. Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
2. Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
3. Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
4. Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
5. Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
1. Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.
