'Five Nights at Freddy's is a fantastic strategy survival horror game that is probably the most scary and most intense game I have ever played. This game will make you sweat, shiver and scream.
The idea of this game is you have been hired as a security guard at Freddy's Pizza place. Your goal is to check all the security cameras, the lights, the doors, your environment, EVERYTHING to keep an eye on Freddy and the other the animatronic droids to make sure they don't get to you. Otherwise they will see you as another droid without a Freddy costume and will try to stuff you inside of one (which will kill you). The objective of this game is to survive the night from 12:00AM to 6:00AM (each hour is around 1.5 minutes in length). You must survive all 5 nights to beat the game (The game saves at the start of each night). There is also an extra night and a custom night where you can choose the difficulty of each droid, on a scale of 1-20.
The warning for this game is "This game contains a lot of Flashing Lights, Loud Noises and Jumpscares" If you really cannot cope with loud noises make sure to turn your game volume down to your satisfaction. The jumpscares in this game happen when the droids get to you. They jump right into your vision and perform a very loud robotic-like scream.
This game I'd say has a horror scale of 8/10. I've always been a fan of Indie horror but this game is a masterpiece. It is scary and intense as F*CK!!! There is a free demo for this game online which only unlocks the first night. You can buy the full version for only $4:99 which is a pretty decent price for this kind of game. It's worht the money.
Overall this game is a very unique and fun idea for a horror game. I rate it 9/10, it is that good. If you are a fan of horror or Indie horror then I Highly recommend buying this game. Special thanks to IndieDB and the youtubers: Markiplier and Yamimash for introducing me to this game.

The sequel to Blocks that Matter, a cutesy but challenging puzzle platformer designed around building tetrominos, this is a very different kind of puzzle game. It's still about manipulating blocks, but that's where the similarities end.
Here, you fly around and stick blocks of the same type together to solve puzzles most of the time, and it's not really possible to get yourself killed. There is a rewind button if you get yourself stuck, which is good because that *will* happen.
You'll go through multi-screen levels, making your way to the exit and collecting 3 memory blocks. The memory blocks aren't really optional, you need enough of them to unlock new levels. But you do get to skip a bunch if you don't see the solution to get them immediately.
At first, each screen will be it's own puzzle, but soon enough you'll be backtracking between screens to solve things.
And at first, things start of simple - 2 types of block (glass and sand), no special interactions or physics extept that they only stick to their own type. This also gets more tricky fast, as you'll learn that fire burns wood and turns sand into glass, metal is can be electrified (to trigger electiricity based switches) and gets pulled in by magnets, slimes can be used to make blocks sticky so they don't fall when they hit a wall etc.
There's even a few boss levels, which really aren't too different from regular levels except for the fact that you'll be shooting things into a huge slime in some way.
The game really shines in it's level layout.  Some really tricky puzzles are included, but mostly the maps are designed in a way to trick you into overthinking. And every new mechanic, instead of having a dedicated tutorial, has a screen or two worked into the level that shows you how it works. Late game example of that is the room where ice and cloud blocks are introduced. A simple switch drops down 2 blocks of ice - one passes a laser and gets turned into a cloud. The cloud blocks the exit, and you can't suck it up. But you can launch the ice cube at it, and that will disperse it. And presto, by finding your way out of the room, you just learned a few important bits.
The music & art style also work well - music sets a sense of mystery, and the art is nice and cartoony. It combines well to give a clear presentation.
Only downside is that sometimes the engine glitches, especially when rewinding - so that blocks don't end up where they should. Rewinding further usually helps in that case though.
Overall, if you're a fan of quirky puzzle games, this certainly deserves a look.

I was pleasantly surprised by this game. It takes place in the Shadowrun universe, which is a tabletop game set to the D&D rules. You can play with other people, but you don't have to. There are henchmen that you can select to control for the missions that require more than one person. There is a bit of research needed while playing, because the game doesn't tell you some specifics, but the community is pretty helpful. There is a chat function like you would find in MMO's, but it doesn't require you to play dependant on other people.
Gameplay is very similar to XCom, as in it is a tactical, cover based shooter. There is a wide variety of classes, but you aren't restricted to one skill tree. Tons of character upgrades.
I would recommend this game to anyone looking for a Classic, Click to move, Steampunk, RPG, that doesn't require a lot of thought.

Had a thriving town of 19 people when in year 14 a tornado hit and killed all but four adults.  One of the survivors was the teacher of the school which had been annihilated along with its single student.  Fortunately she was gathering rocks in the woods while he waited in confusion for his lesson on woodcutting or whatever to begin at the time 90 mph winds buried him permanently under his desk.
Also destroyed were the fishing wharf, trader's dock, town hall, hospital, all but one house, tailor, and the storage barn with everything inside it.  One sheep survived.
Although there was enough room in the remaining house, the couple living in the house (including that teacher with questionable professional ethics) decided that if God hadn't wanted the homeless couple to be homeless then He wouldn't have knocked their house over.  So in obedience to divine providence, they kept their doors firmly locked to their neighbors.  Since the storage barn was gone, that also meant that they kept that slovenly forester and hunter away from the only stored food in town.  They promptly starved.
The two survivors decided that the wife would gather food while the husband would try to fix the barn, since taking food directly from the woods to the house evidently violates some other divine law about sanctifying your food with a barn or wagon before eating it.  Very complicated.  Anyway, there wasn't enough stone to fix the barn meaning that the fellow must first tear down the ruins of their ill-fated neighbors' homes to get the necessary barn supplies.  Naturally, his tool broke.  Ripping and tearing at the bloody stump of the herbalist's house, he freed almost enough stone to fix the barn.  It would've been enough if the final act of the starved woman that spring hadn't been to deliver those stones to the incomplete site of a coal mine.  Her preemptive revenge sealed the two survivors' fate.
The man went to the blacksmith's shop, untouched by the raging gropery of nature's wrath, and drew from the town's plentiful iron and wood supplies.  With his bare hands, the man shaped white-hot iron into useful tools.  But when unassigned from the blacksmith's shop he did not retrieve one of the new tools.  Duty-bound by forces he could not comprehend, the man refused to pick up a tool until five were sitting in front of the smithy.  He instead walked across town to pick up a piece of iron and place it in a distant stockpile.  Then he and his wife went to the quarry and just sorta idled for a while.  She went back into the woods to pick more roots and berries, leaving baskets at neat intervals in her work area.
Meanwhile, food ran out in the house.  Realizing that they simply could not eat anything that hadn't traveled through a barn, husband and wife made a final valient effort to disassemble the former town hall to build their sacred shrine to municipal storage.  The man continued to rip at the dusty husk with his bare hands, losing his final fingernail on a loose nail.  His wife starved to death right across from him, but he continued his task until he as well dropped dead in the snow.
There was a box of fish beside their house.
The remaining sheep confusedly bleated, wondering when he would be fed.

It's straightforward.  The mechanics are simple.  The purpose is clear.  There's no confusion as to what you are expected to do and what tools you have to do it.
It's diabolical.  The puzzles are sometimes bananas, requiring some pretty twisted logic and lateral thinking.  While you strive for a solution, there's a constant nagging feeling that sometimes your solution is just
and you need to do it better.
It's oddly darkly humorous.  There's a strange undercurrent of defiance against your alien overlords, from listening to the audio diaries of the project managers who came before you, from resenting the food pellets that drop into your cell when you complete sections of the game.
It's also gorgeous - not so much in graphics, which are perfectly adequate, but in the efficiency of the presentation.  No main menu.  No weird visual effects cluttering up the screen. No unnecessarily ostentatious setpieces.  No splash screen! On load, the game drops you right into where you left, so you can literally load the game and get building.  There's a gorgeousness to seeing your machine, your factory do its work, and the satisfaction that comes with it makes the effort all the more worth it.
It's one of the most interesting puzzle games I've ever played, and I'm enjoying it hugely despite not being great at coming up with particularly creative solutions.
You might find comfort in this game if you're an artist who is struggling or having a fight with your muse which happens be an extension of yourself.

This is an excellent puzzle game that provides a very accessible visual analogy to writing a computer program (something I do for a living). The premise is that you are a human who has been kidnapped by a malevolent alien race. In each scenario you face, you are compelled by your new masters to design a factory process by piecing together machinery components about the size of minecraft blocks. You are given input blocks that spit out of magic holes at a pre-determined frequency. You are given a goal of what the end product of those input blocks should look like after rolling through your little factory.
Often there are many different ways to skin the cat presented to you, some being more efficient then others. It's really neat to skim the forums and see all of the different ideas that people come up with to accomplish the same goal.
The game doesn't distract you with alot of filler. It's presentation is very straight forward and simple. The solutions you come up with probably won't be, which is alot of the fun.
This is a solid, fun game that makes you think and create. It's also not all that expensive. Definately recommend it.

This game absolutely nails the importance of good gameplay and atmosphere.
Truth be told, the set up makes little sense. Anyone who knows much about how 'power' actually works will know that the power-usage setup makes no logical sense. In fact, there's no logical sense for you to be there.
Instead, this game focuses on what it SHOULD focus on, great gameplay. Just a lowly security guard with a job to do, only to be haunted by animatronics behaving as terrifying as you'd imagine them to be. Each time you're too late, or even just unlucky, you're treated with an oh-so lovely jump scare death. The game knows how to really use jump scares as an advantage, not just a cheap gimic or scare, and the jump scares constantly work so well because they're reserved for your own demise. Most of your time in the game will build up an atmosphere so thick and tense and even stressful, that you can't help but feel that moment of terror whenever you die.
Course, when you don't die, you're just treated to a LOT of tense creepyness, constantly wondering if they're gonna jump out yet... or dreading your power running out as 3% is left and your door lights have been jammed. :)
All in all, it's a very creepy, atmospheric game with a simple, easy-to-grasp gameplay that actually manages to be enjoyable and stressful at the same time. For the price that it's asking, you seriously cannot ask for anything better, and my personal hope is that this game will allow for this type of gameplay to become more famous, thus allowing other future fantastic games to come about.

In regards to the Game itself:
I still think quarrys and mines could use improvements, especially is regards to thier resource rates, and the negatives (the main issue with quarries is that there are alot of negatives, and few possitives e.g. high accident rate, high cost, permanent land occupation, slow resource rate, requirement to go on FLAT LAND).  real quarries are generally not built on flat land, but usually into an escarpment or a mountain. flat land is extremely important in this game, because most buildings will not be placeable on any kind of grade.(should be able to bring land to grade as labour activity like clearing resources, but it should take a while unless you have alot of steel tools).
The Death Spirals, and interesting as it is to watch an entire town die, is very frustrating if your trying to stop for a few reasons. but ONE SMALL change would certainly help.
allow the condeming of houses. one button - CLICK, and nobody can occupy it. now I can control birth rates (somewhat) and somewhat force people to live where I want (near thier work).
Pathing button doesn't do anything more then show paths, would be nice to be able to change. also known as switching workers manually.
as a result of these balance issues, I feel that each game is very similar. I'm curious how mods will help, maybe adding new "Tiers" of buildings (one I did check out offered a Water Wheel Powered Lumber Mill, which is a great idea. because with higher populations you need 10+ woodcutters)

Before playing this game my only other Shadowrun experience was the exceptional Shadowrun: Dragonfall.  I realize that game was made by a different developer but both games take place in the same universe and both have tactical combat systems.  Personally I much prefer Harebrained Scheme's approach a lot better.  The gameplay was a little bit deeper and more robust.  I also felt the story was quite a bit more clever and meaningful.
That being said Boston Lockdown does have a couple fun characters and a decent story-line.  However, most of you time will be spent in fights, making this game better suited for those who like the battles more than anything else.  Its a challenging and rewarding combat system but there is only a handful of stages that get repeated over and over again.  You'll see this a lot in all the haphazard side-quests that only feature the most basic plots-lines.  All the side-quests really just feel like filler but are very compelling to play for the karma (experience points) you receive, making them very hard to pass up.  I feel that if this game had been a refined and polished 10 hours instead of the 25 hour grind-fest it turned out to be it could have had a lot more potential.
Its hard to know to recommended this title or not.  I would definitely recommend playing the Harebrained Schemes series first and only trying out this game only if you really badly want more a lot more content.  I also realize that this game can be played multiplayer, which is really neat.  I didn't try it myself but I think that is definitely one of the major selling points.  Honestly, with so many similar and better games out there I have to think you'll find better use of your time elsewhere.

This game is not anything like a Shadowrun game should be, especially when compared to another readily available offering.  It reminds me of the differences between the Sega game and the SNES game a couple of decades ago: both are based on the same IP, but that's where the resemblance ends.  Each had something the other lacked, but one was definitely superior to the other.  The same could be said for Chronicles (when compared to SR Returns).
This game's major offering was supposed to be the multiplayer element, however, due to the incredibly limited multiplayer interaction and severely anemic active playerbase, it no longer can even claim that as a selling point.  Failing that, little remains to recommend it. Fans of the tabletop game won't even recognize this game, beyond a few cosmetic elements. Game play is stilted and offers little reason to play one class over another.  The story what there is of it) is forced and mundane, and offers no alternative solutions beyond the mission objectives.
While no Shadowrun game has yet to live up to the full potential of the tabletop RPG, this one falls furthest from the mark.

Heroes VI is a difficult game to review. Does it stack up to previous HOMM games? Definitely not, this is a simplified version of what we have come to love. There are less resources and much less micro management in terms of obtaining the correct resources and even spells. If you still fire up HOMM 3 every now and then this wont even seem like the same game.
And that is exactly how you have to treat it, as a different game and then you can see some of its merits. There is fun to be had in this game. The creatures are well thought out and the battles are satisfying. This is without a doubt the worst HOMM game but if it is on sale it is worth it if you are looking for a less intense HOMM session that generally will be a much shorter game.
I also have to mention the performance of the game, it is very very poorly optimised and will struggle to produce decent framerates even on a high end computer. When it was launched, it was loaded with game breaking bugs, but for the most part these have been fixed.
HOMM VI is a game I do recommend but with a very large asterisk next to it.

Before I start this review I'd like to mention 3 things:
1) If you do what I do and look at the negative comments first, don't.
2) I wish I had bought this game from the developers, I got it from humble bundle.
3) This game is extremely short. If you want a game that you can spend hours in it's probably not for you, but I'd say give it a try anyway.
I saw the trailer for refunct, didn't read about it, and thought it would be longer. A sort of open world game that was relaxing and somewhat mindless. The only thing that I got right was that it's relaxing. The game throws you in immediately and you have to figure things out on your own, in a way very reminiscent of older games. I mean back during the 16-bit wars. They didn't tell you how to play, they just expected you to figure it out on your own. Nothing holds your hand in this and you might get lost a bit despite how small the world is.
The music is beautiful, the gameplay is simple, and the ending is rather cute. I put the gameplay at around 20-minutes, if you're trying to run through as fast as possible. However don't rush it, take your time. The controls are fluid which is saying something because I played on a keyboard. In my experience games that look like they are meant to be played with a controller lack the fluidity on keyboards. They don't work as well. This game doesn't have that issue.
Also to address some of the negative reviews it is a game. These things like "It's a nice tech demo, not much else" and "if you bought this game you got swindled".. these are the reviews of people that have gotten used to the mainstream view on things. The view that a game has to be long; that you have to be able to pour hours into it to have fun; that things have to be overly challenging; that games are built for the player.
I saw a comment that called this pretentious crap. It's not. At least it's not in my opinion. To me it feels like this game was built for the developer. What I mean by that is the developer probably wanted a game that was simple, that was relaxing, and if others enjoyed it? awesome, but probably wasn't the main goal. A seemingly mindless world that at the end had a purpose.
I won't tell you to buy it. That's your choice to make, but give it some consideration. It's cheap enough and definitely worth it.

It is very hard to review these kinds of games because there is, admittedly, very little to measure them on. Is it a walking simulator? Quite possibly. Is it for everyone? Absolutely not. That's the wonderful thing about The Beginner's Guide. It's different, and it is definitely a game that you would see more as an experience than something you really participate in.
In the terms of the narration it showcases some really neat things in it's presentation, some of which can really open your mind to new ideas. The narration is easy to follow and it's something you will want to listen to. It's engaging and deep. For a product that openly advertises itself as not including standard game mechanics or goals, it is just that. That is the only expectation you should go in with.
It's absolutely a game I will need to ponder for a little while, and that's a good thing, as a creative person, I find value in what this game explores. Not everyone will, and that's okay.
Similar to everyone else's reviews, I don't want to spoil anything. However, in likeness to other people's reviews, I will say that if you are a game developer, or even a creative person, a musician, an artist, a filmmaker, or anyone who makes content for people to consume in any way, this will likely appeal more to you. This isn't something I would be putting onto a 'game of the year' list, it's simply an experience worth experiencing. Go into it with an open mind. You won't regret it.

Valley is an amazing, beautiful gaming experience. This is just one of the best games that I have found here on Steam, and I happened upon it just because someone mentioned it was on sale, on Gamng on Linux. Graphically it is splendid. The level design is perfect: it is the outdoors exploration sim that I have been craving. The gameplay is awesome - so far it is about using your powers to improve life around you (imagine!) You are managing your environment to enrich and not to destroy, but not in a dull preachy way. It is just part of the excellent gameplay that makes you feel part of the environment as you are also moving through it.
Give you an example of the gameplay: you are in the woods, see that the trail leads down to a river, you run full speed down the path, the motion blurring happens and there is a sound of air rushing past you, you leap into the air - over the river - and down into some photorealistic trees that are swaying in the wind, with a crunch that can almost make you feel the impact, and a plume of dust rises around you.
That is one of the many just-so-happens moments that this game gives you, just moving from place to place. I am not even going to try explaining the really special things that Valley delivers. And it gives a bunch of cool ideas.
It is challenging and compelling. I keep looking forward to coming back for the worldbuilding, the story, the level design, and everything else. And I bought this at such a huge discount that I feel like I robbed the developers. This is one of the very few games that I have picked up on Steam that I would have really been completely satisfied to pay the full price. I just cannot say enough about how thrilled I am at getting a chance to play Valley.

RPG make is an interesting program...asset wise comes pre-packed with a full smorgasbord of characters, items, tiles, audio, and a pre-balanced battle system. While you'll still ultimately be limited by what assets you have (you should see my really ugly improvised boats), they go a very long way, especially with the character creator that creates unique sprites giving you a wide cast.  DLC asset packs can bolster it further, just note integrating them into the game takes a little messing around with folders and isn’t automatic. Haven’t looked up fan made/modder’s asset packs, but I bet those a great as well. (edit: they are, especially easy now with Workshop)
Scripting events and designing scenarios is very straight forward and ridiculously easy, you’ll be easily self taught if you have enough technical knowhow to write as much as a batch script. Occasionally it underwhelms with options, for example, I was unable to have party members move independently of the leader outside a cut scene. However, there's a good deal of mods out there that fixed this for me and more, and should definitely be looked at for more complex projects. I was still able to do plenty of neat things without mods, like having a desaturated flashback with a different playable character and storm effects.
Overall, if you ever had the passing interest in making a video game with zero skill, this is probably your best bet. You don’t need to be a coder, artist, or writer to get really far into something pretty decent, and at 18 bucks on sale its worth every penny.
As a side note, this gave me a lot more respect for game production, 55 hours in and I can’t even get through making a introduction...

Steam Risen.exe is not compatible with 4GB patch as it trips Steams Large Address Aware flag. If you plan to mod and want to use more than 1.2GB of RAM on this game then do not buy the Steam version. If you still want to use the Steam version as it is on Sale, be aware you will not be using texture mods with high settings and ini increased draw distances without crashing due to lack of RAM due to how the game is coded regardless if you have a 64 bit Windows.
Steam's Risen is already patched to 1.10, instead of fan patch get Radical Rebalancing Mod which has a modified version of the 1.3 fan patch already in it. Then get Risen - ModStarter 1.3.4.0 (Online DB version), this modding tool has all of the patches other than Radical Rebalancing. Avoid adding any general rebalancing mods except the A.R.B.M. mods that is designed to work with Radical Rebalance, as the rest will cause the game to crash due to conflict. Add in only 1 of the 2 music mods. If you using Steam you probably want to use Vurts DarkRisen texture Pack or possibly (not sure on the texture size) Autumn in Risen and not the high resolution option and this means you do not need the Grass Mod. Pick any other mods you want that will not cause conflict and have fun.

Team Fortress Classic is the predecessor of the Free to Play game we all know and love, Team Fortress 2. It is a team-based FPS very much like TF2. It was originally a mod based on the 1996 game Quake and was eventually adopted by Valve to be it's own game in 1999. Hell, this game is as old as I am. Runnin on the Source engine, this game is one of, if not, the best game Valve has ever made. It's gameplay of having classes is what makes it stand out from the rest of the FPS games we all see nowadays. It has changed the gaming world and still is to this day with TF2. There are games out there like Battleborn and Overwatch that take on the class-based approach to FPS's, but none of them can compare to Team Fortress. If you're a die-hard Valve fan such as myself, then you NEED to buy yourself a copy of this staple in FPS gaming history!

Team Fortress Classic is much like Team Fortress 2 , and it still has hundreds of servers running so you won't find it difficult to find yourself servers to play.

This is an absolutely fantastic puzzle game. For those whom played blocks that matter and didn't like the platforming aspect, don't worry, this doesn't have any platforming to speak of. The only related things in the game are the characters and the use of blocks.
The game actually controls through point and click mechanics, moving your character from place to place through just clicking there. The games main focus is using a combination of different blocks which interact with eachother in different ways, in orde to solve a puzzle. Placing blocks involves you shooting them out instead of using the tetronimo mechanic from the last one. Each block has specific functions hinted to ingame once you find them. The game constantly throws new block types at you, as well as special new funtions, mixing things up. They continued to throw new mechanics all the way to the end of the game, and all of them felt well implemented.
You're main objectives in a level consist of two things; getting to the end, and collecting the memory blocks. You can beat a level without getting all chips, but in order to progress to certain stages, you'll need to obtain the memory blocks. You'll also need to 100% a section to unlock the bonus stage for keys to the small boss puzzle stages (using the term "boss" lightly, as it is really a series of puzzles).
The game features no way to die, and if you do mess up a puzzle, there is always an undo button to push things back to where you need them in an instant. The game never felt tedious or boring; always throwing new ideas and puzzles types your way. The puzzles, while challenging, never felt too easy, or too hard. The game also never feels the need to hold your hand at any given point.
The only flaw that I can think of is that there is a bonus challenge later in the game which requires knowledge of the konami code, but it's not required, and is overall a terribly minor flaw on an otherwise great puzzle game.
To me it was worth every single cent. If you are even remotely into puzzle games, I highly reccomend it.

I think that this is a great puzzle game until you're about 60% of the way through when they introduce more timing elements into the solutions.  The timing detracts from the game in my opinion, up until then if you understood how to solve something you could solve it in one or two tries.  Once the timing got involved however the 'undo' button was used a lot.  It's very frustrating understanding how to solve a puzzle and having trouble executing that solution.
Another thing to keep in mind which may have an effect of your enjoyment of this game is that if you intend on getting all of the brick pieces (which are the bonus objectives) you may end up undoing a lot of your work in any given level.  The reason behind why you would undo your previous solution is that it may not have been ideal, meaning that you could have saved a block or two which would allow you to get a brick piece.  I'm not sure how I personally feel about it since this is something that has provided me with enjoyment and frustration at different times.  One of my level designer friends really liked this aspect of the game though.
That being said, I think that the basic mechanics of how the blocks work in relation to each other is very intriguing and leads to a lot of interesting puzzles.  The art is sleek, the music is charming; it feels cohesive.
.  The first half is definitely worth your time and depending on your preferences you might like the second half too.

So I got this game as a gift from a friend, so we could hang out and listen to funny people tell funny jokes. Thought it would be more like being at a comedy show than anything but wow was I wrong.
Where to start? The rooms are hosted by other players, (nothing wrong with this in particular) the problem stems from people who want to join rooms and get on stage just to yell something really racist, or some kind of "joke" with humor more befitting of a 12-year old who just learned slang for male or female genitalia. There is a, what's supposed to be, cleaner room where people would host rooms with cleaner jokes, but it doesn't stop people from doing the exact same thing in those rooms.
Then there's the audience. 90% of the time no one can get through a whole joke without being voted or kicked off the stage. People are loud, crude, rude, and for some reason enjoy blasting music through their mic while everyone else is trying to listen to the people on stage. The only good thing about this is there's a way to mute the audience, but then you miss out on the very few people that actually have funny and witty remarks regarding the people on stage. Yes, you can absolutely mute people in the audience, but it really is a pain to get into a new room and have to mute half of the poeple in there just to hear someone on stage.
There are a few positives to this game. You will occasionally run into a few people who are genuinely funny, but for the most part you'll just hear vulgar language yelled through the mic over and over again until the person finally gives up and moves to another room. There is a pretty cool avatar-customization at the home screen in which you can customize your looks and the pitch of your avatar's voice. I spent about an hour on this game so far, and I do hope to spend more in the future, but all-in-all, in its current state I cannot recommend this game.
PROS:
-Occasionally very funny people
-Great to waste time with, especially with a friend
-Player-hosted rooms where you can manage the audience
-Player customization
CONS:
-Loud, rude, crude audience. You'll be spending more time muting people in the audience than you'll be spending enjoying the "show"
-Most people get on stage to yell racial slurs
-The "clean" rooms are just a bit tamer than the "mature" rooms, although just as unfunny and crude

Normally I don't ever write reviews but I thought this game deserved one as a lot of misinformation is spread about it. Sure it has its faults but it is no way as bad as some of the people in the reviews make it out to be. Tbh just from looking at the reviews I wasn't even going to download this game because all I saw was the term P2W thrown around and we all know how games like that are. So after much talking to my friends who play this game I decided to dive in and see for myself what this game had to offer. Today I would like to discuss the Pros and Cons of this game from a pure PVP prospective.
Pros
1. New Players.
-They start new people in lobby's of people lvl 1-12  and you can't play ranked or with people above till you reach lvl 13. Now reaching lvl 13 isn't hard at all but it does give people time to learn the game and how to play. This helps new people vs. new people and get to learn the game with each other. As well experienced players don't have to have their game ruined with people still trying to figure out how to do basic things. I honestly wish most companies would make it mandatory to do this like Warface does.
2. The guns in this game are easy to get
- I find the guns you can get from loot just the same as you can get with the money you earn in the game.Right now I use the S60B3 sniper and MS Radek Assault riffle and I have no problem killing people with or without loot guns. Honestly the only thing good about loot guns normally are their skins. I don't find myself getting out gunned at all. In this case I don't see it as P2W at all. Now for this first 20 hours I didn't spend a dime but after I wanted to see if these loot guns are better and spent some money on this game. I got one and honestly I do just the same as I do with MS radek if not worse some matches.
3. The Community isn't bad at all
- Coming from CSGO, PUBG, and a MOBA *Heroes of the Storm* this game is by far less toxic then what I experience over there. In my games so far I only ran into one toxic person and most people just ignored him instead of fuelling the fire like in most games.
4. Game Mechanics
- Honestly the running around , sliding, vaulting over walls, and having people assist you up in higher places is really smooth and nice in this game. To be able to move around the terrain is always fun and nice a refresher from how games are today.
5. The Map design
-Honestly the maps in this game are far better then most games and make for some fast gameplay. They are very well decided and pretty balanced for both teams.
Cons
1. The severs
- Honestly the severs in this game are probably worse then PUBG and CSGO combined. Who knows what my ping is during the match as well as others because all you see is little service bars like on a cell phone.I mean sure I can view it in the launcher but it doesn't help once i hit the game. As well most of the players I played with and against are either 3 bars or that famous red bar. Its really annoying playing on severs like this in a FPS game. Also I don't like how the players base is split into two different channels. I feel like this just reduces the time for lobbies and a really unnecessary thing.
2. The Consumables
- Now what they did to consumables is just dumb. You have to spend in game money you earn or real money to have a chance to get a consumable like blue smoke or an anti personal mine. Yes that is right you can not straight up just use in game money to get it right away you only a chance to get it in a box. O wait you can get it right away though if you are willing to use really money to extend your uses of them. Now if you play the game enough there is no doubt you can get enough of these boxes to keep your consumables more then stocked but the fact that you can't just buy them with in game money is the strangest thing,
3. HitReg
- When it comes to things like sliding the hit registration in this game is really buggy. Now I don't know if this is do from the sever or from the game itself. When you slide in this game it become a crazy broken way to just get free kills most of the time. Just go around sliding with a shotgun and you will see what I mean.
4. Communication
-  I don't know if im blind or what but is there no voice chat in this game. That is crazy considering it is a FPS in today's world. They really need to add this to the game or make it easier to see if its even there.
5. Repairing Guns and Gun Contract
- Just let us buy the gun one and done instead of this renting things with some of the guns. Also the idea of spending in game money to repair your guns is just a task that shouldn't be added to a FPS game.
Overall I have had a pretty fun time on this game. Sure it has its downside but I don't see how people can say its P2W at all. If you want you don't have to spend a dime and you will do just as well as people who spend money. A lot of things can be unlocked just by playing the game. Its a free game and its fun I would recommend.
TLDR - Game has some problems but overall is fun. Its free and not really P2W.

A wonderful experience, this game lets you be a shadowrunner with your friends and explore the streets of Boston during a rather frightening nanomachines outbreak. Solid x-com like tactics mixed with a variety of abilities and strategies make it a fun must-play for any tactics fans.
The game isn't perfect though. Though the addition of a rotatable camera is nice, there are still some targeting issues in regards to AoE and playing with very experienced players can make it difficult for newer players to get the feel of the game. Especially since it allows players of any skill level to party up. It's less of an issue since the game is co-op but it does remove the challenge.
On the other side of the coin, while the main game is very much completable with henchmen, the end game content is impossible to do without other high level players. And its not always possible to find someone who wants to play those things with you. Much less three others.
I also have a few nitpicks in regards to what damage types can and cannot affect as well as the degree of simplifying the karma spending system got. Being able to eventually max everything out just makes things a bit less fun overall since it removes a lot of core strategy. But there's still a lot of stragegy in what you bring and how you interact with your teammates. So not a complete loss. Still, it would have been nice to be able to to customize things more metculously like in the single player games. Especially in regards to magic so people can run builds that are not just "nuke everything."
These balance issues and nitpicks aside I can still reccomend this game. It's a blast to actually do stuff with friends and when you're on the harder missions and manage to complete them through careful strategy and teamwork (provided your team communicates) is extremely rewarding. Certainly not the best of the series, but absolutely worth it for a group of friends who want a cyberpunk strategy fix.

This game has it's good points and it's bad, but I am leaving it a recommended thumbs up because overall it is fun.  I only recommend picking this game up at below $10.  And really you should have a friend or two to play with, or it's not as fun solo.  This is a very watered-down version of Shadowrun, and if you like the tabletop or other versions of the game, you will find that there are a lot of limitations and missing options for a true shadowrun universe.
PROS:
*  Overall Fun Gameplay
*  Can be challenging at times (Mainly Early on - Later can be super easy)
*  Decent Storylines
*  Most interactions with NPCs are Voice Acted
*  Decent Graphics
*  Rotating Camera Angle Option
*  Highly customizable character (Clothes anyway) if you are in to that sort of thing.
CONS:
*  Lack of true shadowrun rules/universe.
For example if you want to have multiple summoned creatures/drones, your entire group has  a max number.  So if you get in a group with a rigger and shaman they will have to share the summon pool, which is quite dumb.
*  There are no docwagons, if someone gets incapacitated you have 5 rounds to finish the mission.
*  There is no way to trade items between other players.
*  Camera will Jump away from the action leaving you wondering how much damage was done and to whom.  (If you turn off the Combat Action Camera- which has it's own issues.)  So Aggravating.
*  Limited or No Options for Graphics / Gameplay / Keyboard Configuration.
*  Bugs - (Bug where you use action points, but they still show up.  Bug where there is an inaccessible open doorway.  Moving/Action simultaneous with other players in group can result in odd or unwanted behaviors - Such as clicking on weapon attack and then someone else moves, it resets your attack you just choose.  Drones can be feared.  Sometimes marked targets will lose mark if hit.  Bug where the character you are speaking with says one thing, but text says another.  Bug at end of game where if your resolution is 1600 x 900, you can't skip past credits.  The Collector has a blurry face and he cares what you think)  So many inconvenient and annoying bugs.
*  AI isn't very smart.
*  Watered Down Shadowrun Ruleset.
*  No Manual.
*  No Matrix.
It's a fun game, but could have been so much better.  It's hard to believe that this late after release it has a multitude of odd bugs that can really be frustrating at times.  But even with all it's faults, it still can be an enjoyable game to play.  My Girlfriend and I play every few nights and as this is her first foray into the Shadowrun Universe, it's rather simple for beginners to pick up.

After 10 months of playing, I figured I should review the game. I know enough at this point to make an informed opinion, right?
The first thing you should know is that there is no story, nor is there an "end game". I see so many people complaining about that in their reviews. This game follows the lives of your little group of settlers and all of their offspring. They are born, they get married, they breed, they die. Some of them go to school, some of them don't, some farm, some hunt-- ALL of them will, at some point, do something to infuriate you. But how can there be an "end game" in a city builder? It goes completely against the point of building, if you have to stop.
This game is flawed, yes. There are bugs. People tend to freeze up when their houses catch fire, which is unfortunate. Playing on easy is usually more difficult than playing on hard. Traders only travel by water (slowly), but nomads only travel by land, and in groups that get larger and larger until you have to start turning them away. My favorite, though, is when people starve even though you have an enormous surplus of food. I've encountered this one a lot. All Messica has to do is go to the storage barn to get food, but noooooooooooo, she goes walking in the forest instead.
Then dead.
There are a lot of positives as well. Your AI is unpredictable, so even if you do the same thing over and over again, they won't. They graphics and sounds are beautiful. And it's true to life. Your mines and quarries will eventually dry out, deforestation causes not only a lack of trees, but a lack of food in that area, too. The maps themselves make you want to see just how big you can push your village, but there's such a delicate balance between growth and resources. It's incredibly hard to find it. I'm still learning how to do things better, even after the amount of time I've put in.
Tl;dr- Sure, the game still has bugs, but it was made and is being maintained by one guy. AI is wonky, game can get repetitive, but, as far as city-builders go, Banished is one of the best ever made.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding cheese cake recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1 cup digestive plain sweet biscuit crumbs
3 tablespoons sugar
3 tablespoons melted butter
40 ounces softened cream cheese
1 cup sugar
3 tablespoons flour
1 tablespoon vanilla
1 cup sour cream
4 eggs
Directions:
For The base:.
If you're using a dark pan, preheat the oven to 350. If you are using a shiny pan, 375.
Combine the crumbs, melted butter and 3 tbsp sugar well and pat onto the bottom of a 9 inch springform pan. I also like to very very lightly butter the sides of the pan so that the cheesecake will not stick later on.
Bake for 10 mins in your preheated oven and remove. Let it cool while you prepare your batter.
For the batter:.
Make sure everything is at room temperature.
Combine sugar, cheese, flour and vanilla in a big bowl and mix on medium speed till well combined. Don't forget to scrape the bowl as you're doing this.
Mix in the sour cream till its incorporated well. Then, add the eggs one by one, mixing well after each addition.
Pour the batter into the springform and let it bake for 1 hour and 10 minutes After the baking time, turn off the oven and leave the door ajar. Let the cake cool in there for about 1 1/2 hours.
Remove the cake and let it cool thoroughly. Refrigerate overnight.
Release the sides of the springform.
Eat.

Alright, ladies and gentlemen - I have just reemerged back into the real world, after almost 100 days (99 days 18 hours) survival in one playthrough. With that up my sleeve, I'll be bold enough to say that I know a thing or two about this game and ready to try and write an adequate review. So gather round, grab a cup of hot chockolate and have a listen to what uncle Chern's got to tell ya :)
I'll split my review into three sections - pros, cons and things that are considered negative by some reviewers, but not necessarily are.
Let us start with the cons, because this list is the shortest... and because I am grumpy old b*****d who likes to criticize. So...
CONS:
MAP - Map in the current version of the game is not very large. There are only a few points to explore and salvage from. So after you have visited them all (which can... and probably should... be done in the first few days of your survival), the game becomes a bit repetitive. Go find meat - go collect some wood - cook - eat/drink - sleep - repeat from step one. Saying that - it does add to realism. Real survival in the wilderness is far from glorious and comes down to just that - get food, cook, keep sated, hydrated and warm. But still it would be nice to have more areas to poke your nose around :)
LOOT (sometimes) - Loot in the game is mostly random... which is a good thing and adds to realism and replayability value, but at some playthroughs it can get bloody stupid. Sometimes you may have enough ammo to get out of Canadian wilds, venture to Afghanistan and assist several ISAF operations, have three knives, 5 packs of MRE rations, ton of medical supplies and good gear. Sometimes it may be evenly and fairly spread-out - so you find a good bit of everything in moderate ammount... And sometimes it gets silly. On my previous to last playthrough i found 5 can openers, no MREs, no repair tools, one almost broken knife and ton of degraded clothing. I still managed 41 days and died of stupidity (went to bed while freezing, and hoped I'll warm up... I didn't), but be warned - never know what you might get and life isn't always fair :)
LONG DARK - No matter what you do, in the end your character is goind to punch that snuff button and check out. That can be quite depressing, that after toughing it out for 2-3 months, heroically navigating through blinding blizzards, savagely fighting wolves for half frozen (and half eaten) deer carcasses, you still going to die. I know - it wouldn't be "The Long Dark" game if you didn't fade into the long dark in the end and it makes this game highly competitive among the players, but it would be nice if there was an option for some sort of happy ending to the game. Maybe they'll do it for story mode later on.
FLUFFY - I am not going to spoil it for you. You'll get to know him as you play the game. Be afraid... be very afraid... and never let your guard down. Cause the very moment you think you're safe and relax, the cruel reality will bite you in the ***... literally.
Other than that - there are no bad things about this game. I wouldn't even use a word "bad" to describe all of the above - there are no bad things, just areas for improvement (just please don't change fluffy - leave him where he is - we all love him really... ok, he's completely evil ***hole, but it wouldn't be so much fun without him).
Now, that we are done with those negative waves, let us switch to the positive side and see how beatiful this game is :)
PROS:
REALISM - Ok,.. let's get this straight - no simulator will duplicate the real thing - ever. As an ex-marine and keen climber and outdoorsman, I could have listed countless things that can be added to this game, from the realism perspective. But, so far, this game is as close as computer game can get to real-life survival (if you know anything better - please feel free to suggest). It is not casual, it is not skyrim with most hardcore "eat, sleep, drink" mods, it does not hold your hand, nor cuts you any slack. It's simple - "ok, you're in **** - get surviving"... and if you can't - hey, it's natural selection for you. So forget all the fancy Bear Grylls shows - no climbing cliffs, no running butt-naked through the winter forest and then trying to replenish your calories by munching on a squirell. Conserve your calories whenever and wherever you can, keep warm and hydrated, keep your gear in working order and adapt adequately to anything the wilderness throws at you - no heroics, no pointless wondering or taking chances, just timely well-planned actions... or it's game over.
IMMERSION - The atmosphere of this game is absolutely marvellous. Nevermind cartoon graphics - sound, tension and your imagination (if you have any) totally do their trick. Howling of the wind outside at night, does set the mood in, whilst howling of the wolves at dusk, will send that tingle down your spine and motivate you to keep your rifle handy and get inside as soon as you can. And there is a really cosy and safe feeling, when you are sitting by the fire late at night, cooking your meal and celebrating your survival for yet another day.
REPLAYABILITY - As mentioned before, the loot is pretty random. So every time the gear made available for the picking would be a little different and so will be your situation. Sometimes it will be bad and other times it will be just plain awful... Deal with it :)
FLUFFY - Well, you know... :)
Finally, let us take a quick look on things, that have been criticized by many players, but that are not entirely that bad.
BALANCE - There have been numerous complaints from the players about calories ticking away too fast or equipment degrading too fast. It's a fair point, but guys - let's not forget that this is a game and players should be kept occupied. There would be a lot less to do if your equipment didn't degrade overtime and so the game would be just repetitive cooking and wood-foraging almost from start to finish. And that's a bit boring - don't we all agree?
If we are talking realism, then how about adding the fact that your clothing will be soaking wet after couple of hours outside, thus will become a lot colder not overtime but right away and will require good bit of drying to become warmer again? Or how about the fact that your ammo may get damp and unusable, or your rifle itself will require good thorough cleaning regularly, or wood that also will require drying, before it can be set on fire with a match and paper? And so on, and so on... Full realism will make some things easier, but will make a load of other things the hell of a lot harder. So stop wimpering, fix those damn woolen socks with a bit of cloth, patch up can opener with some rusty scrap metal and get out there :)))
WOLVES - To my surprise I've seen quite a few complaints about abundance of wolves in the game and the wolf AI. Personally I do not know why anyone would complain about wolves - wolves in this game are your best friends, right after your winter coat, rifle and knife. In fact you may not need rifle when you got those guys around. On my last playthrough I have run out of ammo, by about 70th day. I survived for almost 30 days more. Guess how? I waited untill some wolf takes down a deer, then scared him off with a flare or fought him off with my fists and hoooray - 8kg of free venison every time. All thanks to wolves... poor buggers - I owe them some beers.
As to complaints about a wolf AI, I don't see what's wrong with it. Yes - the hungry wolf in the middle of the winter will try to have you for lunch - if there's no easier prey to be had, they will attack human (both in this game and for real). Once again - be thankful for "non-realism" and having to deal with lone wolves every time. In real life you'd have a whole pack of them on your ***. Do you feel lucky? :)
It seems like my word limit is up... Shame :) Anyway - get this game and play it. It's 100% worth it.
Thanks for reading :)

Like it's predecessor,
,
is a block-manipulation puzzle; you can grab blocks located horizontally from you, and shoot them in like directions. However, Swing Swing Submarine made two design choices that I feel makes this game inferior to its predecessor.
The first is that while
is a puzzle-platformer, Psychobot (the protagonist of this title) flies, removing the platforming element entirely. While this makes sense from a business standpoint (I imagine they have tablet devices in mind for this game eventually, if it doesn't already exist), it does remove a significant layer of gameplay that made the first game so enjoyable.
Secondly, each stage is broken into Zelda-style rooms, with pipes that connect rooms together. While it certainly makes the content look cleaner, there are several instances of puzzles being broken up between rooms in such a way as to render the gameplay unintuitive (as an example, in the early water stages, there are several puzzles that require you to know the spacial locations of other objects in adjacent rooms prior to firing yourself from a cannon). Given how these puzzles tend to interact, either larger rooms when appropriate--or at least the ability to view other rooms from a mini-map or the like--would have been welcome, and made these puzzles more intuitive.
Ultimately, while I do feel this is a solid game at a fair price point, the fact that this game is simply more shallow and less skill-based than
is rather disappointing. If you're looking for more
, delve into the custom levels there. If you're wanting a straight puzzle game without any frills, pick up
.

I was one of the folks who supported this game on Greenlight, and I was really rooting for it - but it turned out to be an almost complete disaster.
I do like the art style and the concept of two sisters traveling in time (in short bursts, mind you), and the pendant that provides time-traveling powers is a cool gimmick. But that's a drop in the bucket, I'm sad to say...
A number of the puzzles are broken, and at times I either had to wait until the 'skip' bar filled up (took about two minutes) or reboot the game if the puzzle becomes unresponsive.
The puzzles and HOG scenes are the meat of the game, and since they're pretty much broken the game is rendered pointless and frustrating - you'd really have to go out of your way to get it working.
Also, the story itself is another issue I have.
It's rushed, and there was a lot of potential to have it go in another direction but I guess the devs were strapped.
And there were some interesting additional characters (like a sooth-saying homeless man and a detective with a mysterious past); they only appear once in the story and it's such a waste to cast their roles aside.
The story was short, choppy, and the ending - while ending on a happy note - it's unsatifying...
I had really hoped that this would be an enjoyable experience, but I just wasted $8 and five hours of my time trying to get past tiresome glitches. There's no excuse for such a poor performance.

This version of RPG Maker is a really unique and easy-to-learn game engine. I have worked with at least five different game engines at this point, and a general rule among them: Trial and Error is too slow of a method to effectively learn the engine. RPG Maker breaks that rule to pieces. Level design takes minutes instead of hours, adding the playable character is at the click of a button, there is a fully customizable set of controls to change abilities, animations, and stats. If you are a programmer you can edit any of the script files to alter the gameplay, alter the battle system, or add your own elements. I personally haven't tried this out yet, but I've heard that if a code is added properly, the engine will add your new controls to its list of attributes. I have made one simple game in it, but since it has a splitting storyline, fully developed turn-based battle system, leveling system, and multiple playable characters, it's been described by friends as "short but complex." Oh, did I mention working in the engine is fun?

Outlast is a really memorable game that is without a doubt is one of my favourite entries into the well established horror genre and will be for a long while. The game overall is a trully horrifying experierence throughout with non-stop fear inducing moments, each memorable in their own right. Each part of the game is wonderfully brough to life be it in the level design, the fantastic ambience and it's creepy inhabitants. Chris Walker and the twins are outstanding in this game, although the twins have, what I feel less screen time than they deserve as they are so interesting and should have had a bigger role. The game was perfect at giving you the feel of helplessness as you explored with nothing more than your camera and your wits. The ending is not one of the best that you would expect from a Horror game but at least makes sense. Overall Outlast is one hell of a game, with an emphasis on the hell, and should be given at least a shot by all fans of the horror genre. I would give it a 9/10.

Below is a list of archetypal shadowrunners and their skills.
Deckers can slide like a whisper through the databases of giant corporations, spiriting away the only thing of real value—information.
Street samurai are enforcers for hire whose combat skills and reflexes make them the ultimate urban predators.
Riggers can manipulate vehicles and drones for a variety of purposes.
Mages, those rare folk who possess the gift of wielding and shaping the magical energies that now surround the Earth, are sought after to spy on the competition, heal and buff their allies, sling spells against an enemy, commit magical sabotage, and any other purpose that their employers can dream up.
Shamans are specialized mages whose attunement to the natural magical forces allows them to support themselves and fellow shadowrunners with a variety of defensive spells, as well as summon spirits in combat.
Physical adepts, who use the awakened magical energies to refine their bodies to the point of absolute perfection and become the ultimate fighting machines.
Not every shadowrunner follows these archetypes. In fact, the beauty of the Karma system for experience means you can combine or dedicate the classes above and become your own Shadowrunner trying to make money in a corportate ran future. Shadorun Chronicles - Boston Lockdown leaves a memorable impression if you are a fan of the genre. First, let's consider what I consider to be the negative factors of the game:
1. The end-game content lacks a matchmaking system to help with grouping. If you are playing solo, you likely won't enjoy the difficulty of the missions.
2. The character levelling system makes it difficult to identify compatibilities when looking for a group throughout your levels. I found it easier to simply run solo or to join random "LFG" requests and hope that I fit in. You can identify what missions are available to you, but that is only a general idea of character strength, and others have to be familiar with the missions to understand. I found this to be the worst part of trying to party up.
Ok, so there are my complaints... Now on to my praise for the  good stuff:
1. The character options are pretty varied and offer elements through race, skills and gear. The variety is impressive.
2. The gameplay is easy to interface with and to learn. It is turn-based, allowing for more control of character actions and cooperation in a party.
3. The overall mission content is impressive. There is a lengthy storyline in addition to hourly end-game missions for endless play.
4. The DLC is value-added and improves upon an already fun experience.
Overall, I recommend the game. It offers some great inspiration for table-top gaming if you need mission ideas for your Shadowrun game. The lackluster grouping feature is overcome by persistent chat channels that allow you to join eventually... and run solo in the meantime.

This game is a drug, that's how addictive and enjoyable this game is. If you're looking for a superb quick fix, this game is a must have! Games as straight-forward, simple (but not easy), and simultaneously relaxing as this game are rare. Simply put, you will not want to stop playing this game because its short levels are just plain fun, providing quick gratification. Before you know it, a few hours have gone by.
You control an orb of energy. The objective of each mission is to collect as much energy as quickly as you can, while you are avoiding asteroids and homing missiles flying at you. There are four "power-up" energies you can collect during your missions as they appear. They appear in two situations: randomly appearing within traps, and when asteroids are blown up. The whitish-blue energy increases your movement speed. The green energy makes you temporarily invincible. The red energy gives you mines to blow up asteroids. The yellow energy increases the chances your attacks are multiplied. What's even better is they can be stacked. You can wield all four energies at once, if you can collect them before they expire. Just be careful as you go for the energies, because they're surrounded by traps.
Your "weapons" consist of mines that you can manually "plant", a circular force field of anti-gravity that surrounds you, repelling asteroids, and the ability to temporarily freeze time, which allows you to maneuver through tight spots.
This game is similar to Asteroids, but but with so many more variables and incentives. You don't actually have to destroy the asteroids, but doing so causes the colored energies to appear. You earn stars after completing each mission. How many stars you earn depends on how well and efficient you perform. The more missions you complete, and the more stars you earn, the more you can level up the energies, amplifying their enhancements, as well as increasing their duration. You can then go back and replay previous missions in order to get more stars, which you can then apply toward leveling up your skills even more.
In a nutshell, this is one of the best games I've played, as far as "casual" games go. Sometimes I just want to sit down and play a fun, simple, and relaxing game, and with this game, the developer has mastered that niche.

I enjoyed SpaceChem in the sense that I enjoyed the emotional pain of creating an incredibly complex "machine" only to discover that it reversed something somewhere along the path and it was easier to delete and start over with the lessons learnt than to try and patch in a fix -- which would inevitably work but break something else (lesson?). Infinifactory is WAY more fun than SpaceChem. I'm not sure whether to attribute that to its satisfying 3D Minecraftesque environment, or the story with all its food nuggets, VHS tapes, and trucker hats, or the wide variety of blocks that such an environment allows. Really, it's all of the above and more. Here is a game in which the developers applied all that experience and feedback from SpaceChem and applied it in a way that manages to be equal parts difficult, frustrating (in a good way), fun, funny, and oh-so-deeply satisfying.
Without ruining everything, I'll say I came to what I thought was the final "mission" of the game and found it an appropriately complex and large build that took a good amount of thought and planning. As I watched the last completed unit pass into what we'll call the recepticle, I thought "this was money well spent, and I'm going to go through and optimize all my earlier builds. Moreover, this was so good that I'm going to go write my first Steam review to send thanks to the devs and recommendations to other logic gamers." That was my thought at that point in the game, and then I found out there's more. More compelling, more complex, and I figured I'd stop here, write that review, and only then get back to the next build.
I've already spent a lot of extra time rebuilding machines that passed but didn't satisfy me, satisfy in the sense that maybe they wasted blocks that could have been put to better use, or managed to build the prescribed number of objects but would have broken had it been asked to cycle endlessly (just one there) without any bugs. Feels good to come away with instant feedback that tells you that you've built something as efficiently as anyone else has been able. Many won't want to strive for that type of perfection, and the truth is that I won't for all the puzzles, but the point is that they've produced an environment and the tools that make you enjoy what would under normal circumstances be a chore and not a game.
If it requires Uplay to run it, stay away, stay far away.

"Refunct is a peaceful, short first-person platformer about restoring a vibrant world."
Let me translate this to you:
Peaceful- calm, relaxing, not preassuring, not blaming or punishing for your errors, no enemy.
Short- no gaming fatigue, won't take whole day, probably won't even take whole hour from your life.
First-person platformer- immersion, jumping and running from point A to point C through point B, easy goal.
Restoring a vibrant world- you have a goal, at least a mere excuse or it. No story, no explanation, no "these guys are enemy because they shoot at us and you have to kill them" kind of stuff. Just restore colors to the world that has appeared under your feet with no explanation. Does story even matters when all AAA titles just use old same "guy X wants to be evil so hero Y needs to defeat it and you are hero Y" blueprint?
For recommendation and review point all i can say is that game is exactly what it say it is- peaceful platformer with a very vague goal of just playing and reaching the end. Best enjoyed after long day of work when you just want to play something, but are just too tired or exhausted for titles like GTA, Skyrim or Terraria (you get the point).
Game is really short, which means you can complete it in one go. There is no rush, no hard action, no fast reflex needed and no hard mechanics, which means that you can just sit and relax. Game is easy, yet, forces you to think once in a while and challenge yourself when outcome doesn't really matter.
Graphics are really good for such short game, not demanding supowercomputer (heck i play on 6 year old laptop while have lots of other stuff open) and I'd like to see more of it.
Pricetag for relaxation in evening after dinner and exhausting day isn't that high.
Highly recommend to people who feel that sometimes they just want to play something, not run'n'gun all over the map in high action titles.

Refunct is a short and sweet first-person puzzle platformer. Your job is to get to some buttons on various platforms through jumping and parkour techniques. Each button you press activates another group of platforms that rise up to be used to help get to the next button, until you complete all of them. It's very much a pick-up-and-play title. There are only a few mechanics, with a few things like tunnels and bouncing platforms being introduced part-way through, and it's all very intuitive. There is no death or failure state, and it's designed so nothing ever becomes inaccessible as more platforms rise (important because you need to hit all of them for 100% completion). The puzzles are quite well designed, and it's fun climbing and running through the maze of platforms.
This is a game for people who want a relaxing one-session playthrough while they have some downtime. It took me a little over half an hour to finish the main puzzles and another half an hour to get 100% completion. As far as I can tell there really isn't much replayability; once you get 100%, there isn't really anything to do except jump around. The devs have also released several updates since game launch, though nothing in the way of new gameplay as far as I can tell.
The art is simple but appealing, with relaxing music in the background and a beautiful starscape that doesn't change.
I got it in a bundle where it wasn't a factor, but in terms of price, I would say that considering what it is, it could stand to be a dollar cheaper (though $2.99 isn't a big deal) so if it's something you care about you could stand to wait for a sale unless you really just want to support the developer. This is one of those cases where I would say that's a good enough reason by itself to buy full-price, though, because this kind of quick and well-designed game by a small indie team is the kind of thing I think should be encouraged.

The Piranha's finest and maybe their best title. Despite a rather small size of the island, every location brims with love and effort spent into creating it. The world feels complete, no unnecessary detail, no location out of place. The combat is engaging and the progression keeps this going well into the endgame, where you might get tired a bit from the final enemy types, particularly if you want all experience.
Why a thumbs down, then?
The game is abandoned and unoptimized for newer versions of OS. This becomes particularly evident on the second playthrough, when you can run out of memory. The only way to fix it is to patch the executable with a program, which will bring it's virtual memory use potential up to 4 GB, in line with 64-bit systems. And guess what, you can't do that with a Steam Risen executable. People on the forums tried to contact the devs/publishers about the issue without success. There are still some very annoying issues in the game, that could be easily addressed by the devs, but never were. I highly suggest you get the unofficial patch from the World of Risen website. A lot of users on the forums report being unable to start the game due to gfx-related problem. I had it too, I think you manually have to change the resolution in the ini file to match your monitor's to make it work, but I'm not completely sure. No support, no Steam cloud, existing in-game achievements never mirrored. You get the picture.
So, would I recommend you play Risen, especially if you're Gothic fan - oh God, yes, absolutely.
There is no need to get Steam version for that, though.

I'll try to keep this review simple for you.
PROS
-Amazing originality as far as mechanics and overall game design. Life and death play a key role in everything you do, in a really cool way.
-Characters with a pulse: despite typicalness of everyone in the game, they still felt lively.  Basically good voice acting and development, pacing was just right on it.
-Quantum puns and Schrodingers Video Game that never was but is at the same time.
-Only a few hours of gameplay, but can easily see myself replaying once I'm done. There are also quite a few things I missed on the first run already, so there's a lot to explore here and there.
-If you like stuff that makes you go "woo", then you'll have a fun time with this one. It's one of those games you'd really love playing in an IMAX theater if you had the opportunity.
-You ♥♥♥♥ing control life and death.
CONS
-A bit redundant here and there. Once you get around to upgrading a few things and learning the overall controls, you find yourself repeating gameplay every now and again.
-It's clunky at times, not nearly enough to be unplayable, but enough to irk you when it happens. Easy fixing w/settings and such, but still a con.
-The enemies were awesome, but very limited for variety. There is basically a bad, baddie, and baddest. Although I did not complete the game at time of this review, may edit later.
-I didn't have trouble personally with it, but my buddy pointed out that this type of game is better on a controller opposed to keyboard and mouse. It's subjective, really, but he brings up a valid point.
-The animations for the rigs and models aren't TERRIBLE....but sometimes cheezy. Would have made this game a lot better for atmosphere if they worked on it more before release.
TL;DR:
It's a solid game, as with any steam game, try to pick it up on sale. If you enjoy first person adventures and interesting little stories that have yet to be oversaturated on steam or by hollywood, it's worth it. It's no gem, could have been a little more worked on, but has replay value, is borderline fun, and at times was even reminiscent of classics like Portal.

I've played through Risen about 2 1/2 times and I enjoyed every minute of it. While it's missing some modern RPG aspects like having a customizable character, it has a lot of classic RPG elements that are well executed and engaging. The voice acting is amazing for being an older game and the characters are very immersive. Some might consider the plot generic, but I really felt captivated by it.
The most satisfying quality of this game has to be the combat system. It's similar to Gothic, but much more refined and 100x less clunky. While you may see enemies dash away from an attack rather awkwardly, that's about the only gripe you could find with this combat system. It has a high skill ceiling, but it is still possible to increase your stats so you don't have to be a highly skilled player. The last chapter of the game is insanely difficult if you are not adept at using your primary weapon, but by then you should be fairly good if you have experience with 3rd person RPG's.
Overall, I consider this game to be one of my favorite open world RPG's. It's better than Gothic, Skyrim, Two Worlds, and maybe a bit better than Oblivion. I got this game from a Humble Bundle, but I definitely think it's worth the $9.99.

Risen is definitly an old school RPG, in that nothing, I repeat NOTHING is spoon fed to you. At best, you get a couple of generic markers for the general location of where you may need to go for some quests, but for the most part it is entirely up to you to keep track of who is who, where people and places are at, and what you need to do next. Unlike games such as Skyrim, in Risen you are forced to figure almost everything out for yourself. Quests take awhile to finish, and are arched out rather than radiant so that you don't feel as if you are repeatedly doing the same stuff over and over. Hours will fly by as you wander about the island and learn how to progress.
Combat is on the wonky side, and can take a bit to get to learn. Many creatures have attacks that are, IMO, a bit too fast and overpowered, and require a little more than just skill to get through. However, there are many things you can take advantage of in order to make it though the combat system.
Graphics wise, i would say that the game has aged considerably well. While most textures arent remarkable or even close to realistic, they are far from being immersion breaking or ugly. In fact. some areas are quite beautiful, and the soundtrack is one of the best from the time.
If you have a short attention span, or don't have much experience with RPGs in general, this game may not be the best place for you to get your feet wet. However,  with how often these games go on sale I would highly suggest that you put at least a couple of hours into the game.

An extremely fun little game. It's a puzzle game and has very simple controls (just click the left mouse button) but some of the levels really make you think. You control a little robot, you move by left clicking on a square. Using this robot you travel through various rooms in a given level searching for the end portal. As you explore the level you may find different blocks (wood, sand, stone, sticky jelly) which each have different properties and can react differently in various situations. For example, if you let a laser or fire get near a wood block it will burn and be destroyed, but a sand block turns to glass. In most levels you need to try and conserve as many blocks as you can.
Of course getting to the end portal on each level usually isn't very difficult. However there are three gold coloured blocks on each level, and obtaining all three of those and then getting to the end portal can lead you into some fiendishly brain-teasing logistical puzzles to think your way through. If you sit and think long and hard enough, nothing is beyond your grasp to figure out. If you get frustrated enough (or completely stuck) there is a brilliant guide with a video for how to complete every level, but it's very satisfying to solve everything for yourself (and if you look at a video you'll feel like hitting your head against the wall thinking "it was so obvious, why didn't I see that").
Give your brain some gentle exercise with this charming, fun, and non-violent game.
