Outlast... What can I say? Well for starters it is fricken terrifying! You spend 3-4 hours hiding under beds or in lockers hoping your pursuer won't find you. Running away from your enemies is very scary and suspenseful as well because you have no idea where you are going most of the time. Mount Massive is an incredible place that is very detailed. Outlast is probably one of the best looking horror games I have ever played. I just like how it feels so smooth when you are playing too. As you get farther and farther into Mount Massive, more and more of the sinister secrets unravel. Outlast has a lot of good things going for it but there are some bad things though. The find three things to unlock this or turn this back on proves to be pretty annoying. You find yourself getting more frustrated than scared in these parts. The inmates aren't very scary when you get up close to them and they all look the same. They could have taken the time to make the enemies look different. I don't know about everyone else, but i didn't the ending to be all that great. This game also isn't really worth the twenty dollars due to the fact that the story is only 3-4 hours long. There is also the DLC that just came out thats eight dollars and that is only around two hours long. So I would wait for this game to go on sale if you are going to buy it. But overall Outlast is a great game and is a step up in the horror game industry.

Cons:
· Unfixed bugs that can crash the game unexpectedly and frustate your gaming nirvana.
· DLC for completing the races to get what it should be a full game? I commited this error that once, but after that, nevermore.

My veredict:
· Save your money and spend it in anything else distributed by someone less evil than Ubisoft, or wait until a DRM-free version (or just DRM linked with Steam) is out.

I love Shadowrun. I used to GM a tabletop game when I was younger, the new Shadowrun Returns -> Hong Kong are great. Look at my Profile, I built up the Level 5 Badge for two of them! That said... Shadowrun Chronicles is just not good. It's a turn based game akin to X-Com, but don't expect half the quality of that sort of game. This does just enough to qualify as a game and that's it.
So what's my issue with it? Firstly, it doesn't stick to anything Shadowrun, it doesn't have the statistics, it doesn't have the skills, it doesn't care about what your character can do, it doesn't care what your character background is. It lets you select two weapons and go from there.
Decking is a weapon. Don't expect any Matrix, it doesn't exist.
So okay, we have a game with orks and trolls, weapons and magic, in a futuristic X-Com style setting, right? Sound good? It's not. You can move, you can shoot, that's it. There's no overwatch, no covering angles, you can sit in cover and watch the enemy run around you and shoot you in the back, even though you had a turns worth of actions left to do something about it. There's no tactics here, it's all about kill or be killed.
It's a shame because, as I said at the start, I love Shadowrun and a multi-player game where you take on runs sounds awesome, but unfortunately.. it's not.
I bought this on a Steam sale so I'm not that annoyed, but if I paid full price I'd be feeling pretty annoyed about now. Avoid. Seriously.

During and after playing this game, all I could do to explain it, was that this game was "me".
As an environment designer, while my designs aren't as out there as the ones presented, I fully understand this game and the mindset of all involved. This game connected to me on a very intimate level, which genuinely shook me while playing it. I found all of my own experience and mannerisms as an environment designer kick in, noticing many little details that normal players would never see, and understanding them from a very personal viewpoint. I fully understood exactly what was meant.
If you are not in game design, this might not speak as strongly to you. I honestly don't know. To me, though, this game has so much more of an impact, if you work behind the curtain. This game, while being sold to the public, feels to me like it is not for the people who play games. It is for the people who make the games to be played.
I do not know if the events portrayed are real or not, but regardless of if they are, I certainly hope all involved, particularly the story focus, get some closure. While it will mean next to nothing, I'd also want to note, for the game developers, that I completely understand this game, and the meanings behind it and every chapter within it. Or at least, I certainly hope I do.

In Depth Review of The Long Dark
*DISCLAIMER, THIS IS WHILE THE GAME IS IN ALPHA AND SHOULD ONLY BE CONSIDERED FOR IF THE FOLLOWING READER WISHES TO BUY THE GAME WHILE IN EARLY ALPHA. SOMETHINGS MAY HAVE BEEN ADDED OR ALTERED IN THE GAME BY UPDATES AND CAN CHANGE SOME ITEMS IN THIS REVIEW*
Graphics: 9.75 out of 10
The graphics of the game are not really detailed and high definition such as Battlefield or The Last of Us. But the graphics run very well and are beautiful for this type of game. With it being an indie game, this can be expected. With having minor glitches such as things disappearing such as wolves in the distance, the graphics deserve said rating.
Gameplay: 10 out of 10
With this being a survival game, you can really enjoy the constant having to run into shelter to prevent hypothermia, or being chased by wolves. The HUD is very likable since it disappears after a few moments of showing important info. The need for food and water really sets the game in a "I will die if I don't do this" kind of mode. The calorie counter, the menu simplicity, the different materials you can find or make to repair items really makes this game wanted.
Audio / Ambiance:  10 out of 10
The audio is to die for in this game. With really high definition surround sound, it is the same type of audio Naughty Dog used for "The Last of Us". Really draws the player in, makes them stop whenever they hear something since you can tell how close it is. The noise of each footstep in the snow, the heavy breathing. This 3-D type of audio really makes a good game. The audio goes with the ambiance since the only real time the ambiance is thrown at your face is when you have to go to a Hydro Dam Facility to scavenge for supplies. You then realize you might not be alone...
Story: n/a
With only sandbox mode available in Alpha, story cannot be rated.
That is my full rating for the game "The Long Dark".

i've only put a few hours into this game so far, and i feel as though i'm probably only starting to scratch the surface on it's complexity, but at this point, i am having an absolute blast with it!
the game works precisely as displayed in the trailer: you are given x inputs, told to produce y output, and you have to figure out how to get y from x using the factory machinery tools provided to you. These tools include conveyor belts, pistons, sensors, welders, and more. It becomes very quickly apparent with any seemingly easy puzzle, that the deceptively simple systems the game provides you can and must be used to created increasingly complex and synergistic structures, as you create more and more intricate outputs.
The game very thoroughly challenges your problem-solving skills, spatial and mechanical awareness, and logical abilities.  I would highly recommend it to anyone looking for a truly unique, engaging, and challenging puzzle game.

The Total War series is tagged under the genre “strategy”. I would use this term very loosely when it comes to the Total War franchise. The idea of two armies battling it out to the death sounds pretty awesome, the issue here is that Total War simulates this in a very boring, unrealistic and unfair manner.
About half of my playtime is in the campaign, and the rest I’ve put into online battles. Both of these game modes aren’t really up to scratch since they miss many features which would make the game more enjoyable.
In the online edition of the game, there is no progression system (although there is a technology tree in the single player campaign), which means that you’ve got nothing to work towards whilst playing the game online. This means that the online gameplay gets very boring, very quickly.
Another reason why the online is quite poor is because of the way the “strategy” in this game works. The only strategy in this game consists of spamming the most over-powered units and running to the top of the largest hill as quickly as you can. I have many hundreds of hours in this game, and I’ve yet to win a single battle. This shows how un-balanced the game is; it also shows the lack of strategy involved in the game (I’ve played many hours so I’ve had plenty of time to get good, yet I still can’t win any battles).
If you want a game which requires strategic thinking, I recommend that you go and check out Call of Duty. Call of Duty is a game which requires a lot of strategy and teamwork if you want to beat the opposing team. You’ll need good communication with your teammates, as well as good knowledge of the maps and guns. There is also a progression system, so you actually have something to work towards whilst playing the game.
I’ve also reviewed other games which claim to be strategic, such as Counter-Strike: Global Offensive (many claim it’s a “strategic shooter”) and I’ve explained why games such as Call of Duty are better. I will leave a video on this below the review.

Very high calibre puzzle game here.
The platforming aspect of Blocks That Matter has been removed entirely (you simply click a location to travel to it), and the puzzle aspect ramped way up to compensate. Additionally, instead of creating tetrominoes you simply chuck blocks around one at a time, however each block reacts to other blocks and environmental hazards differently. This minimalist design philosophy may initially seem to have dumbed down the game, however, like Toki Tori 2, it quickly becomes apparent that the significantly decreased array of options simultaneously makes the puzzles themselves more apparent, and the solutions more laterally realised.
I enjoyed my (considerable) time with Tetrobot and Co. immensely and highly recommend it to anybody in search of a puzzle game which is simple and intuitive to learn, without being simplistic in the execution of the puzzles themselves.

I was looking for a new game to play and happened to find this one. I read some mixed reviews on it, some saying it was too hard, and some saying it was the best game they had played. It's one of those games that you can lose so many hours to without even knowing it. One thing that you should DEFINITELY know before buying this game is that it can be very challenging. I just finished playing a game on normal difficulty with disasters turned OFF, and all of my followers just died from various things (cold, starvation, etc...). Once you get the hang of it though, it is a very fun game. The fast forward feature is simply amazing, and the custom world generation seems like a cool feature that I need to play with. If you do buy this game, I HIGHLY recommend going through ALL the tutorials. There are many factors that help make your town sucessful, and it is very helpful to know all of them. Overall, this is a great game, and even though I just lost, I am going to keep playing (probably on easy until I get the hang of things!). If you fancy yourself a city-builder fanatic, you aren't living without this game in your collection.

This is another of those times that I'm having so much fun with a game, that I feel the need to sit down and share why it is that I feel this way. I first tested DD2 very, very early on, before it was redone to be much closer to its predecessors, Dungeon Defenders, and Dungeon Defenders Eternity. Team Trendy was still deciding on the direction they wanted to go with the project. At the time it was PvP, and I for one am extremely happy that they went back to the tried and true formula that makes the series great. After trying the game again, post-redesign, I bought into the Defense Council, and it's not often that I feel thrilled to have paid $70 for a game. Here are the things this game does SO right:
DD2, even still in alpha, trumps the first 2 games already. The tavern is bigger, better, and packed with things to unlock and discover as you play. The game features quests, NPC's, mad amounts of loot and items, a solid campaign, and once beyond that, multiple new game modes to dive into. For an Early Access title, there is a tremendous amount of content here already, with more updates pouring in every 6 weeks or so. I do look forward to plenty more maps coming in in the future, those are pretty limited currently, but not so much so that you get bored.
Trendy Entertainment, once again, shines in their interactions with the community, in addressing bugs and issues, and in building a great experience. These guys GET IT. I mean REALLY get it, when it comes to how to treat the community, and even in alpha they're right on top of things. You'll see them reply to nearly every thread, and for a game with around 14,000 concurrent users at the time of writing this, that's impressive to say the least. They've gone above and beyond the call, even compensating the community when issues arise which reset quests or cause the players to lose progress. This is an alpha, we will ALL lose progress at times, but these guys still know how frustrating that can be!
One of the big surprises for me in DD2 was getting into the campaign and seeing more than just the same crystals to defend. There are interactive traps on the map, and other things to defend besides just the main crystal. In one case, there were even NPC's on the map, cowering up near the throne while you defended them and kept them alive. Tel ya what, having actual characters there made it feel so much more worthwhile! Who wants to defend an empty throne? I love the added depth they've brought to DD2, it brings so much life to the game!
Trendy has done a perfect job with the cash shop. There is absolutely nothing pay to win in DD2, and never will be. It's a promise they made, and have stuck to like glue. You can buy costumes, bags, things like that, but never boosts, or anything that changes the way the game is played. You can't go to the cash shop and make your game any easier, or make it impact the experience. You can sure look great though! The costumes for each character are quite cool, and worth a spend for people looking to support the development of the game.
Additionally, even with an already bustling community, I LOVE the option for private taverns/friends only gameplay. Let's face it, most people don't want to play with "that guy", who presses ready before the towers are even placed, or who afk's mid battle. There are plenty of players around, and getting into a public tavern/game is definitely easy to do, but if you want to chill alone or with the best friend, being able to do that is a huge plus for me. The game has taken the best of what makes a free to play game fun, and added in the way to play the way you want to play.
To sum up:
Pro's:
-The game is already head and shoulders above previous games in the series
-The development team is ROCKING this!
-The game has depth, immersion, and a ton of fun, even for an alpha release
-It's Free to play done beautifully right
Cons:
-It is an alpha, so you are going to find the hiccups and bugs that come along with an Early Access game
-Maps are still limited this early on, but there are enough to keep you going for hours even now

I enjoyed it, but i have a ton of issues with the game.

2. I personally found the mouse sensitivity too high. A menu option to adjust sensitivity would be nice, and the high sensitivity led to me making very slow and tiny movements that went way further than i wanted (especially with the speed power up), and led to what i feel are unfair deaths because the controls are as precise as i would like.
3. While the upgrades are nice and it's cool to see some overall progression built into a game like this, the yellow upgrade (which lowers your ability costs) feels incredibly unsatisfying as i never felt like any of the abilities other than timestop was any good. The other three powerups have immedite effects upon collection that feel really good to use (inbulnerability, speed up,  and mines).

The first level is as big a complexity bump as you're going to get, Once you figured out the basics, the game does very little to introduce new obtacles or powerups for the player. All in all, cool game if a bit clunky. Play it if you want very simple dodge mechanics and some tough levels. Or don't, there are plenty of better games on the store.

Not too different from the Harebrained Shadowrun that you probably know and love -  a bit more combat and mission focused, with a stronger emphasis on a trinity of damage types (physical, magic, tech). The campaign is fine, with some regular Shadowrunney stuff going on (Dragons! Computers! Infections!) and long enough that you'll probably finish it just before you begin to notice the maps being recycled.
Gameplay is mostly skirmishes with another small squad or 'get to a point on the opposite corner of the map' - pretty boring compared to the robust dialogue and characters you get even in Shadowrun Returns, but I don't think this game had a huge team working on it, and the content and assets they were working with probably came with the caveats/restrictions of whatever engine they were porting it from (possibly a Jagged Alliance remake, but I am probably wrong.)
Anyway, it's mostly fun and good! You can customise your character and crew with a lot of different cosmetic junk since there's a very basic loot system where you can find, say, a new glowing arm tattoo in a dumpster during a mission, and it's great to see other people's characters pop up in the squad selection lineups, and even better that you can hire them. Haven't really experimented with the multiplayer since I don't know if it mixes well with the control-freak-enabling nature of tactical games.
One other thing that works surprisingly well - considering this is a Shadowrun game, after all - is since it's an instance-based multiplayer squad game in nature, there's a global chat (with people who are usually not completely stupid) which really pleases me in a lot of ways - it fits in perfectly with the game lore and is useful mechanically, and I just think the immersion this adds just really makes up for a lot of the things this game is missing compared to the Harebrained Shadowrun series. Anyway, it's a minor thing, but sometimes that's what makes everything come together.

With a plethora of indie survival games, it's nice to see a fresh take on the genre. Most survival games focus on horror, far fetched post apacalyptic scenarios, or combat. The Long Dark takes survival back to its eery roots. You find yourself alone in the Canadian wilderness with next to no tools to survive with. The landscape is vast, dreary, and filled with sights and sounds to explore, as well as wildlife that could potentially sustain you, or kill you. The gameplay is fairly simple, with nothing but keys to move, sprint, crouch, and the mouse buttons to interact with the environment.
There's something about the art style and the sense of isolation within the game that gives the game an overall scary tone yet wondrous tone. I appreciate the focus on survival, but the game still needs some obvious tweaking. The game is in alpha, so there is a lot of work to be done before final release, but judging from where the developers are headed I am a little worried. Instead of focusing on an episodic story mode (aka you will have to pay per episode -- Walking Dead style), which I cannot imagine having a lucrative story, I would prefer to see a focus on fleshing out the environment, and perhaps seeing a procedurally generated sandbox mode. As of now, there is only one map to play on, with limited resources.
I would like to believe that once the resources in an area run out, the 'survivor' would move on. After the first 5-10 days, you will most certainly have run out of all loot to discover in the map. At that point you rely on the very grind-filled gameplay element of hunting for wolves/deer, foraging for wood, and boiling water. The game is boiled down into these three elements as of now.
Here are things I would like to see:
- A more balanced calorie/thirst system.
- Larger maps.
- Procedurally generated maps (preset maps are okay, but it would be interesting to explore a never-ending wilderness!).
- Crafting (this is actually in the works).
- More forgiving item wear (knives and hatches last more than a few days in real life, why not in game?).
- Potential for minor shelter personalization (for example, it would be nice to remove dead bodies from given shelters).
- More realistic wood foraging (having a hatchet in the middle of a forest should produce high yields of acquired wood).
- Wildlife diversity (needs more than just deer and wolves).
- Wildlife traps, sleds for higher carrying capacity, and snow shoes!
Great game so far, but needs some work done for longer replayability. Please focus on fleshing out the survival experience before focusing on a story mode!

is an exploration game/platformer that gets one thing right: it understands that movement itself can be fun if it's cool-looking and fluid enough. There are issues, of course (clipping and invisible walls are unforgivable in a game about freedom of movement, and what's up with the camera often sliding down to the character's crotch level?); but generally, the jumping and movement in
feel great.
The level design is hit and miss. Mostly levels are great to navigate. However, there are two different types of levels in
: some are fast theme park rides that want to pump your adrenaline with special effects, speed, and huge jumps; others are calmer and reward exploration. The issue is, they play completely differently, and it's not obvious at first glance which type of level you're on.
I did, however, very much love the final run, that has you traverse a huge exploration-based level that is collapsing around you, turning into a linear path. It's a smart way to add spectacle and wink at the player, while making it clear what is expected of them.
The mechanics are numerous, but added gradually, so as not to overwhelm the player. And while it's definitely not a walking sim, it actually felt like one to me, since most challenges felt easy, and the mood was very relaxed; more than anything,
invites you to absord the atmosphere, look for secrets, jump around, and hug trees.
Unfortunately, the setting and story of
are... shall we say, confused. They combine a mystical valley inhabited by Ghibli-like cute magical creatures, a Greek-named bomb, the Aztecs, a random explorer finding a military-grade suit, a semi-serious plot about a scientist competing with Oppenheimer, but also a plot about his fellow researcher trying to sabotage their work because the bomb HURTS THE TREES. It's an incomprehensible mess of references and styles that wants to be mystical, gritty, thoughtful, social, and emotional at the same time—but ends up just silly.
Still, if you don't pay close attention to a supposedly serious military researcher qualifying the newly-found source of unknown energy as 'cute' and thus worth more than human lives,
provides an array of nicely-looking locations, good atmosphere, and fun, if easy, parkour. Would definitely recommend waiting to buy this on sale though.

Tetrobot & Co is the most fun i've had playing a puzzle game in a long time.  Morusque's soundtrack is great and manages the challenge all puzzle games face, which is to produce tracks that are enjoyable to listen to on a loop, and avoid being tedious or formless.  The puzzles themselves are challenging and require some thought but never rely on obtuse jumps in logic, and game mechanics are introduced gradually and with some fun.
As for the gameplay itself, you pilot psychobot, a nano-sized repair bot, through damaged tetrobots in order to restore the larger robots to working order.  Piloting is achieved through pointing & clicking where you'd like psychobot to fly to.  Psychobot can vacuum up blocks of varying sorts in direct line of sight, and fire them as projectiles along the same path (subject to any environmental hazards that might intercept a block).  Blocks themselves are subject to gravity, and stick to like blocks, and it's through these mechanisms that many of the puzzles are crafted.

This game is a fun little 3D platformer with high production values, and an engrossing (if short) plot line. It doesn't go out of it's way to kill you with punishing jump sequences, and instead focuses on providing cool movement mechanics and giving you opportunities to put them through there paces as you bound across the landscape.
The atmosphere was amazing, lots of great scenic outdoor locations, strewn with some ancient ruins and retro military-industrial facilities. The game is quite short, and the plot advances quickly, which keeps things fresh since you're constantly moving into new areas and aquiring encountering new mechanics.
I did find the combat encounters a bit weak, even the big boss went down easily on the first try, but ultimately the combat was more a sideline than the focus of the game so this wasn't a huge problem. Also there are collections-- I know some people like these, but I find they force me to slow down and poke around in all the out-of-the-way corners instead of enjoying the flow of the game. Not a fan, but your mileage may vary.
What makes this game great:
* smooth control mechanics
* great scenery and background music
* unusual plot concept
What's holding it back:
* combat not challenging
* collections

Each game in the Total War series since its inception with Shogun Total War in 1999, has increased in size and scope, rendering all as monumental strategy tests in every way, Napoleon Total War being no exception.
The tutorials are a must.
The beauty of this series lies in being given a strategic campaign overview to control, which works well being turn-based, as well as offering the exciting, frenetic, real-time drama of being in charge of each battle itself.
Combat is certainly exciting to watch and be involved in.
The one huge and fundamental drawback to this whole series was that often what in reality would have been epic, long drawn-out battles, end up being ludicrously over condensed to such a short space of game-time that unless one is constantly pausing the action to give specific orders one feels like a general having to make seven decisions, all within a few moments whereas in real life you would have had much more time.
Overall, however, this is a vast and sweeping strategy test which is head and shoulders above every other RTS ever made.

Slightly interesting collect-em-up game mechanics can't save this poor title. Control a small ball of energy, collecting other coloured balls of energy for powerups, and clouds of energy to complete the level before a time limit, all while avoiding a constant flow of asteroids, which cannot really be shot. They can be blown up with mines or homing missiles, both of which are rather pathetic in practice.
I was a bit dissapointed when I first played this game, with the word "destroy" in the title, and "bullet hell" in the description I was expecting a shoot-em-up. How wrong I was. There's very little destruction going on here. Ok, so you can blow up the occasional asteroid, but the game requires you to collect such a large amount of energy that even when fully powered up you won't be able to fire off lots of missiles or mines very quickly. I guided my people though many years of growth and happiness. After several generations of potato farmers, a lucky trade resulted in peach tree seeds. Our orchards were just beginning to yield fruit, with which we could start brewing peach ale!  Then, I had a tools shortage one season because I had iron surplus stored in the trading dock, and tried to build too much at once. That had a negative effect on crop yields (fewer tools), which were only just keeping up with my booming population anyway. The next several years were a slow downward spiral, as the farmers, hunters, gatherers, and their children all slowly died of starvation, each year producing less food for everyone else as there were fewer workers. Almost turned it around by clearing out food reserves, but the winter had set in, slowing down everything. Not enough woodcutters for firewood, or laborers in general. My people either starved or froze to death until no one was left, leaving a sad,empty town. No more picks clinking or trees falling or axes chopping, just the sound of the wind. Total and absoute despair. 10/10. Can't wait to try again.

This is Horror at its finest... This is 'Outlast'...
You awaken, numb from head to toe after being heavily sedated.
Your arms and legs tremble as you come to the realisation, you're still trapped...
You pick up your trusty CamCorder and look at your surroundings.
"Rest in Peace"
The words Hastily written in blood all around your would-be tomb.
You approach the door only to be greeted by a Patient, although he isn't as far gone as others as he unlocks your Cell door and scurries off as if he was ordered to do so.
You approach the rickety balcony infront of you curious, after hearing what sounds like a watermelon being pulverised...
As you look down you feel a sickness in your stomach like no other...
"They're in my blood and they wanna get out...Can feel..."
A patient is pounding his head over and over onto the dust and grime covered walls of Mount Massive leaving his forehead indented and sanity no where to be found.
You see a flicker of light radiating from a broken glass window in a Cell below you.
Anxious, you slowly begin your 10 metre journey to the blood-stained stair case...
Suddenly you hear a loud smash as a Tortured, disfigured hand is thrust towards you from a cell window.
Instinctively, you weave and dodge the grip of what may have been your death...
As you venture on your short journey you hear voices.
Not insane, nor harsh voices but rather calm and collected tones echoing through the darkness.
You raise your camera quickly, as though they may help you.
You scurry to find the damaged Night Vision swith on your mangled CamCorder.
As you flick the switch, all hope fades...
Two men, naked and dripping in blood stand before you.
The only thing seperating you from their blunt, bloody machetes is an Iron door that, in this moment, feels like a God-send.
The men speak of a Priest who has apparently ordered them to not kill you...
"We should give him a running start" Says the taller one.
"Such Patience" whispers the shorter one.
In this moment you seize the opportunity to dash down the stairs and into the room where the beacon of light is.
As you stop to raise your CamCorder to help find your way in the Abyss of the everlasting darkness you hear the two men again.
"I want his tongue, and his liver"
"They are yours..."
As much disgusted as you are trembling with fear you proceed throught the 'Body-size' gap in the wall and enter what seems to be a maintenance hallway.
As you make your way through the narrow hallway you hear voices from above, but not the Naked Men.
One voice quietly whispering under their breathe what seems to be a lullaby.
The other only repeating the words "Silky, Silky, Silky..."
You see a small hole with a more then convienent crate underneath.
You steadily climb the crate and enter the small hole onto the Pitch Black floor above.
As you race to find you CamCorder you realise the Lullaby singer is directly infront of you.
You attempt to steady your breathing as you slowly raise what is, your second pair of eyes...
A Disfigured Face meets your gaze as he wriggles around in what appears to be a Jacket designed for patients such as himself.
As your horriffic 'stare off' continues you ask yourself.
"Where was the other voice?"
As the Disfigured man steps aside, your vision focuses on a sight as unholy as the devil himself...
You stare in horror as you witness a man thrust backwards and forwards into what appears to be a headless, unidentifyable corpse.
You feel a churning sensation in your stomach as you throw your head back to keep what may have been your last meal ever, down...
The man stands up, furious at you watching him, 'in the act'
He calls you many things but what stands out to you most is, "Sick"
"You're a Sick F***, watching like that. You like to Watch?"
You close your eyes, take a deep breath, turn.
And just like that, You're off again.
Running from what seems like an inevitable doom.
As you leap and bound your way through blood soaked corridors and Ripe-smelling hallways you stop.
No.
It can't be.
The stories you've heard all make sense now
All the things you've discovered about Murkoff now all fit together
Entrails, Guts, blood
Scattered across the room in which you stand.
The one word that sends shivers down your spine and tingles down your neck is written in blood in front of you....
You take a deep, fear induced breathe and tremblingly mutter the Phrase...
"Walrider........"

Pros:
+ "New" concept with set items on the heroes
+ An online connected item system (dynasty) which enables you to level up weapons as your hero gains experience. (too bad for people who cant connect to the internet all the time)
+ You can choose your hero type and still select abilities from both might and magic classes
+ All heroes can learn spells of higher ranks, and not randomly
+ Challanging campaigns and nice boss battles!
+ Interesting mix of abilities.
+ Good looking graphics and designs.
Cons:
- Set items are a bit booring, they give general stats and mostly nothing awsome. 6 set items should give a big bonus.
- Dynasty items require ALOT of experience to level.. During campaigns you are stuck using the same weapon all the time, because it has a healing spell... So not much variation possible.
- Campaigns are very long, and creeps increase in size so fast you are not allowed to lose any units. (therefore you need all the healing spells available)
- Enemy heroes magically always knows what castle is unprotected and the exact size of your army. Enemy armies also grows in an rate far greater than your 10 vs 1 castles.
- Stunn spells doesnt work. Examples:
* Succubus charm/seduce spell clearly states it stunns for 2 turns. The creature is in fact stunned for the remaining turn(even after their turn has passed).
* Time statis spell clearly states 4 turns, it randomly stunns between 2-4 turns.
* Chilled/frozen usually works for 1 turn as well (they can attack the next turn, after they got stunned).
* All stunn spells counts one turn even though the creature has already done its turn. Makes sense?
- Auto combat always makes you lose units, which mentioned earler you cannot afford. every battle (up to 100 times) has to be done manually as a result of the increasing size of the creeps, which also almost never retreat, even if your army is much, much larger.
- Still bugs in the game. I could buy 100 units when there were 11 available and won the map. Stunns are buggy.
- Hero movement is buggy. I got boots, hero trait, stable, etc etc and still cant get far. But the enemy can always ride further. A hero without an army however can ride through the whole map with the same buffs.
- Very less information of the hero stats.. How many movement points does the hero have? How does it get increased mana? What does one might power do? Some spells cant be cast because of lacking information..
- Lacking tool tips everywhere..
- Campaign doesnt follow a chronological pattern, its very confusing.
- I can go on for ever.

Overall I give this game a thumbs up because despite it's flaws the main campaign offers a very good tactical turn based experience and unless XCOM is all you'll ever want to play then Shadowrun Chronicles is a good alternative for some solid 30h of fun.
It's certainly not worth the retail price though, so wait for a sale :)

Here we go again, another game where, I wish there was a "maybe" button, but I think I have to go with "No" on this one. I was curious about this game because I like the creepy horror titles like the
games that freak you out without all the blood and gore. The concept of this really piqued my curiosity. The idea of being a night watchmen with a 12am to 6am shift in a Chuck E. Cheese-style restaurant with the weird animatronic characters seems like a good setup. But seriously this "game" has such minimalistic "gameplay" that there isn't much to it other than some, admittedly effective, jumpscares.
Here's the gameplay in a nutshell:
The game tries to concoct some sort of narrative reason why you can't just keep the doors closed constantly (it takes power and your bosses are cheap so you have a set amount you can use) and why the robots start walking around at night, trying to kill you (the owners don't want the robots' servomotors freezing up, or some such nonsense), but it makes me feel the same way I do about the aliens in the movie
coming to invade Earth, which is three-forths covered in stuff that is fatal to them. To say that this is all contrived is an understatement.
I feel like the first night is pretty much handed to you as a way to present you with some narrative exposition (however laughable), but I had a lot of trouble getting through night #2 without running out of electricity; I kept getting to 5am but couldn't survive until 6. Now that I am on night #3, I am not sure there is much point in pressing forward. Honestly, I feel like you can see everything there is to see in this game by looking at the screenshots on the Steam Store Page. I don't feel like nights 4 through 5 are going to offer much more; the critters are just going to move faster or be more unpredictable. Just go watch some videos on youtube of other people playing nights 3, 4, and 5. Seriously, one video I watched of a guy playing night #3 was him flashing the door lights on each side, back and forth, occasionally checking the Pirate Cove stage to keep Foxy at bay, and then, when necessary, closing a door temporarily. Back and forth, back and forth; click, click, click. That's not gameplay, it's boring repetition.
This game has a somewhat cool concept that tries to get away with very minimal gameplay by some weak narrative reasoning. If you really must check this game out, wait for it to go on sale, because even at only 5 bucks, it feels a little thin.

I actually think a Sonic the Hedgehog game could be cool from first person after playing this game.

Other than that, this game is legit. Very unique gameplay, interesting story and beautiful outdoor areas which are tied together with an excellent soundtrack. I hope the developers make some kind of sequel that expands on the gameplay mechanics.

I got this off a bundle, and while I wouldn't go out and buy it for $3 myself, I think that's the perfect price for it. It's short, sweet, polished and while it left me wanting more, it didn't feel incomplete. I would absolutely buy a pack of handmade levels like Refunct's singular playspace, with varying difficulties, even if it was just that.
It is, or it felt, shorter than I expected, even when reviews called it "a nice 30-minute thing". The visuals are fantastic, though I feel like they could've been used to a greater extent, making the "weather" more dramatic -that fog in particular, very atmospheric- and the audio that accompanies them is relaxing, with nice intuitive sound cues.
Controls brought me back to Portal and Mirror's Edge, very responsive, making navigation feel wonderfully natural. They're not bogged down by transitions and don't really allow for 'tech', but that plays in their favor. A wallrun seems suited for the movement expected from the player, but doesn't feel necessary given the less intrusive wall-hop. I had to turn mouse sensitivity to 200% to make it feel responsive, the option's there and it works well.
Potato graphics. Great gameplay. Highly recommend.

This game is awesome. I'll give it 10 / 10 in the future.
It has one wonderfull thing, which few of today's games have - it's own, specific CLIMATE. You feel it from the first seconds of play. Things which build up for it are:
1. STORY
You wake up in the middle of nowhere, with no weapon, nor food. The heat of your body constantly falling. There's no time to think, you must act. The game pulls you in at the very beginning and keeps it that way.
2. GAMEPLAY
You constantly need to do something. You're either hungry, thirsty, cold or exhausted. At some point it may gets little tiresome, because you wish you had more time for exploring things and this beautiful world, but if you carry on, you'll explore it anyway (Sandbox).
The game is hard. There's only sandbox mode available with one area, but it gave me 10 hours of solid gameplay anyway. I consider full game with story mode and few more sandbox areas will give at least a couple of times this.
3. GRAPHICS
It is made by a renowned artist Hokyo Lim, author of i.a. The Unfisnished Swan
. He's an out-of-the-box thinker.
Sometimes, you feel like watching a very good movie. But mostly, you feel like you're actually there. Standing there at the top of the mountain and admiring views. Some people may consider it looking a bit too fairy-tale-like, but for me it is suiting.
4. SOUND
The sound effects are what builds up the atmosphere and they are very real. At some point even the howling wind gives you chills because it sounds similiar to the wolf's howling.
The music is heard only occasionally, but the moments choosen to play it build up the atmosphere even more.
There are two PC available - man and woman. Man is vioced by the Mass Effect no.1 voice actor Mark Meer. Female - I don't know, but I think she's not a professionall voice actress or at least for me her voices are disturbing.
CONS:
The game got kind of tiresome after ~10h and a few deaths. There's lot of walking in the beginning and tt's also easy to die. If you die you loose your save. So, if you're hunted down on 2nd day due to distraction, you have to replay the whole part before it really got fun. I think it requires some sort of calibration yet.
To sum it up: This game is made by professionals, who left big gaming companies to create offbeat titles. It has great graphics, music, and nice gameplay. When the story mode will be available, it will be unbelievably good. I predict it will deliver one of the best gaming experience in a long time. And I don't mean survival enthusiasts.

Another game from Zachtronics that I cannot recommend enough. Many people are calling it "SpaceChem in 3d" which is a fair description, but doesn't really capture the fun of finally guiding your blocks through twists and turns to get them synced up and in the right position at exactly the right time to have your construct output correctly.
The overarching storyline is a bit minimal, but the real fun is in solving the puzzles in new ways. There's that sense of accomplishment when you see your machine completing the task, especially when your results compare favorably with the global statistics. There are audio logs from previous solvers scattered throughout the levels which add to the world, but are not needed to enjoy the game.
As with SpaceChem, on occasion, I find some puzzles to be immediately obvious even at later levels, while others I sometimes have to think about for a while before a possible solution emerges. There are also some quirks of which control block takes precedence that you will have to work around and/or exploit to get the jobs finished.
Community created puzzles are available in the Steam Workshop, but prepare to be challenged by them. The community seems to pride themselves on devious puzzle crafting.
Overall, one of the most fun games I have played all year.

Besides writing and studenting I work as a night security guard to pay for my extravagant, luxurious needs (food, water, shelter). And it doesn't matter the setting or location, working at night can be very unsettling. Alone with your thoughts in a dimly lit ANYPLACE during the witching hour can be literally the worst thing ever. The clock tick tocks mockingly as time slows to a crawl and the night grows darker with each passing hour. I'm not a spiritual person... but around three or four in the morning, third cup of coffee in hand and heavy-lidded eyes blinking in futility at the specter of sleep, you start to hear things. Snaps and cracks from the wind. Chittering and chattering from various nocturnal animals. A flash of light across your face as a lonely car makes a very slow u-turn. A bang from something somewhere. And you start to wonder: are you experiencing auditory hallucinations or did you just hear a baby cry? So you walk outside for some fresh air. And just where the light from a distant street lamp falters to the shadows you see something standing. Just. Barely. Noticeable.
Just waiting for you to shut your eyes.
That paragraph best sums up my experience with “Five Nights At Freddy's.” It is a panic attack simulator ingeniously disguised as a game. You're a recently hired security guard at Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, a kid friendly pizza party parlor with a sordid, spotted past. For instance, most previous night guards are MURDERED BY HAUNTED ANIMATRONIC ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥T. And you will be too unless you're hyper diligent. See, not only is Freddy's HAUNTED BY THE LIVING EMBODIMENTS OF EVERY CHILDHOOD NIGHTMARE YOU'VE EVER SUFFERED, it also has an incredibly tight budget (Freddy's is likely crippled financially by dozens of lawsuits). They have only so much energy to expend from twelve at night to dawn. Your working hours. You'll have to manage that as you check video camera feeds, turn on the lights just outside your office, and seal your two office doors.
When your night begins everything is hunky dory and all the animatronic monstrosities are SILENT AND STILL AS THEY SHOULD ALWAYS BE. But as the night progresses and you check your feed you'll find some things... off. Wait, wasn't Freddy on stage a minute ago? Now he's in the dining area. And huh, where did the ♥♥♥♥ing rabbit goooooOOOOHHHHHHHH ♥♥♥♥!
And then you find out where Bonnie the Bunny went.
He went into your office.
To eat your eyes.
So you'll have to be, as I said, diligent. Keep your eyes peeled for the scoundrels as they make their way towards your office. If they get too close (go on, turn the light on just outside the door and have a heart attack) just seal the door. But for every nervous glance at the feed, every light flicked on, and every door slammed shut, your power will drain, eventually leading to an outage. And God help you if that happens. I'm just kidding!
There is no God.
Only Freddy.
At the end of the night (assuming you survive) you'll start another... if you'd like.

What this game gets right though is what I think it was going for: the awesome feeling of speed and momentum. That is what kept me playing to the end. It was awesome to run on rails that gave you superspeed, jump right before a giant hole, and fly through the air to the next part of the corridor. Awesome feeling... one that I don't think I've had in a game before.
But in my mind, sadly there is a huge con...
It's made in Unity, and it seems to be quite unoptimized. I have an i7 7700k, gtx 1080 and 16 GB Ram, as well as have this  game installed to my primary ssd. As it's Unity it's very GPU based. My GPU immediately shot up to 99% for the entire game, while my CPU stayed around 20%. My fps would swing from 144 (rarely) and around 28-32 (most of the time.) Even if I turned own AA to medium, it would only push the average up to about 38-40. That's just unacceptable, especially in a game based around movement. Now, I will say that it didn't seem to lag even though the fps were as low as they were, but there's no reason they should have been in the first place.
Regardless though, I'd still recommend it. I had it on my wishlist for quite awhile, but luckily found it in a bundle. I'd be hard pressed to say $20 is worth it (for me, at least) but it's on sale all the time, so if you can get it for $5-$10 and have a couple hours on a rainy day, it's well worth it.

How to solve a puzzle in Infinifactory:
1) Look at the output and think, "That's not so hard, let me put this here and that over there."
2) Run your experiment.
3) Swear because it's nowhere near what you thought it would be.
4) Swear again.
5) Come up with a rickety solution that works under one use case but falls apart on others. (This is exactly like some real-world programming!)
6) Marvel as your friends come up with more elegant, faster solutions.
7) Realize that you're having a tremendous time.
I don't know what Zachtronics has against the human brain or why he wants to punish it so, but I encourage his behavior. Great game, they've been very good about expanding it and refining puzzles. Recommended.

While at this point the Tetrobot is the most popular and best robot around, it is not immune to problems. The Psychobot’s job is to go into Tetrobot and fix whatever problems my lay inside.
So what exactly do you do in this game? Well, you move blocks. Blocks that matter, to be specific. The game follows an extremely similar style of logic and mechanics that Blocks that Matter does, since they both play out in the same universe. The goal is to maneuver throughout the Tetrobot, finding as many pieces of memory that you can along with getting to the end. Unlike the puzzle platformer style of game play the previous game had, this plays more like it is on a  grid. The Psychobot flies through Tetrobots to wherever it needs to be.
Fixing a Tetrobot isn’t easy, though. It is actually quite the puzzle, as they get a lot of blocks clogged up into their system. You have to manipulate these blocks so that you can continue on through certain passage ways and areas. Blocks connect to blocks of the same matter. So stone will connect to stone, wood will connect to wood, and so on.  Knowing how to correctly stack blocks will be very helpful for maneuvering through these levels.
It is never hard to relax and play this game. Everything about the game is very soothing. If you would like you can slowly make your way through each puzzle, taking your time and taking in everything the game has to offer. Just as Blocks that Matter was, this game is very charming. I always manage to have a smile on my face when playing through it, either it be the satisfaction of solving the puzzles or even just picking up on some of the funny references they have to different games, books, movies, and music!
The pacing in the game is pretty nice as well. In total there are 8 sections in the game, each containing 5 normal levels and one key level. Each section slowly adds new mechanics, making game play more complicated yet all the more fun. You never feel overloaded on all of the things you have to learn or solve, but it never drags on either. The Tetrobots act as the sections, each having their own issues. Either they be flooded with water or even frozen! Each Tetrobot’s problem will advance and change the game play, which makes for an excellent thrill when going into a new section.
Besides the overall satisfaction of being able to solve some of these complicated puzzles, the game really helps you feel rewarded for your efforts to progress through the game. There are a lot of cool and interesting unlockables from not only completing the puzzles but collecting the 3 memory blocks there are in each level. Either it is more pieces to the story, a few extra levels, or a collection of all of the soothing songs available. You really have this drive to continue playing through the game.
Tetrobot & Co. was a unique game to play through. Its charming style kept me relaxed as I challenged my mind with each level. Swing Swing Submarine really has a way with puzzle games. If you really enjoy puzzle games then I highly suggest you give this one a try.
If you want some video footage going a tad more in depth on how it plays, then make sure you check out my video on it!

Outlast did a lot of things right, but a few crucial things very very wrong.
Let me strart off by saying that this game can definitely play in the same league as Amnesia TDD, when it comes to being scary. The problem is, though, that most of the scary parts in this game, especially early on, are jumpscares. Those really only work once.
That is a concern, as the game uses a checkpoint system. Be aware that the "save & quit" option in the pause menu does NOT work like the one in Amnesia. All Outlast saves is your collected notes, NOT your actual progress. Same goes for dieing in the middle of a puzzle. You'll have to do it over again from the last checkpoint (which is usually before the puzzle). This takes away a lot on the immersion for me, and completely eradicates any fun  in playing the game.
The controls also felt akward for me, since you have to manually toggle out of crouching to be able to sprint. Usually pressing sprint would automatically untoggle a crouch, in my experience. Especially if you just failed sneaking by an enemy, that can be fatal to the ingame character, and make you loose all progress since the last checkpoint.
I find it incredible how such little things can ruin the fun in a game. I wouldn't buy this again, that's for sure.

Infinifactory is my favorite puzzle game I've played in a long while, maybe ever. It's all the programmy goodness of Spacechem (and Zach's earlier browser games) but in a beautiful 3D environment with some cool storytelling mixed in.
Infinifactory is a puzzle game, but different than what you may be used to in this genre. You're given a set of input blocks, and must maneuver, combine, and reconfigure these blocks to match a specific output on the other side of the map. It's incredibly open-ended in how this is accomplished, allowing for some brilliantly simple, or horrifyingly overly complicated solutions to the same problem.
Difficulty curve is nice and smooth, reaching a peak difficulty that will require some serious time and thinking to work through, but was never hard enough to get me to give up entirely. Adding a bunch of folks to your Steam friends to compare scores with adds an extra level of replayability by giving you the opportunity to optimize your solutions to get a few cycles under your buddies.
Infinifactory was further reviewed by myself and my good friend Gary in episode 38 of our podcast Check it Out, Comrade! Give it a listen!

I bought this through a recent bundle deal and wasn't sure from the description whether I'd like it or not. It's quite different from any other 1st person game I've played and is quite relaxing to play in some ways. It's never frantic like a lot of shooters tend to be, the gameplay isn't that hard and the levels are enormous.
Pros:
The outdoors look fantastic and you get a real sense of size and space.
Easy to get into and play.
Gameplay is fun.
Levels and game is well designed and makes you want to play just one more mission!
Playing for 20 minutes turns out to be 3hrs ;)
The music is quite good (and really irritating too, see below).
Cons:
Controls! I'm a lefty and you can't change the key mappings (set for right handed players!) in the game. You have to launch the config utility for the game from within your Steam library in order to remap keys. What a pain in the backside that is!!! Oh, and if you launch the game any other way than via the library, it will ignore your mappings. From what I've read, this is a problem with the Unity Engine and not the game itself.
Music - every time I launch the game, I have to go into options and turn the music off. Even though it's set to silent in options, it still plays! Some new levels loading cause the music to start playing again and you have to turn it off, again. Really, really annoying bug!
Linear - Ok, so the outdoor scenes are massive and look open. You can explore as much as you like and there are hidden crates in some odd places. The problem is that despite this illusion of it being an open game, there's only one exit to each scene/level/mission or whatever name you want to use. It's a linear game dressed up (cleverly, I might add) as an open world. That is a con because I don't like linear games and yet hasn't spoilt the game because it's well hidden in the level design.
Variety - I think I'm almost near the end of the game after 4hrs+ and it is becoming a bit samey now. There's just not quite enough in each level to keep me as interested as there was to begin with.
All in all, a very good game and it does deserve all the positive reviews and praise. Full price is currently just under £15 and I don't think it's worth quite that much. For me, just under ten would have been more realistic.

The Forgotten Ones is an interesting enough game for fans of the Horror genre. While it falls short of many other small independantly developed games, in the same genre. (Cry of Fear comes to mind, when I think of small, independently developed Horror games. That I hold to high standards.)
It's still a worthwhile title to check out, and waste a few hours playing. Despite many of the negative reviews this title has recieved. I feel that the game is getting a much worse rap than it in all honesty, deserves.
Finishing the game, and getting all of the achievements. I've say I'd have my fair share of the game, to give it a reccomendation.
However, this game is indeed for the niche crowd that does not mind playing with the games mechanics in order to survive.
In short, abusing exlpoits in the games engine in order to complete the game.
Now you may be able to get through the game without resorting to abusing the enemy AI, I for one, found it all but neccesary.
Pros:
+Good atmosphere, has a very unsetlling setting in some areas in particular.
+Decent ambient soundtrack and noises, although some can get pretty repetitive when they loop infinitly.
+Varied weapons, and they all feel and sound powerful.
+No Crosshairs, you must use the iron sights if you wish to hit an enemy accurately, and the iron sights are well done.
+Scarce ammo and health pickups, you can only carry one spare medkit at a time, you can only save at certain locations. It really hit homes the survival horror vibe it's going for.
+I really dig the puzzle elements and inventory management system that is included with the game. Though the puzzles are not the hardest. They more than enough suffice for such a small dev team on this game.
Cons
-First and foremost, the enemies are incredibly hard to survive unless you abuse the enemy AI. (i.e. Jumping ontop of a high placed object, just out of reach of an enemy's attack.)
They require lots of ammo to put down, unless you consistantly place headshots. They are very fast, and worse of all, their attacks will stun lock you, making you move to a snails crawl and most certainly will spell your doom, if you get backed into a corner.
-There are several bugs that are common I have experienced. Getting stuck in place after loading an area, requires you go back through the door and back again to move, or in worst case's, a full restart from last save.
Constantly getting stuck on objects, where you have to pick them up and throw them in able to move.
-The framerate is absolutely inconsitent. I have a GTX 970 SLi setup, and it goes from 200+ to 20's and lower many times. So prepare yourself for a slide show at times.
-And lastly, picking up key items, and ammo is maddening. You have to be a pixel perfect reach in order to pick up anything, and most of the time there is no indication that you can grab it or not, so may pass up some ammo, thinking that you are full for that weapon, only later to realize you can grab it later on, just you weren't approaching it at the right angle.
Overall, I would say try this game out, if you are a horror fiend. And don't mind a few glitches and bugs here and there.
I will warn you that it is tough as nails, thanks to the incredibly reslient and fast enemies.
If you don't mind lots of trial and error, than this game may worthwhile for you to pick up.

I have thus far played through what I take to be the majority of the game and have really enjoyed it. I have found it to be refreshingly different from anything else I've played. Its free flowing movement system and clever way of unfolding the narrative are very well paired with an affective music score and beautiful environments. I do have two particular gripes with it however, which have given me reason to write this review granted that I don't usually bother to do so.
Firstly the save system is pretty old school in that you start at the beginning of each level whenever you load up the game. It's not an awful hindrance given the fast pace at which you can traverse the levels, but it does seem to be an unneccesary bother.
Secondly and most significantly is the lack of reward for exploration. There is a MASSIVE potential for exploration in this game because of its sprawling level designs and the way in which the L.E.A.F suit enables you to traverse the environment. I have continually exploited this, but am very rarely rewarded for it. There are item pick-ups throughout the game, but the vast majority are in plain sight. There are also "acorn doors" which are non-essential to the games completion and the majority of these are in plain sight too. I wonder if the developers have done this to encourage a fast paced playing style, but given that the game lends itself to that naturally I think they ought to have made room for a slower pace too. I have continually felt let down that my exploring yields no extra reward and feel as though the developers have gone to the trouble of designing something huge without providing an extra incentive to explore and make the most of it.
All of that being said the pros still very much weigh out the cons here. I have been continually drawn back to the game to unfold its story, environments, sounds and game mechanics.

Gosh, it's hard to review this game without saying what's already been said times and times again. In short, this game is probably the most enjoyable sandbox-blow-everything-up game you'll ever play. It's still to be surpassed, which Just Cause 3 failed to do, though it's also a fairly enjoyable game.
Graphics-wise, it's still holds up for its time, and is arguably much better done than a lot of games lately : it's detailed, it's colorful, it's dynamic and it's optimised.
The gameplay is where the game truly shines, and where all the fun and enjoyment are coming. It's fast paced, easy to get used to and just really, really, REALLY fun. You go around with your infinite grappling hooks and parachutes and destroys buildings upon buildings, military bases upon military bases, and you never stop. Some people might find this boring, and I can understand, as it tends to be repetitive, but the visuals and the gameplay go hand in hand to give the player an enjoyable experience.
The story, the characters and this kind of stuff is where Just Cause 2 truly lacks audacity and overall quality. The dialogues are mostly boring and uninteresting, the characters are shallow AF, and the story is, well, almost inexistant. This is a shame, because even though one will play this game for its gameplay and explosions, it would have been nice to have a story to actually follow.
The music is pretty good, though you don't pay attention to it often.
Overall, a really nice game with a solid gameplay and nice graphics that promises explosions and gives you tons of them. A must-have for anyone wanting to blow stuff up !

I think this game was rougher during the launch window, but as a fan of the Shadowrun Returns series, I also like this game.  The main campaign is fun so far, and has decent to good voice acting, and the tactics are simplified from Shadowrun Returns, but still enjoyable.  Honestly, I like the streamlining for the most part, although I don't like how you can't switch to real time travel outside of combat.  It's turn based all the time, even when you're done fighting and want to explore and collect things.
That's the main flaw with this game, alongside the fact that it's got a mostly linear story with not much choice.  The graphics, sound and music are good, albeit low-poly with no lip-synching, but I don't mind that.  The character customization is surprisingly good, with a lot of fun clothes, although the small number of pre-made portraits can be disappointing, especially the 2 (count them 2 total) for the Dwarf Female.
I wish there was a way to just use your avatar's 3D model as a portrait, and that you could just switch to real time for times outside of combat.  Other than that, it's a surprisingly enjoyable game.  I'm glad I took a risk and bought this game in the Humble Store's create your own bundle for THQ Nordic games.  Fans of turn-based strategy, story, and Shadowrun can probably find something to like in this game.

Unfortunately, unlike SR: Dragonfall and SR: Hong Kong this game completely throws out the unique 'classes' of Shadowrun and opts instead for classes built around whatever weapon your holding.  The 'classes' in this game are called Skills: Blunt, Blades, Summoning, Spellcasting, Shotguns, Automatics, Pistols, Rigging, Hacking, Body, and Mind.
The games graphics are a mixed bag.  The players and npcs are poorly rendered however the backgrounds are gorgeous.  You can customize your characters looks (and the game gives you plenty of options to pick from).  You randomly get new “loot” during missions by finding new pieces of clothing for your character to wear to further customize your appearance.
There is one saving grace for SR Chronicles and that is the multiplayer component.  You can higher NPCs to go with you however they are by far weaker than players.  The game really shines when you take friends with you on the very difficult tower defense type missions that you normally have no chance at winning solo.  So far this has kept me coming back to a game that is only SR in name.
I can only mourn what could have been here.  If this game used the same assets that made SR: Dragonfall/Hong Kong (Physical Adepts, etc.) AND the multiplayer aspect here then this game would be a must get.  For now, skip it unless you are willing to overlook that its only SR in spirit,  fun co-op game.

Five Nights at Freddy's is  a one-note joke, a single mechanic, and a single location and manages to take it to a hilarious extreme. Despite the overall lack of depth in gameplay and frustrating difficulty, I still find this game to be a unique experience. It's refreshingly simple and does a good job of breaking free from a lot of the cliche's of modern horror games, especially once you realize that this game does not take itself seriously. At all.
The game is simple: you are a security guard at a pizza parlour that includes animatronic animal entertainers. You work the night shift. The animatronic animals like to "roam around" at night. You have a limited amount of power with which to use security cameras to keep track of them, and keep the doors to your office (the only physical location in the game) closed when the animals get too close. If you don't keep track of their movements and they enter, then you're dead. Power tends to run out pretty fast, so the main aspect of the game is that of resource management.
It's a simple mechanic, yes, but it will have you frantically switching between the cameras as you lose track of one of the bots, and as panic mounts you'll realize that HE'S RIGHT OUTSIDE THE DOOR! I can see this game being a big hit if played on a big screen at a party or something, considering how fast it plays and how simple it is. As power drains and tension rises it can be hard to focus on conserving power, and when the end comes it is usually hilarious.
My main problem with the game is that it's a one-note joke that wears thin after awhile. If you are wanting to play this as a serious game, then move on. It's a gag that will entertain you for 3 hours max, until you let someone else play and don't tell them anything about it. Then you'll get more enjoyment. And probably fewer friends :D
For five dollars, I recommend this game. I think it's a good price for something that's a light-hearted, more competent and slick version of the scary maze game. It tells me that the makers understood what they were doing and didn't want to make the game out to be anything more than it is. And for those of you that think you shouldn't buy it because you've seen a youtube video of it, I'd give the game more credit than that. You don't know what it's like until you're sitting in the security office panning frantically between cameras, hearing them singing ominously in the dark halls of the pizza parlour. YOU DON'T KNOW WHAT IT'S LIKE, MAN!

Is it possible to really understand another human being? Is it even meaningful to try? When we try to analyze something, are we just projecting our own biases onto it? These are tall, open-ended questions that The Beginner's Guide tries to answer. What you get out of it, like most things in life, depends on you.
The game opens with Davey Wreden introducing himself as the writer of The Stanley Parable, a work he proudly calls "absurd". This game, he says, will be different. Delivering on that promise, The Beginner's Guide asks you not to make a series of choices, but to try and understand where a person was coming from as he created a series of video games. Wreden lets you play these games, frequently interjecting to give you his opinion on what everything means, but what really matters is what you take from the experience.
Traditional gameplay elements are sparse and accusations of being a "waking simulator" will probably appear in droves, but that shouldn't impede players interested in the process of making and understanding games.  The Beginner's Guide is one of the most unique experiences of 2015, staying with you long after you exit the game.

A survival horror game that needs a little bit more polish and a few bug fixes. A new update to the game improved on alot of the problems. There is still more work to do however.
What i liked:
-The game uses the cry of fear ammo mechanic (which means when you reload any bullets in that mag are gone) which punishes those who always reload after firing 5 rounds in a 30 round mag
-the weapons feel good as well as a nice variety
-Fun to shoot those evil things
-interesting bleed out mechanic
-enemies spawn randomly keeping tension up
-good atmosphere
-voice acting is pretty good (props to the guy that dies first [the character he voiced was Gregor])
What i did not like:
*-Optimization issues (large framerate drops) lack of video settings such as: shadows, Anti Aliasing etc.
-cliche "they killed my loved ones, they must pay!" plot (should have just stuck with you are a police officer investigating and hunting down a nazi war criminal from WW2)
-annoying ambient sounds can be irritating to the eardrums (the spot where you first encounter edward)
-The final boss is a bullet sponge. Which means the only way to beat thim is to A) use your teamates as canon fodder or B)create a barricade and then play peek a boo. (well at least he was a boss unlike the halo 4 didact which was QTE bs).__*the boss has been improved his accuracy has been reduced however i still recomend using step A or B
*---------------------*
Changes i liked:
-melee weapons have been removed, however now when you quick melee it knocks enemies back which is very handy and much apreciated
-Enemies damage and attack speed have been toned down (very apreciated) players now have a chance to actually survive close encounters
-2 more random enemy spawn have been added
-The character will now be able to pick up ammo first instead of phys objects (much apreciated)
-The diner scene has been improved, it no longer takes forever cycling through dialog with sheizel
Changes i did not like:
-Inventory now takes a few seconds to open and close as opposed to previous version that you could open up in an instant.
-the ending has changed *spoiler alert* you now meet mafiosos, i have been unable to find a way to avoid them since the only way to go is either thru the cellar or you get teleported straight away to them.
Side note: A few extra monster spawns are needed in the Library, staircases in rightwing area, the main room at the front entrance of mansion, the room above the diner and after beating the boss statue as well as the courtyard.

Nothing more eerie than the Canadian wilderness to really immerse yourself in a survival sandbox. You ever watch those survival shows and imagine what you would do in those situations if they dropped you off in the middle of nowhere? Well look no further - The Long Dark does not hold back in the harsh bitter cold as it drops you off with no hand holding as you have to very quickly figure out how to survive. At this stage, it is definitely still an alpha - not all features are enabled yet, and there are some features that I don't really like:
- Clothes are destroyed way too quickly - I understand that they deteriorate, but within a day? Realistically, that is not the case
- Even the cheapest can opener can last longer than a few cans - some of the tools break way too quickly
A nice thing (or not so nice thing) is that there are no real instructions - learning is trial and error (and in most cases, death) so a lot of gameplay potential.
Overall, I am quite pleased with the gameplay so far - but there is still quite a bit of work to be done (especially with the main storyline still to be released), but the sandbox can be very fun for those who relish in such a challenge. I look forward to seeing the improvements and new features to be added.

My first challenging mission in The Forgotten Ones:  To work out how to pick up my gun and ammunition.  This alone took me many minutes, as the keyboard mapping section of the Options didn't seem to cover an "action" button, and "E" was apparently already taken (and un-remappable).  Trial and error eventually informed me that the key I was searching for was "F" (this would not be the last "key" I would have to find in the course of this cliché-ridden if somewhat enjoyable quasi-mess of a game, just for the record).  My second mission:  To, er, go get some take-away food for some greasy friend of mine in a hotel lobby.  He didn't even seem particularly grateful once I gave it to him - quite dismissive, actually - but hey, you can't always expect substantial rewards for all the good deeds you commit in this world.  I guess that this and a couple of other bits where you get to choose what you say to people - to no apparent consequence - are this game's concession to the oh-so-modern notion of "open-world gaming".  (Thank ♥♥♥♥, it was mostly linear from there on in.)  Then it's into my beaten-up old jalopy, and off into a crazy, incomprehensible world of horror and (mis)adventure...

The Forgotten Ones is daft, but fun.  Not entirely competent, but fine.  Hardly inspired, but reasonably entertaining, and perhaps all the more crucially, FREE.  It's actually quite scary and suspenseful, thanks in no small part to the excellent sound design (apart from the bits where characters actually TALK, which are borderline inaudible...but perhaps thankfully so).  It's also quite hard, but not TOO agonisingly so (though the combat is frankly appalling - melee weapons being a vast improvement over GUNS most of the time! - but said fights are thankfully few and far between).  Think of it as a second-rate Cry Of Fear - itself a flawed but charming game - then add in a trashy (if lovingly realised) WWII/nazi setting, and you're mostly there.  Not a masterpiece by any stretch, but what do you expect for nuthin'?  Recommended to any horror game fans who can lower their expectations suitably when they're given something for free.  Certainly preferable to a swift kick in the eye, if only by a small margin.

Verdict: 6.5/10.

(PS I somehow managed to get an achievement where I spotted Slenderman...even though I completely failed, in the event, to see him at all.  There's also a bunch of Pewdiepie/Stephano references, and a visit to the Resident Evil 1 mansion.  Welcome to the era of post-post-post-post-modernism, kiddies.)

(PPS Didn't even bother to finish it, though walkthroughs tell me I was close to the end.  I'm sorry, but I simply lacked the willpower to work out where all the valves I had to turn were.  And besides, the end "boss battle" looked decidedly♥♥♥♥♥♥♥and anti-climactic anyway.)
