- The class you develop is bond to certain questlines you may or may not follow (details down aswell)
- Miserable graphics even for the year it came out
- Interaction with the game world is non-existent
- Characters are anonymous, uninteresting and inexpressive. It looks like talking to (badly) animated tree stumps.
===
This is an extraordinaire section i made just for THIS review, in which i will explain to you, esteemed reader, the abyssal flaws i have described up above.
1. Combat System: Risen's combat system, regarding melee mostly, is such a mess i have rarely witnessed in my whole gaming career. First of all, attack patterns, movement animations, speed, parry system are wholly flawed beyond repair. Enemies can dodge your attacks which is fine, but they can aswell attack just after they dodged, in the span of a tenth of a second, which you cannot do at all, and then repeat their attack animation a random number of times consecutively, this can very certainly end up with your character being 1-shotted by an unstoppable series of attacks you cannot parry, for there is a little delay between when you are wounded and when you can again parry; this delay is larger than the delay between the enemy attacks, so you cannot do any action while under a barrage of attacks.
Secondly, facing multiple enemies is totally unfeasible: you can focus your attention on just one direction while attacking, your attacks are bond to follow that direction as long as the animation goes on. This means, you cannot, say, hit one enemy with a slash then hit another one near him and then a third one. Attacking one enemy leaves you totally exposed from all other directions, from which enemy can attack you like i described before. Player cannot even lure single enemies, as triggering combat with one will very likely trigger the whole enemy field and drag you to a multiple combat you have zero chances to win, unless said enemies are very far below your level.
Third, animations are clunky, unresponsive and generally really messy. Players will have trouble timing attacks and also to spot when an enemy is going to attack, since there is no pre-attack animations, nothing, enemies just stand there then attack instantly without any little notice, and then return to their idle animation.
2. Character Development: Oh boy here we go. first of all your class is bond to the storyline you might want to follow: for example if you choose to be a bandit, you will not be able to be a mage. This because when you level up, this game has no normal RPG style level up system, but instead gives you Learning Points, and nothing else. These points can be used at specific trainers around the world to improve your Statistics or Abilities. Fact is, certain branches of the Main Quest will allow you only to learn certain classes' skills as i said before. This limits the experience a player may want to pursue heavily. Also, trainers cost Gold, each ability you learn costs gold, and also Statistics cost gold, other than Learning Points.
This system is totally failed and limits the developmetn of your character by a lot.
===
Risen could be a nice game with its setting and storyline, but many gameplay-breaking issues and bad art direction flaw this game beyond salvation.
I do not recommend this game at all, unless you just want a world of pain and suffering.

This is probably the best Heroes of Might and Magic game. While Heroes II had better campaigns in it, the Heroes VI campaigns remain good. The AI is excellent - a serious challenge to beat in some battles.
Heroes VI also removes one of the most tedious things about HOMM (and i say that as someone who loves these games), which is having to do a running tour of all your cities to keep your armies equalling or outnumbering the AI's.
In Heroes VI you can recruit troops with a hero in any town, from any town, speeding things up massively.
The option to build advanced town portals that let you teleport between towns you control speed things up again. And since the AI can build the same portals it doesn't make the game any easier.
Heroes of different factions also get completely different skill trees from one another, which adds to the variety of the game a lot.
The graphics are nice, so is the music.
The one downside to Heroes VI compared to earlier games in the series is that to get the best starting bonuses you can get you have to play it online via uplay, which, when you're playing single player, is just a bit of a pain that slows starting a new game or loading a saved one down a bit.
This is a minor annoyance though in what is basically a really great game.
Some HOMM fans deride Heroes VI for having made some changes to previous games. The mess of Heroes VII resulting from trying to go backwards instead of forwards shows how mistaken those people are imo.
The one thing that Heroes VI hasn't changed is that it's still in big part a matter of who can recruit more troops faster - but that's a flaw in the basic type of game it is, not this version of it.

A fantastic puzzle game. It's rock solid stable, looks good and has lots of content as well as an interesting storyline. If you liked SpaceChem then you'll love Infinifactory.
As others have said It's basically SpaceChem in 3D, concepts of reactors and piping are more or less combined, with conveyers taking the place of the latter, and the entire level being the reactor. The same concept of optimising cycles (time), number of components used and now overall footprint of components is present.
Finding a solution, and then tweaking to optimise is a dream come true for us OCD types out there! The game will rank your solution for a given challenge against the population playing the game, so that you can see where you score. It's difficult, and sometimes impossible to rank highly in each area. Decreasing cycle time will increase block count for example. Improving one of the three scores will usually come at the cost of one or both of the others.
Zachtronics stands out for me as a real leader in modern puzzle games. Great challenge, lots of replayability, user created content and a sandbox mode! For those that like their puzzle games, I can't reccomend it enough.

Let me just put this straight: This game is absolutely amazing. Despite the Early Access tag, it feels fully fleshed out, I have not yet found a single flaw or bug and I've been enjoying Infinifactory with every new puzzle being thrown at me.
You get a few blocks as inputs, you rotate them, stamp them, weld them and do other stuff to get the required output. When you get 10 outputs, you complete the puzzle. It sounds simple, but as the later levels introduce new mechanics, blocks and other stuff, the game becomes a thousand times harder, but in a challenging way. You try your best to solve the puzzle, you fail, you modify your design, fail again, try to change things up and voila! It works! And it's extremely satisfying to see your contraption work flawlessly after you're done. I found myself looking at every single block in my factories for at least a few minutes before moving on to the next puzzle. What I absolutely love doing is just randomly picking one block and looking at where it'll end up in the finished object.
From the start of the game to about its half, I went through each puzzle in about 15-25 minutes, so it wasn't hard. Right now I'm at the last few puzzles, and I just can't solve them! I manage to solve one a day, and even then I realise that there must be a better solution! It drives you to improve, optimize your factory and just look at the mechanisms doing their work, slowly combining little bits and pieces into one cool-looking object.
There was one time when I built the complete factory for a puzzle, then I see the very first finished 'instance' of the output making its way to the finish line, and then suddenly the game yells at me. It says that I have a hole in my object that shouldn't be there! I look at the object that arrived, I look at the needed output... and then I realise that it's true. I made such an easy way of solving the puzzle at the start, then I just had to add a few small pieces and ship it to the output point, and now I have to come to the very beginning of my solution to try and change it to fit what is required, and I have no clue how to do that. I spent approximately 15-20 minutes just trying to fix the flaw in my existing design, but it was really satisfying to see it work in the end, and have another 'puzzle completed' tick in the menu.
80% of people have already stopped reading this, but I'd like to add just one more thing. Since I'm a person which absolutely loves sandbox games, unlocking the Level Editor after completing a bit more than half of the game was a "♥♥♥♥ YEAH!" moment for me. I instantly jumped in and saw that there were two options: "Simple" and "Advanced." I went for Simple first, it gave me an open hangar and a few blocks to build my puzzle with. I built something, solved it to be able to upload it to the Workshop and then uploaded it. However, there were barely any blocks from the full game that I could place down, and the space in the hangar was still limited. I wished I could build in other environments from the game and add features that you come across in certain levels but never do again. I became really sad, and I was going to find a suggestion thread for the game to ask to improve the Level Editor by adding more stuff into it. However, I completely forgot about the "Advanced" mode of the editor. After I quit my custom puzzle, I glanced at the menu, saw it and remembered that there was another mode! I hastily clicked on it and what I saw completely blew my mind! It was a genuine Level Editor, it had all the different environments from the game, EVERY single block type, EVERY feature that the game had and slightly modified and expanded puzzle options! It felt more like a genuine developer editor than a small thing for players to build their own puzzles with. There were special blocks like invisible conveyors, invisible blocks, level borders, a starting position block, the map origin and so on and so forth.  In the block menu, all the blocks are labeled with text instead of icons, that's because there are hundreds of available blocks. At first it's a bit hard to navigate, but after you get used to it, you start finding all the blocks you need in no time. Granted, this kind of editor would not suit every single player, and it's good that Zach seperated the two editors, but for players like me, which are really into game design and understand how developers actually make their game, it was really easy to get used to and I'm really glad that it's possible to create the same environments as the actual game instead of sitting in the same hangar with the same blocks and very limited options available to you.
Overall, the game is amazing, if you like puzzles, buy it right now. You get your money's worth completely, if not more than what you've actually payed for. The game is interesting, it has a very good difficulty curve and is worth playing until the very end. Now, the game was developed by a single person, and seeing how great and flawless everything in the game is, it's more than a huge achievement for the developer, Zach. I'd say that puzzle-lovers should definitely buy the game even in Early Access because it's as good as the consumer version would be. It's great.

Everything considered this is a fantastic game and if you have any interest you would be a fool not to give it a try.

This game was wonderful! Terribly addicting. I have to admit I love the choose-your-own adventure aspect of it all, and the storylines behind each of the dynasties is fascianting. It was fun to spot the little references to one another and to The Deed itself. Although I've managed to get all the achievements (and those last few were a fun pain in the tuckus to try to get!) I probably will still come back to it at some point just to try out all the different lines of dialogue and see what happens.
I also really loved the moral struggles that I ended up going through with this as I tried to hit all the achievements, and the way the MC themselves reacted to said struggles at the end.
Of the three dynasties, I probably found 1868's storyline more compelling, though 1401 had more play time. The endings of 1895 felt a little dissatisfying at times, but I have to admit I personally love Margaret Percy and all the intrigue that's hinted at in her interactions with the different characters-- That's probably the one I'll be going back to the most to see what happens of just picking any of the responses!
Overall, highly highly recommend, though I'd say definitely use with a proper mouse as it makes certain aspects of gameplay a little easier, IMO. If you don't feel like feeling a little morally wrong after this may not be the game for you, but if you don't mind that and love stories, this is the one for you!

1. Game Mechanics : classic RPG maker game so simple key was used (arrow/ esc button/ mouse). Nothing special game related. Fortunately there is Shift button to faster the MC movement.

3. Sounds : well, it match the situation in the game, but no special made up OST.
4. Story : this is the part where this game is special and different than the rest of games I've played so far. There's three different story, with three different characters and motives. The MC is always a person who wants to kill someone so badly based on revenge or hatred. We now must kill the target and try to blame someone for the deed. Basically this game resembles CLUE the boardgame, if you're familiar with it. There's a person, a murder weapon and alibi.
5. Replayability Value : trust me, to achieve all the achievement is the challenge for this game. Killing a person is so much easier compared to achieving all the achievements. Good luck to replay them 1000 times and try to complete all the achievements ^^.
6. Fun Factor : who said it isn't fun to kill person and try to get away with it?
7. Value for Full Price : to support the great developers out there, why not? This is the first game I buy on Steam, because it cost less than $5. Now I really am grateful to buy this one and look at my gameplay hours!
8. Others : Never judge a game by it's price, it's cover, it's reviews (unless it's buggy and crashy of course). You'll never know what treasure is buried inside dirty land.

Perhaps you'll get into the editor with stars and dreams in your eyes and an outline in your hand. You'll draw world maps, towns and dungeons with the easy to use tools. There will be many hours of work put into your hopes and dreams and after much toil and hard work, you'll get to begin the exciting journey of promoting and marketing your game that you've made.
Or, perhaps you'll open up the database editor and cower at the number of things that need customizing and changing. Maybe you'll be happily chugging along before you find some effect that your game absolutely Must Have, but it requires you to delve into the depths of Ruby and RGSS3 to make it happen. Maybe your hopes of getting your game done at all will be dashed by hundreds of commenters informing you that your game looks like "RPG Maker trash" and that you should "go kill yourself" instead of making your game.
This tool is a great tool for making JRPG inspired games. It makes many things easy. But do not enter with illusions about how much work and effort is required in getting even a simple game done.

It looks great and plays great. Playing through the story is relatively quick(finished in 2.5 hours) other than that, I really have nothing to complain about. I honestly enjoyed the story to this game. It's played in the form of tape recordings that are qued at certain points within the chapters. The story is alos backed by bits of lore spread throughout the environment. Yes you can speed run through a good portion of the game, but you may find yourself missing out on some plot points.

For the most part the controls are smooth and easy to use(sometimes I found myself overshooting a platform). Since you're piloting an exoskeleton that grants increased speed and agility. And I actually feel it. The physics of the game are based on momentum. Running down hill, you will see a significant increase in speed. Running uphill, you slow down. This in turn will affect jump height and distance.
The suit is upgradeable throughout the story to include a grappling hook, jump boost, push rods(makes for a fun sequence running through tunnels) and more. There is also the use of an energy based life-death manipulator. You can use it to bring dead things-trees, deer etc- to life or take the life from organic objects. The suit operates off energy that comes in the form of glowing orbs around the environment or you can retrieve this energy from living creatures if you need a boost in a pinch.
The combat is, well, simple. There are four types of enemies(5 including a boss fight) and these are normally won by using the life-death manipulator against them.
Overall, I would recommend this game. I had fun playing it, and if you're into platformers and parkour type games, then this one should be up your alley

I haven't played Gothic, but I've heard Risen is more or less a reboot/rehash of Gothic I and II.
This being said, if you've never played Gothic, here's what to expect from Risen :
The game starts just as I like them : Thrown in an unknown island after the ship you sailed with got wrecked in what appeared to be a storm, you're given a weapon, a couple of items and here you roll.
The game's an action-rpg, so the combat is both important and reflex-based.
There are three factions you can side with in order to get their exclusive stuff (usually, the armor) and each faction puts the emphazis on some specific skills (The rebels are about hunting and thievery since they're cast out of the city and living in the swamp, The inquisitor's followers put the emphazis on staff-wielding, the mages are ♥♥♥♥ing mages) while most skills are available everywhere (weapons, crafting etc).
Most npcs from the three hubs (The rebel camp, the Monastery and the city) will react to events regarding the island or yourself (been promoted captain of the Don ? Here go the salutes from the troops) which is great.
The combat system gets good as you unlock skill levels in a type of fighting.
Now for the problems :
Risen tends to copy/paste encounters in the last part of the game. To the point of being absolutely awfully boring. You'll fight reptilian undead again and again and again.
Itemization is pretty straight-forward. Better weapons usually mean more damage and require more stats. Don't expect anything fancy. Even the massive legendary end-game weapon is actually a regular axe with a regular moveset.
In addition to copy/pasted encounters, have some copy/pasted quests ! Not only will you have to reckon the island to recover the necessary artifacts for the main quest to keep on at chapter II, you'll have to do it again at chapter IV !
Overall though, it's mostly good. The end-game is very tedious though as I said but the experience you'll have is very satisfactory, mostly due to the different possiblities of progression (working for the don, being captured by the inquisitor's men, asking the mages to take you in) and the different quests you'll have in the different factions.
Concerning the story, which I haven't really talked about, it got two axises : the first one is the struggle for the control of the island. This one is cool. The other one is the actual main story and, let's just say it's both cliché and boring.

An excellent first person horror game developed by Red Barrels! Outlast puts you in the shoes of an investigative journalist called Miles; he wishes to explore an asylum whose name and address were specifically mailed to him by one of the asylum's employees stating there are horrible things going on and that he should promptly investigate.
Upon arrival you immediately notice that the game gives you a camera and... nothing more. In the dark the device's night vision mode provides you with visibility but that's all - Outlast does not give you any weapons. Those of you who played Frictional Games' Amnesia may find the concept similar - yes, here, just as in Amnesia, the dark places are your best friend. When encountering enemies you immediately need to hide as you can easily die after a couple of hits.
As your equipment consumes batteries you frequently need to search for these throughout the game. And while the game's story unfolds as you progress further it's worth checking every corner for collectibles - these are dossiers further explaining the things going on in the facility.
The atmosphere is one of a kind! The game reminds you of those found-footage horror flicks that started in 1999 by Blair Witch Project. While in well-lit (or barely lit) places you do not need to use your camera it is still advisable as Miles takes notes only when pointing his camera at certain things / events. Through these notes can you really see how he's getting more and more desperate and crazy as he further ventures into the horrors of the asylum!
The game is full of scripted events. While you think hiding is always successful, sometimes Outlast wants you to be seen by a monstrous, homicidal patient and deliberately puts you in a chasing sequence. Miles can easily vault over the obstacles  while running but nothing is more frightening when you have just escaped into a room and just closed the door behind you but you can hear the bashes of your enemy on the door while trying to hide!
Graphics look good thanks to Unreal Engine 3. But the game's score and sound effects make it stand out! There is a reason why a lot of people say a headset is a must! While it is an indie game Outlast offers you roughly 5-6 hours to complete the story. Greater difficulty settings give you fewer batteries and those of your thriving for the maximum can complete the game on Insane difficulty: here there's no checkpoint so in case you die you can start it all over again!
Outlast is a great game! It has a terrifying atmosphere not many horror games can offer these days. Its DLC completes the story for you and helps you with some unanswered questions. Gameplay-wise it offers fewer puzzle sequences as many of the players found these too repetitive - the developers did listen and made an even better game!

Risen is a third person open world action roleplaying game made by the team that gave us the Gothic games, and it shows. It is very much like Gothic 1 & 2. Characteristic features of these games are:
- Exciting melee combat: just spam-clicking the mouse will get you nowhere, you need to actually think and time your moves (blocking, parrying, hitting). This is a challenging game, maybe even difficult for some.
- Learning curve for your character: there isn't just a learning curve for the player but for the character, too. He needs to learn to fight better. As the game progresses and you level up, you actually feel your character get better. At first, his fighting style is pretty clumsy and you can barely kill a wolf. But later on, you'll fight with more style and finesse, and you can start killing stronger monsters that you had to avoid before.
- Factions: there are three factions you can join. Each faction has their own set of preferred skills, weapons and armor. This adds to replayability. Playing a mage type character will be a completely different experience from playing a sword-and-shield type character.
- Trainers: when you level up somewhere in the middle of the forest, you don't just 'learn' new skills or get stronger or more dexterous right there out of the blue. Instead, you'll need to visit a trainer who can teach you to get better or who can teach you new skills.
- Great atmosphere: the settings, the NPCs, the music, the different 'hubs' for the factions, ... everything adds to a distinct atmosphere that only Piranha Bytes can create. Although I must admit I think Gothic 1 & 2 had even more 'heart' than Risen, it's there at its core. Risen has what Gothic 3 lacked and what made Gothic 1 & 2 the timeless classics they are today.
Note about achievements: this game has achievements but they aren't visible in Steam, only in the game itself. From the game menu, click 'Game' and then 'Achievements' for an overview of the achievements. Risen does have classic Steam Trading Cards.

I picked up all of the Shadowrun reboots and recently finished Shadowrun Returns and Shadowrun Dragonfall. If you want to play Shadowrun Chronicles, be sure to play it before playing any of Harebrain Schemes' games or else you'll be disappointed for sure.
Graphics:
There are more special FX in this engine, but they use some sort of overlay system for symbols. So if you pan your screen, the symbols will float as they strive to catch up with the background. The spectrals look good and there was a neat effect where I missed a shot and hit a car whose windshield cracked. They also try to do some sort of cinematic zoom-in periodically when you kill stuff. That might be neat when used sparingly, but it did it when I killed a Lvl 1 dog... which was silly.
Sound:
Music is decent, but the previous Shadowrun soundtracks are more catchy. Voice acting feels like it was done by a bunch of C-list actors. The quality is there, but it doesn't feel believeable at all. It might be because some of the lines that they have to read are terrible, or maybe the lines feel terrible because they read them poorly. In either case, I found myself skipping past most of the voiceovers once I finished reading the text.
Gameplay:
This is just a Shadowrun themed game, so don't expect it to feel the same as the previous Shadowrun games. The skill trees move away from RPG style characteristics and instead focus on skills. If you played Dragonfall, remember the options that you had for upgrading your secondary characters? It's similar to that except you have to use the same pigeonholes for your main character. Also, hackers hurt people by... hacking at them? They don't have guns, you just click on someone to hack and then little blue data beams fly over and hurt them somehow.

Given, it's still a very hardcore puzzle game, which is really not for everyone.

What

A polished, or even simply finished, MMO. There's no trading anything with anyone ever; why, you can't even sell those spare clothing unlocks, either. multiplayer to do.

Sold as an MMO RPG, and absolutely deserves a thumbs down as that - irrespective of whether it is a decent game otherwise.

I am dissapointed but still pleased by VX Ace. Since it was released I've used XP, but because of XP's age and lack of larger screen resolutions I decided to buy VX ACE.
I haven't gone too in depth with VX Ace, so far only using stock tilesets and this is where my biggest dissapointment lies. While most people that are serious about making their own RPG will more than likely use Parallax backgrounds, for those of us that lack artistic skill, the stock map maker and tilesets are where its at.
The problem with it though is that it automatically merges similar tilesets together if they touch (I'm not sure if this was an issue in XP since it's been a year since I've messed with it). Say you want to make a Large home with a little shack attached. Well if the top of the roof on the shack matches the height of the main building, they merge and look like the roof is a single part of the building and the only way I have found to prevent this is to use two different tiles.
I would STRONGLY encourage people, who are thinking of buying VX ACE, to learn how to use a good image editor such as Photoshop or Gimp, to create Parallax backgrounds for their worlds. It's a little more labor intensive, but you'll have a better look and feel to your game!

Do you enjoy puzzle games that will result in you getting stuck on a level for hours on end, but make you want to strive to complete it, knowing that what you learned in the current challenge will apply to all the ones to follow? If so, then this game is for you!
Infinifactory is by far the best puzzle game I have played in years, though it can be very tricky at times. Since you are basically creating a space factory of sorts, you have to pay close attention to the timing of every individual part of your machines. Having one single element of your design slightly off in timing can throw the whole thing out of whack, and will cause you to loose levels. Fortunately, the machine only runs when you tell it to do so, and you can pause it in action for a closer look at what exactly is happening at any time.
The learning curve is decent and starts out fairly simple, but it does ramp up the difficulty quickly. Infinifactory gives you just enough hints to get started, and leaves the rest for you to figure out on your own. This is the sort of game that will force you to think spatially, and have a tendency to throw complete curveballs at what you though you knew about how to complete a level. Later in the game, when you start unlocking new components, you can return to your previous levels with the new components, and try to improve your score using them and any new techniques you have figured out.
As an added bonus, the music is very well done. It is very relaxing, but not to the point that it will put you to sleep.
Overall, If you love challenging puzzle games, then I absolutely recommend picking up Infinifactory. It is very challenging, but also very rewarding, and should keep you busy for quite some time.

I really love the way this software works.
It is simple enough to be highly usable for someone who is not an expert game-designer and programmer and artist, but if you are any of those things, this program will work for you too, because it extends nicely, as you can add in your own scripts and art, to some extent.
It does have its flaws: It's severely limited to making 16-bit style RPG games. It is not 3D, nor can it be. It cannot make any kind of game you can imagine. You can do awesome stuff with it beyond RPG games, adding elements of other things here and there, but it may require scripts and coding knowledge and could be very difficult.
Some of the tile-sets in the game are confusing, and the way those are structured can be tough, but the base art that comes with the game is very pretty and well-thought out, and can take you a long, long way.
The fact there's so much DLC for this game concerns me, I won't lie. To buy it all separately will be very expensive, but it is nice it is sorted into packs for different types of games (like Sci-Fi, Adventure/Fantasy, etc.)
It also has a good community of people modifying files and building resources for it, which is always nice.
I used it because I had to for my game-design program for school, but I always was one to buy RPG-Maker games on PS2 because I love creating RPG games.
If you enjoy RPG games, and you seriously want to build one, and don't mind doing a huge amount of work (it won't be that easy, it'll take a ton of time and energy!) and you're okay with using most of the art that exists already, or have the capacity to produce and import your own, then you want this program.

Basic Tutorial and Video Review:
A solid 4X Economic Turn-based game that is SO FREAKING HARD. Due to a lack of a tutorial, and an incredibly minimalist HUD, this game can only be learned through trial and error. The AI has one difficulty, ruthless and expansive and will quickly outpace you if you waste too many turns. However, despite these faults, this game has the most interesting take of the economic portion of a 4X game I've ever seen. The entire goal of the game is to make a ton of money to colonize at least 50% of the galaxy. You make money by building mines that each specialize in the production of 1 resource. As you build up, you start to build factories which can create commodities which sell for significantly higher profits than just plain resources. If you don't have the required resource needed to produce the good then you buy it off the market automatically which, obviously, diminishes your profits. So you benefit by colonizing planets and varying what resources you're mining. To add on to this strategy, there is the Patent System. Summed up, this system means, if you have all the resources needed to produce a commodity, then you can purchase a patent on it causing your profits to increase by 500%. However, patents are in limited supply and there are only so many combinations of resources that can be patented meaning the faster you expand, the more money you make, thus the better chance of taking over the galaxy you have.
Now there is a military side of the game where you build massive fleets to attack either independent worlds or AI controlled worlds which have the resources you need. However, fleets and militarys and even the research required to make them more effective are ungodly expensive! Even a small fleet of 4 frigates can cripple a burgeoning Company, so you only go to war when necessary.
I definitely recommend this game, it's hard and can be incredibly punishing but anyone who is willing to take the time to play the game will quickly find a Gem amongst indie Space Strategy games.

This is an impressive piece of software.  If you ever wanted to make your own JRPG this a great tool to do it with.  However you should do so with the right expectations up front otherwise you might be disappointed.
First, there's a lot of depth here.  Expect to spend a fair amount of time just learning how the software works.  I found an excellent tutorial on the web that was ~170 pages long that walked me through creating a small RPG including a world map, town and buildings inside the town, mobs, NPCs, items, shops, etc.  Even at 170 pages, there were a lot of pieces of the program that were skipped or only mentioned briefly.  Everything that you'd want to have or would see in a typical old school JRPG is possible but there is a learning curve so expect to put some time into that.
Second is the time required to create your own RPG once you know how the tool works.  Classics like the original Zelda were not made in a day, so if that's your ambition then plan on spending a lot of time to get there.  The tool is fantastic as it takes care of the technical aspects of rendering the screen, handling input, playing audio, tracking game states and dealing with more complex things like how character levels progress, building a shop or handling combat.   It's still up to you to paint the world, write the story, the dialog, add the event triggers, define how characters progress, what items and spells do, what they're called and how much they are work as well as defining the monsters and bosses and then assembling this into a coherent game.
Bottom line is if you have any interest in making a game like this, or just want to see what's involved in making a game like this then this is a great tool to do that with.  I'd suggest that if you get it, don't get any of the DLC until you've had some time to go through a tutorial  and had a chance to try it out to see if it's for you.

This game wants to be a horror title, that shows insights to the horrors of WWII, while also realistically portraying the human desire for revenge. It manages to do none of those.
One of the main things I noticed is that the team put so little attention to detail that many of the props with no bottom texture like the filing cabinets (and at one point a dresser) are see-through on the bottom. That's the scariest part of this game: How little attention the developers put into making this a pleasant experience.
The controls are clunky, ambushes are cheap, enemies have about three frames of animation each, and the voice acting is so fakely German that as someone of Austrian descent I'm kind of offended. Have you considered hiring actual English-speaking Germans? That'd go a long way towards fixing it.
Also the jumpscares are laughable at best. Monsters cheaply ambush you, but I reacted with anger at how unbelievably cliche it was, not with fear.
The notes are unbelievably dumb, there were enough typos I almost thought it was translated by a first year immigrant. At one point they spelled 'despair' as 'dispair' on one of the notes in the illogical maze known as the mansion.
Also for the graphics I could forgive someone for thinking this was a Playstation 1 game, the weapons feel so clunky that it makes me want to go play Half-Life 2 instead, or if not the classics, maybe an actually good source mod. If you're looking for something fun, this is not it. I was nothing but frustrated the entire time.
I will give you five points for effort though, because clearly it took you 'some' time to do this.

Valley is a great game that gives you a feeling of freedom, not in the sense of choices necessarily, the story is pretty linear. Instead the L.E.A.F. suit your character wears gives you a liberating feeling of movement. When I first was able to run in the suit, going extremely fast downhill while the music picked up to a cheery little tune I couldnt help but smile. You can jump high, run fast, skim over water- the environment feels like a playground in itself. While it does pose a few dangers (dont go too slow over water or you'll sink) it never feels nerve wracking.
There is little in the sense of combat, a few enemies here and there as you go through the story, but they are all relatively easy to beat. I didnt mind. The puzzles of how to use the suit to move forward in each area were plenty for me.
The story is quite intriguing, slowly being painted as you move along. I found myself worrying what was going to happen to these characters, even though you're only contact is listening to old recordings and readings of what happened. They did a great job making a story you want to keep going to uncover.

As a bit of background, I should be clear that I'm pretty into the Shadowrun universe and lore (I started with 4E and have been really getting into 5E as of late, as well as the HBS Shadowrun games). A buddy of mine and I have a weekend game day each Sunday and we were looking for something to try, so I pitched this game to him (I knew very little of it when I started out, other than "hearing things" that people had said about the state of the game). With that in mind, we started the main campaign together and hoped for the best.
For my buddy, I'm pretty sure he had a good time despite him having little understanding of the Shadowrun universe. Myself, on the other hand... I fraggin' loved this game for what it tried to accomplish with the limited resources available.
The best analogy I can give is that it's like X-COM with light MMO elements. Abilities have cooldowns or use mana (which regenerates per turn). Cover provides evasion bonuses, so position on the battlefield matters. Missions are based in instances and start off simple but ramp up in difficulty quickly (by the Infected! expansion, the difficulty spiked a LOT - can be a real sticking point for some players, but I enjoyed that the runs got more challenging and required more of a plan of attack). The story takes a while to get going, but once it builds its momentum it does a good job establishing the basis of the most recent craziness to hit the Sixth World.
But the main feature that drew me in to the game (and why I'm leaving this review) was that it was a game that allowed me to share an experience with a buddy of mine together. If you're even slightly interested in the Shadowrun universe and have a buddy who is as well, and the two of you enjoy turn-based tactical gaming... then this game is a really good value for what you get out of it. I logged 50 hours - all of them playing with my gaming buddy - and we had a blast together every step of the way.
The game isn't perfect, obviously. A lot of resources are reused, some interface and tooltip descriptions aren't clear, and there are occasional typoes here and there. But given what the developers had to work with in terms of funding... I really think the final product here exceeded my expectations.
I really hope that I'll be returning to the shadows some day, whenever the next chapter unfolds.
-Grimm

Fallout 3 is large open world FPS-RPG which takes the narrative of "what would happen if there had been a nuclear exchange in the 1940's and the citizens of the United States was trying to struggle with the after math of a nuclear exchange". Developed by everyone's favorite open world developers Bethesda Game Studios and released in 2008.
Welcome to Vaunt 101, while there aren't any Vault Hunters searching for it
there are quite a number of treasures to be found within this vault. The Vault was designed to house and take care of it's inhabitants in the aftermath of a nuclear holocaust.
You spend a good chunk of time learning about vaunt 101, meeting the other citizens, and growing up. Literally, you start as a baby being born in vault 101, then as you grow up you learn more about core mechanics within the Fallout 3 game, ethics, V.A.T.S., S.P.E.C.I.A.L., combat, and more!
The games story really doesn't start until your father suddenly disappears and you go searching for him! I won't spoil anything else about the story, but it does go on for quite a while, as you would expect and hope for in a Bethesda game!
*
"Notice: Fallout 3 is not optimized for Windows 7 and later" EHHHHHHHhhhhhhhh..... My brother and I had to tinker with the files and do some trouble shooting to get it to work on my windows 7 computer in 2015. Then I directly transferred the game data to my new Windows 10 Computer Rig.
I can say we got it to work, however I cannot say for certain if any changes were made that would allow you to simply download from steam and get the game working. I can say that right now with the changes we made it works on windows 7 and 10.
Wheeeew, where to start? Lets start with the simple first: Fallout 3 controls like a FPS, I trust 99% of the people reading this review understand what direction to point the gun and click to KA-BOOM.
Next to explain V.A.T.S., the game probably will do a better job of explaining it, but V.A.T.S. stand for "Vault-Tec Assisted Targeting System", and will allow you to pause the game, and take aim for you at a specific part of an enemy. But hitting your target is based on percentages, so if you shoot at point blank and have a 99% chance of hitting your target, there's always that 1% chance you'll miss.
Since my luck is terrible, I tend to try to avoid using VATS, but over stream someone pointed out I could use them for explosive weapons and grenades, since I particularly STINK at hitting my target when I'm throwing a grande.
Next we move on to S.P.E.C.I.A.L.! S.P.E.C.I.A.L. is an acronym for the primary attributes in Fallout3. They stand for: Strength, Perception, Endurance, Charisma, Intelligence, Agility and Luck.
All the other qualities of the game can be broken down into the "par for the course" as far as RPG's and Open World games are concerned. Expect a lot of exploration, expect gear with different perks, expect optimization strategies online; explaining where to go and how to play.
Something I didn't expect was: Fallout 3 is hard! I fancy myself an average skilled gamer
, I'm constantly eating Stimpack for breakfast while I play
. I've sunk a crazy amount of caps
into hoarding Stimpacks, I'm like a doctor or someone doing illegal drug related stuff.
At this time there aren't any steam achievements for Fallout3, this may change someday, depending on if Bethesda decides to add achievements.
Fallout3 is priced at $9.99, the Game of the Year Edition is priced at $19.99. You'll get more mileage
out of your game by purchasing the the Game of the Year Edition. Over twitch someone suggested I play through the DLC to get power armor, and it would make the rest of the play through easier.
Fallout 3 is to some, what Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion is to me; a wonderful game that opened them up to the amazing size and scope a game can actually be. While I will always personally prefer Oblivion, I have enjoyed playing through this game, and can easily recommend it to anyone who's even remotely interested. Fallout 3 is totally worth your time.
I recommend this game to anyone whom enjoys a challenge, likes Open World games, mods, enjoys RPG's, isn't intimidated by large open spaces, and has A LOT of free time to explore.
Thanks for reading my review!

Well guys, as far as an RPG goes this one's a bit messed up. First, lets get the things they've done okay to well noted down: The pace of this game very good but the story is about average, Cliche, but better than some. This is NOT a short 10 hour romp of patheticness that RPGs made now are and the leveling/advancement of your character are at about where you would expect. In addition the world looks amazing especially for when it was made and it doesn't hold your hand as much. NO LOAD SCREENS! Well, Almost none, you WILL be hitting quick load a lot, but I'll get into that later. For the world, story, and looks I'd give this game a 7/10. But, like nearly all seemingly good things this is completely ruined by the following:
It commits close to, if not ALL of the unforgivable combat gaming sins:
-all enemies physical attacks are normally twice as fast as yours.
-The game randomly slows your attack to 1/10th your normal speed, giving all enemies
around you free hits as you can't get out of the animation, thus killing you by default through
no fault of your own.
-Your enemies, including wild animals, can parry your parries, but you as a player can't even
with max skills.
-All enemies can attack and hit you instantly, you cannot. Your sword can literally be
connecting with them in your attack and the enemy will often instantly get a super powerfull
atack in that is so fast you can bearly see them move,
doing massive damage to you. You as a player are not capable of this.
-Dodging is of no use as your enemies can track you through it perfectly and hit you anyway. You as a player can't
track or hit, even by chance, a dodging enemy.
-Enemies have unlimited numbers of attacks they can string together while the player, even with the skill that
supposadly allows such, cannot.
-All enemies recover from recoil 3 times faster than you do.
-Enemies sometimes become invulnerable and cannot be harmed, this is also not fixable by reloading a save and
requires the game to be restarted.
-Your character is sometimes spun around by enemy attacks and of course, you are not able to do this to them.
-If you save after you have an enemy's attention any reload of that save will load that enemy within stricking range of
you and attacking, no matter where they were when the original save was created. This renders such save unusable
as you end up dieing the moment the game loads every time, no matter what the cercumstances before the save.
-All enemy melee weapons have greater range than yours no matter what. Enemy has a dagger and you have a two
hand sword? Their dagger out-ranges your sword. Even animals out range your weapons with their horns and teeth.
-Enemy gaurding has a good wide range of defense from the front, But you only have defense for a tiny sliver of angle
that leaves you pulling your hair out as you watch blades swing THROUGH your shield to hit you.
So, all in all I'd give non-combat parts of the game a good 7/10. It is a good story and environment but it isn't anything we havent seen before and the story is cliche. But for combat I give it a definate 0/10, that's right, an actual ZERO out of ten. Combat is so buggy and un refined it renders the game completely unplayable a lot of the time and melee combat is based purely on you getting lucky. So unfortunately, I have to give an overall score of 3/10 and can't at all recomend this game to anyone who doesn't want massive levels of frustration.

Aside from the title, I don't intend to fill this review with much in the way of superlatives or hyperbole, simply because saying something along the lines of “This game changed my life” doesn't really mean anything in a literal sense whether or not it's true.
The statement made by the title is, however, true. Through its narrative and interactivity, The Beginner's Guide provides insight into game design – specifically insight into game designers and the games they work on. Developer commentary, rather than being a separate bonus, is integrated directly into the experience as Davey walks the player through the game while telling them a story.
On the surface, this blend of hand-holding and storytelling makes the game play out rather like a documentary. However, the interactivity of the game is vitally important to the experience. Despite how little my choices actually meant to the game as a whole, I was stricken by the feeling that I am actually an
piece of the overall experience; stricken by the realization that a story told only has value if someone is there to listen. I needed only an inconsequential amount of agency to still feel like I, as a gamer, mattered to the game I was playing – and that's exactly what I got.
What really hooked me was feeling like Davey was speaking directly to
. Not to me as a character, or even necessarily to me as a player, but to me as a
. It was a remarkably human feeling, and I can safely say that no other game I've ever played has validated my existence to quite that degree. It didn't take long before I was completely invested in the experience I was having.
Imagine, for a moment, having a conversation with your favorite game designer. If such a thing doesn't exist, imagine having a conversation with your favorite author, movie director, musician, or entertainer. While playing The Beginner's Guide, I felt like I got something akin to what I'd imagine that to be. A direct line of communication from game designer to gamer
the game I was playing.
I felt like I not only got insight into the game I was playing, but also into Davey as a person. And it was a reminder of the people who give me the experiences I indulge in on a daily basis.
Being so casually reminded that there are actually human beings, with lives, experiences, and stories to tell, behind every single game I've ever played was… an eye-opening experience, to say the least.
And it's left me with so many questions.
Do those people design games with the explicit intent for them to be played? Do they show every single game they've worked on, or are their drives full of unfinished or scrapped projects (if those don't get deleted outright)? Do they make games for business? For profit? Or simply for the joy of it – whether it be their joy as a game designer, or the joy others feel when playing their games? Or do they make games because… it's the only way they can reflect on themselves and grow as people?
I write because it allows me to look at myself objectively and learn from myself. And I didn't even realize that's why I write until I had this experience. Could it be that many game designers actually do the same thing? Are their games, like eyes, windows into their soul?
These are questions I
asked myself until I played The Beginner's Guide.
Now I can't stop asking them.

I played only a few minutes and I can already recommend it. Here's why:
I love horror games. I do. I enjoy the thrill of being scared and all that, but this game is beyond scary. It somehow reaches into your brain and embeds an itch inside. An itch to look at the monitors. To make sure everything is in order. To make sure THEY didn't move. And if they did, pray to gods they are not coming for you. Gradually, it embeds in your psyche the CCTV picture of those terrifying, creepy THINGS, those... animatronics... and then when the image of their grinning faces with their cold, dead eyes is firmly in your head, it puts it right in front of you with a terrifying, mechanical scream! And then you have to turn the game off for a few seconds. Go back to the familiar desktop, check your pulse and decide it's too late to play this game. Then play it the next day, when it's no longer night time, when the sun is up and the room is no longer dark. But let me be clear - it's not just an any old jumpscare-fest we're talking about here, oh no no no. This is mastery of the expected-unexpected. The buildup of tension and the reveal are amazingly well executed. This is what I'm looking for in a horror game - even what seems like a whole lot of nothing terrifies you, brings you to a breaking point, and then, when you're most vulnerable, when you're starting to lose sanity, that's when it strikes. And it strikes hard. Not just in the sense that it's fast and loud, which it is, but in the sense that it's just uncanny. Creepy. You know that feeling when you stare into the bathroom mirror late at night and expect something to come out of the shower behind you? There is a split second moment when you're no longer certain which of your thoughts are real and which are just imagination, and that's when you decide to turn your eyes away from the mirror. Well, imagine if you looked away only to see your worst fears materialize right in front of your face, right there! That's how scary that game is. That's how it works. It messes with your head, brings the anticipation to a boiling point and then taps on your shoulder and screams in your face once you turn your head. Genius! Love it, but must not play now. Too dark.
All things considered, this game is a little gem. A little, shiny gem which reflects a dark figure standing 2 inches behind your left shoulder. It will test you. You will have nightmares. Consider yourself warned.

Powerful enough on it's own, yet enriched by any DLC or fan based materials you can find and add to the resource manager.
This engine has a lot of potential behind it if you are willing to exploit everything it has to offer.
Events and scripts work best together.  Your ability to control events will dictate how fast your game will develop.
For the beginner there is a tremendous amount of free resource manager loadable content available from minotaurs to prefabricated maps and recolored RTP sprites.
For the advanced user the engine takes on a new form and allows you creative freedom to load script based commands to further control and customize your players experience.
With Windows exporting exe files, soon to be joined by an Android export for games you will have a wide audience for whatever it is you choose to create.
Materials included for the engine are a wide array of fantasy genre sprites, battlers, battle backs and preset items.  This means you can start making a game immediately without the tedious task of making spells, items, classes, portraits, and equipment.
The free version has all the same utility minus the preset content, and shortcuts to commonly used events like transferring a player through a door and making a standard treasure chest.
If you are willing to learn 'eventing', or are a returning user to the RPG maker franchise like I am you will enjoy this engine immensely and all the countless hours of fun and development it can bring you.
A warning though.  You reap what you sow.  That means you need to find problems and solve them as they happen.  You need to be able to work through commands and actions logically in order to catch mistakes you make, and you will make mistakes.   Those are half of the fun!  The more you add, the more chance something will conflict or go wrong.
If you are unable to get a handle on evening, or you need assistance there are a number of forums on third party sites dedicated to increasing your skills with which ever area you help to utilize the editor.
I strongly recommend a third party site like drop box to store a backup of your game.  Nothing is perfect and the more you measures you take to protect your work the better for the amount of time invested.
I highly recommend this product not only for the customization elements, but because you can share what you make.  Be it a 15 minute coffee break adventure rogue like, or a 20+ hour RPG nostalgia fest from the golden age of Super Nintendo gaming 2-D graphics.
To date I have bought this engine 5 times and gifted it to 4 friends as well as bought a number of the DLC packages.
For those willing to buy the DLCs, please note that nothing gets added to the editor when you buy them.  As a developer you need to load all additional content from the steam DLC files under "Steam\steamapps\common\RPGVXAce\dlc" and that includes scripts as well.
You have total control over the game you make.
It is possible after all your hard work you want to encrypt the files to protect it, or simply keep the players from cheating by loading it into an editor and manipulating the database.  RPG Maker gives you the option to encrypt your work, or leave it so a player can has the option of editing it.  This is handy for bigger projects and play testers.

This has been on my wishlist forever, it seems. It looked intriguing, but I had this nagging feeling it was going to be like Myst, and I'd never get it done because I'd just eventually get board with the games needed to progress. Last night I had a few hours to kill before heading to bed and this was on sale for pretty cheap. Reviews were all very positive and I read it was a fairly short play through so I figured I'd get it finally and play for a bit.

Long story short, I was up till 1:30 am because I just couldn't stop playing. I finished the game, start to finish, in 1 sitting, not getting all the achievements, just a playthrough. It took approx. 4.5 hours and my 11 year old son even sat with me the entire time and we had a blast figuring out the next steps needed to progress, and just enjoying the the game in general. The power running sequences were, by far, our most favorite parts.
To sum up, buy it! A nice short game to just pass a few hours with.

Banished is a city builder; a simulation where your goal is for your people to survive the world and to make your city thrive. If you have played city builders before you will recognise the classic elements: Get resources, grow or hunt food, make tools, expand your town. There are no threats from other rivaling cities, only the harsh dangers of nature with cold winters or the ever-present danger of a catastrophe such as fires, diseases or a bad harvest.
I had high expectations on Banished. I have for a very long time waited for a city builder where nature is the only hinderance. I try Sim City every once in a while only to discover I still don’t like the gameplay and most other games about city building are mostly RTS games focusing on military and defence (one example is Stronghold).
So did Banished live up to my expectations? Yes! It’s fun and it keeps me constantly on my toes. It doesn’t tell you what to do: Start a game and you have an open landscape and a build menu – knock yourself out. (But yes, there is an optional tutorial about the different buildings.) There is no “clippy the paperclip” to tell you what you need to fix: Only warnings in your event log (and that is if you decide to enable the event log.) Learn by your mistakes, find a balance in your production, think ahead so that you have all you need for winter. Start over, try again.
I have played two games (on medium difficulty) so far: On my first one, my population became too old and I didn’t get enough children to keep the town going. Turns out people aren’t happy enough with roofs above their heads: In order to make new babies families want a house of their own.
In the second one I traded away most of my tools in order to get sheep to breed only to find out my total tool output must’ve been negative. In just a few seasons none of my villagers had tools. Which meant bad food production. Which meant starvation. (After a rage-quit after the last one it took less than an hour before I started itching to start a new game.)
When it comes to appereance I also like the game: Banished isn’t graphically mind-blowing but it is enough not to be an eye-sore and the graphics never get in the way for gameplay.
If you like city-builders you should definitely try out Banished. It’s a game that can make you happy, angry, or sad; but whatever mood it takes your to I am sure you will still love it.

Short: This game could have been really good, all the stuff was there it was just all done very poorly. Also the load times make Skyrim look like Usain Bolt.
The game does have a good horror atmosphere to it. I think if this was picked up by an actual game company with the original creators giving input it could be a big seller.
The combat system is very unforgiving and little to no help is offered. Normally when it comes to melee/gun first person combat you don't need any guidance but this game failed on that aspect. The enemies completely destroy you if you so much as make 1 error. As far as the difficulty goes it's a very difficult game but not in a fair way, more like a Silver Surfer NES way. Makes things feel like more of an annoyance than a challenge. At the very least put in a difficulty option.
Picking up items is a task, half the time you end up picking up random books, buckets, bikes, trash bags, boxes, etc. just to find out you could only pick up 1 of the 2 clips on the shelf after squatting and checking different angles.
A very annoying this is how far the camera tilts when you strafe, it's so bad that I initially thought I was hitting the key intended to be used for peeking around corners, but no that's the regular way that you strafe in this game.
Backtracking and not the good kind either! If you don't check absolutely every piece of junk on the ground you are going to miss things and constantly end up backtracking and trust me there is a lot of junk to check everywhere. It's very time consuming.
The story line might be a bit easier to follow if the gameplay didn't leave you frustrated and you could hear it over ambient sounds like rain. You pretty much need subtitles to get a rough idea of what's going on and even then it's kind of confusing.
The only redeeming qualities to the game is that it does provide a good horror atmosphere and it does have the potential to be a great game with a large amount of polishing. The game as it is now seems like an alpha to something good coming. The best though is that it's free, nobody would pay for this as it is but like I said polish it up and I would pay money for it.

An excellent first person horror game developed by Red Barrels! Outlast puts you in the shoes of an investigative journalist called Miles; he wishes to explore an asylum whose name and address were specifically mailed to him by one of the asylum's employees stating there are horrible things going on and that he should promptly investigate.
Upon arrival you immediately notice that the game gives you a camera and... nothing more. In the dark the device's night vision mode provides you with visibility but that's all - Outlast does not give you any weapons. Those of you who played Frictional Games' Amnesia may find the concept similar - yes, here, just as in Amnesia, the dark places are your best friend. When encountering enemies you immediately need to hide as you can easily die after a couple of hits.
As your equipment consumes batteries you frequently need to search for these throughout the game. And while the game's story unfolds as you progress further it's worth checking every corner for collectibles - these are dossiers further explaining the things going on in the facility.
The atmosphere is one of a kind! The game reminds you of those found-footage horror flicks that started in 1999 by Blair Witch Project. While in well-lit (or barely lit) places you do not need to use your camera it is still advisable as Miles takes notes only when pointing his camera at certain things / events. Through these notes can you really see how he's getting more and more desperate and crazy as he further ventures into the horrors of the asylum!
The game is full of scripted events. While you think hiding is always successful, sometimes Outlast wants you to be seen by a monstrous, homicidal patient and deliberately puts you in a chasing sequence. Miles can easily vault over the obstacles  while running but nothing is more frightening when you have just escaped into a room and just closed the door behind you but you can hear the bashes of your enemy on the door while trying to hide!
Graphics look good thanks to Unreal Engine 3. But the game's score and sound effects make it stand out! There is a reason why a lot of people say a headset is a must! While it is an indie game Outlast offers you roughly 5-6 hours to complete the story. Greater difficulty settings give you fewer batteries and those of your thriving for the maximum can complete the game on Insane difficulty: here there's no checkpoint so in case you die you can start it all over again!
Outlast is a great game! It has a terrifying atmosphere not many horror games can offer these days. Its DLC completes the story for you and helps you with some unanswered questions. Gameplay-wise it offers fewer puzzle sequences as many of the players found these too repetitive - the developers did listen and made an even better game!

To say I regret the time I spent playing Risen would be like saying the holocaust was a little unfortunate. If ever a game was created to frustrate and punish (not by way of skill cap) an rpg lover, it would be this game. Risen has all the appeal of dating a toothless Little Debbie taste tester without the great bjs or free snacks.  It boasts so many cool concepts and executes on NONE of them.  Easily one of the ugliest least enjoyable Rpgs I have ever played.
Making a list of pros for this game is next to impossible;  maybe the interesting creatures in the world could be appealing to some, but definitely not when weighed with all the filth this game manages to churn out.  The combat is complete trash, you button mash for melee and god forbid you try to use ranged.  No reticle unless you zoom and the zoom takes 2 seconds to focus. Now try to get a shot off while groups of melee  enemies rush your face.  Basically the only ranged strats consist of shooting before in combat and switching to melee (O don't switch weapons while zoomed cause it will stay there and u will have to manually zoom back out...derp) or breaking the stupid AI by diagonally strafing into enemies and shooting them when their character models begin turning.
The AI is laughable and insanely easy to take advantage of,  Running a group of enemies over tree roots and getting them stuck allows them to be easily picked off.  And again since most enemies are melee it makes it that much easier.  Enemies have one attack pattern that never changes, charge into you and do 1 of their often times 2 possible combos.  The game tries to mask this huge failure by making the difficulty extremely high.  If you're playing on hard enemies will kill you in a couple attacks.  Im perfectly fine with a game having a high difficulty curve...If it's fun (Dark souls).  This game is not fun at all.
While the game says it has character customization and varying skill paths it basically boils down to being a bandit or a mage both of which have as much depth as a mud puddle in July.  Much like the skills, the quests have different ways of completion that would appear to have morale consequences tied to them but in the end its essentially more gold for making the "correct" decision and even if you completely screw over the npcs related to the quest  and they say they hate you, they will still interact with you the same way. The quests reminded me of an MMO, a whole lot of fetch and kill quests with almost no substance; given by countless npcs you will never care about.  Every npc has the same melancholy tone and you will remember none of them, much like your own character.  You can literally go into a town, find someone in their house, beat them till their health is gone, loot all their items, wait for them to get up and beat you to death (you dont die) and get up and keep everything.  Rinse and repeat. Such a well coded game.
The world is open for each map and you're free to explore as you like, likewise with quests you can pick the order of completion for many outside of crucial story quests.  This is a wonderful model for an rpg to have, unfortunately for this game the maps are bland and almost always dark.  There was no place I visited during my playtime that was memorable and quite frankly the game is ugly, like early original xbox ugly.  It's only fair to note that I never actually beat the game even though that was my primary goal.  So it is possible that the quests might have started to pick up and became somewhat interesting, but this in no way excuses the snore-fest that was the first part of the game.
So we have an ugly role playing game with terrible AI, boring combat, forgettable quests and a depressing cast of characters that only reflect how you will feel inside after you start playing.  The only way I would ever recommend this game is if it was at least 85% off and you have played almost every other rpg on steam. Piranha Bytes really dropped the ball on this one.  3/10 for this walking steamer.

Having enjoyed the other Shadowrun games I got this expecting more of the same.  I was dissapointed to say the least.  When you spend more time picking out your characters underpants than their skills something is wrong.  You have two "Statistics" both of which offer bland variations of combat upgrades and one or two skills that access locked off rooms in a map.  Melee you pick Blades or Blunt, but don't worry they are effectively identical with the only real difference being a bonus against a particular enemy type towards the end of the line.  Yes, line as skills are simply there to give you abilities that use that item.  You have basic proficiency in every skill from the start and the only real gain from putting points into a skill is a shorter cooldown on some abilities.  Ranged you have the greatest variety of options with a whole THREE skills to pick from Pistols, Shotguns, or Automatics.  Magic is reduced to only two options as well with one featuring different ways to summon the same critter and the other containing both direct damage spells in the game.  Tech based skills get the same gutting as everything else with deckers being possibly the furthest deviation from archetype I have ever seen in a game.  Deckers do not jack in or access the Matrix, instead they have been reduced to crippled mages.  Supernatural enemies are immune to tech damage so there is an entire third of them who you cannot effect and you have only a direct damage ability and an aoe with a medium cooldown.  The mission hub is tiny and could have been completely replaced with a post mission debriefing screen where you decide if you want to buy one of the two upgrades you have for your items and then pushes you on to the next mission.  Instead you have a different vendor for weapons, armor, magic and tech and each has between two and nine items total since there are only three variations of any particular weapon and only two options for armor.  Cyberware? nope none for sale.  All in all if you want a bland easy turn based non tactical blast em up to play with a buddy buy this crap on sale, or better yet buy a couple nerf guns and an egg timer you will have more fun.

Like SpaceChem, every level in Infiniactory leaves you feeling like an all powerful being who can make and produce anything... Then the next level involves almost the exact same thing but turns out to require a totally different solution and you have to go back to the drawing board and start building a new thingamajigger. And after you finish it and fix all the "bugs", your magical spinning pushing pulsing factory of doom starts purring. It's mesmerising to watch.
It's not (yet) as hard as SpaceChem, I suspect because there's a lot more open space to work in, or perhaps because some of the "tricks" for optimizing in SpaceChem work fairly well here too. (or I got smarter :D?) That said there's plenty of new ideas here - you can tell it's related, but it's also a whole new bag of tricks, surrounded by the great infrastructure of histograms and "hacks".
I recommend this to anyone who likes puzzles or making stuff or tinkering about, though I warn you, you might start dreaming of conveyor belts and wondering why your food doesn't slide out the fridge and cook itself when you open the fridge door.

Several Moments at Samuel's is a great visual novel, dating-sim doujinshi game that has ever been made. You are an employee at this popular restaurant called Samuel's Sassy Sweets, were both children and adults go to enjoy desserts and sweets. You are the security guard, and you work along with 3 talking and sentient anthro animals. Your objective is to strike up a relationship with one of them without Samuel the Panda finding out! You can choose from these three:
Daphne the Duck: A very friendly and kind duck who loves taking care of the kids as if she was their mother, but has a habit of working too much for them. Good luck getting her attention!
Barbie the Rabbit: A rather shy rabbit that doesn't talk much, but from the very beginning she seems to feel an attraction to you, as you constantly see her staring at you. But can you get her to talk to you instead of always look at you?
Wolfy the Wolf: A kind of though looking wolf that prefers to be alone for the most time, he doesn't actually work that close to the kids. He is the equivalent of "tsundere" of the male genre! So be very careful how you treat him, as he can get very mad at you!
Later in the game you can actually choose to try and get Samuel as your mate, but he's the hardest of the three to "get"!
With lots of lovely scenes (and some lewd ones :X), this game is the future of dating sim for every player out there that has always wanted to marry their favorite animal!

I nominated this game for Steam's "Mom's Spaghetti" award based heavily on the one of the best gaming moments I've ever had, that happened in this game. The about four minute non-stop, high speed run on electrified rails at the Soma Reactor was Pure. Freaking. Bliss. It certainly elicited a real physical response as I got shivers and a raised heartbeat. I replayed it. And I replayed it again. And again. I would sometimes boot up the game just to do this run - it's such a rush. Pretty on the eyes with the visual effects and boon for the ears with the sweet soundtack that played into the experience. From the story and universe standpoint this whole bit is near pointless, which makes me even happier that it was included in the game just to indulge the player in a bit of crazy fun.
Enough of praising that one part lol. I just love it, so well done.
I meant to write a review earlier but with this award nomination I simply had to (and give my thanks to the devs). Because that is what this game is - simple, rewarding fun. All the mechanics revolve around moving freely in the world and explore, they've been carefully honed to ensure a great experience. The character is very responsive and there isn't much to remember to maximize the focus on the world around you. The visuals are simply stunning, beautifully crafted levels - there's a ton of treasures hidden in the maps and the combat is non-existent to minimal so it's encouraged to take your time to enjoy. Kudos to the composer for an incredible, atmospheric soundtrack. It compliments the world really well.
My only complaints are the lack of a save system, the somewhat forced combat, and the "horror" elements of the later levels.
- There isn't a clear distinction where one level ends and another one starts, and if you exit the game at the wrong point you have to navigate through the entire level to get to the next one. It's bad design to make your player to commit to playing one full level, that can take 20-40 minutes, in one sitting if they want to progress. This was hindering my own experience.
- The combat, as many others have said, isn't particularly well executed. It was clunky and the preset of the game doesn't support it to make it a seamless part of the whole experience. The angry bug clouds I could understand, but not the stuff later on...
- By "horror" elements I mean exploring the dark indoor facilities. At some points I had to check if I was still playing the same game, and not something like SOMA. Atmospheric, sure, but when you spend most of the game in open world, and build it to be a mostly peaceful experience, it's a notable shift in the mood. Of course the storyline and the build-up supports it but there was absolutely no need for the corridors to be so ominous - I was afraid something would jump at me at every corner, and wasn't really enjoying the stress it caused.
A minor complaint is the strange timeline - it's hard to say how long these facilities and junk have been lying around because they're all clearly abandoned, but the immediate events affect the main character in the present. That being said, the story and the world/setting are engaging, and the voice acting well executed. The "bad guy" was a very believable character.
I would definitely recommend giving this little gem a run. It's a light game, with about 8-10 hours of playtime, depending how thorough you are. The devs picked a few simple elements that succeed in making the player really enjoy the time spent with the game. The sense of movement and the unique momentum mechanic was something I personally enjoyed, and like mentioned earlier, visuals and audio are very notable strenghts. Thanks Blue Isle Studios for your game! It was a good experience.

Here goes my take on SRC-BL: There is some good, bad and ugly here, I'll break it down.
The Good:
I love the art and combat style, more so than the Hairbrain version of the game. Shooting NPCs and watching them ragdoll replete with blood slowly flowing from their headwounds ...lends itself to an awsome sense of violent immersion. (Be forewarned, if such is not your thing...then move on.)
Missions are not ball-busting yet, they're not mind-numbingly easy. They take ample tactics and forethought. They got ths one just right.
Sound is comparible to its predecessors.
Some have complained about lag though performance for me has been adequate (getting around 60 fps on my humble rig.)
Character creation is awesome - nuff said.
The Bad:
Hencemen cannot be customised, any gear you find can't be equipped nor can their skills. You're left choosing from a list of prefabbed hencemen the skills and equipment of which automatically advance as you advance.
The skill tree is rather shallow compared to the HB version of the SR games.
The game can become a grind of: kill this,..return; escort that...return and so on.
The "hub" (where you buy gear, pick up quests) is significantly smaller than in previous SR games.
The Ugly:
First thing I noticed was that there was no "collision detection" in the hub. I would spawn on top of other toons and walk through them. (the Hub needs work.) Maybe not a big deal...but it sort of kills the immersion for me.
Don't come into this game expecting a huge MMORPG experience. I would say that this is more/less a co-op version of the typical game. Rather disappointed when the focus was changed from online to "lockeddown".
Voice acting vs. text. The voice acting is plausable though not  good enough to resist the desire for the interactive text-based version that allowed you to choose alternate direction/personality to your mission objectives.

Conclusion:
All-in-all I enjoy the game, short-comings notwithstanding. If your a SR fan, you probably will too...if not, don't bother.
