For years I have watched crazy Minecraft videos of people using redstone to build microprocessors and all kinds of impressive feats of recreational engineering, but every time I tried to play I just came up blank on ideas.  Plus, if you want to build things in the context of your own game, you have to spend hours mining for the components to begin with.  I've always felt that Minecraft genius was just out of my reach.
This game is the precise answer to my problem.  It gives you a problem to solve and an infinite toolkit to solve it with.  It's been a long time since I've felt absolutely gleeful playing a game.  You look at a puzzle and think "this is literally impossible."  Then 2 days later you'll be talking to someone and just shout "THAT'S IT" in their face and run away mid conversation to go home and solve it.  Every puzzle makes you feel like a moron until it makes you feel like a genius.
My only suggestion to the developer would be, stop calling it Early Access!  I avoid Early Access games as a rule, I only caved this time because the consensus in the community is that it is a fully fleshed out game and calling it Early Access is mere modesty.  I have yet to come upon a single bug or crash.

DO NOT buy this game, the constantly online DRM is ridiculous. I finally had enough and decide to write this review to vent some of my frustration.
As a long time HoMM fan, there are many issue other people complain about which I can give it a pass. I can give Uplay a pass, since it works for me most of the time. There are bugs that crashes the game, like the time when a griffin dives under the effect of fear aura, the game simple crashes. The dynasty weapons' ridiculous reverse effect bug where reduced mana cost becomes increased mana cost is okay for me, as I can simply avoid these weapons.
But god damned it the conflux system is awful. A bit of introduction, this game HoMM6 has a system called Conflux, where some of the weapons and game features need to be purchased using in-game currencies. These features includes dynasty weapons, avaters, custom heroes and game-start bonus. To use these features, you need to be constantly online. It is fine if you decide to play offline, but obviously you will not have access to these features. It is designed to punish piracy, but in the end, this game is so bad nobody wants to play both the pirated version and licensed version.
They could have done many things to smoothen the experience, but they refused do it. When you are suddenly offline due to 1 second of unstable connection, the game forced you out without save. The online save and offline save do not work with each other. The worst offence of all, the conflux only works half of the time, as it is right now.
Ubisoft has then stopped using this kind of online DRM for their games after HoMM 6 which is praise-worthy. However, unfortuantely they never release an update to get rid of this stupid mess for this game.

Love the program. I have used it for a long time now and can say that most of the things I can't do with it aren't needed anyway. In addition to the DLC there is a lot of player-generated content avaliable on the steam community (but be respectful of those who made them)
That said, the engine itself is plug-and-play and thus has many practical limitations. There are things it can do and things it can't and not a lot of in-between. Because of this and because of the built-in script editor knowing Ruby languege will greatly enhance your ability to make use of this engine.
Notes to potential buyers:
because of the cost, I would caution casual buyers to be sure this is a program they would actualy use. As I recall there is a demo ("lite" version) avaliable on the official site for this program that you might want to try. I have not tried to use it myself. It is also available here on steam if you search for it.
Some of the music packs also have sample music avaliable on the game's official website:
Most DLC expands your avaliable content; it is not nessisarialy a straight-up upgrade so don't just buy all of it without looking at it first.
Not all of the content shown in the trailer exists in vinilla: spesificaly I noticed the pop-up immages of characters are not included and the "name bar" for character conversations dosen't exist in vanilla. They can, however, be created and added. They might also be avaliable in the DLC or from the community.
One last note: I have seen several people buy this engine only to lose interest a couple months in and never finish a project. Make sure you are comitted to completing your game and set reasonable goals based on your current ability. To use this engine you need to know how to work. Although my own goals were overly ambitious initialy I don't plan on quitting until I have at least completed one project. Look at my number of hours, consider that I haven't completed a project, and tell me why you'll need to be comitted to work before you can use this program.

Secondly, It seems that the pistol has no purpose considering the only ammo I'm finding is for my rifle. Same goes for the mele wepon, I'm taking more damage fighting the enemies in hand-hand combat and losing quite easy. If you want to make a balanced combat system make sure you dont under or over power your wepons like the mele. Finally, too many unnecessary loading screens. I can't tell you how many times I was about to get into the game when all of a sudden I enter a tiny room to only be hit by a long loading screen.      However, there is alot of good in this game. Starting off with the atmosphere. Its great! There isnt that much music and every moment has put me on the edge of my seat thinking something is going to happen, its brilliant. Secondly, the enemies are terrifying, they have the uneasy walking with everyone loves in a scary game, and half the time you barely see an enemy and when you do you know you have to be carful because they are srong and hard to kill. Finally, as many people would say a good horror game isnt complete without a great story and so far the story this game provides has is great! Your not aimlessly walking around killing enemies without a purpose. I love how your on a mission for justice and is willing ti do anything to achieve it. Other than the cleche post WWII or after WWII its brilliant. Other than a few of those minor problems that can be fixed you did an amazing job creating a horror game!

Team Fortress Classic is a complete joy. At first it's a hard game to jump into and can be quite annoying from time to time. There are many things that make this game what it is.
First off, this game set the standard for what every class-based shooter should be. From the fast-running scout to the hefty Heavy Weapons Guy, this game introduces most-needed diversity in what any game should have to keep it running, and to keep players playing. Sometimes, however, it just doesn't seem like the classes are doing what they should. On maps like 2fort (CTF) or Dustbowl (TC), the Medics are the ones that are the guys pushing the flag by using their frag and concussion grenades to propel themselves towards the capture point, rendering the Scout useless and completely diverts the MEDIC'S role away from what it seems.
The game play of this game will keep you sitting at your desk for hours on hours. The on-going struggle to carry a piece of cloth on a pole to an enemy base will be as if you're running with a piece of pie dangling in front of you -- Long and annoying at first, but rewarding in the end. The stalemates of the grenade tosses at the beginning of matches can be aggravating, but you'll feel like a secret agent slipping through as a spy.
Overall, this game is absolutely marvelous, and will live on forever. This game is worth the five bucks, it's tons of fun, and it will keep you entertained for years to come.

I purchased this game solely for single-player play. I have not played and will not play any multiplayer. I have played through the entire game once with a pistol/blades elf. I don\'t regret playing it and generally had fun, but there are some major shortcomings. I won\'t be replaying or buying any DLC.
PROS:
1) Turn-based squad combat is fun.
2) Even if rather limited, it is set in the Shadowrun universe. There is no substitute for that.
3) Character customization is pretty well done.
CONS:
1) Requires login to servers to play and you are forced to see the global chat.
2) No choices to be made in the story until the very end. You can choose not to do side missions, but those are just inconsequential grinding for money and experience.
3) Writing was boring and lifeless. Didn\'t use contractions.
4) Weapon progression seemed silly. You save up a bunch of money waiting for new weapons and armor in the shop and then buy the best new weapons an armor. Thing is, you don\'t even know what you are saving up for until it\'s available and once it is, you can probably just buy everything you want immediately.
5) No documentation
6) No Matrix
7) Deckers doing damage to everything short of magical creatures with their deck seemed silly.
8) Mages not having access to a physical attack seemed like an artificial limitation.
9) Henchmen (NPC runners) can only have single offensive skill. This made melee henchmen nearly useless. You need to use cover in this game and it is not easy to do that if you have to get up close to contribute at all.
10) Henchmen can\'t have tactical items (e.g. medkits)
11) No overwatch capability
12) Wild camera movement during enemy turn makes it hard to see damage amounts as they appear
13) Lots of map reuse. You can start me at a different end of the map, but it\'s still the same map.
14) Missions started to feel very formulaic. I began using the same set of henchmen for every mission (Halon, Bats###, and Jimmy Mac). Cover, mark, fire, slice, rinse, and repeat.
15) Every character gets two actions per turn and attacking ends the character\'s turn. Unless you get a temporary bonus, you can\'t just attack twice. You can\'t attack and then reload. You can\'t attack and then run for cover. This felt so limiting, simplistic, and artificial.

That said, the engine itself is plug-and-play and thus has many practical limitations. There are things it can do and things it can't and not a lot of in-between. Notes to potential buyers:
because of the cost, I would caution casual buyers to be sure this is a program they would actualy use. Some of the music packs also have sample music avaliable on the game's official website:

Not all of the content shown in the trailer exists in vinilla: spesificaly I noticed the pop-up immages of characters are not included and the "name bar" for character conversations dosen't exist in vanilla. They can, however, be created and added. They might also be avaliable in the DLC or from the community.
One last note: I have seen several people buy this engine only to lose interest a couple months in and never finish a project. Make sure you are comitted to completing your game and set reasonable goals based on your current ability. To use this engine you need to know how to work. Although my own goals were overly ambitious initialy I don't plan on quitting until I have at least completed one project. Look at my number of hours, consider that I haven't completed a project, and tell me why you'll need to be comitted to work before you can use this program.

As someone who's played every single fallout game, yes, even THAT game. The one on PS2/Xbox that nobody wants to acknowledge. I can safely say while Fallout 3 was a drastic change for the series, it's still very enjoyable. It's arguable which is better, fallout 1/2/Tactics, or 3/NV/4. Me, I'm more of a Fallout 2/Tactics/FNV guy. But this isn't for Fallout 2, Tactics, or FNV.
Fallout 3 begins with your birth. Your mother dies from cardiac arrest shortly after you pop your little head out, and dad begins to question this freshly born infant on it's name, and what it wants to grow up to look like. After your mother dies, the game skips a year or so, and you pick your S.P.E.C.I.A.L here. For reference, mine is usually something like this. S: 7 P: 5 E:7 C: 4 I: 6 L: 1. Then, you go through life in the vault, eventually getting your very own Pip-Boy 3000, a BB gun, and taking your G.O.A.T to determine your tag skills. One day, dad leaves the vault, and everything goes to♥♥♥♥♥♥ With the help of your childhood friend (or not), you escape Vault 101, and emerge blinking into the wastes. You eventually find your way to Megaton, and get info from a supposed friend of your father's. Then you make your way to Galaxy News Radio, meet the brotherhood, acquire a nuclear catapult, and ♥♥♥♥ up some giant roid rage mutant with the help of a bunch of dudes in power armor with laser guns. After meeting the charismatic Three Dog, your eventually find your way to vault 112, and free Dad from the horrific simulator that the man who built the Garden Of Eden Creation Kit rules. You then enlist the help of some scientists who live on half of a big♥♥♥♥♥metal boat, who are also apparently your dad's pals. Once more,♥♥♥♥♥♥goes to hell when the batman army, also known as the Enclave, attacks the purifier, intending to take it over. Your father sacrifices himself to kill a bunch of batmen, but Colonel Autumn survives because of some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t mystery drug. You enlist the help of the Brotherhood of Steel, and run off to vault 87 to retrieve the G.E.C.K. The Enclave somehow kidnaps you, and then you get to be interrogated by a now-gray haired Colonel Autumn. President Eden tells him to ♥♥♥♥ off so that he can meet you. On your way there, Colonel Autumn makes the batmen ignore Eden's order, and attack you. After carving a bloody path to Eden, you find out the president of the Enclave is just a genocidal computer, which you can then trick into comitting suicide, or obey his orders to posion the purifier for some reason. You then escape, and find out that the Enclave has fortified their position at the purifier, and so the Brotherhood of Steel finally unveils Liberty Prime, who then proceeds to bend the enclave over, and roughly ♥♥♥♥ them up the♥♥♥♥♥while you make your way into the rotunda, and activate Project Purity. Then you die. Unless you have Broken Steel. Then you awaken two weeks later, and find out that the batman army is still hanging on for dear life. You once again work with the BoS to finish off the Enclave, the penultimate blow being when you use their orbital missile thing to nuke their mobile base crawler back to the stone age. Then you're free to explore the Capital Wasteland as you please.
There's a lot to this game, and I only covered the main story, and the DLC that allows you to continue after activating Project Purity. Tons of sidequests for you to do, loot to find, allies to befriend, enemies to make, all that jazz. Fallout 3 is defintely one hell of a game, and if you can muster the (very little) brainpower to make it work on newer OS, then I reccomend picking up a copy.

I'm a fan of the Shadowrun setting and I liked Shadowrun Returns, so I thought this game should be fun as well with the ability to play co-op as well. Well, I was partly right, because it is pretty decent as long as you have someone to play with. The reasons I'm not recommending the game is:
- I'm a fair bit into the story, but shops never sell anything new so it feels like I'm just accumulating nuyen (money).
- Skill trees feel very bland and at higher levels you need tons of karma (xp) to advance in a seemingly pointless skill.
- Magic is done wrong. A pure mage can't really harm robots in this game, while in the game system there are plenty of spells to do so with. Also, troll mages seem to be the best choice, because they do more magic damage. No clue why.
- Speaking of magic, hit% is really weird. Often I can have a 90% chance to hit with an AoE-spell and still miss, and every time I miss the spell hits one or more friends instead. Like, why would I throw a manaball backwards just because I missed the particular tile I was aiming at? This is almost game-breaking at times.
- The further you progress, the more you realize that the developers were lazy and just reused the same levels over and over again. The only things that change are where and which mobs are placed.
- Story isn't really engaging, so far it's mostly been "meh".
This being said, if you'd really like some (simple) turn-based shadowrun action together with a friend or two, go ahead. I'd recommend you to first look up some gameplay-videos on YouTube though and get the game on a sale.

Lets review!
This game is intense, and not for your usual survival elements that make big name games what they are.
You are confined to a single room. This room has a monitor which provides your only eyesight about Fazbear's Pizza, and two switches; a door switch and a light switch. Your objective is deceptively simple. Survive the night, using these three tools as your only means to see 6 A.M. alive.
Might seem easy, at first. The first night will be a breeze, a true tutorial of the game to get comfy. By night 2, you might be surprised to pop open your cameras only to find out one of the animatronics is already out and mucking about.
By night 3 you'll understand what real horror is. It isn't in 'Do I have enough bullets', or 'oh damn, I have to outrun this big bad oogy boogy thing'. It's in watching a power gauge go from 100%, and praying to God it doesn't hit 0% before dawn comes. Or hoping Chica will finally go away from the window, while you're trying to maintain three different things and watching your reserves just drop and drop.
The jump scares are pretty okay. They'll surprise the hell out of you, and may cause you to scream loudly and in a broad, colorful stream of obscenities. But this is only the icing on a seven layer cake straight from the bakery of Hell. The atmosphere, and tension are the real key factors here. Combined with a resource management scheme that works really well, and becomes significantly harder to deal with, this is a real gem of a game!
There are some cons. For instance, your neighbors next door of your apartment will not appreciate the sudden stream of slurs you echo throughout your apartment building. Also, a great deal of the A.I. is either left up to luck itself on whether or not you'll survive, or I somehow was... good, I'm not sure which. Foxy never broke out of Pirate's Cove during my five nights, though he did come sneaking out of the curtain. And Chica decided to jsut take up a five minute vigil outside of my door, which quickly became annoying and cause my only death due to dealing with her while trying to keep an eye on everything else. But at the same time, I'd chalk up such paranoia inducing shennanigans as all part of the experience.
Welcome to Freddy's. It's one half skill, and the other half luck. Will yours hold out til 6 in the morning?

Review as of 10/16/2015 with 238.7 Hours on record.
Gameplay: Is almost the same as DD1 with some stark differences. Combos are being added, meaning if an enemy is frozen from an ice turret, and hit with a rock turret, they have a chance to shatter. Towers are much MUCH larger then in DD1 as of the last patch of DD2, yet this also makes the towers more imposing and shows the true details of how much effort was put into the towers themselves.
Controls: While gamepad is supported, it still needs some fine tuning which can be done on the options menu. Pretty much any command can be re-binded to keyboard, mouse, or controller so have at it. The camara angles can be funky at times but that mainly applies to close quarters or strange builds that puts you and your towers against a wall.
Characters: Your favorites return with more to come! So far only the 4 original heroes from DD1 have made a return, with more in the works! They each handle differently, they all have their own advantage, and the gameplay with each one varies while still working together in such synch to cover each person’s weakness is astounding.
Multiplayer: As of right now you can play solo or use matchmaking. Matchmaking is still being fine-tuned to get you the best matches. Out of my full time playing I have only ever been matched with 2 rude people and that in itself is astounding! The community is amazing for this kind of game. Everyone is working together to achieve the same goals as you so they help each other out!
Inventory: There is still much to desire here, yet it is still being fine-tuned and made. Trading will hopefully be around soon, yet your own loot is instanced so you don't have to fight others on who gets what loot. Pick up everything you see as its all yours!
Overall: I was hesitant for a bit during the early parts of early access. The gameplay was lacking, and then Nightmare Mode was released. And boy, was no one ready to take that on! It is the current endgame mode and ultimate challenge as of right now. With everything now falling into place, this game will last for, hopefully, a very very long time.

I loved the first game... Not at first, though. In fact, when I first saw all the DLC, I thought Dungeon Defenders was a horrid cash grab. I only got into it because I was cooerced by my friends...

Dungeon Defenders was a true pleasure to play, and nice breath of fresh air in a genre I never even considered. Since then, I have played Sanctum (1 and 2), Orcs Must Die 2, but neither really cured the itch the first left behind.
Then I played this... and I didn't really stop until my friend and I crushed the main campaign.
Dungeon Defenders 2 is a true successor to a truly wonderful game, which even runs beautiful on my PoS laptop. The gameplay feels faster, the loot plentiful to the point of slowing you down a moment in the menus to see and sell --which works in the game's favor; it has you stop, take a breather in between missions for each one to really feel unique and not just more fodder for the slaughter.
The game is nowhere near perfect, but there's no denying a lot of love went into this... and it's F2P, so there's no harm in trying it. Don't take my word, don't take anybody's; if you have a toaster, try it out. Worst case is you are sucked into the game for hours, and left wondering why you haven't put any pants on yet.
Edit: This game has changed way too much, and for the most part not for the better. Another currecny to unlock champs, with heavy incentive to pay instead when the amount you gain through quests is apalling; I liked this game, but I do not like where it is heading, esp. when the new characters have major legs up on their basic cousins.
Hopefully I'm proven wrong in the future, but for now I cannot recommend this game in its current state.

--**FULL REVIEW FOR SHADOWRUN CHRONICLES - BOSTON LOCKDOWN (
) INCLUDING DLC**--
[Initial version: May 11, 2016]
SCOPE: All story-specific content that has been released to date, which includes the main story campaign and the Infected DLC. All remaining content is effectively grinding gear and Karma (exp), and will have its own section.
This review is also completely
.
Oh, and for clarity:
is NOT an 'MMO' in any real way, save for the mandatory servers. There is no resource trading to speak of (even between a player's own runners), and open "grinding" isn't an option until after the end of the main story.
For all practical purposes, treat SRC: BL as a turn-based PVE game with the option of inviting human players along...and it's all hosted online.
-GAMEPLAY: The short, dirty version is that the gameplay is way too simple and "streamlined" for Shadowrun. If I had to use a relative comparison, I'd say it's like XCOM: Enemy Unknown, possibly even a bit simpler.
There's ZERO "legwork", no real resource trading or management, no Matrix runs or even Shadowland banter (to be fair, there's a good story reason for that), and character building is bare-bones even compared to its sister game series, Shadowrun Returns.
Normally I wouldn't hold something like this against a game, except it's supposed to be SHADOWRUN; and in an era where online games as complex as EVE Online remain popular and viable, I don't think it was too much to ask for at least a little bit more depth.
-ENGINE, GRAPHICS, AND AUDIO: This game is low-budget and it shows. The 3D graphics look ~12 years out of date vs the modern high-def bloom-fest of current gen gaming. Personally, I have no issue with that, because the visual style fits well enough (well, the models could afford to look less "toony"), and it isn't an offensive departure.
The main campaign has some voice-acting, and it ranges from 'passable' to 'plain ol bad'. Nothing painfully offensive, but I routinely found myself re-reading text and doing better takes than most of the droning VAs, in-situ. Yikes.
Music...it's completely unremarkable. I have nothing to say about it, good or bad.
-INTERFACE: Best thing I can say about the interface, is that it's "functional" (not great).
There's a number of improvements I can and will suggest, including:
There are times where moving around specific hazards in a single turn isn't possible, despite having the total movement available, because the game automatically uses the shortest path for everything.
Using movement queuing (that is, letting the player map a specific path before confirming) instead of always forcing "shortest distance jog" would allow for more in-depth hazard design.
-STORY, DIFFICULTY AND OVERALL PACING: The story is pretty meh, with one, maybe two really interesting moments in the entire thing. The difficulty curve will depend heavily on how many player character runners you bring along, and at what relative "level" each one is to the mission.
The base campaign's story missions curve up fairly evenly, with only one or two anamolously hard missions along the way. Post-campaign missions are (initially) off the charts in terms of difficulty, spiking WAY beyond what you had previously dealt with (barring possibly the very last mission).
One big upside I will mention, is that at least
has pretty damn accurate/honest Hit%; it doesn't hide the enemy's personal evasion bonuses or quietly skew successes like it does in Shadowrun Returns. Or at least, I didn't embark on any of my "Miss 3 shots at 95%+ in a row" streaks like I did so often in SRR.
-INFECTED MISSIONS: This DLC is...pretty bad IMO. All signs point to a rush job.
1) There's no voice-acting, even for all the characters that previously had VA. This wouldn't be so bad if not for the fact that this forces the player to read the text...which brings me to my second criticism of the Infected DLC...
2)...The text is LITTERED with errors; mostly typos, but more than a couple of flat out broken sentences.
3) Little original content. Apart from the maps (and the Ex-Pacis faction mobs), most everything else is a reskin of previous content.
4) The difficulty spikes are wildly uneven.
The second mission was an unwinnable slug-fest the first time; second attempt it was a slow cakewalk. As in, the encounters were very different, despite having the same characters and resources available.
4a) Oh, and making Achievements purely luck-based,  is a stupid enough concept. Making it so you only get ONE crack at a given story mission achievement with that character is just cruel.
OVERALL: I would wait on a sale, or possibly just pass entirely. I don't want to leave the impression that I hate this game, not by a long shot.
It's just...as a long time Shadowrun fan, it's far too simple and bland. As a generic turn-based RPG, it will kill some time, but is otherwise not terribly memorable.
I really want the Shadowrun video games to do well, or at least well enough to warrant more ambitious Shadowrun projects; hence the length of this review. If you're a fan looking for more SR lore and story, I'd stick to the tabletop, novels and the last two SRR games (Dragonfall is an excellent story, and Hong Kong has been pretty great so far).
Boston Lockdown has a strong potential setting, and pulls a couple of big name-drops in the story's crisis, but ultimately leaves no lasting impression.
(it also makes many mistakes with the in-universe physical laws; namely involving hacking and magic, but these changes were clearly done with the interest of gameplay mechanics in mind, so I let them slide purely on those grounds. It still makes me roll my eyes watching drones say IMMUNE TO MAGIC when a POWER bolt hits them)

Zachtronics has taken an engineering simulator and disguised it as a puzzle game. You start off building simple constructions and transporting from point A to point B. Before long you're constructing separate sub-assemblies simultaneously and piping them to various juntions to be fitted together in a vast labyrinth of conveyor belts, power conduits, welders and blocks, then when you finally step back and look at your masterpiece, you wonder how the heck you got it all to work. The game also has tremendous replayability, challenging you to craft more efficient designs; a smaller overall system footprint and seamless manufacturing processes. You can compare your design efficiency with the general public and with your individual friends. If you're the patient, problem-solving type that loves to think outside of the box, this game is a real treat. I've had many a laugh testing out a system that I nearly perfected, watching my creation come together, only to have the boxes piling up at input 3 simply because I forgot to wire one of the pistons.

Fallout 3, a tale of exploration, family, the collapse and rebuilding of society, and revelations. You are the silent, lone wanderer of the wasteland, discovering what in the wasteland  happened and how the world became so bleak and grim. The story, while not quite as good as New Vegas' is full of plenty of twists and turns down the main quest line. But the side quests are where the real truth is revealed. Touching stories of children trying to find their parents to blowing up an entire town, just for a fancy apartment, there is some massive variety (more so than in a game like Skyrim or Fallout 4). The gameplay is fine but not great, with a unique twist in VATS. What Fallout 3 may lack in story or gameplay, it definitely makes up for in its world. The Capital Wasteland is one of my favorite video game open worlds ever. The size, although not that large, never feels small and you never feel locked in a specific area. The really impressive part of the world is that Bethesda nailed the wasteland feel to it. Overall, a spectacular game that I would recommend to anyone that hasn't played it before, or played it on consoles and wants mods.
Verdict: 9.2/10

-VATS

Cons:

-Mediocre story compared to the other Fallout games

In over 5 hours I've discovered so much wrong with this game.
The entire server/matchmaking system is a mess. The devs expect you to stay grouped with some strangers the game matches you with. Additionally, people will make you wait for 5 minutes or longer, and that's in a 10 minute match. It's not their fault, however, it's how the devs made the game. Even after finishing a mission you're forced to wait for up to 2 minutes if not everyone readies up. And often they won't, instead be chasing after gear and gold coins which get AUTO COLLECTED, except most people don't seem to know of this function.
If you want to go your own pace, be prepared for a great source of frustration right here. Extra effort, extra time lost, all for nothing.
Meanwhile you often get thrown into a mission that just started, meaning you won't be getting any green mana to build towers with, at least not the first wave. To all TD fans out there: Missing out on your first wave income - is this something you enjoy? As an avid TD fan, I can tell you this is extremely unsatisfying. It's one of those little mechanics that'll easily drive one away.
This game is obviously not made to play on your own pace. Apart from what I described above, every map is multiplayer oriented, and while you can go at it alone, the game really tries to force you not to.
Difficulty. Sure, it slowly curves up, but i'm still meeting zero challenge. Over 5 hours in, and I haven't had a single moment where I thought there might be the slightest possibility of losing. The devs treat you like an infant, slowly pacing you. In the end this backfires, as people who are enjoying the lack of challenge will quickly quit once the challenge is suddenly thrown in their face, and people preparing for the challenge won't be prepared at all due to the lack of experience fighting off a serious situation - as so far they have had their hands held on every single turn.
Max towers. This is a big one. You will be dealing with a lot of different people as you play the game. Most of them simply lack common sense when it comes to tower building. They will spam garbage all over the map, or clutter a single lane with limitless low level structures. Even if you are playing with pro's, this is an issue. It's a mechanic I do not like, do not agree with and forms a huge barrier in my mind whenever I think of starting the game up. The max towers really limits your options and creativity, it takes away from the idea of a "Tower Defense" game and further promotes you to focus on your hero.
Which brings us to my final chapter, as i'm getting tired of writing about this "mediocre at best" game. The focus on the action part of the game... While the levels are designed with both tower builders and action players in mind, there's just no real balance to speak of. You can choose whether you want to focus on towers or on hero, but in the early game it really doesn't make a difference. Can't speak for the mid-end game. But I can tell you this often results in people almost completely ignoring the side they haven't focused on. You'll see tower builders camping near their towers, occasionally casting some abilities, and you'll see action players hack n slash their way through a wave while completely ignoring their green mana (tower currency) bar, not even taking the time to upgrade someone else's structures.
There are plenty more annoyances and issues. From inventory system/infinite amounts of crappy loot to dig through, to the quite limited amount of classes=/=towers, this is feels less like a TD and more like an action game than the first one. For some people this might actually be a good thing, however.
I'm not even talking about the graphics which I do not care for, or the lack of any sort of voice acting, which I don't expect to ever see.
The game is a mess, it's frustrating, and it's most definitely worse than the first one.

Mind you that most what I described here are simply core mechanics, and have little to do with the fact that the game is in Alpha.

The Deed Dynasty is a sequel to The Deed. It features three new murder scenarios set in three different time periods with different casts, they are all (almost) up to par with the original though there is little variety. The original had a bit more depth, such as flashbacks that could be encountered in the household, but overall all murder scenarios are of a good quality. However, despite them taking place in different time periods they are all quite similar, since while the story and characters change the mechanics do not. It also does not expand on the original formula, it is the same game except three times as large. With that said, I liked the first game, meaning I also like this one. The dialogue trees are quite intricate and do remember a lot of details, and with the numerous ways to assassinate the targets you can get lots of different endings. The writing itself is good, and the characters, while not memorable, certainly do feel real. If you like interactive storytelling I would reccomend this to you, especially with its low price. However, if we ever get a third game I would like to see some innovation in the mechanics or simply even more reactive dialogue trees. Overall, I say buy it.

Valley is a first person platformer with light combat elements. It reminds me a little of another game I played entitled "A Story About My Uncle," so if you're a Valley fan, the one might be worth checking out too.
Almost immediately after starting the game, you find a "LEAF" suit. It's basically an exoskeleton that allows you to run faster, jump higher, and get this: revive or destroy local flora and fauna. When you're charging down a hill, gaining momentum the whole time, and you launch across a crevasse, the game is exhilarating. There are quite a few moments like this, and things get especially exciting when you find train tracks that seem to interface with your suit to generate more and more speed. In addition, it creates an oddly tranquil feeling in the player to revive deer and dead trees that you come across.
However, I can't say that the story really resonated with me. First of all, your character is exploring ruins that seem to be at least 50 years old. The game attempts to create an immediate crisis that the player is responsible for solving, but the thought that these ruins have been sitting here without incident for so long really undermines the pressure and immediacy of the crisis. It is true, though, that someone else could happen upon the site and abuse the technology found within. So perhaps it's good that the protagonist stopped by, but she definitely doesn't need to be in a hurry.
Secondly, and at the risk of giving too much away story-wise, I felt that one of the big "reveals" in the late game could be read as an allegory for the stem cell debate. This came to mind as I was playing, and actually soured me a little on the title as I tired long ago of conservative legislators delaying potentially life-changing medical advances.

To summarize it simply, it is a very cost-efficient, well-written and designed murder scheming simulator. The gameplay involves gathering gossips about others, hiding your true motive by choosing conversations carefully, selecting from a variety of weapons, and using certain evidences all in order to frame others (or make it look like a suicide) and ultimately get away with murder. There are a wide number of outcomes based on your every action and interaction with others.
The game is in fact a sequel for the game "The Deed". To be precise, it is a sequel that is a prequel which expands on the "Bruce" bloodline introduced in the first game with 3 new stories set in older eras. While the first game only had one scenario, "The Deed: Dynasty" is, in a sense, like an expansion pack which maintains the general gameplay formula and offers 3 new scenarios with a lot more interesting characters, stories, and motives for murder.
While I had never been a fan of such genre, this game has definitely enlightened me to it with the abundant amount of various paths and outcomes it offers under the objective of murder. It is certainly an experience worth trying out for its generous price.

Ah, Valley...
When you were very little, do you remember running down a hill to get that speed boost, to feel that sensation of flying forward at the limits of your balance and experiencing the exhiliration of moving faster thatn you ever could on flat ground?  This game is that feeling bottled when it wants to be, and a visually assisted audiobook when it doesn't.
A common rule of cooking is that if you are going to do something simple, you have to do it well.  Blue Isle Studios must have had that as a mantra when designing this game.  It doesn't do anything extravagant, simple story, simple mechanisms, simple linear path.  However, in doing those things it also does them very well.  The controls are tight and natural and work well with the level design so that movement along the path feels exhilirating and yet natural.  The music is built to make you feel the sheer joy of effortless movement.  The combat neither feels overly forced or completely ignorable.  Everything in this game is simple, and yet simply perfect.

Fallout 3, a tale of exploration, family, the collapse and rebuilding of society, and revelations. Do you want an excellent horror experience filled with blood and fear? Than Outlast is for you.
Miles Upshur, an investigative reporter, receives a tip from an employee of the Murkoff Corporation. The tip says that the Corporation is conducting potentially illegal operations at the Mount Massive Insane Asylum. Armed only with his video camera with nightvision, Miles investigates.
What he finds is worse than he could have imagined.
Now, trapped inside the Asylum, stalked around every corner by its' inhabitants, you must guide Miles to freedom and help him reveal the truth to the outside world.
While the setting may be off-putting to some (Ohh, an insane asylum. How original.), Outlast's atmosphere and intensity will make anyone who plays immediately forget about that. The game has a good length, totaling at least four to eight hours in length.
Instead of a standard flashlight, you are equipped with a camcorder with night vision. The night vision runs on batteries, which can be few and far between in the beginning, but grow slightly more common as the game progresses. But one must use them sparingly, as they have the lifespan of an exploding firework. The camera also allows you to collect notes if you focus on a certain event or object of interest for long enough. These notes add a bit more of character to Miles, detailing what he thinks about the event or object. You can also collect files that are scattered throughout the game, offering a look into how this madness all began. These notes and files give you a clearer view on the game's story. The camera changes along the way, sustaining a crack in the lens and occasionaly distorting with static late in the game.
But enough about the camera, let's discuss our main character, Miles Upshur. Miles is a regular, everyday person. So he doesn't know how to fight; your only options being run, hide, or die. The character model is fantastic, allowing you to see your body and arms. Your hands wil grab onto doorknobs as you open them, press against the wall if you're leaning against one. I will say there is a moment mid-way thorugh the game that temporarily effects you character, but I wont go further than that.
You can use the "Q" and "E" by default to look around corners, or look behind you when you are running away from that knife-weilding psychopath.
Speaking of psychopaths, let's briefly touch upon the game's antagonists.
There's a big, ugly, guy who acts as the "Main Villain" for the first part of the game. He will be following you throughout the game, and will not discuss this further.
The patients are diverse, although facial models do end up getting re-used quite a bit, but that doesn't detract from the experience that much. Since these are mental patients, they can be unpredictable. Some simply sit in a corner, crying. Others are actively hostile, a few try to help you escape, and smome are friendly one moment and hostile the next. This adds a layer of suspense to each encounter.
Some of the encounters do get a little repetitive, using similar variations of "Collect 'X' amount of items for 'Y' object to activate 'Z' objective.". And it does become predictable as time goes on, that the moment you press a button, chances are something will start stalking you. But they do throw some different scenarios in there every so often, like being trapped in an extremely dark courtyard with a bad guy audibly moving near you. The A.I. is pretty good, actively looking in places you could be hiding in. Stealth is key at times with certain enemies, while other encounters have you sprinting for your life, slamming doors and pushing barricades in front of them as whatever's chasing you gets closer.
The graphics are great, bearing an extremely gritty, realistic resolution to it. The motion blur can be disoreinting to some, so feel free to disable it if you want, it doesn't detract from the immersion in my opinion. The screen has an apparent "Film grain" quality to it, becoming more noticeable when you use your camera. There is little to no HUD of any kind, besides the camcorder overlay, offering a very immersive experience.
This game is horror at its' finest. And while Outlast isn't the perfect horror game, it is still a fantastic journey. My only complaint is that they could have offered a little more variety with the encounters and objectives. Instead of, perhaps, having an enemy appear when you activate something, have nothing happen. THis would cause the player a massive amount of anxiety, waiting for something to happen. And when nothin does, and they start to calm down, hit them with a jump scare!
Overall, I would give this game a 9 out of 10. A fantastic experience overall, that any horror fan worth their salt should give a try. I will not spoil the ending, but I will say that it leaves a lot to be desired. Besides that, this was one of the best horror experiences I have ever had in a video game. And I would highly reccommend you play by yourself, at night, with headphones on, for the ultimate experience.

Fallout 3 is an amazing game with incredible story that sticks with you forever.
Several hundreds years after the world destoyed itself with nuclear holocaust you emerge from a haven, only introduced into the hellish wastes of radioactivity and barbaric cultures who murder and steal for survival. You will do things that you regret, you will help the people who need it the most and you will survive, one way or another.
Choices matter here, you can murder people decimate communities or you can help fix the broken and worn out towns and ease the pain these poor souls must suffer from every day life. Someone upset you? bash their skull in with a hammer. Did someone take your teddy bear? blow their brains out. How about that ugly green mutant shooting hot lead at your face? MELT IT. You choose your skills, your weapon and your tactics. Be it melee weapons, guns, explosives, energy weapons or big♥♥♥♥♥versions of these, like say a minigun or laser equivalent. What about a gun that shoots nukes? The variety of traits and skills gives a different style each time you play. You can choose between light, medium and heavy armours that come with pros and cons along with stat changes.
Fast travel is a option if you want to move quickly from discovered locations. This gives incentive to explore more areas and gives you the ability to travel more freely between the large landscape. The trademark S.P.E.C.I.A.L (Strength, Perception, Endurance, Charisma, Intelligence, Agility and Luck) gives you the choice of adding points to each. Be a well rounded person, or dumb as a brick with super strength. Okay, from a story and gameplay perspective this game DEFINITELY has potential. I can't really criticize a lot cuz it's still early alpha days, so I'll simply stick to some selected pros and cons:
The most significant PROS:
+ excellent atmosphere for a survival game, nice choice of area (winter wilderness)
+ nice ambient sounds and character voiceover (cud be more varied, though)
+ nice semi-cartoon semi-real graphics, reminds me a bit of "The Last Express" (1997 adventure), I wouldn't mind if it stayed that way, but entirely realistic graphics wud be awesome as well
+ a good variety of survival items and methods (not too easy, not too complicated)
+ creepy areas (without any monsters or zombies - finally, thank god!)
The CONS (Mind you I'm quite picky, but we all know this is an early alpha, yet hopefully designers take such feedback into account):
- GENERAL BALANCING needs to be improved a lot, I'm not saying surviving shud be made easy, but atm it's a lil hard to even stay alive for a couple of RL hours
- ONLINE multiplayer MODE must be added, cuz searching for other survivors and teaming up in a hostile environment wud be way cooler than doing this all on ure own
- in doing so, it wud be great to add real CRAFTING and e.g. shelter BUILDING FEATURES with full visual animation effects (e.g. take down a tree with a hatchet, carry the logs to your building site, build a hut in very customizable ways, craft weapons, armor, traps, etc. to defend ureselves and ure shelter/village)
- furthermore, CHARACTER DEVELOPMENT (skill trees, etc.) shud be introduced/enhanced
- various gameplay DIFFICULTY SETTINGS wud be nice, e.g. more food & survival gear and less beasts in easy mode, etc.
- GRAPHICS need improving, there are still many glitches i.e. at the border of the maps, getting stuck while ducking etc.
All in all, imho a good survival game shud be:
- highly customizable in terms of items used, character development, non-linear gameplay
- realistic yet simple to navigate

Having played Harebrained Studios' excellent Shadowrun Returns and Dragonfall RPGs I came to Chronicles with information like this is an online-only co-op focused game made by another studio and which initially had some pretty terrible reviews that have since improved with the regular patches. Being a single player person I was wondering whether this game would do it for me but after giving it a chance I have to say it is a good game.
While Boston Lockdown may not have the full-fledged RPG mechanics of SR and SR:D (favouring a somewhat simpler skill tree) it is a Shadowrun experience with turn-based tactical combat, good 3D - if simple - graphics and - more importantly to me - you can solo the story campaign without problems if you build your character carefully. The story is interesting and there is character building across the campaign. One thing to bear in mind is that multiple aspects of the rich Shadowrun world (which is a long running pen and paper RPG first) are not fully introduced so it would be better if you play another Shadowrun game first to familiarise yourself with the setting so as to fully enjoy it.
Of course this being an online co-op-focused game, the game's hub is one relatively small map that acts as a stop-over shopping and discussion location where you will see other players walking around but you can solo the whole thing without problems. As the main story progresses the hub changes to reflect current events and you do get side missions regularly after the introductory missions are over. The only thing preventing this being a serviceable offline SR game is the always online requirement (saves are server side) and the small easy to ignore chat window on the bottom left. As the developers do not have the rights to make an offline game this is an understandable compromise but I do hope it gets a full offline mode sometime in the future so the game lives on past the servers. The difficulty especially in the beginning is quite high which makes for an interesting challenge and pushes you to plan and execute carefully.
So TL;DR: Yes, this is a good Shadowrun game for single player types and scratches that turn based Shadowrun itch in between the Harebrained studios core entries.

Shadowrun Chronicles is a decent attempt at making a heavily multiplayer focused turn based strategy game and to some extent it does succeed, but unfortunately for me it's failures heavily outweigh it's innovations.
----
+ Unique in that the turn based tactical gameplay is fully co-op.
+/- Gameplay can be fun, but is shallow compared to other similar games (see the other Shadowrun games, XCOM, Massive Chalice, Final Fantasy Tactics, Tactics Ogre, Front Mission, Fire Emblem, etc)
+/- Costume collecting elements exist, but many of them are very similar to each other
- Terrible story telling
- Wonky, nonsense filled dialogue
- Terrible voice acting
- Very little end game content without DLC
- No matchmaking other than spamming global chat
- The same battlefields are used multiple times
- Outside of missions, you are restricted to one small and boring hub area for the whole game.
- Some minor bugs and strange design choices give the game a slightly broken feeling
----
This is probably not the shadowrun game you are looking for. This is not a part of the other more popular Shadowrun series which is also on steam and which I would highly recommend.
First off, I am a complete sucker for turn based tactical games of this nature. I absolutely can't get enough of them. The idea of being able to play a game like that with some buddies is an intriguing one to say the least. I am grateful this game exists, if only for the possibility that more games might attempt a similar formula and hopefully do it much better.
Sadly though, there may be a story in Shadowrun Chronicles, but other than there being a lockdown in Boston in which you and your pals are stuck, i'm really not sure what it is. There's some nonsense about increasingly stupidly named "corps" (the big corporations which are the social leaders in the shadowrun universe) being up to no good in some vague way and there are AI zombies and dragons involved somehow. That's about all I was able to gleam from the ridiculously inept story telling and confusing, poor dialogue.
Also, the voice acting made it difficult to concentrate for any length of time on what was being said. My orc character seemed to me like the voice was copied straight from the normal human male and pitch shifted down with some cheap software. It really sounded awful.
The game quickly devolves then into a series of pointless missions that go on for just a tad too long before culminating in a boss fight so difficult that the universally accepted way of beating it involves hiding in a small room for long periods of time.
Overall, it's not a game I would recommend to anyone but the most die-hard of Shadowrun fans or turn based tactical connoseurs, and even then I would only recommend it with the affidavit that it is mostly not very good.

I tried really hard to like this game, but in the end there is just no way I can.  For me, Heroes 5 was the pinnacle of the series and every step 6 takes is a step backwards in my opinion.  Here are the 5 biggest problems I have:
1. The AI programming completely ruins the game.  In the single player campaign, the AI does not play with the same rules or even close to the same rules as the player.  Every creep monster it encounters runs from it, which allows it to pillage everything on the map as quickly as it can walk to it.  It also doesn't actually build its cities up.  It starts with a predefined city build and just gets flooded with many times more troops per week than the player gets.  Additionally, defeated AI heroes respawn with very large armies.  This forces you to rush through every map as quickly as possible because the longer you give the AI, the exponentially more numerous his army becomes.  Its rate of growth is far beyond what you can keep up with.
2. The skill system is awful.  Every hero has some base stats and beyond that, they are all otherwise exactly the same since every hero can be trained in any skill you want.  Have a warrior?  Spend your skill points and turn him into a spell caster.  Have a wizard?  Spend some skill points and make him the strongest warrior on the map.  It's silly.
3.  You can convert towns to different factions.  Some people surprisingly like this, but its actually just a bandaid to help compete with the terribly unbalanced/poorly scripted AI.  Yes, with just a few ore, wood and gold, you can convert any town of any faction to your faction.  Just like magic, instantly.  Again, it's just stupid.
4.  The campaigns aren't really campaigns.  You can bounce around between campaigns mission by mission and ironically have to in order to actually follow the story chronologically.  It basically kills any attempt to keep a coherent story line going.
5.  It has 2 additional layers of DRM.  Uplay is bad enough, but the Heroes 6 "Conflux" always on internet connection requirement is just too painful to bear since half the time it doesn't even connect.  There are plenty of times where you can't play the game because the conflux servers are down.
All in all, the game is a nice looking, shallow disaster.  Avoid this like syphillis.

Except for one particular aspect, The Last Journey succeeds in building an engaging story in an interesting world with good voice acting and beautiful pixel graphics. Only its gameplay is ultimately and unfortunately a discouraging drag.
Despite the exciting premise and well made story assets, exploring the vast empty space still feels incredibly exhausting. The ship flies automatically at a set speed. About every ten to twenty minutes an object of interest, namely a planet, star or spaceship wreckage, appears nearby with an uplifting tune playing and an arrow indicating the objects location. Randomly occurring asteroids, which can greatly damage the ship's hull, don't have such indicators and can be hard to dodge, especially with the upgrade that accelerates the ship's speed installed.
There's simply nothing else to do than watch the screen and occasionally move the ship every few minutes. That in itself is not so much of a problem. A slow-paced game with few mechanical interactions can be relaxing. But in this case the game forces the player to be constantly on edge in order to advance, making it more tiresome than relaxing.
Then again, the lack of (inter-)action promotes the moments where supposedly important discoveries are made. There's a suspense that stems from the story and builds up due to the quietness in space and basic survival mechanics that require the player to find oxygen, platinum for ship repairs and thorium to fuel the ship. Resources are found on planets, stars and spaceship wrecks and usually cover the consumption generously.
The Last Journey demands undivided attention while offering only short story snippets leaving the player staring at empty space for dozens of minutes without action. The great amount of artistic integrity and promising story proposition sadly doesn't spur the motivation to push through seemingly endless hours of doing nothing.

I recommend this game to most people on the basis that it offers an immersive experience by executing on gorgeous graphics and a brilliant soundtrack to augment an intriguing foray into the unknown. You'll enjoy plenty of beautiful vistas and heaps of atmosphere which evolves as you move through the valley's various "biomes" and uncover gameplay and narrative elements. Incidentally, the pacing of each of these is really nicely done.
It's no spoiler to reveal that there are collectables in this game, and this element is never prohibitive of story progression. I would recommend a measured vigilance as you move through areas, and returning after concluding the story to complete your gathering of collectables. Pedantic search for them will cause the experience of the game to drag during its slower sections for all but the most fastidious of dispositions.
PvE Combat features, but its generally secondary or even tertiary nature as a theme is reflected in its simplicity. Depending on your taste, this might encourage or deter you. Consider this, then, an exploration and adventure game that delivers on all its major points. The various activities that you'll undertake typically involve conveying yourself to a new part of your environment; and in this, the game strikes me as a rigourous "walking simulator" at times.
I must stress, though, that it remains engaging throughout, as from the off, you'll have a suit which augments your movement drastically. Moving around the map in various ways really capitalises on the audiovisuals of the game and can feel a fairly liberating, joyous experience as it's not so bonkers as to seem fantastical and takes place in a world that looks real enough to allow you to suspend disbelief.
I'll also add that I'm so pleased to have bought the soundtrack at the same time, so consider doing that if you know what's good for you.

-- SUMMARY - EXTENDED REVIEW FOLLOWING --
Despite many other recent reviews, I personally feel that Warface could be a great FPS; one of the best currently available for free on Steam. The pay-to-win elements that other players describe follow suit of almost every other free-to-play video game - that being that because players have to unlock better weapons OR buy-in, the game is therefore pay-to-win. Incidentally, the more attentive of you will likely find that in the vast majority of cases, your weapon choice really doesn't matter that much (until you discover snipers).
The connectivity is oftentimes, unfortunately, atrocious. The game has an autokick bot that smashbats anyone who meets the ping limit during a match, but either the limit has too much leeway, or the bot doesn't always work. In good faith, I'm opting that the issue is the former...thus, my review will change if the developers can once and for all eradicate these players that haven't heard of broadband. The connectivity in some matches is the only unfair portion of this game to date of this review and it is the blight behind the so-dubbed 'hacker problem', which everyone seems certain exists.
I half-arsedly recommend Warface, though, since there are still more ridiculous free-to-play alternatives on Steam, if you dare to try them. I'm one of the many unlucky players that can only operate Black Squad in safe mode because my Direct X9 isn't installed (it is), Blacklight has gone straight down the metaphoric drain, and PlanetSide 2 is the very epitome of neglect and salted with the most bitter portions of the dark side of online humanity. I firmly believe that if Warface's developers pull their finger out, it could become one of the number-one FPSes available not just on Steam, rather, everywhere.
-- SOCIAL --
I have seen that one important point seems to have gone amiss; this is a game that crows its multiplayer cooperativity in your face from the beginning to the end, yet it separates players - regardless of whether or not they're friends or clanmates - into concentration-camp-like rank tiers. Friends cannot join you in games other than PvE cooperative situations until they too have reached rank 13 if you have already surpassed that rank by the time they join, which for any PvP player is a bit of a dull notion. Your newbie friends won't be joining you for at good few hours. That matters circumstantially.
To add insult to injury, you're more than likely to find that the difference between this 'noob tier' and 'MLG tier' is non-existent, if not for contenders with new rank ratings. Whatever the development team think that their rank segregation system is helping or otherwise doing...it isn't. It's a pain in the rectal opening for any social construct.
The playerbase is what one might expect of something free to play - salty and prone to whining. When I'm not being accused of hacking, I'm being greeted by the most precociously unfiltered ten-year-old, self-proclaimed cougar-dominators that one might usually only see in online console games.
-- GAMEPLAY --
All things said and done thus far, the majority of the reviews on this game don't do it as much justice as it should get. I don't have a glorious computer, but mine can handle Warface very smoothly. That might mean bugger-all to you, but to me, especially for a game that looks 'alright', it is nice to be able to run without (much) issue.
I have experienced slight lagging and warping, but I did note that these only really occur when other players in a match have high latency spikes, which leads on to my other jab; connectivity, explained in the following section.
The maps - in particular, for the Free for All and Team Deathmatch game modes - are, for the most part, far too small. This is more noticeable in Free for All when you're squashed into a tiny map with fifteen other players as you're constantly backstabbed and spawn-killed as the game struggles to find new, fair spawn points. I would like to say that it is only a few maps, but, sadly, it is nearly all of them...so I can only suggest lazy map design.
Team Deathmatches are somewhat better, but only because not everyone is out to murder you. Yes, they all look great, but a map becomes cheap when it becomes unplayable. The group sizes should be smaller, or the maps should be larger. Moreover, I personally feel like we should be given the option of group sizes, and maps ought to be larger, either way.
As in most FPS games, several weapons are far too easy to use in certain situations - Warface is no exclusion, in that the sniper rifles are just far too easy to use in variety of circumstances for which they were certainly not designed. CQC is too easy - as a bulky weapon, players find it too easy to quickly manouevre with them. It is especially ridiculously unrealistic when players kamikaze slide toward you, granted one-shot kills with rifles that armour simply has no defense against on almost any part of a player's hitbox. The snipers make more effective shotguns than the actual bloody shotguns. Go figure...
-- USER INTERFACE --
The UI is utter bullsh*t and needs serious reform. Sure, it is simple, but who cares about that if finding your way around is worked about largely by trial and error? Half of the information I know about the UI's usage came from Google, and finding all of the appropriate answers was not the 'walk in the park' that it should have been.
-- CONNECTIVITY --
I felt that it was important to include a section on this. The connectivity to Warface servers might sound inherently bad after you have read about the 'special 75%' as I fondly call them, but I'm connecting from the UK to the Luxembourg server at 22ms; that's not bad, and in fact, I should get good latency in all matches...and I do, at least when I'm looking.
While your connection might be sound, the connections of others approximately 75%(!) of the time (which is an educated guess, by the way - not at all an exaggeration) fall between the 'barely acceptable' and the 'connecting via McDonalds Restaurant smoke signals' end of the scale. As most PvPers from ANY game know, a player's high latency generally has an adverse affect on both themself and/or others - in most cases, others. I honestly had no idea that connecting via facial expressions, hormones and Morse Code was a thing in online gaming...but there you go. Some of the horrendous lag you see on some players makes their two tin cans and a piece of string look far superior to your fibre optic.
The problems begin when multiple players join a match with silly-high latencies. It's not fair on them, and it's even less fair on the players with good latency. We're expected to submit to paying the developers? Not until you get rid of your latency nukers.
Another way of looking at it; exploiting the 'tactics' of the enemy team in every respect is considered fair play - in fact, that's how you might achieve victory in most FPSes. But as soon as you start to exploit the bad connection of a player as you see online, that player might start seeing you killing them in exactly the same sort of bullsh*t ways that they had originally began to kill you in. It looks like you shot them through walls and buildings when you saw them on your screen legitimately, for example. You eventually best their score, and in time, many of these players are childish enough to call you out as a hacker without enough self-awareness to realise that the fault is theirs - not yours - that they saw one of your ancestors waddling around as a different class.
I can only imagine what the threshold is for being reported for hacking - but I gather that the initial ban is automatically applied.

I have been out on my gaming for awhile; I use to play a lot of games then felt burnt out and overall just bored with video games in general. Its been around a year of me not playing games besides the brief occasions of dabbling for a few hours for the nostalgia. I recently had an urge to get into a fun rpg, something open world that had a survival feel to it. though I was very limited on games I could get, because I sold all my consoles, and all I have is a 4 year old 300 dollar HP pavillion laptop. So with hours spend looking up reviews then checking if my laptop could run them I decided on risen. I AM SOOO GLADD I DID!!! My choices were down to gothic 3, two worlds 2 and risen. Which all of them have mixed reviews so it was hard to decide. So HERES MY REVIEW.  GRAPHICS - To me graphics really don't matter much if the game is really fun and this is the case here. keep in mind I play on all low for better performance but even at that I think the world is beautifully done. The weather and the lighting are awesome. When the sun is shining its really bright and actually looks like how bright it would be in real life. When its dark its as dark as it really would be in real life. its soo awesome looking when its dark out, your exploring, its storming and lightening and you get flashes of bright light where you see everything, it really looks badass. (now on high settings the graphics are really nice for its time.) so torches are actually a must if your going in really dark caves or traveling at the dark of night or you can wait to journey and sleep in a bed till morning.  I think it really immerses you in the world. GAMEPLAY- Now what I really really like about this game is the overall small details that a lot of games overlook, that really make the world feel alive IMO. For a RPG I think these details im about to explain are really important to a RPG because theirs people who play and really wanna get into the role of there character and the world hence ROLE playing game. First I'll start off with getting food and cooking it. in this game food really does matter idk how many times i was out exploring and if i didnt have food to boost my health I would of died. and you can find water barrels to drink from that will boost your health when your in need like being out of potions or only having a few. I like how when you cook food you see your character really cook the food, and when you drink you see your character really drink or when you eat whatever your eating he will actually take it out and eat it. when you kill someone in the game no matter who it is they will stay dead for the whole game, IT MAKES SENSE. when you go into someones home they will get mad and threaten you, it makes sense. when you want to up your stats in lets say pickpocking or swords you have to find someone who specializes in that art and pay them to train you, again it makes sense. The map isnt that big compared to like gta or skyrim but I think its pretty much perfect because there is a lot of content packed into it and it feels actually pretty damn big because you only run as fast as you do in like fallout 3 and new vegas. Plus in the beginning there is a lot of unknown places you cant explore because there are monsters their that are just to hard to kill untill you get stronger and better gear. So it gives you something to work for on the side. youll find a cave and get halfway through it then find there to be a monster that is just to strong, so you take note, leave, build up, gear up, get stronger, and go back later. The game has so much dialog and you can basically talk to anyone, your character actually speaks what you pick and he is such a smartass 98% of the time I love it. The story is not that special but I think its cool! its kind of like star wars with no force, instead magic, and theres the iquisition(which is like the empire) and then the bandits/dons men (which is like the rebels) your fighting for control of the island basically, you have the choice to choose what side you want to support. Now a lot of people dont like the combat and a lot love it, I love it even though it is basically 2 buttons, block and attack, what makes it really fun is you have to be really good with timing, its kind of like a timing mini game. if you attack at the wrong time you leave yourself open to get hit. Blocking is really important and swinging at the perfect time is also important, cause this game is really hard and if you dont play smart you will die tons. If you like games that hold your hand this isnt for you. But if you like games that really give you a challenge then it is for you. #noquestarrows. theres a lot more I can say about this game but it would go on too long. This game has became one of my all time favorite open world RPGs. It is underrated. Overall I give this game a hardcore 9.5/10

Risen is tailored for a niche audience, the hardcore RPG crowd. If you've never played a Gothic game before, then Risen might be a great place to start--if you know what to expect.
Without some explaination, you might find the game a deeply flawed, boring experience or you may grow fond of the game despite its faults. The worst flaw that would otherwise make this a classic is its replayabilty, specifically past Chapter 1.
I'm going to save you hours of trouble with some useful tips.
One, turn the difficulty down to Easy--trust me, you'll thank me for Chapter 3. (See Padding.)
Two, there is always another option. Magic can be just as practical to non-mages to beat the game.
Here are some helpful reminders on how to win:
Three, exploit the game's looting mechanic. Whenever you knock down a human NPC, you can steal their stuff and they'll come right back with little to no punishment. (See a good weapon/shield? Take it.)
Four, abuse the brewer for gold. In the Swamp, there is someone who will buy weed from you (10 for 70 pieces of gold). You can then beat him down, steal it back and sell  him the same stuff. This is a great way to earn gold if you are lacking funds, and because the game is difficult already I don't feel bad using the exploit.
Five, get trained ASAP. The game won't let you max your character out with gold alone. You have to gain XP to earn Learning Points--I don't think there's a max level--which you can then use to earn talents (swords, sneak, etc.) as well as stat increases.
Six, focus on talents and stats. Talents are to improve your character itself via better combat skills/animations; stats are to get you better gear. The game expects you to manage both as you'll need counter-parry for Chapter 3 enemies (+7 for Swords) as well as decent gear to deal out enough damage.
If you know this information before starting, then you'll have a much better time than most players. The game is intentionally brutal at the start, but it is the good kind of challenge where it relies as much on skill as awareness on your character. Get past that hurdle and you'll find a worthwhile experience in the first chapter of the game.
(You're still going to die a lot.)
Risen's combat is... complex. That's as nice and as nuanced as I can describe it, and in some ways I think the combat makes Dark Souls feel streamlined in comparison.
You can read the attacks of enemies--but the animations are somewhat sporadic and poor. You can use a wide array of attacks--when you unlock them. The game requires you to use your positioning, sometimes, but also mastering the parry system, other times.
But that's not what makes this game brutal to something like Dark Souls.
Your character's animations are hampered at the start. You will notice a change in combat gameplay from the beginning of the game towards the end, so leveling up your talents and stats is mandatory to win. (Or you can be a bigger masochist.)
For example, in the early part of the game, you'll rely on dodging/faking-out enemy attacks than the late-game parrying system. Your animations improve and the enemies require different tactics.
This never felt aggrivating because the game felt designed that way.
Enemies are not scaled to the player, discouraging players from areas they shouldn't be exploring, and the ones in my way were were reasonable compared to the hordes later on. And compared to the initial enemies, they do become more complicated towards the end--except for the Titan boss fight--that I was required to master my specilizations to win.
However, what I don't understand is why the game locks your camera. It works for 1-1 engagements, but clunky when you have to fight multiple enemies at once. If they had enabled it as a lock-on button, then I wouldn't compliain.
The other main issue with combat is the lacking variety of enemies. You'll quickly notice color-palatte/text swaps and grow tedious of engagements. (Thankfully, enemies will taunt you before actually attacking you.)
These two problems don't detract from the thrill of every engagement, but they are areas of improvement and the monotony of the game is something that becomes a problem once the game falls short of its introduction.
Whenever people praise Risen for its open-ended routes to play and the wonderful sense of world building, they are usually referring to the first chapter of the game. And there's a good reason why that is the case.
In the game's first hours, you find yourself in the conflict between the "freedom fighters" of the Don as well as the Inquisition's hold on the island with the mages' Monastary of the Order.
Simple enough, right? You may be surprised to know that you actually have three initial paths to choose--all of which have multiple ways of accessing them. And in order to advance to Chapter 2, you have to visit three main areas of the game. Some are based on your choice; others on your failures.
For example, you could start by going to Harbour Town (a neutral area). To enter the town, you can bribe the guards to let you in or you can do some farmwork to sneak in. (Or you can be taken away by the guards to the Monastary for being outside the walls.) Once inside, you can do quests for either faction--be sure to choose one side for the best rewards--that will have multiple ways of success.
From there, you can either enlist with the Inquisition to get some training (especially for magic) or you can meet with the thieves' leader to find the hidden exit that the Don's men use to  carry out ther operations. You'll either find yourself in the Swamp (the Don's headquarters) or the Monastary.
Or you can start out in the Swamp to train your skills and rise up within the ranks doing laborous tasks that can be challenging early in the game. Then you'll recieve orders to find out the situation in Harbour Town and then set up a peace agreement at the Monastary. (This is the route I took for my playthrough.)
Or you can be caught by the Order--at any point in the chapter--and forced to enlist.
As you can probably tell, there are many alternatives to choose. That's not even talking about the island itself. The island is actually a very contained, expansive environment that has multiple entrances and paths from one side of the island to the other. From Chapter 2 onwards you recieve teleportation stones to save time.
While most games would portray one as the noble underdog and the other as the tyrrant, Risen doesn't portray either side as the good side. In fact, no one is the "good guy" other than how you portray your character.
Unfortunately, the end of the first chapter is where the game begins to fall short of itself.
Chapter 2 -4 suffer from serious padding. I wouldn't have a problem had the game not spammed enemies or deviated me to put me on fetch quests. It doesn't ruin the game, but I have little desire to replay past Chapter 1.
I enjoyed the temple quests, but I wished the two factions were relevant. And because the three areas and the factions become forgotten, the game feels more linear than it is.
If the game simply condenced these chapters into one, I think it would be a masterpiece.
Funny enough, the Eye of the Tiger is an apt way to describe the "thrill" of Risen. For every failure, you learn something new--and that's the essential thing Risen does right.
I wonder how many people will be forgiving of this game in a post-Steam refund world. It's a slow-burner RPG that warms the heart with enough time.
