I like flight sims, but they don't like me. I'm a terrible pilot.
But I picked up flight in Simpleplanes very quickly. The flight model has some sense of realism, but anyone should be able to fly and land with very little trouble.
The act of building a plane is also easy to pick up. You have a diagram that tells you where the centers of lift and mass are, and the tutorial explains how these things work and what you should be trying to do. Within half an hour, I'd finished the tutorial and had shot down a plane while flying a piston engined fighter of my own design.
But it isn't TOO easy. I placed the guns in the wrong place at first and shot off my own propeller. The aircraft is very unstable. And if I don't constantly hold the stick back while taking off, I'll pitch into the ground the second my tail wheel leaves the tarmac. There's quite a bit of room left for mastery, in other words.
If you want a specific type of plane, say a B-17 and you don't want to build it, you can download it from what seem like hundreds of planes available on their site. The program will connect directly to the site and save the plane where it is supposed to be, so you don't need to do anything manually in order to add planes how you like.
I'd compare this game to Kerbal Space Program. It's nowhere near as deep, but it is in a similar vein.
A couple of things I don't like:
1. There aren't many scenarios and there doesn't seem to be a way that you can make your own. Like I can't set up a battle with 5 of my planes, 4 of which are controlled by the AI, against 3 AI mustangs escorting 2 AI B-17's. It's not that type of game at all. There is a 'dogfight' option, but when I flew it I was shot down by a second enemy plane that I didn't even know was in the air. I was like, wait, how many opponents do I have? I thought I had just one? The scenarios that you have aren't customizable either.
2. The site could be much better organized. From what I saw, they don't have planes in categories like WWII, WWI, helicopters, cars, etc. It's just a list. Sort by the highest rated vehicles of the month, year, day, or week, and click an arrow until you blunder into something that you find interesting. If it really is set up like that, then it's kind of a disservice to the players and to the aircraft creators who put quite a bit of time into that stuff. (this has been addressed by the dev below).
But the basic gameplay and aircraft design mechanic makes this game well worth it even with those flaws. It's a great sandbox.

I've been playing this game with my RL pals for the last couple of weeks and I must say that I think it's been given a really bad rap. Sure, the Harebrained Schemes titles are far better RPG and single player games - of course they are, that's what they were designed for! Boston Lockdown is simply about four mates getting their co-op on Xcom-style in the Shadowrun universe. I know Xcom is over-used as a comparison in reviews for isometric turn-based games, but in this case the similarity runs deeper than the format. Boston Lockdown uses a skill system which is akin to the way you advance troops in Xcom. You equip your character with 2 weapons, each of which opens a corresponding skill tree. Advancement on a skill tree offers many either/or decisions at given levels, so you must choose wisely as there is no going back. Yes, it's pretty simplistic - but nuanced enough in the choices you have to make as you invest in the trees to feel rewarding. Synergising your skills with the people you run with is pleasing, too. I think if one views this game as having more in common with a title like Helldivers, it would better serve. Don't bother with pick-up-groups, just get three of your pals and work the campaign together, arguing about who goes first during your action phase or whether that grenade was meant to bounce off that wall.
To surmise, I played pen&paper Shadowrun RPG in the late 80s and this is the closest I've felt to actually doing a run with my buddies since. Sure, it's got it's quirks - but there's nothing else out there like this.

Spacechem is one of the most fantastic puzzle games I've ever played. It really is an amazing game.
Infinifactory is the successor to Spacechem, but this time in a first-person 3D environment.  Although I don't see Inifinifactory matching Spacechem's elegant simplicity, it is a very interesting game on its own.  The addition of a 3D environment both enhances and detracts from the puzzles.  On the plus side, 3 dimensions to work with mean you can create some very intriguing solutions.  On the minus side, navigation in the 3D world can be a headache sometimes.
While there was a storyline in Spacechem,  it almost felt secondary to the game, and you could easily ignore it if you chose (although it was interesting to read).  Infinifactory's storyline seems to be more integral to the game.
Infinifactory has a dark sense of humor, which I enjoy.
It is also still a work-in-progress, with many changes and enhancements having been added since I first purchased this on Early Access.  However, even in its early-access state, it does not disappoint.  The puzzles have been fun and challenging (some more or less than others), and the game has a lot of potential that, as the updates show, is being actively realized.
I will say that since Spacechem was so fantastic, purchasing Infinifactory was a no-brainer.

Five Nights at Freddy's isn't the deepest game, or the most terrifying in my book, but what it is is clever, well done, and tense. As the night security guard at Freddy's, it's your task to make sure the Chuck E Cheese style animatronics don't murder you in the night, easier said than done with limited power to see, watch the screens, and close your emergency doors. It's game about calculating how much energy you can and can't spend on watching the animatronics, closing your doors, or just sitting... waiting... hoping that the morning is close. The helplessness creates a tense atmoshpere, broken by your inevitable failure, and generally punished with a jumpscare. The jumpscares aren't bad, but the gut wrenching moments beofre them are much better. I've had a lot of fun with it so far, the mechanics are clever, and it's a good thrill.
I will say that all your failures end in horrifying jump scares, animatronics screeching in your face, with the promise of visions of your mutilated corpse in a suit. The AI can also be a little cheap at times, while the helplessness creates a tense atmosphere, it can also be frusterating when the rabbit stands at your door and eats all power to game over you real quick. Game Overs can also be seen coming. If you can't close your door, the animatronics have already won, and it's an annoying feeling knowing you now sit waiting for a jump scare, nothing you can do about it.
Over all though, I'd say it was worth the five dollars for a game I'll probably open time to time for a tense scare.

A generally great follow up to the original Deed. The 3 new scenarios have excellent variety in terms of settings and characters and allow for interesting creativity for how you go about trying to pull off the crime and get away with it. I also liked how the last scenario here ties things together with the first game, appropriately in a bittersweet way.
However, as much as I appreciate having more scenarios included, the original game had only one, and the dialogue choices here pose a bit more of a challenge, at least initially, I miss some of the odd humor that could found in the first Deed. More often than not these choices would very much derail your attempt to commit a perfect murder, but I also believe added to the replay value. There was entertainment, even if your character is doing everything spectacularly wrong.
In any case, I still strongly recommend The Deed: Dynasty. The developer is excellent and delivers great value for a very fair price. I look forward to playing more Pilgrim Adventures in the future and hope that at some point they revisit The Deed concept again.

reminds me a little bit of Drakkhen: Order of the Flame. the world building and quests are good, and the environment is exciting to explore, but quest objectives aren't always all that clear. i might just be dumb, but i spent a lot of time going in circles. combat isn't anything new, and it's pretty difficult -- i tried making a spellsword and it worked out pretty well.
one feature i really like is the way you obtain skills. instead of automatically being alloted skill points to distribute, you have to do quests/interact with NPCs in order to train from them. if you want to learn how to lockpick, you can talk to a blacksmith and he'll eventually share his mechanical skills. if you want to be a better archer, you need to find someone who knows that kind of combat (a hunter in the wilderness?).
along the same lines, you don't start out with a map -- you have to find one. and you can even hire a cartographer to draw you a more detailed one. features like this (that newer RPGs usually lack) add a nice layer of immersion, but also add a lot of difficulty and process to simple things. fun if you like challenging exploration, but i'd be prepared to be frustrated at least sometimes.

Shadowrun Chronicles: Boston Lockdown is a turn-based tactical game that has a similar battling system to XCOM. It's part of the Shadowrun series, but doesn't really seem to fit in with the other games that where mad ein thsi series. It has it's good and bad points, one of the main points being the new 4 multiplayer co-op mode that adds a bit more depth to the game itself from the other games in the series.
Shadowrun Chronicles: Boston Lockdown starts with a really nice character design screen. ou are able to design your character, it has a large variety of tools that you can use to make your character unique and what you want yiur character to look like. Unfortuantly, this customization isn't carried over to the AI that are with you, letting the game down a little bit, but not by all that much. It would've been nice to be able to fully be able to customize your entire team, but it's not possible in this game. The missions do start off rather well, you might get a feeling that you are playing in XCOM, but with a cyberpunk feel and many different characters. Although to start off with the missions seem to be nice and flexible, it does start to get that feeling of just being the same mission, but with a different location that you are in and different enemies that you have to kill. The weapons that you can equip on your character seem to be all nice, and they all seem to be different from one anther. But in actual fact all the weapons that you find aren't really all that great, you don't really get that satifaction when you find a weapon in this game. I would say that playing co-op with some friends on this game would definatley be recommened, just because your friends will probably bring along useful items and equipment rather than the AI. It also makes it run a lot faster than having to play single player with the AI running with you as well.
The graphics of the game are great, and what really helps the game pull itself back up from some of the negative things that I have listed above. The graphics of each area that you go into seem different from the last and gives you a new change of scenery throughout the game. The lighting and shadowing isn't really focused upon that much throught the game, but some points here and there did stand out to be rather nice looking and such.
+ Fun Cooperative play
+ Great character customization
+ Nice Graphics
+ Trading Cards & Achievements
- Samey sort of missions
- Not fully customizable squad
Shadowrun Chronicles - Boston Lockdown is a fairly fun and enjoyable game. I would recommend playing it in short bursts of say 30 minutes - 1 hour, as you may get bored of the samey missions and not come back to the game. The graphics are well designed and the character customization is well done.

This is the most immersive survival game I have ever played. It really makes you believe you are freezing cold, or dying of starvation. Every day you survive feels like a victory, and this is something great considering the genre this game belongs to.
The gameplay mechanics include keeping yourself well-fed, drink enough water to avoid dehydratation, keep yourself warm against the cold winter, control your caloric consumption, and maintain the shape of your tools and clothing. Add aggresive fauna to that equation, and you will have a survival challenge. Right now, the effects of all these mechanics are being tweaked by the developers in search of balance as there are a few inconsistencies, but that is what Early Access is for (among other things).
The game will feature two different game modes: Story and Sandbox. The Story mode probably is not going to be shown in the EA phase, so during the following months we only have the sandbox mode, which is worth the buy by itself.
The biggest thing to keep in mind before buying the game right now, is that there is only one small playable map/area, which you can explore in a relative short time. The items are spawned randomly with each game, while the map is hand-crafted (not procedurally generated). There are more areas to come to experiment with the sandbox, and if they keep the quality of the one we have been shown, it will be a blast, because the game is really, really beautiful.
If you are looking for a single player survival game, with lots of atmosphere, mood and immersion, challenging but fair (being balanced right now) with somewhat complex mechanics, look no further, this is your game. But keep in mind that right now the content is a bit short (though there is a lot more coming).
In my case, I am loving every single hour I am playing with it. This is the survival game I was looking for since a very long time.
PS: Can't wait for the Oculus Rift support (confirmed by devs) :)
------------ UPDATE: 19/11/2014 ----------------------
So far I am liking how the devs are managing Early Access:
- They are addressing detected bugs at a very fast pace, releasing hotfixes in very short time.
- They have also released one content patch where they added a new area/map which is very interesting and quite different from the existing one. This is a good sign, as it adds variety of scenarios to play in. It makes me eager to see more...
- They are tweaking and balancing gameplay mechanics after listening to the users' feedback.
It's too soon to say, as the game has only been in EA for a short period of time, but it looks like it's heading in the right direction. I must point out, if you don't enjoy difficult problems and solving those problems, this game probably isn't for you.  It's not instant gratification, it's grueling visualization and planning, only to watch your brilliant idea fail miserably and need many revisions and modifications before even working correctly, and then further modifications to actually optimize a build.
Still, it's not nearly as difficult as making a real assembly line, but that's basically what this game is, assembly line simulator.
That's not why I am giving this game my recommendation though.  While it is a great assembly line simulator, it goes above and beyond that in thoughtful design and detail.  It could have easily been a game that was purely solving puzzles, but they instead opted to include a story line, one with many subtle implications, both dark, terrifying and humorous.  These story parts are sparsely distributed between small cutscene like performance reviews by terrifying and confusing aliens, and other dead humans that came before you.
Probably the most intriguing thought that came to mind for me was after the story picked up a little, and after thinking for a bit on how the ones before you dealt with their predicament...  I thought it was funny how many of them saw their prison as horrible torture, and how the charcater you play is obviously some sort of engineer.. I had a good laugh at the idea that it was torture for everyone but an engineer, who must surely find it to be the greatest thing to ever happen...
No intrusive troglodytes to obstruct your work, no bosses that don't understand engineering, no stupid monetary constraints.  Just you, the problem, and the machine.  An Engineer's wet dream really...  Also abducted by a giant Alien mega-empire...  Just to stroke the Sci-fi fanboy deep down inside every engineer.
I love these little touches, it brings the game to life in a way that a menu and empty room never could.  And the game could have easily been just menus and bland puzzle rooms, but instead you are transported to various alien worlds...  You see the failed attempts of those that came before you, and you listen to the intriguing storyline that plays out as you play the game.  It gives reason to the puzzles, and that makes all the difference.
All that being said, it is a fairly difficult game.  I don't think I've played a game before that required this much cognitive excersize in order to advance...  You really have to be able to see the machine working, step by step, in your mind, long before you place the blocks...
For me personally, that's one of my greatest joys of being a sentient being.  I love using my imagination to create working devices, and I especially love it when I finally manage to bring it into the game world, and it works perfectly...  Brings a tear to my eye...
So if you're up to the task, pick up this little gem and see if you can get a better cycle score than me...  Just remember, I pretty much start all the puzzles now by switching input to max and working it out from there first, and taking away input as needed.  I've noticed it actually doesn't make much of a difference, and in many cases makes it much easier, to just do max input.  It's a bit overwhelming at first, but all the same rules apply, just with a much smaller range of error...  But often times I can make it work with very few sensors and a few well placed conveyor belts...  Definitely much easier when you're thinking about the whole thing moving and going at the same time...
Also it's quite deceptive... You'll get most of the way through a problem, switch the machine on, and realize that every 7th manufactured part causes the whole assembly line to back up because one block moved into the right place at the wrong time....
So... be ready for ragequit.

It was clear that this game was going downhill when the Kickstarter team started back-pedaling on their plans, contradicting their earlier claims, and ran one of the most mis-handled campaigns since CLANG.
The gameplay is clunky and forgetable, with minimal customization. Further, the game is setup so that you can become good at EVERY skill. Basically, like Skyrim without a level cap, you have nowhere to go but towards some ungodly singulariy. It's not about "What will I specialize in?" but "What will I specialize in FIRST?". Sink enough hours in and you can max out every single skill tree. I understand that this is a nod to tabletop Shadowrun, which revels in its class-less nature, but that only really works for games in which a character has a reasonable chance of dying permanently before becoming the best at everything ever. In an online game, a realm famously lacking in permadeath, it results in a power escalator with a top floor at which you are expected to be before interacting with other players.
Just... disappointment on every level.

Alright, now for my actual review of the game; firstly I'm going to assume you played about 0.1 hours or less of the game and ragequit from the issues I gave fixes for above, so let's assume you have a basic understanding of what's going on.
Now dialogue in this game is quiet and the story doesnt provide too much early on (when I wrote this review) so I'm going to make up names and some backstory.
You start the game as colonel douchieebag whom just got a phone call from Professor Hubert Farnsworth that he can find some really good burgers at the  In n' Out in Fort Swastika; and some other silly dialogue.  So he jumps around he room, grabs his gun, and runs out of the building as fast as he can; crosses the street and visits the king of garbage and gets stopped by invisible walls everywhere till he finds his car right outside his headquarters.  Then the game goes from looking like crap, and playing like crap, to looking actually pretty great.
The game has a pretty spooky atmosphere, feels well decorated, has slight jumpscares of reasonable spookynes, and gives you a sense of unease at times when you're not sure what to expect around the next corner.
Don't worry about thinking of saving as a cheat, it saves a lot of time from opening the menu at the same item, and you're going to die a lot; especially if you run around often considering this game suffers from the Obese Man Disorder when it comes to stamina drain, and I believe enemies even drain your stamina when they hit you; so if you get cornered by a couple with your crappy rifle you're probably dead.
Anyways, what I think of the game;  it's a surprisingly good job.  The game runs smoothly, looks good, is spooky, and pretty fun.  Some parts are kind of lulz such as the time when someone gets killed by a really generic 3d model being rushed by them.  lol  You'll see what I mean.

TL;DR: Fun and exhilarating, simple but good mysterious story. Non-violent, centred around movement through—and state of—'Valley'.
The game mechanics are centred around the locomotion enabled by the L.E.A.F. suit, that you get very early in the first area and it is to say very enjoyable experience.

Overall, I can't recommend this enough for something so unique and nice. Although £15 does seem a bit too much. Pricetag of £10 would suit it perfectly—definitely get on discount if you were keeping an eye on this.

I was a little unsure of this game, considering the subject matter of murder is a little dark and sinister, but I was pleasantly surprised to say the least. It feels to me like a good old fashioned puzzle or story-driven adventure game. You need to a pay a lot of attention to what characters say through the conversations, and you need to choose your responses very carefully. Its not just enough to try and frame somebody else by planting their weapons on the body and a bit of evidence in their room - you need to have engineered as many conversations as possible to make it look like they have motives and reasons for the deed. At the same time, you need to be careful and consistent in your own responses. You don't want to say anything that might make you look like a didgey character, or somebody raking up dirt on everyone else. Plus, whatever you say to any of the npc's will come out in front of the local law later, so be consistent in whatever story you spin about yourself!
All in all I found this more in depth than I expected, and a good deal of though is required to succeed. I suspect it is possible to frame any of the npc's (or make the murder look like suicide) in any of the three scenarios, and here is where the games replay value lies. While all the weapons and evidence are the same each time you play, the conversations (ie, the most important part) may not be (although there are a finite number of possibilities). Hence, it is possible to see many different endings to each scenario.
More information and some gameplay in my review of it on Youtube here:
But overall I enjoyed the game, and for the price you will get a lot of hours of puzzlement out of it.

I really wanted to like Refunct, as I'm a fan of nonviolent, world-restoring games (the best example I can think of in this genre is "de Blob" for Wii, which I thoroughly enjoyed), but the game unfortunately failed in almost every category for me, and I cannot recommend it in any capacity.
The game's premise is simple: you step on gray platforms to turn them green, step on buttons to raise other gray platforms, and repeat until the archipelago of squares and rectangles is all green.  There are a few other mechanics that you can interact with as well, but they mostly just help you jump to reach taller platforms.  There's no story, save for an endgame celebration when you hit all the red buttons (somewhat satisfying) and an endgame celebration when you 100% green the archipelago (strange and very lackluster).  It's also not made clear what you are - a person, or maybe a ball?  The gameplay overall, is boring and repetitive.
The controls are never explained - you have to look on the options menu to see them.  What's more, they're a little ambiguous (It took me a while to figure out what "climb" meant - you certainly can't climb, but you can pull yourself up ledges).  They're also barebones - the game relies a lot on precision jumping, and the precision jumping is either easy or annoyingly hard, depending on the situation.  You can wall jump, and sometimes that's a little tough too, but not a fun kind of challenging.  Overall, the controls feel horrible.
The visuals are the one area in which Refunct shows potential - the game is simply designed but visually quite striking.
The area in which I believe the game has failed the most, however, is sound.  It's a clear missed opportunity for a musical score to start simple, then grow and flesh itself out based on the percentage of the archipelago restored.  Instead, there is no score, just a selection of electronic background tracks that feel somewhat out of place with the supposed theme of nature.  When diving underwater, instead of these soundtracks muted over an eq filter, the music completely stops and is replaced with ticking, as if to suggest you have a limited time underwater.  You don't, though - you can't die in the game, so the ticking doesn't make sense.
At the end of the day, I cannot recommend Refunct.  As a school project, it's a great effort that I imagine would receive (deservedly so) a high grade.  But as a game, it falls short in far too many areas.

You will dedicate most of your population to producing food, most of your time to cultivating your resources, and most of your space to managing your population. It is a bit of a niche market, but if you're the type of person that enjoys focusing on a more base level of survival than the traditional kill-or-be-killed style of game that's so popular these days, you may enjoy this.

The Deed is a murder mystery, except this time you're the Murderer and you have to get away with it! If you enjoy the idea of making the perfect kill, evading and fooling the police and getting away scott free, then you should take a closer look at this game.
This release was a quite a suprise to me, I enjoyed the first game, but never expected a sequel. Fortunately its a good suprise, and anyone who enjoyed the first game will enjoy this game, with more refined gameplay and three scenarios to play instead of one.
The core gameplay involves finding an item and weapon that incriminates your patsy (or an item that leaves the impression the target took their own life), then planting that item in the right place so the police find it, and using the weapon to kill your target. If all goes well then the police will find the item in their search and that combined with the weapon you used makes your patsy look suspicious enough for them to be arrested. You will also need to minimise suspicion against yourself, for example in one scenario bringing up an argument with the victim makes the police suspect you more, but changing the subject allows you to avoid the suspicion.
Environments are small, but this allows you to really understand the environment and people in it, allowing you to easily execute your devious plan and control the way events proceed. The only real flaws this game has are repeated dialogue getting tedious as you replay scenarios and cases where the your own plan isn't one the game designers thought of (however I haven't run into this situation yet).
There are three scenarios in this release, and I've only played one and still I can wholeheartedly reccomend this game, its a unique experiance worth playing especially for such a low asking price. If you're still skeptical then I can reccomend the first game in the series which is only $1 so you have little to lose.

Risen is a game that does not steer from the traditional recipe of its developer, Piranha Bytes. For those that haven't played any of their games - it's an open world 3rd person RPG, in which your character finds itself in the middle of an unknown environment, trying to survive against the odds.
If you have played any of their Gothic series of games, i'll immediately recognise the recipe. You explore the immediate suroundings, make first contact, get pointed to or lead to the nearest faction camp, then decide to join said faction or explore other factions. After this you'll be introduced to the big problem of the world, and embark on a quest to solve the aforementioned issue.
The story structure is almost identical to the one from the first Gothic game. If However, you haven't played any of their earlier games, i'd highly reccomend playing this title. It has a rich, enticingly explorable environement and the graphics are in my opinion quite good, even for today's standards. Even if you played any other Piranha Bytes games before, it's an enjoyable game, and far far better than the last Gothic title.

This game is a dream come true.  If you are a survival fan, get it.  It is ready for you.  Outstanding developer, goes above and beyond the call of duty with Early Access player relations.  Already worth every penny.
THE GAME
The ambience is brilliant.  You really get that sense of isolation and loneliness that you look for in a survival game.  Graphics create a wondrous, realistic but almost dream-like, world for you to explore.  The sky is beyond beautiful at night.  Careful consideration has been paid to sounds, enhancing immersion.  Footsteps in the snow, the clicking and popping of a safe dial and its tumblers, the rush of a freezing wind, the distant cry of a wolf in the hills.  This is immersion at its finest.  The game forces you into survival situations in which you must think critically, plan for trips, react in a crisis, and adapt to your environment.  It is exciting, challenging, and at times stressful and unnerving.  Everything you want in a wilderness survival.
THE DEVELOPER
The Hinterland team is just amazing.  These guys know what they are doing.  You will not be disappointed.  If you are like me, you will have bought Early Access titles on Steam, and found unfinished products, empty promises, incompetent teams that do not respect their customers.  The Hinterland team?  You're in for a different experience.  These guys are setting a new standard of performance for Early Access programmers.  I give them my gold seal of approval.  They are respectful, attentive, responsive, engage with customer feedback, are true to their word, and have a great vision for their product that they are consistently executing as they write it into reality.  They release regular updates, pay attention to users in the Steam forums, rapidly squash bugs, and are constantly tuning the game to create a more refined experience that is fun, challenging, and true to their vision.  A+.
IN CONCLUSION
Get it.  If that doesn't convince you, I don't know what will.  You'll be thankful you did.

NOTE: This is a review based on Early Access Alpha.
Also note: Summary at the bottom of the review.
You find yourself alone in a frozen wilderness. The only signs of human activity are empty buildings and frozen corpses. You have one goal, survive as long as you can, using your wits and what you find on the aforementioned corpses and in empty buildings. You have four priorities: food, drink, warmth and rest. You have to hunt, you have to gather firewood, melt snow and boil water. Your tools may break, so you have to repair them and your clothes. You have no-one to help you, and a wolf just picked up your scent.
No, civillization didn't collapse while you were sitting at your computer, you are playing "The Long Dark". a brilliant and relatively (see under "Con" below) realistic survival game.
Pro:
*A (fairly) realistic survival game that pits you against nature and the elements.
*Simplistic but beautiful graphics.
*The choices you make have a real impact on your survival chance.
*You have a very limited amount of stuff you can carry before it gets too heavy, leading to tough choices.
*The weather and where you walk in the terrain impacts how quickly your body temperature falls (as far as I can tell).
*Take a fall or carry too much in steep terrain, and the result will be a sprained ankle or even a broken leg.
*Eat uncooked or tainted food, or drink unboiled water, and you will become ill and have to use antibiotics and resting time to recover, things you can ill afford to waste.
*NO ZOMBIES!
*Did I mention that there are no Zombies?
*There really aren't any zombies, finally a survival game without them!
Con:
*Your tools and items degrade very quickly, which isn't really that realistic. After all, your axe shouldn't break after foraging for just a little firewood, nor should your rifle need repairs after just a few shots fired. I understand why this is done, it compacts the playing experience, and adds another layer of challenge, but shouldn't there be an "Easy" setting where things are either easier to repair, or degrade a lot slower? This also applies to the next two points:
*Just repairing things in a nice, warm cabin makes you exhausted, which seems a bit unlikely.
*Eating until you are as full as you get seems to keep you going a surprisingly short time, given that the average human can survive for a very long time without food, so long as water is avaliable. In the arctic and when working hard, you do need more food than ordinary, but even so...
*Random spawn of items in containers and buildings adds a challenge, but if you cannot find a knife or an axe early on, you may be placed at a serious disadvantage. This is a minor matter though.
Con, but likely to be addressed before launch:
*There is currently just one gamemode (sandbox) and one area with another marked as "comming soon". Hopefully, we will see larger areas and a lot more of them to chose between as the game moves into Beta and towards Launch.
Summary:
A survival sandbox game without zombies, The Long Dark is a game of a different stripe than most of its brethren, and in a positive way. It is challenging, it always ends with your death (for now, anyhow) and yet...it keeps drawing you back in with its simple, yet artful graphics and simple premise: Survive. At any cost.  8/10 -Recommended!

If you like puzzle games (and who doesn't, really?), you'll like Infinifactory.  There isn't really that much of a story here per se, but the puzzles are challenging (after a gradual ramp-up, then a steep jump after you've gotten the basics), and the concepts in the game are unique.  I really enjoy playing, and I would recommend everyone at least try this out.  I'm sure it will only get better before it leaves Early Access status and is released Gold, but frankly, the core mechanics are solid in this game.
I have found that some puzzles were rather challenging later in the game, but I prefer my puzzle games to challenge me to think creatively instead of being a snore fest.  I really liked the Portal series as well, but those puzzles were WAY too easy and linear.  This game requires you to think ahead, and can be especially challenging if you are trying to find an optimal solution in terms of cycle count and foot print.
There were quite a few that I completed thinking "Wow, I think I have this just about perfect" only to find that many people found MUCH better solutions! It makes me feel like I have much to learn, and at the same time enjoy the learning experience.
10/10, would buy again.

I have been following this game since the Kickstarter last year. (Which I backed)
I had pretty high hopes for this game and it showed great potential.
As many other reviewers pointed out, when this game first released into Early Access it was almost unplayable. You froze within minutes of starting, or you died of hunger within minutes of starting, or you ran out of calories within minutes of starting, or you died of thirst within minutes of starting or you get killed by a wolf within seconds of starting. Yes, seconds. Once a wolf had you in sights, you might as well restart because there was no escaping or surviving. If you managed to somehow survive a wolf attack, you would quickly die of infection or bleeding out. Why in the hell can't you use your hatchet or hunting knife or rifle to kill it when it attacks you?!? Cooking the food did no good. You still got food poisoning even after cooking the food. RIDICULOUS! Sitting ONE inch away from a BURNING FIRE didn't even help warm you up a single degree, even while you're using one of the pits inside the house. How does a fire in a house not warm you up past 40 degrees?!? Especially when you're basically standing INSIDE the damn fire.
But since the latest update, they have addressed ALMOST ALL OF THESE ISSUES! Calories don't burn QUITE as fast. Still really damn quick though. You definitely don't freeze as fast. A fire finally seems to warm you up when you're sitting next to it. Hunger takes a TINY bit longer to kick in and thirst is pretty easy to quench so long as you have even the tiniest amount of water. The wolfs no longer home in on you like a heat-seeker missile. You can actually run away now, but only IF you are far enough away. Cooking the food finally seems to help from getting food poisoning(ABOUT TIME).
They still haven't addressed being able to use the HUNTING knife or Hatchet to fight the wolf off. You still have to fight it off with your bare hands, which is ALMOST impossible. Seriously, why have a HUNTING knife if you can't use it when you get attacked?!?
The game is beautiful and the artwork is amazing. The sounds and music are both really good. It just needs some minor tweaks to help make it a lot better.
I'm glad I waited until after they did a few updates before I did this review, because if I hadn't then it would have just been all negative. But instead I waited to let them get the updates out. This way I got to try it both BEFORE and AFTER the updates. The game has IMPROVED VASTLY with these new updates. I really hope they continue to listen to feedback and make adjustments accordingly. The Forgotten Ones is a Half-Life 2 Mod designed to tell a story of madness and vengeance. I suppose I should start off by saying I'm most certainly not one for the horror/scary game style, but after a year of keeping this game in the corner of my mind, I finally broke down and tried it out. The Forgotten Ones introduces you to several ideas I actually wish more games would embrace and more developers would try. Instead of rehashed characters/sprites from the Half-Life 2 library, The Forgotten Ones actually attempts originality with creatures and does not bog you down with constant enemy spawn points. While the many grunt enemies require a gratuitous amount or well placed bullets to silence, the several bosses that are strewn amid the chaotic mansion require critical and quick thinking to overcome. Puzzles, although mostly simple find item/use item style, are distanced from each other rather well; however, the enemies you will encounter between puzzles are the real test.
The Forgotten Ones does have its issues: The enemy AI humorously falters here and there, items do not always want to be picked up, there are save locations instead of quick or even checkpoint saving, and one or two places where you may no-clip through a wall or object and get stuck. Even with all those issues, The Forgotten Ones is an interesting take on the horror genre for gaming utilizing good ideas for cover and trapping enemies to conserve ammunition, a very solid mix of music and terrifying sounds that will keep you checking behind your computer chair, and a satisfying duration.
I most certainly hope you consider trying out The Forgotten Ones, its an exciting, a little rough around the edges, horror First Person Shooter with some serious attention and care in its execution.

This is the sequel to the hugely overlooked, obscure mystery detective 'The Deed', RPG made by Pilgrim Adventures; who are slowly climbing up my ladder of favourite indie developers. Dynasty expands on the original's concept and foundation with deeper storytelling, more and diverse characters, who strangely seem to be incredibly memorable despite their generic appearance and names. This could be due to the fact this game's art style, whilst looking plain and brown, strikes a resemblance of old school mixed with modern sprite work.
Of course, the meat of this and the prequel game is the "choices matter" mechanic. Does it work? In short, yes. Yes yes yes yes yes yes! Whilst the game is limited in scope due to its short, linear nature and small world to explore, which isn't a bad thing I might add, the idea that you will be judged for your actions and un-actions is a satisfying, tense experience. Knowing that if you talk to him, or her, and collect this or that, will definitely effect the outcome is immersive and thrilling, and graphics be damned. Without specific spoilers, here's an example. To have the murder look like somebody else committed it, you'll be required to talk to a certain character and ask them about the character you want to frame to learn more about their past, which you'll use against them in the chain of evidence you have setup against them. I would say it's more about finding the "correct" choices to make to win the game than having absolute freedom to do anything and get away with it, which again, I actually find to be a logical game design choice.
Audio wise... meh, it could be better, but it isn't explicitly terrible or unpleasant. I like the BGMs, but I would like to see things like footsteps and ambience added just to put the cherry on the cake. But please, keep the no voice acting. I love to read and I love reading the dialogue with my own voice that I allocate to these characters, much like a novel. In this game, the lack of voice acting, I think, enhances the atmosphere and enjoyment.
I'll re-iterate the character portraits and art style again. Somehow, for some reason, I really love them. Yes, they are just plain blank faces, but the way they are styled and portrayed is... cool...? I would like to see this style return for a potential sequel, among all the other compliments as above.
For the negatives, I think the inherit bias towards the player character should be dropped and less alibis for the NPCs to be limited to only 1 or 2 and not all of them. It's quite annoying to have a sheriff turn up and immediately suspect you just because he hasn't heard your name before. Also the sound design complaint as above.
To finish this review, and if the developer bothers to read this far down, I would like to say I love The Deed and this game, but I would LOOVVEEE to see a game made by them where YOU are the detective, and YOU solve a murder mystery - where the killer is random per playthrough, in the style of The Deed games.
Again, great sequel this is bar some personal gripes, well worth the asking price and more!

What I like about The Deed: Dynasty is that it is a truly unique gaming experience. Its not going to 'wow' you with visuals, or have you on the edge of your seat. Its a slow burn effect where you slowly see your actions come to fruition. It really forces you to think before speaking (or, choosing a dialogue option hehe)  The evidence and planting techniques don't feel forced like they sometimes did with the first game (The Deed) its not as simple as 'bloody knife > put bloody knife in person's bed' "they did it!" you're forced to really think through fully the situation, who is this person you're framing? what was thier relationship with the victim?
I started to really feel quite sinister as I hunted through dialogue looking for things to help incriminate others, while also being careful not to raise too much suspicion about myself.
If anything this game has taught me I'd be a terrible murderer.
And, for this low of a price, c'mon, totally worth it.

I really don't know how to feel about this one. It's not poorly designed, but there's also not much design to it. It's really short, but it does quit before it makes itself repetitive and boring. It's as long as it needs to be, which is not long at all, but there's very little reason to experience it a second time, with so little reason to play it the first. It's hard to say it's overpriced when it's only $3, but it does certainly feel like any other free to play game. Basically, it's hard to love or hate Refunct because all of its pros and cons are canceling each other out. That is, bar two cons.
To elaborate on the game's length, I beat the whole game; that is 100% completion, grabbed all of the collectibles, saw the ending presentation, got all of the achievements, and even had enough time to wander around some more,
I got the very first Steam Card drop. It took a total of 30 minutes to experience
this game had to offer and there's still another 2 card drops left! I could do 2 more 100% completion runs before I would get all of the card drops. That's how short this game is!
But, by far, the biggest complaint I have is easily the lack of content. All you do is run, jump, wallhop, and slide your way to the next Portal button. Now don't get me wrong, those are perfectly fine elements to have in a game and I wish more did, but it shouldn't be the
elements in your game. There are no enemies. You can't drown. You can't fall to your death. There simply is no threat at all. I remember a time where a game like that would be laughed out of the room, and anybody who admitted to playing it would get beaten up every day for the next week. And that's no joke. When I was a kid, I got into actual fist fights because I said I enjoyed playing Kirby's Adventure on the NES.
because of that. But I digress. In addition to no threats, there's also very little reason to keep playing. The only reason is to see if you can actually get to the next button, but even that feels more like you're just checking another item off of your bucket list. It has all of the same impact as balancing a spoon on your nose. In other words, I'm really only doing it because I'm bored and mildly curious to see if I can.
But, rather than shame the very obvious flaws the developer(s) are no doubt aware of and have actually embraced in Refunct's description, I would like to offer a suggestion. How about a rocket launcher? You could blow up enemies with it, which would give enemies a reason to exist, and you could also rocket jump. I'm a huge fan of rocket jumping and a game where rocket jumping is its central gameplay mechanic would be awesome. And Refunct is the perfect game for it because the look, feel, and already existing gameplay mechanics are practically built for a rocket-jumping, wall-hopping, butt-skidding, super good time party. It seems like a rocket launcher is the one element that's completely missing from Refunct.
Another suggestion would be to create a modding environment so other people could add content to Refunct themselves. That way you wouldn't have to worry about trying to please everybody at once, or breaking Refunct's motif. The game could even quickly become a smash hit if the environment is done right. Just look at what a good modding environment did for Minecraft. Outside of multiplayer, why else would anybody play it?
As for the final verdict, I suppose I'll probably have to give Refunct a thumbs down. Not because I think it deserves a thumbs down, but because I believe it certainly doesn't deserve a Steam score of "Overwhelmingly Positive". A "Very Positive" score? Sure. But not a score games like Team Fortress 2, Rocket League, CS:GO, Steamworld Heist, Civ5, GTA5, Axiom Verge, and the entire Fallout franchise (except New Vegas) couldn't even get. That's right, none of those games have a Steam score of "Overwhelmingly Positive" and all of them have way more content and way more replayability than Refunct. So I'm afraid I must say 'sorry' to Refunct and its developers, but somebody has to help balance out this upvote frenzy.
With all of that in mind, I'm actually looking forward to the next game from Dominique Grieshofer. What little Refunct does, it does very well, and you could certainly take Refunct and build a very fun game out of it. That's why I'm hoping this isn't Dominique Grieshofer's last work. Dominique, don't give up!
Oh and BTW, I left Refunct running in the background while writing this review and I wrote the whole thing before I got the 3rd and final card drop. So I experienced
this game has to offer, including the critique, before Steam could give me the 3 card drops. Did I mention it's a short game? Cause I think it might be a short game.

No pogramming skills are required to develop a basic jrpg game so you can fully concentrate on the creation of immersive gameplay. Imagine that  you  have a programmer and an artist in your team who have already done their work - you only have to piece everything together! Not as easy as it sounds though. The flexibility of the program also lies in the fact that you can write your own scripts if you are familliar with programming.
That said, I can definitely recommend this powerful tool for the beginning game designers who don't know what to start with.

RPG Maker VX Ace is a piece of software to make your own old school role-playing games along the likes of the Super Nintendo, GameBoy Advance, and original NES days. This is the 5th generation of the RPG Maker series and there is none better, nor will there ever be. In fact I'll tell you right now its worth the $70 and worth even $100. Now I'll tell you why.
You make your own game, your own actors, your own armors, weapons, classes, skills and so on, but with RPG Maker VX Ace there is a much better handle of things that makes it far less tedious than previous versions. There is even more customization without making your head explode or needing plug and play scripts made by the community. You can give your actors weapons skills. It gets detailed from there, because you can make skills need weapons. Give armors stats.
From there, create enemies, put them in groups and make them use skills based on turns. You craft the enemy intelligence to what you want it to be. Either random chance, specific needs like if an enemy has 50% of its health, then attack, use a skill or run away.
The real difference between RPG Maker VX Ace and previous versions is the depth without using scripts made by the community. There is also a graphics generator like a paper doll maker that lets you get some real diversity in each character's sprite and faces. Its all so easy now and I can't stress that enough.
RPG Maker Ace is so easy to use and quick to map with. Just like painting with titles. Battles and stats are easy to manage in fact the program has a pre-made maps, stats, enemies, weapons and everything you need to quickly make your own game.
You can pour hundreds if not thousands of hours into this and have fun doing it. I know people that have quit their job to make RPGs using this program and have been doing it successfully for years now.
The only big catch is the program comes with stock art, stock music and so on that is quite lacking compared to previous years, but really that's why you get someone to make it for you or you just import content into the game. Want to fight Zelda? Import her into the game.
With scripts the game can really be tailored to make it your own. If you don't want to make a Dragon Quest or Final Fantasy style of game... get a script to make a Zelda game. I've even seen people make space shooters with this game. The Ruby scripting language offers some good versatility.
Now that I've said the good, its time for the bad. The engine itself is starting to feel dated. Not only is RPG Maker VX Ace the sequel to RPG Maker VX, but the engine as a whole feels a decade old. The maximum resolution is around 640 x 480, even when you program it to be changed, the compiler won't allow it to be the size you want.
There needs to be a search feature. As an advanced user, I need this. My in game scripts, dialog and events become horrifyingly complex. There's an easy find feature for scripting, but not the events, which is everything on a map or in the game. Its been over 15 years and RPG Makers still don't have it. More complex things like lighting and even a lot of moving sprites at once become an issue and cause slow down when playing your games.
In all if you're a creative person, this is a great outlet for you. In fact you can have a lot of fun playing your own RPG and adding to it as you progress. I'm usually the person that says wait for a sale to buy things, but $70 - $100 is well worth it, but since this is Steam wait for a $35 sale :-)

Six days.
Six days, seventeen hours and twenty some odd minutes. That's how long I've been out here.
You know, I thought the lack of food would get me. I spent the first two days after the crash ransacking some camp of all their candy bars and canned beans. There were ice fishing huts out on the lake; when I spotted those halfway through the first day I thought I was home free.
No such luck. Not a soul around. I held onto a glimmer of hope that somebody would come by to check on the buildings or something, or maybe the camp office would have a phone, or just a friggin' radio - anything! But that evaporated when I started finding frozen bodies.
I don't know what happened to the outside world, but whatever it was stranded these people here.
I stayed at the camp for a day or two, getting my bearings, waiting for the weather to clear, patching my clothes.
Dodging a wolf.
I didn't even see it sneak up. Out here, you get used to being alone. Besides the birds and the wind there is nothing around. I was trudging between fishing huts and I noticed movement to my right. I glanced over and did a double-take at a mean looking black wolf trotting the opposite direction on the shoreline. I probably could have hit it with a snowball if I cared to.
Thankfully, it seemed completely disinterested and we went our separate ways.
After a couple of days I realized I needed to move on, if I could. Much to my chagrin sodas and beef jerky don't grow on trees and I was pitifully low on food. I had seen a few frozen deer carcasses around, but without any kind of cutting tool they might as well have been rocks.
Some absent-minded camper had left an awesome jacket behind so I wasn't completely back to square one, but I wasn't exactly happy to be trudging out into the wilderness once again.
The trappers cabin was a surprise and a god-send. Food! Firewood! A lantern! A rifle! A
! It was almost civilized.
I had been drawn in by the birds circling a body nearby - presumably the trapper himself, badly gored and thoroughly frozen. His hunting licence had his name as Max, and over the next hill was the cabin.
Sorry, Max. I know this stuff is yours, but I didn't want to come to the same end you did.
I thought I had it made, then.
It took a few tries to get used to the rifle - never fired a gun in my life, and my first shot at a deer went wide and sent it running - but after nailing three bucks I was almost buried under venison steaks.
You know, Max, would it have killed you to stock a knife or hatchet in your cabin? Seriously. I nearly killed myself twice trying to drag an entire deer back to the cabin because I didn't want to let it freeze.
A few days later things started to go wrong.
I was lining up a shot on a deer and stepped off a ledge, into thin air. The drop was only a few feet but I wasn't expecting it - twisted an ankle, bad. That laid me up for about a day.
Then, I realized that I had run out of matches.
You know, it's amazing how something so simple and so...stupid can suddenly become so critical in a survival situation. There is no gas station nearby or corner store or Wallmart. I couldn't get a fire started. No cooked food. No way to melt snow. And I had just spent a day laying in bed, running my supplies down without any kind of return of gain.
There was nothing for it. I ate what I had left, packed up some tools and equipment, and stepped out into the wilderness once again.
I knew there was nothing in the direction I had come from except some cold, empty cabins, so I headed away, through a small valley and into a forest.
I then made a stupid decision: I ate some of the raw venison I had brought along. I was hungry, starving even. I knew it was a risk, and it turned out my number was up. An hour later I started puking my guts out. Food poisoning, I guess. I popped some antibiotics, finished off the last of my water and managed to stumble into the next valley. To make matters worse the wind was picking up and it was getting late.
There was a lifeguard shack or look out or something next to a pond here. Any port in a storm, or so they say.
I'm writing this on the back of a 'don't pet the mountain lions' pamphlet right now with a 'Camp Mystery Lake' pen. I keep having to stuff the pen under my jacket to keep the ink from freezing solid.
Can't say the same for me. The wind chill is nasty, even in this shelter and in my bedroll. My ankle is killing me, my stomach is doing flip flops. I'm hungry, thirsty, and freezing. Weak and tired.
I'm going to go to sleep now. I'm not going to sugar coat it; I don't think I'm going to get out of this.

I usually don't go into much depth in my game reviews, but I will with this one. And I am just going to say this right now. Outlast is the scariest game I have ever played in my entire life.
There are so many things that are good about this game. For one, the graphics and just the overall athmosphere is amazing. You really feel like you are in an insane asylum and you are fighting for your life. The entire time you NEVER feel safe, and even just walking down a corridor makes your heart rate go up. The jump scares are so perfectly placed and not so much overused to where it gets annoying and you expect it, but it also never makes you feel like nothing will happen. One of the best things about Outlast is that you never know what will happen next. You could just be walking past a bunch of dead bodies, and none of them pop out and scare you, yet when you have to come back around they jump and scare the living sh-- out of you.
Another great note is the story. The whole time you are playing you are trying to understand the secrets behind this asylum-gone-mad. Figuring out the story at then end is so worthwhile also. NOTE: This game is not for younger children. There's tons of blood, gore, jumping moments, and some sexual content, including male nudity.
All-in-all, Outlast is a great horror game that we need more of. The overall game is great, if not amazing, and there's no reason on why you shouldn't play this game.

The numbers in this game are awful at present.  Most notably: the food and thirst mechanics are absurd.  I burn more calories sewing in my room than I do sprinting through snow.  I'm eating 3-4 pounds of meat per day and burn through carbs like a lunatic.
Today, I lived until day six by spending 100% of my time walking to and from various dead deer, cooking meat, and boiling water.  Water takes forever to boil and the idea that it takes an hour to melt snow is laughable.
You'll be stunned how much of the world you can't take.  Maps on walls, cups on shelves, etc. that you of course would grab in real life because you can use it all.  Can openers die after opening six cans and hatchets die after five hours of "finding wood" -- which is another mechanic fatally flawed.
If you play, never ever try to live outdoors.  This is an exploration game, not a survival game.  Even if you've had survival training and know how to build a lean-to and lay down foliage under your bedroll, this game isn't built for you at the moment.  Run as fast as you can to one of their better buildings and live there instead.
This game is not random; it's one map and you'll learn where the best stuff is around playthrough #207.

This game went to the top of my wishlist the moment I saw the trailer, and it doesn't disappoint.
Before you get into the game, the download is really surprising. The game itself, if I remember correctly, is less than 500mb while the download is compressed to less than 300mb. Very tiny for what's packed into this neat little find.
The initial impression is purely visual, before you experience anything, and the detail and beauty is just obscenely good - I spent a good few minutes just looking around the (randomly chosen) starter area.
After a snowstorm started to pick up around me, I decided to head down some nearby train tracks and came to a train loading area with trailers I could explore, loot, and rest up in, before heading out further down the valley and up some steep slopes (which seemed to make my character out of breath as my calorie meter went down faster - wonderful feature). At the top was a lookout post with first aid, extra layers of warm clothes, and some canned food I had to bash open due to lack of a can opener. Some beans were lost to the floor but I was fed nontheless.
While the game does supply you with cans of soda and granola bars dotted around (maybe some canned pork and beans if you're extra lucky), you will need to sustain yourself to survive. Snow can be melted on stoves to produce water of questionable sanitation, and animals can be hunted for meat if you can find the tools before you starve to death.
It's best to do all this during the day however, since the nights are pitch black if you don't have a light source, and even those won't do you much good in wide open areas where wolves could be prowling.
If you want to live longer, I'd suggest using the night time to search interior spaces. Secure a base, scavenge for food, and have a reliable place to rest nearby incase a storm hits.
While story mode isn't availabe in the alpha, sandbox mode gives you a choice of two nameless characters (male/female) who do more than just give you a sense of gender. Each add their own narrative pieces and react to what's going on around you which really gives an extra layer of immersion. Falling down a hill a little too sharply can leave you literally hobbling on a sprained ankle, and if you put off eating for too long the sounds of a growling stomach float up to you.
While I haven't put an incredible amount of time into this game, it's already going straight into my top 3 and I can see myself having a lot of fun with this.
Shout out to the wonderful Tamara for the gift!

Spacechem was my favorite puzzle game of all time - Infinfactory ties it, if not beats it.
The game is conceptually similar to Spacechem: You're given a goal to construct, you're given a supply of various parts, and you're tasked with making a contraption that can mass-produce the intended product. Both games share a similar creative element that makes them great. Since there is no "right" way to solve a puzzle, every solution you come up with feels like it's uniquely yours, and you get a massive sense of satisfaction from seeing your creation in action after a long period of head-scratching.
Difficulty wise, I found it slightly easier than the previous game, but still an extremely challenging puzzler. I've heard complaints about it being too obtuse, with tutorials too hard to understand, but I found that the game had a great sense of discovery and experimentation that would have been ruined by less subtle guidance. The puzzles themselves offered some great brain-straining, though I ultimately found myself running into less frustration and fewer dead-ends than I did with Spacechem.
The scoring system deserves mention for being unusual, but brilliantly designed. In addition to the obvious scoring of solutions based on how fast and efficently they complete the goal, the game also scores you on your "footprint". What this means is, looking on the solution from the top down, how many squares are covered by machinary or have moving parts passing over them during a run of the solution. So, ten machine parts only count as one footprint if they're all stacked on top of on another. This is different than Spacechem's scoring of how many parts (symbols) are used to make a solution. In addition to creating a different way of thinking for those looking to get the best possible score, it allows a surprising amount of creativity that would have been lost if it simply counted the parts. For example, a large assembly can easily be moved by one conveyor belt, but it looks quite strange. A floor covered in multiple conveyor belts would look better, and would have the same footprint score as the more basic solution. This even allows some artistic freedom, as you can construct roofs and other shapes above your moving parts without penalty.
The game features a humorous, but very dark story of alien abduction and enslavement, most of it told through audio logs found on dead bodies, holding their last words before they died trying to solve the very puzzle you're trying to solve. They range from funny to heart-wrenching, and I found myself getting far more invested in the lore than I expected to. Cool-looking factories would have interested me enough, but instead I was making cool-looking factories at the behest of my evil alien captors and questioning just what I was making and why. Even the puzzles themselves had humor and personality, eventually making me feel like I was constructing actual products, not just assemblies of cubes. If I had one complaint, it was how the ending left me hanging. Obviously I don't want to spoil anything, and this may be the only "Early Access" part of the game, but it seemed like there was a LOT more story to tell after the last puzzle.
Speaking of Early Access, this game is probably the most complete early access game I've ever played. I ran into absolutely no bugs or crashes, no missing or placeholder content, and a campaign that lasted me well over a dozen hours. Infinifactory could have easily been released as a finished game and I'd have no critisism about its current state. I hope for and look forward to the potential additions in its early access development, such as new parts, continuations of the story, and of course, new puzzles.
I'd highly recommend Infinifactory to anyone who likes a challenging puzzle, as well as those who like creative production games like Factorio or automation-based mods for Minecraft. And of course, for people who liked Spacechem, I would call this a 100% must buy.

The Forgotten Ones is one of those games. You know the ones. The "We won't help the player and instead have them learn it themselves" type of games. The game re-introduces tactics and mechanics used in popular Source horor titles, such as Cry of Fear, and somehow find a way to mess them up. The controls are sloppy, and the default button placements are odd for a source game.("E" does not activate/pick up items, "F" does). The atmosphere, on the otherhand,is well made. It can keep the player on edge for long periods of time, without wearing off the fear factor too quickly. Sadly, though, most of this is neglected due to over-the-top hard enemies. The first enemy you face can deplete your health quickly, keeping you from running away. Also, if you are hit two times, you lose the ability to sprint, and walk 1/2 as you could, making certain levels almost impossible without finding a medkit. Sprinting is also terribly broken. You can't run for about 3-5 seconds without having your character slow down to 1/3 of their walking speed AND hearing an obnoxious breathing sound for well over 7 seconds. The weapons do no damage to even the weakest enemies, so I found close combat easier. The rooms are too clausterphobic, mostly consisting of corridors with 1-2 enemies. Also, most bosses are easier than the normal enemies. So that sucks. But seriously, you can find better F2P games out there, such as Unturned and the previously mentioned Cry of Fear. Please, don't try to waste your time with this game. You will most likely be killed by one of the millions of props. That is why I give this game a solid 3/10

At its original full price it certainly wasn't worth getting. But it got a reduction and now it's available for almost nothing in a Humble Bundle. First off, and the reason it has done badly, it's NOT what you would expect from a Shadowrun game after having played the HBS offerings. There is far less depth to story elements, there is no overwatch mechanic and hacking, lockpicking etc is reduced to clicking on your target and a seccess or fail roll. Missions are taken from a single central "market" hub contributing to its not being great in an RPG sense.
All this said, it has a lot of positives as well and is certainly enjoyable purely as a TBS more geared towards co-op fun. You can play it fine as a single player game but it quickly becomes clear that this isn't where the main fun lies. My advice is to get it in its Humble package and only grab the DLCs if you find it's to your liking. Overall though it's a perfectly good tbs based in the Shadowrun world and quite unique in that it offers tbs co-op. It's really not the pig Shadowrun fans have made it out to be and despite its faults I'm going to give it a thumbs up overall. As long as you approach it "eyes open" that it's not like the other shadowrun games then you should enjoy it.

For the first 24 hours or so of playing this game, I was sure that I'd be giving it a positive review if for no other reason than because I had spent nearly all of my free time playing it since I started. By the end of it the best thing I can say about it is that I'm still interested in trying Risen 2.
The tone of the first half and the second half of the game is alarmingly different. From when you first wash up on the beach with a fellow castaway who proves entirely irrelevant to the point where the main plot is actually explained to you, the game spends its time impressing upon you how much of a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the island you arrived at is and how the population is the exact mix of workshy, cynical and desperate to put you in a position of solving all their problems for them out of sheer exasperation. It's a fairly interesting setup that manages to keep the usual RPG fetch quest formula while also completely justifying it and making sure it never feels like irrelevant busywork.
The second half of the game is killing lizardmen in a dungeon crawl.
I'm barely exaggerating. Chapters 3 and 4 of the game are spent almost entirely in one dungeon or another, fighting wave after wave of lizardmen. While the early half of the game was fairly restrained in its call to violence, to the point where I don't think I killed more than a dozen humans over the entire course of the game, limiting combat mostly to fending off ill-tempered wildlife, the latter half has you cut down hundreds of lizard men.
And to be clear, there's a good reason the combat was so restrained in the first half - Risen's combat is AWFUL. Take Dark Souls, remove the stamina bar, but also take away dodge-rolling, slow block speed to a crawl, and only give the player five armor upgrades over the entire game. I admit with zero shame that I eventually got sick of this and activated godmode at around 2/3rds of the way through Chapter 3. The combat is tolerable in controlled doses, but the second half of the game is almost nothing BUT combat, which the system clearly wasn't designed with in mind.
A few more warnings to keep in mind should you try it for yourself:
- Don't sell your scrolls, at least not the Telekinesis, Levitation, or Nautilus ones. Despite the ostensible freedom of the RPG mechanics, most of the 'puzzle' mechanics blatantly only have one solution, that being magic. Maybe one in five will give you a problem that can be solved with a bit of athleticism or archery.
- Speaking of, don't bother with archery. It doesn't do much damage and the entire group will immediately bumrush you after the first arrow. Additionally, the ranged weapon skills only upgrade draw and reload speed in 10% increments, with no further abilities.
- The jump mechanics are quite possibly the absolute worst I've ever seen in a game. In addition to being just really floaty, Risen's edge physics are absolutely terrible. There were roughly a dozen instances where I'd climb up or dump down from a ledge only for the game to be unable to decide whether I'd landed on the ledge or was supposed to slide down, and instead of pushing me down like most games do, it simply left me hovering in the air forever, forcing me to either load a save or restart the program entirely. Unfortunately the game requires you to climb or jump more than a few times to progress, so all I can recommend here is to save often.
While the overstuffed combat and the tedium of the second half thoroughly alienated me, I enjoyed the game's opening hours well enough that I'm still going to give Risen 2 a try, but personally I'd say this is one to skip.

It's the first time I'm writing a negative review for a game and this game is the only game that I have refunded. I bought it on winter sale for 1€, but I still felt that that money could be better spent elsewhere and there are so many games that deserve it so much more. Maybe it's just not my type of game, but Refunct managed to bore me during 20 minutes I spent in the game to 100% it. What other people found relaxing, I found boring and underwhelming. What other people found as a great design and beautiful assets, I found to be more like a product of someone messing around with a new engine, trying to write something simple to learn its basics.
I know I'm being a little harsh, but that were my feelings when the game ended after really underwhelming 20 minutes. As I said, it's probably just not my type of game - I really enjoy being challenged by the games and when I think of Refunct, the somewhat similar game that comes to mind is DeadCore. Similar in gameplay, but when you read negative reviews for DeadCore, they are the opposite of what is praised in Refunct. DeadCore is accused of being too hard, aimed only for an audience of hardcore FPS speedrunners. Despite not being FPS speedrunner, I really liked DeadCore, because it was really engaging and challenging. Refunct, on the other hand, just feel dull.
TL;DR:
I'm writing this review mainly to warn some people that it just might be not for them. Despite Refunct being like 20 minutes long, it managed to bore me. If you seek challenge and enjoy games that are hard - seek elsewhere.

Overall, I’m happy to give this game an 8/10. I very strongly recommend people buy it if it’s on sale, and I applaud supporting the developers by buying it at full price.

Spacechem was my favorite puzzle game of all time - Infinfactory ties it, if not beats it.
The game is conceptually similar to Spacechem: You're given a goal to construct, you're given a supply of various parts, and you're tasked with making a contraption that can mass-produce the intended product. Both games share a similar creative element that makes them great. Since there is no "right" way to solve a puzzle, every solution you come up with feels like it's uniquely yours, and you get a massive sense of satisfaction from seeing your creation in action after a long period of head-scratching.
Difficulty wise, I found it slightly easier than the previous game, but still an extremely challenging puzzler. I've heard complaints about it being too obtuse, with tutorials too hard to understand, but I found that the game had a great sense of discovery and experimentation that would have been ruined by less subtle guidance. The puzzles themselves offered some great brain-straining, though I ultimately found myself running into less frustration and fewer dead-ends than I did with Spacechem.
The scoring system deserves mention for being unusual, but brilliantly designed. In addition to the obvious scoring of solutions based on how fast and efficently they complete the goal, the game also scores you on your "footprint". What this means is, looking on the solution from the top down, how many squares are covered by machinary or have moving parts passing over them during a run of the solution. So, ten machine parts only count as one footprint if they're all stacked on top of on another. This is different than Spacechem's scoring of how many parts (symbols) are used to make a solution. In addition to creating a different way of thinking for those looking to get the best possible score, it allows a surprising amount of creativity that would have been lost if it simply counted the parts. For example, a large assembly can easily be moved by one conveyor belt, but it looks quite strange. A floor covered in multiple conveyor belts would look better, and would have the same footprint score as the more basic solution. This even allows some artistic freedom, as you can construct roofs and other shapes above your moving parts without penalty.
The game features a humorous, but very dark story of alien abduction and enslavement, most of it told through audio logs found on dead bodies, holding their last words before they died trying to solve the very puzzle you're trying to solve. They range from funny to heart-wrenching, and I found myself getting far more invested in the lore than I expected to. Cool-looking factories would have interested me enough, but instead I was making cool-looking factories at the behest of my evil alien captors and questioning just what I was making and why. Even the puzzles themselves had humor and personality, eventually making me feel like I was constructing actual products, not just assemblies of cubes. If I had one complaint, it was how the ending left me hanging. Obviously I don't want to spoil anything, and this may be the only "Early Access" part of the game, but it seemed like there was a LOT more story to tell after the last puzzle.
Speaking of Early Access, this game is probably the most complete early access game I've ever played. I ran into absolutely no bugs or crashes, no missing or placeholder content, and a campaign that lasted me well over a dozen hours. Infinifactory could have easily been released as a finished game and I'd have no critisism about its current state. I hope for and look forward to the potential additions in its early access development, such as new parts, continuations of the story, and of course, new puzzles.
I'd highly recommend Infinifactory to anyone who likes a challenging puzzle, as well as those who like creative production games like Factorio or automation-based mods for Minecraft. And of course, for people who liked Spacechem, I would call this a 100% must buy.

User Interface is well designed, you will always easily see if your city is running well or if problems are arising.
There are no major gameplay issues. The military part of the game is not that bright, as is often the case with this kind of games.
