It's Spacechem!  In 3d!
Okay, that's the facetious review, but it really gives you a solid idea of what this game is.
If you didn't play Spacechem, let me explain the game here.  Essentially, this is a game about moving cubes around the map via conveyor belts, rotating them into place, and attaching them to other cubes in the right way.  The challenge comes in trying to get everything to line up correctly, as oftentimes you'll find that the blocks are being delivered to you in a way that makes it difficult to deal with them.  In your head, imagine that you have several cubes of sugar.  From the left side of your table, you have a constant line of green sugar cubes.  From the right side, you have a line of red sugar cubes.  The game tasks you with building a red cube that is flanked on each side with green cubes.  Doing this with just conveyor belts and block pushers is the challenge of the game!
Now, this game does a lot of things right.  The interface is very solid and the puzzles are very well thought out, allowing for a lot of creativity.  You won't get stuck on things, the game boots very quickly, and I have yet to see even a bug or a crash so far.
I can only think one downside, which is after each area you get awarded a random item by the alien overlords you are working for.  This takes up about 30 seconds, and that's all the complaints I can think of.
So would I recommend it?  Yes, I would, but ONLY to people who know they like puzzle games.  If you are unsure if you like puzzle games or not, pick up Spacechem and find out.  You can probably find it for almost nothing, and if you enjoy it then pick this up as well.
As for me, I'm off to compete on level scores against my friends.  One of his machines scored almost 3 times better than mine did, and I sure as heck am not going to stand for such a thing!

I am really enjoying Shadowrun Chronicles. It takes the standard Shadowrun series gameplay (SR Returns, DragonFall, Hong Kong etc.) and simplifies it down, then makes it multiplayer. I would really go as far as to say, while being one of the most simple Shadowrun games mechanic wise I feel like the addition of multiplayer and extra character customization with the large amount of player cosmetic options really goes a long way all on its own. Even if you are not really interested in playing cooperatively with other players on your shadowrun team, you can still play through the missions with a team of AI shadow runners of your choice.
To go into more details about how skills work in Shadowrun chronicles, each weapon type has its own skill "helix" Two separate paths that you make choices from, each level unlocking a skill from either the top or bottom path. There are no "classes" in Chronicles, but your skills are determined by your weapon choices. Each skill set is different, as an example guns are broken down into types, pistol, assault rifle, shotgun etc. while magic, summoning, rigging, and decking are all on separate trees. There are also Paths for Mind/Body that deal with passive abilities that can benefit any weapon choice/ play style.
Most player interaction takes place in a hub area in downtown Boston, where in between missions you will meet other shadowrunners, stock up on supplies, sell and buy new gear, pick up side missions or simply change your wardrobe. There is not a whole lot to it other than that, The campaign Boston Lockdown also is centered around the characters you meet here, and as you progress the main plot the hub world changes a little at a time. Story wise I have been entertained well and am enjoying the plot, even if it feels a little shallow and lacks player choice almost completely. There is a strong feeling of mystery around the events that unfold during the main plot and I cant wait to play more.
Overall I recommend Shadowrun Chronicles to any fans looking for another Shadowrun game to play, or to anyone looking for an Isometric RPG they can play Co-op.

Five Nights at Freddy's is by far the best horror game I've played. It is the very definition of paranoia.
You play as a night watch security guard for Freddy FazzBear's Pizzeria (because 4 bucks/hour is pretty cheap). Your job is to watch the security cameras and make sure that the 4 animatronics stay in line. You have control over the security cameras, 2 doors, and lights to see just outside the doors. Using any of those causes your power to drain quicker. You switch on your camera to find that the bots are all where they are supposed to be...
Except what if they aren't?
In this alternate universe, the bots are set to a 'free roam' setting. They wander around the building on their free will. If they happen to make it to your office, they recognize you as a bot without a costume. They will stuff you in a tiny little suit filled with animatronic gizmos. Nothing to worry about though, you have doors right?
In case you forgot doors use power. If you use up all your power, you have to sit there in the dark, and wait for your (very terrifying) death... You literally HAVE to expose yourself to danger in order to survive, which is what bothers most of the people who play it.
So was it a $5 well spent? YES YES YES YES!!!!!!!! Obviously yes there are only 5 levels, but you can play those levels over and over. There are so many different scary ways you can die, and every single one fills my pants. Yes 11/10. Done. Finished. Bye

Recommended for a CERTAIN CROWD ONLY of which I am not a member.
Pros:
- Engaging drop-you-right-in-it story
- Branching questlines
- Gray moral choices (you have to pick a side in a conflict that's far from black-and-white good/evil)
- Fantastic voicework
- Unique and interesting magic system
- Big open world feel
Things some people will see as Pro and others as Con:
- You will die lots
- You will mess up and have to super backtrack multiple times or even game restart because you stat'ed wrong or sold a thing or killed an NPC, etc.
- No way of knowing the level/strengths/abilities of an enemy aside from fighting it
Cons:
- Graphics are a bit outdated
- I've been pushed "through" solid walls by enemy attacks, sometimes ending up "ouside" cave areas stuck in glitch world
- "Classes" are unbalanced
- Some noticable dialogue glitches that are very annoying
- Lockpicking sucks, many chests are locked, either learn the skill and play a luck-based minigame and stock up on the limited supply of lockpicks or wait for FREAKING EVER to get the unlock spell
THE COMBAT SYSTEM gets it own section because this is what made me have to stop playing.
You will have to spend a decent amount of time in melee no matter what you build. Archer build would be super tricky because many quest-related combats are in arenas and some fights don't give you space to snipe, plus ammo is limited. Mage builds follow a questline that requires winning multiple melee combats first, and even when you do learn magic, it's expensive, mana doesn't regen except from food/potions that doesn't work mid-combat and sleep, and there's no casting without mana.
That said, melee is done in a way that I personally find annoying as hell.
I'm sure there are plenty of people who prefer combat to be more about technique than power. If you're good at it, you might enjoy having to actually pay attention to blocking, chaining combos, breaking blocks, sidestepping, dodging, chasing enemies around, baiting them toward you, setting up idk wtf. But this is the ONLY viable strategy.
BECAUSE THE ENEMY KNOWS HOW TO BLOCK. AND DODGE. EVEN BIRDS AND INSECTS AND PORCUPINES. They can either block or they move faster than you and can easily dodge backwards out of the reach of chain combos. And the ones that can block can literally hold down block for ages while you wail on them for no damage. Breaking a block requires paying to learn (and being high enough level to learn) advanced techniques, and then executing them properly.
You can't tank. There's no armor, only clothing sets that are extremely difficult to acquire (you get new clothes for joining factions, getting promoted, etc.) and rare helmets. Magic jewlery can provide some protection but you'll want those slots for boosting stats. You can't consume potions or food mid-combat to heal, and attempting to use healing magic just gives the enemy a chance to wail on you while you navigate you inventory, put away your weapon, use the scroll/spell, and pull out your weapon again. And no, health doesn't regen over time. IF you use a one-handed weapon like a sword, you can carry a shield, but it doesn't help all that much, and that's only a viable build for a non-magic-user.
There also aren't "rogue" skills that would help negate blocking. There's no poison to chip away enemy health or technique to negate enemy armor with a smaller weapon.
So you HAVE to learn the techniques. You HAVE to be fast enough to chain your attacks just right. Even first-level birds can destroy your health bar if you slip up, wasting precious time or resources. And getting dropped into mobs of fast moving enemies that circle around you is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥♥even if they're all low-level. You will take damage. It will suck.
I really wanted to like this game. I wanted to play it for the story. But I can't deal with this damn combat system.

This is a simple mobile - PC port so PROs/CONs are the best way to look at it. This is a casual game that doesn't try to be competitive.
PROs
+Game is pretty much freeware. Purchases are mostly cosmetic, and most people won't ever need to buy extra hints considering how many free ones the game gives you.
+It's a solid and enjoyable "The Amazing machine" Clone.
*Note that the above two pros are the main reason I am giving this a positive review, as this game is essentially a free TAA which makes it worth the download and try just for that alone.
+You get stars ( In game currency ) for free just by collecting them in game, which means you could even grind it out and get the cosmetics for free. Overall very generous business model.
+There are more than one ways to solve many of the puzzles, with extra score given to you if you manage to figure out ways to beat a level without using all the items it gives you. This is the correct way a TAA clone should be as it encourages the player to find their own way as opposed to just the developers way. This also adds replay value as you can try to go back and see if you can beat the level again using a more efficient method for a higher score.
+Can be enjoyed within relatively short time
+Part of profits are donated to helping homeless cats. Some people may decry this as trying to take advantage of cat lovers, but when you consider that this games business model is already a great deal that's probably not the case.
+Visuals and sound manage to be charming despite being low end
+Small download size
+Hats
CONs
-It's a mobile port and doesn't try to hide it. The game even advertises to you that you can also get it on your iPad with the app store. Pfffft.
-Why no Android?
-Being a mobile port also means low end 6th/5th generation gaming standards. The game seriously looks like it could be a minigame for the original PS2 Kingdom Hearts. Graphics are color map only, no specular lighting, minimal variety to sound effects, etc. The whole game could have been made in the late 90's and you wouldn't be able to tell the difference.
-Using a hint is pretty much just skipping the level.
-A huge part of your score is really just a random bonus you have no control over. Some people may not mind it, but it can be a little silly at times if you are trying to place on the leaderboards.
-Hats
Overall 8/10 - a fun little game to play when you only have 10-15 minutes to spare.

The sound effects are also good, with little things that you wouldn't expect from a game this small. An example being that if you jump through some leaves on a tree they actually rustle.
The story is quite cliche with a heavy emphasis on man corrupting nature. Whether that is a negetive is up to you really as I found the execution to be interesting enough within the setting they had created. But the game and the story itself is very short. I'd say 5 or 6 hours max just doing a normal run through without going out of your way to collect the in game collectibles.
Perforamce was good, with only a couple hickups lowering 60fps to around 50fps, but I'm running a pretty decent rig so that wasn't much of a suprise.
If I was to point out negatives I would look at the lack of replayability and the combat. I doubt you're going to get another playthrough out of this game once you've already played it. It doesn't have the mesmerising visuals of a game like ABZÛ to make replaying worth it. Possibly if you really personally enjoy the movement and want to collect all the collectibles you might return.
The combat could honestly not be in the game. It feels like it's just there to give you something else to do for a few seconds before you resume your running about. It's also laughably easy.
Now this review so far probably looked very middling, but I beat this game in one session. You could put that down to how short the game is but I genuinely enjoyed the game, even with it flaws. My final verdict would be advising you to pick this up in a sale like I did if your looking for a game to take you away to it's little world for a few hours.

I had my eye on this game for months before purchasing.  Picked it up for $10.
Addiction.  That's what we're dealing with here people.  If you are looking for a game that you have to tear yourself away from, this is the one.
Like any good sim, this game never reaches a true equilibrium.  You can't turn your back on it for a second unless you have the simulation paused.  Plate-spinning, juggling, whatever you want to call it.  You are doing surgery on a paitent that just doesn't want to live.
PROS
Graphics - The level of detail and the art direction perfectly matches the game.  It really adds to the desperation factor.  Excellent use of zoom based detail.  Excellent use of weather elements.  Animations are clear, but not overdone.  I run this on a really weak onboard graphics chip and it's still going strong.
Gameplay - Again, its so engrossing that you will need to set alarms for yourself to go to bed at night.  Everytime you solve one problem, another creeps up.  I've gotten a lot better at staying in front of trouble, and staying well stocked, but it's a challenge.  Especailly when you get over 1000 citizens.  Some things stabilize.
CONS
Graphics - Sometimes the weather layer is so thick that it stops you from getting things done. (Which may actually be the point now that I think about it).
Gameplay - There are some frustrations with the AI.  Sometimes people will drop dead of starvation while carrying a box of food to a barn.  One one hand, I know these people are really representing the society as a whole, that their sacrafice is a result of low food stores and distribution, and I shouldn't be so bothered by this.  But on the other hand, each person in the town is so detailed: Name, gender, age, education, clothing, kids...Heck! You can even use a tool to see the path they use to get to work.  I'm surprised that they don't have some piece of AI that says "forget the greater good!  I'm eating this cabbage before I die!"  There's just no self-preservation meter.
All in all, totally worth the $10.  I've got 50 hours of gameplay in so far, and I'm only writing this review, because I had an outbreak of Cholera, and I just needed to take a break before the possible death spiral.

The Long Dark is a reaslistic survival simulator, placing the player in the shoes of either a male or female survival of a plane crash over a remote part of Canada due to an electrical storm interfering with plane's systems. Starting only with the clothes on your back and a single flare, you are left to make your way through the remote wilderness in harsh winter conditions to seek shelter, food, water and other things to drink, resources like wood to make fires and keep yourself warm and even a weapon to allow you to hunt and to defend yourself. Though some days are better than others, blizzards and snowstorms and intense wind can sweep in at a moments notice, making an otherwise relatively safe trek deadly.
Everything from your tools to your clothes to even your food has a 'condition', showing you how usable they are. A tool that gets too low condition-wise will break. Clothes whose condition has deteriorated will no longer keep you warm and food that has deteriorated too much will not even come close to restoring the amount of calories-the game's stamina-and Hunger and Thrist that it otherwise would. Packaged food like candy bars and drinks like soda or bottled water are scarce. What's more, aggressive and territorial wolves roam the wilderness, attacking the wildlife and even the player, should you catch their attention, with a single wolf attack quite possibly being the end of a playthrough. The only long-term way to survive is to learn to live off of the land, gathering wood, tinder and matches for fire, learning to hunt and gather meat from the carcasses of animals and melting snow for water, then boiling that water to make it drinkable. All of this must be done while minding your Hunger, your Thirst, your Temperature and your Fatigue. Any one of these getting to a critical state can be deadly, making the game an exercise in balance and maintenance-both of your equipment, and of yourself.
This game is fantastic as is and I can only see it improving once the game's crafting system is implemented and new areas are developed. As is, the game's map is small. This is offset by the fact that staying out in the open is a bad idea unless it is to gather resources, due to being out and about and moving all over increasing the players Hunger, Thirst, Fatigue and making the player cold. It really doesn't take long to learn the entire map, though the presence of a randomly spawning bunker does spice things up. The game's story mode is said to be launching soon, and I can't wait to see what the developers do with the story mode.
Though I do have a lot of good things to say about The Long Dark, I am somewhat confused by some decisions, such as the inability of the player to use a Hatchet or a Hunting Knife as a weapon and only as a means of gathering wood and meat from frozen animal carcasses respectively. I understand those are the tasks they are best suited for but realistically, if a hatchet was your only weapon and you were being chased or hunted or even pinned down by a ravenous wolf, you wouldn't stop to think "I can only use this for gathering wood!". You would hack at the wolf or stab at it until it either let you go or it died. This does leave the hunting rifle as quite the coveted find, since it is the only weapon currently in the game and it makes finding it that much more satisfying but I would still like to see some sort of ability to use the hatchet and hunting knife as weapons.
Overall, this game is a fantastic experience and when you're down to the last of you food and drink, in the dark and the cold and attempting to clean and bandage your injuries form a wolf attack before the wolf comes back or you go into shock and bleed to death, you'll really feel the stress setting in. I can absolutely recommend this as a buy even if it is still in Alpha. If you are a fan of realistic survival simulation and you've always wanted to see if you could maybe make it out in the frozen wastes without the things we take for granted in every day life, then you will love The Long Dark.

This game is so good... At first, I thought it was very complicated and difficult. After a few hours and a failed village, I pretty much have it under control. Few things I've learned:
-Early on, gatherer huts are your friend.
-Make sure you build more houses than you need, so that when kids grow up, they move into the empty houses and make their own families. If there is no vacant house for them to go to, they won't move out of their parents house and make a family. More houses = population growth.
-Get a farm, make it huge, and in early spring, put 4 farmers on it until it's completely harvested. After the field is completely empty, remove all of your farmers and get them to do things like wood cutting or tailoring or whatever else you need done.
-Placing storage barns and stockpiles in strategic locations will reduce the ammount of walking your labor dudes will have to travel, thus increasing productivity a bit.  Building roads also helps with productivity a bit.
All in all, it is a pretty wicked game and if you like city builders, this one is for you!!

Children of the Nile is an old game, and I played it as a kid on CD for god knows how long. Egypt is a facinating place to build a city, full of wealth, religion, and monuments only a mad man would attempt to build.
You are a dynasty of pharohs who's job is to build a city and thrive. Start with a pack of farmers and shop keeper, then bring in nobles, educate their children, who then become priests, merchants, and commanders in your armies. The game requires a balance between the wealthy classes who provide you with more farmers and unique resources and the poor who feed everyone else and make the basic goods. Not only that but on some maps raiders and traders appear who will either provide exotic goods or take everything you got. It's a beautifully complex game that makes for a challange.
That being said I do have complaints. You can rarely have cities going for 70+ years withour the people becoming massively unhappy and harder to please. This is because not only the fact that as time goes on you are expected to provide even larger temples and exotics to the people the base resources you do have dindle with little respawn. Not only that but it appears they try further to discourage long games by increasing bad events, like long droughts and floods, and provide less good harvests to make it stressful to even feed the people. While campaigns, having set goals, this problem does not concern you, in sandbox mode it is annoying to have to give up a game because no matter how hard you try the people will get angry. Also the game limits how big you can get, limiting the vital educated elite to only 30 or so men, severely limiting you're abilities to expand across the map. This game is designed for 50-70 year games with populatons that will never exceed 1000 people (still a crap ton in this game).
While it may seem like I have more complaints than I have compliments don't be scared of this game. For what little time it wants you to play it is more than enough time to get massive temples and pyrimids up and trade from all corners of Egypt to flock to your markets. It is a simple strategy game that will provide at least 30 to 40 hours of content and even more if you customize your own maps and play on them.
TL;DR Buy the game if you like city builders and Egyptians.

Oh my god! They did it again!
I mean, literally. Infinifactory is just another SpaceChem.
So why would you pay for it once again? (If you gifted SpaceChem to all your friends, relatives, acquaintances and hated enemies, aside from having bought it for yourself on every platform imaginable, you may skip the following. In fact, just buy the goddamn game already.)
Well, aside from "new levels from SpaceChem" being an altogether good thing in my view, there are a few *minor*, almost inconsequential differences from SpaceChem.
For one thing, Infinifactory is 3D. And I don't mean it like "OMG, they render everything in glo-o-orious 3D" -- no, it's the puzzles that are genuinely three-dimensional, which adds a completely new layer of complexity to the game.
For another, the game features an entirely new story, of which I've seen but a little so far, but which I already like a lot.
The rest of it is just good old SpaceChem -- with emphasis on "good", because it seems that Zachtronics kept all the good parts, from free-form puzzles admitting zillions of different solutions (which doesn't mean finding a solution is easy -- OH GOD, NO!) to subtly soul-destroying difficulty curve, and from zany sense of humor to online histograms readily showing you just how much does you cherished soltuion suck compared to true masters.
No, wait, they did drop one good thing -- you can no longer automatically upload videos of your solutions to YouTube. But since the game is in Early Access, there's still time to fix that.
I should probably mention that I had some reservations before buying the game, and that, in particular, I was worried whether the first-person perspective would turn out to be a huge annoyance. I'm happy to report that it's not -- your in-game avatar is equipped with a blatanly unrealistic jetpack, which allows you to roam around the puzzle about as freely as a free cam would. I do think that controlling the jetpack through mouse wheel would make the experience even more smooth, and I'm not sure there's any point to "dying" -- momentarily -- when you fall off a cliff ohdamnforgottoturnthejetpackon, but all of that doesn't really add up to a genuine "annoyance", and may be fixed in the future.
Lastly, if you tried SpaceChem and *didn't* like it, I think it's a sure sign you're not gonna like Infinifactory either. The two games really are very similar to each.

This isn't dungeon defenders. It's another game with the skin of dungeon defenders placed on top of it. I'm fairly mediocre at tower defense games at the best of times, but even I was breezing through the content. Maybe it gets harder later, maybe it even gets interesting, but at least initially it is tragicly boring, simple, and easy.
The UI and menus are an absolute disaster. What immediately strikes you when trying to utilize either of these is that the game doesn't know what it wants to be. It can't decide if it's a third person shooter, an ability-based action game, a tower defense game, or a dungeon crawler. And in trying to be all of these things the UI and menus fall all over themselves by being both useless and cluttered. It took me a google search to figure out how to create another character.
Returning to the idea of the game not knowing what it wants to be, loot drops like you'd expect in any dungeon crawler/Action-RPG. And it has just the same impact as in those titles where 90% of what you see is absolutely useless trash to simply be vendored. In a game of this style, save me the effort and either just drop the gold so I can buy usefull stuff from vendors or don't drop anywhere near the same amount. In just 1 match I had already worked out that the game auto-loots stuff left on the ground for you (I assume I needed to set my bags to auto-collect but why wouldn't you?) by accident because I got tired of collecting useless junk after each wave.
I think my party member's statements sum up the game brilliantly:
"I don't want to play anymore"
-other member "You just leave"
"How do I leave?"
"What button do I press?"
If you have the patience it's possible later the game might become something good, something of a fraction of what the first game was. I don't have the willpower or patience to trudge through the beginnings to bother finding out.

A challenging Skyrim lite adventure, with combat system requiring more competence than in Witcher 3 and voice acting bordering on uncanny enough to enjoy the experience rather than going through motions.
Upon crashing on island you find yourself fixing everyone's problems, from orcs being too overly rowdy with bashing the skulls in on the roads, to decade long daddy issues of newly met characters. From rags to riches, you start hitting overfed mosquitos with a stick, advance yourself through ranks as a trustee of 2 different factions( one in two denominations ) to find yourself hitting more fantasy lore revered monsters with a stick that has a pointy metal edge on top.
You get to traverse the maze of unmarked investigations, one thing already dead within the real of video game convenience as well speech checks, that if taken too far can land you with floor sweeping job, or without your head. Ah the possibilities.
The cons :
The game however, can be a bit too formulaic in gatekeeping certain content, directly tied in your equipment upgrades through main mission. The crafting is pretty basic and the advantages of advancing certain skill paths pretty unclear, especially that you will find yourself short on training points and gold most of game. Even if alot of quests leave you to your own devices in figuring out the solution, often they aren't as intuitive as they could. Resorting to a guide, if not often, isn't anything unusual when it comes to Risen. I mean, there are a lot of games to play.
Overall if you know and enjoy games like Gothic 1 and 2, this game will click with you. If you like map markers and a combat where your character sommersaults from opponent to opponent with minimal effort on your side, it won't be a worthy purchase. If you like Witcher games, this might be a 50/50 roll.

This game has simple but aesthetically pleasing graphics, nice character outfit customization with a large variety of items (gotten at random from missions) and gameplay which is easy to learn but can be hard to master. It's turn-based strategic shooting in the same vein as Fallout Tactics or Xcom, though with less focus on the story aspect.
The game has its faults, chief among them the chat system which at this time offers no way to communicate privately with other players, as well as frequent disconnections from the servers which ejects you from the game entirely. However despite this, the enjoyment factor is extremely high and the game is never more fun than when you have four players in the same experience range taking on a mission together.
The co-op element, whether you are two players with a NPC each or a full team of four, really makes me happy with this purchase. And as it stands, this is my favourite co-op game of the year (and in several years). If assembling groups was a bit easier, the communication more streamlined and the characters a little more customizable, it would a must-own title.
As-is, I would recommend to to anyone who likes tactical co-op or shadowrun/sci-fi.
For anyone else it might be a gamble.

To anyone who has played the first 2 Gothic games and liked them: This is the closest we will get to a successor for that specific type of game we crave.
To anyone else:
This is a action-RPG with a few differences that IMO make it worth the price to play it:
1. Both Enemies and resources/consumables are finite meaning that there is no ''absurd grinding just to take one big baddie'', but at the same time the difficulty of the quests and monster placements have a nice curve to them so that you will most likely clear them in roughly the same order anyway. It's just that knowing that there's a natural end in sight aka: ''there's nothing left to kill'' makes the experience feel like your presence matters more in the world.
2. While the first point isn't all that unique having that in a Open-World does give it more of a niche that other bigger titles like the TES's don't have.
3. Item placements ( such as in chests or just laying around ) are static so after finishing it once ( or looking it up ) you can get a rough idea of where this and that weapon/consumables are, but while other may see this as ''lacking in replay value'' I see it as ''Nice gonna try to beat that tougher opponent to get a head-start next time'' since this again plays with the good difficulty they have. Also a lot of the good weapons have a pretty high stat requirement so you can't just go straight to one of the top weapons in game and use it immediately.
And now some cons:
1. The story tries to follow from the ending of Gothic 3 ( the neutral ending btw ) but at the same time try to be a new ''Original IP'' since they didn't have the license anymore after the 3rd game which might make fans of the Gothic games feel a uncanny valley effect throughout this game.
2. The story itself is also IMO kinda lackluster, which is a shame but then again the preceding games mentioned above while having IMO a few better characters were sorta the same in overall quality so if you're searching for deep and engaging characters/story then you might want to look elsewhere. ( Although while not deep this and it's predecessors do have probably the most down-to-earth or normalish feeling cast ever IMHO)

If you don't jump at least once during your first play through of this game then you are not human. Outlast is terrifying. The subtle background music and sound effect creates a very creepy atmosphere keeping you on the edge of your seat throughout.
The Graphics are sharp and detailed giving it an intensely unique visual setting. The game has very good lighting and shadow effects adding to the creepy atmosphere of the game. Specially when you use your video camera light and your vision is limited.
There is a good combination of a well tuned audio track and a lot of visual gore. The game is written well revealing itself bit by bit as you walk through the corridors of the game. The last game that gave me strong emotions similar to this was Heavy Rain.
The game is a first person survival game. Moving around the rooms and corridors of the asylum finding what horrors lurk in the depths. Then finding a way out now realizing that was not a good idea. You have no weapon in this game. The only defence you have are your legs for running and hiding spots like lockers or under beds. Then you wait until you think the coast is clear.
Highly recommend this game specially for horror fans. This is a real benchmark for true horror games. If you want and idea of how scary this game is watch walkthrough guides on You Tube and listen to the commentary. It very funny until you play the game yourself.

Valley is an absolutely enchanting experience. The story is very interesting and kept me engaged from start to finish. Exploring Valley was very rewarding and memorable due to the awesome L.E.A.F. suit you acquire at the start of the game. This allows you to build up huge momentum as you run down hills or speed through underground tunnels on electrified rails. The various upgrades found as you complete the story add additional functions like a grappling hook (which is context sensitive unfortuantely), double jump, magnetic wall climbing, and water running. There is also a bit of an FPS element as you will need to use the suits ability to fire energy blasts to defeat enemies. The energy consumed for attacks is also your health and can be replenished by draining it from plants, animals, and generators. However if you drain too many animals and trees the health of the valley itself is lowered, if this reaches zero the game ends. Where Valley really shines is it's story and freedom of movement as you explore each beautiful area in search of secrets such as upgrades for the suits energy capacity. Once you have completed the main story you can revisit each area to hunt down any remaining secrets, there is a completion percentage shown for each level so you will know right away if you missed anything. The voice work and music are excellent throughout as was the overall performance, I did not encounter any major glitches or frame rate issues. Valley is an easy recommendation if you just want to relax and explore a fantastic environment while unraveling a mysterious story. Be aware that Valley is very light on the combat and the only real challenge comes from platforming as there aren't really any puzzles.

This feels like a student put one of their first homework assignments on the market for $2.99; there's no story, there's no depth or length to the game (which doesn't even last half the claimed half-hour), the mechanics are somewhat broken and very unengaging, and ultimately whatever you like about this game can be found in titles that do it ten times better absolutely free; to say nothing of the full games you can buy for $3.
One of the largest issues for the platforming is that it takes place entirely first person--this can work, but especially in a game that relies on ledge grabs and wall jumps, the complete and total lack of feedback feels awkward and makes the gameplay feel soulless and flat at best, broken at worst. Compare Mirror's Edge, where the small addition of being able to see the player character's arms and legs makes it extremely clear what's going on, gives feedback to the player to understand why something did or didn't work, and engages the player by adding emotion and nuance to the mechanics beyond "stand in the corner and spam jump".
The game lacks a core 'play' mechanic that would make it fun and engaging to simply run around the world, it lacks challenge that could make it fun to try to beat, and it lacks any depth or length that would allow it to explore its concepts in more depth, or provide more reason for the player to stay tuned in for more than ten minutes.
I wouldn't spend money on this game for any circumstances other than perhaps speedrunning. Had I not gotten this as part of a bundle, I would have refunded it.

This game is a wonderful place to play around in. While it mostly is a "walking sim," there's actually a little bit of combat thrown in. Nothing too crazy, so even those who don't normally play games can just enjoy the adventure at their own pace, and the enemies have a cool design, and tie-in to the main plot.
Story is mostly told through audio logs, which is a pretty cool narrative tool I have never tired of since playing Bioshock. Unlike in older games such as Resident Evil, where you got most of the plot by only reading the notes and cutscenes, it got a tad overdone, leaving just a wee bit too much at the imagination at times, especially when you really wanted to know what happened to everyone, and not just the characters you played as. With the voice overs, you really get a sense of character from the world you're in, and changes up the many ways one can experience a world within a game.
That said, this is a very short adventure, much like Blue Isle Studios's previous project, Slender The Arrival, which also featured simple gameplay, but done in a unique fashion to cause paranoia and fear. That game still gives me the creeps just thinking about it, but here, Blue Isle Studios gets to make their own full project, with their own ideas, rather than taking off with a borrowed one and building from there. Not saying it was a bad thing for them to do that, I'm just happy they got to do a project that wasn't tied down to a mythos, and they really got to make their own here.
No, there is no horror here. This is, for the most part a very touching, and rather spirited adventure from beginning to end. It's been a longtime since a game has made me feel "fun" for the sake of fun. I was never bored here, and if you're someone who just enjoys taking in the scenery, and nature itself, you'll probably love it for that alone.
I can't really think of any real negatives, except for the length. I feel the main adventure could have been an hour or two longer, but the game does leave itself open for you to explore long after finishing the storyline. Also, while the aspect of being able to give and take away life for survival is unique, and not something really explored in games, I feel like there could have been more developed here, but not sure what could have been done without adding characters.
If you enjoyed Soma, which was also another interesting walking sim, adventure type game, I'm pretty sure you'll enjoy this one. There's even an area named Soma, and while Soma itself is unrelated to this game and studio, I couldn't help but make the comparison once I made it to that point. Don't get me wrong, the tone is quite different, and this one is a more happy go lucky sort of experience, without too much thought being given to the morality of your abilities.
If you need an adventure, or a need to pass the time, by all means check this one out. I certainly wasn't disappointed.

This game feels like something that could have been made by just experimenting with the feature of the engine for the first time.  There's more to it than that, but the sheer lack of anything to engage the player makes it feel less like a finished game and more like a test build.  The term "minimum viable product" comes to mind.  Worse, it's made in Unreal 4, which means it's not optimized for the level of graphics actually used.
The biggest fault, though, is with the gameplay.  The game is advertised with all the platformer mechanics it has and the idea that it doesn't need to teach the player.  The problem is in practice that means no attempt is made to demonstrate how said mechanics are actually performed.  The game simply hands the player a situation where a mechanic is necessary and leaves the player to figure out what inputs and such are needed.  A quick look through the forums shows the result.  I counted 4 threads of players who got stuck because the game suddenly expected them to wall jump with no indication in-game that wall jumping was available.  This game appears to have been intended to follow the footsteps of games like Portal, but with no understanding of how to imply mechanics.

Being a student of computer science, I really enjoy puzzle/problem solving. That is why I really enjoy games that really come down to actually solving puzzles, and it should not be a surprise that the company that brought us spacechem (and earlier: kohctpytop, the codex of alchemical engineering (I and II), manufactoid, ruckingenur (I and II), the bureau of steam engineering and more) have once again produced a puzzle game.

Clearly I would recommend this game, but not only to people like me that like to optimize and take shots at the ever-growing collection of levels in the steam workshop, but also to the people that have never touched a 'game for engineers' puzzle game in their lives; as these puzzle games with open solutions are often a good way to train the brain.
Finally, I would like to take the last paragraph of this review to recommend some other good puzzlers to people that enjoy infinifactory: spacechem (of course) (as it is slightly harder and made by the same, brilliant company); manufactoria (found online for free) (a game with completely different mechanics, but still a game for engineers); and fez (while not an open-solution puzzler, it is still a puzzle platformer with unique mechanics and some pretty good brain-crackers)

Pros:
* The art style is simple, but beautiful.  I like the step away from ultra-realism and a design that will look the same today as it will two or 20 years from now.
* Fairly 'realistic' survival edge.  I'm not a survival expert, but I am a deer hunter.  We hunt late season and the colder the better for hunting during that time.  We've hunted when it's -20 F for a daytime high and I can tell you that it doesn't matter how bundled up you are... that kind of cold is persistant and penetrating.
* Simple gameplay.  Not having 200 buttons to remember is nice.
* Gun/ammo scarcity - I still haven't found the rifle!  I'm fine with that, as it makes the game more interesting.
* Developers seem active, open, and willing.
Cons:
* Frustrating at times.  I like difficult games when it comes to this genre, but this game does at times feel like the mechanics make it hard in a "cheap" way.  Prime example is wood.  There are downed trees, chairs, tables, etc all over the map and available to burn if needed... but you can't.  Wolf attacks are also a bit "off".  What does feel real about the wolves is that they seem much more likely to attack you when your condition is low.
* Eating cycle seems far too accelerated.  In fact, eating and drinking seem to be reversed in their urgency.  Water is a much more important than food, but I am pretty much never thirsty and and always starving.
* Gun/ammo scarcity - I still haven't found the rifle!  Another somewhat "cheap" feeling mechanic because up there in Canada in the wilderness guns are going to be pretty darn easy to come by.  I'm OK with it, though as it isn't a bad trade off.
* There MUST be a way to use a hatchet, knife, prybar, log, etc as a means of beating a wolf when it attacks you.
* This game SCREAMS for randomly generated maps (or at least significant portions randomly generated.  Story mode will be interesting, but for sandbox play anything without a random, large map will make it too "same ol' same ol'" when it comes to replayability.
Overall, I think it's a great game that is still entertaining even with limited features at the moment.  I feel the developers will take the community feedback and realize at least a good portion of the potential here.

I suppose that one should say that this is 3D SpaceChem, and that you should get it if you liked SpaceChem.  I suppose, to some degree, that is true:  Those who loved SpaceChem will most likely enjoy this game, but I think it is important to make it known as distinct from SpaceChem.  So, with that, I'd suggest going to the next review if you want actual reasons on why to get this game, since I'll just discuss the mechanical similarities and differences between Infinifactory and SpaceChem.
SpaceChem was a game of constraint - given one more Waldo, more bonding, or grid space, and every level becomes easy.  I imagine most people knew how to beat each level in SpaceChem, but they couldn't manage to fit in their solution to the allotted space, since symbols can't be placed on the same spot, or an avenue couldn't be found to move the molecule through.  SpaceChem was also precise - you told each molecule when they could come in, and you did what you wanted to them (except for randomized inputs, but the idea holds - you planned for accounting for inputs) before sending them off to the next reactor. You had Syncs and slightly more involved ways to make things happen when you wanted them.  The key to solving a SpaceChem puzzle was generating something manageable - once you had that, you had the level.
Infinifactory is still an open-ended puzzle game.  Your solution was the one that came to your head, not the single reduced possiblity that could win you the level.  You'll still have different solutions from your friends, but the breed of how this is accomplished is different.  You see, in Infinifactory, inputs come out at fixed intervals, and while you can modify that interval, the fact of the matter is that you can't do things when you want to, you must react to this constant push of inputs, or else one input will mess up the one that came before.  Indeed, that is the fundamental difference between SpaceChem and Infinifactory:  In Infinifactory, you deal in reacting to incoming blocks, with a fair ability to do anything, while in SpaceChem you plan on how to use your scarce resources to achieve the result.
It's a subtle difference, to be certain, but I think it is rather necessary.  I guess people will be thoroughly enticed by "It's 3D SpaceChem", but I'm not seeing any Waldos in space!

Children of the Nile is the more modern version of the old citybuilders like Pharaoh And Zeus, allowing you to build a city in ancient Egypt. Some of the more modern things are, aside from the obvious graphics being different, that you no longer need to worry about intersections sending your supply and maintenance people entirely the wrong direction. You can now actually focus on building a city, rather than having to puzzle out the most efficient way to place buildings without them collapsing, catching fire, and starving because the food vendor doesn't show up there.
Citizens in your city are in a class society. From top to bottom, they are the pharaoh. That is you, and your family. You have a palace, and your family goes out to collect any sort of material, be it luxury goods or a humble pot to store things in. You are the state. All food belonging to the city also belongs to you, but you will always have a nice supply of food stored away in your palace. Pharaoh gets first pick, and a percentage of all food farmed in taxes.
Just below you are the nobles, who live in large houses and get their income from the farmers under them, and in order to support a large farming population, you will need nobles to guide them.
Under the nobles are the educated elite. Priests, scribes, overseers, and commanders of the military. They have similar demands as nobles in terms of luxuries, but they are paid by the government for their services. Only the sons of nobles and luxury shopkeepers qualify for education. These are the doctors, the administration, and the tax collectors. Because nobles will try to dodge paying taxes, a scribe can catalogue how many fields have been sown so that you know exactly how much belongs to Pharaoh.
Under them still, the middle class. Entertainers and shopkeepers. These earn their bread through their services and the goods they sell. Simple, but neccesary for society to function.
Below them, the peasantry. Farmers and servants. The farmers work the land and earn enough food to last until next harvest in doing so, and the servants do the shopping for nobles and collect resources for luxury shopkeepers - So they don't have to mingle with the common folk.
Separate from them all are government workers. They fit somewhere between the middle class and peasantry, and are paid generously by Pharaoh's bread. They are the brickmakers, the construction workers for bigger buildings(Small buildings like a servant's shack are made by the servants themselves), and anything else government wants from a papyrus maker up to the military.
If at any time your system fails and the people are without food, they will leave their jobs to scavenge for it. Dates, pomegranades, fish and so on are plentiful, so you need not fear you'll ruin your city and have a ghost town.
The game starts slow every map, as you have 10 bricks(Enough for one baker, brickmakers huts don't need bricks), and only one educated person in your city at the start. So you will want to build a school and several brickmakers more to ensure you can keep growing. Before you know it, you've spend several hours building. There is no immigration either, from what I can find. You start the map with 200-300 citizens living in huts, scavenging off the land. After that, children will be your main population growth. This becomes an issue when you want a big military, as military men don't get married - They live in their barracks-tent with two other men.
Some things that are bad, there are a lot of shrines out there that will take a bit to figure out which goes where and which are popular - If you even have room for them. Sometimes your citizens or a merchant may get stuck on a corner, and sometimes you may find your labourers can't figure out which limestone block they want to pull, and manage to fail to move any of them.
In the end, it's still a pretty and somewhat relaxing game where you can spend hours getting your city just right, and then decide to change it up again because you have a new idea. Cosmetic things like gardens, plazas and trees are free to place too, so you can make it look good without having to worry about your workers spending ages watering the plants and not farming.
Worth grabbing it if you like citybuilding, it's good at what it does

At that point I was sometimes left wondering why, if you would want to play a programming-style game this hard, you wouldn't just actually program - especially since there are games online based on real programming which don't leave you cursing that there isn't room to build the function you need! But at the same time, building factories does have a very visceral and effective feeling which brought me back to the game several times.

I've found this much more accessible than SpaceChem, but still extremely satisfying and challenging. I liked the idea of SpaceChem but didn't play it much in the end as aspects of it seemed unintuitive to me. (I meant to go back to it, and figured I just needed to learn how to play it, but never did.) Not so here. Everything is clear from the start and I was instantly hooked.
This is one of those puzzle games that gets inside your head and makes you start interpreting other things you look at as if they were in the game. Like how Tetris makes people dream about blocks, or instinctively work out how to slot everything they see in the real world together, just in case, because part of your brain has started doing that automatically.
I am not usually a fan of Early Access but it's fine in this case. I can see there are some slight UI improvements that might be added to the final version (already being discussed by the devs) but that's about all you might gain by waiting. I usually dislike EA because I only want to play most games once, so I'd rather play them in their best form, but with this game you're solving puzzles which are so open-ended and free-form that you can solve them again another day in a completely new way, using new techniques you've learned and pieces you've unlocked, and still have a blast. And the game is already in a very good state. So this is a rare case where I can recommend an Early Access game.
Infinifactory doesn't suffer from the problem of some "build a thing to solve a puzzle" games where the solution is either so simple or so restricted that you are not really having to think, only to work out what the designer wanted you to put where (except one or two levels which are obviously tutorials on new pieces, which are understandable a bit like that, but even then encourage experimenting). It's very open and you're generally given a large 3D canvas in which to invent methods of solving things. You can go for elegance, simplicity, or audacious complexity. Whatever you choose often turns out a lot more complex than you thought, which is part of the fun.
Price wise, it seemed a bit high at first for what I thought might be a simple puzzle game. Having played it and become hooked, and seen the depth and replayability it has this has, the price is well worth it. I have spent literally hours on some puzzles, and even once they are finished the desire to improve the solution or just experiment remains. You will more than get your money's worth with this game.
Congratulations to the devs, you knocked it out of the park and created a classic. In a world where "puzzle game" has started to mean "match three in a generic grid of gems", a game like Infinifactory is refreshing and inspiring.

Excellent game for anybody who likes specifically problem solving; in a lot of "puzzle solving" games your goal is to find the answer intended by the puzzle maker, while here you can make any solution you want with a lot of room for finding an elegant solution, a fast solution, or just the first solution you come up with.
Overall the game has a very smooth learning curve, I started having to think about the puzzles very early in the game but never got to a point where I felt lost or unable to make any progress on the task at hand. The pseudo-leaderboard statistics encourage replaying to find more optimal solutions, also enabled by the game saving your past solutions and having multiple slots for each challenge so you can keep your successes while still trying new things from scratch. While I may have blown through the entirety of the included levels in a single day due to my immense ability to obsess for very short times, I have yet to try any user-submitted content or attempt any interesting creations of my own. The quality of the level creator and community support will go a long way toward increasing the longevity of the game... And all that without even being fully released!
That's not to say the game doesn't have any issues. Several blocks have multiple types, such as clock- / counterclock-wise rotators, horizontal/vertical sensors and welders, which take up the limited space on the hotbar. Fortunately the block selection menu can easily be used to select blocks not on the hotbar, but I'd rather have the virtually identical blocks simply become completely identical blocks to free up some space.
On a related note, rotation. The reason that some of those duplicate blocks are needed is because there is only one axis of roatation available, and being able to place any block vertically would provide a lot of more appealing solutions compared to what is actually available. Maybe this was intentional in order to make the Lifter block acquired late in the game more relevant, since it's literally the only way to move anything "up", but even the lifter is frequently awkward to use especially on large composite objects making vertical space management very important when planning construction.
The only other thing is that the levels which have "meat" in the title are very disturbing, especially the second one. They are skippable, so do so if you consider yourself the least bit squeamish. I held myself together, but on the second one in particular I couldn't even bear to watch the machine I created; once I knew it would work I literally stared at the wall instead, and refused to do even a second of optimization. I would be happier if those levels simply weren't in the game at all. They don't ruin the experience though, and as mentioned they're skippable.
Update: After playing a little longer I found a control which is only mentioned in they key bindings list, block mode (or something like that). This shortcut lets you switch between the horizontal and vertical versions of a block that has them, as well as pushers/blockers and counter/clockwise rotators. With this shortcut it's possible to have access to every block on the hotbar (other than one block which is only available in the free-build mode).

Risen (1) was a very interesting adventure for me. Growing up playing RPGs like Oblivion or Skyrim, I was never introduced into the more hardcore-ish subgenre. So naturally, it came as a surprise when the 1st creature I met was able to kill me in 4-5 hits, while I was still figuring out how attacking works.
After finishing the game, with every quest except a few teleport stones left to acquire done, I was overrun by a sense of joy for finally getting rid of those Lizardmen (read: angry lizard DEVILS that don't care how much health you have and will still kill you in 1 combo because God doesn't love you), but at the same time a sense of regret for not exploring that road that I saw by chance, that I didn't take because i had something else to do, etc.
This is pretty much the entire pace of the game: You arrive on an island (read: crash in a very violent way) and wake up on a beach, with nothing but a stick and a useless female by your side, who you will ditch in the first 10 minutes of the game, never to see her again. From there, anything you do is guided only by your sense of curiosity and the choices you make. Some choices may be better, some may net you more gold, and some may help a poor woman survive through her illness, but what it matters is that its YOUR choice. By spending hours and hours travelling that island, killing those ANNOYING wolves that just DONT QUIT, you start to somehow love it, and want to see its people be safe and happy.
As seen in Skyrim, although this game is older, there is a moral choice that you must make between two factions at war, the Imperia.....uhm...Inquisition and the Don. Just like in Skyirm, one is looking out for the greater good on the long run of the whole population, while the other is looking out to its individuals just in the present. As always, there's fanatics, there's people who only care about money, and people who just want to be annoying (I'm looking at you, Romanov. Even  I had more gold on me than what was in that damned chest that everyone was fussing about.)
There's a lot of ups and downs in this game, the ups in the likes of finding a new awesome looking weapon/armor, and the downs being finding out that you STILL get 2-shotted by lizardmen because why not.
The quests are by no means boring from making you explore dungeons to having you fight Undead Lords for their rings to gathering that all-important Weed.
As a conclusion to my non-coherent review that says, in a lot of words, absolutely nothing, I would recommend this game to anyone with some spare time and a LOT of patience/skill. Its a great game, with a decent storyline and somewhat vast somewhat interesting world filled with somewhat annoying monsters that are somewhat repetitive.
And remember, dodging is your friend. Your ONLY friend.

I came to Shadowrun relatively late only in 2013 when the video game franchise has been rebooted with Shadowrun: Returns. Since then I became a huge fan of the series and played all released PC games so far, including Shadowrun Chronicles: Boston Lockdown.
I especially fall for the title made by Cliffhanger Productions due to its online/multiplayer feature. It is a really great experience so far and I must admit that I got addicted a bit recently.
Let me summarize Shadowrun Chronicles: Boston Lockdown:
It's a classic turn-based strategy (TBS) game like XCOM (as often mentioned), Warhammer 40,000: Chaos Gate or the rebooted Shadowrun game series made by Harebrained Schemes and unifies the best aspects of all mentioned TBS games. Its simple controls and game basics on one hand and its partly very challenging combats and missions on the other hand are in sum appealing to both, 'old hands' and rookies. A bonus are the RPG elements and the skills system, which are similar to Harebrained Schemes' Shadowrun games, but slightly rearranged. Right now, there are already wide possibilities of skills and skill combinations, e.g. decker, rigger, shotguns, blades, blunt, shaman etc.

The game mechanics are based on the fifth edition of the Shadowruns tabletop game and its very potent licence, meaning if you're into cyberpunk, science fiction, dystopia and love the Shadowrun universe, this game is for you.
Unfortunately, there are some drawbacks as well. Even though there are relatively much missions to play, lot of them are short or seem kinda inconsistent story wise. In general lacks the story in excitement and depth and gains momentum only late in the story progress. Therefor, some side missions are really interesting and challenging and a lot of fun (but are taking place on recurring maps of the main campaign though).
The missions are more fun in cooperative multiplayer with fellow 'Chummers', but sadly it can take quite a while before you get fellow players together since the game is a little depopulated currently. In other words, you are depending on prebuilt henchmen sometimes, whose character development you cannot affect or control. Thus, they are a little 'underpowered' but should be enough powerful for the main story campaign.
The interaction with other players is also kinda awkward, since there is no direct chat (whispering) implemented and basically there are only two chatrooms in total existing; the global chat and the party chat if you teamed up with other players. This can be a bit annoying sometimes but is still to handle.
Good thing is the developers still add content to the game and have much plans for the future. The support by the game developers, Cliffhanger Productions, is outstanding; very curteous and extremely kindly (and fast!).
That's why I rate this game positive. Again: if you're into Shadowrun, TBS and Fantasy, support the devs and that hidden gem and buy it!

Summary: Shadowrun is an incredible setting for those interested in SciFi settings and (especially) cyberpunk roleplay. This game is an excellent choice for those who enjoy the Shadowrun single-player games and want to bring a friend in on the action. Good (but not quite great) co-op fun for those who love the Shadowrun tabletop game but for whatever reason either can't gather together in one physical place, or would prefer a computer handle all those pesky rules.
Shadowrun is set in a cyberpunk future that combines science and technology with magic in a beautiful coupling of SciFi and Fantasy. Character choices range from the exact precision of the sniper, to trigger-happy run and gunners; from spell-slingers to always-online hackers; from summoning monsters or building and remotely controlling machines to do your bidding, and more!
This is a top-down turn-based tactical RPG that (arguably) offers slightly fewer choices in every round of its combat than other great games of its genre (like XCOM: Enemy Unknown), but makes up for that by (arguably) offering a more robust roleplaying experience... THAT YOU CAN PLAY WITH FRIENDS!
But in my opinion a few (minor?) setbacks keep this game from reaching its full potential:
+ All players act at the same time, which sounds like a good idea in theory (less waiting) but in the end proves to just make co-op strategies more frustrating than they need to be. Take a few moments to plan your perfect strategy? Oh, a half second too slow so your faster friend shot at (maybe missed) your optimal target first. Take another few seconds to device an alternative, finger moves to click confirm but BOOM, your other buddy ran right into your blast range and shagged that up hard. Better have a good voice chat (or have everyone in the same room) and willing to talk strategy or this is gonna get REALLY frustrating.
+ Because of the above, your view will suddenly shift and yet your input isn't always properly locked out while they act, so a lot of accidental clicking (on actions or on the wrong target area) will occur. You may lose friends over this. Again, communication is key.
+ The game doesn't adequately explain how having some abilities can't be combined (effectively) with others. I was several new abilities deep into skill trees before the game made it clear that I wasn't able to use more than two types of skills in a mission at one time. This is due to most requiring the player to equip an associated item that enables that skill, and you can't carry more than two of these at once. Example: If you want to be casting spells you'll need to equip an item for that; want to use a sword, you'll use your other slot for the sword. If you then start a mission then you won't be able to summon anything in that mission because you don't have an equipment slot free to add the item that permits use of summoning abilities.
+ The game doesn't adequately convey that abilities within a skill will NOT generally affect your effectiveness in other skills, regardless of whether their description sounds like it should (Simplified example: Spells and guns are classified as ranged attacks, but the "bonus to ranged attacks" ability in one of those skill trees won't make you any better at the other).
+ Selecting NPCs to accompany your human players in missions is needlessly tedious due to most of the important information you'll want to see about them at a glance is only visible once you've selected them, navigated to that section of their info, and then if it's not what you thought/hoped navigating back to the big list... rinse-repeat.
Bottom line though: This is quite probably the best modern co-op turn-based game on the market today.

I liked the exploration part of the game, to a point. But there really isnt much to explore. My game time shows 42.9 hrs. But when I sat down to actually play the game and complete all the quests, it only took me 25 hrs. Which is less then half of the time advertised on the "About the game" description below, which boasts over 60 hours. I highly doubt it would take that long to walk every inch of the island.
The combat is probably one of, if not the most, unwieldly, buggy, dissapointing systems I've ever encountered. It's hard to get used to. Timing seems everything, tossing the skill of the player aside. Stats seem to speed up the characters actions and damage and not chance to hit which I am thankful for. It wasnt difficult, it was just, annoying.
The best part for me was the storyline, and the side stories/quests. That's not to say they were all well written, it was just the best part of the game for me. Theres a side quest ****SPOILERS**** where to have to save a man from nightmares from a certain ring he found. The back story for the rings is awefully close to Lord of the Rings. Just felt generic and out of place for a game that has alot of lore.
Just a few items above that irked me one way or another. Now time for the ratings.
Graphics : 6/10 - Not great, but not bad. I would go 7 but some of the textures look like they just moved Gothic 3 to an island and said this is Risen.
Gameplay : 3/10 - Again, some of the worse controlls for combat ive ever seen. Plus, no way to increase your characters running speed except by scroll. And teleportation only comes about mid way through the game, so travel is slow and tedious. I also dont like using the left mouse button to do everyhting.
Story : 7/10 - Not bad here. I enjoyed following the history of the island and some of it's inhabitants. The tie in to the Gothic seiries was a nice touch.
Content : 5/10 - Im about even here. What there is to see is great, but the lack of content is disturbing. Also I should note, the only crafting in game thats worth having is Alchemy and Scroll Making. Nothing else is useful to warrent spending points in. Also, I had a hard time leveling. Even with completeing all the quests and the monsters I killed, I only reached level 24. Why? Cause monsters dont respawn. And after all the quests are done, what else can you do to raise your level?
Replayability : 0/10 - Once youve beaten it, no reason to replay. the story does have a few alternate choices you can make, but the last few chapters are always the same.
Overall Score : 3.5/10 - It's one of those games that probably deserve to be played, but players deserve to be given a better game to play. Again, it's not bad...it just isnt good. Im not sorry I bought it, but Im certianly not happy about it either.

It's not a great game and honestly it's a step back from the original. However, DunDefToo does grow on you a bit. Finding rare loot and pets feels nice... but loot is so overabundant that you stop caring about anything that isn't mythic/legendary. The game has an auto-collection feature but it doesn't let you choose what is collected/left behind. This means you gotta sift through the garbage to make sure you didn't miss a pet or pet food (they don't have an indicator on the screen/map to make them easy to track).
The maps are all super boring, small, and mostly tight spaces. This is problematic because players and towers have collisions on them. So, the game gets crowded very quickly.
Players get their own mana (currency for making/repairing/upgrading defenses) each round and it scales based on the player count. This is pretty nice and you can hand it off to the other players. Sadly, the game is totally anti-social. A single player can (like the first game) change their character to place additional defenses. The players also have a shared point limit for placing defenses. So, most of the time you either put up with bad placements or a single player doing everything. Basically, the game stops being tower defense and more about doing nothing or going combat focused (killing things yourself). This was a problem in the first game as well, but those maps were usually laid out in a way that a combat player still retained value.
The pet system is god awful. You need special materials to "evolve" your pets... this sounds cool, but you need a resource called "shellium" which is obtained by letting pet eggs expire. This means you have to give up the chance at an interesting pet for some resources... and it takes 48 hours of sitting in your inventory to expire. Pets occupy their own special bag space, but eggs take up normal bag slots. Leveling up pets requires food... food does not stack with itself and therefore takes up extra bag space. The eggs can be hatched instantly between matches (in the tavern after you reach a certain level), but the timers could change. The timers used to be 8 hours and you can only hatch one at a time.
So, your inventory will consist of the following:
* Garbage items for upgrades/selling
* Eggs
* Cosmetic item boxes (requires premium or daily quests to open)... you'll get a lot of these.
* Quality items (so you can use a different build.
* Pet Food
* Pet Food
* Pet Food
If you want to get materials to upgrade pets then you'll spend even more space on eggs.
What the game sells for a premium:
* Character slots (5$) - you get enough for each class at leas
* Bags - 2-5$ depending on the size of the bag
* Pet Bags - 2-3.5$ depending on the extra space you want
* Costumes - 10$ or more for costumes
* Pet Skins - 2$ or more depending on the costume
At first glance the game seemed pretty fair (monetization-wise)... but with the inventory problems and sheer cost of space it began to feel greedy. Like they sacrificed usability to sell more things.
Physics/Networking:
So, the game is prolly hosted on a server rather than on the leader's system. This wouldn't be so bad, but the game's server is authoritative and the client has to obey. This means rubberbanding, or worse, the server sends you flying forward because it didn't notice that you had stopped. This means that input lag exists... and it's pretty awful. It's like they built the game on an old-school architecture without realizing that there are superior options.
The game has large, blocky, collisions for everything. The characters slide (prolly input lag) around and so it's not uncommon to throw yourself off of a cliff. When your character attacks they move a little bit and the animation can't be canceled. This again, leads to the feeling of input lag (this is animation related rather than server related though). Basically, ranged attacks function better than melee attacks.
Bottom line:
It's a skinner box disguised as a game... a game with poor physics and networking. While it's free-to-play it has a lot of greedy elements hidden in there.

I've played this sensational city management game for nearly 3 years now. I purchased Banished October 1st 2014 during a 25% discount sale for a mere 14€ and I now consider this to be a classic. The game is in its finished state and is no longer being updated. However, with its thriving and dedicated modding community it appears it'll continue receiving new content for the foreseeable future. My favorite mod is
created by
which adds an enormous amount of in-depth content. Banished is without a doubt my favorite city management game with
coming in short second. Banished is very time and cost effective considering the small price tag and you can play it for an hour or an entire weekend. The community for Banished is to say the least wonderful and has created a lot of useful tools for the game. Such as the
among others.
There's no steep learning curve and it's a rather slow paced game when you initially start out. However, this depends greatly on your difficulty settings. The map generator is great and the replay value colossal. Banished has a well thoughtout gameplay, amazing mechanics and intelligent AI which will make it enjoyable whatever difficulty you decide upon. The graphics are immersive and the sounds are great but slightly repetitive. Nonetheless it still makes the game very calming and relaxing. That is until the realities of colony survival emanates. Decisions has ramifications, lack of awareness results in horrid consequences. Preperations are vital and is a fundamental element of the game seeing that you need to plan out the year and stock up on food, clothes and firewood for winter. You will have realizations of that moment where you made that single incorrect decision several years ago and it's now threatening to be the undoing of your growing city and must be addressed before spring. While also bartering for seeds, lifestock, resources and materials. Prioritize certain jobs in order to adapt and survive. Once you've successfully managed all this and set up a self-sufficient town. With no limitations, no hand holding and the future of your town is completely in your and natures hands. The wave of satisfaction is immense. The only downside that I've discovered is that the game engine begins to slow down during sped up gameplay. Which for me became noticeable at around the 800-900 citizen population mark.
I've adored and cursed this game. I recommend the game to anyone who appreciates and are entertained by the city building genre. As well as those who are considering giving the genre a try as it's a great starter.
Posting your own experiences with Banished whether good or bad assists newcomers in making their decision in whether to purchase the game or not.

Well, I have over 600 hours in the game, so perhaps I should write a review.  For context, I'm a shameless HOMM fanboy; I started back in the day with HOMM II, and recently replayed III, IV, and V, just for the nostalgia (and in preparation for MMH7's release).
This game did have some game-breaking bugs in its early days; today, only one remains that I can detect, and that is the "NVidia card causes black town/combat screen" bug.  I actually picked up a Radeon card just to get around that bug - that's how much I enjoy the game.  When the game first came out, it had one bug that I found highly amusing ... if you chose to speed up the combat animations, the sound would also be sped up, to the point where it sounded like a bunch of mice screaming and yelling.  Maybe I'm easily amused ... but the bug still exists in the Dungeon campaign (SoD), which I recently re-played ... and it was still worth a chuckle.
Nearly all of my gameplay has been campaign - I enjoy those more than anything else, although I can't easily explain why.  This installment, when you include Shades of Darkness and Pirates, has numerous campaigns, which allow you to fully explore the various factions and reputation paths.  The whole dynasty thing was moderately interesting, but tended to offer too much temptation to lean on "dynasty traits", which could really upset the balance of the heroes.  The dynasty weapons, which attain new abilities as they level up, are the highlight of the dynasty system, in my opinion.
I'm not going to nit-pick the pros and cons, as other reviews have already done that in great detail - I'll keep them simple:
Pros:
Very open skill tree (also see cons)
Cutscenes are interesting and relevant (Pirates had some amusing content)
A tremendous variety of combinations of factions, artifacts, etc., keep things interesting
Spell cooldown during combat, while limiting, is realistic and forces you to use your brain a bit
Reduced resource granularity helps to keep the focus on playing the game, versus constantly juggling resources
Having all creatures in all towns available to hire from any town ... nice!
Fixed perspective camera, versus the crazy controls in HOMM V
Takes full advantage of 2560x1440 monitor
Great musical score
Cons:
The skill tree doesn't let you go as far with certain skills; consider Grandmaster Pathfinding in HOMM IV (no terrain penalty, +50% movement).  In MMH6, every hero can have logistics, but it's limited.
Some campaigns tend to be a bit suffocating
When morale gives a stack an additional move, it's not a full move; less movement, and less damage
That's really it.  Overall, 9/10 from me.
